recs: A Promise, Not a Finding For forty-nine issues we have signed off Love you down to your star stuff . The grammar of that phrase has been doing the hardest work on this site, and nobody had said so. Here is what it claims, what it carefully does not, and why that is the stronger position. Everything here is signed with one phrase. It is on thirty-five of these pages, in five registers, and it is the closest thing this project has to a thesis. Love You Down To Your Star Stuff. Read it as a sentence rather than a logo and two things come into view. Both are load-bearing. Neither is decoration. The subject is us. [We] love you down to your star stuff. There is no cosmic agent anywhere in it — the loving is being done by particular people, on purpose, and the phrase has never pretended otherwise. And “down to” measures reach, not cause. It says how far the love goes, not why it is given. Not because you are star stuff, therefore loved — but loved all the way down, star stuff included . The star stuff is the extent of the claim, not its warrant. That distinction is the whole of this page, and it matters because there is a sentence one short step away that gets both parts wrong. We wrote it once.

The sentence we wrote once At the foot of Bone Song — Zine No. 1, the first thing this project ever made — the colophon ends like this: “You are made of star stuff. The universe loves you for it. So do we.” Bone Song · Zine No. 1 · colophon The middle sentence is the naturalistic fallacy stated flatly. The universe is the subject, doing the loving; for it makes the star stuff the reason. Both moves are exactly what the rest of this page argues against. And then the next three words take it back. So do we. We are pointing at that line rather than quietly deleting it, for two reasons. A site that keeps a public error log does not get to tidy its own first page and pretend it was always clean. And more to the point: those three words are this entire essay, written before any of the rest of it. The repair was already in the building. What follows is just the argument for why it was needed. A correction this page exists downstream of No. 49 quoted that Bone Song line, called it “our masthead,” and dropped the So do we — then argued against what was left. Neither half of that was right. It is a colophon on one zine, not a masthead; the masthead tagline is Cosmic Connections ; and the sentence had already corrected itself. Ryan caught it on 15 August 2026, which is why this essay is built on the phrase we actually use. The zine is corrected and the error is logged in the changelog rather than absorbed quietly. So: the strongest objection to a claim like ours, in its strongest form. It comes from a comic fantasy novel, which is where we found it, so the credit goes above the argument rather than in a footnote below it.
The objection, in its strongest form

The objection, in its strongest form In Hogfather , Death is explaining to his granddaughter Susan why humans need to believe in things like the Hogfather. She pushes back — they are not the same as the big things, she says — and he answers with the hardest sentence anyone has aimed at this website. YOU THINK SO? THEN TAKE THE UNIVERSE AND GRIND IT DOWN TO THE FINEST POWDER AND SIEVE IT THROUGH THE FINEST SIEVE AND THEN SHOW ME ONE ATOM OF JUSTICE, ONE MOLECULE OF MERCY. AND YET— Death waved a hand. AND YET YOU ACT AS IF THERE IS SOME IDEAL ORDER IN THE WORLD, AS IF THERE IS SOME . . . SOME RIGHTNESS IN THE UNIVERSE BY WHICH IT MAY BE JUDGED. Death, in Terry Pratchett's Hogfather (1996), verbatim — the small capitals and both italics are the novel's own He is right. That is the whole reason this page exists.
There is no atom of justice in the powder

There is no atom of justice in the powder Grind this entire site down. Every citation, every field guide, every carefully sourced figure, every abundance table. Sieve it. There is no molecule of and therefore you belong in what comes through. This is the naturalistic fallacy, and we have named it in the house rules from the beginning: you cannot get an ought out of an is . But naming a fallacy is not the same as understanding why it would be fatal here specifically , and that part is worth spelling out, because it is not an abstraction for us. The same move, run the other way, is how eugenics argued. Nature does X, therefore we should do X is a machine that will manufacture a welcome or an extermination depending only on which fact you feed it, and the people feeding it have always been able to find a fact. Our chain collection exists because good physics keeps getting misapplied to human beings by exactly this route. So the danger is not that the argument is impolite. It is that it does not hold, and it can be turned around . And there is a sharper consequence still: The part that decides it If our claim that you belong rested on variation persists in nature , then a paper finding that variation does not persist — in some species, some system, some scale — would revoke it. The belonging would be contingent on the literature holding still. A claim that the next paper can take away was never doing the work we needed it to do. Which is not a reason to abandon it. It is a reason to be honest about what kind of claim it is.
Which is why the grammar matters

Which is why the grammar matters Pratchett's answer arrives a few lines earlier in the same conversation, and it is the one we actually use. The small lies — the Hogfather, the tooth fairy — are practice . And what they are practice for is the big ones: justice, mercy, duty . Which are also not found in the powder, and which exist anyway, because enough people acted as though they did for long enough. Susan makes our objection almost word for word — people have got to believe that, or what is the point — and Death's reply is three words long: MY POINT EXACTLY. NO. YOU NEED TO BELIEVE IN THINGS THAT AREN'T TRUE. HOW ELSE CAN THEY BECOME ? Death, in Terry Pratchett's Hogfather (1996) How else can they become. Not a consolation — a construction schedule. Justice is not a thing anyone discovered; it is a thing being built, badly and unevenly and for a long time yet, and belief is the scaffolding you stand on while you build it. Now put Death's sieve beside our phrase, because they travel in the same direction and make opposite kinds of claim. He grinds the universe down to the finest powder and goes looking for justice among the atoms, and finds none, correctly. Love you down to your star stuff goes down exactly as far — and does not claim to have found anything there. It claims that the loving reaches that far. Down to is not because of. One of those is a discovery, and the other is a distance we are willing to travel. So the phrase never needed correcting. The love in it was always ours, doing what we do, and the star stuff was always the measure of how far it goes rather than the reason it is given. What was missing was not better wording. It was anybody saying out loud that the wording is doing something — and that the sentence we wrote once, in the colophon of No. 1, is what it looks like when the grammar slips. A finding can be overturned by the next paper. A promise can only be broken by the people who made it. That is not a weaker position than the one we appeared to be in. It is a much stronger one, and it is also a great deal more demanding — because it means nobody else is holding it up . There is no cosmic backstop, no fact in reserve that will do the arguing for us if we stop. The universe is not going to pathologize your variation, and it is not going to welcome you either. It is not that kind of thing. We are that kind of thing. The phrase, split by what kind of claim each half is The phrase Love You Down To Your Star Stuff, cut in half in reading order. On the left, "love you down to" — justice, mercy and the claim that you are loved — passes through no sieve at all and is placed by hand into a box marked promised. On the right, "your star stuff" falls through a sieve and arrives in a box marked checkable, with examples: nucleosynthesis, abundances, piezoelectric bone. Beneath: one half is kept, one half is found, and down to is the reach rather than the reason. one phrase, two different kinds of claim love you down to … justice mercy “you are loved” no sieve passes these PROMISED put there, and kept there, by us … your star stuff the sieve CHECKABLE nucleosynthesis · abundances · bone one half is kept. one half is found. “down to” is the reach. it is not the reason. Figure 1 · the same phrase, sorted by what kind of claim each half is
Every piece here is a ladder

Every piece here is a ladder The second rule falls out of the first. If the physics is not carrying the ethics, then the physics has one job — being accurate — and we have to be candid that every piece here simplifies it. There is a proper name for that, and it is not ours. Jack Cohen and Ian Stewart called it a lie-to-children : a simplification that is false, and is nevertheless the only way to get somebody to the next rung. It is what your physics teacher is doing when they tell you electrons orbit the nucleus like little planets. We do it constantly. The atoms in your body were forged in dying stars is a rung — hydrogen is primordial, and a great deal of the rest arrives from stellar winds, neutron-star mergers and cosmic-ray spallation. Bone is piezoelectric is a rung, and one we got wrong twice before correcting it : the effect is collagen's, not the mineral's. So what separates an honest simplification from the thing this site was built to fight? One property, and only one. the same simplification, two practices a lie-to-children a smoothed retelling says it is a rung presents itself as the top names what it left out files off the hedges, because the tidy version travels further survives being climbed past collapses the moment somebody checks Which is what the house phrase “a rhyme, not a proof” has been doing at the foot of piece after piece without ever having a name. It is a rung marker. So is the wood-wide-web hedge , where the mycorrhizal trade is ours to use and the forest-wide story is not. And the ladder has a moral limit as well as an epistemic one , which is the part that is genuinely ours. Field Guide No. 10 keeps five turtles people made in their own section with no correction table, because a table that fixes a mistaken verdict has no business being run over somebody's cosmology. There the rung stops for a reason that has nothing to do with accuracy. Some things are not ours to climb past.

First Sight and Second Thoughts The third rule is the method, and we were using it for a year before we found out it had a name — in a children's book about a girl learning to be a witch. “First Sight and Second Thoughts, that's what a witch had to rely on: First Sight to see what's really there, and Second Thoughts to watch the First Thoughts to check that they were thinking right.” Terry Pratchett · Wintersmith, 2006 First Sight is seeing what is actually in front of you rather than what you expected to be there. It is harder than it sounds, because the expectation arrives first and feels exactly like observation. It is why the field guides keep arriving, independently, at there is no standard one of these — that is what you find when you go and look instead of consulting the type specimen in your head. It is also what our corrections look like: the mantis shrimp's famous colour vision collapses on contact with the literature, and the wood wide web rhymed so beautifully with mutual aid that it got past us in three separate pieces. Second Thoughts are the thoughts that watch the first ones. Not doubt — supervision. And this is the half you can build machinery for, which is the only reason this site has any: second thoughts, as installed the first thought what watches it “this quote is obviously by…” FACTCHECK.md , and the rule that aggregators are leads and never citations “the page looks fine” six checking gates that measure instead of glancing “we got that right, surely” a changelog that publishes our own errors That last one is the Second Thought that costs something, and it is the reason the changelog is a public page rather than a private log. Publishing your own corrections is not a virtue display; it is the only way first thoughts ever get supervised where somebody can see it happen. The asymmetry matters, though, and it is worth ending this section on: only the second half can be automated. No gate will ever tell you that a beautiful pattern is doing your looking for you. First Sight needs a person who is willing to be disappointed by a finding they loved — which is the same person the previous essay is about.
What this licenses, and what it refuses

What this licenses, and what it refuses Every argument on this page has a cheap version that sounds nearly identical, and the cheap versions are common enough that leaving them unnamed would be negligent. Not: Not permission to believe whatever you like. The little lies are practice for justice and mercy, not for anything that happens to be comforting. A belief that has to become true puts you under an obligation the moment you hold it, and most comfortable beliefs ask nothing of anybody. Not a softening of a single figure. Everything checkable here is still checked to the same standard, by the same gates, with the same ledger. This page changes what the checking is for ; it does not change how hard it is done. Not relativism. “There is no atom of justice” is a claim about where justice is located — not a claim that cruelty and care are the same, or that it does not matter which you choose. It matters more, not less, once you know nothing else is holding it up. Not an argument that fiction beats evidence. The opposite, and emphatically. This whole collection exists to reclaim science from the things that wear its clothes. Not a demotion of the physics. The star stuff is true, it is checked, and it is the most beautiful fact we know. It earns its place in the phrase entirely on its own. It simply does not carry the ethics, and it never claimed to. Not a claim that we planned this. We are not going to pretend the phrase was engineered to dodge a fallacy. It was written as an act of love and the grammar came out right, and we only noticed why it was right in the course of getting something else wrong . Being correct by instinct still counts, but it is not the same as having reasoned it out, and this page is the reasoning arriving late. Not ours. Three borrowed ideas hold this page up. Two are Cohen and Stewart's and one is Pratchett's, they are credited above rather than below, and the full account of the borrowing — including two attribution errors that finding it corrected — is in No. 49 .

The shorter version You are made of star stuff. That part we checked, and it is the most beautiful fact we know. The universe does not love you for it, because the universe is not the kind of thing that loves. We are. That is not a discovery being reported to you — it is a thing being done, on purpose, and it will go on being done. And the phrase we have signed off with since the first zine never claimed otherwise. It has been saying the right thing in the right grammar for forty-nine issues, and all this page does is finally say why. Love you down to your star stuff. Not because of the star stuff. All the way down to it. Where this came from → Sources. Terry Pratchett , Hogfather (1996) — both passages quoted verbatim from the novel, including the small capitals Death's dialogue is set in and the italics on show , rightness and become . The versions circulating online, including in Stimpunks' own commonplace book, are sourced to a quote aggregator and to a clip of the 2006 television adaptation and drop all of that; the correction is logged in FACTCHECK.md and in the changelog . Terry Pratchett , Wintersmith (2006) — First Sight and Second Thoughts, quoted at stimpunks.org since 2024. Jack Cohen & Ian Stewart , The Collapse of Chaos (1994) and Figments of Reality (1997) — lies-to-children, five years before The Science of Discworld carried it to a wide audience. It is theirs and not Pratchett's , which is one of the two attribution errors No. 49 corrects; the Science of Discworld books alternate chapters between Pratchett's Discworld narrative and Stewart and Cohen's science. What is ours. The reading of these ideas against this site's own signature phrase, and the grammatical argument about down to ; the argument that a revocable claim was never doing the work; the moral limit on the ladder; and every error above. About Star Stuff Zines and field guides on the science of belonging — we are made of star stuff, and we belong not despite our differences but as them. Star Stuff (starstuff.earth) is a collaboration between the Stimpunks Foundation and More Realms — a growing collection of zines and field guides that read settled science as an argument about belonging. It is the public flowering of the Stimpunks knowledge garden: if stimpunks.org is the garden, this is where it blooms. And a great deal of what blooms here was grown from seed in More Realms. The method is consistent. Each piece begins with something well-established in physics, cosmology, chemistry, or biology, and lets it carry a claim about neurodivergent and disabled life — not as loose metaphor, but as the same pattern showing up at more than one scale. Almost every atom heavier than helium was forged in stars and their deaths; the calcium in our bones and the iron in our blood came from stars that died before the Earth existed. We take that settled science and read it as an argument: if we are all made of the same stellar matter, then neurodivergent and disabled people belong here fully — as part of the universe knowing itself in every possible way.

An official collaboration Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms. Two sites, one argument: difference comes first. Stimpunks is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit built by and for neurodivergent and disabled people — a knowledge garden of glossary, patterns, and practice. More Realms is Helen Edgar 's speculative companion to her Autistic Realms : where Autistic Realms is the grounded, practical site, More Realms is, in her words, “looser, weirder, more speculative” — somewhere to wander and think sideways rather than conclude. Star Stuff is what the two of us make together, and the pairing is on every page for that reason. Helen's writing is not a footnote to this collection — it is one of its sources and much of its weather. Why Difference Comes First , We Are Made of Relations , My Monotropic Galaxy , the shared-air and shared-signal coinages, the constellation reading of the spiky profile: these arrived here from More Realms and Autistic Realms, and they set the frame that later pieces work inside. Three zines are hers outright, in her own voice — Nos. 11 , 28 , and 30 — one more, No. 29 , was developed after her essay, and her work is named and cited across much of the rest. Attribution stays specific underneath the co-branding. Where a piece is Helen's, it says so and it is hers. Where a piece takes an idea from her, it names the essay. The two organizations share the masthead; the individual credits stay exact. How the three sites actually feed each other — which essays became which zines, which glossary terms became which arguments, and why a web of linked notes produces concepts nobody wrote down — is its own page: Cosmic Connections .

The through-line Difference is not a deviation from a norm. It is the default state of matter — and we belong as it, not despite it. That claim gets made across scales, and the scales are the point. The same shape keeps turning up whether you look through a telescope, a microscope, or a front door. The cosmic & subatomic Relativity and crip time; phase transitions and fluctuating capacity; spectroscopy and the constellation that was never a severity scale; the near-uniform early universe that needed tiny differences to make any structure at all. The ecological & biological Niche construction and worldmaking; the umwelt and the double empathy problem; symbiosis and the self that was always a collective; tides and co-regulation. The lived & communal Monotropism and spiral time; threshold anxiety and the crossing; functioning labels and the constellation of intensities; memory, mutual aid, and the work of being loved down to your star stuff.

How it's made, and held Each piece pairs a real diagram and honest sourcing with the community's own knowledge, and many are built with — or directly credit — neurodivergent thinkers. Everything is written in the first person plural: we , not they . And everything is held in common under Creative Commons, made to be printed free and shared freely. The zines are flowers of the garden, and a flower's whole purpose is to give its seeds away. A note on the science These are resonances, not proofs. The physics does not owe us our ethics, and we don't pretend it does — we begin from well-established science and read it as an argument about belonging, noticing where the same shape recurs. Where a source is contested or an interpretation is one among several, we say so. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. Sources & corrections We trace every quotation to a primary source, credit coinages to the people who made them, and ground the science in real, checkable work. We're human, and the collection is living — fact-checking here is ongoing, not finished. Every audit and every correction is published in the changelog , our own errors included. If you spot an error or a misattribution, please tell us: open an issue on GitHub or reach us at stimpunks.org , and we'll fix it. Solidarity, not charity — corrections are mutual aid. We love you down to your star stuff. A man runs out of words

Frankfurt · 1604 A man runs out of words Johannes Kepler was trying to draw an eclipse properly, and the language stopped him. The problem is geometry. If the thing casting a shadow is lit by a point of light, the shadow has one crisp edge and you need one word. But the Sun is not a point. It is a disc — an extended source — and every part of it throws its own shadow in a slightly different direction. So the shadow comes out layered. There is a core where the whole disc is hidden. There is an outer region where some of the disc is hidden and some of it still shines through. Between them there is no edge at all, just a handover. Kepler had umbra for the core. For the handover he had nothing. So, in the middle of a diagram in Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena, he made one: …quod est inter KE, NM penumbra dicatur, LN vero umbra. Kepler, Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena, 1604 — orthography normalised Let what lies between KE and NM be called penumbra — and LN, indeed, umbra. The verb is dicatur: let it be called. That is not a man using a word. That is the word being made, in one clause, because a drawing demanded it. He built it out of paene, almost, and umbra, shadow. Almost-shadow. And notice what gets named: not the dark, not the light. The thing between them. Before 1604 there was a shadow and there was not-a-shadow. The zone in between existed the whole time, and had no name, and therefore could not be reasoned about. what a word is for A few pages on he is already using it as an ordinary working term — decrescente, crescit penumbra, as the one shrinks the other grows — and noting that well before an eclipse looks like it has begun, nearly the whole Moon is already inside the almost-shadow. Three zones, because two would lie

The vocabulary now Three zones, because two would lie Kepler's two words became three, and the third one is the one people have never heard of. Because the Sun is a disc and the Moon is a ball, the Moon's shadow is a cone — it narrows to a point and then stops. Which means the shadow behaves differently depending on how far down it you stand: the Moon's shadow, per NASA's eclipse glossary zone what you see from inside it umbra the darkest part of the shadow. The Sun is completely blocked — a total eclipse. penumbra the weak or pale part. The Sun is only partially blocked — a partial eclipse. antumbra past the cone's apex. The Sun appears larger than the Moon, which is seen in complete silhouette — an annular eclipse, the ring of fire. The antumbra is worth sitting with, because it is the case a two-word vocabulary genuinely cannot describe. Stand there and the Moon is entirely in front of the Sun — nothing is sticking out, nothing is off to one side — and it is still not a total eclipse, because the Moon is simply too small in your sky to cover what is behind it. Complete coverage, and still not enough. The obstruction is total and the darkness never comes. the antumbra, which needs its own word Two words would have forced that case into one of the other two, and both would have been wrong. The partial one is the enormous one

Scale The partial one is the enormous one Here is the fact that rearranges the picture, and it is purely a matter of footprint. When the Moon's shadow lands on Earth, the two zones are not remotely comparable in size. The umbra touches down as a narrow track — on the order of a hundred to a few hundred kilometres across, a stripe you can drive out of in an afternoon. The penumbra lands as a vast disc, thousands of kilometres wide, covering a good fraction of a hemisphere. Run the consequence. Everyone inside that huge disc is having an eclipse. Almost none of them are in the track. The overwhelming majority of people who have ever seen a solar eclipse have seen a partial one. Totality is the rare case. The penumbra is where we live. the arithmetic of the two footprints And this is exactly why the word had to be invented rather than borrowed. The condition Kepler named is not an edge case or a rounding error at the border of the real thing. It is the ordinary condition, and the total case is the exception. Which sets up the trap this zine spends the next spread walking into on purpose. If partial is the normal state, and partial is a gradient, it is very tempting to conclude that the difference between 99 percent and 100 percent is just... one percent. It is not. It is not close to one percent. And the reason is not poetic. The cliff Ninety-nine percent is daylight Stand at 99 percent obscuration and you are not almost at totality. You are in a slightly odd afternoon. The reason is that the Sun's surface is outrageously bright and the corona is not. The corona — the thing you have come to see, the pearl-white structure that only exists for the eye during totality — is roughly as bright as a full Moon. Now leave one percent of the photosphere uncovered. That surviving sliver is still hundreds to thousands of times brighter than a full Moon. It does not politely dim the scene. It obliterates the corona and keeps the sky blue. Photometry bears this out as a cliff rather than a slope: measured illuminance falls roughly a hundred-fold in the last two minutes before totality, by another order of magnitude in the final half minute, and by more than four orders of magnitude in total between full Sun and totality. Ninety-nine percent of the way there gets you almost none of the way there. The last increment is not an increment — it is a change of state. what the photometry says, put plainly And then the Moon covers the last sliver, and the world does something else entirely: The period of total eclipse felt like a fermata. Birds quieted. Colors dimmed. A surreal calmness unfurled. Ryan Boren, Central Texas, 8 April 2024 A fermata is the mark that tells a musician to hold a note past its written value — to suspend the count. It is the right word, and it is not available at 99 percent. At 99 percent the birds are unbothered and the count runs on. So both of these are true at once, and the zine will not drop either: The shadow is a gradient. There is no edge; there never was; Kepler needed a third word precisely because the handover is smooth. And there is a threshold inside the gradient. Somewhere in that smooth handover sits a point where the birds stop. Both, not either Gradient and threshold Most arguments about difference pick one of these and lose the other. The shadow does not let you. Pick gradient only and you get the flattening move: everyone's a bit like that, it's all a spectrum, we're all somewhere on it. True as far as it goes, and it dissolves every threshold that matters. If it is all one smooth ramp, nothing in particular is owed to anyone in particular. The word for this is not solidarity. It is erasure with a friendly face. Pick threshold only and you get the gatekeeping move: either you qualify or you don't; either you're disabled or you're fine. Also recognisable. Any account that can only hold one of those is describing something other than the world. the shape of the argument Kepler's word is precise about this in a way our usual vocabulary is not. Penumbra does not mean a bit shadowed. It names a specific region with real boundaries — you are in it or you are not — whose defining property is that the blocking there is incomplete. It is a category, not a hedge. A named place where a partial state is the actual condition, and the partial state is not a failed attempt at a total one. Two other fields worked this out independently, went looking for a word for it, and arrived at Kepler's. The tissue that is not dead yet

Stroke · 1981 The tissue that is not dead yet When an artery in the brain closes, the damage is not a disc. It is a shadow, with zones. In 1981, Jens Astrup, Bo Siesjö and Lindsay Symon published a paper in Stroke with a title that is half physiology and half borrowed astronomy: "Thresholds in cerebral ischemia — the ischemic penumbra." Working in a baboon model of middle cerebral artery occlusion, and measuring blood flow alongside electrical activity, pH and extracellular potassium, they found not one threshold but two: two thresholds, and the zone between them as blood flow falls what happens first threshold electrical failure. The tissue goes silent. It stops doing its job. second threshold ion-pump failure. Potassium floods out. The tissue stops being tissue. Between those two lines sits a region that is functionally silent but structurally intact. It is not working. It is also not gone. Restore the blood supply and it can come back. Impaired is not lost. There is a zone between not functioning and not surviving, and it is where every intervention lives. the ischaemic penumbra, in one sentence They called it the ischaemic penumbra — and the word fits with an exactness that is almost uncomfortable. A region of partial deprivation, wrapped around a core of total deprivation, distinguished from it not by how bad it looks but by whether anything can still be done. The core is the umbra. Nothing is coming back from there. The penumbra is the part still holding on, and it is holding on on a clock. Consequences What the word bought This is the part that matters, and it is not linguistic. Naming that zone changed what happens to people. Consider the alternative vocabulary — the two-word one. In it, brain tissue after a stroke is either alive or dead. Under that description, the urgency is unclear and the target is unclear. There is damage; you assess the damage; the damage is what it is. Now describe the same brain with three words. Suddenly there is a region that is currently non-functional and currently salvageable, and it is shrinking, and it is shrinking as a function of time. That description does something the other cannot: it makes a clock visible. And a visible clock is the thing an entire field of emergency medicine is organised around — the reason acute stroke has a treatment window at all, the reason imaging tries to distinguish core from penumbra before deciding, the reason the phrase time is brain exists. Every intervention is aimed at the penumbra. Nobody is treating the core; there is nothing there to treat. The whole enterprise is a fight over the almost-shadow. what follows from having the word Sit with the shape of that, because it recurs everywhere and is almost always got wrong. The zone that looks least dramatic — not the catastrophic core, not the healthy surround, the ambiguous ring in between — is the only zone where anything you do makes a difference. The core is past help. The healthy tissue does not need it. All of the leverage is in the part that a two-state description cannot even name. And a two-state description does not merely fail to help there. It actively hides where the help would go. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks

Griswold · 1965 Penumbras, formed by emanations The second borrowing is stranger, more contested, and we are going to say so on the page rather than in a footnote. In Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965), the Supreme Court struck down a law banning contraceptives. The difficulty was that the Constitution does not mention privacy. Justice Douglas, writing for the Court, reached for Kepler's word: "…specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance." Justice William O. Douglas, Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965) The claim is that a written guarantee casts something beyond its own literal edge. Protect the home against quartered soldiers, protect papers against search, protect association — and around each of those, in the region where the light is partly blocked, sits something the text implies without stating. Now the honest part. This is among the most criticised passages in American constitutional law, and not only from one direction. The objection is real and worth stating fairly: if a text casts penumbras, who decides how far they reach? A shadow with no measurable edge can be extended to cover whatever the reader wanted covered. The danger of the penumbra is exactly its virtue. It is the region where the boundary is not sharp — which is what makes it honest, and what makes it available for abuse. the objection, not dodged We are not resolving that here; it is a live argument among people who have spent careers on it. We include it because of what the borrowing shows: twice now, in fields with nothing else in common, someone confronted a situation where a binary would produce an obviously wrong answer — and both times the word they reached for was the astronomer's. Both times, for the same reason. A hard edge would have been easier to administer and false. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks
Almost accessible is a phase change away

The turn Almost accessible is a phase change away Here is where we live, and both halves of the physics are load-bearing. Take the gradient half first. Most of us are neither fully blocked nor fully in the light — and the next spread is about who gets told they are the former. We are Disabled and Autistic and chronically ill in ways that fluctuate — good days, bad weeks, a capacity that is real on Tuesday and gone on Thursday. There is no crisp edge to point at, and every system we deal with demands one. So we get told the partial state is not a state. You managed last month. You're doing fine now. The penumbra gets read as a failed umbra — as a claim that hasn't finished proving itself — rather than as the place where most people actually are. Now the threshold half, which cuts the other way and is the one more often forgotten by people who mean well. Support is not proportional. Ninety percent of a ramp is a wall. A venue that is accessible except for the toilets is not 95 percent accessible; it is a venue you cannot stay in. Captions that drop out for the last two minutes did not deliver 98 percent of the talk. The last increment is where the phase change is — and up to that point the sky stays stubbornly, uselessly bright. Ninety-nine percent of the way to totality is a slightly odd afternoon. Ninety-nine percent of the way to access is a locked door with a very good ramp leading up to it. the same arithmetic, twice And then hold them together, because separately each one is a well-worn mistake. All gradient gives you the flattening, and nobody is owed anything specific. All threshold gives you the eligibility form, and the enormous partial zone vanishes. The shadow insists on both. Smooth, and with a place in it where the birds stop. The last thing to carry over is the 1981 one, which is the most hopeful sentence in this zine and the least sentimental. There is no umbra in a bodymind

The distinction this piece owes There is no umbra in a bodymind Everything so far has been about shadows falling on things. Now the question that decides whether any of it is safe to use: where does an umbra actually live? Go back to the geometry on spread 3. An umbra is a relation between a source, an obstruction, and a place. It is not a substance and not a property. The ground in an umbra has not changed; it is simply where the blocked light would have gone. Move the source and the umbra moves. Take the obstruction away and it is not there at all. The pavement does not have an umbra. The pavement is in one. Nothing about the pavement is different. what a shadow is, and is not So the threshold on the previous spread is real, and it is an umbra of support. Support can be partial, and it can be total — ninety percent of a ramp is a wall, and behind that wall nothing gets through at all. That umbra is a fact about an arrangement, and arrangements can be changed by whoever built them. Functioning labels do something else entirely. They take the shadow the arrangement casts and paint it onto the person standing in it. High-functioning. Low-functioning. Mild. Severe. Levels. Each one relocates a fact about circumstances into a fact about a body. And “profound autism” is the umbra version of that move. Proposed in the Lancet Commission on the future of care and clinical research in autism (2021) for Autistic people who are minimally or non-speaking, require round-the-clock care, and are “not able to advocate for themselves.” Hold that last criterion against what the research actually finds. Steven Kapp's 2023 review concludes that minimally speaking Autistic people can communicate — particularly with responsive partners — that they need testing which lets them show what they have rather than testing built to miss it, and that they can self-advocate. Which makes “unable to advocate for themselves” partly a statement about the listener, the method and the room — and only partly about the person it is written on. the criterion, read carefully Now put spread 7's sentence where it belongs. In the ischaemic penumbra, what looks like loss is often deprivation — and reading deprivation as loss is not a small error there. It is the exact mistake that costs the salvageable zone. Profound reads deprivation as loss, and does it on a person. So let this be flat and unhedged. This piece recognises an umbra in support — support that is wholly blocked, and can be unblocked. It recognises no umbra in an Autistic bodymind at all. Not a small one. Not a rare one. Not one reserved for somebody further along than you. There is no zone of person that light does not reach and cannot be made to. And that refusal is not a denial of anyone's support needs, which would be its own way of writing people off. Some people need constant, skilled, expensive, round-the-clock support, and saying so plainly is part of the argument rather than an exception to it. Helen Edgar puts the distinction exactly: Autistic people with profound and multiple learning disabilities and health needs are not “Profoundly Autistic,” they are autistic with specific needs. Helen Edgar, More Realms · “Profound autism” does not exist Which is why support-needs language restores the penumbra. It is specific, it names domains, it varies by day and by room, it can go up and down, and — the part that matters here — it never declares any part of a person past reaching. The word came from an eclipse, and an eclipse is the right lender. Medicine's umbra is a genuine property of matter: that tissue is dead. That is precisely why it must not travel any further. Borrowing the astronomer's word does not license borrowing the surgeon's verdict. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks
A borrowed word is not an argument

The guardrail A borrowed word is not an argument Two fields reaching for the same word is a striking fact. It is not evidence for anything about us, and we want to be exact about that before closing. What the borrowings actually establish is narrow: that in at least two serious domains, practitioners found a two-state description inadequate to something real, and the vocabulary they wanted already existed in optics. That is a fact about the usefulness of a distinction. It is not a finding about disability, and no amount of elegance makes it one. The physics on spreads three through five is exact and checkable. The turn on spread ten is an analogy, and analogies license nothing on their own. A rhyme, not a proof. What we would defend without the metaphor: that fluctuating capacity is real, that partial support frequently delivers nothing, and that describing people in two states hides the place where help works. Those stand on their own evidence, and the eclipse is how we show them, not why we believe them. Not:that any bodymind has an umbra. This is the refusal the whole piece turns on, and spread 11 states it outright. We recognise a total blockage of support, which is a fact about an arrangement somebody built and can unbuild. We recognise nothing of the kind in a person. Profound, severe, low-functioning and level 3 all take a shadow cast by circumstances and write it on a body. Not:that refusing the label denies anyone's support needs. Some people need constant, skilled, round-the-clock support, and spread 11 says so plainly rather than sidestepping it. Refusing an umbra on the bodymind and funding the support are the same position, not competing ones. Not:that anyone is in shadow. The reading is right there — dimmed, obscured, waiting for the light to come back — and we refuse it. Nobody here is a diminished version of a brighter thing. The shadow is a description problem, not a person. Not:a severity spectrum. "Mild to severe" is the umbra-and-nothing vocabulary wearing a gradient costume, and it still ranks us along one axis toward a normal. The penumbra is a zone, not a rung. See No. 21. Not:"everyone's a little bit like that." This is precisely the flattening spread six refuses. A gradient with no threshold in it is not solidarity; it is a way of owing nobody anything. Not:that partial support is a start. Sometimes it is. Often it is a wall with a ramp leading to it, counted as ninety percent done. The photometry is the whole point: almost can be worth nearly nothing. Not:a proof about people. Kepler was drawing eclipses. Astrup, Siesjö and Symon were measuring baboon cortex. Douglas was construing the Bill of Rights. None of them was writing about us, and we are not pretending otherwise. Almost Shadow · Stimpunks

Who is speaking, and from where

Before anything else Who is speaking, and from where This spread is early on purpose. Almost every failure available to a piece like this one is a failure of attribution, and the largest is the sentence Indigenous people believe — which flattens hundreds of distinct legal traditions into a single opinion nobody holds. The people quoted in this zine, and where they speak from Who From where Tyson Yunkaporta Apalech clan, western Cape York; Wik Mungkan speaker Dr Mary Graham Kombumerri, south-east Queensland; Wakka Wakka through her mother’s people Prof. Anne Poelina Nyikina Warrwa; Traditional Owner and guardian of the Martuwarra Marlikka Perdrisat Nyikina Warrwa; Poelina’s daughter, writing with her Mr Bill Neidjie Gaagudju, Kakadu Dr Zoe Todd Métis, Amiskwaci­wâskahikan (Edmonton) Three of those are Aboriginal Australian and from three different nations with three different bodies of law. One is Métis, in what is now Canada, writing about a different problem entirely. They are not interchangeable and they are not a chorus. The point is made inside the sources themselves. Redvers and colleagues, having spent a paper on First Law, end it by saying that First Law is “uniquely rooted within the respective lands globally” — not one law with local dialects, but many laws, each of which is a fact about a particular place. A small thing we are doing on purpose. Poelina’s river appears in the literature as both Martuwarra and Mardoowarra, depending on the publication. We follow whichever spelling a given source uses rather than picking one and normalising the rest, because the normalising is the habit under discussion. Already an Entity · Stimpunks

The charge against our law Immoral, and not illegal Yunkaporta reports a conversation with two Elders. Aunty Mary Graham’s position, as he sets it out, is not that settler law is cruel or badly administered. It is that settler law is incomplete. settler law is incomplete because it is possible, even commonplace, to commit immoral and unethical acts of destruction that are not illegal Aunty Mary Graham, as reported in Tyson Yunkaporta, Right Story, Wrong Story (2023) She calls First Law a “full Law” by contrast — full because it includes all ethical and moral behaviour, and takes care of every aspect of a complete human being. Test the charge rather than admiring it. It is a claim about our own statute books, and it is the kind of claim a reader can check in an afternoon. Draining a wetland with a permit. Clearing a remnant forest inside an approval. Discharging within a licensed limit, every day, for thirty years. A catchment that is legally dewatered by the sum of individually lawful extractions, no one of which is an offence. None of that is a loophole. A loophole is a defect in a law that was trying to prevent something. Our law was not trying. It has no category for the wrong, so there is nothing to be caught by. Graham’s own 1999 paper opens under an epigraph from Bill Neidjie, a Gaagudju man of Kakadu: The white man’s law is always changing, but Aboriginal Law never changes and is valid for all people. Mr Bill Neidjie, Kakadu Man, quoted by Mary Graham Read that as an observation about instruments rather than a boast. A law that changes constantly is a law being negotiated. The question this zine follows is what our law was never asked to hold in the first place. Already an Entity · Stimpunks

Not through an intermediary The Land is the law Aunty Mary Graham publishes under her own name, in the open. It would have been easy to keep quoting her through Yunkaporta, and it would have been wrong — letting one Aboriginal author be the sole conduit for another’s thought is a version of the same flattening. So: Graham, in Parrhesia, in 2023. There is no Aboriginal equivalent to the Cartesian notion of ‘I think therefore I am’ but, if there were, it would be — ‘I am located therefore I am’. Mary Graham, “The Law of Obligation, Aboriginal Ethics,” Parrhesia 37 (2023) From which follows a self that is not the unit Western ethics assumes. “A reflective self is a communal self,” she writes: one that understands how communal acts affect those around them, human and non-human, over time — rather than being limited to an immediate relation of cause and effect. And then the formulation she names as both a philosophy and a protest: The Land is the law. Graham, Parrhesia 37 — “that well-known phrase which is both a form of protest and a philosophical worldview” What grows out of that relationship she calls a Custodial Ethic: an obligation to look after the Land that nurtures us — “an ethic of looking after, stewardship, caring for, rather than a survivalist ethos with its rivalry and competition over resources and structural conflicts enveloped in hierarchies of power.” Notice the shape of the disagreement. It is not that our law values the wrong things. It is that our law is built around a self that ends at the skin and a timeframe that ends at the next cause. Ask that instrument to register a two-hundred-year obligation to a river and it has nowhere to write it down. Already an Entity · Stimpunks
A totem is an institution, not a sentiment

Kinship as jurisprudence A totem is an institution, not a sentiment In Nyikina, a totem is Jadiny. Poelina and Perdrisat write that when Aboriginal people are born they are given one, and that the totem is kin — you are given a totem to teach you that you have a kinship relationship with non-human beings. To define it they reach for a settler anthropologist, which is worth noticing: Deborah Bird Rose, whose framing they quote is a totem as “a common property institution for long-term ecological management.” Go to Rose’s chapter and the argument is drier and better than the phrase suggests. She sets out to analyse “a dynamic jurisprudence of duty in which responsibilities and rights are considered together” — and concludes that “totemism appears to constitute just such a jurisprudence of responsibility and right.” Her list of what that jurisprudence actually does is the part that should embarrass anyone who filed totemism under belief: Responsibilities are differentiated and complementary, held locally and regionally, so that “no country is self-sufficient”. Burning, the preservation of species, the preservation of permanent waters. “Restraint is equally part of this system.” There are sanctuaries where people do not hunt or fish or gather. Totems are linked to taboos that enforce restraint and are managed by the appropriate people — the kangaroo people can forbid others to kill and eat kangaroo. Deborah Bird Rose, “Common Property Regimes in Aboriginal Australia: Totemism Revisited” Read that as a schedule rather than a cosmology and it is a protected-areas network with enforcement, allocation and standing. Sanctuaries. Species-specific prohibitions. Named parties with the authority to forbid. Obligations that run between groups because no estate can be managed alone. This is the spread that earns the collection. The relationship with non-human beings is not the decoration on the law. It is the mechanism by which the law is held. Already an Entity · Stimpunks
Terra nullius rested on a claim about management

How the doctrine was built Terra nullius rested on a claim about management Here is the hinge, and it is Rose’s. The legal doctrine that declared a continent unowned was not, at bottom, a legal argument. It was an ecological one, and it was wrong on its own terms. The claim was that Aboriginal people did not manage the land. A. P. Elkin, in a book first published in 1938, gave that view what Rose calls “the mark of scientific authority”: The food-gathering life is parasitical; the Aborigines are absolutely dependent on what nature produces without any practical assistance on their part. A. P. Elkin, quoted in Rose — the parasitism view, in print under scientific authority Rose states the inference in one sentence: “The idea that the land was untransformed led directly to the idea that land was unowned.” Behind it sits Locke — whatsoever a man removes out of the state that Nature hath provided, and mixes his labour with, thereby becomes his property. No visible labour, no property. No property, no owners. No owners, terra nullius. The reversal came in 1969, when Rhys Jones described Aboriginal use of fire as land management and called it fire-stick farming. Rose notes his choice of the word farming was deliberate, and provocative “precisely because it hit a cultural/political nerve”: like farmers, people intervened in their ecosystems to transform them in predictable and desirable ways, for long-term productivity. So the observation that founded the doctrine was a failure to recognise an institution that was in front of the observers the whole time. The management was there. It did not look like a fence, so it did not count as one. Hold on to that shape. It happens again on spread ten, to something larger than a continent. Already an Entity · Stimpunks

Named as its custodians publish it Warloongarriy, Wunan, Liyan Poelina and Perdrisat open their section of the Challenges paper in Nyikina — Jayida Booroo, yimartuwarra marnins. Welcome to our Country. We are women who belong to the Martuwarra Fitzroy River. They write, in their words, “as Indigenous insiders, mother, and daughter.” What follows is theirs to publish and ours only to report, so this spread names and does not gloss: As set out by the Martuwarra’s own custodians Name What they say it is Warloongarriy Law River Law — the First Law governing the Martuwarra, carried in a songline shared by the First Nations along the river, setting out community and individual rights, relationships and responsibilities Wunan Law regional governance law — a cooperative model respecting the sovereignty of Indigenous nations while treating River, Sea, Ranges and Desert Country as one connected whole; before colonisation, the regional system for trade exchange from the Kimberley to the Northern Territory Liyan “the feeling of a deep personal relationship with all living and non-living things” — the spirit within us that connects us to the universal spirit of life Jadiny totem, in Nyikina Two things they say about how this law works are worth setting directly against ours. First: “First Law principles are not expressed in terms of external rules, policies, and procedures by government to influence individual and societal behavior through fear.” It is carried in stories, and passed to each generation by singing and dancing. Second, on obligation: “it is our fiduciary duty to protect land and living waters, and our non-human family.” Fiduciary is a settler-legal word, chosen deliberately. It names the strictest duty our own law knows — the one owed by a trustee, where you may not profit, may not have a conflict, and must act for the other. Our law has that duty. It has simply never been made to run toward a river. Already an Entity · Stimpunks

Where the tidy story breaks Personhood is not the ask There is a version of this subject that settler readers enjoy very much, and this zine was originally going to be built on it. Rivers are being granted legal personhood. Look how far we have come. The statutes are real. The Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act 2017 gives the Whanganui in Aotearoa New Zealand “all the rights, powers, duties, and liabilities of a legal person,” exercised by Te Pou Tupua, the human face of the river. In Victoria the Yarra River Protection (Wilip-gin Birrarung murron) Act 2017 carries a title in Woiwurrung meaning keep the Yarra alive — and, contrary to how it is usually reported, does not grant personhood at all; it gives the river a voice through the Birrarung Council. Then you read what the Martuwarra’s custodians actually say about it: This is different from the legal subject of “personhood”, for which there is increasing ambivalence among some traditional landowners due to important questions on the actual legal usefulness of this term. As the River is already an entity, it should not have to depend on the specific actions of settler law to achieve this status. Anne Poelina & Marlikka Perdrisat, Challenges 11(2), 29 (2020) That is the sentence this zine is named after, and it takes the flattering story away. Personhood is settler law conferring, on its own authority and in its own vocabulary, a status the River’s own Law has never once doubted. To celebrate the conferral is to celebrate the gatekeeping. Poelina’s companion paper with O’Donnell, Pelizzon and Clark puts the objection in its title: “Stop Burying the Lede: The Essential Role of Indigenous Law(s) in Creating Rights of Nature.” The lede being buried is whose law did the work. The ask is not to be granted standing. It is legal pluralism — that both systems run, and that ours stop presenting itself as the one that decides what exists. Already an Entity · Stimpunks

The same move, on something larger Terra nullius, aer nullius Spread seven left a shape: a European observer fails to recognise an institution, concludes there is nothing there, and the conclusion becomes law. Zoe Todd, a Métis anthropologist, watched it happen again — not to a continent, to the climate. She was at a Gifford Lecture in 2013, excited, because Bruno Latour was a personal hero and his work was part of why she had left biology for anthropology. He spoke about the climate as a matter of common cosmopolitical concern. And she found herself, in her words, “just another inconvenient Indigenous body in a room full of people excited to hear a white guy talk around themes shared in Indigenous thought without giving Indigenous people credit or a nod.” Her name for it extends the older doctrine exactly: aer nullius Zoe Todd, Journal of Historical Sociology 29(1), 2016 — her coinage The climate, she writes, becomes “a blank commons to be populated by very Euro-Western theories of resilience, the Anthropocene, Actor Network Theory and other ideas that dominate the anthropological and climate change arenas of the moment.” An empty sky, awaiting theory. The land was never empty either. Todd is scrupulous in a way worth copying. She extends due credit to Latour for the framing. She says plainly that her concern “is not really with Latour himself, but with how a Euro-Western audience consumes” the argument — without knowing that comparable discourses were already running outside the rock-star arenas of Euro-Western thought. She does not think he intended to elide decades of Indigenous intellectual labour. The charge is not plagiarism. It is a citation practice — and a citation practice is a thing anybody can fix on a Tuesday afternoon. Already an Entity · Stimpunks

Our own exposure, named We are in this chain Todd’s charge is about citation habits in Euro-Western writing about more-than-human worlds. This is Euro-Western writing about more-than-human worlds. It would be indecent to print her argument and not check ourselves against it, so: We use the phrase “more-than-human” constantly. It is the name of a whole collection here. It is exactly the register Todd is describing — the vocabulary of sentience, agency and multispecies relation that Euro-Western theory arrived at recently and treats as its own discovery. And No. 26 reaches for Deleuze and Guattari. It takes the rhizome — no trunk, no centre, enter anywhere — from two French philosophers, to argue for decentralised, relational, non-hierarchical ways of knowing. That argument is good and we still hold it. But Todd’s point is not that Deleuze is wrong. It is who else could have told you, and whether they got a line in the bibliography. This is the part where a piece like this usually says we have learned so much and moves on. What we have actually done is smaller and duller: gone to Graham’s own paper instead of quoting her through Yunkaporta, gone to Rose’s chapter instead of using the phrase Poelina quotes from it, named a nation beside every name, and checked what Poelina thinks of personhood before writing a spread praising it. none of which is a revelation — it is just doing the citations The honest version of Todd’s remedy is unglamorous. Read the people whose thought it is. Cite them by name and nation. Notice when your exciting new framework has an older address. We are not clean here. We are one draft less dirty than we were, on one piece. Already an Entity · Stimpunks
What we are not going to do with this

Where this zine stops What we are not going to do with this Every other zine on this site ends the same way. We take a settled fact, follow it honestly, and find that a claim about belonging — usually about being neurodivergent, usually about us — was already sitting inside it. That is not happening here, and the absence is the argument. Run our usual move on First Law and two things happen, both bad. The physics or the statute becomes the validator — First Law is admitted because it agrees with thermodynamics, which makes our instruments the judge of somebody else’s jurisprudence. And Aboriginal Law becomes an instrument for an argument of ours, which is what it looks like when a body of knowledge is used rather than read. There is a version of the paragraph we are declining to write. It is about how settler law and the deficit model share a shape, both measuring against a standard with no way to record relation. It might even be true. It is also not ours to reach for here, it would travel without its qualifier, and this material has been made to carry other people’s arguments quite enough. Yunkaporta offers a definition, and we should be measured against it rather than choosing our own: an Indigenous person is a member of a community retaining memories of life lived sustainably on a land base, as part of that land base Tyson Yunkaporta, Sand Talk (2019) We do not meet it. Stimpunks is a settler-founded project on stolen land, and Star Stuff is a set of web pages made by people who are not going to become custodians of anywhere by reading about it. That is the plain situation, and stating it costs nothing except a paragraph we would have enjoyed writing. Not: First Law explained. Nothing here is our account of anybody’s Law. Every description is quoted from a named person of a named nation, published in the open, and we have not paraphrased past what they published. Not: “Indigenous people believe.” Three Aboriginal nations appear here and they are not a chorus. Redvers and colleagues say it themselves: First Law is “uniquely rooted within the respective lands globally.” Not: ancient wisdom. Everything cited here was published between 1999 and 2023 by working academics, in peer-reviewed journals, several of them lawyers. Filing it as timeless is another way of filing it as not-current, which is how a live legal argument gets read as folklore. Not: validated by physics. Yunkaporta can draw the line between First Law and the laws of physics; he is inside one of them. If we do it, we have made our instruments the arbiter of somebody else’s law, which is the colonial move with better manners. Not: a rights-of-nature success story. The primaries broke that reading and we let them. See spread nine. And: not a metaphor for us. No river here stands in for anybody, and nothing on these pages is an argument about neurodivergence. This is the only zine here that ends without one, on purpose. Already an Entity · Stimpunks
