The Moon Is Always Half Lit

53 Star Stuff The Moon Is Always Half Lit on phases as geometry, the far side that was never dark, and why waning is a word about the angle 50.2% · 59% · 27.32 d · 29.53 d · 1959 · a rhyme, not a proof L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely
There has never been less Moon

The fact There has never been less Moon The Sun lights one hemisphere of the Moon. Not usually. Not on average. Continuously, for four and a half billion years, without a single interruption that was not an eclipse. This is worth sitting with, because almost nobody pictures it that way. A crescent Moon looks like a Moon that has had most of its light taken away. It is not. It is a fully half-lit Moon seen nearly edge-on to its own daylight — you are looking at the boundary between its day and its night from almost alongside, so the lit part presents to you as a sliver. The illuminated hemisphere is exactly as large at new Moon as at full. Nothing dims. Nothing is withheld. Nothing is recovering. The same amount of Moon is in the same amount of sunlight the entire month, and the entire month is a story about where you happen to be standing. A phase is not something that happens to the Moon. It is something that happens between the Moon and you. One refinement, because precision is a form of care. Slightly more than half is lit — about 50.2 percent. The Sun is not a point and it is much larger than the Moon, so the tangent lines that define the terminator close a little past the geometric halfway line. It is a small number and it is the honest one, and we show the arithmetic in the colophon rather than asking you to take it. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
A phase is an angle, and you are one of its arms

The geometry A phase is an angle, and you are one of its arms Three bodies are required to make a phase: the Sun, the Moon, and somebody looking. Remove any one of them and the phase does not become something else — it stops existing. There is no fact of the matter about "what phase the Moon is in" that does not include an observer's position in it. The quantity astronomers actually compute is the angular separation between the Sun and the Moon as seen from where you are, and that number has your location baked into it as surely as it has the Moon's. So the month-long procession of shapes is not the Moon doing anything. It is the Moon and the Earth carrying you around a lit object at a steadily changing angle, and your line of sight sweeping across a boundary that, on the Moon itself, has not moved at all. The Moon is not changing. The three of us are moving. Figure 1 is the standard diagram with one thing insisted upon: every Moon in the ring is drawn with the same lit half, facing the same way. That is not an artist's simplification. That is the finding. Eight orbital positions, one unchanging lit hemisphere Sunlight arrives from the left. Earth sits at the centre of a dashed circular orbit. Eight Moons are spaced around that orbit, and every one of them is drawn with its left-hand hemisphere lit and its right-hand hemisphere dark, because every one of them is lit by the same Sun in the same direction. The apparent shape a viewer on Earth sees differs at each position only because the viewing angle differs. every Moon here is exactly half lit only the angle to the viewer changes Figure 1 · the lit half never moves Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
Four of the eight last no time at all

The names Four of the eight last no time at all Everyone has seen the chart: eight little Moons in a row, eight names, eight equal boxes. The chart is a convention laid over a continuum, and it is lopsided in a way the drawing hides. The US Naval Observatory is precise about this. New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon and Last Quarter are defined to occur when the excess of the Moon's apparent ecliptic longitude over the Sun's is 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° respectively — which makes them instants. Moments. They have no duration. The Moon is Full at a specific second and is not Full a second later. The other four — waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning gibbous, waning crescent — are the entire rest of the month, about a week each. Four knife-edges and four long weeks, drawn as though they were eight equal things. Underneath the chart the illuminated fraction changes smoothly and without steps, every value between nothing and everything, all month, every month. There is no moment at which the Moon crosses from one kind of thing into another kind of thing. The boxes are ours. We drew them because a chart needs boxes, and then we started reading the boxes back as though we had found them. This is not an argument against the names. They are useful, they are precise where they claim to be, and the USNO states their status plainly rather than hiding it. It is an argument about what happens when a naming convention outlives the page it was drawn on. One synodic month: four instants and four intervals A horizontal band represents one lunar month. Four bright vertical hairlines mark New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon and Last Quarter, which are defined as instants with no duration. Between them lie four wide blocks, each about a week long, labelled waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning gibbous and waning crescent. A smooth curve beneath shows the illuminated fraction rising and falling continuously with no steps. 0° 90° 180° 270° 360° wax cres wax gibb wan gibb wan cres underneath, no steps at all Figure 2 · the boxes are ours Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
Three people, three crescents, one Moon

The observer Three people, three crescents, one Moon Because you are one arm of the angle, moving you changes the answer. Take a single instant — one waxing crescent, one illuminated fraction, one Moon. In Edinburgh it is lit along the right-hand edge. In Melbourne, at the same moment, it is lit along the left. Near the equator it rides low as a bowl, lit along the bottom, and there is a lovely folk name for it: a wet moon, tipped up to hold the rain. Nobody is wrong. Nobody is seeing an illusion. The Moon is not doing three different things. Your horizon is tilted differently relative to the plane the Sun and Moon lie in, so the same lit edge presents at a different roll angle — and since up is defined by where your feet are, the picture rotates with you. Three drawings. Three correct answers. The difference is entirely in the observer. If somebody handed you these three sketches and asked which was the real Moon, the question would be malformed — and yet it is exactly the question we ask about people constantly, in reports, in assessments, in the sentence but she seems fine with me. The same crescent seen from three latitudes Three identical Moons at the same instant with the same illuminated fraction. The first, seen from the northern hemisphere, is lit along its right edge. The second, seen from the southern hemisphere, is lit along its left edge. The third, seen from near the equator, is lit along its bottom edge like a bowl. NORTHERN SOUTHERN EQUATOR lit on the right lit on the left lit underneath one instant · one lit fraction · one Moon Figure 3 · the picture rotates with your feet Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
There is a far side. There is no dark side.

Luna 3 · 7 October 1959 There is a far side. There is no dark side. The far side of the Moon receives exactly as much sunlight as the side we know. It has days and nights of the same length. It has noon. And at new Moon — the one night of the month when we can see nothing of the Moon at all — the far side is in full daylight, the whole hemisphere blazing, entirely unwitnessed. The phrase "dark side" is not poetic licence. It is simply a mistake, and it names the wrong property: the far side is not dark, it is turned away. We found out what was there on 7 October 1959. Luna 3 swung behind the Moon and took twenty-nine photographs of a hemisphere no one had ever seen, developed the film in a small automated darkroom it was carrying, scanned the negatives with a moving light beam, and radioed the result back across the vacuum. The pictures were grainy and covered about seventy percent of it. What came back was not a shadow. It was a landscape — sunlit, crowded edge to edge with craters, and almost entirely lacking the great dark maria that make the familiar face familiar. It had been like that the whole time. Unseen is not unlit. It never was. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
Tidally locked was never rigidly held

Libration Tidally locked was never rigidly held "The Moon always shows us the same face" is the second thing everyone knows about the Moon, and it is also an approximation that dissolves by about nine percent if you watch carefully. We see roughly 59 percent of the lunar surface from Earth, not fifty. The Moon rocks, and it does so for two unrelated reasons that happen to compound: Why we get more than half Motion Cause What it shows us In longitude the orbit is an ellipse, so the Moon runs fast near perigee and slow near apogee while its spin stays even a little around the eastern and western limbs, in turn In latitude the axis is tilted about 6.7° to the orbital plane a little over the north pole, then a little over the south So the lock is real but it is loose. It is a tendency the system settled into, not a bolt. The Moon is very slightly out of step with itself all month, and the reward for noticing is nine percent more world. Even the thing we describe as fixed turns out to be negotiating. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
New Moon here is a full Earth there

Complements New Moon here is a full Earth there Stand on the Moon on the night we call new, look up, and Earth is full — a complete blue-white disc, four times as wide as the Moon looks to us, and far brighter. This holds all the way round. The phases are complements. When we have a thin crescent, they have a fat gibbous Earth. When we have full Moon, they have new Earth, a black disc ringed in red by every sunrise and sunset on the planet at once. At every instant, the two phases sum to one whole. Which means the light is never missing. It is only ever distributed differently between two vantage points. Nobody in this system is having less; somebody is having it elsewhere, and the arithmetic is exact. There is no moment in the Earth–Moon system when anybody is in the dark. There are only moments when the light is somewhere you are not standing. This zine is about light. The other half of the relationship — nearness, tides, and what a body close by does for another body's rhythm — belongs to No. 17, The Nearest Body, and is deliberately not re-walked here. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

The ashen light The light we send back Find a thin crescent a few days after new Moon, on a clear evening, and look at the part that should be nothing. It is not nothing. The whole round disc is faintly there, ash-grey, the dark part visible. That glow is our light. Sunlight strikes Earth, bounces off cloud and ocean and ice, crosses to the Moon, and comes back to your eye. English has an old name for the sight: the old Moon in the new Moon's arms. Leonardo da Vinci worked out the mechanism around 1506–09 and drew it in the Codex Leicester, and — being Leonardo — never published it, so it did nobody any good for a century. He also got it slightly wrong: he thought the light came off Earth's oceans, where in fact most of it comes off clouds. The first published explanation is credited to Michael Mästlin. Mästlin taught at Tübingen, and among his students was Johannes Kepler — who, a few years later, ran out of vocabulary while drawing eclipse geometry and had to invent a word for the region that is neither full shadow nor full light. He called it penumbra. That story is No. 51. The teacher explained the light on the unlit part. The student named the shadow that is not quite a shadow. Neither of them would accept a picture with only two states in it. And note what earthshine actually requires. The dark limb is visible because something else is lit and facing it. Nothing about the Moon changed to make it appear. It became visible because of what was turned toward it. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
You can finish the circle and still not count as returned

27.32 · 29.53 You can finish the circle and still not count as returned The Moon completes one full orbit of the Earth — a whole circuit, 360 degrees, measured against the fixed stars — in 27.32 days. That is the sidereal month, and it is the orbit the Moon is actually on. But it is not back to new Moon. Not close. Because while the Moon went round, Earth moved too, about 27 degrees along its own orbit around the Sun, and "new Moon" is defined by the alignment with the Sun. The target slid forward. The Moon has to keep going — past a full circle, roughly 29 degrees further, about two more days — to catch an arrangement that did not stay put. That gives the synodic month: 29.53 days. It is the month everyone actually lives by. It is the one calendars are built from, and it is longer than the orbit it is made of. The cycle you are counted by is longer than the circuit you are actually completing — because the thing you are measured against keeps moving. There is a whole second piece in this — 29.53 days will not divide 365.24 days, and every calendar humans have built is a patch over that refusal. That is a chain for another day, and it is not this zine. The synodic month overshoots the orbit A dashed circle represents one complete lunar orbit of 360 degrees, taking 27.32 days. An additional short arc drawn outside the circle at the top right represents a further 29 degrees, about 2.2 days, that the Moon must travel to return to the same phase, because Earth has moved along its own orbit meanwhile. Together they make the synodic month of 29.53 days. +29° · 2.2 d the overshoot 360° · 27.32 d the orbit the phase cycle is 29.53 days a full circle was not enough Figure 4 · past 360° to arrive Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

The turn Nothing about it waned Here is the whole of it: waxing and waning are words about the geometry. They are not words about the Moon, and nothing in the Moon does them. We are described in phases constantly. Verbal on Tuesday and not on Thursday. Fine at home and struggling at school, or the reverse, which is usually taken as more damning. Capable in the assessment room and not in the corridor outside it. Someone writes down the sliver they were standing at the right angle to see, and it enters the record as how much there is. Those are not two quantities of person. Nothing was withheld in the first case and released in the second. The whole hemisphere was lit the entire time. What changed was the angle, the conditions, and who was doing the looking. A functioning label is a phase recorded as a substance. It takes the crescent and files it as the whole Moon there is. And the observer is in the measurement — that is the part that keeps getting dropped. But she seems fine with me is not a fact about her. It is a report of one angle, offered as though it were the object. So is he never speaks. So is every profile assembled from people who each saw one edge and none of whom were asked where they were standing. The spiky profile that No. 21 is about is exactly this, seen from inside: not a person who fluctuates in amount, but a whole person meeting differently-angled conditions and being measured as though the conditions were neutral. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

A case, first-hand Full time and part time The previous spread is an argument. Here is what it looks like from inside one school career — Ryan Boren, writing in 2022 about being read at both extremes at once. He is hyperlexic and Autistic. School did not know he could read, because he would not read aloud: situational mutism and exposure anxiety, in his words, “locked my lips.” Then one day, in a quiet corner with what he calls a semblance of psychological safety, he read a book cover to cover to his teacher in a whisper, and asked: “Can I go now?” “During my school career, I was both r-word and genius.” Ryan Boren, R-word and Genius: Situationally Mute Hyperlexic Autistic, 2022 Note what actually changed, because it was nothing about him. The reading was there the whole time — the entire lit hemisphere, at full brightness, before the quiet corner and after it. What moved was the room. And he names the variable exactly: “R-word and genius. The difference in impressions is due to psychological safety, it’s presence and absence.” Then the sentence this whole zine has been building toward without knowing it. He describes going “from being a full time r-word to a part time one, depending on who was in the room with me and if I felt safe enough speak.” Full time to part time. That is a phase, recorded in the vocabulary of proportion — as though there were an amount of him, and it had gone up. And depending on who was in the room with me is not a metaphor for the observer's position in the angle. It is the observer's position in the angle, stated plainly by the person being measured. He goes further than we would have dared, and he is right to: “Autistic people are psychological safety barometers.” Which inverts the whole measurement. A barometer's reading is a fact about the air around it. If the apparent phase tracks the safety of the room, then the instrument was measuring the room the entire time — and the room wrote the result down as a fact about the child. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks
The crescent really is less light

The guardrail The crescent really is less light There is an easy, wrong version of this zine, and it is one sentence away from the right one. The easy version says: since the Moon is always half lit, the difference is imaginary, so nothing is really harder on Thursday than it was on Tuesday. That is false, and it would be a cruel thing to hand anybody. A crescent genuinely delivers less light to you. Measurably. A full Moon can light a path home; a crescent cannot. The geometry is not a trick and its consequences are entirely real for whoever is standing under it. The correction we are actually making is narrower and holds up better: the difference is located in the arrangement, not in the body. Not in the Moon, which never changed. In the angle, the conditions, the room, the lighting, the hour, and the position of whoever is writing it down. That is exactly where an arrangement can be altered — and exactly where a diagnosis cannot reach. This is the same move No. 51 makes with shadow, and we are borrowing it rather than re-deriving it: an umbra is a relation between a source, an obstruction and a place, never a property of the ground it falls on. Same here. A phase is a relation between a source, a body and an observer, never a property of the body. Not:that the hard days are not hard. They are. This zine is about where the difficulty is located, and relocating it out of the bodymind is not the same as denying it. Anyone who reads this as "cheer up, you're always full" has been handed the wrong sentence, and we would rather say so on the page than hope. Not:that support needs are an illusion of perspective. Some of us need substantial, skilled, continuous support, and nothing in the optics touches that. What the optics refuse is the inference from seen as a crescent to is a crescent. Not:that inconsistency is a character flaw. Unreliable, attention-seeking, could do it yesterday — all of these read a changing angle as a changing will. Fluctuating capacity is ordinary, and the demand for a flat output is a demand no orbit has ever met. Not:the masking compliment. "You'd never know" is a description of the observer's angle presented as praise for the object. It is the same error as "the dark side," and it costs more. Not:that we are unknowable. The far side was unseen for the whole of human history and it was never unreal — and then Luna 3 went and looked. Hard to see from one position is an instruction to move, not a mystery to romanticise. See No. 48 on where that guardrail sits. Not:a proof about people. The USNO was defining ephemeris terms. Luna 3 was a spacecraft. Mästlin was explaining a glow. None of them was writing about us. Spread eleven is an analogy, and analogies license nothing on their own. A rhyme, not a proof. Not:that psychological safety is the only variable. Spread twelve is one person's account and it names safety because that is what was decisive for him. Sensory load, processing time, energy, pain, interoception, the demand itself and plain accumulated exhaustion are all real angles too. “Just make them feel safe” would be a new flattening, and a cheap one — the point is that the variables are in the arrangement, not that there is only one of them. Always Half Lit · Stimpunks

L★S The lit half was never in question. Only ever the angle, and who was standing at it. No. 17 The Nearest Body — nearness beats mass, and co-regulation is gravity No. 21 Not a Line — a spectrum is not a ranking No. 44 You Cannot Flatten a Sphere — what a summary must throw away No. 48 The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing — known only by its effect No. 51 Almost Shadow — the named zone in between No. 53 The Moon Is Always Half Lit — the phase is the angle ← you are here Reflection Which of your crescents has somebody written down as the whole of you? Where were you standing the last time you decided how much someone had in them? What have you called waning that was only ever the room, the hour, or the light? Whose far side have you called dark, when the truth was that nobody had gone round to look? If someone’s apparent phase is a reading of the room, what has your room been reading out lately? What would it take for the people describing you to be asked where they were standing? Sources The four principal phases are instants — quoted, not paraphrased. The US Naval Observatory's Astronomical Applications Department states that “the phases New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon, and Last Quarter are defined to occur when the excess of the apparent ecliptic (celestial) longitude of the Moon over that of the Sun is 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees, respectively,” and that the dates and times computed this way “are instantaneous and well defined.” The same source describes the crescent and gibbous phases as intermediate, “each of which lasts for about a week between the primary phases.” Spread four's whole argument is carried by that asymmetry, which is why it is quoted rather than characterised. The 50.2 percent figure is ours, computed, and shown so you can check it. No source is cited because we did the arithmetic rather than finding it. For a sphere of radius r lit by a larger sphere of radius R at distance d, the terminator falls beyond the great circle by an angle α with sin α = (R − r) / d, and the lit fraction is (1 + sin α) / 2. With R = 695,700 km, r = 1,737.4 km and d = 1.496 × 10⁸ km, that gives sin α ≈ 0.00464 and a lit fraction of ≈ 50.23 percent. Wikipedia's article on the solar terminator corroborates the principle for Earth — “a little over one half of Earth is illuminated at any point in time” — but not the lunar number, so we are not claiming it as sourced. It is a grace note; the load-bearing claim on spread two is that one hemisphere is always lit, which needs no decimal. Luna 3. Launched 4 October 1959; the first photograph of the lunar far side was taken at 03:30 UT on 7 October 1959, from roughly 63,500 km, after the spacecraft had passed the Moon and looked back at the sunlit far side. Twenty-nine photographs were returned, covering about seventy percent of the far side; the film was developed onboard and the negatives scanned and transmitted to Earth. Per NASA and the NSSDC, the most striking feature of the images was the near-absence of the large dark maria that dominate the near side. Figures are as reported and the resolution was low; nothing in this zine rests on the image quality. Libration. That roughly 59 percent of the lunar surface is visible from Earth over time, through libration in longitude (orbital eccentricity against uniform rotation) and libration in latitude (an axial tilt of about 6.7 degrees to the orbital plane), is standard positional astronomy. The 59 percent figure is the conventional one and is an accumulated total over time, not a fraction visible at any single moment — spread seven says “from Earth,” not “tonight,” deliberately. Sidereal and synodic months. Sidereal month 27.32 days, synodic month 29.53 days. The synodic month is the longer because Earth advances roughly 27 degrees along its own orbit during one sidereal month, so the Moon must travel about 29 degrees past a full circuit — about 2.2 days — to restore the same Sun–Earth–Moon alignment. Both figures are mean values; the true synodic month varies by several hours either side, and Figure 4 is schematic rather than to scale. Earthshine, and what we can and cannot claim about who explained it. That the ashen glow on the Moon's dark limb is sunlight reflected from Earth is settled. Leonardo da Vinci gave a correct explanation around 1506–09 in the Codex Leicester and never published it; he attributed the reflection to Earth's oceans, where most of it in fact comes from clouds, and spread nine says so rather than tidying it. That Michael Mästlin was the first to publish an explanation is stated by the history-of-science writer Thony Christie (The Renaissance Mathematicus), and we mark it plausible rather than verified: it is a single strong secondary source, Wikipedia's Mästlin article does not mention earthshine at all, and we did not confirm it against a primary text. What we cut during the check: a much better story, that Kepler credited Mästlin for earthshine in Astronomiae pars optica (1604) — the same book in which he coined penumbra for No. 51. It would have been a perfect joint between two zines, which is precisely why we distrusted it. What the sources actually support is that Mästlin's 1596 Disputatio de Eclipsibus is often referred to in Kepler's 1604 work — not that Kepler credited him for this. So the spread claims only what is documented: Mästlin taught Kepler at Tübingen (Kepler studied there 1589–1594, and learned Copernican astronomy from Mästlin's lectures), and the two men's work sits either side of the same problem. Also deliberately not claimed: a publication date for Paolo Sarpi, whose writings on earthshine are variously dated to c. 1578–83 and variously described as published or not; we could not settle it, so he is not on the page. The wet moon. The bowl-shaped crescent seen from low latitudes is a real observational fact following directly from the geometry, and wet moon is a genuine folk name for it. We give it as folk usage, not as a technical term, and attach no cultural claim to it. Spread 12 is Ryan Boren's own account, quoted verbatim from a published post. “R-word and Genius: Situationally Mute Hyperlexic Autistic,” stimpunks.org, 19 September 2022. Every quoted phrase on that spread — locked my lips, a semblance of psychological safety, Can I go now?, During my school career, I was both r-word and genius, the difference in impressions is due to psychological safety, it’s presence and absence, from being a full time r-word to a part time one, depending on who was in the room with me and if I felt safe enough speak, and Autistic people are psychological safety barometers — is his wording, not a paraphrase, and the post was read at the source rather than through a summary. The slur is written as “r-word” throughout because that is how the source writes it, and that convention is deliberate on stimpunks.org rather than our own softening. The barometer inference is ours, not his: he wrote the sentence; the observation that it inverts the direction of measurement — that a barometer reading is a fact about the surrounding air — is this zine's addition, and it is an interpretation of his line rather than a claim he made. The two terms that spread carries, credited to their originators. Exposure anxiety is Donna Williams's, from Exposure Anxiety — The Invisible Cage: An Exploration of Self-Protection Responses in the Autism Spectrum and Beyond (Jessica Kingsley, 2003); Williams was herself Autistic. Psychological safety as a research construct is Amy Edmondson's, from “Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams,” Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2):350–383 (1999) — a study of work teams, not of Autistic children; the application to classrooms and to Autistic people is Ryan's, not Edmondson's, and the distinction is kept here rather than allowed to blur. We write situational mutism rather than selective mutism, following the source and the Stimpunks glossary, because selective implies a choice that is not being made. What this zine deliberately does not do. It does not restate the tides, nearness or co-regulation argument of No. 17, which is the Moon's gravity and a different physical story from its light. It does not take up eclipses, which belong to No. 51 and No. 52. It does not make comparative claims about non-Western lunar phase systems, which we did not research and will not gesture at. And it does not follow the calendar problem — that 29.53 days will not divide 365.24 — which is a Burke chain rather than a zine, and is parked as a candidate rather than half-told here. No claim is made that the geometry proves anything about people: spread eleven is an analogy and spread thirteen says so on its face. Spread twelve is not offered as evidence for the optics either — it is a life that the optics happen to describe well, which is a different and smaller claim. A rhyme, not a proof. the same tug, at every scale 30 Migration Always Migrating migration, monotropism, and the galaxy you're already made of Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · never fixed, never finished L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·
Reading the world as felt knowledge

Inner compass Reading the world as felt knowledge Every migrating body is made of matter that has already migrated once — forged inside a star, scattered across unthinkable distance, and gathered again by gravity into a bird, a whale, a galaxy, you. Migration was never a metaphor borrowed from animals. It's the oldest fact about star stuff. Birds cross oceans using a compass sense we still don't fully understand — something in their eyes that responds to the Earth's magnetic field, tied to quantum effects still being worked out (Mouritsen, 2018). No map. Just the world, read directly, as something felt. Salmon return to their birth river through magnetic imprinting and the memory of water. Humpback whales cross hemispheres between calving and feeding grounds. Elephants walk the routes their grandparents walked. Even a seed migrates, carried on wind or fur, landing on new ground — every one of these bodies built, ultimately, from the same stellar matter, just arranged into a different way of moving through the world. It's easy to think of migration as a straight line — departure, journey, arrival. The workshop pushed against that. Migration is transformation across time as much as displacement across distance. Gilles Deleuze (1994) circled something close to this in his work on difference and repetition: no repeated pattern is ever a true copy — each turn carries its own small variation. Migration, read this way, is a spiral. With every movement, everything changes. the tug begins here not arrival — transformation a spiral, not a loop every turn carries its own variation Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

inside a bird's eye earth's faint field light cryptochrome two spins, still linked separated — not separate a compass made of relation warm, alive, and airborne A quantum compass Linked, even at a distance Here's the strange part of the bird's compass that's worth slowing down on. Inside a bird's eye, light striking a protein called cryptochrome creates a pair of electrons whose spins become linked in a way physicists call entanglement. Once two particles are entangled, what happens to one is tied to the other — even after they've separated. That linked pair turns out to be sensitive to the Earth's very faint magnetic field, and that sensitivity is thought to be part of how a bird reads direction (Hore & Mouritsen, 2016; Mouritsen, 2018). This is one of the only places we know of where this kind of quantum behaviour seems to do real, working, felt-in-the-body science — not sealed in a lab near absolute zero, but warm, alive, and airborne. A bird's felt sense of direction may be, quite literally, a small piece of quantum physics happening inside a living eye. Entanglement means: once two things have been in relation, they stay in relation. Distance doesn't undo it. Separateness was always the less accurate story. Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

Relationship first Not fixed-thing-first, relationship-second There's a related idea in physics called relational quantum mechanics (Rovelli, 1996). In this view, a tiny particle doesn't quietly hold fixed properties of its own, waiting to be measured. What it is only becomes definite in relation to whatever it's interacting with — another particle, an instrument, an observer. Writing on Rovelli's work, philosopher George Webster (2026) draws out the wider stakes: objects don't come first and then differ from each other — they emerge out of something more fundamental, a process of difference and relation that was already under way. Not fixed-thing-first, relationship-second. Relationship first, all the way down. I'm not a physicist, and this is one interpretation among several that physicists still argue about. But as a multiply neurodivergent person, it's closer to how I actually experience being myself — not a fixed, separate thing moving through the world on its own, but something that shows up through relationship and encounter (Edgar, 2026a). A bird doesn't carry its compass in isolation from the field around it. Maybe none of us carry ourselves in isolation from the fields around us either. the tidy story a thing, then its relations the closer story definite only in relation difference and relation come first; the standalone object is what got built relation, then thing one reading — physicists still argue Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

in motion · not yet decided Milky Way Andromeda ~50/50, not fated Sagittarius dwarf — still arriving trajectories, revised as the data arrives a tug, not a destination an itinerary that keeps being rewritten The same tug, at galactic scale Galaxies migrate too Zoom out far enough and the same pattern is still running. The stars in the Milky Way's halo aren't all original residents — many arrived. The Sagittarius dwarf galaxy has been streaming its stars into our halo for billions of years, a slow-motion migration first identified by Ibata, Gilmore, and Irwin (1994) that is, in a very real sense, still arriving. For decades it was treated as settled science that the Milky Way and Andromeda are on a fixed collision course, due to merge in roughly four to five billion years. The most recent modelling, using the latest Hubble and Gaia data, found something more honest: closer to a fifty-fifty chance of that merger happening at all within the next ten billion years, once the pull of smaller nearby galaxies is properly accounted for (Sawala et al., 2025). What looked like an inevitable itinerary turns out to be trajectories, still being revised as better data arrives. In the meantime, the Milky Way is far more likely to slowly absorb one of its own smaller satellites, the Large Magellanic Cloud, over roughly the next two billion years. Nothing here is a fixed itinerary. It's motion under gravity — a tug, not a destination — the same shape as a bird's restlessness before flight, revised at every scale as new pulls make themselves felt. Always Migrating · Helen Edgar
The restlessness that arrives before thought

The tug The restlessness that arrives before thought Brigit Anna McNeill writes of the tug of migration — a bodily restlessness that builds before anything is consciously decided. The pull comes from within, shaped by season and sea, and the sense of direction follows from inside it. I recognise that tug. Monotropism (Murray, Lesser, & Lawson, 2005) describes the way Autistic and ADHD attention gathers intensely around a small number of interests rather than spreading evenly across many. I've written elsewhere about picturing my own attention as a galaxy rather than a chart — energy gathered gravitationally into a few bright points, rather than spread out in an even, undifferentiated glow (Edgar, 2026b). The tug is that gravity. It pulls the same way a star's gravity gathers the matter that will become its next generation of planets: not evenly, not by choice exactly, but by an attraction real enough to bend everything nearby around it. Many of us are taught early to override this. Autistic masking research describes suppressing natural responses in favour of alternatives judged safer in non-Autistic spaces (Pearson & Rose, 2021). The tug gets read as too much, too narrow — and over the years we learn to quieten it, moving further from our own inner compass, until we may not recognise our true self at all. Csikszentmihalyi (1990) described flow as the state where attention and challenge align closely enough that the sense of separate effort disappears. Monotropic hyperfocus may be one of that state's clearest expressions — often carrying an undercurrent of wonder, where the world briefly widens around whatever has caught you, the way a night sky widens once your eyes adjust to it. the even glow spread evenly, nothing gathered the galaxy a few bright points, gathered by gravity the tug is that gravity attention as a galaxy not evenly — not by choice exactly Always Migrating · Helen Edgar
Learning to trust the pull again

the needle was never broken N your own north the "correct" default pulled off, not demagnetised trust returns unevenly deflection, not defect the pull was outside you Letting go of neuronormativity Learning to trust the pull again Trusting our inner compass again isn't easy, and there's real privilege in being able to unmask and be your Autistic self among others. Neuronormativity — the assumption that evenly distributed, easily legible attention is the "correct" default — doesn't just ask us to behave differently. It makes us distrust ourselves. Neuroqueering (Walker, 2021) is an ongoing practice of subverting and resisting that assumption. Not a destination to arrive at — no more than a galaxy's merger is a fixed destination — but an ongoing refusal to be ashamed of who you are. Pernille Fraser's poem "Can We Trust?" names this same rupture from the other direction — not what we lose faith in within ourselves, but what has to be earned from everyone around us before that trust can return. Shared through Stimpunks Foundation, it repeats its question across sensory load, pacing, correction, and whether we'll be believed: "Can we trust the space you offer?" (Fraser, 2019/2024). It never resolves into an answer. It stays in the asking — the way migration stays in the tug, before any destination has been decided. Nota flaw to be corrected, or a phase to be outgrown. Notsomething owed only once you've proven yourself safe to include. Nota straight line, or a fixed orbit — trust returns unevenly, and it can be withdrawn. Always Migrating · Helen Edgar
No single frame is the fixed one

Many ways of moving through No single frame is the fixed one Migration is only one expression of the many ways living things exist in and move through the world. Tarragnat (2025) names this range ethodiversity — the variability of behavioural and existential styles within and across species, opening neurodiversity out beyond a purely human-centred neurological framing. A bird's compass, a salmon's imprinting, a whale's crossing, a galaxy's slow absorption of its neighbour, a human's monotropic pull — not the same mechanism in different costumes. Genuinely different ways of being, each valid on its own terms rather than measured against one baseline. That sits alongside Milton's (2012) double empathy problem, which cautions against treating any one frame of reference as the fixed one against which others are read as deviant. Difference here is already a form of connection. A migrating salmon doesn't just pass through a river — its body becomes part of it. When Pacific salmon return to their home streams to spawn and die, they carry marine-derived nutrients into freshwater and the ecosystems around it: something taken from one world into another. Whales do something similar at ocean scale, helping move nutrients such as nitrogen and iron back into sunlit waters and redistributing them across great distances. Neither salmon nor whale sets out to feed a forest or an ocean. But each unique way of moving through the world is, at the same time, an act of shaping it — and of being reshaped by it in turn. Barad's (2007) intra-action: a self, a species, a migrating body, a galaxy doesn't exist as a separate thing that then relates to its surroundings — it comes into being through the relating itself. The liminal space a migrating creature passes through isn't empty transit between two solid states. It's where the shaping actually happens, at every scale there is. the crossing is not empty self field shaped in the relating not before it — intra-action no frame is the fixed one intra-action the self forms in relation, not before it Always Migrating · Helen Edgar

a profile still measures axes · edges · a baseline a constellation moves no baseline · no rank always connecting, always becoming from chart to constellation never fixed, never finished Nothing stands still A migrating galaxy of intensities The workshop's real gift was permission: to stop treating change as the exception that needs explaining, and start treating it as the base condition everything else moves through. I used to picture the shape of my own bodymind as a spiky profile — real peaks, real troughs, instead of one flat line of neuronormativity running across the whole of who I am. It's a truer picture than the flat line. But a profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all — it's a constellation of intensities, an ever-shifting arrangement of sensory, cognitive, and relational ways of being, always connecting, always becoming, never fixed, never finished (Edgar, 2026c). This zine is what happens when you let that constellation move. We are made of matter that has already migrated across unthinkable distances — forged in stars that lived and died before Earth existed, scattered by their deaths, gathered by gravity into a solar system, a planet, a body, an interest, a self. Not a chart with a fixed baseline, and not even a fixed arrangement of points — a galaxy, always in relationship with itself, always in motion. Migration isn't a metaphor borrowed from birds, whales, and galaxies. It's one of the oldest facts about life on Earth. Every one of us is a small, temporary constellation inside a much larger migration that hasn't finished, and is always moving. Life doesn't hold still and occasionally migrate. It migrates, and it moves, it transforms everything and everyone around it, living and non-living. We were never a line. We are not a chart. We are migrating stardust — never fixed, never finished. Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms Stimming and Belonging with AURORA Twenty-eight performances, weighted toward live — because the argument is the body — and the physics of the light she shares a name with. The companion rack to Warriors and Weirdos, Zine No. 13. Playlist & essay · Sound
She watched herself back, and did not change a thing

One She watched herself back, and did not change a thing Asked about the way she moves on stage, AURORA gave one of the more useful answers anybody has given about a body in public. The first time I saw myself playing live… on a video was kind of a terrifying. I didn't know that I looked like I was doing an exorcism or having a heart attack while performing live… but I can't really do anything about it. I'm a very emotional person, and I guess when you have songs with lots of emotions… I have to use everything I got to sing those songs, and I have lots of things to work with. AURORA, in the Red Bull session for “Conqueror.” Lightly condensed from her spoken answer; ellipses mark cuts. Read that again for the order of events. She saw it. She was shocked by it. She kept it. Not because she reframed it into something admirable, and not because someone reassured her — she says plainly that she can't do anything about it, and then, in the same breath, that she needs it. The movement is not decoration laid over the singing. It is part of how the singing happens. I have to use everything I got. Anyone who has been told to keep their hands still knows how rare that sentence is. The usual sequence runs the other way: you catch sight of yourself, you feel the shock, and you spend the next twenty years editing. Whose word is which She calls it emotion. We are the ones calling it stimming, and that distinction belongs on the page rather than buried in it. AURORA has spoken publicly about being neurodivergent, using that word; she has not, as far as we can find, described her stage movement as stimming, and we are not going to put the term in her mouth. What we are saying is narrower and, we think, still worth saying: a great many of us watch her move and recognise something — the whole body recruited, the motion arriving with the feeling rather than after it, the flat refusal to hold still for the comfort of onlookers. The recognition is ours. The title of this page describes what her work does for us, not a claim about what is happening inside her.
What the light she is named after is actually doing

Two What the light she is named after is actually doing The aurora takes its name from the Roman goddess of the dawn. So does she. That is a coincidence and we are going to make nothing of it — but the coincidence points at a piece of physics that turns out to be about exactly this. Here is the part everyone knows: charged particles from the Sun spiral down the magnetic field into the upper atmosphere and the sky lights up. Here is the part that matters. The colour is not the Sun's. The solar wind delivers energy and nothing else; what you actually see is an oxygen atom, having been knocked into an excited state, dropping back down and releasing a photon at the one wavelength its own structure permits. The famous green is 557.7 nm, and that number is not a property of the Sun or of the wind or of the weather. It is atomic oxygen's own line. Energy came from outside. The colour is the atom's. Now the part that stopped us. That green line is a forbidden transition. Atomic oxygen's auroral transitions, and the altitudes at which each is seen On the left, three energy levels of atomic oxygen: the 1S state at the top, the 1D state below it, and the 3P ground state at the bottom. A green arrow from 1S to 1D is labelled 557.7 nanometres with a lifetime of about 0.7 seconds; a red arrow from 1D to 3P is labelled 630.0 nanometres with a lifetime of about 110 seconds. Both are marked forbidden. On the right, an altitude scale showing red emission above roughly 150 kilometres, green emission between roughly 100 and 150 kilometres, and below that a crowded region labelled collisionally quenched where neither completes. Atomic oxygen ¹S ¹D ³P ground state 557.7 nm · green forbidden · waits ~0.7 s 630.0 nm · red forbidden · waits ~110 s Where it completes red above ~150 km — thin enough to wait out 110 seconds green ~100–150 km below that: nothing too crowded — a collision takes the energy before it can emit Altitudes approximate. “Forbidden” is a term of art. It does not mean impossible — it means the transition breaks the electric-dipole selection rules, so it happens slowly. An allowed transition is over in nanoseconds. The oxygen ¹S state sits for about 0.7 seconds before it releases the green photon, and the ¹D state waits about 110 seconds for the red. And that waiting is why altitude decides the colour. Low down, the air is crowded: long before the atom can complete its slow release, something collides with it and takes the energy away instead. Physicists call it collisional quenching, which is as bleak a phrase as it sounds. The green shows between roughly 100 and 150 km. The red needs to be higher still, because 110 seconds of undisturbed waiting is not available anywhere denser. The most famous light in the sky is a slow release that the rules call forbidden, and it only completes where nothing crowds it. Both halves matter. The label was never a verdict on whether it could happen. And the room is what decides whether it does. We are not going to spell out the analogy. You can see it. What we will say is what the physics licenses and what it doesn't: “forbidden” is a description of a ruleset, not of a possibility — the sky does it constantly — and whether a slow thing gets to finish depends on the density of what surrounds it, which is an argument about rooms rather than about atoms. A rhyme, not a proof Oxygen has no stake in any of this. Selection rules are not social rules, and quenching is not a metaphor for a classroom — the word is doing a specific job about collision cross-sections and it does not transfer. Nothing about the 557.7 nm line obliges anyone to make room for anyone. We are noticing that the sky's best-known trick has the same shape as the thing we keep asking for, and noticing is the whole of the claim.
The same song, again, and again

Three The same song, again, and again There is a word for the other half of this, and it is ours rather than the industry's. Stim listening — listening repetitively to a single song, album or playlist — was coined by Jim Irion, who describes using it to start work and to hold focus. It is the listening practice almost nobody designs for. Streaming services are built to move you along: the next track, the fresh recommendation, the endless lateral drift. Plenty of us want the opposite, and want it for good reasons — the same song forty times because the fortieth is doing something the first could not, because repetition is regulation, because you have found an auditory samefood and samefoods are not a phase. AURORA's catalogue takes this unusually well, and the rack below is arranged for it rather than against it: the same song appears more than once in different rooms, because Conqueror at a Red Bull session and Conqueror on late-night American television are not the same event, and running them back to back is a legitimate way to listen. Ryan keeps a YouTube playlist called Stimming with Aurora, and it is worth noticing what is in it: almost nothing but live performances. Not the studio versions, not the official videos — the sessions, the radio spots, the concerts. That is not an accident of collecting. When the body is the argument, you need the footage where the body is.
Queendom, and a people that names itself

Four Queendom, and a people that names itself The belonging half of this page is argued at length in Warriors and Weirdos, so we will not repeat it here. One thing is worth restating, because it is the mechanism. Queendom (2018) does not describe a place that exists. It describes one being declared — a country announced for everybody the existing countries had no room for, which is a different act from asking to be let into somewhere already standing. And her audience did the corresponding thing from the other direction: they took a name. Weird stops working as an insult at the exact moment a people picks it up and uses it as an address. That is the same move the word stimpunk makes, and crip, and mad, and neuroqueer. It is also why the reclamation is never available to bystanders: the word only turns when the people it was used against are the ones turning it.
No cure, and the wounds nobody can see

Five No cure, and the wounds nobody can see Two of her songs do work this collection keeps needing, and they do it from opposite ends. Cure for Me (2021) takes the brightest, most danceable arrangement on the record and puts it underneath a refusal — which is the correct setting for that refusal, because the demand for a cure is usually delivered warmly, by people who are sure they are helping. Invisible Wounds (2024) goes the other way and stays with the part that does not photograph: the injury nobody can see is still an injury, and the absence of a visible mark has never been evidence of anything except the limits of looking. Between them sits the practical fact that every access conversation eventually runs into. What can't be seen still has to be believed.

Six What this page refuses A page about a beloved performer's body carries specific risks, and it is better to name them than to hope nobody notices. Not a diagnosis. AURORA has said she is neurodivergent and we use her word, exactly as Zine No. 13 does. Aggregator and SEO pages have begun attaching specific conditions to her name; we are not repeating them, and neither should anyone citing this page. Not her art explained by her brain. “She makes music like that because she is neurodivergent” sounds like appreciation and works like a reduction — it turns a body of deliberate craft into a symptom with a soundtrack. Not stimming attributed to her. She describes emotion. We describe recognition. Those are different sentences and this page keeps them apart. Not inspiration. She is not evidence that being different works out fine if you have enough talent. Most of us are not going to be given a stage, and the argument for making room cannot depend on the person in the room turning out to be extraordinary. Not stimming as acceptable only when it is beautiful. This is the one that matters most here. Her movement is celebrated because it is on a stage, set to music, and lovely to watch. The same body doing the same thing in a classroom gets a behaviour plan, and a child who flaps in a supermarket gets stared at by people who would applaud this. If the movement is only permitted once it has been made into art, nothing has actually been conceded. Not physics as permission. The aurora does not authorise anything. It is a rhyme, and it is fenced as one above.

Warriors and Weirdos is the thirteenth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the one about AURORA (Aurora Aksnes) — read as a way of being star stuff: the alien who came home. We feature, quote, and embed her work across our site, on our pages for alien, keep on livin', stim-listening, happy-flappy, find your people, reframe, weird, different, wild, gender, and normal. born herefounds onenot cast out — in transit L★S · 001 The Wolf Between Packs Grey wolf · Canis lupus aged 1–3 · roughly 15–20% of a population A lone wolf is almost never a wolf that was cast out. It is a disperser — young, in transit, crossing the neutral ground between territories to find a mate and found a pack of its own. a life stagecalled a floatercrosses buffer zonesmay join another pack ▸ Field notes Field notes · Grey wolf · Canis lupus The phrase has been borrowed so thoroughly that it now means a dangerous man acting without a group. In wolves it means something close to the opposite. Wolves disperse from their natal pack between roughly nine and thirty-six months of age. A dispersing wolf — biologists often call it a floater — moves through the buffer zones between established territories, the neutral strips no pack claims. It is looking for unoccupied ground, or a mate, or an existing pack with room in it. Some disperse a second time, having not found a breeding opportunity the first time. Wolves can move between resident and dispersing states across a life. At any moment, something on the order of 15 to 20 per cent of a wolf population is doing this. It is not the exception. It is how the population reaches new ground at all. So the lone wolf is not the one the story failed. It is the one carrying the next pack in it, walking through empty country to get somewhere the species has not been. Every pack was founded by two animals who were, for a while, alone. We keep the borrowed phrase in the community — lone wolfing, as Betsy Selvam uses it in the essay this guide grew from — and it is worth knowing that the animal it came from was never the loner we meant. She was already right about the practice. The wolf just turns out to agree. under 1 in 10all of these L★S · 002 Nine in Ten Bees Solitary bees · most of Anthophila social species: under 10% of all bees Honey bees and bumble bees are fewer than one bee species in ten. The overwhelming majority of bees build alone, provision alone, and never meet their own offspring. the hive is the exceptionmason and leafcutterno colony, no queenmost nest in the ground ▸ Field notes Field notes · Solitary bees · most of Anthophila Of roughly twenty thousand described bee species, the social ones — honey bees, bumble bees, stingless bees — are fewer than ten per cent. Everything else is solitary: mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, carpenter bees. A female builds a nest, stocks each cell with pollen and nectar, lays an egg on it, seals it, and moves on. She will not be alive to meet the adult that comes out. This matters because of what we did with the other ten per cent. The hive is one of the most heavily worked metaphors in the language — busy as a bee, worker bees, the hive mind, the queen. An entire vocabulary of virtuous collective industry, built on the rare case. The typical bee works alone and the whole world eats because of it. Solitary bees are, per individual, often far better pollinators than honey bees; they carry pollen loosely, visit more flowers, and fly in colder weather. Nobody has ever suggested that a mason bee is under-socialised. It simply has a different way of being a bee — and there are eighteen thousand more like her, which is what a norm actually looks like. solitaryeusocialsame species L★S · 003 One Species, Two Answers Sweat bee · Lasioglossum albipes solitary or eusocial · and it is heritable The same species nests alone in some populations and in cooperative colonies in others — and reared side by side in a lab, each population keeps doing what it did at home. social polymorphismboth forms are typicalcommon-garden testedno correct version ▸ Field notes Field notes · Sweat bee · Lasioglossum albipes Lasioglossum albipes is a halictid — a sweat bee — and it does something that should be more famous than it is. In some populations, females nest solitarily: one bee, one nest, no helpers. In others, they nest eusocially, with a foundress and a worker brood. Same species. Reared in a common garden — both forms in the laboratory under identical conditions, and again under swapped photoperiods — each population kept the behaviour it had in the field. That points at a genetic component rather than a purely environmental switch, and resequencing has since identified variants that differ between the social forms. What we want from this entry is only the shape of it: a single species in which "how much do you nest with others" has two answers, both normal, both heritable, neither pathological. Nobody has proposed a treatment for the solitary populations. There is a further finding here that we are deliberately not building on. It is named in the refusals below, and the reason it is refused is the more useful lesson. left to be foundthe trail others walk L★S · 004 The One Who Writes Ahead Giant panda · Ailuropoda melanoleuca over 80% of marks aimed at the trail A solitary animal that maintains a whole community by chemistry — leaving scent messages on trees, deliberately positioned where others will pass, for animals it may never meet face to face. asynchronous contactaimed to be foundidentity, age, statusa network without meetings ▸ Field notes Field notes · Giant panda · Ailuropoda melanoleuca Giant pandas are solitary, and they are not out of touch. They deposit urine and anogenital gland secretions on trees, and those marks carry individual identity, sex, age, reproductive status and social standing. Other pandas read them. The result is a maintained community structure among animals who have very little direct contact. Two details lift this out of the ordinary. Over ninety per cent of the marks used are the longest-surviving kind — the message is matched to how long it needs to last. And over eighty per cent of marks are oriented toward animal trails, on ridges, on locally dominant trees. Pandas go out of their way to put their marks where someone will come past. That is not withdrawal. That is effortful, deliberate, asynchronous outreach — composing something, placing it carefully where it will be found, and walking away before anyone reads it. We have a whole argument about this already, in Shared Signal (No. 21): a message that arrives later is not a downgraded version of a conversation. Most of the animal kingdom is doing it this way. Asynchronous is not the fallback channel. It is the majority channel. known · calmstranger L★S · 005 Dear Enemies Territorial neighbours · across many taxa Fisher, 1954 · and the inverse, 1994 Once two territorial animals have settled a border, they stop fighting over it — and respond far more strongly to a stranger than to the neighbour they have known for years. familiarity lowers aggressionbirds to crustaceansthe nasty neighbour inversea relationship at distance ▸ Field notes Field notes · Territorial neighbours · across many taxa Fisher named it in 1954, watching territorial birds: two neighbours, once their boundary is established, become dear enemies. They stop spending energy on each other. Present the same animal with a stranger and the response is immediate and much stronger. It has since been documented across birds, mammals, amphibians, reptiles, fish, insects and crustaceans. The logic is plain enough — a neighbour who already holds ground is not trying to take yours, and repeated non-aggressive encounters make them cheap to predict. The energy saved goes into foraging and breeding. Then the honest part. It does not always run that way. Temeles reviewed the cases in 1994 and named the inverse: nasty neighbours, where residents respond more strongly to the animals next door than to strangers — typically where the neighbour is the one actually competing for what matters. Both patterns are real and which one appears depends on where the threat is. We are keeping both, because the interesting claim survives either way: a solitary animal is not an unattached one. It holds specific, individually recognised, long-running relationships with animals it hardly ever meets. Some of them are peace treaties. Some of them are feuds. All of them are relationships. The territorial geometry is genuinely strange. Male coalitions hold small territories covering less than ten per cent of a solitary female's home range, an arrangement described as unique among mammals. The female moves through many male territories; the males hold ground and wait. Two details are worth keeping. A single male, without a coalition, is usually a non-territorial floater — the same word the wolf entry needed, and the same disadvantage. And while coalitions are typically brothers who never separated, in the Serengeti roughly thirty per cent of coalition members are unrelated males who joined. So: within one species, at the same time, in the same grass — an animal who lives alone by default, an animal who lives in a permanent small group, and an animal who joined a group of people it was not born to. Nobody is doing cheetah wrong. same group, all dayhour by hour L★S · 007 The Party That Changes Hourly Fission-fusion species · Kummer 1971 chimpanzees · spider monkeys · elephants · dolphins Some of the most social animals alive do not stay in one group. Their parties split and re-form through the day, changing size and membership hour by hour — and nobody calls it instability. leave and rejoin freelysize and composition varynamed 1971, framed 2008a whole social system ▸ Field notes Field notes · Fission-fusion species · Kummer 1971 Hans Kummer used the term in 1971 for primates whose groups change size by splitting and merging according to what they are doing and what food is available. Aureli and colleagues formalised the framework in Current Anthropology in 2008, defining it along three axes that vary independently: spatial cohesion, subgroup size, and subgroup composition. Species are not in or out of this category — they are described by their degree of fission-fusion dynamics. Chimpanzees and spider monkeys are the classic cases. Elephants, hyenas and dolphins are in it too. Here is the part worth sitting with. These are not marginal or antisocial animals. Chimpanzees and elephants are among the most socially sophisticated species on the planet, and the way they do sociality is by constantly leaving and coming back. An individual peeling off to forage alone for six hours is not a warning sign. It is the mechanism. What makes it work is that the bond survives the absence, and the return is unremarkable. Which is precisely what a fission-fusion social life asks of a group: that leaving costs nothing, so that coming back costs nothing either. one fortnightseventeen years under L★S · 008 Seventeen Years, One Fortnight Periodical cicadas · Magicicada 13 or 17 years under · then all at once Nearly the entire life is spent alone underground drinking from a root. Then, on a schedule kept to the year, millions surface at once and the whole thing is loud, brief, and over. five instars undergroundsynchronised to the yearpredator satiationlongest-lived insects ▸ Field notes Field notes · Periodical cicadas · Magicicada Seven species of Magicicada live in eastern North America — twelve broods on a seventeen-year cycle, three on a thirteen-year cycle. A nymph spends those years underground through five instars, feeding on xylem from tree roots. Alone, in the dark, for longer than most vertebrates live. Then the brood comes up together, all of it, within days. They are among the longest-lived insects on Earth and they spend the visible part of it in a matter of weeks: moult, sing, mate, lay, die. The synchrony is doing real work. It is understood as predator satiation — arrive in numbers so overwhelming that predators are simply full, and enough survive to lay. Any cicada that emerged early, on its own initiative, would be eaten. Nobody can do this alone, and the only way to do it together is to spend seventeen years apart, counting. What we want from it is the shape: a life that is almost entirely solitary, punctuated by one enormous, non-negotiable, gloriously loud social event — and the long quiet is not a failure to socialise. It is the preparation. the runsame spots, each year L★S · 009 The Same Stretch of River Brown bear · Ursus arctos solitary all year · then the salmon run Solitary animals that gather in numbers when the salmon arrive, sort themselves out without much fighting, and return to the same fishing neighbourhood year after year. temporary aggregationa dominance hierarchyneighbourhood fidelitythen apart again ▸ Field notes Field notes · Brown bear · Ursus arctos Brown bears are solitary. Then, for a few weeks, they are not. Where salmon are forced to concentrate — a waterfall, a shallow stretch — bears assemble. At Brooks Falls in Katmai, as many as fifteen at once. What makes it possible is that the food is abundant enough that tolerating each other is cheaper than fighting. What makes it orderly is a dominance hierarchy: a dominant bear arrives, subordinates step aside, and often there is no growl exchanged at all. Work on Alaskan brown bears at small salmon streams has found something further — fidelity to particular foraging neighbourhoods. Bears return not just to the river but to their stretch of it, alongside a recurring cast. So it is not a random pile-up. It is closer to an annual gathering: same place, roughly the same people, understood rules, and everyone goes home afterwards. Set this beside the octopus entry at the bottom of the page, which is the same situation with one variable changed. Here, the resource is abundant and the gathering works. There, the resource is scarce, and it does not. Whether proximity becomes company depends almost entirely on whether there is enough to go around. 7.7× backnot kin L★S · 010 The Ledger of Who Shared Puma · Puma concolor 7.7× more likely to share back The textbook solitary carnivore turns out to share kills with animals it is not related to — and to be markedly more generous toward the individuals who once shared with it. reciprocity, on a slow clocknot predicted by kinship1,000+ carcassesa social network after all ▸ Field notes Field notes · Puma · Puma concolor Elbroch and colleagues put GPS collars and motion-triggered cameras on pumas in northwest Wyoming and watched what happened at more than a thousand prey carcasses. Pumas are the standard example of a solitary carnivore. The results, published in Science Advances in 2017, did not behave like it. Every puma in the study shared food with another puma at least once. Many did it repeatedly. Crucially, who they shared with was not predicted by kinship and was not random. Individuals were 7.7 times more likely to share with a puma that had previously shared with them — direct reciprocity, of a kind usually documented only in animals we already call social. The authors' framing is the useful one: the same social strategies as group-living species, over longer time scales. A puma's social life is not absent. It is slow. Encounters are rare, so each one carries more, and the accounting runs across months. This is the entry that keeps the guide honest about Symbioses. Mutual aid is not confined to animals who live in groups. It is here too, in the most solitary carnivore we could name, kept as a running tab between animals who mostly avoid each other. party sizemore fruit → L★S · 011 A Function of Fruit Orangutans · Pongo party size 1.05 → 1.9, by forest How sociable an orangutan is turns out to depend less on which species it is than on how much fruit the forest is producing. Change the food supply and the sociability changes with it. semi-solitaryparties above chancesociality tracks fruitthe old contrast revised ▸ Field notes Field notes · Orangutans · Pongo Orangutans are described as semi-solitary: usually alone, but forming temporary parties more often than chance would predict. Those parties appear to be for social reasons — mating, play, company, protection from harassment — rather than being accidents of two apes reaching the same tree. The textbook line used to be that Sumatran orangutans are the gregarious ones and Bornean orangutans the solitary ones, and that this was a species difference. Field data has been revising it. Average daily party size runs about 1.6 to 1.9 in West Sumatra against about 1.05 to 1.3 in East Sumatra and Borneo — but the between-site differences track fruit availability, not taxonomy. A forest with more fruit produces more sociable orangutans, whichever species is in it. Read that again slowly, because it is the whole collection's argument arriving through an ape. Sociability here is not a fixed trait of the animal. It is a property of the animal and its forest together. An orangutan in a poor-fruit forest is not a less social orangutan. It is an orangutan in a forest that cannot currently afford company. We say this constantly about ourselves and it is usually taken as special pleading: that whether we can manage company depends on the sensory and social conditions we are asked to manage it in. Here it is in a great ape, measured, in party sizes to two decimal places. You change the field, not the animal. one nest, one birda year out L★S · 012 A Sabbatical Year at Sea Wandering albatross · Diomedea exulans divorce rate ~0.3% Months alone over open ocean, a year off between breeding attempts, and one partner for life — a bond that survives more absence than almost any other on Earth. biennial breederchick-rearing to ~280 daysbonds take years to formuntil one of them dies ▸ Field notes Field notes · Wandering albatross · Diomedea exulans A wandering albatross rears a chick for up to about 280 days. Because that consumes most of a year, they are generally biennial breeders, and most individuals take what the literature cheerfully calls a sabbatical year at sea after each attempt — alone, over open ocean, for months at a stretch. And the pair bond holds. Divorce runs at about 0.3 per cent; pairs usually stay together until one of them dies, which for a bird that can live forty years and possibly longer means decades. Forming the bond in the first place is slow — an average of 3.2 years for males and 2.3 for females. Put those two facts against each other. This animal spends the overwhelming majority of its life physically alone, further from another member of its species than almost anything else alive. It is also about as pair-bonded as vertebrates get. Proximity and attachment are not the same measurement. We treat them as one all the time — assuming the person who is often alone must be less attached, and the person constantly surrounded must be well connected. The albatross takes a year off and comes back to the same bird. Slow to bond, then bonded for life, with long stretches of necessary solitude in between and no damage done. Many of us would recognise the pattern. the only hard groundevictions at the edge L★S · 013 Octopolis and Octlantis Gloomy octopus · Octopus tetricus Jervis Bay · ~23 dens · 10–15 animals Two dense octopus settlements on the sea floor off New South Wales, widely reported as proof that octopuses are secretly social. What the surveys describe is closer to a housing shortage. scarce hard substratedens on shell middenevictions and chasingno reframe table ▸ Field notes Field notes · Gloomy octopus · Octopus tetricus Octopolis was found in 2009: a bed of scallop shells two to three metres across, with a piece of scrap metal at the centre, and up to fourteen Octopus tetricus seen there at once. Octlantis, surveyed from December 2016, has no human debris at all — about eighteen metres by four, roughly twenty-three dens in three clusters built on rock outcrop and shell midden, with ten to fifteen animals present. The reporting was jubilant. Octopuses are the standard-issue solitary invertebrate, and here were octopus cities. Read the surveys and a plainer account appears. Both sites sit in soft sediment, where hard substrate to den in is scarce. Where a rock outcrop exists, octopuses accumulate on it, and the shell middens they generate by eating create more denning surface, which draws more octopuses. The interactions observed at these densities are largely den evictions, chasing, posturing and colour change — animals in each other's way. That is not a society. It is what happens when the only affordable housing is one small patch, and it produces exactly what forced proximity produces. We have not given this entry a reframe table because there is no misreading here to correct. The popular verdict is not wrong about the octopuses; it is a wish about us — that closeness follows from being put close together. Compare the brown bear nine entries up: same crowding, abundant food, and it works. Proximity is not company. Proximity plus scarcity is a fight. Anyone who has been put in an open-plan office, or mainstreamed into a classroom with no accommodations and told that the proximity itself would socialise them, already knows the finding. No reframe offered not every crowd is a community · L★S 013

fed you, and you fed methe record, not the pedigree L★S · 001 The Ledger (see No. 64) Common vampire bat · Desmodus rotundus handed off — full argument in Zine No. 64 The best-measured case of care that keeps accounts. Stated here in one entry and argued in full next door, because telling it twice would be telling it worse. 8.5× relatedness64% unrelateddies at 70 hourshanded off to No. 64 ▸ Field notes Field notes · Common vampire bat · Desmodus rotundus A common vampire bat dies after roughly seventy hours without blood. A bat that fails to feed can be fed by a roost-mate, who brings up part of her own meal to do it — a costly act, and exactly the kind kin selection was built to explain. Carter and Wilkinson (2013) tested it under conditions that strip the usual confound out: over two years they individually fasted twenty bats and induced sharing on forty-eight days, with relatedness mixed and familiarity held equal, so nobody could be helped merely for being nearby. Food previously received was the best predictor of food given, and 8.5 times more important than relatedness. Sixty-four per cent of sharing pairs were unrelated — against the sixty-seven per cent you would expect if nepotism were absent altogether. Two details close off the cynical readings. Donors initiated more often than recipients, so this is not harassment. And the sharing network tracked mutual grooming, which means the bond is maintained rather than inherited. The full argument is next door. No. 64 spends a spread on it, and this guide would rather point than repeat. What the bats contribute to the catalogue is the mechanism: a record of who has fed you, kept well enough to act on. two sons+ one stranger, later L★S · 002 The Stranger Let In Pied kingfisher · Ceryle rudis two kinds of helper · one of them unrelated A breeding pair may be helped by two quite different sorts of male: sons, and strangers. The strangers are driven off at first, tolerated later, and accepted only when the pair cannot feed the brood without them. primary helpers: sonssecondary helpers: unrelatedadmitted under hardshipReyer, 1980s ▸ Field notes Field notes · Pied kingfisher · Ceryle rudis Pied kingfishers breed with helpers, and Heinz-Ulrich Reyer's work in the 1980s separated them into two kinds that behave nothing alike. Primary helpers are usually sons of the breeding male. They feed the nestlings and guard the nest, investing at close to a breeder's rate. Secondary helpers are unrelated males. They turn up a few days after the nestlings hatch, are warded away at first, and are eventually tolerated — at which point they feed the female rather than the chicks, and contribute less than the primary helpers do on both feeding and defence. The honest part is the condition of entry. Secondary helpers are accepted when environmental conditions are poor enough that the parents' own time and energy will not raise the brood alone. The stranger is not admitted because the family became generous. He is admitted because the family ran short. We are keeping that, rather than trimming it. A catalogue of non-kin care that only printed the warm cases would be selecting its evidence. And the fact cuts both ways: the door opened under pressure — and then it opened. Hospitality that begins in need is still hospitality, and a great deal of human kinship has started exactly there. No. 64 makes the same move with the helpers who stay because the habitat is full.
