It builds a nest — and then shares it. Several unrelated pairs lay into one clutch, and all the adults incubate, brood and feed. This is Christina Riehl's study system, worked at Gatún Lake in Panama under the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute since 2006, across as many as forty-five nests in a season. It is also the reason her review matters to No. 64: she came to the question of non-kin cooperation from an animal that could not be explained with kin selection, and then went and counted how common that was across the birds. Two findings are worth keeping separate. The first is simply that the arrangement exists and is stable: unrelated adults, no helper caste, no dominant breeder, sharing the work of a single nest. The second is experimental — anis tested for kin discrimination do not appear to discriminate. It is not that they weigh kin slightly less heavily. The mechanism looks absent. What holds it together instead is the relationship. Riehl's later work reports that stable social bonds between unrelated females raise individual fitness — meaning the thing being rewarded is not who you are related to but who you have kept turning up with. Which is the bats' ledger again, at the scale of a household. Superb fairy-wrens breed cooperatively: a group holds a territory, and all the males contribute to feeding and defending the young. The expectation is obvious — paternal care ought to be going to relatives, so the helpers should be fathers, sons and brothers. DNA fingerprinting found that 76% of offspring — 138 of 181 — were sired by extra-group males who contributed no care whatsoever, and that 95% of broods, 38 of 40, contained young fathered from outside the group. At the time it was the highest recorded rate of cuckoldry in any bird. Sit with the shape of that. In the nest there is a brood. Around it there is a group of males feeding it. And the genetic fathers of most of those chicks are elsewhere, doing nothing. The family that is present is not the family that is related, and it is the present one that does the raising. Two cautions, because this is the entry most likely to be over-read. First, this is a fact about paternity and provisioning, not about intention — we are not claiming the wrens have made a decision about kinship. Second, it is not a moral: nothing a fairy-wren does licenses anything about a human household. What it does is dismantle a claim, which is the only work No. 64 asks the animals to do. The nest that gets fed is the nest somebody is standing next to. no line abovefounded together L★S · 005 Founding a Territory Together Brown skua, Galápagos hawk, green wood-hoopoe three lineages · one route A third way to end up with a group of unrelated adults raising young: skip the family entirely and establish a territory jointly, from scratch, with somebody you are not related to. coalition formationunrelated foundersthree separate lineagesfrom Riehl 2013 ▸ Field notes Field notes · Brown skua, Galápagos hawk, green wood-hoopoe This entry is a route rather than an animal, and it is taken directly from the review that No. 64 is built on. Riehl (2013) sorts the ways a cooperatively breeding group can end up containing non-kin into three. Delayed dispersal where high adult mortality or extra-pair paternity erodes the relatedness of a group that started as a family — the fairy-wren case above. Immigration, where an outsider joins an established pair — the kingfisher case. And coalition formation, where unrelated individuals establish a breeding territory together from the beginning. The examples she names for that third route are brown skuas, Galápagos hawks and green wood-hoopoes — a seabird, a raptor and a passerine, in three unrelated lineages. The reason it earns a card: the other two routes can be told as stories about a family that changed. Something diluted it, or something joined it. Coalition formation has no family in it at any point. The group is a partnership that was founded, and the young are raised by the founders. Held honestly: this card is the thinnest in the guide on purpose. We read Riehl's review, not the primary literature on each of these three species, and we are not printing figures we have not checked. It is here because the category matters to the catalogue — care can begin with an agreement rather than a lineage — and leaving it out to keep every card equally heavy would have made the sort dishonest. ?born the same nightno pup is claimed L★S · 009 A Veil of Ignorance Banded mongoose · Mungos mungo 64% give birth on the same night Mongoose females give birth synchronously into a single communal litter, which makes it effectively impossible to know which pup is whose. The care that follows does not sort by relatedness — and the literature argues the not-knowing is why. 64% same nightcommunal litterescorts don’t sort by kinup to 30 pups ▸ Field notes Field notes · Banded mongoose · Mungos mungo Banded mongooses live in groups where several females breed at once — and they give birth on the same night. Reported synchrony runs to 64% of females delivering on exactly the same night, producing one communal litter that can run to around thirty pups. The pups are then reared communally. Adults called escorts feed, carry and guard individual pups through the vulnerable period, and escorted pups survive better than unescorted ones. And the finding that matters here: there is no evidence that escorts and pups assort by parentage or relatedness. Where escorts do show a bias, the work points at the pup's sex, not its relatedness. Why the synchrony is not incidental. Birth synchrony of this kind is understood as a product of reproductive competition — it limits the opportunity for infanticide and reduces the competitive asymmetry between pups born to different mothers. And because everything arrives in one pile on one night, the information required to favour your own is simply not available. The Nature Communications paper on this titles the effect exactly as we would want to: a veil of ignorance promoting fairness in a mammal society. This is the strangest card in the guide and the one we are most careful with. It is not that mongooses have chosen equality. It is that a competitive arms race between breeding females produced an architecture in which nobody can practise nepotism, and equal treatment is what falls out. The result is fair. The reason is not kindness. Which is worth holding onto, because a great deal of human fairness works the same way — anonymised marking, blind auditions, need-blind admissions. We build veils on purpose because we do not trust ourselves to be fair with the information. The mongooses got one by accident. these two matchkin, heard not known L★S · 010 Kin, By Accent Long-tailed tit · Aegithalos caudatus helpers are failed breeders · sorted by call A genuine kin-directed helper system — and the recognition appears to run on how alike the birds sound. Failed breeders go and help relatives, choosing males whose calls resemble their own. redirected helpingcall similarity tracks kinshippeaks at mid predationHatchwell, long-term ▸ Field notes Field notes · Long-tailed tit · Aegithalos caudatus This card is here to keep the guide honest. No. 64's central figure is that 55% of cooperatively breeding bird species nest primarily with kin — family is the plurality, and a catalogue that printed only non-kin cases would be lying by selection. Long-tailed tits are a clear case of the majority. Ben Hatchwell's long-term study describes redirected helping: a bird whose own nest fails may become a helper, usually at a relative's nest. So helpers are not queuing juveniles; they are this season's failed breeders, spending the rest of the season on somebody else's brood. Which means the amount of helping depends on the supply of both failures and survivors — cooperative behaviour peaks at intermediate levels of nest predation, and there are more helpers in shorter seasons when there is less time to re-nest. The mechanism is the beautiful part. Call similarity correlates with kinship, and failed breeders choose to help males whose calls are more similar to their own. Breeders, for their part, react aggressively to the calls of non-kin near the nest. So the family is being identified by ear. And here is why a kin entry belongs in a guide about chosen family. Long-tailed tit calls are learned — birds acquire them in the natal group. So what the bird is matching is not a genome but who it grew up hearing. The cue is social, even though the correlation it tracks is genetic. Put a bird in a different nest and you would be changing what it recognises as kin. Held honestly: the vocal story is a plausible and evidenced mechanism, not a closed case. Helpers fine-tune how much they provision according to relatedness, but their effort was not correlated with vocal similarity itself — so calls look like they are doing the addressing rather than the dosing. The distinction is in the papers and we are not flattening it. still breedingstopped · gives more L★S · 011 The Grandmother Who Stopped Resident killer whale · Orcinus orca post-reproductive · and helping more for it Grandmothers improve their grandcalves’ survival — and the ones who have stopped breeding do it best, because a grandmother still raising her own calf has less to give. post-reproductive helpinggrandmothers matter mostcapacity has a ceilingNattrass et al., 2019 ▸ Field notes Field notes · Resident killer whale · Orcinus orca Nattrass and colleagues (2019) analysed decades of resident killer whale records and found that post-reproductive grandmothers improve the survival of their grandoffspring — and that they do so more than grandmothers who are still breeding. The proposed reason is not sentimental and is the whole reason this card is here. A grandmother with her own dependent calf is constrained: her movement and activity are organised around that calf, so she cannot provide the same support and leadership, and she has less to invest in her grandcalves. The grandmother who has stopped is the one with capacity. The authors connect this to killer whales having evolved one of the longest post-reproductive lifespans known outside our own species. This is a kin story throughout — grandmothers, grandoffspring, matrilines — and it is in the guide precisely for that reason. But notice what the finding is actually about. It is not about how related the whales are; relatedness is held constant across the comparison. It is about who has the room to give. Two grandmothers, identically related to the same calf, differ in how much they help according to what else they are carrying. Which is the least sentimental and most useful thing in this guide. Care is not a feeling that scales with relatedness. It is labour, and labour has a ceiling. A great deal of human family arrangement fails not because anybody stopped loving anyone but because the people who were nearest were already at capacity — which is the argument No. 64 makes about the private household, and No. 59 about what a nervous system is owed. That spread exists so the zine cannot be read as a warm story. This card is the experiment. Jan Komdeur (1992) translocated Seychelles warblers to Aride Island, previously unoccupied. With no competition for territories, young males bred, in high-quality territories, rather than helping. As the good habitat filled up, birds increasingly became helpers, territory-budders or floaters. Take away the shortage and the helping largely goes with it. But the fuller finding is more interesting than the shortage, and it is why the paper's title names two things. It is not only saturation; it is territory quality. Young birds hatched on high-quality territories stayed as helpers rather than take breeding vacancies on lower-quality ones. And the effect of a helper depends on where it is: one or two helpers on a good territory raise their parents' reproductive success, while helpers on a poor territory reduce it. So the honest reading of constraint is not "trapped." It is arithmetic: sometimes home, even in a subordinate position, pays better than the independence on offer. That is a harder thing to sit with than a wall, because it is recognisable. People stay in arrangements that are working out better than the alternative available to them, and calling that either devotion or captivity gets it wrong in both directions. Which is the point of putting it in this section. The card cuts against the guide's grain. If we only printed cases where care exceeded kinship, we would be doing to the evidence exactly what the textbook did when it printed only the family cases. not obligate after allmost disperse alone L★S · 013 The Eusocial Mammal That Wasn’t Damaraland mole-rat · Fukomys damarensis the obligate story, withdrawn For decades the textbook case of a eusocial mammal — a queen, non-breeding helpers, insect-like castes. Recent work finds pairs breed perfectly well without helpers, and most breeders got there by walking off alone. not obligate after allsolitary dispersal is the normno fixed casteswalked back 2016–2023 ▸ Field notes Field notes · Damaraland mole-rat · Fukomys damarensis This card is the guide checking itself, and it belongs here more than any of the others. The Damaraland mole-rat has been the standard mammalian answer to "does eusociality happen outside the insects?" — a single breeding pair, a burrow full of non-breeding adults doing the digging and the pup care, the whole arrangement read against ants and termites. A run of work since the mid-2010s has taken most of that back. They are not obligate cooperative breeders: pairs can and frequently do reproduce without any helpers, and breeders do not appear to rely on helpers for reproduction or survival. Solitary natal dispersal is the commonest route to breeding for both sexes — prospective female breeders typically disperse and settle alone in a new burrow system, surviving well and staying in good condition, sometimes for years, before a male arrives. Inheriting the dominant position is uncommon. And the helpers show no fixed divergent developmental pathways or task specialisation; the differences between them look like age-related polyethism. The verdict in the literature is that the similarities to obligately eusocial insects were over-emphasised. Now: why put this in a guide arguing that care exceeds kinship? Because the mole-rat was a case in our favour — a mammal supposedly so committed to cooperative rearing that it had gone functionally insectile — and it did not hold. If we are going to say the family-as-nature's-unit story got oversold, we have to say this got oversold too. The bias that inflates a cooperative story is the same bias that inflated the nuclear one: a satisfying picture travelling further than the evidence for it. It also carries a specific caution about this whole genre. A charismatic social arrangement gets described, becomes a textbook example, and is then cited for decades by people who are not tracking the primary literature. That is the mechanism Too Good to Check is about, and it does not spare findings we like. No. 31 and No. 36 are both about a reading that outlived its evidence. So is this — except this time the reading was ours. “Better Get Used To It” Ask for a slower pace and you will meet one answer so often that it has an acronym. Homework young because there's homework later. Grades young because there are grades eventually. No accommodation at school because the real world won't accommodate you. The logic never changes: life will be hard later, so hardship now is preparation. Hardship now is not preparation. BGUTI · named by Alfie Kohn, 2005 · early adversity is not a vaccine It has to ignore them The argument treats the timetable as the fixed thing and the child as the adjustable one. But children arrive at things at genuinely different rates — so “everyone gets this at this age” guarantees some are handed what they cannot yet use. BGUTI doesn't overlook developmental difference by accident. It cannot survive noticing it. And it isn't true Kohn again, and it is exact: people don't really get better at coping with unhappiness because they were deliberately made unhappy when they were young. Early adversity is not a vaccine. It mostly teaches you that adults will do this to you. Where it does its worst Behaviorism watches compliance and reaches for consequences, so it has no way to represent a child who needs longer. Needing longer shows up as refusing; refusing gets a consequence. The consequence never changes the pace. It only adds fear to it. “Almost by definition, the BGUTI defense ignores developmental differences.” Alfie Kohn · “Getting Hit on the Head Lessons” · Education Week · 7 September 2005 the full argument and every source: starstuff.earth/two-hundred-years-zine · Zine No. 34 print freely · share freely · CC BY-SA 4.0 See reverse Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms look at the water, not the creature Broadside · Open edition Side B of B The animal, and its bill 272 years, and 156 to grow up. The Greenland shark lives in water near freezing and grows less than a centimetre a year. Nielsen and colleagues dated 28 of them in Science in 2016: a life span of at least 272 years, the largest animal at 392 ± 120, and age at maturity of at least 156 ± 22 — inferred from body length, not observed. And that is not a superpower. A species that takes 156 years to reproduce even once has almost no capacity to replace losses. They were hunted in very large numbers and still turn up in trawls. The IUCN lists them as Vulnerable . Slowness is a strategy with a bill attached — superbly fitted to an ocean that held still, nearly defenceless against one that changes in decades. So look at the water. A ruined cornea is a disaster in bright water and nothing at 400 metres. A 156-year childhood works in an ocean that holds still and is fatal in one full of trawlers. None of those outcomes is a fact about the shark. You cannot tell whether a pace is a problem by looking at the creature — you have to look at the water. What to ask instead Not “how do we get this child up to speed?” But: what is this environment demanding, who chose that, and what would it cost to stop? Name the model. The social model of disability distinguishes a body's condition from the disabling produced by environments built as though that condition didn't exist. Stairs disable a wheelchair user. The pace of a school day disables a kid who needs longer. Ask for the design change, not the indulgence. Slow pedagogy — unhurried time, room to revisit, the present treated as though it counted. Not a kindness extended to slow children; a change that stops manufacturing failure. Change the water and hold the person. Naming the environment is not a reason to leave anyone without help while the world gets redesigned. Not: Not slow is better. See the bill, above. It's a set of trade-offs, and some are brutal. Not everyone just needs more time. Sometimes it's a different route, a support, a tool, or dropping the demand. “Go slower” is one accommodation, not the answer. Not “but the real world won't wait.” Sometimes true, and still no licence for BGUTI — and the real world is also built, also by someone, also changeable. Not a reason to skip support. Naming the environment must never leave anyone without help while we wait for it to change. Not biology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof — a person's pace would deserve respect in an ocean where everything moved at one speed. We don’t prepare students for a world of potential oppression by oppressing them. She named it first, and that order matters

Dark Matter Field She named it first, and that order matters In My Monotropic Galaxy (More Realms, June 2026), Helen Edgar maps twenty constellations of her own Autistic self. The first of the twenty is the Dark Matter Field. Much of the lived experience of being Autistic for many people is weighed down by what I have called the Dark Matter Field in my galaxy. This is the heavy darkness of neuronormativity, reflected in the accumulated weight we carry around of a world that does not meet our needs, and does not love us down to our star stuff. Helen Edgar · My Monotropic Galaxy · More Realms, 2026 She reached for the cosmic vocabulary on her own, for her own reasons, before anybody asked what the physics of it was. We have left this constellation alone twice — No. 45 and No. 46 both took other namings from her map and said in their colophons that Dark Matter Field was being deliberately kept back. This is the piece that spends it. The direction of travel is the whole discipline of the thing. Her naming came first; the astronomy is set beside it afterward, to see what the careful version of that inference actually looks like. The reverse move — physics first, then a claim about people because the physics said so — is the one this whole collection exists to refuse. It has a name, and it has a body count. So: nothing on the next eleven spreads is evidence about a nervous system. What follows is a method, worked all the way through by people who were very good at it, and then the same method held up against how the question got answered about us. Which way the borrowing runs An arrow from her naming to the physics is marked allowed. He counted the light and weighed the cluster

Coma, 1933 He counted the light and weighed the cluster Fritz Zwicky did something very simple, with seven galaxies. He measured how fast they were moving relative to each other, and asked how much mass it would take to keep them from flying apart. Then he counted the light and asked how much mass that implied, assuming the stars were like our Sun. The two numbers did not agree. They did not nearly agree. the average density in the Coma system would have to be at least 400 times greater than that derived on the basis of observations of luminous matter Zwicky 1933 · Helvetica Physica Acta 6 · English translation Four hundred times. Not a rounding error, not a calibration problem, not something you argue away over lunch. The discrepancy was the finding — a gap between what a model predicted and what the bodies were actually doing. And he did name it. The translation has him writing that this “would lead to the surprising result that dark matter exists in much greater density than luminous matter.” So the word was there from the start. What he did with it next is the part nobody quotes. The two masses of the Coma cluster A short bar for the mass implied by the cluster's light sits beside a bar roughly four hundred times taller for the mass implied by the galaxies' motions. The tall bar is drawn broken to indicate it is not to scale. from the light from the motions ≥ 400 × bar broken · not to scale Figure 2 · the gap that started it Beyond the Optical Image · Stimpunks
And then he called it an unsolved problem

What he declined to do And then he called it an unsolved problem Zwicky had a factor of four hundred and a name for it. He could have announced a discovery. Here is how the section actually ends: These considerations indicate that the large velocity dispersion in the Coma system (and other dense clusters of nebulae) holds an unsolved problem. Zwicky 1933 · closing the argument Read that again with the four hundred still in mind. He had the measurement. He had the word. He filed it as unsolved. That is not modesty and it is not hedging. It is a precise report of what he was entitled to say: a discrepancy of this size exists, and I do not know where it lives. He lists three candidate accounts in the paper and settles on none of them. The first thing a careful person does with a discrepancy is decline to place it. Hold onto that sentence. In ninety-three years it does not get improved on, and on spread ten we are going to want it badly. Zwicky's ledger Two columns. Under claimed: a discrepancy of at least four hundred, and the word dark matter as one possibility. Under not claimed: which account is correct, that the matter had been found, and that the problem was solved. The paper everyone cites never says dark

ApJ 238, 471 · 1980 The paper everyone cites never says dark Vera C. Rubin, W. Kent Ford, Jr. and Norbert Thonnard took spectra of twenty-one Sc galaxies out into their faint outer regions and published the rotation curves. It is the paper the whole story hangs on. Almost everything said about it is slightly wrong. the retelling · and the abstract You have heard The paper says flat rotation curves “Most rotation curves are rising slowly even at the farthest measured point” Rubin discovered dark matter “must have significant mass located beyond the optical image” a paper about dark matter subject heading: galaxies : internal motions The curves are not flat; they are still climbing where the light gives out. The negative claim in the abstract is narrower still and more careful than either version: “Neither high nor low luminosity Sc galaxies have falling rotation curves.” Not they are flat — they do not fall. That is what the data could carry. And then the conclusion, which is the sentence this zine is named after: Sc galaxies of all luminosities must have significant mass located beyond the optical image. Look at what that sentence does. It says where. It refuses to say what. The word “dark” does not appear in the abstract at all. Forty-seven years after Zwicky, with better instruments and twenty-one galaxies instead of seven, the claim is still only about the location of mass — and the paper is filed under internal motions, because that is what was measured. Twenty years on, she still would not place it

PASP 112, 747 · 2000 Twenty years on, she still would not place it In 2000, Rubin wrote a retrospective called One Hundred Years of Rotating Galaxies. By then she was the most cited person alive on this question. Here is what she was willing to say. Surprisingly, we cannot yet rule out a modified gravitational potential, rather than dark matter, as the explanation of our observations. Vera Rubin · PASP 112, 747 · 2000 Twenty years after the famous paper, the woman the discovery is named for is still holding two rival accounts open: maybe there is unseen mass, or maybe our law of gravity is wrong at these distances. She does not pick. She reports that the observations cannot yet decide. And then this, which is the reason this zine exists: It is folly to believe that we know what a galaxy is, while the extent, the density distribution, and the composition of ≥90% of its mass are still a dark mystery. Vera Rubin · the same essay Folly. Her word, about her own field, about the object she spent a career measuring. Not we are nearly there. Not the details remain. It is folly to believe that we know what a galaxy is. Then they placed it — and this is where we were wrong

ApJ 648, L109 · 2006 Then they placed it — and this is where we were wrong Two galaxy clusters collided. The hot gas — which is most of the ordinary matter — got slowed by the collision and left behind. The galaxies sailed on through. So for once, the ordinary matter and everything else were in different places. Clowe and colleagues mapped the gravity by how the cluster bent the light of things behind it, and found that the gravity was not where the gas was. It was out with the galaxies. Their title is not shy: “A direct empirical proof of the existence of dark matter.” An 8-sigma significance spatial offset of the center of the total mass from the center of the baryonic mass peaks cannot be explained with an alteration of the gravitational force law, and thus proves that the majority of the matter in the system is unseen. Clowe et al. · ApJ 648, L109 · 2006 This zine was proposed on a sentence that is wrong, and we are leaving the correction on the page. The pitch said the field is “never directly observed, only detected by its distorting effect” — and offered gravitational lensing as evidence of that. But lensing is the instrument that made the direct detection, and this paper explicitly rules out the modified-gravity account Rubin was still holding open six years earlier. The premise had to go. We publish our own errors; that is the house. Gravity where the gas is not Two lobes of hot gas sit near the centre of a collision. Unseen is not the same as unfindable

Two claims, held apart Unseen is not the same as unfindable Here is the thing the smoothed retelling flattens in both directions at once. The mass is established. The identity of that mass is not. Those are different claims and the field keeps them scrupulously apart. Deep underground, in tanks of liquid xenon, people have spent decades waiting for one of these particles to bump into something. LZ has now reported hundreds of live days of exposure and found nothing. XENONnT, tonne-years of exposure, nothing. The searches are widening to lighter and stranger candidates — axion-like particles, dark photons — because the obvious ones keep not being there. Ninety-three years after Zwicky, the ledger reads: we know it is there, we know roughly how much, we know where it sits, and we do not know what it is. Both halves of that get abused. Say only the first half and you have a settled science that brooks no questions. Say only the second and you have “scientists don't even know what dark matter is” deployed as if it discredited the measurement. The honest version is harder to shout and it is the only one that is true. Settled and open Two columns. Settled: a discrepancy exists, its size, where the mass sits, and that the force law cannot explain it away. Open: what the particle is, its mass, whether it interacts at all beyond gravity. Three places a discrepancy can live

The structural question Three places a discrepancy can live Strip away the galaxies and this is the shape of the whole thing. A model predicts what a body will do. The body does something else. The gap has to go somewhere. There are exactly three places to put it. In the mass: something is there that we are not seeing. In the law: our model of how things work is wrong at this scale. In the measurement: we are reading the instrument badly. Astronomy has spent ninety-three years arguing all three, out loud, in journals, with the rival accounts named and the failures published. Zwicky listed candidates and picked none. Rubin held mass and law open for twenty years past her own famous result. Clowe closed one of them and said precisely how — 8-sigma, and here is the configuration that made it possible. The null results from the xenon tanks are published, which is why anyone knows the particle is missing. None of that is a courtesy. It is the machinery that makes the eventual answer worth anything. A verdict is only as good as the alternatives that were allowed to compete with it. Three doors, all opened A measured gap leads to three labelled doors: the mass, the law, the measurement. This is not evidence about you

Where it breaks This is not evidence about you The proposal for this zine called the parallel “an exact structural match.” It is not, and here is the failure at full strength rather than tucked in a hedge. Dark matter is hidden by nature. Neuronormativity is hidden by convention. That is a different kind of hiding, and it changes everything about what follows. The field warping us is not undetected. It is written down. It is in the diagnostic criteria, the intervention targets, the compliance goal on an education plan, the phrase “culture fit” in a hiring rubric, the seating chart, the lighting spec. You do not need a tonne of liquid xenon a mile underground. You need to read the paperwork. The right word is not invisible — it is unmarked. It goes unnamed because it is the baseline, and the baseline is the one thing a measurement never lists among its objects. And that difference is good news. A particle that has evaded ninety-three years of the best instruments ever built may simply be beyond us for another century. A convention is a decision, written by people, and it can be read, quoted, contested and changed this year. Two kinds of hiding Hidden by nature requires new instruments and may take another century. Hidden by convention requires reading the existing paperwork and can be changed this year. The physics chooses neither, and that is the tell

One field, two readings The physics chooses neither, and that is the tell Helen's Dark Matter Field is the accumulated weight — the heavy darkness, the thing pressing down. That reading is hers and it is true to her life. Now take the identical fact. Unseen mass is most of what holds a galaxy together. Without it the thing flies apart. Read that way, the very same physics is the perfect emblem of something else entirely: the co-regulation nobody logs, the care work nobody bills, the friend who answers at 2am, the accommodations that never made it into a report. The unmeasured is not the unreal, and it is often the unmeasured that is holding everything in place. Same field. Same evidence. Same ninety-three years of measurement. Crushing weight and the only reason anything is still standing — and the physics does not adjudicate between them, because it was never asked about you. If one fact can carry two opposite morals, the moral was never in the fact. the whole reason we mark it This is the cleanest demonstration we have of why this collection keeps saying a rhyme, not a proof. Someone has to choose which reading to make, and then own the choosing rather than hiding behind the galaxy. Helen chose weight, in her own galaxy, about her own life, and said so in the first person. That is what an honest use of a metaphor looks like. Not:dark matter proving the field is real. Ninety-three years of rotation curves say nothing whatsoever about a nervous system. If you needed astrophysics to believe us, the problem was never the evidence. Not:an argument against evidence. The opposite. Careful public attribution is the thing we are asking for. Nulls published, rivals named, verdicts withheld — give us that and we will take our chances. Not:modified-gravity advocacy. Rubin's 2000 sentence was true in 2000. Clowe answered it in 2006 and we quote the answer, at 8-sigma, on spread seven. Not:“you are mysterious.” Rubin's folly line is about a galaxy. Turning it into mystique about Autistic people is the move we are refusing — being unexplained is not the same as being unknowable, and we are neither. Not:the inspiration story about Vera Rubin. She was shut out of observatories and she was scrupulously careful. Only the second one is our argument here, and borrowing the first would be doing to her what gets done to us. Not:a claim that bodies never contribute. A gap can have more than one source. The objection is to the question being closed, not to any particular answer. Not:Helen's reading corrected. Her galaxy is hers. Spread twelve adds a second reading to the same physics; it does not take hers away. The sentence this zine is named for is the one to keep. Rubin, Ford and Thonnard had twenty-one galaxies and every reason to reach, and they wrote: mass located beyond the optical image. Exactly what was measured. Nothing about what it was made of, or what it meant, or what anybody deserved. Ask for claims about us that narrow, and that honest. There is a great deal of you beyond the optical image — and the loving does not wait on the inventory. One fact, two morals A single central fact, unseen mass dominates a galaxy, branches to two readings: the weight that presses down, and the mass that holds it together. Neither branch is marked as the one the physics chooses. unseen mass dominates the galaxy the weight that presses down the mass that holds it together both true of the physics · neither from it somebody chooses · say who Figure 11 · the fork the fact will not take Beyond the Optical Image · Stimpunks

L★S · 001 Alex African grey parrot · Psittacus erithacus · one bird, three decades named the colour of an object, and the object of a colour Irene Pepperberg spent thirty years with one parrot, and the task that mattered was not vocabulary. It was cross-classification: shown a set of objects, Alex could name what colour a given object was, or which object was a given colour — the same items, two independent questions, answered on request. vocal labelling with contentPepperberg, from the late 1970sone animal, thirty yearsthe reviewers did not believe it ▸ Field notes Field notes · African grey parrot · Psittacus erithacus · one bird, three decades What was asked. Not can a parrot make the sound — that was never in doubt — but whether the sound was attached to anything. The cross-classification task is the sharp version of that question: the same objects on the table, and two orthogonal questions about them. What colour is the key? Which thing is green? A response cued by the handler, or bound to a single memorised pairing, cannot answer both. What the field said at the time. Pepperberg began this work in the late 1970s, when the doctrine of the small, non-cortical, therefore-incapable bird brain was strong enough that she received reviewer comments along the lines of asking what she was smoking. How that quotation reaches us, stated plainly. Through Güntürkün, Pusch and Rose, who cite Pepperberg's own memoir Alex & Me (Harper, 2009) at page 72. We have not opened the book. So it is a reported quotation at one remove, and it sits here in the notes rather than on the face of the card, where a reader would fairly assume we had checked the page. If you want to quote it, get the book. Why it is in the guide at all. Because it is evidence about the field rather than about the parrot. A result that needs three decades and a hostile review to establish is a result whose delay says something about who gets believed — the same mechanism this house tracks in human contexts under other names. Held with care. The strongest honest version of this entry is not Alex proved parrots have language, a claim Pepperberg did not make. It is the narrower and sturdier one: a vocal label in a parrot can be detached from its referent and re-applied on demand. The claim How it circulates As it checks out A parrot that talked mimicry — a tape recorder with feathers the finding was never the imitation. L★S · 002 The Warble Budgerigar · Melopsittacus undulatus · the most-kept parrot on Earth open-ended vocal learning — rare, and not something we got by being primates The bird in the kitchen cage is one of a small scatter of animals that learns its vocalisations instead of inheriting them — a capacity shared with songbirds, hummingbirds, parrots, some cetaceans, and us, and absent in our own nearest relatives. open-ended vocal learningshared with us, not with apesabsent in the great apesstudied because convenient ▸ Field notes Field notes · Budgerigar · Melopsittacus undulatus · the most-kept parrot on Earth Included as the counterweight to Alex. The African grey is the famous parrot. The budgerigar is the one in a hundred thousand living rooms, and it carries one of the rarest capacities in the animal kingdom. The pattern is the interesting part. Open-ended vocal learning is scattered across unrelated groups — parrots, songbirds, hummingbirds, some cetaceans, humans — and is absent in the great apes. Whatever vocal learning is, we did not get it by being primates. A capacity distributed like that is exactly the kind of pattern that makes the inherited-or-invented question in the companion zine genuinely hard rather than rhetorically hard. What this card does not claim. That a budgerigar's warble carries propositional content. That question is open, and it is not answered by the fact of learning. The claim here is about the mechanism of acquisition only. Sourcing, graded. L★S · 007 Tomorrow Common raven · Corvus corax · ≈1.2 billion pallial neurons refuses food now for a token it can barter tomorrow The sharpest planning result in the guide. L★S · 008 Thirty Thousand Clark's nutcracker · Nucifraga columbiana · high-elevation cacher up to 30,000 pine seeds · recovered up to six months later A nutcracker at high elevation caches up to thirty thousand pine seeds across a wide area and recovers them up to six months on. Move the landmarks twenty centimetres and the bird searches twenty centimetres off — which is how we know what it is actually using. Clark's nutcrackers living at high elevations cache up to 30,000 pine seeds over a wide area and recover them up to six months later — a load that demands highly proficient long-term spatial memory. Reported in Emery's 2006 review, citing Balda & Kamil (1992). The experiment that shows the mechanism. Vander Wall (1982) let nutcrackers cache in an arena containing multiple objects. Between caching and recovery, the arena was extended 20 cm to the right and every small object in the right half was moved 20 cm with it. One large landmark on the left — a rock — stayed put. The birds' recovery errors were about 20 cm, for exactly the caches in the shifted half. That is a beautiful result, and it says something more precise than "good memory." The bird is not storing a location. It is storing a relationship to landmarks, and when you move the landmarks you move the bird's answer by the same amount. Related work finds these birds preferring large, nearby landmarks to small distant ones, which carry more information than a general sense of where. Why it is paired with the scrub-jay. Same family. Completely different problem. One bird caches tens of thousands of a single durable item and needs where, for months. The other caches a variety of perishable items and needs when. Neither is the standard corvid, and there is no version of this pair where one of them is the better mind. And the honest connection to the raven card. Ravens match great apes on the Primate Cognition Test Battery except on spatial skills. Here is a corvid whose whole life is the spatial problem. Nothing in this literature suggests a single scale that both birds sit on. Cited via review — Emery, "Cognitive ornithology: the evolution of avian intelligence," Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2006), for both the Balda & Kamil and Vander Wall results. Neither primary was read for this guide. L★S · 009 What, Where, When Western scrub-jay · Aphelocoma californica · California integrated memories of what was cached where, and when Scrub-jays cache a variety of foods that perish at different rates, and recover them over shorter periods. Clayton and Dickinson found them forming integrated memories of what item was cached where and when — the closest thing in the animal literature to remembering a particular past occasion. A nutcracker caches one durable thing and needs to find it. A scrub-jay caches a variety of items that perish at different rates, over shorter horizons — so where is not sufficient. If a worm rots in four days and a nut lasts months, retrieval order matters, and getting it right requires holding the deposit time. The finding. Clayton & Dickinson (1998, 1999) trained scrub-jays with foods of differing decay rates and found them forming integrated memories of what was cached where and when. Emery's review adds a second capacity — experience projection (Emery & Clayton 2001) — and notes that at the time of writing these two capacities had not been demonstrated in other animals. Why we write "episodic-like" and not "episodic." Because the field does, and the hyphen is doing real work. What the experiments establish is the content structure — what, where, when, bound together and used. What they cannot establish is whether the bird experiences remembering. That is not a hedge we added; it is the literature's own care, and flattening it would be the exact move this house objects to. The bit that unsettles a tidy story. The social-intelligence hypothesis says complex cognition is driven by complex social life. Scrub-jays are semi-territorial and comparatively non-social, and they carry the most sophisticated memory result in the corvid literature. One clean counterexample does not sink a hypothesis, and this is not offered as sinking it — but it is the sort of fact that a smoothed retelling of "social brains" quietly omits. L★S · 010 The Pigeon Rock dove · Columba livia · the bird the argument was measured in Stacho's imaged species · numerosity with Weber's law · ⅓ the glucose The most disparaged bird in the guide, and the one the current dispute is built on. The right-angled fibre architecture that started it was imaged in pigeon forebrain. Pigeons discriminate numerosity showing distance effects and Weber's law, like monkeys. Three-dimensional polarised light imaging of pigeon forebrain showed radially and tangentially organised fibres crossing at right angles across the whole extent of the Wulst and the sensory dorsal ventricular ridge, with an iterative circuit motif repeating across somatosensory, visual and auditory zones. The honest boundary, which the paper prints: the non-sensory parts of the dorsal ventricular ridge showed a mosaic-like arrangement instead, not the tidy architecture. The algorithms. The fuel. von Eugen and colleagues (2022) found avian neurons consuming roughly a third of the glucose mammalian neurons do. This is the fact that makes the rest of the arithmetic work: the bird did not get a bigger brain, it got a cheaper one, and spent the saving on packing. The point of the card. The evidence that dismantled the ranking came from the animal at the bottom of it, and it came from there for reasons that had nothing to do with respect. L★S · 011 The Atlas Chicken · Gallus gallus domesticus · the most numerous bird on Earth the whole pallium, sequenced cell by cell, across eight stages in ovo The bird our culture ranks lowest and eats by the tens of billions is the bird whose pallium was mapped at single-cell resolution. Zaremba and colleagues built atlases of the adult chicken pallium and eight developmental stages inside the egg, and that map is what took the inherited-or-invented dispute down to the level of cell types. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics across the entire adult chicken pallium and eight in ovo developmental stages, compared against corresponding atlases from mammals and non-avian reptiles. What it found, in the shape it actually has. Conserved expression patterns in inhibitory neurons across amniotes, with one cell type expanded in birds — a type sitting predominantly in the mammalian amygdala but found throughout the avian pallium. Conservation of excitatory neuron types in the hippocampal regions. And elsewhere, homology in some places and transcriptomic convergence in others. Partly inherited, partly arrived at twice, and the boundary does not fall where gross anatomy would have predicted. Why the chicken. Not because it is the cleverest bird. Because it is a tractable laboratory animal whose embryos can be sampled through development — which is the one thing you cannot do with a wild kea. The prior single-cell work had covered adult reptiles and restricted areas of songbird pallium; key regions such as the hyperpallium had no cell-type data at all, and the development of the pallium had never been studied at single-cell level in birds or non-avian reptiles. The thing worth sitting with. Chickens are killed for food in the tens of billions a year — we are not printing a precise figure we have not sourced, and the order of magnitude is the part that matters. It is, by a wide margin, the bird whose worth our culture has settled most confidently. And it is the bird holding the map of the structure the whole cleverness argument is about. We are not going to turn that into a tidy moral. We are going to leave it on the card. L★S · 012 The Second Species Barn owl · Tyto alba · the bird that turned a measurement into a finding the same circuit motif · a more sub-differentiated Wulst One brain showing an architecture is an observation. Two distantly related brains showing the same architecture is a finding. The barn owl is the second species in Stacho and colleagues' study — and where it differed from the pigeon, it differed in a way that tracks its life. The whole weight of Stacho and colleagues' result rests on the word iterative — the motif recurring across modalities, across regions, and across species. A pigeon alone leaves open that you have found something about pigeons. A pigeon and a barn owl, which last shared an ancestor a very long way back, closes that door. The difference, and why it is reassuring rather than awkward. The paper reports that although both species showed a comparable column- and lamina-like organisation, small species differences were discernible — particularly for the Wulst, which was more sub-differentiated in barn owls, fitting the processing of stereopsis combined with high visual acuity in that structure. That is a good sign about the method. A technique that returned identical results for a ground-foraging generalist and an aerial nocturnal ambush predator would be suspicious. A technique that returns the shared motif plus a difference that maps onto how the animal hunts is reading something real. Why the barn owl is in the "never asked" section. Because nobody put an owl in this study to find out how clever owls are. Owls, for all the folklore, are not standouts in comparative cognition. The barn owl is here as an anatomical control — and controls are where findings come from. The bird contributed nothing to the cleverness argument and everything to the evidence. Ströckens and colleagues found corvids carrying more associative pallial neurons than chickens, pigeons or ostriches — a crow matching an ostrich with a brain two and a half times smaller, in a body more than two hundred times smaller. L★S · — Inherited, or built twice? an open dispute · three papers, three answers no reframe table, because there is no verdict to correct The question at the centre of this subject has no settled answer. Did birds inherit the cortex-like circuit from the last common stem amniote, or arrive at it independently? Three papers behind this guide give three different answers, and the version that circulates picks one. Stacho 2020 — conservedGüntürkün 2024 — convergentZaremba 2025 — partly eachnot ours to settle ▸ Field notes Field notes · an open dispute · three papers, three answers Stacho and colleagues (2020) end with inheritance. In their own words, it is likely that an ancient microcircuit that already existed in the last common stem amniote might have been evolutionarily conserved and partly modified in birds and mammals. Note the doubled hedge — it is likely that … might have been. It is offered as a proposal. Güntürkün, Pusch and Rose (2024) end with independent invention. Their four proposed features for complex cognition have, they argue, convergently evolved, which is what makes them hard to replace. Their reasoning is structural: the bird's prefrontal-like area sits inside the dorsal ventricular ridge and therefore cannot be homologous to the mammalian prefrontal cortex, so on their account it must have been built separately. They also call their own list speculative. Zaremba and colleagues (2025) end with both, in different places. Conserved inhibitory neuron types across amniotes; conserved excitatory types in hippocampal regions; homology in some places and transcriptomic convergence in others. Why this card has no table. A "how it circulates / as it checks out" table asserts two things: that there is a verdict, and that we hold it. Here there is a live disagreement between working researchers publishing in Science and in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, and running the apparatus over it would be us borrowing the authority of a settled finding for an open question. Same rule as Field Guide No. 10, where the turtles people made get a different card rather than a smaller one: a subject that cannot take the apparatus gets a different card, not a lesser one. What does circulate. Search any of this and you will meet convergent evolution as the answer. It may well be right. It is one of three positions, and the reason it travels is that two independent inventions of a mind is a headline, while partly conserved, partly convergent, boundary still being mapped is a research programme. And the belonging claim does not depend on the outcome, which is the whole argument of No. 86. If it was built twice, the layered cortex is one implementation among at least two and is not the entry fee. If it was inherited, the kit is older than either lineage and neither of us designed it. A shared inheritance cannot be a hierarchy. Not filed as an entry not filed as an entry · an argument in progress

L★S · — Is the comparison even fair? a methodological question its own authors raise no reframe table, because the authors got there first Every "bird matches ape" claim rests on a comparison between structures that are not the same structure. The researchers making those claims say so themselves, in the same paragraph. That self-hedging is the part the coverage drops, and it has no verdict either. "not entirely fair" — the authorsassociative neurons beyond the PFCdomain-general or notthe qualifier is the finding ▸ Field notes Field notes · a methodological question its own authors raise The specific hedge. Corvid associative pallial neuron numbers come out roughly on par with prefrontal neuron numbers in chimpanzees — a striking figure, from a brain of eight to ten grams. And Güntürkün, Pusch and Rose add, immediately, that this comparison is not entirely fair, since mammalian associative neurons also reside beyond the prefrontal cortex. In other words: the bird's total is being set against a part of the mammal's. Why we are not treating that as a debunk. Because the authors raised it, and because they went on to argue the comparison is still informative — it highlights an unexpected quantity of associative neurons in a very small brain. Both things are true at once, which is why this is a card without a verdict rather than a correction. The larger version of the same question. Could birds excel in a few domains while primates have genuinely domain-general cognition? That was asked properly and answered: a detailed comparison across eight cognitive domains (Güntürkün & Bugnyar, 2016) and a subsequent review across 28 domains (Lambert et al., 2019) both concluded that corvids, parrots and non-human primates possess similar domain-general capacities. And on the algorithms, the tested birds appear to use mental processes similar to mammals' — pigeons showing numerosity distance effects and Weber-law compression, corvids passing through object-permanence stages in the same order as children and making the same errors at the same stages. Which is genuinely strong evidence, and still leaves this card open. Because "similar performance via similar algorithms" is a claim about outcomes and processes, not about whether the underlying quantities being compared are commensurable. The ruler question and the performance question are different questions. Why it matters beyond birds. This is the same shape as the argument in No. 36, where the long-finned pilot whale's neocortical neuron count came out above ours and the ranking survived anyway — because it was never resting on the count. When a measure keeps needing a qualifier to produce the expected ordering, the measure is doing something other than measuring. Not filed as an entry not filed as an entry · a question about the ruler

You are a body of water

Mostly water You are a body of water Roughly sixty percent of you is water. Your blood runs close to the salt of an old sea; each of your cells is a droplet that learned to hold a shape. Before it was ever "you," this water was rain, river, cloud, glacier, and the warm inside of other creatures. Astrida Neimanis puts it plainly: we are, each of us, a body of water — not a sealed vessel with water stored inside, but water itself, gathered for a while into the shape we answer to. And it doesn't stop at your skin. You drink the sky and breathe out the sea; you pass your water on. You are less a thing than a place — somewhere the planet's water is briefly passing through. You are not a container of water. You are water, briefly holding a shape. ≈60% drink · breathe in breath · sweat · give on a place water passes through ≈60% water · always in transit a place, not a container Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

the membrane is permeable born of another's water water moves across the line permeable · borrowed · shared we are all downstream Transcorporeality Nothing here is only yours Every one of us began inside another body of water. Neimanis calls this gestationality: your first world was someone else's inner sea. We are each born of a body of water — and built from water that others, human and not, once carried. Stacy Alaimo's word is transcorporeality — matter moving across the line we like to draw around a self. What is "environment" one minute is "you" the next: the river becomes your blood, your breath becomes the weather, the fish carry traces of us and we of them. So there is no clean edge. We are all downstream of one another — of every creature and cloud that held this water first, and every one who'll hold it next. The membrane is real, but it leaks. Belonging isn't a bond we add on afterward; it's the water already moving through. We are all downstream of one another. Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

Differentiation The confluence keeps the difference Here's the trap to refuse. If we all flow together, doesn't difference dissolve — everyone melting into one? Neimanis is careful: watery belonging is not a blur into sameness. Water is the great archive. It carries what passed through it; it stays particular; it remembers. You can watch this where two rivers meet. A confluence runs braided for miles downstream — one channel, two waters, still visibly distinct. Joined and different at the same time. That is the neurodiversity paradigm in a single image. Belonging as flow doesn't sand us down to a common shape. The spiky profile survives the merge. We are in it together and each unmistakably ourselves — no baseline to dissolve toward, no norm the water is trying to reach. Belonging doesn't ask you to lose your shape. you us one channel · two waters · still distinct joined and different at once interbeing without erasure Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

deep channels, turned the same way shared flow · the watering hole channels aligned · flow shared deep, together Collective flow Where the currents pool Attention flows too. Monotropism (Murray, Lesser & Lawson) describes minds that pour attention into a few deep channels at a time — a strong current, not a thin spread. In flow, the channel becomes the whole world. And currents can meet. When our attention tunnels line up — same interest, same rhythm, working side by side — they join into collective flow: parallel play, shared hyperfocus, the easy company of people deep in the same thing. Autistic Realms (Helen Edgar) names it shared flow — attention turned toward one another's, holding a channel open together. A watering hole is where flows gather — the literal one, where creatures meet to drink, and the kind Stimpunks builds into Cavendish Space: a place made for attention to pool without anyone being pushed out of their own channel. Belonging, here, is a confluence of attention. Flow isn't only solitary. Currents find each other. Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

Belonging as flow Build the watering hole If belonging is a flow, the work isn't to make people fit. It's to keep the water moving. You don't answer a drought by lecturing the fish about resilience — you restore the flow. So we build watering holes: places where currents of attention and care can gather; where you can drink without being drained; where no one has to leave their channel to be let in. More-than-human kin included — every body that shares this water has standing at the pool. Belonging isn't earned by sameness or paid for in masking. It runs upstream and downstream of you already. The task was never to prove you deserve the water. The task is to unblock it. Notdissolution — belonging never asks you to lose your shape. Notthe sealed self — no body of water is only itself. Notpurity — "clean vs. contaminated" is the old language of eugenics; water mixes, and so do we. Notflow-as-productivity — we reclaim flow as joy and company, not output. drink without being drained keep the water moving restore the flow Bodies of Water · Stimpunks
We are all bodies of water

interstellar ice comet ocean you older than the Sun · on loan to you the same old sea The oldest water We are all bodies of water Follow the water back far enough and it leaves the planet. Much of Earth's water is older than the Sun — formed in cold interstellar clouds and carried in on ice and comets before there was an ocean to hold it. The sea in your cells is partly starlight's leftover frost. It has been vapour, rain, river, glacier, whale, fern, and stranger — and it will be again, long after us. You are one shape it is taking, on loan, for a little while. So when you feel the pull toward others — toward shared water, shared attention, shared air — that isn't neediness to apologise for. It's the truest thing about you. We are all bodies of water, all made of star stuff, all borrowing the same old sea. Love you down to your star stuff. We are all bodies of water. You were never a closed thing. Bodies of Water · Stimpunks

1 Bone Song Bone Song on piezoelectric matter, star-forged calcium, and the universe that doesn't pathologize its own variation L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Yasuda, 1954 — 1957 Your bones are electric Dr. Iwao Yasuda discovered something extraordinary in the mid-twentieth century: human bone is piezoelectric. Press on it, bend it, move through the world, and it generates voltage. The word comes from the Greek piezein — to squeeze, to press. Squeeze the crystal and it sparks. The crystal, in this case, is you. Collagen and hydroxyapatite — the structural proteins and minerals that make up your skeleton — are arranged in a lattice so precise that mechanical stress becomes electrical signal. Every step you take is a small current. +V −V stress piezoelectric bone under compression hydroxyapatite lattice · collagen fibres · voltage potential Bone Song · Stimpunks

Ca Fe C Mg P N O Si forge stellar nucleosynthesis elements forged in dying stars · Ca, P, C, N, O Stellar nucleosynthesis Forged in a dying star The calcium in your bones was not born here. It was forged — fused in the nuclear furnace of a star that lived and died billions of years before our sun ignited. When that star collapsed and exploded, it scattered its elements across the galaxy. Over eons, gravity pulled the debris into new configurations. Eventually: a solar system. A planet. An ocean. A cell. A bone. You are the universe's way of turning its own ash into something that can walk and feel and think about where it came from. The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, the carbon in our apple pies were made in the interiors of collapsing stars. — Carl Sagan, Cosmos Bone Song · Stimpunks

The poem Your bones are electric. Not metaphorically. Not as a figure of speech borrowed from the poets who came before. Literally. Measurably. Piezoelectric. Press on them and they spark. Move through the world and they sing voltage. Dr. Yasuda knew this. He pressed on the crystal and it answered. The crystal was bone. The bone was yours. The calcium that carries that current was forged in a star that died before our sun was born. You are walking around with stellar ash in your skeleton. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Storms are not disorders. Variation is not deficit. The electric bone that bends differently is still making the signal. We love you down to your star stuff. To the calcium. To the charge. To the exact configuration of atoms that has never existed before and will never exist again. L★S. Bone Song · Stimpunks
The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation

The paradigm The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation The neurodiversity paradigm says: difference is variation, not deficit. It names a lens — one that the DSM cannot offer — in which the full range of human neurological experience is part of the natural distribution, not a deviation from it. A star doesn't diagnose its own magnetosphere. A fault line doesn't pathologize its seismic activity. Turbulence is how the universe moves energy from one place to another. You were told your signal was noise. You were told your frequency was wrong. But the bone still made its electricity. The calcium still remembered the star. Reclamation The punk in Stimpunks is this: we take the diagnostic language back into the lab and ask a different question. Not what is wrong with this person but what did the instrument fail to measure? Not why can't they be like everyone else but what is the universe trying to do through this particular configuration of matter? Every kind of mind lights up the sky differently. That is not a problem to solve. Bone Song · Stimpunks
