70 Star Stuff Both Arcs, One Drop on the raindrop that makes both bows at once, the lab that tried to erase both of you, and why entwined turns out to be a claim about the source rather than a feeling about the self for everyone told to file one of themselves under later L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely

The fact this zine runs on One drop makes both A double rainbow is not two rainbows. It is one optical event with two visible arcs, and the reason is a single sentence in an atmospheric-science textbook: A single raindrop produces both: entering rays undergo either one internal reflection (primary) or two internal reflections (secondary) before exiting. Roland Stull, Practical Meteorology, ch. 22 One drop. One beam of sunlight going into it. Both arcs, at the same time. The light that bounces once inside the drop leaves at about 42.7° from the antisolar point and makes the inner bow. The light that bounces twice leaves at about 50° and makes the outer one. The drop is not choosing. It is doing both, continuously, to every ray it catches. Which means the second bow is not an extra that sometimes shows up. It is always being made. Whenever there is a primary, the two-reflection light is being produced by the very same water from the very same sun. Whether you can see it is a question about the brightness of the sky, and about nothing else. Hold onto that shape, because the rest of this zine is built on it: two things that look like two things, coming from one source, produced together, neither one waiting its turn. One drop, two ray paths, both at once A single raindrop catches sunlight along two different lines. One path reflects once inside it and leaves toward the inner bow; the other reflects twice and leaves toward the outer bow. Both are happening in the same drop at the same time. two bounces → outer bow sunlight one bounce → inner bow same drop · same light · same instant Figure 1 · the drop is not choosing between them Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks

The geometry of not ranking The reds face each other On the inner bow, red is on the outside. On the outer bow, red is on the inside. The extra reflection reverses the order, and the consequence is worth saying slowly: the two red edges point at each other. They are not a sequence, and they are not a ladder. They are mirror images, facing across the gap between them, with the rest of each spectrum fanning away behind. If you were looking for a shape in the sky that refuses to put one thing above another, this is the one you would draw. And that gap has a name, from about 200 CE: Alexander's dark band, after Alexander of Aphrodisias, who noticed the sky is darker between the bows and wrote it down roughly eighteen centuries before anyone could say why. The why is exact: Neither the primary nor secondary rainbows return light in the viewing-angle range between 42.7° and 50°. Hence, the sky is noticeably darker between these rainbows. Stull, Practical Meteorology, ch. 22 So the dark band is not a wall between two things. It is the region neither arc reaches — the shadow left behind because the light piled up somewhere else. The separation you can see is a by-product of the concentration you can also see. Nothing is in the gap because everything went to the arcs. It is a strange comfort, and an exact one. The space between the two halves of a double rainbow is not evidence that they are separate. It is evidence of where the light went. Red facing red across Alexander’s dark band A profile of the sky measured outward from the antisolar point. The inner bow runs violet at about forty degrees to red at 42.7 degrees; the outer bow runs red at about fifty degrees to violet beyond it. Between them is a band where neither bow returns light, and the two red edges are the two edges facing it. 40° 42.7° 50° red — inner bow red — outer bow Alexander’s band measured outward from the antisolar point ↑ Figure 2 · mirror images, oriented toward each other Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks
Fainter is a fact about the path

The number we are not going to hide Fainter is a fact about the path The outer bow is dimmer. Stull gives it plainly — “the secondary rainbow is faint — only 43% as bright as the primary rainbow” — and a zine that quietly left that out would be a zine you could not trust with the rest. So here is why, exactly. Every time light meets the inside surface of a drop, only part of it reflects; the rest escapes out of the drop entirely. The outer bow's light has to survive two of those encounters instead of one. More of it leaks away. That is the whole mechanism. It is a fact about how far the light travelled and how many times it was asked to turn around. Dimmer is not lesser. Dimmer is later along a longer path, and the path was longer because it did more. Two things follow, and they matter more than the number does. First: the outer arc is never absent. It is produced by the same drop from the same beam, always. Nothing about a double rainbow involves the second arc arriving late or optionally. What varies is whether the sky behind it is bright enough to drown it. Second: visibility is a fact about conditions, not about the arc. A thing can be fully real, continuously present, and hard to see, all at once, and none of those is in tension with the others. Our own Your Shadow Is the Centre (No. 69) spends a whole spread on the version of this that is about the observer's position. This is the other half: not where you have to stand, but what else is in the sky. The turnings, in Ryan’s words The dimmer arc takes more turnings. I relate to those turnings as a queering and neuroqueering of path and destination. The arc is not lesser because it is dimmer, it just emitted light along more turnings. One drop. One light. Two pathways. One brighter in fewer directions, one distributing more of itself along the way. Both always there. — Ryan Boren Which is why the next spread refuses to do the obvious thing with all of this. Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks
This zine will not give you one bow each

The refusal, and it goes here rather than at the end This zine will not give you one bow each The obvious move, at this point, is to hand you one arc for being queer and the other for being neurodivergent. We are not going to, and the reason is structural rather than delicate. If you assign the arcs, one of them is the 43% one. You can write around that for twelve spreads and the shape will still be doing the ranking underneath, because the reader can see the sky. A metaphor that needs constant correcting is a metaphor that is already saying the wrong thing. And the physics does not support the assignment anyway. Go back to spread two: one drop makes both. The two arcs are not two objects that happen to co-occur. They are what a single drop does with a single beam of light, always, simultaneously. Nothing in the optics divides them between two owners, because the optics never divided them at all. The drop is not a metaphor for having two identities. It is a demonstration that one source can produce two whole things at once, neither of them a consequence of the other. So: the drop is a life. The light is one light. Both arcs are being made the entire time. Neither is the second one, because there is no first one — there is one event, and it has two arcs, and the numbering we gave them is a fact about the order we happened to explain them in. “Primary” and “secondary” are our words for our convenience. The drop has never heard them. Why this zine refuses it, in Ryan’s words I’m queer and neurodivergent. I feel both of these aspects of myself equally and fluidly. They’re both important to me and my identity. I feel them intrinsically without one being subordinate to the other. They are entwined in the whole of me. Thus the title of this zine, “Both Arcs, One Drop”. I don’t have a neurodivergent “primary” arc and a queer “secondary” arc, or vice-versa. Same drop, same light. In borrowing the double rainbow as a rhyme and metaphor, we don’t force a hierarchy or rank. We are omni-directional. Our light follows multiple paths of arrival and becoming, none lesser to another. — Ryan Boren Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks

Where entwined stops being a feeling The same lab People say queer and neurodivergent liberation are entwined, and it can sound like a warm claim about solidarity. It is not. It is a claim about a source, and it has a citation. In 1974, the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis — the flagship journal of applied behaviour analysis — published “Behavioral Treatment of Deviant Sex-Role Behaviors in a Male Child”, volume 7, issue 2, pages 173–190. The authors were George A. Rekers, then at Harvard, and O. Ivar Lovaas, at the University of California, Los Angeles. Thirteen years later, in 1987, the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology published “Behavioral Treatment and Normal Educational and Intellectual Functioning in Young Autistic Children.” The author was O. Ivar Lovaas, at the University of California, Los Angeles. One name, on both. Two of a discipline's most consequential papers, one aimed at a boy who liked his mother's jewellery and one aimed at Autistic children, from the same man at the same university. That is not an interpretation, and it needs no theory of history to hold it up. It is two entries in a bibliography. Anyone can check it in a minute, and the checking is the point — because the version of this claim that circulates as vibes is exactly the version that can be waved away. The 1974 paper states its own purpose in its own abstract, and we are going to quote it rather than characterise it: This study suggests a preliminary step toward correcting pathological sex-role development in boys, which may provide a basis for the primary prevention of adult transsexualism or similar adult sex-role deviation. Rekers & Lovaas, JABA 7(2), 1974, p. 173 Primary prevention of adult transsexualism. Written down, in a peer-reviewed journal, as the aim. Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks

A door No. 38 stopped at It was the same room Our own Eight Tenths of a Second (No. 38) follows the measuring apparatus out of an observatory in 1796 and down through Wundt, Cattell, Thorndike, Pressey and Skinner, and it ends in a spread called “A room with a child in it” — Lovaas at UCLA, and the 1987 paper. That chain is complete and correct and it stops at a door. This zine opens it, and reports that there was more than one kind of child at that table. The connective tissue is not thematic. It is methodological, and it is the same in both papers: operant conditioning — identify a behaviour, define it so it can be counted, reinforce what you want, punish what you don't, chart the line going the direction you chose in advance. The 1974 paper uses a multiple-baseline design. So does the autism work. The apparatus does not care what it is pointed at; that was always its selling point. Behaviourism did not have one theory for Autistic children and a different one for gender-nonconforming children. It had one theory, and a list. Which is why the entwinement is not a coalition that queer and neurodivergent people chose to form out of good will. It is a fact about who was in the room, and it was decided for us, by other people, before we could object. Eric Michael Garcia, writing about why a book on autism includes queer history, put the reason as plainly as it can be put: “The same people who want to stop queer kids from being themselves are the same ones who want to stop me from flapping my hands.” Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks

Read at the paper, not at a summary Kraig The paper calls him Kraig. He was four years and eleven months old when he was referred. His real name was Kirk Andrew Murphy. Everything on this spread is quoted from the 1974 paper itself, which is open access and which we downloaded and read, because the account that circulates online is second-hand and in one place slightly wrong — the pseudonym is often given as “Craig”, and the paper says Kraig. His mother was “trained to be his therapist”. In the home, the method was a token economy: Red and blue standard poker chips were used as “tokens”. The blue tokens … could be directly exchanged by Kraig for the “back-up reinforcers” according to a “price list” set by the mother (e.g., five blue tokens were required for a candy bar). The red tokens (Sr-) were discriminative for (a) a response-cost condition …, (b) a timeout procedure …, or (c) physical punishment by spanking from the father. Rekers & Lovaas, JABA 7(2), 1974, p. 180 Here is the detail that undid us, and it is a sequencing detail. Before the chips were pointed at anything to do with gender, the researchers ran them on ordinary household behaviour first, because — their words — “it was judged ‘clinically safer’ to apply it initially to nongender behaviors in the home.” In that phase, red chips were given for “slamming doors”, “cursing at mother”, “tracking dirt on carpet”. Then the same red chip — the tracking-dirt-on-the-carpet chip, the one whose meaning the child had just been taught — was extended to playing with girls, playing with dolls, feminine gestures, and female role play. The behaviours on the home checklist are listed in the paper: “plays with girls”, “plays with female dolls”, “feminine gestures” — specified as “limp wrist, ‘swishy’ hand, arm or torso movements, sway of hips” — and “female role play”. Kirk Murphy died by suicide in 2003. We state that the way Austin H. Johnson states it in the behaviour-analytic literature: as a fact, adjacent to the study, without a causal claim attached. His family have said publicly what they believe the treatment did to him. That is their account to make, it is not ours to convert into a finding, and the record does not need it in order to be damning. What the paper does not contain: the widely repeated detail that Kirk's brother hid the red chips to protect him. That comes from the family, reported later — not from the study. We have kept the two apart on purpose, because the study is quotable and a grieving family should not have to be. Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks

What the field has done about it since Fifty-two years, and it stands A paper like that could have been retracted at any point in half a century. Here is the actual record, which is short. In October 2020 — forty-six years on — JABA published an Editor's Note, a Statement of Concern. It did not retract. Its reasoning is worth reading exactly: By today's standards…the study would be considered unethical…However, the available evidence does not make it clear that the original study was unethical by the standards of that day. JABA Editor's Note, 2020 — as quoted by Johnson (2022) In 2022, Austin H. Johnson answered it in Behavior Analysis in Practice, arguing that the paper should be retracted, and that “the available evidence strongly suggests that the original study was unethical and misaligned with the principles of Applied Behavior Analysis.” Johnson is also where the child's name and pronouns come from, established through conversations with Kirk's sister. The defence offered in 2020 was the standards of that day. The 1974 paper printed its own aim in its own abstract: the primary prevention of adult transsexualism. Nothing about that has ever required a later standard to read. The paper is still in the literature. Cited, indexed, downloadable, with a note attached. That is not us characterising a field; it is the field's own filing, and it is why this zine leans on the record rather than on outrage — the record is worse than anything we would have said. And be exact about what this does not establish. It does not establish that a behaviour analyst today endorses 1974. Most would be appalled. What it establishes is lineage, and lineage is the claim being made here: the suppression of queer children and the suppression of Autistic children came out of one method, one lab, and in the crucial instance one author — and the discipline has not yet been willing to say so by taking the paper out. Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks
Entwined is a claim about the source

The claim, stated carefully Entwined is a claim about the source Put the two halves of this zine together and the sentence comes out precise. Queer and neurodivergent are entwined not because the experiences are the same — they are not, and flattening them would be its own erasure — but because they came out of one drop. The pathologising was one method. The lab was one lab. In the sharpest instance, the author was one man. Whatever else divides the two, the machinery built to remove them did not distinguish between them, and that is a fact about the source rather than a feeling about the self. There is already a word for the entwinement, and it is a coinage, so it gets credited properly. Neuroqueer is Nick Walker's, who has dated his own use to around 2008; in early 2014 he found that Athena Lynn Michaels-Dillon had arrived at the same term independently, while Remi Yergeau had been working the same ground as neurological queerness. The three of them began putting it into public use from there. Walker's Neuroqueer Heresies collects the argument (2021). Three people, working separately, reaching for the same word at the same time. The word for two things being one thing was itself arrived at twice over, by people who had not compared notes. And the history is entwined at the root as well as at the wound. Nick Walker's reminder is worth keeping in the front of the mouth: Gwen Nelson, who created Autistic Pride Day, is a trans woman. There is no version of Autistic pride that was not, from the start, also this. So the double rainbow was never two flags flown at one address. It was one drop, doing what a drop does, and the light coming out of it twice because that is what light does when something turns it around. Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks

What this does not say What this does not say A zine that names a dead child and a living discipline has to be exact about its own edges. So, plainly: Not:one bow each. Stated on spread five and repeated here because it is the thing most likely to be read back into the piece anyway. No arc belongs to an identity. One drop makes both, always, simultaneously — and the 43% is a fact about path length, so the moment you assign the arcs you have invented a hierarchy the optics never contained. Not:that queer and Autistic experience are the same experience. The claim is about a shared source of suppression, which is a much narrower and much more checkable thing. Plenty of people hold one of these and not the other; plenty hold both and find them pulling in different directions on a given Tuesday. Entwined at the root does not mean identical in the hand. Not:that the 1974 treatment killed Kirk Murphy. He died by suicide in 2003. His family have said what they believe. We report the death as the behaviour-analytic literature reports it — adjacent, uncaused, unadorned — because a causal claim we cannot support would weaken a record that needs no help, and because his family's grief is not a rhetorical device. Not:that today's ABA is 1974. It is not, practitioners will say so, and many of them mean it. The argument here is lineage, plus one specific institutional fact: the paper was examined in 2020 and left standing. Those are different accusations and only the second is aimed at anyone currently alive. Not:a claim on the Pride flag's colours as the physical spectrum. No. 69 already refuses this and it stands: the flag is a chosen set, and the Philly stripes were added precisely because a “natural” spectrum was being used to leave Black and brown queer people out. A banner and an atmospheric phenomenon are different objects, and only one of them is legislated about. Not:the egg-crack argument. That the neurodivergent egg-crack moment is borrowed from trans communities — and is better in its original — is The Shell Was Your Calcium (No. 57), which spends it properly. Two entwinement pieces, two different mechanisms, no re-running. Not:a proof. A rhyme, not a proof. The refractive index of water demonstrates nothing whatsoever about a person. What the optics supply is one honest shape — a single source producing two whole things at once, neither derived from the other — held up next to a documented history that happens to have the same shape. The history is the evidence. The rainbow is why we could see what the history was shaped like. Both Arcs, One Drop · Stimpunks

The Bow-ery Ten bows · one scale Every list of rainbow kinds shows you ten photographs taken from ten places at ten focal lengths, and asks you to believe the captions about how big each one is. This is the same ten drawn to one scale. The third of the “-ery” sheets, after The Hatchery ’s twelve cosmic eggs and The Quillery ’s eight Esmx. Same rule as both: every drawing carries one checkable thing , with its source under it. The companion catalogue is A Field Guide to Rainbows (No. 20), which sorts bows by what physically changed. This sheet asks the smaller question that a catalogue cannot answer in prose — how big is it, and where in the sky do I turn to look? The one thing to know before the plates Three units to the degree, and every plate is centred at the same point. The dot at the bottom of each drawing is the centre of that bow — the antisolar point , in the direction of your own shadow, for everything made of water; the sun itself for the two plates made of ice and the one that bounced three times. Radii are true against each other, so a bow that looks half the size of another is half the size of it. Every plate also carries the 42° primary as a faint dashed ghost , whether or not the primary is what the plate is about. That is the reference line: it is the bow nearly everyone has seen, and it is the only way a drawing can tell you that a 22° halo is not a small rainbow but a different thing at half the radius, on the other side of the sky. What the scale cannot show: brightness, which varies by more than an order of magnitude across these ten and is drawn only suggestively; and the sky itself, which is left out so the geometry is not competing with weather. What this is, and what it is not These are drawings, not photographs, and not data. The radii are computed from published angles and are trustworthy to the width of the stroke; everything else — the thickness of a band, the intensity of a colour, the exact spread of a fogbow — is drawn to be legible rather than measured. Where a figure is doing real work it is printed as a number on the plate, and the source line carries it. Eight of the ten reproduce their counterpart glyph from Field Guide No. 20. That guide draws each bow at 104×96 with two labels in six-and-a-half-point type, because the glyph has to survive being a diagram in a card. The plates here are 400×232 — roughly eight and a half times the area — and they exist because a diagram is drawn to explain itself and a drawing is not. Putting both on the plate is the honest version of that claim: you can see what the small one had to give up. Two plates carry no glyph, and the reason is worth stating. The field guide has no entry for a plain rainbow, because it sorts bows by what changed and in an ordinary rainbow nothing has. So the most familiar object on this page is the one the catalogue could not card — and it leads the sheet.

The ten The Primary Bow A rainbow drawn to scale as a band of seven colours, violet on the inside and red on the outside, forming a semicircle of about 42 degrees radius centred on a dot at the bottom of the frame that marks the direction of the observer’s own shadow. Two of the seven bands, indigo and orange, are ticked and labelled — they are the two Isaac Newton added to reach seven. indigo orange RED OUTSIDE · VIOLET IN bands drawn ~2.8× true width true spread ≈ 1.9°

The Primary No. 1 · the one the catalogue could not card The bow nearly everyone has seen, and the only plate here with no counterpart in Field Guide No. 20 . That guide sorts bows by what changed , and in this one nothing has. It is the reference, not an entry — which is why its dashed ghost appears on all nine of the others. The bands, though, are ours rather than the sky’s. Newton’s optical lectures of 1670–72 name five : red, yellow, green, blue, violet. Opticks , in 1704 , prints seven — orange and indigo added at exactly the points where the half-steps fall in the Western diatonic scale, the seven-note division of an octave. Newton offered the correspondence between the harmony of sound and the harmony of colour as an analogy and hedged it carefully; the seven survived the hedge and became what children are taught. The light has no bands in it at all. It is a continuum, and every boundary drawn across it — including the six drawn here — is a decision somebody made about where one name should stop. The sky supplies the gradient. The categories are ours. Sources: Newton’s five-colour spectrum in the Optical Lectures (1670–72) against the seven of Opticks (1704), and the diatonic-scale explanation for the addition of orange and indigo: Topper, D., “Newton on the number of colours in the spectrum,” Studies in History and Philosophy of Science (1990), which is the scholarly treatment of the question rather than the popular retelling. Newton framed the sound–colour correspondence as an analogy, not a result, and we keep that. Related here: Not a Line (No. 21), which argues the adjacent thing — that a spectrum is not a severity scale — from the emission-line side rather than this one. No counterpart glyph. Field Guide No. 20 has no entry for a plain rainbow, because nothing about it changed. The Secondary Bow and Alexander’s Dark Band Two arcs drawn to scale around the same centre. The inner one, at about 42.7 degrees, has red on the outside. The outer one, at about 50 degrees, is fainter and has its colours reversed so that its red faces inward. The sky between the two is shaded distinctly darker. REDS FACING ACROSS THE GAP Alexander’s dark band 42.7° · one bounce 50° · two · 43% as bright

The Secondary No. 2 · the second bounce, drawn at true separation One internal reflection leaves the drop at about 42.7° . Two leave it at about 50° , and the extra bounce flips the colour order, so the two reds face each other. The outer bow is 43% as bright as the inner — an extra reflection is another chance to lose light, and a longer path loses more. The gap between them is Alexander’s dark band , and it is drawn here as what it is: not a shadow and not a missing band, but a direction into which neither bow returns any light at all. Alexander of Aphrodisias noticed the sky was darker there around 200 CE and wrote it down, roughly fourteen centuries before anyone could say why. The reason this plate exists rather than a photograph: in a photograph the separation is whatever the lens made it. Here it is 7.3° of true angular distance , measurable against every other plate on the sheet. Sources: Angles, relative brightness and the no-light-returned explanation of the dark band all follow Stull, R., Practical Meteorology , and are the same figures printed in Both Arcs, One Drop (No. 70) and Field Guide No. 20 — deliberately, because a sheet and its zine disagreeing about a number is worse than either being wrong alone. Alexander of Aphrodisias, c. 200 CE, for the band’s first record and its name. The argument this plate does not make — that “secondary” is a rank the physics does not contain — is No. 70’s. reds facing, 42.7° / 50° dark band between As Field Guide No. 20 draws it: same two arcs, no scale, at 104×96. Supernumerary Arcs The primary bow drawn to scale, with five progressively fainter pale pink and green arcs crowded just inside it, their spacing narrowing as they go inward. RAYS CANNOT PRODUCE THESE fringes crowd inward Young, 1804

The Supernumeraries No. 3 · the arcs that broke the ray model The faint pink and green fringes that sometimes crowd the inner edge of a primary. They are not weak repeats of the rainbow. They are the one feature of a rainbow that geometric optics cannot produce at all — not “predicts poorly”, but cannot, in principle, which made them a standing refutation of the complete ray account sitting in plain sight above every rain shower on Earth. Thomas Young explained them in 1804 , by interference: two rays can leave a drop at the same angle having travelled different distances inside it, and on recombining they reinforce or cancel by wavelength. Because that requires light to have a phase , the arcs became evidence for the wave theory at the moment that argument was live. The half worth keeping is what happened next. Airy dismissed Young in 1838 as “the imperfect theory of interference”, on the real ground that it put the arcs at the wrong angles. Young’s numbers were off because he had not known a ray crossing a focal line picks up a 90° phase shift. Put it in and his account is surprisingly accurate. A correct mechanism, rejected for a missing term, and overshadowed for well over a century. Sources: Young’s 1804 interference explanation, Airy’s 1838 dismissal of it as “the imperfect theory of interference”, and the missing 90° focal-line phase shift: Lock, J. A. & Adams, C. L., “Supernumerary arcs of rainbows: Young’s theory of interference,” Applied Optics 56(19), G104 (2017), read at abstract and summary level. Fringe spacing is drawn schematically — it depends on drop size and is not printed as a figure. rays cannot make these Young 1804: interference As Field Guide No. 20 draws it, with the ray model crossed out. The Fogbow A broad, soft white band forming an arc slightly inside the dashed reference position of a normal rainbow, with faint additional white arcs inside it. The band is many times wider than the coloured band of a rainbow. BROAD, AND WHITE BY ADDITION droplets under 0.05 mm dashed: the 42° primary

The Fogbow No. 4 · the same bow, drawn with a wider pen Rain falls at around a millimetre. Fog and cloud droplets rarely exceed a hundred micrometres, and a fogbow wants them at roughly 0.05 mm and below . At that size the light diffracts around the droplet, and diffraction widens every colour band. Widen them far enough and they stop sitting side by side and start sitting on top of each other; overlapping colours across the visible range add to white. Nothing is missing. Every colour is present and in order. The white is the sum, arrived at by addition — which is the opposite of what “colourless rainbow” implies. The plate also shows why sorting these by appearance was never going to work. A fogbow looks nothing like a rainbow and differs from one in a single parameter . And it runs on a slope, not a switch: as droplets grow the bow narrows and colour returns at the edges, so waterfall spray at 100–500 µm gives bows that are neither. Sources: Droplet-size thresholds, the diffraction mechanism and the intermediate spray forms follow Les Cowley’s Atmospheric Optics (atoptics.co.uk), an expert secondary source and named as one. Radius is drawn as a representative value inside the primary; the real figure is a range , about 30–45°, because it varies with droplet size — which is why no single number is printed on this plate. small drop bands overlap = white As Field Guide No. 20 draws it: colours beneath, white on top. The 22-Degree Halo and Sun Dogs A ring of 22 degrees radius drawn around the sun, which sits at the centre of the frame. Two bright patches — sun dogs — sit just outside the ring, level with the sun. The dashed 42-degree rainbow reference arc is drawn much further out and labelled as being behind the observer. A small hexagonal ice plate is drawn in the corner. a rainbow would be out here — and behind you ice CENTRED ON THE SUN 22° · about half a rainbow sun dogs, level with the sun

The 22° Halo No. 5 · the plate this sheet was built for Put the two on one scale and the argument stops needing to be made in words. A 22° halo is not a small rainbow. It is a different phenomenon, at about half the radius, formed in hexagonal plates of ice rather than spheres of water — and, decisively, it is centred on the sun . To see the dashed arc on this plate you would have to turn around. That single fact disposes of most of the genre. Lists of “rainbow kinds” routinely file sun dogs, the 22° halo and the circumhorizontal arc alongside real bows because they are coloured arcs in the sky, and coloured arc in the sky is a description of appearance. The mechanism, the medium and the direction you face are all different. Sun dogs are the same ice at the same 22°, concentrated where the plates are horizontal — which puts them level with the sun rather than anywhere on the ring, and is why they come in pairs. Sources: Hexagonal plate and column crystals, the 22° minimum-deviation angle, and sun dogs as the horizontal-plate case: standard halo optics via Atmospheric Optics . Drawn with the sun on the horizon so the geometry is legible; at any real solar elevation the ring rides with the sun and the dogs stay level with it. Field Guide No. 20 files all of this under a single withheld card, The Ones That Are Not Rainbows , with no reframe table. hexagonal ice plate not a rainbow As Field Guide No. 20 draws it: the crystal, and a bow crossed out. The Circumhorizontal Arc The sun drawn near the top of the frame with a dashed 22-degree halo around it, and a broad band of colour running horizontally across the lower part of the frame, 46 degrees below the sun. Labels give the sun-elevation requirement of 58 degrees and the annual hours available in London and Los Angeles. 46° below THE SUN MUST BE ABOVE 58° London ≈ 140 h/yr Los Angeles ≈ 670 h/yr impossible north of 55°N

The Circumhorizontal Arc No. 6 · where “rare” turns out to mean “not from here” Sold everywhere as a fire rainbow . It is ice — sunlight entering the vertical side face of a hexagonal plate crystal in cirrus and leaving through the horizontal bottom face — and it hangs 46° below the sun , which is why this is the one plate whose centre had to move. The scale is unchanged. It needs the sun higher than 58° . That is a hard geometric condition, and it has a consequence the genre never prints: the arc is impossible north of 55°N or south of 55°S . Not rare there. Impossible. Where it is possible, availability varies enormously. The sun clears 58° for roughly 140 hours a year in London and roughly 670 in Los Angeles . Same crystals, same cirrus, same physics — a once-in-a-lifetime sight in one city and a regular summer one in the other. Every rarity ranking in this genre is partly a ranking of where the reader lives, and this is the entry where you can put a number on it. Sources: The 58° solar-elevation requirement, the impossibility above 55° latitude, and the London/Los Angeles hour figures come from the halo literature via Atmospheric Optics and Wikipedia’s circumhorizontal arc entry, which agree. No primary computation was reached, and these are the numbers on this sheet we would most like to improve — they are also the ones carrying the most argumentative weight, which is exactly when a figure should be flagged rather than trusted. No counterpart glyph. Field Guide No. 20 files this inside its single ice-halo card rather than giving it one of its own. The Glory Three small concentric coloured rings, only a few degrees across, drawn tight around the silhouette of a person’s head and shoulders at the centre of the frame. The dashed 42-degree rainbow reference arc is drawn far outside them for scale. A question mark sits beside the rings. the primary, for scale ? A FEW DEGREES ACROSS centred on your own shadow still not fully explained

The Glory No. 7 · the open question on this sheet Coloured rings a few degrees across, tight around the shadow of your own head on cloud or fog — from a ridge, or an aircraft window. The scale is the point of drawing it here: set against the dashed primary, a glory is tiny , and photographs never tell you that because they are taken with whatever lens was to hand. It is also the one entry on this sheet whose mechanism is openly unfinished . Mie theory computes the glory in full colour and offers no explanation of it . Debye-series analysis says the light has undergone one internal reflection. In 1947 van de Hulst proposed surface waves — light grazing the droplet and shedding radiation as it travels round — and that remains the consensus. The standard statement of that consensus is that the precise mechanism remains rather obscure . So this is the plate that keeps the sheet honest. Nine of these ten are settled to a fraction of a degree. One of them you can see out of a plane window most cloudy flights, and it is not finished. A specimen sheet that only drew solved things would be teaching that the sky is solved. Sources: Mie theory computing but not explaining the glory, the Debye-series single internal reflection, van de Hulst’s 1947 surface-wave proposal, and the “remains rather obscure” assessment: Laven, P., “How are glories formed?”, Applied Optics 44(27), 5675 (2005), with the surrounding Atmospheric Optics material. Ring radius is drawn at a representative few degrees; it varies with droplet size and no single figure is printed. ? centred on your shadow mechanism still open As Field Guide No. 20 draws it, question mark and all. The Third- and Fourth-Order Bows Two faint arcs at about 40 and 45 degrees drawn around the sun, which sits at the centre of the frame surrounded by concentric washes of glare. The arcs are much fainter than on the other plates. BEHIND YOU, IN THE GLARE 3rd ≈ 40° · 4th ≈ 45° first photographed 2011

The Third and Fourth Order No. 8 · present for centuries, photographed in 2011 Light can go round inside a drop more than twice, and at three and four bounces the bows turn around . They do not appear outside the secondary; they appear on the other side of the sky, at roughly 40° and 45° from the sun itself. The glare on this plate is not decoration — it is the entire reason they went unphotographed. Their existence was worked out long before anyone saw one. The obstruction was never theory; it was contrast. Both were first photographed in 2011 , the third-order by Michael Großmann with Elmar Schmidt and Alexander Haußmann, and a natural fourth-order by Michael Theusner, in the same issue of Applied Optics . It took knowing the exact angle, a rain shaft in the right place, heavy contrast processing, and persistence. The common correction follows straight from the drawing: three arcs in a photograph are almost never a “triple rainbow.” They are the primary, the secondary and a reflection bow. The real tertiary is at the centre of this plate’s geometry, behind the photographer. Sources: Großmann, M., Schmidt, E. & Haußmann, A., “Photographic evidence for the third-order rainbow,” Applied Optics 50(28), F134–F141 (2011), and Theusner, M., “Photographic observation of a natural fourth-order rainbow,” Applied Optics 50(28), F129 (2011); both confirmed at the publisher. These are a small number of confirmed images obtained by specialists under heavy processing, not a survey — the phrase the literature uses is “photographic evidence,” and we keep it. these sit around the sun photographed in 2011 As Field Guide No. 20 draws it: rings around the sun, no scale. The Moonbow A rainbow at the standard 42 degrees drawn in flat grey, with one wedge of the same arc — the upper right quarter — drawn in full colour, connected by a dashed line to a small camera symbol. A crescent moon sits in the upper left. TO THE EYE TO A SENSOR the same 42° every colour, unreported

The Moonbow No. 9 · the bow was complete; the instrument was not Moonlight is sunlight that bounced off the Moon, so a moonbow is a rainbow in the most literal sense: same geometry, same 42°, same colour order. The only difference is intensity — and intensity is enough, because of how eyes are built. In low light vision falls back from the cone cells, which discriminate colour, to the rod cells, which are far more sensitive and report no colour at all . A moonbow generally sits below the threshold at which cones respond, so the arc arrives at the retina with its full spectrum intact and is reported in greyscale. Open a shutter for thirty seconds and every colour appears. The plate draws both readings of one arc, because that is the honest picture. The bow is not deficient, and neither are the rods — they buy their sensitivity by not sorting wavelengths, which is the job they are for. Two instruments, two accounts, and a third settles it. The colours were present and unreported. Sources: Scotopic vision falling to the rods below the cone threshold, and the full spectrum appearing in long-exposure photographs of moonbows: well-established visual science and atmospheric optics, given as such rather than from a paper read for this sheet. The colour wedge is drawn as a quarter of the arc for legibility; a real long exposure records the whole bow. to the eye: grey to a camera: all of it As Field Guide No. 20 draws it: grey bow, colour bow, moon and camera. The Full Circle A complete circle of rainbow colours at 42 degrees radius. The upper half is drawn solid; the lower half is dashed and faded, and the lower part of the frame below the horizon line is shaded dark to show that the ground is in the way. ALWAYS A FULL CIRCLE the ground is in the way get above it and it closes

The Full Circle No. 10 · the arc was never an arc A rainbow is the set of directions 42° from the antisolar point, and that set is a circle . It is always a circle. Nobody sees one because the antisolar point is below the horizon whenever the sun is above it, so the lower half would have to be made by raindrops that are underground. Get above the drops — an aircraft, a cliff, the top of a waterfall — and the obstruction goes away and the bow closes. Which means the famous “rare full-circle rainbow” is not a kind of rainbow. It is the only kind there is , seen from a position where nothing is standing in front of its lower half. This plate is the sheet’s own argument about itself. Nine drawings above it stop at the horizon line because that is what the ground does to a cone of directions — and the shape you were taught to call a bow is a fact about standing on a planet. Sources: Geometry, and it needs no citation beyond the antisolar point being below the horizon whenever the sun is above it. Drawn with the centre exactly on the horizon, which corresponds to the sun exactly on the opposite horizon — the case that gives the largest arc anyone on the ground can see. Field Guide No. 20 makes the same point in prose at The Arc Was Never An Arc . always a full circle the ground hid the rest As Field Guide No. 20 draws it: solid above, dashed below.
What we left out, and the colour that is not here

What we left out, and the colour that is not here Notes The colour these are drawn in is in none of them. This site’s palette runs on a pink, #f472b6 , and it appears on nine of the ten plates above. Magenta is not in the spectrum. There is no wavelength that produces it: it is what the visual system builds when the long-wavelength and short-wavelength cones fire together and the middle one does not, and the brain closes a ring that the physics leaves open. So a sheet of ten bows, drawn as carefully to scale as we could manage, is drawn partly in a colour that no rainbow contains — and there is no version of these drawings that fixes it, because the pink is doing a job the spectrum has no way to do. We are not going to pretend that is a flaw we overlooked. It is the most interesting thing on the page. We left out the sea spray bow, the twinned bow and the Titan bow, and the reason is this sheet’s own rule. All three are in Field Guide No. 20 and all three are good. None of them can be drawn to scale in a way that tells you anything: a sea spray bow differs from a rainbow by 0.8° , which at three units to the degree is 2.4 units — about the width of the stroke it would be drawn in. A twinned bow’s split comes from drops flattened by one or two per cent. A Titan bow is at 49°, which would look like a slightly larger rainbow and teach nobody anything, because the interesting part is the liquid and not the angle. A specimen sheet organised around scale has to decline the entries where scale is not the story , and saying so is better than quietly dropping them. The reflection bow was cut for a worse reason, and it is worth admitting. It belongs here by every test — it is a scale-and-position phenomenon, it is beautiful, and it is the single commonest cause of a photograph captioned “triple rainbow.” It came out because drawing it honestly needs a second centre on the plate (the reflected sun has its own antisolar point above the horizon), and two centres on a sheet whose entire premise is one shared centre would have undermined the thing the sheet is for. That is a limitation of the format we chose, not a fact about the bow. It is carded properly at Field Guide No. 20 . Two plates break the shared centre, and both say so on their own faces rather than here. The Circumhorizontal Arc moves the sun to the top of the frame, because the arc sits 46° below the sun and would otherwise be off the bottom of the plate; the scale is unchanged. The 22° Halo and The Third and Fourth Order are centred on the sun rather than the antisolar point, which is not a break in the convention but the whole content of those two plates — they are on the other side of the sky, and the drawing is how you find that out. What the scale is worth, stated plainly. The radii here are computed from published angles at three units to the degree, and they are as good as those angles. Everything else is drawn for legibility: band widths are exaggerated (the primary’s by about 2.8×, and the plate prints that), brightness is suggestive rather than measured, and the sky is left out entirely. Where a figure is load-bearing it is printed on the plate and sourced under it. The two figures we would most like to improve are the circumhorizontal arc’s London and Los Angeles hours, which reached no primary computation and carry more of the argument than any other numbers on the page. On paper, this sheet loses its colour, and that is the right trade. The shared print stylesheet turns every SVG stroke to a single dark grey, because our five accents measure between 1.7:1 and 2.9:1 against white and not one of them clears the 3:1 a graphic needs to be legible. So a printed Bow-ery is line art. The geometry — which is the whole point — survives intact: a 22° halo still prints at half a rainbow’s radius, and Alexander’s dark band still prints 7.3° wide. What is lost is band order, which is why every plate whose argument is a colour order also prints that order as a label. A page about colour that cannot print its colour is worth writing down rather than hiding. Printed in grey. Every stroke on this sheet is a colour the shared print stylesheet flattens for legibility — the radii and the labels are unaffected, and the colour version is at starstuff.earth/bow-ery. Why a third “-ery”, and why it is an Easter egg. The Hatchery came from the small egg at the foot of the front page; The Quillery from the mascot beside it. This one comes from a catalogue that had to draw sixteen bows at 104×96 and could not show you how big any of them was. An egg is not a lower standard here — same sourcing, same fact-check ledger, same eight gates, same changelog entry as anything else on this site. Only the door moves. Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms Nobody Got His Eyes Right Thirty-one songs across a career — and the two things everyone knows about David Bowie that are not true. Both of them make the difference tidier than it was. The companion rack to Turn and Face the Strange, Zine No. 12. Playlist & essay · Sound
He did not have different-coloured eyes

One He did not have different-coloured eyes This is the most-looked-at face in the history of pop music, and the single fact everybody repeats about it is wrong. Bowie is very widely said to have had heterochromia — two irises of different colours. He did not. Both of his irises were the same colour. What he had was anisocoria: two pupils of different sizes, one of them permanently open. In February 1962, when he was fifteen, his schoolfriend George Underwood punched him in the left eye during a row over a girl. A fingernail caught the eyeball, and the muscles that contract the iris were left paralysed. From then on the left pupil could not close. A pupil stuck wide is a hole full of shadow, so the left eye photographs darker — and next to a right eye whose pupil is doing its ordinary job, the pair reads as two different colours. That is the whole illusion. Why one eye looked darker: a fixed pupil beside a working one Four eyes in two rows. The top row is dim light: both pupils are wide and the two eyes look alike. The bottom row is bright light: the right pupil has contracted to a small dot while the left pupil stays wide. The irises are the same colour in all four. A caption notes that only the lower row produces the apparent difference in colour. Same iris colour in all four. Only the pupil differs. Dim light — they match Bright light — they don't Right eye · pupil works Left eye · pupil fixed open contracted still wide — reads darker Iris colour is drawn identical in all four, because it was. The apparent difference appears only in light bright enough to make a working pupil close — which is to say under stage lights and camera flashes, which is where nearly every photograph of him was taken. Schematic, not a portrait. So the correction is not pedantry about a word. It changes what kind of thing the famous feature was. Heterochromia is a variation you are born with. Anisocoria from a punch is an injury, and this one had consequences: a pupil that cannot contract cannot limit the light coming in, and Bowie was reported to have had impaired depth perception for the rest of his life. The look that a million people have called otherworldly is one eye working and one eye damaged. Glamour is not an accommodation. Nobody ever seems to ask what a fixed pupil is like under a follow spot. He and Underwood stayed friends for the rest of his life, and Underwood — a painter — went on to make artwork for Bowie's records. Bowie himself said the eye gave him an interesting appearance and was, on balance, useful to him. Both things are allowed to be true. He made an injury into a signature, and it was still an injury, and neither half of that cancels the other.
And the constellation is not a constellation

Two And the constellation is not a constellation The second thing everyone knows is nearly as widely repeated and fails in the same direction. In January 2016, days after he died, the MIRA public observatory in Belgium and the radio station Studio Brussel announced a constellation for Bowie: seven stars near Mars, arranged in the lightning bolt from the Aladdin Sane sleeve. It is a genuinely lovely gesture and thousands of people posted about it. It is not a constellation. There are 88 constellations, the International Astronomical Union fixed the list in the 1920s, and it has not changed since. What MIRA made was an asterism — a line figure, a way of joining dots — and to their credit they said so themselves, describing it as an invented Bowie-asterism rather than an addition to the sky's official furniture. Nobody can register a constellation. Nobody can sell you a star, either, whatever the certificate says. Both errors lean the same way Notice what these two have in common, because it is the reason this page exists rather than just a rack of songs. Neither mistake is random. Heterochromia is prettier than a punch in the eye. An official constellation is grander than a radio station's tribute. Both errors take something real — a damaged iris, a nice gesture by a small observatory — and round it up into something more elegant, then travel further than the truth did. That is the exact mechanism Too Good to Check is about, and it is the reason we keep a field card for it. A claim that flatters its subject gets less scrutiny, not more. And there is a cost that is not just tidiness. When the story about somebody's difference is more beautiful than the difference, the practical part stops getting discussed. Sixty years of writing about that eye, and almost none of it about light sensitivity, or depth perception, or what it takes to perform under those conditions. The myth is a very comfortable place to stop.
What he actually did was set selves down in public

Three What he actually did was set selves down in public The argument about Bowie and difference is made at length in Zine No. 12, so this is the compressed version plus one thing the zine does not have. The zine's claim is that Bowie inverts what masking means for the rest of us. Many of us wear the involuntary kind — kept up to pass as normal, kept up until it costs something. His masking was authorship: selves made, shown in full view, and then put down. Ziggy, Aladdin Sane, the Thin White Duke, Major Tom. Unmasking, on that reading, does not have to mean excavating one true self from underneath. It can mean the freedom to be several things out loud and mean all of them. The thing worth adding is that he demonstrated the putting down as literally as anyone ever has. On 3 July 1973, at the Hammersmith Odeon, he told a sold-out room it was the last show they would ever do — and killed Ziggy on stage, mid-tour, at the height of it. Most of the band found out at the same time as the audience. The popular telling is a little too clean You will often read that he told nobody. Not quite: Mick Ronson knew, and by some accounts the stage manager was told shortly before, and the road crew were in on it. It was most of the band who were blindsided, not all of it. We are correcting a detail that makes the anecdote marginally less punchy, on a page whose whole first half is about stories getting rounded up. It would be a poor look to do the same thing ourselves two sections later. A persona you can end on a Tuesday in July is a persona you were authoring. That is the difference between a costume and a diagnosis, and it is why the zine reads his career as direction rather than deficit.
The ending was written down first

Four The ending was written down first And then, at the very end, he did the same trick one last time, in public, with the timing controlled to the day. ★ was released on 8 January 2016, his sixty-ninth birthday. The video for Lazarus — in which he sings from a hospital bed and then backs into a wardrobe and out of sight — went up the day before. He died on 10 January. Almost nobody outside his circle knew he had been ill. He made Blackstar for us, his parting gift. I knew for a year this was the way it would be. Tony Visconti, his producer, on 11 January 2016 — the day after. What that means for this collection is specific. The L★S Playlist already notes that Blackstar is not the bright burning kind of star but the collapsed kind — still massive, still present. Set beside the eye, the arc finishes an argument the whole career was making: the parts of you that got damaged, and the parts you decided to author, end up in the same body of work, and you do not have to sort them into the good ones and the bad ones before you are allowed to be here. That is what we mean by star stuff, said as plainly as we can say it. Not the difference redeemed. The difference included. Not: Not a diagnosis. Anisocoria is a documented physical injury with a date and a named cause. We are not reading anything else into his mind, his neurology, or his sexuality from his songs, and nothing on this page should be cited as though we had. Not damage as the source of the art. The punch did not make him Bowie. Suffering-as-fuel is one of the oldest and laziest stories about difference, and it conveniently excuses never fixing anything. Not the injury erased either. The opposite error, and the more common one here: calling the eye iconic and stopping. It cost him something, permanently, and the celebration usually skips that part. Not one true self, located and held still. The zine's refusal and this page's too — be yourself as an instruction to pick one and stop is not liberation. Not weird as a phase. Difference is not a stage on the way to normal. Not a correction offered as debunking. We are not scoring points off people who said heterochromia; nearly everyone did, including publications with fact-checkers. The point is how a flattering claim travels, not that anyone was foolish.
One — The capsule · 1969–1971 Untethering, read both ways at once: as loss, and as the only available exit.

Cut loose Space Oddity David Bowie · 1969 Major Tom drifts out past the capsule and decides not to come back, and the song refuses to tell you whether that is a death or a release. The ambiguity is the whole point and he never resolved it.
The Man Who Sold The World

Meeting yourself The Man Who Sold The World David Bowie · 1970 A song about running into a self you thought you had finished with. Later carried to a much larger audience by somebody else's cover, which is its own kind of Bowie joke.

Turn and face it Changes Live, Hammersmith 1973 · song 1971 The anthem the zine is named for. It turns to face the adults doing the assessing and tells them not to say the kids will grow out of it — the children being spat on are perfectly aware of what is happening to them.

The next lot Oh! You Pretty Things David Bowie · 1971 Addressed to the generation arriving to replace the one in charge, and cheerfully unbothered about what that will cost them. Hunky Dory's most quietly threatening song.

Watching from outside Life On Mars? David Bowie · 1971 A girl with mousy hair at the pictures, watching a world she has no part in. The most precise song anyone has written about being on the outside of the story and looking up instead.
Two — Selves, worn in public · 1972–1974 The personae, made in the open and set down in the open. Authorship, not concealment.

The clock starts Five Years David Bowie · 1972 The opening of Ziggy Stardust, and an unusual way to start a record about a rock star: with a deadline, and a long list of ordinary people noticed on the way to it.

Someone's out there Starman David Bowie · 1972 An alien who has been watching and wants to meet the kids specifically. Performed on Top of the Pops in a way that a great many people have since described as the moment they understood something about themselves.

Freak, claimed Moonage Daydream David Bowie · 1972 He names himself the alligator, the space invader, the mama-papa — a pile-up of self-descriptions that refuse to settle into one. Reclamation by sheer accumulation.

The persona itself Ziggy Stardust Live · song 1972 A song about a made-up rock star, sung by a real one pretending to be him, describing his own downfall in the third person. The seams are left showing deliberately.

You're not alone Rock 'n' Roll Suicide David Bowie · 1972 The closing track, and the reason the album is not actually bleak: it ends by insisting, at volume and directly to you, that you are not alone. Read it as a keep-on-livin' song, because it is one.

The bolt Aladdin Sane David Bowie · 1973 The next self, and the source of the lightning bolt that a Belgian observatory would later join seven stars into. Mike Garson's piano solo is the sound of a persona coming apart on purpose.

Permission slip Rebel Rebel Live · song 1974 Four bars of guitar and a flat statement that your mother's inability to tell what you are is not your problem. The most useful thing on this rack to hand to a fifteen-year-old.
Three — Plastic soul, then Berlin · 1975–1979 The stretch where he was least well and made some of the best of it. Not a redemption arc.

Borrowed and admitted Young Americans Live · song 1975 He called this phase plastic soul himself, which is more honest than most artists manage about a genre shift. Borrowing, named as borrowing, is a different act from passing.

Hold on Golden Years David Bowie · 1975 Made during the period he later said he could barely remember, and it sounds like glamour with something badly wrong underneath. The instruction in the chorus is to hang on; take it literally.

Blue room, low stimulus Sound and Vision David Bowie · 1977 A pop single about sitting in an empty room waiting to be able to work again, with the vocal arriving a minute and a half late. As accurate a description of a recovery week as anything on this rack.

No words needed Warszawa David Bowie · 1977 Six minutes with Brian Eno and almost no language — the vocal is in no actual tongue. Here because not everything that needs saying is available in sentences, which is a fact this community knows well.

Just for one day “Heroes” David Bowie · 1977 Note the quotation marks in the title — they are his, and they are ironic. The heroism on offer lasts one day, is available to two ordinary people by a wall, and is not offered as a permanent identity. That limit is what makes it bearable.

Camp as a crowbar Boys Keep Swinging David Bowie · 1979 A song listing the privileges of being a boy, sung so archly that the list collapses. The video, in which he plays his own backing singers in drag and wrecks the illusion on camera, is the argument.
Four — Ashes, and the years of being enormous · 1980–1986 Where he becomes a stadium, and the strangeness gets harder to find and is still in there.

Revisiting the capsule Ashes To Ashes David Bowie · 1980 Eleven years on he goes back for Major Tom and finds him a junkie — a sequel that refuses to flatter the original. Very few artists return to their most beloved character in order to disappoint you about him.

Compulsory style Fashion David Bowie · 1980 Not a song celebrating fashion — a song about being told to turn to the left, turn to the right, and do it because everyone is doing it. Read it as a compliance song and it gets much colder.

Give love one more chance Under Pressure Queen & David Bowie · 1981 Improvised in a room in Montreux and never really rehearsed. Its subject is the ordinary unbearable weight of things, and its answer — love, one more go — is delivered by two people who are both, plainly, out of their depth and singing anyway.

The enormous years Let's Dance David Bowie · 1983 The biggest record he ever made, and the video is about the dispossession of Aboriginal Australians — a fact almost nobody dancing to it in 1983 registered. He put the difficult thing in the most popular place he ever had.

The alien, loved Loving The Alien David Bowie · 1984 From a record he later disowned, and the best thing on it. Loving what you have been told is foreign, while knowing the story you were handed about it is wrong — which is roughly the job description of this whole collection.

Nothing much, and everything Absolute Beginners David Bowie · 1986 A vast, unembarrassed love song from a period nobody rates, in which he admits he knows almost nothing about anything except this. Sincerity with no persona in front of it, which was rarer for him than strangeness.
Five — The long way back · 1996–2013 Including ten years of saying nothing at all, which turned out to be a decision rather than an ending.

Spaceboy again Hallo Spaceboy David Bowie & Pet Shop Boys · 1996 The Pet Shop Boys remix, which pulls the Major Tom thread back in and asks, more or less, whether the whole gender arrangement is not something you could simply decline. In 1996, on the radio.

Ten years of silence, broken Where Are We Now? David Bowie · 2013 Released with no warning on his sixty-sixth birthday after a decade of public silence that everyone had read as retirement. Quiet, slow, and about Berlin. He came back by being smaller, not louder.

Fame, examined The Stars (Are Out Tonight) David Bowie · 2013 Stars as predators who need to be watched to stay alive. Coming from him, at that point, it reads less as complaint than as a technical report from someone who has done the job for forty years.
Six — ★ · 2016 Released on his sixty-ninth birthday. He died two days later. Nearly nobody knew.

The collapsed kind ★ (Blackstar) David Bowie · 2016 Ten minutes, jazz musicians, no interest at all in being a single. Not the bright burning kind of star — the collapsed kind, which is still massive and still present and bends everything near it.

Staged as a rising Lazarus David Bowie · 2016 He sings from a hospital bed, with buttons over his eyes, then backs into a wardrobe and closes the door. The video went up the day before the album and three days before he died. Nothing about the timing was accidental.

The plain one Dollar Days David Bowie · 2016 The least costumed thing he ever recorded: an admission that he is not going to see England again, delivered without a single persona standing in front of it. Forty-seven years after Major Tom, no capsule.

The last track I Can't Give Everything Away David Bowie · 2016 The final song on the final record, and its title is a refusal — after a career of bringing everything to the front, he keeps something back. The right place to stop, and he chose it.

Weird on purpose Turn and face the strange David Bowie built a whole career out of the thing the rest of us are told to hide: strangeness. Not strangeness survived, or managed, or apologised for — strangeness led with. "Changes" (Hunky Dory, 1971) is the anthem for it: a song that turns to face the people doing the judging and tells them, plainly, not to tell the kids to grow up and out of it. The children spat on are quite aware of what they're going through. That is our register exactly. Weird isn't a phase to outgrow or a deficit to correct. It's a stance. To turn and face the strange is to stop treating your own difference as a problem to be solved, and start treating it as a direction to move in. Difference is not a stage you pass through on the way to normal. It's a place you can choose to face. “Changes” · live, Hammersmith 1973 turn and face the strange Turn and Face the Strange · Stimpunks

“Ziggy Stardust” · 1972 a persona, worn in the open Many selves The masks were the point Ziggy Stardust. Aladdin Sane. The Thin White Duke. Major Tom. Bowie made selves and set them down in public, on purpose — a career of personae worn in full view and then let go. Many of us know a different kind of mask: the involuntary, exhausting kind, worn to pass as normal and kept up until it costs us. Bowie turns that inside out. His masking was authorship, not concealment — something you choose and show, not something that shows you up. Here's the liberating turn. Unmasking doesn't have to mean finding the one true self hidden underneath. It can mean the freedom to author your selves out loud — to be many things and mean all of them. Not one true self, hidden and recovered. A constellation of selves, all of them yours. Turn and Face the Strange · Stimpunks
Everything hidden, brought to the front

The hidden, visible Everything hidden, brought to the front One of our taglines could be a description of his whole method: Everything that was normally supposed to be hidden was brought to the front. Star Stuff · a tagline Bowie did this for a living. Queerness, artifice, tenderness, fear, the seams of the costume left showing on purpose — brought forward instead of tucked away. He kept the machinery visible and dared you to call it fake. We keep him close on our Bring to the Front page for exactly this reason. Visibility is risk and liberation at once — and to bring the hidden to the front is to refuse the shame that insists it should have stayed back there. “Starman” · 1972 brought to the front, on live TV Turn and Face the Strange · Stimpunks
From the capsule to the blackstar

“Space Oddity” · 1969 the capsule “★ (Blackstar)” · 2016 the collapsed kind Untether · ascend From the capsule to the blackstar "Space Oddity" (1969) sends Major Tom drifting out past the capsule, and the untethering reads both ways at once — as loss, and as liberation. Being cut loose from the ground as a way of being free. Blackstar and "Lazarus" (both 2016), recorded as he was dying, stage the ending as a rising. Not the bright, burning kind of star — the collapsed kind. Still massive. Still present. He sings from a hospital bed and then backs out of sight, a goodbye staged as an ascension. Across a lifetime, Bowie kept returning to the cosmos as the one place difference could finally breathe. Which is our register too. Cut loose from the ground is one way to say free. Purest freedom Authenticity is our purest freedom Bowie complicates authenticity in a way we find useful and honest. He wasn't authentic by being one true, unchanging self. He was authentic by refusing to pretend there was only one. That's a liberating correction for anyone who has been told their real self is the wrong self. Authenticity as self-determination — the freedom to change, to contradict, to become — rather than authenticity as a fixed thing you're required to match. Authenticity is our purest freedom. “Lazarus” · 2016 the most naked, and the most free What this is not The reframe only works if we refuse the counterfeits that usually travel under the same words. Notauthenticity as a single fixed self you must locate and hold still to be believed. Notweird as a phase — something to grow up and out of. Notmasking as the price of admission, the cost of being allowed in the room. Not"be yourself" as a command to pick one self and stop. The freedom isn't to be found out. It's to keep becoming, out loud, without shame. Turn and Face the Strange · Stimpunks

“Heroes” · 1977 we can be heroes The whole constellation Made of star stuff Every persona, every change, every strange and luminous thing Bowie set in front of us — all of it made of the same forged elements as the rest of us. He read the cosmos as a home for difference, and so do we. Bowie opens our L★S playlist for a reason. His whole arc is a long argument that you were never meant to be one fixed, quiet, normal thing — that difference belongs here, fully, as part of the universe knowing itself in every possible way. So: turn and face the strange. You belong here — not despite the strangeness, but as it. You were never one fixed thing. Neither was he. Neither is the universe. Where in your life is "authenticity" being used to mean "pick one self and hold still," and what changes if it means the freedom to keep becoming? Whose strangeness taught you to face your own? Turn and Face the Strange is the twelfth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the one about David Bowie — read as an example of ways of being star stuff, and of being defiantly, joyfully weird. The songs referenced are real and worth naming precisely. "Changes" appeared on Hunky Dory (1971) and as a single in 1972. "Space Oddity" was released in 1969. "Heroes" was released in 1977. Blackstar arrived on 8 January 2016, Bowie's 69th birthday, two days before his death on 10 January 2016; "Lazarus" was released as a single in December 2015, its video days before he died. The personae named — Ziggy Stardust (1972), Aladdin Sane (1973), the Thin White Duke (1976), and Major Tom — are his own inventions, worn in public and set down again. This zine is commentary and celebration. The performances on each spread are embedded from official YouTube uploads; the songs, recordings, and personae are the work of David Bowie and his collaborators, and we quote only the briefest hook and reproduce no lyrics or artwork. The two taglines — "Everything that was normally supposed to be hidden was brought to the front" and "Authenticity is our purest freedom" — are Star Stuff's, and appear across our work, including Bring to the Front. The reading — Bowie as a way of being star stuff, unmasking as authorship rather than exposure, difference as direction — is ours. Bowie belongs on the L★S playlist, which his whole career opens. Link 1 · Frankfurt, 1604 The theory of the hole documented Start with an instrument so simple it is barely an object: a hole. By the late sixteenth century, European astronomers measured the Sun by letting it shine through a small aperture onto a screen. You cannot look at the Sun; you can look at what gets through a hole. It was the standard method, and it had a fault nobody could explain. Solar diameters measured this way came out systematically too large. Not randomly — consistently, in one direction, against what the same astronomers got by other means. Tycho Brahe built careful apertures into his instruments and developed a correction, but the correction was empirical: a fudge that worked, with no account of why. The missing thing was a theory of how an image forms behind a small opening. Kepler supplied it in Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena (1604) — the same book that, a few pages away, needed a new word for the region between full shadow and full light and made one. The blockage was already the instrument. What was missing was an account of what the blockage was doing. the first link, and the shape of all the others Note the order carefully, because the whole chain repeats it. The method came first and worked badly. The understanding came second and fixed it. Nobody theorised the pinhole and then built one; they built one, got wrong answers for decades, and eventually worked out what the hole was doing to the light. Which is a thing worth knowing about instruments in general: using one is not the same as understanding it, and the gap between those two can be measured in centuries. lightbuilt 1 · 1604 · the theory of the hole We Learned to Build the Eclipse · Stimpunks

Link 3 · Guntur, 18 August 1868 The line in the fire documented A total eclipse crossed India on 18 August 1868, and a great many people had travelled a great distance to point spectroscopes at it. A spectroscope spreads light into its colours and shows you the bright lines that particular atoms emit. Aim one at a prominence during totality and you get a handful of lines, each one a signature. Among them, that day, was a yellow line sitting very close to — but not on — the familiar pair emitted by sodium. It was seen by several people. The 1868 eclipse detections are credited to Jules Janssen and also to Georges Rayet, Captain C. T. Haig, Norman Pogson and John Herschel. This matters, and the popular version of the story loses it: a lot of instruments caught that line. What Janssen took from the day, though, was not the yellow line at all. It was something about the brightness. The prominence lines were not faint. They were blazing. And a blazing line does not necessarily need a dark sky — it needs to be picked out of a bright one. what Janssen noticed at Guntur He had come to use the eclipse. He left having realised he might not need it. lightbuilt 3 · 18 Aug 1868 · Guntur We Learned to Build the Eclipse · Stimpunks

Link 4 · the next morning The next morning documented This is the hinge of the whole chain, and it happened within twenty-four hours. On 19 August 1868, the day after the eclipse, Janssen set up again — in ordinary daylight, with no Moon in the way — and successfully observed the prominence spectrum anyway. The trick is to use a narrow slit and enough dispersion. Spreading light out dilutes the continuous glare of the sky across the whole spectrum, while an emission line stays concentrated at its own wavelength. Push it far enough and the line climbs out of the background. The eclipse had been doing that job crudely by removing the glare; the instrument could do it precisely by spreading it thin. The eclipse was never the method. It was a demonstration of what the method would have to achieve. the sentence this zine is built on Sit with the timing. He waited years for the alignment, travelled to India for it, got his few minutes — and the thing the alignment actually gave him was the knowledge of what to build. He then built it immediately, and never needed the alignment again. Every subsequent link in this chain is a repetition of that morning at a larger scale. lightbuilt 4 · 19 Aug 1868 · the next morning We Learned to Build the Eclipse · Stimpunks
One medal, two men, no eclipse

Link 5 · London, 20 October 1868 One medal, two men, no eclipse documented Meanwhile, in London, someone had been trying to do exactly this for two years without ever leaving the country. Norman Lockyer had conceived the same idea in 1866 — that a good enough spectroscope should reach the prominences in daylight — and had then spent two years failing to obtain an instrument adequate to the job. He got there on 20 October 1868. Both men reported to the Académie des Sciences, and the reports arrived within days of one another. The Académie, faced with two independent claims to the same method, struck a medal for the pair of them. It is a genuinely nice piece of history, and it is nearly always told as a coincidence — two men, same idea, same season, how remarkable. It is not much of a coincidence. It is what a well-posed problem looks like when the instruments finally catch up. Lockyer had the idea in 1866 and was blocked by hardware. Janssen got the idea from the eclipse and was not blocked at all. The idea was available; the glass was the constraint. Two people arrive at the same door in the same month because the door has just become openable, not because the universe arranged a story. what simultaneous discovery usually means Both were awarded for the method. Link 7 · 1868–1895 No bench, no element contested Lockyer and the chemist Edward Frankland proposed a name — helium, from hēlios, the Sun. For roughly a quarter of a century, a great many chemists simply declined to accept it. The objection was not that the spectroscopy was sloppy. The objection was that nobody could put the gas on a bench. Nineteenth-century chemistry was a science of substances you could handle: weigh them, dissolve them, heat them, combine them, hand a sample to a rival so they could fail to disprove you. That was what an element was, operationally. A thing you could only ever see in light that had left a body 150 million kilometres away was, to a working chemist, not really a thing at all. the reason helium waited 27 years And notice what makes this hard rather than stupid. The sceptics were applying a real standard, for real reasons. Spectra had already produced false alarms — the next spread is entirely about two of them. Demanding a sample was not obstinacy; it was the discipline's best available guard against exactly the failure mode that was, at that very moment, also occurring. They were rigorous, and they were wrong. Helium was real the entire time. What was actually being argued about was never the Sun. It was which kinds of evidence get to count — and the answer being enforced was: the kind we can hold. Everything reachable only at a distance, only by its light, only through an instrument, sat outside the category of the real until the instrument caught up.
