Stability on a slope and shell strength do the work instead. In the last band, walking away turns out not to be the failure state: a megapode chick hatches under 40 to 150 cm of compost, digs out unaided in a median forty hours, and can fly the same day; a brine shrimp cyst waits up to eighteen dry years and resumes where it stopped; and a cuckoo's shell has a second job no other egg here has, since it must survive being looked at — matched to host retinal function rather than to our eyes, by host-specific female lineages, with the arms-race framing now under live challenge. Then the sixteenth card, dashed, with no reframe table : the egg-crack accounts, borrowed from trans communities and credited as unowned, because there is no mistaken verdict about the morning your own life rearranged itself behind you. One thing the biology does supply is a limit rather than a licence — across birds, squamates, turtles, crocodilians and the echidna, the tool that opens an egg is on the inside . You cannot do it for anyone. You can only be audible. The tenth guide to arrive independently at the same sentence: there is no standard egg. Field Guide No. 17 A Field Guide to Resting Field Guide · 15 + 2 · companion to No. 59 there is no standard way to rest — not an amount, not a posture, not an organ Fifteen ways of resting among our Terran kin, sorted by what is doing the resting . An animal with no brain and no clock. A bird ten months airborne. A squirrel below freezing. And the famous twenty-hour bat, which is one measurement at one temperature. 15 entries → Details Companion to No. 59 , and it asks the question the zine assumes an answer to: what does resting actually look like, across kin who share almost no anatomy? The bands sort by what carries the rest rather than by taxon or by amount. Hydra and Cassiopea have a nerve net and no brain and meet every behavioural criterion for sleep, and Hydra has no circadian clock either — a roughly four-hour cycle instead (Kanaya et al. 2020). C. elegans rests for two to three hours before each of its four moults (Raizen et al. 2008). Great frigatebirds sleep 42 minutes a day aloft, in the soar and never while flapping; common swifts spend over 99 per cent of a ten-month phase airborne, and the record is not uniform — some individuals roosted in midwinter, others never landed (Hedenström et al. 2016). Sperm whales hang vertically and go silent, unresponsive to a boat until it touched them (Miller et al. 2008). Bears keep their skeleton through six months of disuse; arctic ground squirrels hold a core temperature of −2.9 °C by supercooling, with no antifreeze in the plasma (Barnes 1989); lungfish seal themselves in a cocoon of living cells for years. Emperor penguins reach 37.5 °C inside a huddle while it is −19 °C outside, and two thirds of the saving is geometry rather than warmth (Gilbert et al. 2008). Parrotfish build a mucus tent for 2.5 per cent of a day's energy and cut parasite attacks from nearly all to about one in ten (Grutter et al. 2011). Northern fur seals suppress REM for weeks and never pay it back . And the card the guide would keep if it could keep one: the sleepiest-mammal figure of 19.9 hours is a single 1960s measurement at 33 °C on an unknown number of animals, which becomes 11.0 hours at 26 °C — and about one per cent of mammal species have had their sleep measured at all (Harding et al. 2022). Two cards carry no reframe table : sponges, because nobody knows yet and writing actually over an open question is bluff; and plants, because nyctinasty was named by Linnaeus and Darwin himself called the daytime version “improperly” sleep, read here from the 1880 primary. Seventeen cards, fifteen entries. Field Guide No. 18 A Field Guide to Unfinished Animals Field Guide · 16 + 2 · companion to No. 61 there is no final draft — and what varies here is not the animals, it is us Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake and tagged for whether the argument is over. Drawn upside down, then back-to-front. Three animals in three groups. A skull on a tail. Two arms for forty-four years. 16 entries → Details Companion to No. 61 , and it asks the question that zine assumes an answer to: how often does the record actually move? Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake, and — this guide’s one addition to the house form, borrowed from How We Got Here — every card carries a status : revised (ten cards), contested (four), or name stuck (two). A catalogue of corrections that will not say which corrections are finished would read as a list of settled triumphs, which is the smoothing it is complaining about. Assembled wrong: Hallucigenia was published in 1977 walking on its spines, inverted by Ramsköld and Hou in 1991, and turned end-for-end by Smith and Caron in 2015 when they found the eyes, mouth ring and tooth-lined throat at the other end — wrong on one axis for fourteen years and on the other for twenty-four more . Anomalocaris spent most of a century as three animals in three groups: a shrimp-like appendage, the “jellyfish” Peytoia , and the “sponge” Laggania , united by Whittington and Briggs in 1985 — and then the correction was itself corrected , when Daley and Bergström found a three-plate oral cone in 2012 and Peytoia became valid again. Cope put the skull of Elasmosaurus on the end of its neck in 1868, reading a neck as a tail; and the famous story about who caught him is wrong — it was Joseph Leidy , on 8 March 1870, with Marsh in the room, and Marsh’s claim survives only in a newspaper piece two decades later. Mantell put the Iguanodon thumb spike on its nose; it took thirty-odd whole skeletons at Bernissart for Dollo to move it to the hand. Known from almost nothing: Deinocheirus was two arms found on 9 July 1965 and named in 1970 by Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz , and it stayed honestly unplaced for forty-four years until two near-complete skeletons showed a humpbacked, duck-billed omnivore. The Spinosaurus holotype burned in the Munich bombing of 24–25 April 1944 , after Stromer’s requests to move the collection were refused — so every reconstruction since argues from photographs, and the aquatic reading is contested. Helicoprion ’s tooth whorl was placed on the snout, the upper jaw, the back and the tail before a 2013 CT scan put it in the lower jaw — of a specimen that had been in a drawer since 1950 . The line moved: Brontosaurus (the short form of the zine). Torosaurus , proposed as merely a mature Triceratops in 2010 and rejected in 2012, still unresolved — the mirror image of the Brontosaurus case, a merge rather than a split, with the opposite fate. Nanotyrannus , dismissed for forty years as a juvenile T. rex and reinstated in 2025 by Zanno and Napoli on a near-adult skeleton from the Duelling Dinosaurs block, with a second species nobody had separated out. And Tanystropheus , one species until a CT scan made it two, both size classes fully grown. Three of those four errors were the same error: explaining a difference by age. The name outlived it: Oviraptor means egg seizer and it was brooding its own clutch — and the card is careful that the 1995 brooding specimen is an oviraptorid later named Citipati , not Osborn’s animal , because the tidy version of that story is the one that travels. Basilosaurus means king lizard and Owen showed it was a mammal within five years; he proposed Zeuglodon and priority refused it. Both names are permanent , which is the band the zine cares about: a label outlives its refutation by rule or by repetition , and only one of those admits what it is doing. Tidier than the evidence: the fish-crawls-out story has a date problem — Devonian trackways about eighteen million years older than the earliest tetrapod bodies — and the retelling of that correction is smoothed too , because those trackways are themselves disputed. The film raptor is not the fossil one. And the tail-dragging dinosaur was corrected by a whole field changing its mind, from one 1969 monograph. Two cards are dashed and carry no reframe table. Mary Anning found, prepared and drew the first complete plesiosaur in 1823 and Conybeare presented it without naming her; women could not join the Geological Society until 1904, and on her only London trip no label carried her name. She is not a specimen , and running sounds like / actually down the side of a person would file her with the misreconstructed animals, which is the injury. And the last card has nothing to correct yet : on the guide’s own argument some entries above are currently wrong, and it says where to expect it — the age explanation, the fragment that fits every reading, and the instrument that arrives before the answer. Arrival line: there is no final draft , and the guide says plainly why it departs from the house formula: what varies here is not the animals but us. Eighteen cards, sixteen entries. Field Guide No. 19 A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Family Field Guide · 13 + 1 · companion to No. 64 there is no standard family — and what varies is not how related anybody is, it is what the care runs on Thirteen ways of being family among our Terran kin, sorted by what the care actually flows through . A ledger. A coalition of strangers. A boundary crossed. A pile of pups nobody can claim. 13 entries → Details Companion to No. 64 , and it asks the question that zine leaves open: if care is not keyed to relatedness, what is it keyed to? The sort is by mechanism, because the obvious sort — a line from kin to non-kin — collapsed on the first entry that had to go at both ends of it. In superb fairy-wrens , 76% of offspring (138 of 181) were sired by extra-group males who contribute no care, and 95% of broods contained such young; every male in the group feeds the brood anyway (Mulder, Dunn, Cockburn, Lazenby-Cohen & Howell, 1994). Greater anis — Riehl's own study species — share one clutch between unrelated pairs and show no kin discrimination at all. Pied kingfishers admit an unrelated helper only when conditions are poor enough that the pair cannot feed the brood alone, which is hospitality that began in need and is kept in the entry rather than trimmed. Two bonobo females at Wamba adopted infants from a different social group , nursing them, with no aggression from the group — the first such record in any great ape (Tokuyama et al., 2021). A bottlenose dolphin at Rangiroa reared a presumed melon-headed whale calf alongside her own for about three years (Carzon et al., 2019). Banded mongooses give birth 64% on the same night into one communal litter, and escorts show no assortment by parentage — the literature's own phrase for the effect is a veil of ignorance . Section five exists because 55% of cooperatively breeding birds really do nest primarily with kin: long-tailed tits find their relatives by call similarity , and post-reproductive killer whale grandmothers help more than breeding ones, because a grandmother with her own calf has less to give. And section six cuts against the guide's own grain — Komdeur's translocated Seychelles warblers stay as helpers on good territories rather than breed on poor ones, so constraint is arithmetic and not a wall; and the Damaraland mole-rat , the textbook eusocial mammal, turns out not to be an obligate cooperative breeder at all. An overclaim in our own favour is still an overclaim. The families people make get the fourteenth card and no reframe table, because chosen family is already the most adjudicated arrangement in the catalogue and does not need another verdict from us. Field Guide No. 20 A Field Guide to Rainbows Field Guide · 16 + 3 · companion to Nos. 69–70 there is no standard rainbow — and rarity, it turns out, is a fact about where the observer was standing Sixteen rainbows sorted by what physically changed — the drop, the path inside it, the light arriving, the surface the cone meets, the instrument at its point. Not a rarity countdown. 16 entries → Details The catalogue for No. 69 and No. 70 , and the guide that takes on a whole genre: every listicle of rainbow kinds sorts by appearance and then ranks by rarity , and both sorts fail. Appearance fails twice, in opposite directions — a fogbow looks nothing like a rainbow and differs only in drop size, its colours all present and diffracted so wide that they overlap into white; a sea spray bow looks identical to a rainbow and is genuinely a different bow, because salt raises the refractive index and shrinks the radius by about 0.8°, so the two stand visibly misaligned in one sky. Rarity fails because it is not a property of any bow: a circumhorizontal arc needs the sun above 58°, which is impossible north of 55°N and happens for roughly 140 hours a year in London against 670 in Los Angeles. Supernumerary arcs cannot be produced by geometric optics at all — Thomas Young explained them by interference in 1804 and they became evidence for the wave theory of light; Airy dismissed him for predicting the wrong angles, and Young had merely missed a 90° phase shift. Third- and fourth-order bows stand around the sun and waited until 2011 for a photograph, found by people who knew exactly where to look. A moonbow carries every colour and a long exposure records them: it is the rods, not the bow, that cannot report them. A dewbow is a hyperbola because a cone met a plane, and a full-circle bow is the only kind there is, seen from somewhere the ground is not in the way. Rainbow light is about 96% polarised, so a lens can switch it off while the sky is unchanged. And the glory is carded as openly unfinished — the surface-wave consensus holds and the precise mechanism is still called obscure. The section on what the light did inside the drop is led by the double rainbow , carded with its mechanism: one bounce leaves at about 42.7°, two at about 50° with the colour order reversed, the outer bow is 43% as bright because a longer path loses more light, and Alexander’s dark band between them is a direction into which neither bow returns any light at all. The mechanism is the catalogue’s; the argument that “secondary” is a rank the physics does not contain stays No. 70’s. Three cards get no reframe table: the ice halos, because they are not rainbows; the antisolar cone — that the bow is centred on your own shadow and no two people see the same one — which is the whole of No. 69; and the flag and the song, which live at the Sound rack. Unique to each observer is not the same as unreal — the guide refuses the word illusion on its own page. Field Guide No. 21 A Field Guide to Third Nature Field Guide · 12 + 1 · companion to No. 74 a support nobody named is a support nobody defends Thirteen habitats we made by accident — and, on every card, the improvement now removing it. Insulation. Cleaner seed. Remediation. Regeneration. None of them should be reversed. 12 entries → Details The catalogue for No. 74 , built out of that chain’s tenth link: matsutake became rare across Japan by abandonment rather than destruction, because fossil fuel replaced firewood and the woodlands nobody was cutting grew too shady for pine. That turned out not to be a special case. Anna Tsing’s third nature is what manages to live despite capitalism; this asks what it is actually living on. The sort is by what made the habitat — the work, the structure, the damage — because the sort we tried first, by how damaged the place is , collapsed: a hay meadow and a lead-poisoned spoil heap sit at opposite ends of any damage scale and are the same kind of object here. Corncockle did not tolerate farming, it was farming — harvested, stored and re-sown with the grain until better seed cleaning screened its large seeds out. The corncrake needed a late, slow cut, and when the requirement was finally written into a scheme the population rose from 480 to 589 calling males in five years, reached 1,289 by 2014, and slipped again when the prescriptions changed. The high brown fritillary is the entry that embarrasses an instinct: leave the woodland alone is the mechanism of its loss, because it needed the coppice rotation to keep opening clearings. Black redstarts , a bird of Alpine scree, bred on Blitz rubble and declined city by city with regeneration; 27–74 pairs remain and they now breed on land defined as available for development. Swifts nest in gaps that insulation closes. Chimney swifts we assumed were chimney-dependent — recent work finds many still nesting in big hollow trees, which changes what to do, and a guide about unnamed supports should be the last place to invent a dependence that is not there. East of the Rockies every documented purple martin nests in a box a person put up, an arrangement recorded in Choctaw and Chickasaw gourd housing in the 1700s; nothing needs to be improved to end it, only ignored. Calaminarian grassland is Annex I habitat 6130 — a legally protected community held open by lead and zinc poisoning, whose spring sandwort miners called leadwort because it showed them where the galena was; the North Pennines survey records a lichen abundant at Nenthead smeltmill “until the restoration of Nenthead Mines.” Oil platforms off California are among the most productive fish habitat per unit area measured, and decommissioning law says remove them. The London Underground mosquito is the card where we had it wrong: a 2025 genomic study puts molestus ’ origin in ancient Mediterranean agriculture, not the Tube — the accidental habitat was real and three orders of magnitude older, and nobody was careless. The peregrine goes the other way and is here so the guide is not a mood. The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone gets a dashed card and no reframe table , because Deryabina et al. and Møller & Mousseau genuinely disagree and filling in an actually column would be picking a winner in a live dispute. Refuses damage-as-good, ruin as an aesthetic, “nature is resilient,” and any suggestion that the improvements should be undone. A brook is a chord of bells, and the pitch of each one is its size. Field Guide No. 22 Under the Word Field Guide · 18 entries · words by Helen Edgar, Marion McLaughlin & Felicity Goodhall eighteen borrowed and invented words for Autistic joy, and what is actually holding each one up Provenance graded rather than flattened — some attested, some real words wearing a word-list gloss, some invented online in the last decade. The sort is by what you find underneath: thirteen have a mechanism, five have a person. 18 entries → Details Built on Words: Inspired by the experience of being monotropic , a free open-source community e-book by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), Marion McLaughlin (Aurora Consulting) and Felicity Goodhall (Flappy Inky Feathers), who credit @aesthetic_logophile and Tom Read Wilson’s On The Tip Of My Tongue among their own sources. The edition read here is the 104-page January 2025 PDF. The words are theirs and the monotropic reading quoted on every card is theirs; what this guide adds is the provenance and the mechanism. The sort was not the one we set out to make: the plan was to file by feeling — joy, longing, solitude, kinship — and it collapsed at once because the feelings overlap almost entirely. What actually divides them is what is under the word. Thirteen have a mechanism , and it is startlingly often variation . A brook’s voice is air bubbles ringing at a frequency set by radius alone (Minnaert, Philosophical Magazine , 1933), so the sound is a chorus that only works because no two bells match. The bright spots under a tree are pinhole images of the Sun , which is why they all turn into the same crescent during a partial eclipse. The glitter path on water is specular reflection from the small fraction of wave facets tilted toward one observer — it points at you, and nobody else’s road shares a single wave. Dark adaptation is a second visual system that takes tens of minutes of rhodopsin to enter and one bright light to destroy. The smell of an old book is the book coming apart, in vanillin and benzaldehyde and furfural. A cloud floats because its water is divided finely enough to fall at a centimetre a second. Blossom order is a chilling requirement — four thermostats, not four runners. Five have a person underneath instead , and that is a firmer foundation rather than a weaker one, because a person can be checked: the famous English definition of toska is Nabokov’s translation note, not a dictionary; duende ’s aesthetic sense was argued by Lorca in a 1933 lecture and the everyday Spanish word means a house-sprite; limerence was coined by Dorothy Tennov and published in 1979 and never entered any diagnostic manual , which the card says rather than borrowing the authority of the word psychology ; anam cara is two ordinary old Irish words carried into English by one 1997 book; and cynefin is a Welsh word with a second, separate career as a decision framework. Three of these words were invented online within the last decade and one is a Latin word wearing a meaning it never had — marmoris is the genitive of marble — and the cards say so on their faces, because a community that reaches for a word, fails to find one, and makes one is the most Star Stuff thing in the booklet; what would be dishonest is selling recent invention as inheritance. Coddiwomple is not old English slang however often it is sold as such, and the behaviour it names is superbly documented in a desert ant that wanders out and runs home in a straight line. The bouba/kiki figure is printed as 17 of 25 languages rather than “universal,” after Ćwiek et al. (2022), because the three languages where it failed are the interesting part. Five refusals, the first of which is the trap the whole guide is walking past: not that the science proves the feeling is real. The feeling was already real, and physics is not a permit. The bird at the bottom of the insult is the bird the evidence came from. Field Guide No. 23 Bird Minds Field Guide · 13 entries · companion to No. 86 thirteen birds, sorted by what we wanted each one to prove Alex, the New Caledonian crow, the kea, the cockatoos of forty-four suburbs, the ravens who wait for tomorrow, the magpie whose famous mirror result failed replication, two cachers with opposite problems — and then four nobody asked, holding the map. 13 entries → Details The sort is the finding, and it was not the sort we set out to make. By taxonomy you get parrots, corvids and everyone else, which says nothing about minds; by cleverness you are building the ranking this house refuses. What actually divides these thirteen is the question a researcher brought to them — a fact about us rather than about birds. Three sections hold the birds recruited into an argument: asked to mean it (Alex cross-classifying colour and object; the budgerigar carrying open-ended vocal learning, a capacity we share with parrots, songbirds, hummingbirds and some cetaceans but not with apes), asked to make a plan (metatool problems solved around tools that are out of sight; the kea’s statistical inference; ravens refusing food they could eat now for a token worth something only tomorrow; the cockatoo bin culture that spread to 44 Sydney suburbs with site-specific styles and provoked a human counter-culture of bricks and bungees), and asked to remember when (a nutcracker holding 30,000 caches for six months by landmark geometry — move the landmarks 20 cm and the bird searches 20 cm off — against a scrub-jay that must hold when because its caches perish at different rates). The fourth section is where the guide’s line arrives. The pigeon, the chicken, the barn owl and the ostrich were never candidates for cleverness, and between them they supplied the fibre architecture, the single-cell developmental atlas, the second species that made one measurement a finding, and the negative control that breaks brain mass as a predictor. Nobody put them on a poster. One card corrects our own shipped work: the Eurasian magpie’s mirror result rested on two of five birds, carried the authors’ own caution that the sample was too small, and failed a close larger-sample replication in 2020 — and Field Guide No. 11 had listed self-recognition in the column a reframe table uses to say what is actually the case. Two cards carry no reframe table at all , and the absence is the argument: the origin of the circuit and the fairness of the corvid-versus-ape comparison have no verdict to correct, so running the apparatus over them would borrow the authority of a settled finding for an open question — the same rule as Field Guide No. 10 . Pallial neuron share runs about 19 per cent in primates against 62 in parrots and 78 in songbirds; brains in this literature run from one gram to twenty-five. There is no standard bird — not among the birds, and not in the sense the insult intends either, since there was never a standard for them to fall short of.
The limit the form found on itself

The limit the form found on itself The best thing this collection has produced is a place where the format stops , and it was the tenth guide that found it. Being a Turtle holds twelve animals and then, in a separate section behind a different card, five turtles that people made: Turtle Island, ao , Kurma, Great A'Tuin, and a Larrakia Star Dreaming it cites rather than retells. They are not entries. They have a dashed border instead of a solid one, and they do not get a reframe table — because the reframe table is a machine for correcting a mistaken verdict, and running “sounds like / actually” over somebody's cosmology would be obscene. The guide says so on its own face, and then makes the point structurally rather than only in prose: the format difference is the argument. A catalogue that had quietly filed five cosmologies as specimens would have been a tidier page and a much worse one. This is the sharpest thing the form has learned about itself, and it is now the standing rule — if a subject cannot take the apparatus, it gets a different card, not a smaller one. The drift Four of the first five guides were cosmological. Guides six through eleven are all biological. Constellations, elements, worlds and stars gave way to symbioses, nervous systems, migration, sharks, turtles and tortoises — and nobody decided that. It is easy to see why it happened: animals come with better-documented individual cases, and the deficit vocabulary this form exists to dismantle is thicker in biology than in astronomy. It is also worth naming, because a collection that drifts without noticing has stopped choosing. The sky has not run out of catalogues. Naming it worked, which is the only reason this paragraph is worth keeping. This section previously ended by saying the honest lead was “a guide that goes back to the sky, or to something that is neither animal nor star.” My Monotropic Galaxy is both at once — cosmic vocabulary throughout, and a subject that is neither animal nor star but a person's inner life. The drift is broken at twelve. Writing the gap down on a public page is what made it get filled. And then the thirteenth went straight back to animals, which is worth admitting in the same breath. The Ways of Being Alone is wolves, bees, pandas, pumas and apes — the drift's exact shape again, one guide after it was named as broken. It arrived that way because it came from Betsy Selvam's essay on Autistic solitude and went looking for what our kin do about company, and biology is where that question is answered. That is a reason, not an excuse. One guide out of the pattern does not make a habit; the sky still has not run out of catalogues. Not Not a cabinet of curiosities. These are not weird creatures assembled to be marvelled at. Every entry is an ordinary member of its group doing an ordinary thing, and the surprise is only ever about how narrowly we had drawn the category. Not diagnosis by analogy. The octopus is not autistic. The slime mold is not a metaphor for anybody's cognition. Where a guide reaches for a human parallel it marks it as a reach, and the entries themselves stay about the animals. Not proof. Biology does not settle questions about human belonging, and the naturalistic fallacy is a trap this form walks straight past if nobody holds it. A rhyme, not a proof is in these guides because it has to be. Not settled where it isn't. The symbioses guide keeps root-to-fungus mycorrhizal trade, which is settled, and hedges the forest-wide “wood wide web” story, which Karst, Jones & Hoeksema found insufficiently supported — “Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests,” Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023. It rhymes beautifully with mutual aid, which is exactly why it slipped past us in three pieces before anyone checked. Not a ranking, however it is read. Numbered guides and numbered entries are an index, not a league table. The number says when a guide was made; nothing in it says which entry won.

What is not here yet Nothing is scoped and waiting, which matches Sound and differs from Print , where a sheet sits deliberately unbuilt. The lead this section used to carry has been taken up. It read: a guide that goes back to the sky, or to something that is neither animal nor star. My Monotropic Galaxy answered it on both counts, and it is left recorded here rather than quietly deleted, because a gap that gets filled is the evidence that naming gaps in public does something. What is open now is narrower and comes from the twelfth guide rather than from the drift. It ends by asking readers to draw their own constellations, and the site gave them nothing to draw on — so The Constellation Sheet was built next and sits in Print : eighty stars, nothing joined, and a blank index on the reverse. It was held back one pass on purpose, so the guest guide could ship as Helen wrote it before we started adding things around it. Naming it here rather than keeping it on a private list is the same practice as everywhere else on this site — the list of what we have not done is part of the record. What the Rest Stands On A Star Stuff collection · ten pieces Every other page here argues about the world. These ten argue about us — what we think belonging is, how we intend to be right, what happens when we aren't, and how the work gets made.

What counts as a foundation A simple test, and it is narrower than it sounds: a foundation is a piece the other pieces presuppose. When a Kin zine says a shark's cartilage is a secondary loss rather than a primitive state, it is leaning on a paradigm it does not stop to restate, an ethic about checking the claim, and a position on why difference is not deficit. Those commitments had to be written down somewhere, once, or every zine would have to relitigate them and none of them would have room left for its actual subject. Which means Foundations is not the important collection and not the hard one . It is the collection whose contents are load-bearing for everything else — and load-bearing is a structural fact, not a compliment.
Ten, and what each one holds up

Ten, and what each one holds up The claim. The Manifesto — six sections and eight declarations, stating the whole argument at full volume so the zines don't have to. The ethic toward people. Inclusion Safety: Owed, Not Earned — belonging is constitutive, not conferred, and harm is the only disqualifier. The ethic after the door. Six Principles and a Room — a professional code names the environment once in 6,825 words, so when the harm is coming from the room there is nowhere to record it. The ethic toward facts. Too Good to Check — the six ways a fact goes wrong here, worked from our own errors. The stance. Who Is Holding the Candle — two Sagans on why skepticism and wonder are both required, and why every observation has a particular person standing behind it. What we may claim. A Promise, Not a Finding — the grammar of the signature phrase, and why a belonging claim that rests on a fact can be revoked by the next paper. The method, and who is running it. Starlight — what is public here and why, the six automated gates and the faults that created them, and the first plain statement of how generative AI is used on this site. The paradigm. Neurodiversity Field Guide (No. 3) — the model everything else is written inside of, stated plainly enough to hand to someone new. The self-portrait. The Garden and the Stars (No. 18) — what kind of thing this collection is trying to be: a garden rather than a stream. Where we stop. Rainbow Serpents — the qualifier that keeps falling off the second law, and a Law that is not ours to explain. Two of the ten keep zine numbers and still sit outside the register collections , which looks like an inconsistency and is a decision. Nos. 3 and 18 were made in sequence with the rest, and the number records when — that is load-bearing for the dated changelog and the number-keyed fact-check ledger, so it never changes. But neither piece is doing what a Star Stuff or Star Gazing zine does: they are not following a fact to an argument about belonging, they are stating the frame that lets the other zines do it. So they keep their numbers and live here. The number says when; the collection says what , and this is the clearest case of the two disagreeing. Founding Document Star Stuff Manifesto Foundations · the claim The argument at full volume, so the zines can be quiet. On the cosmic origins of who we are, and why we belong — not despite difference, but as difference. The science of how we carry the universe in our bones. An Essay Rainbow Serpents Foundations entropy increases in an isolated system — and the qualifier keeps falling off A criticism of our physics, arriving from outside our discipline, which turns out to be correct. Three of our own pieces walked up to this line and stopped. essay → Details The second law says entropy tends to a maximum in an isolated system — one exchanging neither matter nor energy. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter and its entropy can decrease ; conflating the two is a documented teaching error, and No. 43 made it on this site. In an open system the law is not suspended but restated: internal entropy production stays non-negative while total entropy can fall, because the system exports it. That is not an exception. It is how anything alive works , paid for by low-entropy sunlight arriving and high-entropy infrared leaving. Tyson Yunkaporta (Apalech clan, western Cape York) argues that applying the second law to open interconnected systems is a curse in a precise sense he defines: not a lie but “a true law or pattern applied where it doesn’t belong,” powered by something in constant motion. The essay checks the physics half and finds it right — and begins by admitting that three Star Stuff pieces each reached an edge of this and stopped: No. 43 states the domain restriction and marks crossing it as its leap ; No. 56 uses the law to show a floor is compulsory; No. 69 shows the rainbow is anchored to the observer. Yunkaporta’s carved club is the argument as an object: an ouroboros etched round the head, which when rolled across clay prints “an endless procession of snakes, head to tail” — the closed figure and the open one, from one carving. Then the discipline the essay exists for: three infinities held apart rather than collapsed. It declines to explain the Rainbow Serpent , which is not one being and not ours, quoting it and stopping. And it features Kaya Oldaker’s Autism Infinity Dragon — public domain by the artist’s own release, and not a Rainbow Serpent, not descended from one. Its place here is geometric and checkable by looking: the head does not take the tail. The mouth is open and the plume passes beneath it — a lemniscate, which crosses itself and continues, where an ouroboros closes by eating. The one claim the essay makes about us is routed through the physics and our own symbol: a deficit assessment is an isolated-system model of a person , and people are not isolated. Refuses lineage between the three figures, refuses “ancient wisdom,” and refuses to un-refuse No. 43’s leap. A name collision we live with Zine No. 3 is called the Neurodiversity Field Guide , and it is not one of the Field Guides . The eighteen guides in that collection share a form — a catalogue of same-shaped entries with diagrams, reframe tables and collapsed field notes. No. 3 is an essay-shaped primer that happens to use "field guide" in the older, plainer sense of something you can carry . Renaming it would falsify the changelog and the number-keyed ledger for the sake of tidiness, so the name stays and the collision is stated instead. It is the same call as keeping Kin rather than naming it "Ways of Being," which would have collided with Field Guide No. 5.
The one that makes the rest checkable

The one that makes the rest checkable If Foundations has a keystone it is Too Good to Check , because it is the only piece here that can be used against the others. A manifesto cannot be falsified. A creed cannot be falsified. But a claim about piezoelectric bone or a quotation attributed to a named thinker absolutely can, and this site makes several hundred of them. So the essay names the six failure modes, works seventeen real corrections through them, and points at the public record: the changelog in Notes & Rationale , where every error we have caught in our own work is published with what was wrong, what is right, and who caught it. An ethic about facts that produced no visible corrections would be a decoration. Its companion, Who Is Holding the Candle , argues the half underneath it. Checking is one of two modes and fails on its own; and the checker is always a particular person standing somewhere, so “verified” with no verifier named is the same deletion this site spends its time undoing. Read together, one says go back to the primary source and the other says somebody has to go, and it matters who . Not Not required reading. Foundations is what the site leans on, not what you have to read first. Most people should start somewhere else and arrive here later, if at all, when they want to know why a zine was so confident about something. Not scripture. These are positions we hold and argue for, and the manifesto in particular is written to be disagreed with in public. Nothing here is settled by having been declared. Not a code of conduct. The creed is about what belonging is , not a policy document with an enforcement procedure. It names harm as the disqualifier and stops there, because a creed that pretended to be a process would be worse at both jobs. Not a claim to have got it right. The presence of Too Good to Check in this collection is an admission, not a boast — it exists because we shipped a Martin Luther King Jr. line credited to Baldwin, a paraphrase dressed as a Sagan quote, and a forest-wide fungal network asserted as settled fact because it rhymed so well. Glimmers A Star Stuff collection · 4 pieces · started 31 August 2026 Hopeful science news, told with a Star Stuff angle. News that stokes our senses of wonder, awe, interdependence and belonging — written close to the event, dated on its face, and held to exactly the same sourcing standard as the slow work.

What holds these together Everything else on this site is slow on purpose. A zine takes one settled, checkable fact and follows it until the claim about belonging is already inside it — and settled facts can wait, which is why that method works. News cannot wait, and that is the whole reason this collection exists as a separate place rather than as a looser standard inside an existing one. A glimmer here is a piece of science news that made us feel better about being alive among other people: a launch that worked, an instrument that saw something, a finding that widens rather than narrows what counts as ordinary. Written while the feeling is still on, and then checked as carefully as anything else here. The four registers we care about are the ones in the name of the thing: wonder , awe , interdependence and belonging . Interdependence is doing more work in that list than it looks. Most of what lands here will be about a large number of people managing to build something together over decades, which is the least reported and most remarkable part of any launch.
The axis is occasion, and that is a new one here

The axis is occasion, and that is a new one here Every other collection on this site says on its own face how it sorts, and this one owes the same disclosure. Star Stuff , Star Gazing , More Than Human , Kin and Stars We Grew Up On sort by register — what kind of argument a piece is making. Field Guides and How We Got Here sort by form . Print and Sound sort by medium . Glimmers sorts by occasion. A piece is here because something happened on a particular day and we wanted to say so while it was still happening. That is a fourth axis, and naming it is the price of adding one. The practical consequences are three, and they are all constraints rather than permissions: Dated on its face. Every entry carries the date of the event and the date of publication, because a piece written close to an event is a piece written with less than the full picture, and the reader is owed the ability to see how close. Unnumbered. Zines carry a number that records when ; that sequence is load-bearing across the changelog, the fact-check ledger and years of prose references. Glimmers entries are dated instead. A date says when better than a number does, and the number sequence should not have news inserted into it. Same eight gates, same ledger, same changelog. Faster to write is not looser. Every claim traces to a primary or agency source, every quotation is graded, and the entry gets its row in the fact-check ledger like anything else. Timeliness is not a discount.
Where the name comes from, including the part that goes against us

Where the name comes from, including the part that goes against us Glimmer is Deb Dana’s word , coined in 2018 in The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy as the counterpart to a trigger : the small moment in which a nervous system registers that things are all right. It arrived inside polyvagal theory, which is influential and scientifically contested , and we say that every time we use the word. Helen Edgar gives the reading this collection actually works from, in Glimmers: Autistic Joy and Monotropism : a glimmer need not relate to polyvagal theory at all, being simply the opposite of a trigger — a moment of joy or comfort, sensory or cognitive. One Word for the Opposite (No. 80) is the piece that argues the general case, and its finding is an asymmetry anyone can check: trauma work built a dozen words for a nervous system going badly, and the opposite got one, in 2018. Now the part that goes against us, because leaving it out would make this page a worse version of itself. Two days before this collection was named, we took the word out of a zine for cause. No. 78 shipped on 29 August 2026 framed around glimmers, and was repointed within hours. The reason was sound and it is worth stating exactly: a piece in Star Stuff has to rest on one settled fact, glimmers has none under it, so the argument was correctly moved onto optics — and then the word was kept as the frame after its foundation had been removed. The piece ended up more rigorous and less alive, pointing at something it could no longer reach. So why is it a good name for a collection when it was a bad frame for a zine? Because those are different jobs, and the failure was specific. A zine’s frame is load-bearing — it is the thing the argument stands on, and it has to hold the weight. A collection name is not a foundation. It is a label on a shelf , and what it has to be is true about the pieces on it . These pieces are moments of registering that things are all right. That is the word, used for exactly what it means, carrying nothing. The rest of the argument — that a good word does not stop being good when the theory it arrived in is in trouble, because words and theories are different objects with different failure modes — is already made at length on No. 80 , and we are not going to re-make it here.
Why this page opened at one member — and closed that gap the same day

Why this page opened at one member — and closed that gap the same day This site holds that collections are outputs, not inputs — they get made when a form has already been observed in finished work, never as a folder opened in advance. The floor is two members. Stars We Grew Up On carried exactly two for a long time; How We Got Here was deliberately deferred until a second chain arrived. Glimmers opens at one, which breaks that floor, and the break is deliberate rather than an oversight. The reasoning: a running log is defined by its cadence , not by an accumulated form, and cadence is the one property you cannot observe retroactively. Waiting for a second entry would mean holding the first one until it was no longer news — which is to say, destroying the exact property the collection is being made to hold. Easter Eggs broke the same floor at one member, for its own stated reason, and the precedent there is the relevant one: a break that is written down on a visible page is a better break than a quiet exception inside a tool. It is Ryan’s call, made on 31 August 2026, and it is recorded here rather than left to look like drift. The gap closed the same day. None of Those Miles arrived hours after Flying Free , which puts this collection at the two-member floor after all — the same way How We Got Here was deferred and then created the day its second chain turned up. That does not retire the argument above, and the argument is the part worth keeping: if the second entry had taken three weeks, the first would still have been published here on its own, because a log defined by cadence cannot wait to be sure of itself. The floor was broken on purpose and then met by accident. Both facts stay on the page. Not Not a looser standard. Written faster, checked the same. Every entry passes the same eight gates, carries the same fact-check ledger row, and grades its own quotations. Where a claim is contested, it is marked contested — including on pages belonging to institutions we are cheering for. Not a press-release feed. An agency announcing something is a lead, not a citation, exactly as an aggregator is. Being glad about a finding is not a reason to stop checking it, and enthusiasm is the condition under which checking is most often skipped. Not toxic positivity, and not a rule about how to feel. Noticing a glimmer fixes nothing, and it is not offered as advice to anyone who is drowning. There is no obligation here to be cheered up. This is a shelf for things that happened to cheer us up, published in case that is useful. Not a naturalistic fallacy. Nothing in the sky owes anyone anything, and no value is derived from a fact anywhere in this collection. Where a piece of physics rhymes with something true about how people are treated, the rhyme is marked as a rhyme and not promoted to evidence. Not restricted to space. The first entry is a telescope because a telescope launched. The collection is for any science news that does the work — biology, ecology, materials, anything.

The pieces Newest first. Dated rather than numbered, for the reasons above. 2 September 2026 Until There Were Ten Glimmers · Ryan Boren A thing that never changes and has no counterexample is very hard to tell apart from a rule. Saturn's hexagon was the only one of its kind for forty-four years. There is now a decagon at the south pole — drawn unevenly, wobbling on a 32.5-day cycle, and possibly temporary. Essay · publication day → Details The tidy version of this story is two poles, two polygons, how balanced , and the paper refuses to let you have it. Saturn's hexagon sits near 78.5°N, was found by Voyager in 1980–81, and has been in every image since — a lifetime exceeding 44 years with no counterexample anywhere on the planet. The south pole was tipped out of view from mid-2012 until 2023; when it came back there was a ten-sided wave at 58°S to 63°S, wavelength 16,782 ± 1,100 km. But it is not the hexagon mirrored. Where the hexagon's sides and corners are equally contrasted, the decagon is “not uniform in longitude” : three corners very prominent, four less so, three barely defined. Its corners oscillate on a mean 32.5-day period with amplitudes of 4.6° to 8.4°, and the wobble travels — each corner peaking about 2.7 days after its neighbour — which the authors call “a complex dynamical behavior, never observed in the hexagon.” It did not exist in Saturn's previous year, and it “could be a transient evolving phenomenon, whereas the hexagon is a robust wave.” Two candidate causes and no way yet to choose: a jet instability, or a 4,000-km red anticyclone at 55°S that resembles one Voyager saw in 1981. Three shallow-water runs, none reproducing the observed drift. Also: a shape drifting at 2.5 m/s inside a 116 m/s jet, so the wind goes through the corners and the corners stay put; a jet whose strength has not changed substantially since 1981; and two of the fourteen authors affiliated to a private observatory in the Australian outback and a French astronomy association rather than a university. The turn is epistemic, not decorative: one example, held still for forty-four years, had looked exactly like a law. 31 August 2026 Came Back Clean Glimmers · Ryan Boren The pair that comes back clean is the one to worry about. A thousand people buried two thousand pairs of cotton underpants across Switzerland. Land use mattered more than anything else — and the ground that came back cleanest was the lawn. Essay · 4 diagrams → Details The intuition runs the wrong way, which is why the finding is worth having. Cotton is nearly pure cellulose, so a buried pair of underpants is a standardised meal: how much disappears tells you how much life was down there eating. About a thousand volunteers ran it at a thousand Swiss sites for the University of Zurich and Agroscope, under the excellent project name Beweisstück Unterhose — Proof by Underpants — and land use turned out to matter more than soil chemistry, texture, climate or altitude. Private gardens had the most soil life of any land type studied. Lawns had the least. The most managed surface most of us own is the deadest, which is No. 8 ’s argument about monoculture arriving as a measurement rather than a metaphor. Around 240 of the citizen scientists are listed as co-authors — not acknowledged, not thanked in a footnote, authors — which is a claim about who counts as a knower and is the methods section rather than a slogan. Also: the Tea Bag Index and the published critique that says macrofauna damage gets counted as decomposition, an objection that applies harder to a whole pair of underpants; the 59%-of-global-biodiversity figure printed with its ±15 and its live argument; and the burial protocol, so you can run it in your own garden. Fig. 1 is adapted from the paper’s own scale under CC BY 4.0 — the same licence question Flying Free asked and could not clear, asked again and answered yes. 31 August 2026 None of Those Miles Glimmers · Ryan Boren It’s happening. It’s really happening. It’s finally happening. Sunlight is the cheapest electricity we have ever made — with a fourteen-word condition the headline keeps dropping. Four diagrams, a learning curve derived from the data, and a supply line with no gate in it. Essay · 4 diagrams → Details The good news is real and it is conditional, and the piece keeps both halves. The IEA’s 2020 finding was that “for projects with low cost financing that tap high quality resources, solar PV is now the cheapest source of electricity in history” — and the version that travels drops the fourteen-word condition and swaps electricity for energy , which silently extends a claim about 22% of the system to all of it. That is the same fault Rainbow Serpents is about, two days later in a different field , and this page nearly committed it. The mechanism is a learning curve, and it is derived here rather than quoted: module prices fell from $128.27 to $0.258 per watt between 1975 and 2024 — a factor of 497 — while cumulative capacity grew 3.4 million times, 21.7 doublings. Fitted on log–log axes that is 23.5% off the price per doubling at R² = 0.979. It is called Swanson’s law and it is not a law: prices rose in six of those fifty years, 2022 by 10.2%. Nobody invented cheap solar; thousands of people iterated it into existence in public, and two governments paid for the early expensive units. Also: silicon as the eighth most abundant element in the universe and a product of massive stars, so a panel is star stuff arranged to catch starlight, both halves literal; the 250-year sequence of US energy crossovers, read twice, because a crossover is not a subtraction ; community solar as a watering hole; and Bill McKibben’s line about ninety-three million miles, quoted from a dated source after finding that its three circulating versions do not match each other. 30 August 2026 Flying Free Glimmers · Ryan Boren I needed to witness something hopeful and wonder-filled, something to make me feel good about humanity. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope left Kennedy at 7:26 in the morning, bound for Lagrange Two. On the teamwork that put it there, and why the most famously balanced place in the sky still needs its thrusters. Essay · launch day → Details Roman lifted off from Launch Complex 39A on a Falcon Heavy and separated 31 minutes later, beginning a hundred-day cruise to a halo orbit 1.5 million kilometres out. The piece takes the launch broadcast at its word and then checks it. Two of the three things Roman is built to measure have no agreed explanation at all — NASA’s own page says dark energy is “just the name that astronomers gave to the mysterious ‘something’” doing it — and the third, the exoplanet census, works only because two detection methods with opposite blind spots are running at once. Shawn Domagal-Goldman called the result the ecology of the known universe, which is exact: ecology needs the whole stand of trees, because a range is something you count rather than photograph. The best fact is the one usually left out of the L2 story. Nothing parks at Lagrange Two; it is an unstable equilibrium, and an unattended spacecraft drifts off in about three weeks. Roman will fire thrusters on a schedule, forever, with fuel budgeted for it from the start — and nobody at NASA files that under failure to be independent. A rhyme, not a proof. Also: Nancy Grace Roman, told by a physics department that he usually dissuaded women but she might make it; a mirror handed on from the National Reconnaissance Office; four budget requests that proposed cancelling the mission and the appropriations that saved it each time; and one word from the broadcast — superpower — that stays with the telescope and does not come home with us.
