Monotropic spiral time and felt time (Helen Edgar, Bergson, Deleuze) are their own real clock, measured in intensity, not minutes; Samuels' time travel, grief time, and broken time hold the hard edges too. The reading: no clock is master, and being “off the clock” is closer to the truth than fitting it. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a closing coda by Helen Edgar on spiral time.

Zine No. 20 The Same Water Stimpunks Zines on phase transitions, fluctuating capacity, and why “you could do it yesterday” was never the point Water doesn't get gradually stiffer as it cools — it holds, then flips to ice all at once. Same substance; the conditions decide the state. 8 spreads→ Details Fluctuating capacity, read through the physics of phase transitions. Water doesn't get gradually stiffer as it cools — it holds, then flips to ice all at once at a threshold. Same H₂O, different state, and the conditions (not the substance) decide which. So the exhausting question — why could you do it yesterday and not today? — has a clean answer: capacity is a state, not a trait, and you were near a boundary. The hardest part is the crossing itself (threshold anxiety is sensitivity to a real edge — broken thresholds, not broken people); you can be supercooled, held past your limit until one small thing tips everything at once; and recovery slows near the edge, because that's how systems behave. Nothing is fixed or broken — fluid adaptation and weather-bodies, re-adapting to a changed climate. Extends Minor Worlds: change the conditions, not the substance. Grounded in phase-transition physics, Cynthia Kim, Helen Edgar, and Stimpunks' own threshold anxiety. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 21 Not a Line Stimpunks Zines on spectra, constellations, and why “mild to severe” was always the wrong picture — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer A real spectrum isn't a ladder — split a star's light and every element signs its own fingerprint. No rank, no norm, no line. 8 spreads→ Details The spectrum was never a severity scale — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer. “Spectrum” is the most misread word in our vocabulary: people hear a line from mild to severe. But a real spectrum isn't a ladder — split a star's light and every element signs its own pattern of lines, a fingerprint, which is the only way we know what stars are made of. And the sky's figure was never a line: it's a constellation. The zine follows the escalation from Helen Edgar's brand-new essay — the line of neuronormativity, to the spiky profile (better, but still a grid measured from a baseline), to a constellation of intensities: no rank, no norm, no line. Patrick Dwyer's autism constellation anchors it; the functioning-labels critique shows how the line gatekeeps support (“not disabled enough” vs “too disabled”). Held with care: refusing the line doesn't erase that some of us need far more support — need is not a rank; name it instead. Cashes in the rainbow motif on every page and hands off to the Constellation Field Guide. Eight spreads, spectrum-forward diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 23 Bodies of Water Stimpunks Zines on hydrofeminism, shared flow, and belonging that moves between us You are not a container of water; you are water, briefly gathered into a shape — and none of it was ever only yours. After Astrida Neimanis. 8 spreads→ Details Hydrofeminism as belonging, read through star stuff — after Astrida Neimanis. You are not a container of water; you are water, roughly 60% of you, briefly gathered into a shape. And none of it is only yours: it was rain, river, cloud, and the inside of other creatures first. Neimanis's gestationality (we each began inside another body's water) and Stacy Alaimo's transcorporeality dissolve the clean edge — we are all downstream of one another, permeable and borrowed. The crucial move, held with care: watery belonging is not dissolution into sameness. Where two rivers meet, the confluence runs braided for miles — one channel, two waters, still distinct. That's the neurodiversity paradigm in an image: the spiky profile survives the merge. A dedicated spread carries shared/collective flow — monotropism's deep channels can align into shared flow (Autistic Realms, Helen Edgar); a watering hole is where currents pool. So belonging is a current, not a border — build watering holes, keep the water moving. Much of Earth's water is older than the Sun. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 24 Shared Air Stimpunks Zines on breath, co-regulation, and the air we hold in common There is only one air, so thoroughly mixed that your next breath very likely holds atoms once breathed by strangers and by trees. 9 spreads→ Details The air we share, read through star stuff and solarpunk — a companion to Bodies of Water. There is only one air: a single, well-mixed body with no walls in it, so thoroughly circulated that your next breath very likely holds atoms once breathed by strangers and by trees across the world. It's a reciprocal breath — we exhale what plants inhale, and our oxygen is the exhaust of ancient cyanobacteria (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago), forged first in stars. Every room we share is a shared-air space (a term coined by Helen Edgar & Ryan Boren): in it we trade breath and co-regulate, nervous systems settling into a shared rhythm. The neurodiversity turn: many of us are the canaries of that room. Miners carried canaries because the birds felt the bad air first — not because they were weak, but because they were sensitive, and their alarm was information. Our sensitivity to fragrance, stale air, and fluorescent hum is an early-warning system, not a flaw: don't blame the bird, change the air — build it breathable for the canaries and it's breathable for all. Which raises the harder question: habitable, and for whom? The burden of shared air falls unevenly, so breathable air is a commons, not a private accommodation one person quietly manages. The response is solarpunk: clean air as infrastructure as resistance — open windows, plants, masks, DIY Corsi–Rosenthal boxes — mutual aid you can build in an afternoon. Move quietly and plant things. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 25 Shared Signal Stimpunks Zines on distance, the clearer channel, and the rhythm we carry when we can't share a room Radio waves and starlight are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths — and shared-signal space is Helen Edgar's coinage. 9 spreads→ Details Connection carried across distance, read through star stuff — a companion to Shared Air. The electromagnetic spectrum is one continuous field: radio waves and starlight are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths, and the same physics that carries a voice call carries a star's light. Shared-signal space — a term coined by Helen Edgar — is the counterpart to shared-air space: a call, a message, a voice note, a synthesised voice, carrying the rhythm on a signal instead of the air of a room. A voice note is breath, timestamped and sent; co-regulation crosses a screen too — thinner, but real (Porges; Streuber et al.). For many of us, text and AAC aren't a fallback from speech but the clearer channel — thinking time, structure, fewer sensory demands, a record to return to (Howard & Sedgewick) — and AAC is the real communication, not a workaround. Aversion to the phone is information, not fragility. Reachable, and for whom? Communication access is a commons; we build our own watering holes — the Autistic Rhizome (Edgar), Discords, AAC — sideways and underground, where lurking counts. The oldest signal of all is a dead star's light still reaching your eye: signal lets connection cross a gap touch can't, so no channel is the master channel (Milton). Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 44 You Cannot Flatten a Sphere Stimpunks Zines on curvature, map projections, and what a single number has to throw away Gauss proved in 1827 that no flat map can preserve everything. An IQ score is literally a projection — so it must destroy information. 12 spreads→ Details Try wrapping a sheet of paper smoothly around an orange. It creases, always, and that is not clumsiness — it is forbidden. Gauss proved it in 1827 and liked the result enough to call it the Theorema Egregium, the remarkable theorem: a surface’s curvature is intrinsic, so bending that doesn’t stretch can never change it. Paper rolls into a tube or a cone because those are still flat in the sense that matters; a sphere is not, and no care gets you there. You have used this today without noticing — fold a pizza slice and the tip stops drooping, because curving it one way forces it to stay straight the other. The consequence: no flat map of the world can preserve everything, and every projection must sacrifice area, angle, distance or direction. Mercator chose angle, in 1569, so a constant compass bearing would be a straight line — superb for sailors, and it swells Greenland to the apparent size of an Africa roughly fourteen times larger. The map never says what it chose, and that silence is the scandal rather than the distortion. Then Tissot’s answer from 1859, which is the honest one: you cannot remove the distortion, so draw it — a grid of ellipses showing exactly what this map did to this place. And then the turn. An IQ score, a DSM-5 support level, a functioning label: each takes a many-axis person and returns one value, which is not a metaphor but literally a projection — so it must destroy information, the choice of what to destroy is somebody’s, and the number never records it. Worse than a map, in fact: a Mercator keeps every place badly, while a single number doesn’t distort the other dimensions, it deletes them. Ask what a summary was optimised for and you learn whose journey it serves — Mercator for sailors, a support level for a budget, a functioning label for a gate. If you must summarise, publish the indicatrix: the axes it came from, the range it moves across, what it was built for, reviewed by the person measured. Closes on the gentlest thing the theorem gives — a globe has no edges and no corners, so being at the margin was never information about you, only about where somebody cut. Companion to No. 21 Not a Line, which asks what shape the thing is; this asks what a reduction costs. Twelve spreads, ten diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 45 The Cloud Phase Stimpunks Zines on the last stage of a supernova remnant, and how long the in-between actually lasts The story we get told about a dead star ends about one step past the explosion. The physics runs further than the sentence does. 11 spreads→ Details The story we get told about a dead star ends about one step past the explosion: the shell expands, thins, cools, and disperses into the interstellar medium. Fade out. But the physics runs further than the sentence does, and there is another word waiting at the end of it. Romano, Behrendt & Burkert (2024) followed remnants through their long cold decline and found the radiative phase divides into four stages — and the last one they call the cloud phase. Not the end phase. Not the dispersal phase. The cloud phase: once nothing is driving the shell and the pressure inside has fallen to match the pressure outside, nothing holds the cavity open, so the remnant falls back into itself and settles as a chemically enriched cloud. That is a 2024 simulation and it is held here as proposed, flagged in place — because the argument's weight sits somewhere firmer. Murray (2011) measured what clouds actually do: in the Milky Way's most luminous star-forming complexes, the star formation efficiency averages 0.08, so ninety-two percent of the cloud never becomes a star — and that is the flattering number, since the Galactic average of 0.005 puts it nearer ninety-nine and a half. A giant molecular cloud lasts 27 ± 12 million years, and the bright episode inside it is short, late, and the thing that tears the cloud apart. Which turns the story the other way round: the in-between is not the wait between the real states. It is the majority state, by mass and by duration — and that is a measurement, offered as fact rather than as comfort. Along the way, SN 1987A: at least 0.2 solar masses of dust condensed inside its own wreckage, grains that did not exist anywhere before the star died. The debris field is a foundry. Written after Helen Edgar, whose Supernova Remnant and Emergence Point map the same stage from the inside — burnout as “remnants of my old self entangled in new ways of being,” recovery as re-assembly rather than return, and deterritorialisation as “a soft loosening of pressure.” A cloud never decides to collapse; it is collapsed upon, by gravity and radiation and its neighbours, so the honest question when one of us reorganises is what the pressure is and where it comes from. Held with care throughout: gestation is not a promise of a star, most of the mass never lights, and the claim is only that the cloud is a real state, not a waiting room. Closes on aluminium-26 in the Allende meteorite — something nearby and freshly dead was in our own birth cloud, and which star is openly contested fifty years on, so we name the contest instead of picking a winner. Eleven spreads, nine diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 46 Companion Stars Stimpunks Zines on gravitational binding, the three-body problem, and why no one's path can be solved alone A star that shares a system with another star already has a name, and it is astronomy's own working word: a companion star. 9 spreads→ Details A star that shares a system with another star already has a name, and it is astronomy’s own working word: a companion star. Helen Edgar’s thirteenth constellation carries it — “the people who orbit close … who don’t need me to perform and who just ‘get it’.” But before any of that, a correction, because this collection exists partly to take science back from the version that travels furthest. You have met the line most stars are in binaries — the Sun is the odd one out. It isn’t so. Charles Lada put the binary statistics beside the stellar mass function in 2006 and published the answer as his title: most stars are single — two-thirds of main-sequence systems in the Galactic disk. Multiplicity climbs steeply with mass (~26% of M dwarfs, 44 ± 2% of Sun-like stars, near-total for the most massive), and the galaxy is overwhelmingly made of the small end. So this zine will not tell you that everybody has their people. The claim it makes instead is smaller and holds all the way down: where the binding is real, here is exactly what it is. Sirius A and its white-dwarf companion trace a 50.13-year orbit about a barycentre lying in neither star — and equal binding is not equal motion, since the heavier body is displaced less, which is worth saying out loud for anyone who has been told they’re imagining who does more of the moving. Then the hardest spread: bring two stars close and they do deform each other — stretched to ellipsoids, drawn to teardrops, finally sharing one dumbbell envelope with matter crossing between them. Proximity is not automatically good. It is the wide pairs — bound out to a parsec, one orbit longer than the whole history of flowering plants — where both keep their shape. And then the turn, which is theorems rather than reading: with two bodies you can write the solution down, but Bruns (1887) proved no further algebraic integrals exist, Poincaré (1890) closed off the single-valued analytic ones, and Sundman’s 1912 series converges far too slowly to use. So these systems are stepped forward numerically, together, and no one body’s path can be solved on its own and the others added afterward. That same work is where chaos was found — and the part the popular word destroys is that nothing is random: every rule is exact and known, and the system is still unpredictable far out. Read beside the language this community built first — David Gray-Hammond’s Chaotic Self (“you can’t unqueer a queer mind”) and Autistic Rhizome, with Helen’s Rhizome Array and Mycelial Stars — and holding the tension honestly rather than smoothing it: the rhizome describes resilience, no node depending on another to exist; the three-body physics describes non-separability while bodies are bound. Both true, neither cancelling. Closes on what actually holds a bound system: no agreement, no shared origin, no similarity, no upkeep, no performance — mutual gravity and nothing else, which means there is no version of a companion star that has to earn it. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. A rhyme, not a proof.
The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing

Zine No. 48 The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing Stimpunks Zines on the black hole nobody photographed, and what can only be known by its effect on everything else Nobody has photographed a black hole, and nobody will — the ordinary way of knowing a thing is simply unavailable, and no better lens fixes it. 12 spreads→ Details Nobody has photographed a black hole, and nobody will. A camera works by catching light that left the subject, and the event horizon is the surface where every outward direction has stopped existing — so the ordinary way of knowing a thing is simply unavailable, and no better lens fixes it. What the Event Horizon Telescope released in April 2019 and May 2022 is a shadow: the set of directions in which light that might have reached you went into the hole instead, ringed by the light that passed far enough out to be bent around and escape. Then the fact this zine is built on, which is exact geometry rather than an impression. For a non-spinning black hole the event horizon sits at 2 GM/c² and the edge of the shadow at 3√3 GM/c² — so the dark circle is about 2.6 times wider than the object casting it. Gravity does not merely hide the thing; it magnifies the hiding. And that magnification is nearly constant across spins and viewing angles (5 ± 0.2 GM/Dc², a spread of about four percent), which is the only reason anyone can work backwards from it. The instrument was the planet: eight radio telescopes at six sites from Spain to the South Pole, observing at 1.3 mm, writing ~3.5 petabytes to helium-filled hard drives that had to be flown to two correlators — the Antarctic share stranded until the winter ended. No site saw the ring; no site could have. Four imaging teams then worked blind to one another, on two different families of algorithm, because everyone involved knew what they hoped to find. M87*’s ring came out at 42 ± 3 microarcseconds — an orange, on the Moon. Sagittarius A* was harder despite being nearer, because its innermost orbit takes about thirty minutes against M87*’s thirty days: the subject rearranges itself while the shutter is open. Then the turn, in two halves. Some things are known only by their effect on everything around them — monotropism, pain, a sensory environment, an access need — and the absence of a photograph was never evidence of an absent thing. But the geometry has a second half, and this piece does not stop before it: what people see of an unmet need is the disruption, not the need, and the disruption is the larger object, inflated by every year of bending and masking and quiet accommodation that got folded into it. In physics you can divide the factor out. In a life there is none, which is exactly why you ask. Closes on the guardrail rather than the warm note: unseeable is not unreal, and it is not a blank cheque either — the collaboration pinned Sagittarius A* to 51.8 ± 2.3 microarcseconds without ever seeing it. Twelve spreads, ten diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set that turns down the obvious reading first. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 51 Almost Shadow Stimpunks Zines on the zone Kepler had to name, why partial is the enormous one, and the two fields that borrowed the word In 1604 Kepler was drawing the geometry of an eclipse and ran out of language — so in the middle of a diagram he made a word: penumbra. 13 spreads→ Details In 1604 Johannes Kepler was drawing the geometry of an eclipse and ran out of language. The Sun is not a point of light but a disc, so every part of it throws a shadow in a slightly different direction and the result comes out layered: a core where the whole disc is hidden, an outer region where some of it still shines through, and between them no edge at all — just a handover. He had umbra for the core. For the handover he had nothing. So in the middle of a diagram in Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena he made one: quod est inter KE, NM penumbra dicatur — let what lies between be called penumbra. The verb is dicatur, let it be called; that is not a man using a word, it is the word being made because a drawing demanded it. Paene plus umbra: almost-shadow, and what gets named is neither the dark nor the light but the thing between them. Astronomy keeps three zones now, and the third is the one nobody has heard of: the antumbra, past the shadow cone’s apex, where the Moon sits entirely in front of the Sun — nothing sticking out, nothing off to one side — and it is still not a total eclipse, because the Moon is simply too small in your sky to cover what is behind it. Complete obstruction, and the darkness never comes. Two words would have forced that case into one of the other two and both would have been wrong. Then the pair of facts this zine refuses to separate. First, the partial zone is the enormous one: the umbral track lands as a stripe a hundred-odd kilometres wide while the penumbra covers thousands, so the overwhelming majority of everyone who has ever seen a solar eclipse saw a partial one. The penumbra is where we live; totality is the exception. Second, and cutting the other way, 99 percent obscured is still daylight. The corona is only about as bright as a full Moon, and the surviving sliver of photosphere is hundreds to thousands of times brighter than that — so it obliterates the corona and keeps the sky blue. Illuminance falls roughly a hundred-fold in the last two minutes, another order of magnitude in the final half minute, more than four orders of magnitude in all. The last increment is not an increment; it is a change of state, and on the far side of it the birds go quiet. Gradient and threshold, and any account that can hold only one of them is describing something other than the world — all gradient gives you “everyone’s a bit like that” and owes nobody anything; all threshold gives you the eligibility form and makes the enormous middle vanish. Two other fields worked this out and reached for Kepler’s word, both times because a binary would cost lives. In 1981 Astrup, Siesjö and Symon found two thresholds in ischaemic brain — electrical failure, then ion-pump failure — and named the zone between them the ischaemic penumbra: functionally silent, structurally intact, salvageable on reperfusion. That word is the reason acute stroke has a treatment window at all; every intervention is aimed at the penumbra, because the core is past help and the healthy tissue does not need it. And in Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) Justice Douglas held that guarantees have “penumbras, formed by emanations” — a borrowing the zine presents alongside its critics rather than beneath them, since a shadow with no measurable edge can be stretched to cover whatever the reader wanted covered. The turn: partial support is not proportional support. Ninety percent of a ramp is a wall; captions that drop out for the last two minutes did not deliver 98 percent of the talk; almost accessible is a phase change away from accessible. And the most hopeful sentence here is the least sentimental one, carried over from 1981 — in the penumbra, what looks like loss is often deprivation, and deprivation is reversible if you can see the zone exists and get there in time. Impaired is not lost. And the distinction the piece owes, which is the sharpest thing in it: an umbra is a relation between a source, an obstruction and a place — never a property of the ground it falls on. The pavement does not have an umbra; it is in one, and nothing about the pavement is different. So a total blockage of support is real and is a fact about an arrangement somebody built and can unbuild. An umbra located inside a person is a category error. Functioning labels perform exactly that relocation — high-functioning, severe, level 3 take a shadow cast by circumstances and write it on a body — and “profound autism”, proposed in the Lancet Commission (2021) for people held to be “not able to advocate for themselves,” is the umbra version of the move. Steven Kapp’s 2023 review finds that minimally speaking Autistic people can communicate, especially with responsive partners, and can self-advocate — which makes that criterion partly a statement about the listener, the method and the room. So profound reads deprivation as loss, on a person. Refusing the label is not a denial of anyone’s support needs, and the zine says so plainly, crediting Helen Edgar: “Autistic people with profound and multiple learning disabilities and health needs are not ‘Profoundly Autistic,’ they are autistic with specific needs.” Thirteen spreads, five diagrams, a “Not:” set that now refuses the bodymind umbra first. A rhyme, not a proof.
The Moon Is Always Half Lit

Zine No. 53 The Moon Is Always Half Lit Stimpunks Zines on phases as geometry, the far side that was never dark, and why waning is a word about the angle The Sun lights one hemisphere of the Moon continuously. Nothing dims — what changes is the angle, and one of the three bodies is you. 14 spreads→ Details The Sun lights one hemisphere of the Moon. Not usually, not on average — continuously, without a single interruption that was not an eclipse. Which means a crescent Moon is not a Moon that has had most of its light taken away. It is a fully half-lit Moon seen nearly edge-on to its own daylight, and the illuminated hemisphere is exactly as large at new Moon as at full. Nothing dims. Nothing is withheld. Nothing is recovering. What changes over a month is not the Moon but the angle between the Sun, the Moon and you — a phase needs three bodies, and one of them is the observer, so there is no fact about “what phase the Moon is in” that does not have your position inside it. The US Naval Observatory is precise about where that leads: New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon and Last Quarter are defined to occur when the excess of the Moon’s apparent ecliptic longitude over the Sun’s is 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° — which makes them instants, moments with no duration — while waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning gibbous and waning crescent are the roughly week-long stretches between them. So the familiar chart of eight equal boxes is really four knife-edges and four long weeks, drawn over an illuminated fraction that changes smoothly and without a single step. The boxes are ours; we drew them because a chart needs boxes, and then began reading them back as though we had found them. And because the observer is one arm of the angle, moving you changes the answer: at one instant, one lit fraction, one Moon, the crescent is lit along the right edge from Edinburgh, along the left from Melbourne, and underneath near the equator, riding low as a bowl — a wet moon, tipped up to hold the rain. Three drawings, three correct answers, nobody seeing an illusion. Then the correction the language has been getting wrong for a century: there is a far side and there is no dark side. The far side receives exactly as much sunlight as the face we know, and at new Moon — the one night we can see nothing at all — it is in full daylight, the whole hemisphere blazing, entirely unwitnessed. Luna 3 went and looked on 7 October 1959, returning 29 grainy frames of about seventy percent of it after developing the film in a small automated darkroom it was carrying and scanning the negatives home across the vacuum. What came back was not a shadow but a sunlit landscape, crowded with craters, nearly free of maria. It had been like that the whole time. Nor is the lock rigid: libration in longitude and latitude shows us about 59 percent of the surface rather than half, so even the thing we describe as fixed turns out to be negotiating. The phases are complements — our new Moon is a full Earth seen from there, and at every instant the two sum to one whole, so the light is never missing, only ever somewhere you are not standing. The ashen glow on a crescent’s dark limb is that light returned: earthshine, the old Moon in the new Moon’s arms, explained by Leonardo around 1506 in the Codex Leicester, never published, and slightly wrong (he credited the oceans; it is mostly clouds). The first published explanation is credited to Michael Mästlin, who taught Kepler at Tübingen — teacher and student either side of the same refusal to accept a picture with only two states in it. And the month you live by is longer than the orbit it is made of: 27.32 days to complete a full circuit against the stars, but 29.53 to return to the same phase, because Earth moved roughly 27° meanwhile and the alignment slid forward. You can finish the circle and still not count as returned, because the thing you are measured against keeps moving. The turn: waxing and waning are words about the geometry. They are not words about the Moon, and nothing in the Moon does them. A functioning label is a phase recorded as a substance — it takes the crescent and files it as the whole Moon there is — and “but she seems fine with me” is not a fact about her, it is a report of one angle offered as though it were the object. And the turn is landed in a life rather than left abstract: Ryan Boren’s own account of being “both r-word and genius” across one school career. Hyperlexic and Autistic, he would not read aloud — situational mutism and exposure anxiety “locked my lips” — until one day, in a quiet corner with a semblance of psychological safety, he read a book cover to cover in a whisper and asked, “Can I go now?” He describes going “from being a full time r-word to a part time one, depending on who was in the room with me and if I felt safe enough speak” — a phase, recorded in the vocabulary of proportion, with the observer’s position stated plainly by the person being measured. And his sentence “Autistic people are psychological safety barometers” inverts the whole measurement, because a barometer’s reading is a fact about the surrounding air: the instrument was reading the room, and the room wrote the result down as a fact about the child. The guardrail gets its own spread, because the easy version of this argument is cruel: a crescent really does deliver less light to you. Measurably. The correction is not that the difference is imaginary but that it is located in the arrangement — and the refusals set turns down “just make them feel safe” as a new flattening, since the point is that the variables are in the arrangement, not that there is only one of them. Fourteen spreads, four diagrams. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 54 How Anything Gets Built Stimpunks Zines the five neurodivergent love locutions, and the mechanisms that actually assemble matter Infodumping, parallel play, support swapping, deep pressure, penguin pebbling — set beside five mechanisms by which matter is actually assembled. 8 spreads→ Details The Five Neurodivergent Love Locutions — infodumping, parallel play, support swapping, deep pressure, penguin pebbling — set beside five mechanisms by which matter is actually assembled, on the argument that these are construction methods, not compensations. The deficit story ranks all five as thin stand-ins for the real thing: real conversation, real play, real gifts. That story needs them to be structurally deficient forms of connection. Structurally, they are how things get built. Infodumping: a star cannot stop telling you what it is made of. Every photon leaving passes out through the star’s own atmosphere and each element takes its specific bite out of the spectrum, so the light arrives carrying a complete, unedited account of the composition, whether or not anyone is reading. Fraunhofer catalogued the dark lines in 1814 without knowing what they were; Kirchhoff and Bunsen established in 1859–60 that each is an element’s fingerprint; Cecilia Payne read hydrogen out of them in 1925 and was pressured to soften a conclusion that was right. We know we are star stuff because stars will not shut up about themselves — which makes the unasked-for infodump the entire evidentiary basis of this collection. Parallel play: filed for decades as a developmental stage, something to be passed through. The sky’s version is the wide binary, and El-Badry, Rix and Heintz catalogue 1.3 million of them in Gaia eDR3, genuinely bound at separations out to a full parsec — 3.26 light years — neither star perturbing the other, orbits so long no observer will see one completed. Nothing is being worked toward; there is no closer configuration this rehearses. Wide binaries are not failed close binaries, they are the commonest stable outcome the galaxy produces. Support swapping: W Ursae Majoris contact binaries overflow into a single shared convective envelope, and energy crossing it from the larger star to the smaller holds both within about 200 K of each other despite a mass ratio near 0.3 — the smaller star running far hotter than its own mass could sustain, because capacity is redistributed by the configuration they are in together. And the complication that keeps it honest, because support swapping is not free: in Algol systems mass flows one way, and the star that was originally more massive gave away so much of itself that it ended up the less massive, less luminous, apparently less-developed one. Crawford resolved that paradox in 1955 — the one that looks behind is the one that gave, its donation written down as apparent deficiency. Deep pressure: the locution with the bluntest name, and nothing fuses unsqueezed. A star simply is hydrostatic equilibrium, the balance between gravity pulling in and pressure pushing out, held for billions of years; the solar core sits near 2.4 × 1016 Pa, over 200 billion atmospheres. Take the crushing away and there is no carbon, no oxygen, no iron, no calcium in the bone. The pressure is not a condition the star endures on the way to making elements — the pressure is the manufacturing process. Penguin pebbling: the one most readily filed as sweet-but-slight, and the one with the sharpest physics behind it. Classical planetesimal accretion could not finish a giant-planet core before the gas disk dissipated — the big collisions were simply too slow, and without a core in time there is no atmosphere to capture. Pebble accretion, named by Lambrechts and Johansen in 2012, gets there in 10⁴–10⁶ years, because millimetre-scale pebbles are aerodynamically braked and captured across nearly the whole Hill sphere. The small offerings did not supplement the big collisions; the big collisions could not do the job and the small offerings could. For those cores, the small offering is not a lesser route — it is the route. It even stops itself: past ten to twenty Earth masses the core opens a pressure bump and the pebbles are halted before arrival, so even the sky knows when someone has had enough pebbles. Then the turn, printed on the face of the zine rather than buried in a footnote, because five-for-five is exactly the shape of a claim that circulates for being tidy rather than true. The physics does not justify the love. The universe is not signing anything off, and if it were, its approval would be worthless — a universe that could approve could also decline. This is the same defect the site caught in a sentence of its own: the universe loves you for it makes the star stuff the reason, and a reason can be revoked, where love you down to your star stuff measures how far the loving reaches rather than why it is given. Down to is not because of. Amythest Schaber originated the five; Stimpunks popularized them and put them into currency from 2022, substituting locutions for languages; the term penguin pebbling reached us later, through Lindsey; and Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms has developed the framework furthest, including the Penguin Pebbling game built with Ryan Boren. Eight spreads, five diagrams. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 55 What Looks Like Chaos Stimpunks Zines Seven weavers, twenty-one nests, and a camera say otherwise — and so does a room somebody told you to tidy. Nest building is the textbook example of pure instinct: a bird constructs a thing it has never seen, without instruction, and gets it right the first time. 10 spreads→ Details Nest building is the textbook example of pure instinct — a bird constructs a thing it has never seen, without instruction, and gets it right the first time, so the nest must be something the bird contains rather than something it works out. That claim is falsifiable, because a template predicts one specific thing: sameness, between individuals and within one individual across attempts. Somebody went and measured whether the sameness is there. Southern Botswana, seven colour-ringed male Southern Masked weavers, territories searched daily so a nest was found at the moment it was started; camcorders square to the branch, three nests filmed per bird — twenty-one nests — and the footage coded by a researcher blind to which bird and which date. During the first phase of construction not one measured behaviour was repeatable within a male: not the direction he carried the grass, not how long he wove, not which quadrant he favoured, not how often he lost hold. Then the individuality: two birds consistently pushed the first end of a blade into the right side of the nest, two consistently into the left, three had no side at all — and pooled across all seven, the bias vanished (G = 0.06, p = 0.81). Personal handedness with no species handedness underneath it, which is precisely what a template cannot produce. And they improved: across a season each male dropped grass less often as he built more nests (p < 0.01), while the birds with the most consistent personal style finished the ring phase fastest (R² = 0.25) — a way of one's own was not an eccentricity to be corrected, it was the thing that made him quick. Thirteen years later the harder finding: forty-three white-browed sparrow weaver family groups build architecturally distinct roosts, some with long entrance tubes and some with almost none, stable across years, differing between groups whose territories sit metres apart in the same trees, and not explained by weather, body size, tree height or kinship — then the closer, that the styles are robust to immigration. Not a template and not the environment: a tradition. Set beside all of this is David Gray-Hammond's account of his own room — the diffuser, the books read several at once, the nothing-tidied-away because some days end in a crash rather than a decision — and his sentence about it: to most, it appears that I live in a state of chaos… I know where every item I need resides. The refusals are printed on the zine's face rather than left implied. Not permission from nature, because a universe that could approve could also decline, and down to is not because of. Not instinct versus learning. Not a clever-animal story, since the authors themselves attribute the improvement to increasing dexterity and say any role for cognition still needs demonstrating. And the honest one: not every mess is a nest — burnout collapses the architecture, and the ruins look from the doorway exactly like the curated version. What the science kills is narrower and sturdier for being narrow: the inference that an order you cannot read is not an order. Two centuries of confident observers looked at a nest and saw a machine executing, and were describing the limits of watching while calling it a fact about the bird. Nesting is David Gray-Hammond's; lilipadding is Tanya Adkin and David Gray-Hammond's, with Adkin's name first on both pieces that set it out — a first draft credited it to him alone, and the colophon says so. Ten spreads, two diagrams. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 57 The Shell Was Your Calcium Stimpunks Zines The egg crack moment is borrowed, true, and kinder than its own retelling. More than eighty per cent of a hatchling's calcium came from the wall it broke. The word is borrowed and this zine says so. 10 spreads→ Details In the trans community, getting your egg cracked is the moment somebody knows and accepts that they are trans; the therapist Essy Knopf extended the term to Autistic and ADHD experience in 2025, and credited its origin himself. The word is borrowed and this zine says so — no individual coined it, and Evelyn Bauer's history for Them traces the earliest documented use to an Urban Dictionary entry in August 2016 and finds even Susan Stryker unable to date her own first encounter with it. What the zine argues with is not Knopf but what happens to the metaphor afterwards, when repetition flattens it into a door: one threshold, crossed once, a settled person on the far side. So we checked it against some eggs. The shell does not get thinner. From about day eleven the chorioallantoic membrane dissolves calcium out of the wall, and Halgrain and colleagues measured the result — thickness between day 0 and day 15 not significantly different (p = 0.110), breaking strength between day 11 and day 15 significantly reduced (p = 0.007). Measure it and nothing is happening. Weigh what it can bear and everything is. Nobody could see it; there was nothing to see. Then where the calcium goes: the shell supplies more than eighty per cent of all the calcium a chick embryo gets, roughly 2.2 grams, and at hatch the skeleton holds about three quarters of the calcium in the whole animal. The container becomes the frame, by mass, and there is no moment where one ends and the other begins — and since collagen is piezoelectric, as Iwao Yasuda showed in the 1950s, the wall you broke is now the part of you that turns pressure into charge. Third, the messy middle is a documented stage: at internal pipping the beak enters the air cell and the lungs begin working while the shell is still whole, a staged handover Margaret Vince traced in three parts. From outside, an unmarked egg. Fourth, quail embryos click, and an egg set in a clutch a day late speeds up and hatches with the others — while a slower click rate retards the ones ahead. Synchronisation runs both ways: the ones ahead slow down and wait. And the close, from Mair and colleagues' 2026 study of 225 posts: not a door but an oscillating Grief, Relief, and Belief Cycle, whose fourth theme is post-diagnosis burnout, with the authors asking that identification be treated as a first step rather than a terminal component of a service. The refusals are on the zine's face. Not cracking somebody else's egg — the egg tooth is on the inside of the shell, and you can only click. Not the person before was fake. Not a graduation. Not permission from nature, because chick embryos have no identities and down to is not because of. And not the egg as the enemy, which is the uncomfortable one, because masking cost us enormously and also got some of us here alive. Ten spreads, four diagrams. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 60 Beyond the Optical Image Stimpunks Zines On a measured discrepancy, ninety-three years of refusing to say where it lives, and the same question closed on day one. The most famous rotation-curve paper never uses the word dark. It says mass lies beyond the optical image — exactly what was measured. 13 spreads→ Details Helen Edgar’s first constellation, of twenty, is the Dark Matter Field — “the heavy darkness of neuronormativity… the accumulated weight we carry around of a world that does not meet our needs.” Nos. 45 and 46 both said in their colophons that this naming was being kept back. This is the piece that spends it, and the order of borrowing is stated on spread two: her naming came first, the physics is set beside it afterward, and the reverse move is the one this collection exists to refuse. Then ninety-three years of the most careful attribution on record. Fritz Zwicky (1933) applied the virial theorem to seven galaxies in the Coma cluster and found the average density “would have to be at least 400 times greater than that derived on the basis of observations of luminous matter” — he had the number, he had the phrase dark matter, and he closed the section by calling it “an unsolved problem.” The first thing a careful person does with a discrepancy is decline to place it. Forty-seven years later the famous paper comes apart under reading. Rubin, Ford & Thonnard (ApJ 238, 471, 1980) do not report flat rotation curves: “Most rotation curves are rising slowly even at the farthest measured point,” and the negative claim is narrower still — “Neither high nor low luminosity Sc galaxies have falling rotation curves.” Their conclusion says where and refuses to say what: “must have significant mass located beyond the optical image.” The word “dark” never appears in the abstract, and the subject heading as printed is galaxies : internal motions. In 2000 Rubin was still withholding: “Surprisingly, we cannot yet rule out a modified gravitational potential, rather than dark matter” — and “it is folly to believe that we know what a galaxy is, while the extent, the density distribution, and the composition of ≥90% of its mass are still a dark mystery.” Then the zine corrects itself on the page. It was proposed on the premise that the field is “never directly observed, only detected by its distorting effect,” with lensing offered as proof of that — but lensing is the instrument that made the direct detection. Clowe et al. (2006) measured an “8-sigma significance spatial offset” in the Bullet Cluster that “cannot be explained with an alteration of the gravitational force law.” The premise had to go, and spread seven keeps the correction rather than quietly dropping it. What is still open is the particle, not the mass: LZ and XENONnT have both come up empty, and the searches are widening to axion-like particles and dark photons. Two claims held apart, because collapsing either one is the misuse. The argument itself is structural. A gap between what a model predicts and what a body does can live in exactly three places — the mass, the law, or the measurement — and astronomy has argued all three in public, with rivals named and nulls published. Asked about a child, the same question was closed on day one and the residual placed in the child: not the fluorescent hum, not the unannounced transition, not the six hours of masking, not Milton’s double empathy problem. The claim is precise and the sloppy version is not ours — not that the environmental attribution is obviously right, but that it was never treated as an open question. No rival funded, nothing in the criteria reading “we cannot yet rule out.” Where the analogy breaks is stated at full strength rather than hedged: neuronormativity is unmarked, not unobserved. It is written down — criteria, intervention targets, the compliance goal on an education plan, “culture fit,” the seating chart. Dark matter is hidden by nature; this is hidden by convention, and a convention is a decision that can be read and changed this year. The close is the sharpest thing here. Take the identical fact — unseen mass is most of what holds a galaxy together — and it reads just as naturally as the co-regulation nobody logs and the care work nobody bills. Same evidence, opposite moral, and the physics adjudicates neither: if one fact can carry two opposite morals, the moral was never in the fact. Somebody chooses, and has to own the choosing. Refusals on the face: not dark matter proving anything about a nervous system; not an argument against evidence, since careful public attribution is what we are asking for; not modified-gravity advocacy; not “you are mysterious,” because Rubin’s folly line is about a galaxy; not the inspiration story about Rubin, since borrowing it would do to her what gets done to us; and not Helen’s reading corrected. The neuronormative paradigm is Nick Walker’s (Neuroqueer Heresies, 2021), dated here via Helen Edgar’s own account at Autistic Realms and not read at the book; the double empathy problem is Damian Milton’s (2012); monotropism is Murray, Lesser & Lawson (2005). Zwicky read in translation, not the German. Thirteen spreads, eleven diagrams. A method, not a proof.

Zine No. 61 Thirteen Changes Stimpunks Zines On the number that gave Brontosaurus its name back, a ruler its makers said would not travel, and an appeal they lost in public. A category boundary that publishes its own provenance, fences its own range, names its dissenters, and can be appealed — and lost. Ask that of a cut-off score. 13 spreads→ Details Every kid who loved Brontosaurus got told actually, it’s Apatosaurus, and the lesson attached was that the enthusiasm was the amateur part. Here is the paper trail. Marsh named Apatosaurus ajax in 1877 and Brontosaurus excelsus in 1879; Riggs folded the second into the first in 1903 on differences recorded as “usually considered insufficient to justify generic distinction.” Insufficient is a quantitative word with no quantity behind it — and for eighty years nobody could say insufficient by what measure, because the measure did not exist. Then Tschopp, Mateus & Benson built one, across 298 open-access pages, scoring 81 specimens against 477 morphological characters. Their methods section opens by conceding the soft part: separation “is somewhat arbitrary, in particular in paleontology, where no tests exist for the biological species concept,” and “subjectivity of these interpretations is especially great.” So they published the calibration, which is the spread this zine exists for. They counted the differences between pairs everybody already agreed were one genus — twelve between A. ajax and A. louisae, eleven between D. carnegii and D. hallorum — and set the bar one step past the largest agreed gap: “a minimum of 13 changes is herein considered necessary for generic separation.” Six for a species, deliberately generous, because “a wider margin is preferred herein in order to be more cautious.” You can argue with a number whose derivation is printed. You cannot argue with insufficient. Then the rarest move in the story: they fenced their own instrument. The numbers “cannot be applied to any other analysis, even of the same clade” — a threshold that declares its own range of validity, in advance, in the paper that depends on it. By that ruler Brontosaurus holds its own genus after 112 years, and even the headline is hedged in the abstract: “considered valid by our quantitative approach.” The method was not a rescue machine — the same pass dissolved “Dinheirosaurus” into Supersaurus and raised Galeamopus, cutting against its makers’ own earlier work. And then they filed an appeal and lost. The type specimen anchoring the whole genus Diplodocus is a partial tail the paper calls a nomen dubium, leaving “the otherwise well-known genus Diplodocus typified by a dubious species.” They petitioned the ICZN to move it — Case 3700, with a comment period and supporters — and on the last day of 2018 the Commission said no: Opinion 2425, Diplodocus longus maintained. Refused in print, with a number on it, by a body whose refusals you can look up and cite. Set the five properties beside the label on a child: published provenance, a declared range, named dissent (Prothero, four months later, under his own name), a route of appeal, a citable ruling. A cut-off score arrives already applied, says nothing about who chose it or where it stops meaning anything, and then travels across ages, countries and purposes it was never built for. The ruler that would not travel one clade sideways gets less latitude than the one we hand a five-year-old for life — and there is no Case 3700, nowhere to file, no numbered Opinion. The paperwork is not always kind either, and spread eight says so: Oviraptor means egg seizer, named in 1924 for a clutch it was brooding, corrected by Norell and colleagues in 1994 and 1995, and stuck with the libel forever under nomenclatural priority. Two ways a label outlives its refutation — priority, a rule written down, and repetition, which needs no rule at all. Only one admits it. Then the turn: Velociraptor was feathered, on the evidence of quill knobs on the ulna, and it is smaller and stranger than the movie and closer to a bad-tempered rooster, because birds are dinosaurs. Not one of these corrections made an animal less interesting. Every one made it stranger. The animals were never wrong about themselves; we were wrong about them, and being wrong out loud is what let them get better. And 298 pages is not what growing out of it looks like — it is what it looks like when nobody does. What get serious asks for is never depth, which monotropic attention already has; it is convertibility. Not that we stop being absorbed, but that we stop being absorbed for free. Bettin’s inversion holds: retained neoteny is not developmental lag but a distributed adaptive capacity that keeps a group from setting into whatever the highest-ranking person already believes. The close earns the collection. Apatosaurus louisae is estimated at about 41 tonnes of calcium phosphate, and calcium and phosphorus are made in stars — so a sauropod walked the Late Jurassic on a skeleton of dead stars, every atom second-hand and every atom still in circulation. Bone is piezoelectric, as Yasuda showed, so those animals were writing their own skeletons by walking on them; that this was true of sauropod bone is marked as an inference, not a measurement. And Sander and sixteen co-authors still report “no direct evidence on sauropod food and food processing” — the biggest animals ever to walk, and we do not know how they ate, which never made them less real. Refusals on the face: not an argument against evidence or diagnosis, since published provenance is what we are asking for; not “categories are meaningless,” because thirteen is a real bar doing real work; not a claim that taxonomy is like being labelled; not “the scientists were wrong and the kid was right,” because being corrected was never the injury and not being correctable is; not a demand that every label be revoked, since some of us want ours; and not the naturalistic fallacy, because down to is not because of. Thirteen spreads, eleven diagrams. A method, not a proof.
The Light Arrived Before the Name

Zine No. 62 The Light Arrived Before the Name Stimpunks Zines On light-travel time, the seventy-one years it took one description of us to reach English, and the difference between what a thing is and what it ends up called. Light leaves with nothing written on it, so every name in astronomy is an arrival record and never an origin record. Seven measured delays, and what they say about the observer. 11 spreads→ Details The physics is one sentence and it does all the work: light travels at a finite speed and leaves with nothing written on it. Sunlight is eight minutes and twenty seconds old when it reaches your face; Proxima Centauri’s is 4.2 years old; Andromeda’s is 2.5 million. A photon carries a wavelength and a direction and not a discoverer — everything a star will say about itself is complete at emission, and the name gets attached at the far end, by whoever happened to be standing there with an instrument. Astronomy is honest about this and has a word for the landing: first light is the moment a new telescope opens its eye, and nobody has ever thought the telescope invented the galaxy in the frame. So a name in astronomy is an arrival record, never an origin record — and almost everything in this zine is those two things being confused, with a person in place of a star. Priority is the version written down: credit goes to whoever publishes first, and a comet takes the name of whoever files. Halley earned his fairly — he worked out that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object and in 1705 predicted its 1758 return — and its passages had been recorded for more than two thousand years before him. The rule never claimed otherwise. The trouble starts when the register stops saying what it is a register of. Then 1925, twice. In Cambridge, Massachusetts, Cecilia Payne submitted the thesis showing the stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium; Henry Norris Russell told her it was clearly impossible, and she published with a line saying the abundance was “almost certainly not real.” Russell restated the conclusion in 1929. In Moscow — not Kiev, and the zine keeps its own corrected error on the page rather than fixing it quietly — Grunya Sukhareva finished a clinical description of six boys at the hospital-school she had founded in 1921, recording the aloneness, the flattened expression, the narrow blazing interests and the giftedness underneath. Russian in 1925, German in 1926, English in 1996. Seventy-one years, and half a century after Kanner’s and Asperger’s names were fixed to what she had described. Spread five is the structural spine: a distance is a delay, and the same quantity exists for a finding. Seven crossings, each an interval between two dated events. 168 years from Caroline Herschel’s Royal Astronomical Society Gold Medal in 1828 to the next woman’s, Vera Rubin’s, in 1996. 123 years from Matilda Joslyn Gage mapping the pattern in Woman as Inventor (1870) to Margaret Rossiter naming it the Matilda effect (1993) — the name for late naming was itself a hundred and twenty-three years late, and Rossiter did the one thing the pattern does not do by itself: she looked back down the beam and put the earlier name on it. 71 years to English. 42 years from Annie Jump Cannon joining the Harvard College Observatory in 1896 to Harvard giving her a regular appointment in 1938. 7 years from the first pulsar to a Nobel that went to Hewish and Ryle. 4 years from Payne to Russell. And Mittag-Leffler’s 1925 letter intending to nominate Henrietta Leavitt, who had died in 1921 — there was never a nomination. None of those is a claim about intent; each measures a gap, the way you measure a parallax, and the delay tells you about the observer, not the object. The Bell Burnell spread is deliberately precise where the popular telling is not: she read roughly 96 feet of chart paper a day, found a signal too regular to be noise, and is the second author on Hewish, Bell, Pilkington, Scott & Collins, Nature 217, 709 (1968), period 1.3372795 seconds. She was not written out of the paper. She was written out of the prize. And the pulses had been arriving the whole time — what 1967 changed was the listening. Refusals on the face, because six women is six situations and flattening them would be the second erasure: not that gender explains Sukhareva, since Sher & Gibson give her Jewish identity, her Russian nationality and her Russian- and German-language publication alongside it, and raise the possibility that Asperger omitted her deliberately under Nazi-era antisemitism; not that a missed prize and Stalinist violence are the same harm, since she was attacked at the 1951 Pavlovian Sessions and colleagues around her lost their lives; not that every woman here was silenced alike, since Cannon took the Henry Draper Medal in 1931 and funded the award whose first recipient in 1934 was Payne-Gaposchkin — honoured from outside, unpromoted at home, and she is the exception and forty-two years of the rule; not that recognition and justice are the same, since Herschel took the medal in 1828 and stayed her brother’s assistant on the payroll; not that these men stole, since Russell cited Payne and reported “very gratifying agreement” — the mechanism varies every time and the direction does not; not an argument against priority or citation; and not the naturalistic fallacy. Then the turn that earns the collection. The six children Sukhareva wrote down were Autistic, and so were Autistic children in 1895 and 1795 and every year nobody was taking notes. 1925 is not when we started; it is when somebody was standing there with an instrument. A diagnosis is an arrival record, and the criteria say so out loud — the DSM-5 requires symptoms “present in the early developmental period” while conceding they “may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life.” The manual is describing light-travel time. Somebody diagnosed at forty-seven has not been Autistic since they were forty-seven; the paperwork is forty-seven years old and the light is not. You can’t have been, you’d have been picked up is that confusion said out loud, and it made the receiver the origin for girls, for Black and brown children, for anyone whose flavour of it stayed indoors. There is a version of this history in which the first thing anybody read about us was written by a woman who noticed the giftedness in the same paragraph as the difficulty — because she did, and it did not arrive in time to set the tone. The close: everything heavier than hydrogen and helium was cooked inside stars and scattered when they died, and the carbon, oxygen and calcium in you crossed several billion years to arrive with no name attached and no signature required. The calcium works whether or not Payne was believed in 1925. Publishing Sukhareva’s name does not reach her — she died in 1981 — it fixes our instrument, the one we are using on the next person whose account arrives in the wrong language or the wrong decade. Down to is not because of. Eleven spreads, five diagrams. The light was never wrong. The paperwork was late.

Zine No. 63 Even Fallen Light Glows Stimpunks Zines · after Helen Edgar On Neruda’s well, a rewrite made in burnout, six syllables that answered it — and the fact that fallen wood glows in the dark for no reason anyone has been able to establish. Every known bioluminescent fungus is a white-rot decomposer, so the thing that glows is the thing that eats fallen wood. After 160 million years, nobody can say what the glow is for. 12 spreads→ Details Three texts and one fungus. Neruda’s untitled poem in El mar y las campanas (1973) says that if each day falls inside each night there is a well “where clarity is imprisoned,” and instructs you to sit on the rim of the well of darkness and fish for fallen light with patience (William O’Daly’s translation, The Sea and the Bells, Copper Canyon, 1988, pp. 94–95 — read at the printed page, because every online copy is an aggregator). Read the grammar and the poem has quietly handed out two roles: the one who fishes, and the light that fell. Ryan Boren’s rewrite, made in deep Autistic burnout, moves the speaker into the well — the rim is distant, no casting can reach, patience broke — and the discovery inside it is structural rather than emotional: sitting on a rim with patience is work you can do, being the light at the bottom is not work at all, and once you are the light every instruction in the poem is addressed to somebody else. Helen Edgar answered in six syllables: even fallen light glows. What makes the reply hold is what it refuses — it does not say the rim is closer, that patience returns, or that you will be reached. It is a claim about the light, not about the rescue, and it pries apart two things the poem had welded together. Then the fact. Foxfire. Perry, Desjardin & Stevani (J. Fungi 11(1):19, 2024) recognise 132 taxa across five lineages — Mycenaceae 96, Omphalotaceae 18, Physalacriaceae 14, Lucentipes 3, Cyphellopsidaceae 1 — and every one is an agaric saprotrophic white-rot decomposer, or rarely a plant pathogen. There is no glowing fungus that lives some other way, which makes the thing that glows is the thing that eats fallen wood a statement of taxonomy rather than a figure of speech. The glow is built out of the log: the caffeic acid cycle runs caffeic acid to hispidin to 3-hydroxyhispidin, the luciferin, which luciferase oxidises with oxygen to caffeylpyruvate and a photon near 530 nm — and then caffeylpyruvate hydrolase turns the spent molecule back into caffeic acid. The end of the reaction is the beginning of the reaction. And in the Armillaria lineage the part that glows is the mycelium and rhizomorphs, threads inside the wood, while the mushrooms are consistently non-luminescent: the showy reproductive part is the dark one. Emission runs continuously, on a temperature-compensated circadian clock (Oliveira et al., Curr. Biol. 25:964–968, 2015), so nothing about it is conditional on a receiver — it does not brighten for company and does not stop when the forest is empty, which is nearly always. The honest centre is spread nine: nobody knows what it is for. Lit mushroom models draw more beetles, flies, bugs and wasps than unlit ones, which is real evidence for spore dispersal — and it explains a cap, not the mycelium and lower stipe, which make no spores at all. A live rival says the luciferin is an antioxidant and the light is a byproduct of handling reactive oxygen while dismantling lignin. The review states outright that a non-adaptive, accidental origin cannot yet be excluded. Spread ten is the guardrail: bioluminescence arose once, about 160 mya, and has been lost or inactivated in lineage after lineage since — so keeping the glow is not an achievement and losing it is the commonest thing that ever happened to it. A zine that says even fallen light glows is one sentence away from so you had better be glowing, and the phylogeny is what blocks it. The turn: if you are the fallen light, glowing is not a task you are behind on, and the casting is somebody else’s work — which is where solidarity stops being a warm feeling and becomes a division of labour. Helen’s constellation is what sits at the rim. Refusals on the face: not that the log is glad it fell; not that burnout is secretly productive, because decay is not a chrysalis and burnout is damage somebody’s conditions caused; not that you must glow to be worth keeping; not that the glow is a signal so try harder to be seen; not a promise that you will be reached; not nature proving anything about a nervous system; and not the rewrite corrected — both poems are on the page, unedited, in order. The consolation is deliberately thin, because a thicker one would be a lie to somebody whose patience has broken. Twelve spreads, one diagram. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 69 Your Shadow Is the Centre Stimpunks Zines On the bow that no two people can share, the man who proved it in 1267 with an astrolabe and no theory at all, and why being unable to show someone a real thing was never a reason to doubt it. A rainbow is a circle centred on the shadow of your own head, so there are as many bows as there are observers — and Roger Bacon used that un-shareability as his evidence, not his problem. 11 spreads→ Details The oldest correct thing anybody wrote down about a rainbow is not about colour and not about water. It is about where you are standing. Around 1267, in the experimental-science part of the Opus Majus, Roger Bacon took an astrolabe outside, measured the height of the sun against the height of a bow, and reported that a rainbow can never stand more than 42 degrees above the horizon. He then wrote something far stranger, and wrote it as a finding: “From these facts we learn by experiment that there are as many bows as there are observers.” He gave the test, too — two people look north at the bow, one walks west and the bow goes west with him, the other walks east and his bow goes east. Hence “it is impossible for two observers to see one and the same bow, although an ignorant person does not grasp this fact”; and the reason, which is this zine’s title: “the shadow of each observer divides the arc of the rainbow into two equal parts.” He put the apex of his cone at the eye and ran its axis to “the nadir of the sun” — the antisolar point — and he did all of this with no theory of refraction whatsoever, forty years before anyone described what happens inside a drop and three hundred and seventy before Descartes could calculate it. Roland Stull’s Practical Meteorology says the same things now: rainbows are “centered on the antisolar point, which is the point corresponding to the shadow of your head or camera,” and “different observers see different rainbows caused by different light rays interacting with different raindrops” — red edge 42.7°, violet ~40°, n = 1.3315. But the spread that earns the piece is the inversion: Bacon did not treat the privacy of the bow as a puzzle to explain away, he treated it as data, and ran controls in 1267. A lit cloud takes a colour that “appears the same to different observers, nor does it follow the motion of the observer”; a fish or a stick seen through water is displaced but “does not follow the observer if he recedes”; the bow follows you at the speed of “a man running or riding as fast as possible.” Three phenomena, one question, one odd answer — and from the odd answer he concluded that the bow must be made of rays that bounce. He landed on reflection alone and was wrong, or badly incomplete; the method was right and the geometry survived into a textbook you can download today. The feature that makes a rainbow impossible to hand to anybody is the feature that told us what a rainbow is. Then the harder claims. Les Cowley: “Rainbows possess neither distance nor linear dimension” — it behaves as though at infinity and “cannot be touched, tickled, walked around or driven through”; a direction, not a place. Your two pupils sit 63 mm apart, each the apex of its own cone collecting its own drops, so you are not looking at one rainbow with two eyes — which closes the standard exit from our own umwelt argument in No. 15, because here the perceivers are identical and position alone is sufficient. And the conditions: sun behind you, rain ahead, unobstructed, sun under 42° or the whole ring sinks below the horizon — Bacon worked the arithmetic for the latitude of Paris (41°12′ at equinox noon) and for a latitude near the Tropic of Cancer, where “no rainbow can be formed at any noon of the entire year.” Rain falling, sun blazing, eyes perfect, and no bow: nothing wrong with the observer, and the arrangement is adjustable. The turn: in the 759 years since Bacon wrote it down, nobody has ever concluded that rainbows are not real because they cannot be shown to a second person. No one demands corroboration. That courtesy is not extended evenly, and if it were real you could show me has a four-hundred-page textbook counterexample in the sky twice a month. Six refusals on the face, the first being the one that matters: not that everybody sees it differently so who’s to say — different bow, same physics, 42.7° for everyone, always, and the most private phenomenon here is also one of the most rigidly law-bound. Also not a claim on the Pride rainbow, which already means something specific in our house. Two claims are marked on the page as ours rather than anybody’s measurement. Eleven spreads, six figures, a “Not:” refusals set. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 70 Both Arcs, One Drop Stimpunks Zines On the raindrop that makes both bows at once, the lab that tried to erase both of you, and why entwined turns out to be a claim about the source rather than a feeling about the self. A single drop makes both arcs of a double rainbow simultaneously, from one beam — so neither is the second one. And the suppression of queer and Autistic children came out of one lab, with one name on both papers. 12 spreads→ Details A double rainbow is not two rainbows. Roland Stull’s Practical Meteorology: “a single raindrop produces both: entering rays undergo either one internal reflection (primary) or two internal reflections (secondary) before exiting.” One drop, one beam, both arcs, at the same instant — which means the outer bow is never absent, only sometimes outshone. The extra bounce reverses the colours, so red sits outermost on the inner bow and innermost on the outer one and the two reds face each other across Alexander’s dark band (Alexander of Aphrodisias, c. 200 CE) — a band that is not a wall between them but the region neither arc reaches, the shadow left where the light piled up elsewhere. The zine states the awkward number rather than hiding it: the secondary is 43% as bright, because its light must survive two internal reflections instead of one. Dimmer is a fact about path length, not about rank. So spread five refuses the obvious move and will not hand you one arc for being queer and one for being neurodivergent — assign the arcs and one of them is the 43% one, and the shape does the ranking however carefully you write around it. The drop never divided them. Primary and secondary are our words, for our convenience; the drop has never heard them. Then the turn, where entwined stops being a warm word and becomes a citation. In 1974 the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis published Rekers & Lovaas, “Behavioral Treatment of Deviant Sex-Role Behaviors in a Male Child” (7(2), 173–190), whose abstract states its own aim as “the primary prevention of adult transsexualism or similar adult sex-role deviation.” Thirteen years later the same O. Ivar Lovaas, at the same university, published the 1987 autism paper. One name, on both. Our own Eight Tenths of a Second (No. 38) follows the behaviourism chain to a spread called “A room with a child in it” and stops at that door; this zine opens it and reports that there was more than one kind of child at the table. The 1974 paper was read at the paper — PMC holds it as scanned images, so the PDF was obtained and read, which is how the circulating pseudonym “Craig” turns out to be “Kraig”. He was four years and eleven months old. His mother was “trained to be his therapist.” Red and blue poker chips: blue toward a candy bar, red for response cost, timeout, “or (c) physical punishment by spanking from the father.” And the sequencing detail that undoes you — it was judged “clinically safer” to run the chips on ordinary household behaviour first, so the same red chip that had meant tracking dirt on carpet was then extended to playing with girls, playing with dolls, and feminine gestures. His name was Kirk Andrew Murphy; he died by suicide in 2003, reported here as the behaviour-analytic literature reports it, without a causal claim attached, because his family’s grief is not a rhetorical device. JABA issued a Statement of Concern in 2020 and did not retract, reasoning that “the available evidence does not make it clear that the original study was unethical by the standards of that day”; Austin H. Johnson answered in 2022 that it should be retracted. Fifty-two years, and it stands. Neuroqueer credited properly — Nick Walker, independently Athena Lynn Michaels-Dillon, with Remi Yergeau’s neurological queerness — and Gwen Nelson, who created Autistic Pride Day, is a trans woman. Seven refusals, including that queer and Autistic experience are not the same experience, that today’s ABA is not 1974, and that the claim is lineage. Twelve spreads. A rhyme, not a proof — the history is the argument; the rainbow is only how we noticed what shape it was.

Zine No. 71 Nothing Is Pushing Stimpunks Zines On escape velocity as a coasting number, the places inside a well that cost nothing to sit in, and a telescope built so that it cannot brake. Escape velocity is defined for a trajectory with no engine running — and it falls as you rise. Two of the five Lagrange points cost nothing at all to occupy, and which two depends on the system, never on the occupant. 12 spreads→ Details Escape velocity is a coasting number, and almost every use of it drops the condition that makes it true. The 11.186 km/s quoted for Earth is vesc = √(2GM/r), and it is defined for a ballistic trajectory — the speed you need if nothing is pushing you afterwards. Two things follow that the motivational reading gets backwards. First, the figure is local: it falls as the square root of one over distance, so it is 7.91 km/s at two Earth radii and 5.59 at four. The requirement is not a property of what you are leaving; it is a property of where you are asking from. Second, it says nothing whatever about anything under thrust, which is not a loophole but the scope of the definition. Dawn is the demonstration. On 5 September 2012 it left Vesta not by jumping from the floor but by climbing on ion thrust until the bar had come down to meet it — JPL’s own words, “spiral away as gently as it arrived”; Marc Rayman’s, “Thrust is engaged, and we are now climbing away from Vesta atop a blue-green pillar of xenon ions.” The zine is careful to say on the spread, not only in the colophon, that Dawn did eventually cross the local threshold; the claim is that it never had to make the jump from the bottom. Then the half the piece was actually built for. A gravity well contains places that cost nothing to occupy. Of the five Lagrange points, L1, L2 and L3 are saddle points and unstable; L4 and L5 are genuinely stable — not balancing, not holding on — whenever the mass ratio clears a threshold. That threshold is μG = (1 − √(23/27))/2 = 0.0385208965…, the smaller root of 27μ(1−μ) = 1, and here the zine performs a precedence correction: it is usually called Routh’s value after his 1875 paper, and Bruno Sicardy (CMDA 107, 2010) says it “should actually be called Gascheau’s value in view of the precedence of his work” — Gabriel Gascheau, professor at Toulouse, published in Paris in 1843, thirty-plus years earlier. A piece arguing that the environment decides the outcome had no business misattributing the theorem that proves it. And the theorem is the argument: the same rock, unchanged in every respect, stays at Jupiter’s L4 for the age of the solar system and wanders off from the L4 of a pair whose masses are too even. Nothing about the rock did it. About 105 Jupiter Trojans larger than a kilometre are sitting there now (Bottke, Marschall, Nesvorný & Vokrouhlický, 2023) — and, kept deliberately, they were captured during the giant planets’ migration, so the stable place was not where they started and they did not choose it. Then the case that closes the loophole: even the unstable places are cheap. Petersen (AAS 19-806, 2019): “The dynamical region about the SEMB L2 point is inherently unstable” — and JWST holds it, per Rigby et al. (2023), on burns “scheduled every three weeks…with typical durations of tens of seconds,” of which “three…were skipped because the computed correction was negligibly small.” The maintenance schedule for an unstable position includes doing nothing. The final spread is the one the piece exists for: thermal limits forbid sunward-facing thrusters, so “no direct observatory-to-Sun vector maneuver directions are allowed” — Webb cannot brake, drifting past L2 would end the mission, and so every burn is deliberately thrown short. Nobody calls that the telescope’s failing; the whole trajectory was designed around it, at a cost the mission simply paid. Against all of this sits Helen Edgar’s Gravity Well, constellation fourteen of My Monotropic Galaxy, whose naming and frame are hers and whose violet is this zine’s accent — and Buckle, Leadbitter, Poliakoff & Gowen (2021), 32 Autistic adults, whose finding reframes the whole physics: starting, stopping and switching are one tendency, and what helps is another person — “a stuck buddy that I text” — where alarms and lists rarely substitute. The paper’s title is a participant’s phrase, “No Way Out Except From External Intervention,” which is not a confession but a correct statement about where energy enters a system.
