Seven refusals, including that the burst is not available on request (participants describe “a literal paralysis”), that you’re not stuck, you’re just orbiting is not an accommodation, and that gravity is not the villain — the well is also why there is an atmosphere. One widely-quoted number was hunted, not sourced primarily, and deliberately left out. Twelve spreads, seven figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 73 Measured Against a Tree Stimpunks Zines On six ways a moss fails as a plant, and the finding that the list is backwards — because holding your own water is the newer trick, and the tree is the one that lost the older one. Desiccation tolerance is ancestral. The vascular plants gave it up to get tall and kept it only in their seeds, and some went back for it. The deficit list was accurate line by line, and measuring the wrong thing. 12 spreads→ Details Take a tree as the definition of a plant and a moss fails at six points. No roots — rhizoids anchor and barely absorb. No xylem or phloem. No way to lift water, so no height. No control of its own moisture, because its tissue simply equilibrates with the air. And no photosynthesis at all while dry. Every line is true, and the zine keeps the whole list intact to the last spread. Botany has proper names for the split: a moss is poikilohydric, its hydration tracking the surrounding humidity, where a vascular plant is homoiohydric and holds an interior against the outside — at the price of roots, xylem, a waxy cuticle and thousands of controllable stomata, with a failure mode that is not a pause but death. Drying is a state a tree cannot occupy. Then the finding that inverts the list. Proctor, Oliver, Wood, Alpert, Stark, Cleavitt & Mishler, reviewing desiccation tolerance in bryophytes in The Bryologist 110(4), 2007, record it as a primitive character of land plants, lost in the course of evolution of the homoiohydric vascular-plant shoot system, but retained in spores, pollen and seeds, and re-evolved in the vegetative tissues of vascular resurrection plants. The moss did not fail to acquire the tree’s solution; the tree discarded the moss’s — kept it for the one job where nothing else would do, so every seed in a packet is doing what a moss does, and some lineages later evolved their way back to it. What drying actually is gets stated without comfort. The cytoplasm enters a glassy state in which molecular mobility is severely reduced; a 2013 Journal of Experimental Botany paper on Syntrichia ruralis is titled for the result, “Evidence for the absence of enzymatic reactions in the glassy state.” It is not idling. It has stopped, and stopping is what conserves it — survival bought with the whole of the time. Then water arrives and respiration reactivates almost instantly, photosynthesis within minutes, net rates substantially normal within thirty to sixty. Nothing had to be rebuilt because nothing was dismantled. Syntrichia recovers after decades dry; Roads, Longton & Convey (Current Biology, 2014) grew new shoots from Chorisodontium aciphyllum frozen at least 1,530 years in Antarctic permafrost — and the zine keeps the two apart on the spread rather than blurring them, because that case is cryptobiosis under freezing, not desiccation. The best spread is the boundary layer, and it is Robin Wall Kimmerer’s, read at Gathering Moss (Oregon State University Press, 2003, pp. 14–19). Friction stills the air against every surface, and the layer keeps what it holds — heat, water vapour, and over a rotting log up to ten times ambient carbon dioxide. Being small is the entry requirement, not a shortfall. But the layer is not merely found: friction makes it, so the long narrow upright leaves, the dense hairs and reflective tips and minuscule spines all deepen it. The greater the resistance, the deeper the boundary layer — and the larger the boundary layer, the larger the moss can be. A loop, not a niche: the moss builds the habitat that then permits it to be bigger, and mosses accordingly run from millimetre crusts to ten-centimetre wefts, a range Kimmerer likens to a blueberry bush and a redwood, tracking the layer rather than the moss. And layers nest — a rock’s sits under the forest’s umbrella, so the tree that wins every contest for light is also the reason a moss can be large. That argues against this zine’s own title, which is why it is on the spread and in the closing line. One more inversion: the green cushion is the gametophyte, the generation vascular plants reduced to a few cells in a pollen grain, and the little stalk above it is a periscope whose length correlates with the layer’s depth — the dependent generation is the one built to leave. Closing on Sphagnum: peatlands, ~3% of land, holding roughly twice the carbon of all the world’s forest biomass — the careful wording, kept because the loose one travels further. Six refusals, including that moss is not secretly tougher, that small is beautiful is not on offer, that resilience is never a demand, and that a mechanism recovering in an hour is not a promise made to anyone about burnout. Twelve spreads, three figures. Developed after Helen Edgar’s Mossy Minds & Monotropism. A rhyme, not a proof — the list was true; the ruler was a tree.
The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed

Zine No. 75 The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed Stimpunks Zines on the most expensive smell on earth, and the reason it is not in the mushroom Two people differ functionally at over 30% of their odorant receptor alleles. That is measured, not asserted — and it means “you’re smelling it wrong” is not a sentence that means anything. 12 spreads→ Details Matsutake is among the most expensive foods on earth and the entire price is for a smell — principally 1-octen-3-ol and methyl cinnamate, both of which decline as the fruiting body ages, which is why the grading and the airfreight and the button-stage picking all exist. Then the same molecules, elsewhere: deer choose it over other mushrooms, bears dig ditches for it, and Oregon pickers told Anna Tsing of elk with bloody muzzles from driving their faces into pumice soil to reach it — while in the same ground “slugs, other fungi, and many kinds of soil bacteria are repulsed by the smell, moving out of its range.” One set of compounds; an elk digs until it bleeds and a bacterium leaves. Nothing about the molecules changed between those two sentences. So the fact this zine follows is ordinary sensory biology: a smell is not a property of an object but a binding event between a molecule and a receptor, and if the shape does not fit, nothing happens at all — not a faint smell, nothing. Humans carry about 400 intact odorant receptors, and somebody counted how much they vary. Mainland et al. (Nature Neuroscience, 2014): “63% of the odorant receptors we examined had polymorphisms that altered in vitro function… on average, two individuals have functional differences at over 30% of their odorant receptor alleles” — with OR10G4 genotype explaining over 15% of perceived intensity and over 10% of perceived valence for guaiacol, and explicitly not explaining it for weaker agonists, a limit the zine prints rather than rounds off. The worked case runs from a letter of DNA to a word said out loud: Keller et al. (Nature, 2007) found androstenone “variously perceived by different individuals as offensive (‘sweaty, urinous’), pleasant (‘sweet, floral’) or odourless” — and traced it to two amino acid substitutions in one receptor, OR7D4. Foul, lovely, or absent; three people, one bottle, and nobody misperceiving. Which returns to Tsing’s own account of the autumn aroma: “It’s disturbing. Many people never learn to love it… Some people liken it to rotting things and some to clear beauty.” Not a failure of taste — exactly what a complex volatile predicts against arrays differing at a third of their alleles. And the title’s other half sits underneath it: seventy years have not produced a cultivated matsutake either, because it is a fungus and a pine root exchanging. You cannot farm the first and you cannot standardise the second; it is the same refusal, twice. The turn refuses “everyone has their own truth” hardest — the variation is public, sequenceable and testable, which is the opposite of soft. What it removes is only an excuse: there was no correct experience you were failing to have. Normal is a statistic about a population, not a fact about a person. Held honestly on its own face: no study links matsutake aroma to receptor genotype, and joining them is the zine’s move rather than a demonstrated result.

Zine No. 76 Forty Minutes to See Stimpunks Zines On the second visual system, the forty minutes it takes to arrive, the one bright light that ends it — and the faint thing that only appears when you stop looking straight at it. Dark adaptation is a handover, not a dial. The system everyone calls the worse one runs at the floor physics allows — one quantum per rod — and it is only available off-axis, after forty uninterrupted minutes nobody can feel passing. 12 spreads→ Details Your eyes do not gradually get used to the dark. Two systems hand over, and the handover leaves a kink in the curve. Cone thresholds fall fast and plateau in five to ten minutes; then the trace breaks downward and keeps falling — the rod–cone break — reaching a second, far lower plateau at forty to fifty minutes and an absolute threshold of order 10−5 cd/m². The steep satisfying part is over in ten minutes; the part that delivers the sensitivity takes four times as long and produces no sensation of progress at all, so anyone judging by feel concludes they are finished at about the ten-minute mark. What the second system is for comes from Hecht, Shlaer & Pirenne, “Energy, Quanta, and Vision,” Journal of General Physiology 25, 1942, 819–840 — read at the paper. Thousandth-of-a-second flashes at 510 nm: the minimum visible energy is 2.1–5.7 × 10−10 ergs at the cornea, “between 54 and 148 quanta of blue-green light.” Subtract the eye — ~4% reflected, “almost precisely 50 per cent absorbed by the lens and other ocular media,” “at least 80 per cent passes through the retina without being absorbed” — and 5 to 14 quanta remain, across a field holding “about 500 rods.” And here the zine corrects the most-repeated result in vision science. It circulates as the human eye can detect a single photon. The paper says something narrower and better: “in order for us to see, it is necessary for only 1 quantum of light to be absorbed by each of 5 to 14 retinal rods.” One quantum per rod; five to fourteen rods for a person. The popular version promotes a precise claim about a cell into a boast about an organ. The costs are stated rather than skipped: one pigment means colour is not a defined quantity, not that rods are bad at it; heavy pooling buys the sensitivity and is paid for in acuity; and forty minutes is forty minutes. A tuning is not a ranking. Then the geometry. The fovea — the patch you point at whatever you attend to — is rod-free, and rod density peaks around 20° out, so a faint enough star goes out when you look straight at it. Astronomers train averted vision deliberately. And it is not an amateur’s trick: it is how the 1942 number was obtained. The methods say “we chose a retinal area situated 20° temporally on the horizontal axis” — there was no alternative, because there are no rods at the centre to catch the quanta. The most precise measurement ever made of the limits of human sight was taken by looking away from the thing being measured. The closing move is the asymmetry: forty minutes to build, an instant to destroy, and the person holding the torch spends nothing while the person who waited pays in full — but rods barely respond to long wavelengths, so red light lets you see and keeps the forty minutes. Observatories, bridges, submarines and darkrooms are lit in red. Nobody arrived at that by asking observers to adapt faster. Assemble the description — needs forty uninterrupted minutes, gives no signal while working, resets to zero at no cost to the interrupter, no colour, poor detail, only works off-axis — and it reads exactly like a deficit list, and nobody has ever treated it as one, because everybody has it. Six refusals, the first being that retinal anatomy licenses nothing whatever about how a person should be looked at. Twelve spreads, four figures. Developed after the Nyctous card in Under the Word. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 77 Nothing Melts Stimpunks Zines On how snow grains bond below the melting point without ever becoming liquid, why the joint grows because it is the joint — and why bonding to each other does not fix what you are all standing on. Sintering joins separate things into a structure that carries weight, and none of them stops being separate. The reading is Leanne Betasamosake Simpson’s; only the physics and the avalanche are ours. 12 spreads→ Details Walk on hour-old snow and you go through it; walk on the same snow two days later and it carries you. Nothing was added and nobody packed it. The name for what happened is sintering, and the whole zine turns on what it is not: the obvious way to make a heap of separate things into one thing is to melt them, and that is not what occurs. Grains bond below the melting point, never liquefy, and stay individual crystals with their own boundaries — you can section a snowpack and count them. Held honestly on the spread, because it partly undercuts the title: ice surfaces carry a quasi-liquid premelted layer below the bulk melting point which can assist bonding without bulk melting, and its onset, thickness and relation to liquid water have been argued over for a century. Nothing melts in bulk and no crystal loses its identity; the surface where the joining happens is not a simple solid either. Why the bond forms where it does is the best fact here. Ice sublimes constantly, and the rate depends on the shape of the surface: a convex grain surface gives up more vapour, a concave hollow gives up less. So vapour leaves the rounded outsides and condenses in the crevice between two grains, simply because that is where the vapour pressure is lowest. The neck fills in because it is a neck — and the tighter the curve, the stronger the pull, so the earliest and most awkward stage of a bond is the one the physics favours most. Nothing arrives from outside: the bridge is made of material that left the grains themselves, so the joint is paid for out of the substance of the things being joined. It happens only at contact — proximity is not contact, and the physics has no mechanism for reaching across a gap — and it is strongly temperature-dependent, fast near zero and nearly stalled in deep cold, which makes the capacity to bond a property of grains-in-conditions rather than of grains. What it buys is not hardness but load-sharing: each grain is as fragile as ever, and no grain has to bear the whole thing alone. Then the cost, which is ours and not our sources’. Sintering is also how a cohesive slab is made, and a cohesive slab over a weak layer is the slab-avalanche condition — the same connectedness that carries weight is what lets a fracture cross the whole of it at once. And the failure is not in the necks: it is in the weak layer underneath, which the bonding above cannot reach or repair. Bonding to each other does not fix what you are all standing on. The reading is Leanne Betasamosake Simpson’s, in Theory of Water: Nishnaabe Maps to the Times Ahead, ch. 4, read at the book: “Sintering is a joining. It is a communal transformation that creates a fabric of former snowflakes bonded to each other”; “It weaves itself into its environment, and it does so in a way that doesn’t destroy its neighbours”; “sintering is how Michi Saagiig Nishnaabeg make worlds.” She arrived at it grooming a ski trail — “I wasn’t expecting the snow to teach me how to live in the world” — and she names the cost more honestly than we did: “Sintering is slow deformation,” and “Sintering in the forest is easy for me; sintering with people I’m currently sharing the planet with, much more difficult.” The application to neurodivergent community is Helen Edgar’s. The order on spread ten — her framework, Helen’s application, our physics — is the order the knowledge actually travelled. Six refusals, including that this is not a metaphor extracted from someone’s cosmology, that the physics does not validate the reading, and that community does not fix conditions. Twelve spreads, four figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 78 You Cannot Correct the Sky Stimpunks Zines On why stars twinkle and planets do not, on knowing exactly where a problem lives — and on the fact that correct is not the same as affordable. The flicker belongs to the air, not to the star. Once you know that you cannot honestly blame the star — and you still cannot afford the mirror, which covers a patch, runs on a subscription, and stops when the money does. 12 spreads→ Details A star that appears to be flickering wildly is not flickering. Its light left years ago, crossed the whole distance without incident, and reached the top of the atmosphere as a flat, orderly wavefront. Everything that happened to it happened in the last few microseconds, crossing air made of shifting cells at slightly different temperatures and densities, each refracting the wavefront a little. What lands is corrugated, and the pattern slides across the ground as the cells drift — so somebody standing a few metres away is receiving your missing photons at that instant. The control experiment is free every clear night: through the same air, at the same altitude, planets barely twinkle, because a star is effectively a point and a planet presents a resolved disc whose parts sample different cells at once, so the fluctuations cancel. The standard phrasing is exact — their angular diameters are so large as to quench the scintillations. Quench, not resist: nothing about a planet is tougher, it is simply wide enough that no single cell can speak for the whole of it. If the flicker is caused entirely by the medium, then the flicker is a measurement of the medium, and observatories use it as one — and nobody reads that report as a complaint about the star. Then the hinge the zine exists for. Every remedy is applied to the conditions: wait until the light is higher, spend billions to get above the air, or cancel the distortion with adaptive optics — which needs a natural or laser guide star, is valid over a small patch, and blurs again within milliseconds of the loop opening. It was never a fix. It is a subscription. You can correct a patch of sky. You cannot correct the sky. And somebody already made this argument about people. The social model of disability performs exactly the relocation on spread two: a person is disabled by a world built to a narrow specification rather than by their body. That move was necessary, and it is also the free part — it costs nothing, takes an afternoon, and has never by itself produced a single ramp. Everything after it is the deformable mirror and has the mirror’s properties: expensive, limited in coverage, requiring somebody to keep it running, and failing at once when the funding stops. So the position is uncomfortable in both directions. The people who locate the problem in the person are wrong, and saying so has never built anything. What it does settle is whose problem it is, which is the argument that has to be won before anyone is asked to pay. Six refusals, including that this is not a complaint about the social model but about treating the relocation as though it were the accommodation — a thing done most often by whoever would have to fund it. Twelve spreads, four figures, and a cover that has been running the argument on every page of this site for years: its twinkling points use the shared twinkle-anim keyframe behind the sitewide starfield, and reduced motion leaves them steady. Published hours earlier as The Star Is Not Flickering, framed around glimmers, and repointed the same day when the tie proved thin — the colophon carries that account rather than deleting it. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 82 The Play You Keep Stimpunks Zines On forty-five bumble bees, nine hundred and ten rolls of a wooden ball, and the definition science had to write down before it could see doing nothing at all. The sugar water was already within reach and the bees rolled the balls anyway. Play has five formal criteria, and the first one is that it must accomplish nothing — so the useless thing got studied seriously, on a standard that never once asked it to pay. 12 spreads→ Details Forty-five bumble bees produced 910 ball-rolling actions in a laboratory where a clear, unobstructed lane led to sucrose they could reach without touching anything. Nothing was hidden under the balls; no bee was ever rewarded for moving one. Galpayage Dona and colleagues tested the behaviour against Gordon Burghardt’s five criteria for animal play and it met all five — and foraging, clutter clearing and mating were excluded by the design of the apparatus and by watching what the bees did. The first criterion is the whole argument: to count as play, a behaviour must produce no immediate adaptive outcome. Uselessness is not the absence of a category here; it is the entry condition, written down, and checkable. A second experiment tested whether the activity was rewarding in itself. Bees learned which of two differently coloured chambers held movable balls; when both chambers were emptied they still chose that colour. They came back for the room, not the toy. Younger bees rolled most, particularly three to seven days from eclosion — independent of whether they had met balls before — which is also the window in which bumble bee mushroom bodies are most plastic, though the authors decline to call the overlap causal and this zine prints that hedge. And the paper’s explanation of its own sex difference is the sentence the zine is built on: males rolled individual balls longer because they had more “free time” in laboratory conditions, while females had constant access to pollen and a colony objective. Play expanded into the hours function had not claimed — a fact about environments, not about appetites. Held honestly, at length: the authors cannot exclude that the rolling followed understimulation in captivity, play-like actions have not been shown in the wild, the motivation is unknown, and their conclusion says resembling object play and a form of sentience. All of it stays on the page. Six refusals, including that prescribed play stops meeting the first criterion, that this is not stimming reframed, that joy is not the receipt for hardship, and that an insect settles nothing about a human life. Twelve spreads, two figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 83 The Width of Itself Stimpunks Zines On the root that opens a channel, the lawn that stays compacted, and why we keep asking survivors to do systems change. A dandelion in soil packed to 1.8 grams per cubic centimetre loosened the ground for seventy micrometres, halved that by a hundred and forty, and changed nothing at the scale of the pot. It is a triumph. It is not a repair, and the difference is the whole argument. 13 spreads→ Details Burr-Hersey, Ritz, Bengough and Mooney built the hostile condition on purpose — sandy loam compacted to 1.8 g cm⁻³ with a penetration resistance of 1.55 MPa, roughly fifteen atmospheres — then grew three wild dicots in it for 28 days and imaged the soil by X-ray computed tomography, so the pore structure could be measured without taking it apart. All three species are plants a lawn is designed to exclude; the experiment is a study of weeds without calling itself one. For the dandelion the porosity was 6.9 per cent in the mantle 0–70 µm from the root surface and 3.9 per cent at 70–140 µm, and the paper states plainly that changes were not observed at the whole-column scale. Seventy micrometres is about the width of a human hair. Which makes the sentence everyone repeats — that dandelions break up compacted soil — the smoothed retelling of a result whose conditions were the finding. Not a lie; a claim that kept the verb and dropped every limit attached to it. Then a second complication the metaphor does not survive intact: most dandelions are clones. The genus reproduces largely by apomixis, setting viable seed without fertilisation, and apomicts are triploid or tetraploid while the sexual minority are diploid. Majeský, Vašut, Kitner and Trávníček found apomictic accessions genetically highly homogeneous, with the genus’s real variety most likely of sexual origin — inherited from its lineage’s past rather than being made now. So the tidy reading, grass monoculture against dandelion biodiversity, has a clone-field on both sides. Nick Covington’s line survives all of it and is sharpened by it: in an environment of total control, every dandelion is a triumph. Triumph is the right word. Solution is not — and if even the weed is not the answer to the lawn, the answer was never among the things growing in it. It has to be the ground. The turn is ours: the Autistic kid who found one corridor, the Disabled worker who found the one manager who said yes. A channel opened by force, the width of one person, in ground that stayed exactly as hard — and then read back by the institution as evidence that the column was fine. The closing spread turns on a second dandelion. In Boyce and Ellis’s 2005 borrowing from Swedish the dandelion child is the low-sensitivity one who does tolerably anywhere, and the orchid is exquisitely sensitive to context; Lionetti, Aron, Aron and colleagues added the tulip in the middle across 906 adults — 29 per cent, 40 per cent, 31 per cent. And the orchid half is not fragility: in good conditions orchids do better than dandelions, so every orchid failing in a compacted room is also a result nobody got to see. Set the two dandelions side by side and both say the same thing about the ground — hard ground does not produce variety, it selects for whoever needed least from it, and the survivors get counted as the normal range. Behaviourism is the machinery that presses down, and its offer is that the ground can stay exactly as hard if the child is trained to tolerate it. Unmaking is mostly subtraction; remaking is Cavendish Space, built for caves, campfires and watering holes alike. Six refusals, including resilience as a substitute for accommodation, and the flat statement that surviving is not nothing. Thirteen spreads, two figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 86 Older Than Either of Us Stimpunks Zines On the right angles in a pigeon’s forebrain, three papers that disagree about where they came from, and what belonging looks like under either answer. A bird’s forebrain has no layers, and it has the wiring motif layers exist to produce. Whether birds inherited that circuit or built it separately is an open argument between three papers — and the ranking has nothing to stand on either way. 15 spreads→ Details Stacho and colleagues read fibre orientation directly, by three-dimensional polarised light imaging, through the forebrain of a pigeon and a barn owl — and found radially and tangentially organised fibres crossing at right angles along the entire extent of the Wulst and the sensory dorsal ventricular ridge. Lamina-like and column-like, in a brain that builds neither layers nor columns. The motif was iterative: it recurred across somatosensory, visual and auditory zones, across two regions, and across two species that last shared an ancestor very deep in the Palaeozoic — which is what makes it a finding rather than a slice. The paper also prints its own boundary, and the boundary is the part a summary drops: the non-sensory parts of the dorsal ventricular ridge showed a mosaic-like arrangement instead, patches of fibres running in different directions. Then the obvious explanation fails on its own numbers. A kea carries about 1.28 billion pallial neurons and a raven about 1.2 billion, against a chimpanzee’s 7.4 billion, and all three perform comparably across a wide range of tasks; Güntürkün, Pusch and Rose say so in the paper the figures come from. What makes the arithmetic survivable is not size but provisioning — about 19 per cent of a primate’s neurons sit in the pallium against 62 per cent in parrots and 78 in songbirds — and cost, since avian neurons run on roughly a third of the glucose mammalian neurons use. The bird got a cheaper brain and spent the saving on density. The zine’s centre is a disagreement, and it is a real one. Stacho and colleagues close by suggesting an ancient microcircuit already present in the last common stem amniote, conserved and partly modified — inheritance. Güntürkün, Pusch and Rose argue the four features required for complex cognition convergently evolved, independently, and are therefore hard to replace — invention, twice. Zaremba and colleagues, sequencing the chicken pallium cell by cell across eight stages in the egg, report conserved inhibitory types alongside transcriptomic convergence — partly each, with the boundary in an unexpected place. “Convergent evolution” is the version that travels, because two independent inventions of a mind is a headline and an unsettled question is a research programme. This piece declines to print one of three as the answer, and shows instead why the belonging claim survives whichever way it lands: if built twice, the layered cortex is one implementation and not the entry fee; if inherited, the kit is older than either lineage and neither of us designed it. A shared inheritance cannot be a hierarchy. Fifteen spreads, two figures, six refusals. Deliberately does not re-argue the yardstick — No. 36 owns that, in the harder case — or the nomenclature, which is No. 85. Companion catalogue: Field Guide No. 23.
Star Stuff A Star Stuff collection · 38 pieces The founding register: one settled, checkable fact, followed honestly, already contains the claim about belonging.

What holds these together Every piece here works the same way. Take one fact that is settled and checkable, follow it honestly, and find that the fact itself already contains the claim about belonging. The calcium in your bones really was forged in stars. Mitochondria really were free-living bacteria that never left. The early universe really did need tiny unevennesses to make anything at all — a perfectly uniform cosmos would have stayed a dead fog forever. That is the difference between physics as argument and physics as decoration. In this collection the fact is the argument , not an illustration of a point already decided somewhere else. If the science turned out otherwise, the piece would have to change. That is the test, and it is the reason this register earns the trust it asks for.
Sorted by register, not by date

Sorted by register, not by date The first ten zines founded this method, and seven of them are here. But thirty-one of these pieces were made much later — The Nearest Body , No Universal Now , The Same Water and Not a Line among them — and still belong here, because they do exactly the same thing. Tidal force really does fall off with the cube of distance, which is why the Moon runs the tide even though the Sun out-masses it some 27 million times. Clocks really do run at different rates by speed and gravity, which is why your phone's GPS has to correct for it. Water really does hold and then flip at a threshold rather than stiffening by degrees. Membership here is decided by mechanism, not chronology . A piece is in this collection if the fact is doing the work. The numbers still say when each one was made — see Cosmic Connections on why we kept them that way. Not Not the naturalistic fallacy. The atoms do not owe us this conclusion. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof, and The Lines We Drew is in this collection precisely to name the trap: the bell curve was recruited to make “normal” look like physics, and eugenics followed. Dressing a human value as a law of nature is the exact move we refuse. Not interdisciplinary as tourism — borrowing a physics word for its glamour and leaving the physics behind.

Stars We Grew Up On A Star Stuff collection · 4 pieces The other kind of star. Icons who made weird into a way of being, and let the rest of us find each other.

What holds these together Here “star” means the other thing, and we are naming that rather than letting it read as drift. These pieces are about icons who made weird into a way of being — Bowie, where unmasking is authorship rather than exposure and many selves are a freedom rather than a symptom; AURORA, the alien who came home by gathering a tribe of Weirdos instead of being cured into fitting; David Byrne, whose stage was built by subtraction, and who wrote down what he was before anyone flattened it into a headline. One of the reasons this project exists is that it is fun , and this is where the fun is loudest. We deliberately did not build a collection called “for fun,” because a bin labelled that way quietly labels everything else homework — and would become the one place where our verify-everything standard could slip. So the fun lives out in the open, in its own collection, held to the same ledger as the rest.

Its companions The L★S Playlist and the L★S Broadside belong to this collection in spirit and are one click away in the Sound and Print sections of the index . Zine No. 66 has its own listening companion in Sound, One Body at a Time , which runs from 1977 to the barefoot stage. Not Not fandom standing in for an argument. Why a start-here at all There is a tension on this page and it is better named than hidden. Cosmic Connections argues that this project runs on links rather than folders , that its categories are outputs rather than inputs, and that nothing here arrived in a straight line. A section called Start Here is the most folder-shaped thing on the site. It stays because the alternative is worse. A reader arriving cold at a wall of seventy-two zines and eighteen field guides is not being respected by the absence of a door; they are being asked to do the curation themselves, which is work we are better placed to do once than they are to redo every time. The fix is not to remove the door. It is to be honest that it is a door and not a queue. So: nothing below is a prerequisite for anything else. Every piece on this site is built to stand alone, because that is what a person reading in a hard week can actually use. If a shark catalogue is what you can hold today, start there and let this page wait.

a centre belonging to neither 46 Star Stuff Companion Stars on gravitational binding, the three-body problem, and why no one's path can be solved alone after Helen Edgar & David Gray-Hammond · most stars are single, and we will say so first L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely

Companion star Astronomy already had the word A star that shares a system with another star has a name, and the name is a companion star. Astronomers needed the word for their own reasons, long before it was any use to us. It is not a borrowed term or a softened one. It is the working vocabulary of stellar astronomy — the second body in a bound system, the one whose gravity you have to account for if you want the first one's motion to make any sense at all. Helen Edgar's galaxy already holds it. In My Monotropic Galaxy (More Realms, June 2026) she maps twenty constellations of her own Autistic self, and the thirteenth is Companion Stars. Companion Stars are the people who orbit close, who understand penguin pebbling, and the Neurodivergent Love Locutions. Those who don't need me to perform and who just ‘get it’. Helen Edgar · My Monotropic Galaxy · More Realms, 2026 Note the plural. Not the person — the people. This zine follows that plural outward, from one bond to a whole community, and the astronomy does the same thing on its own: two bodies, then three, and at three something changes that changes everything after it. But first there is a fact to get straight, because the popular version of it is wrong — and this collection exists partly to take science back from the smoothed retelling. Where the word comes from A bright primary star with a smaller companion beside it, joined by a line marked gravitationally bound, over a caption noting the term is astronomy's own. gravitationally bound primary companion not a borrowed word standard stellar astronomy Figure 1 · the term is already theirs Companion Stars · Stimpunks

The correction goes first Most stars are single You have almost certainly met the line most stars are in binaries — the Sun is the odd one out. It is repeated constantly, and it is not what the measurements say. In 2006 Charles Lada put the binary statistics next to the stellar mass function and published the result as his title: most stars are single. Two-thirds of main-sequence stellar systems in the Galactic disk are composed of a single star. The reason is arithmetic rather than romance. Multiplicity climbs steeply with mass, and the galaxy is overwhelmingly made of the small end: fraction with at least one stellar companion primary multiplicity source M dwarfs ~26% Duchêne & Kraus, 2013 solar-type (F6–K3) 44 ± 2% Raghavan et al., 2010 the most massive near total Duchêne & Kraus, 2013 M dwarfs are the majority of stars by a wide margin, and about three-quarters of them are alone. The big ones almost all have someone; there are hardly any big ones. So we are not going to tell you that everybody has their people. The sky does not say that, and saying it anyway would be the kind of comfort that costs somebody else something. the refusal this zine is built on Which leaves a smaller claim, and it holds all the way down: where the binding is real, it is real physics — measurable, long-lasting, and structured in a way worth looking at closely. That is the zine. Not you will be found. Just: here is exactly what being bound is, and what it isn't. Multiplicity climbs with mass Three horizontal bars. M dwarfs about twenty-six percent, solar-type forty-four percent, the most massive near total — with a note that M dwarfs are most of the galaxy, so two-thirds of systems are single. Neither one circles the other A centre belonging to neither Two bound stars do not have one sitting still while the other goes round it. Both move, about a point between them called the barycentre, which is not located in either star. Sirius is the worked example, and it is the brightest star in our sky. Howard Bond and colleagues combined two decades of Hubble imaging with photographic plates and nearly 2,300 measurements going back to the nineteenth century, and pinned the orbit down: Sirius A and its white-dwarf companion Sirius B trace their paths in 50.13 years, with dynamical masses of 2.063 ± 0.023 and 1.018 ± 0.011 solar masses. Now the part that keeps this honest. Equal binding is not equal motion. The barycentre sits nearer the heavier star, so Sirius A moves in a small ellipse and Sirius B in one about twice as wide. The heavier body is displaced less. What is symmetric is the force. Each pulls on the other exactly as hard. What is asymmetric is how far each one has to move — and neither of them gets to stand still. Newton's third law, in an orbit That distinction is worth keeping. A relation can be genuinely mutual and still ask more travel of one party than the other, and pretending otherwise is how the person doing more of the moving ends up told they are imagining it. The pull is equal. The displacement is not. Both are facts about the same system. Why it took 2,300 measurements. One orbit is fifty years, so no single astronomer's career covers many of them. Bond et al. are drawing on other people's observations from before anyone alive was born. Some things can only be known collectively, across generations — which is not a metaphor here, it is the method section. Close enough and you deform each other

Distance is doing work Close enough and you deform each other Here is where a warmer piece would say and neither star has to change shape to stay in relation. That is not true, and the way it fails is the most useful thing in this zine. Bring two stars close and they stop being spheres. Tidal forces stretch each one along the line joining them — the same effect that raises Earth's ocean tides, scaled up until it is the shape of the star itself. Astronomers see it directly: the brightness of a close pair rises and falls as those stretched shapes turn, which is why the effect has its own name, ellipsoidal variability. Push closer still and the deformation runs to its conclusion: what proximity does to a star's shape separation shape wide both stay round; each evolves as if alone close stretched into ellipsoids, brightness varying as they turn closer drawn to a teardrop, its point aimed at the other star touching a shared envelope, dumbbell-shaped — matter crossing between them At the last stage the star can no longer hold its own outer material: it spills across to its companion, and what each one becomes is rewritten by the transfer. Proximity is not automatically good for a star. Being bound does not deform you. Being bound too closely deforms you — and the star cannot choose its separation. We can. the only part of this we get a say in And the far end of the range is enormous. Gaia has resolved over a million bound pairs out to separations of a parsec, with orbital periods running to a hundred million years. Those stars are genuinely companions — held by mutual gravity, one orbit longer than the entire history of flowering plants — and each of them keeps its own shape completely. Distance does not weaken the binding. It only stops the binding from being the thing that reshapes you. Separation and shape Three pairs of stars. No path can be solved alone

At three, the mathematics changes No path can be solved alone This is the argumentative centre, and it is not an interpretation. It is a set of theorems. With two gravitating bodies you can write the solution down. Newton did. Give the positions and velocities now, and there is a formula that returns them for any time you like, exactly, forever. Add a third body and that stops being available. Not because it is hard — because it was proved not to be there: what was actually shown who result Bruns, 1887 beyond the ten classical conserved quantities, the three-body equations admit no further integrals that are algebraic in the coordinates and their derivatives Poincaré, 1890 and none that are single-valued analytic functions either — the stronger closure, and the one that ended the search Sundman, 1912 a convergent series solution does exist (non-zero angular momentum, no triple collision) — and converges so slowly it is useless for computation or for understanding So astronomers integrate these systems numerically: step the whole configuration forward a little, recompute every force, step again. There is no shortcut, and there is no way to do one body at a time. You cannot solve for one body's path on its own and add the others afterward. The paths exist only as a solution to the whole system, together, at once. the sentence the zine turns on The same work is where chaos was found. Poincaré discovered that arbitrarily small differences in the starting conditions can lead to completely different outcomes later — and the crucial part, the part the popular word destroys: nothing is random. Every rule is exact and fully known. The system is deterministic and still unpredictable far out. Those are compatible, and holding them together is the whole idea. What this does not say. It does not say the bodies stop being distinct — each keeps its own mass and its own light. It says their trajectories are not separable. That is a claim about dynamics and prediction, not about what a thing fundamentally is; the ontological version belongs to No. 29 and is not being re-argued here. Two bodies solve; three do not On the left, two bodies on a single clean closed ellipse marked solvable exactly. On the right, three bodies whose two nearly identical starting paths diverge widely, marked step by step, no formula. two bodies one closed curve solved exactly three bodies two near-identical starts step by step, no formula exact rules · unpredictable far out deterministic, not random Bruns 1887 · Poincaré 1890 · Sundman 1912 Figure 5 · the shortcut that was proved absent Companion Stars · Stimpunks

The Chaotic Self & the Autistic Rhizome Two names we already have This community named both halves of that spread before we went near the astronomy, and the naming is David Gray-Hammond's. Writing with Katie Munday, he describes the Chaotic Self as “our sense of Self being a fluid and moving entity, constantly changing and reshaping as we receive new information and interact with the environment” — and, on why the change does not run backwards: “You can't unqueer a queer mind.” That is a claim from lived experience, not from physics, and it should stay that way. But it names the same shape the theorems name: a self that is rule-governed and still not walked back, still not predicted far out. His Autistic Rhizome is the community version — “communities that exist of networks with no single point of origin. They are interlinked but not dependent on one another for their existence” — and the two ideas meet exactly where this zine does: as one of us changes, “the relational change with our immediate environment transfers the process onwards to the rest of our community in somewhat of an unpredictable manner.” Helen's galaxy holds the matching constellations, the ninth and the sixth: Rhizome Array is the Autistic community itself — non-hierarchical, constantly connecting with other people and forming new communities and nodes. Creating something together that none of us could make alone. Helen Edgar · My Monotropic Galaxy · constellation #9 Mycelial Stars represent the underground networks of connection that sustain the neurodivergent community of Autistic researchers, advocates, writers, families, and educators. It is our community network of care and interdependence, all growing toward each other in ways that don't follow a straight line or a hierarchy. The foundation of mutual aid, care and well-being. Helen Edgar · My Monotropic Galaxy · constellation #6 Now the honest part, which we are not smoothing. A rhizome and a bound system are describing different things, and both are true: two true statements that do not cancel the rhizome says the three-body physics says no node's existence depends on another, so cutting one tie does not collapse the network while bodies are bound, their paths cannot be worked out apart from each other resilience non-separability A network can be resilient in exactly Gray-Hammond's sense and any cluster inside it can still be behaving exactly as spread six describes, at the same moment. Neither claim needs the other to be weakened. A rhyme, not a proof. Chaos in dynamics and chaos in identity are not the same claim, and this zine does not argue that one demonstrates the other. Gravity does not know anything about us. What is being offered is a shape that shows up in both places, and a vocabulary this community built for itself first. On the right, three bound bodies with mutual arrows, labelled as paths that cannot be worked out apart. the rhizome cut one tie — the network holds the bound three no one path solvable apart resilience · and non-separability both true at once Figure 6 · two claims, neither cancelling Companion Stars · Stimpunks

What the binding is made of Nothing but mutual gravity Strip a bound system down to what actually holds it, and there is one item on the list. No agreement. No shared origin — many wide pairs formed apart and were captured, or drifted from a cluster that has long since dissolved. No requirement of similarity: Sirius A is a bright main-sequence star and Sirius B is the burnt core of one that died first. No maintenance, no renegotiation, no performance. Mutual gravity, and that is the whole of it. And it does not fall off with familiarity. It falls off with distance, and even at a parsec it is still there, still doing the one thing it does. The binding asks nothing of either star except that it have mass. There is no version of a companion star that has to earn it. what gravity does not ask for That is the claim, kept small enough to be true. Not that you will be found — spread three forbids it. Not that closeness is safe — spread five forbids that too. Only this: where the binding exists, it is made of nothing that can be revoked for underperformance, and where three or more of us are in it, no one of our paths was ever the kind of thing you could work out alone. Not:a promise that everyone has their people. Two-thirds of stellar systems are single. We opened with that on purpose, and we are not walking it back at the end. Not:a claim that closeness is automatically good. Close companions deform each other into ellipsoids and teardrops and finally take each other's material. Distance is what lets both keep their shape. Not:a claim that being single is a lesser state. It is the majority state, and a single star is a complete description of a star. Nothing here reads solitude as a shortfall. Not:the individual dissolving into the group. Every star in a bound system keeps its own mass and its own light. What is inseparable is the paths, not the bodies. Not:chaos theory proving anything about the Chaotic Self. Chaos in dynamics and chaos in identity are different claims. They rhyme; a rhyme is not a proof. Not:“unpredictable” meaning random. Every rule in a three-body system is exact and known. Determinism and unpredictability sit together, and flattening that is how the word gets misused against us. Not:an obligation. The physics describes what mutual dependence looks like where it exists. It does not say anybody owes it to you, or you to them. The three-body problem. Heinrich Bruns (1887) showed the equations admit no first integrals beyond the classical ten that are algebraic in the coordinates and their derivatives; Henri Poincaré (Acta Mathematica 13, 1890) extended this to integrals expressible as single-valued analytic functions, and the same work is where sensitive dependence on initial conditions — later called chaos — was first identified. The objection that was perfectly good

1543–1838 · the long objection The objection that was perfectly good If the Earth really moves around the Sun, then over six months your viewpoint shifts by the whole width of that orbit — and nearby stars should visibly slide against the distant ones. They don't. Not to the naked eye, not to Tycho Brahe's superb instruments, not to anyone for nearly three hundred years after Copernicus. So the Earth does not move. That was not stupidity. It was valid reasoning from careful data, and it is the strongest empirical objection the heliocentric model ever faced. The answer — the stars are simply much, much further away than that — sounded like special pleading, because the distances required were, by the standards of the time, absurd. And there was a second trap underneath, which is the part that should make anyone nervous. Through a telescope, stars show small discs. Take those discs as real and you can compute a physical size — and at the distances parallax would require, stars come out grotesquely, impossibly enormous. Tycho ran that calculation and rejected the conclusion. The discs were not there. They are an artefact of light passing through a finite aperture — the instrument drawing its own signature on the sky and handing it back as data. the trap under the trap So the chain opens on a failure with three parts, all of them still with us: absence of evidence read as evidence of absence; a conclusion rejected because its implications felt too large; and an instrument's own artefact mistaken for a property of the thing observed. What eventually broke it was not a better argument. It was somebody measuring the shift. documented the missing parallax → Bessel The shift nobody could see Two observing positions at either end of Earth's orbit, with sight lines to a near star that barely changes its apparent place against the background stars. The angle is marked as too small to detect. Königsberg · 1838 Somebody measured the shift Friedrich Bessel picked 61 Cygni because it moved. Not much — but its motion across the sky was unusually fast, and fast usually means near. With a Fraunhofer heliometer, on every clear night he could get, he tracked it against two neighbouring stars. In 1838 he published the result: a parallax of 0.3136 arcseconds. That is an angle it is worth trying to feel. A two-centimetre coin, seen from thirteen kilometres away. That is the entire wobble on which the first known distance to a star was built. It gave about 10.4 light years; the modern figure is near 11.4. He was narrowly first. Thomas Henderson had Alpha Centauri and Friedrich Struve had Vega at almost the same moment. Three people, three stars, one method, within months. Three hundred years of "we looked and saw nothing" ended the moment the instrument got good enough to see a coin at thirteen kilometres. The stars had been moving the whole time. what actually settles an argument And here is the detail this collection has to stop and mark. Bessel did this at Königsberg — the same man, at the same observatory, who established the personal equation: the finding that observers differ from one another systematically, and that the right response is to publish a constant for each of them and correct the data rather than correct the observer. Twice, from opposite directions, the same person demonstrated that knowledge requires a located, particular observer. Once by needing their displacement. Once by needing their difference. documented the measurement → what the method implies Nought point three one three six arcseconds A coin drawn at one end of a long dimension line and an eye at the other, thirteen kilometres apart, illustrating the size of the angle Bessel measured. 2 cm 13 kilometres 0.3136″ 61 Cygni · Bessel 1838 ≈ 10.4 light years modern value ≈ 11.4 Figure 2 · the whole wobble baselinethe chain 2 · Bessel · 61 Cygni Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

The geometry · and what it forbids No baseline, no depth Strip parallax down to what it actually is, because the whole zine is in the geometry. You look at a star. You wait six months, which carries you to the far side of Earth's orbit. You look again. The star appears to have moved a little against the far background, and from that angle and the width of your orbit you get the distance. The width of your orbit is called the baseline. It is not a nuisance in the measurement, not a source of error to be minimised, not contamination from the observer's situation. The observer's displacement is the instrument. Take it away and you have not made the measurement purer. You have made it impossible. the sentence this zine turns on Consider what a genuine view from nowhere would be. No location, therefore no second location, therefore no baseline, no angle, no distance. An observer at no position sees a flat sky and cannot tell a nearby star from a far one. Not "with difficulty." At all. The god's-eye view is, in the one domain where we can check it exactly, the blindest possible position. And the reverse holds too, which is the constructive half. The more your positions differ, the better your measurement gets. That is why space astrometry beats ground-based: a wider, better-known baseline. Difference between viewpoints is not noise to be averaged out. It is signal, and it is the only signal there is. documented parallax → the whole distance ladder Two positions, and none On the left, two observing positions with a baseline between them yield an angle and a distance. On the right, a single point with no baseline yields a flat sky and no distance at all. from somewhere baseline → distance from nowhere all equally far no baseline → nothing the view from nowhere is the blind one Figure 3 · position as instrument baselinethe chain 3 · the baseline Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks
Everything rests on the bottom rung

Everything above it Everything rests on the bottom rung Parallax only reaches so far. Past that, astronomy does something audacious: it builds a ladder, and calibrates each rung against the one below. Rung one is geometry — parallax, an observer moving, no assumptions required. Rung two is the period–luminosity relation. Certain variable stars pulse at a rate that tracks their true brightness, so if you can read the period you know the intrinsic luminosity, and comparing that to how bright it looks gives distance. Calibrated by rung one. Rung three reaches further still with exploding stars of standardisable brightness. Calibrated by rung two. And so on out to the expansion of the universe itself. Every distance in cosmology — every one — is ultimately anchored to somebody standing in a particular place and moving to another. what the ladder is bolted to Which means the ladder inherits the bottom rung's fate. Move the calibration and every rung above it moves. This is not hypothetical: recalibrations of the variable-star rung have historically resedimented the entire extragalactic distance scale, and disagreements about that calibration sit near the centre of live arguments about the expansion rate today. Hold that structure, because the rest of the zine is about a different ladder with the same property. When the bottom rung is a person in a position, and you have pretended there is no person and no position, everything built on top inherits the error and none of it knows. documented rung two → who built it The distance ladder Four stacked rungs — parallax, period-luminosity, standard candles, and cosmic expansion — each labelled as calibrated by the rung below, with the bottom rung marked geometry, an observer moving. cosmic expansion exploding stars period–luminosity parallax · geometry an observer, moving each rung calibrated by the one below move the bottom and everything moves Figure 4 · anchored to a located observer baselinethe chain 4 · the ladder Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks
The woman not permitted to observe

Harvard College Observatory · 1895–1912 The woman not permitted to observe Rung two of the ladder — the one everything above it stands on — was built by a person who was not allowed to use the telescope. Henrietta Swan Leavitt joined Harvard College Observatory in 1895 as one of the women hired as computers: paid by the hour, assigned tasks rather than choosing them, employed to measure photographic plates that men had exposed. On those plates she found and measured the periods of roughly 1,700 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds. And she noticed the thing nobody had: because everything in the Small Magellanic Cloud sits at essentially the same distance from us, differences in apparent brightness there are differences in actual brightness. That single observation converts a pattern into a ruler. The result — the period–luminosity relation, the Leavitt Law — appeared in Harvard College Observatory Circular 173 in 1912, titled "Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud." It was published under the name of the observatory's director, Edward Pickering. It opens by noting that the statement "has been prepared by Miss Leavitt." HCO Circular 173, 1912 Prepared by. The measurement of the universe rests on rung two, and rung two is credited in a subordinate clause. Now put that next to the argument of the last three spreads. Parallax says knowledge requires an observer in a position. Leavitt was denied the position of observer and made the discovery anyway — from a chair, with a magnifying glass, on somebody else's plates. She had a standpoint. The institution simply declined to record that it was hers. documented this erasure → the pattern Who is at the telescope and who is at the plates A telescope with a named observer beside it, and a desk of photographic plates where the discovery was actually made, with the credit line reading prepared by Miss Leavitt. the observer named on the paper the plates where the law was found “has been prepared by Miss Leavitt” Figure 5 · rung two, in a subordinate clause baselinethe chain 5 · Leavitt · rung two Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

1988 · the name for it The god trick In 1988 Donna Haraway gave the fantasy its name, in an essay about vision, and about who gets to be looked at. "I would like to insist on the embodied nature of all vision and so reclaim the sensory system that has been used to signify a leap out of the marked body and into a conquering gaze from nowhere. This is the gaze that mythically inscribes all the marked bodies, that makes the unmarked category claim the power to see and not be seen, to represent while escaping representation." Haraway, "Situated Knowledges," Feminist Studies 14(3), 1988, p. 581 Read the mechanism slowly, because it is precise. There are marked bodies — visible, particular, available for study. And there is an unmarked category, which is not neutral but simply unexamined: it holds the power to see and not be seen, to describe others while never appearing in the description. Haraway calls the whole manoeuvre a god trick — "the god trick of seeing everything from nowhere" — and is blunt about its status: "that view of infinite vision is an illusion, a god trick." She is not describing something exotic. She is describing the default voice of a methods section: subjects were observed. Observed by whom, from where, with what stake in the result? The sentence is constructed so the question cannot be asked. And note where the essay is set, because it is not incidental. Haraway's examples are satellites, space probes, planetary imaging, the “brilliant space platforms of the powerful.” She even quotes a magazine's epigraph on the infinitesimal: “The stuff of stars has come alive.” The critique of the view from nowhere was written, from the start, in the vocabulary of looking at the sky. documented the god trick → her positive claim Marked and unmarked An eye at the top, drawn without a body and without a position, looking down at three marked figures who are fully rendered and labelled as available for study. unmarked · no position marked bodies · fully visible to represent while escaping representation Figure 7 · the power to see and not be seen baselinethe chain 7 · the god trick Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

The line that usually gets dropped "Only partial perspective promises objective vision" Haraway is routinely read as an opponent of objectivity. She is the opposite, and she says so in a sentence she flags as the moral of the essay. "The moral is simple: only partial perspective promises objective vision. … Feminist objectivity is about limited location and situated knowledge, not about transcendence and splitting of subject and object. It allows us to become answerable for what we learn how to see." Haraway, 1988, p. 583 Not objectivity is impossible. Not all views are equal. Partiality is the precondition of objectivity — and what you gain by having a location is the ability to be answerable, which a view from nowhere structurally cannot be. You cannot check the work of an observer with no address. Now set that beside the geometry from spread four. parallax no position → no baseline → no depth situated no location → no accountability → no objectivity They are the same claim in two vocabularies. In astronomy it is a theorem you can check with trigonometry: the measurement is constituted by the observer's position, and pretending otherwise destroys the measurement. In epistemology it is an argument. The astronomy does not prove the epistemology — but it does demonstrate that the shape of the claim is not mystical, because there is at least one domain where it is exactly, boringly true. Marked contested, and here is what is contested. Haraway never mentions parallax, and we are not claiming she had it in mind. The parallel is ours. What makes it more than a pun is that both claims have the same structure — position is not a contaminant of the measurement, it is a component of it — and that Haraway independently reaches for astronomical imagery throughout. What it is not is a proof: a theorem in trigonometry cannot settle an argument in epistemology, and if this spread reads as though it does, it has overstepped. contested parallax → situated knowledges The same shape, twice Two parallel three-step arguments — one in geometry ending at distance, one in epistemology ending at objectivity — both beginning from having a position. geometry a position a baseline depth measurable epistemology a location answerable checkable objective same shape · one is a theorem, one an argument Figure 8 · a rhyme, and we mark it as one baselinethe chain 8 · partial perspective Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks
Relativism is also a god trick

The guard rail · in her own words Relativism is also a god trick The obvious misreading of everything so far is therefore all views are equally valid. Haraway blocks that exit herself, in the same essay, and more sharply than her critics do. "Relativism is a way of being nowhere while claiming to be everywhere equally. The 'equality' of positioning is a denial of responsibility and critical inquiry. Relativism is the perfect mirror twin of totalization in the ideologies of objectivity; both deny the stakes in location, embodiment, and partial perspective; both make it impossible to see well. Relativism and totalization are both 'god tricks' promising vision from everywhere and nowhere equally and fully." Haraway, 1988, p. 584 That is as complete a refusal of "it's all subjective" as anyone has written, and it comes from the person the phrase is most often blamed on. The geometry says the same thing, and it is worth spelling out because it is not obvious. Two well-known positions give you a distance. Infinitely many positions, none of them recorded, give you nothing at all — you cannot form a baseline out of viewpoints you refuse to specify. Relativism is not many baselines. It is the refusal to state one, which is the same epistemic position as the view from nowhere wearing different clothes. She is equally careful about the standpoints of the subjugated, which she says are preferred but explicitly not "innocent": they are preferred "because in principle they are least likely to allow denial of the critical and interpretive core of all knowledge," and they remain subject to critical re-examination like any other. And: "not just any partial perspective will do." documented the guard rail → what happens without it Two positions, no positions, all positions Three panels: two stated positions give a distance; no position gives nothing; and unlimited unstated positions also give nothing, labelled as the mirror twin. two, stated depth none nothing all, unstated nothing mirror twins relativism is not many baselines it is refusing to state one Figure 9 · the exit she closes herself baselinethe chain 9 · the guard rail Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

2010 · the unmarked sample The unmarked sample Here is the god trick with numbers on it. In 2010, Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan asked a question nobody had bothered to ask systematically: who are the people in the studies? The answer, across the top journals of the behavioural sciences: 96% of samples from Western industrialised nations 68% of subjects from the United States 12% share of world population those countries hold They named the sample WEIRD — Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic — and made the finding that turns it from awkward into serious: on many measures these subjects are not merely unrepresentative but frequent outliers compared with the rest of the species. Notice what the problem actually is, because "unrepresentative sample" undersells it. The results were not published as facts about American undergraduates. They were published as facts about human beings — the population went unstated because the researchers' own position was the unmarked category. A methods section that does not say where you are standing is not neutral. It is a claim to be standing nowhere, and it is always false. the god trick, operationalised And this is the ladder problem again, exactly. Rung one was a narrow, unstated sample. Where it lands on us Research done on us Autism research is close to a controlled experiment in what the god trick costs, because for most of its history the observers and the observed were disjoint sets. Look at what that arrangement produced, using findings this collection has already walked. Outcome measures chosen from outside: the endpoint inherited from 1987 was indistinguishability — how much like everyone else the child seemed — a target nobody standing on the inside would have written down (No. 38). Harms not measured: 150 intervention studies, 11 mentioning adverse events (No. 40). You do not ask about harms you cannot imagine, and you cannot imagine harms you have never been on the receiving end of. And the finding that only exists because somebody moved. Damian Milton's double empathy problem (2012) reframes the communication breakdown between Autistic and non-Autistic people as mutual and relational — a mismatch between two positions rather than a deficit inside one of them. That is a parallax result. It is invisible from one position and obvious from two, and getting it required an Autistic researcher — an observer at the other end of the baseline. why the sample includes the analyst Decades of research described the deficit as a property of the Autistic person, the way Tycho described stellar discs as a property of the stars. In both cases the finding was partly an artefact of the apparatus — and in both cases you could only see that by observing from somewhere else. Which is what participatory research is for. Not courtesy, and not a legitimacy ritual. A second position on the baseline, which is the only way anyone has ever measured depth. documented the failures → what the correction actually is One position and two From one position the gap between two people is read as a deficit located in one of them; from two positions the same gap is visible as mutual, sitting between them. one position “the deficit” located in one two positions the gap is mutual it sits between same people · same gap only the number of observers changed Figure 11 · double empathy as a parallax result baselinethe chain 11 · research done on us Conquering Gaze · Stimpunks

The correction Publish your coordinates Two exits are closed. You cannot remove the observer — that destroys the measurement. You cannot declare all views equal — Haraway refuses it, and so does the geometry. What is left is the answer Bessel gave twice, and it is embarrassingly practical: state where you are standing, and publish the constant. In 1838 that meant recording the baseline: which two points the observation was made from, how far apart, how accurately known. In the personal equation it meant recording the observer: this one runs 0.2 seconds late, here is the number, correct the data and keep the person. The research equivalents are unglamorous and already invented: Say who the sample was, in the claim and not only in the appendix. Say who the researchers were and what they had at stake. Put people with the experience in the design, not the debrief. Choose outcome measures with the people who will be measured. Report harms. Name the coordinates the work was done from. the baseline, in a methods section Every one of those is usually filed under ethics or inclusion. They belong under method. A positionality statement is not a confession or a disclaimer — it is a published baseline, and it does the same job Bessel's constants did: it makes the reading correctable by somebody who was not there. And it is the reason "nothing about us without us" is an epistemic claim before it is a political one. A study of us that contains none of us has one position. Whatever else is wrong with it, it cannot measure depth. Marked contested. The synthesis is ours: Bessel did not think of the personal equation as a template for research ethics, and Haraway does not cite him. What we are claiming is a shared form — make the observer's position explicit and correctable rather than invisible or irrelevant — not a historical descent. And the practical claim underneath, that participatory methods produce better findings rather than only fairer process, is an empirical question that deserves its own evidence and does not get to lean on the analogy. contested the personal equation → research practice Two answers from one man Bessel's two results side by side: parallax, where the observer's displacement is published as a baseline, and the personal equation, where the observer's difference is published as a constant. The turn The sky is not flat There is a real answer to how far away 61 Cygni is. It is about 11.4 light years, and nothing in this zine softens that. We got it by knowing exactly where somebody was standing, twice, six months apart, and by publishing both positions so anyone could check. The precision came from the situatedness. It did not survive despite it. So this is not an argument that science is only perspective, and it cannot be turned into one without contradicting both halves of its evidence — the geometry says a position is required, and Haraway says relativism is a god trick. The view from nowhere is not too rigorous. It is not rigorous enough, because it has thrown away the one thing that makes a measurement checkable: a stated place to have made it from. Objectivity is not the absence of a position. It is a position you have written down, so that someone standing elsewhere can correct you. what the chain arrives at And nobody built this road on purpose. Tycho was doing his best with an instrument that lied to him. Pickering ran an observatory whose employment practices he had not invented. The researchers in the WEIRD survey were using the subjects who were available. Each did competent work from an unexamined position — which is exactly the failure the whole chain describes, performed by the people describing it. Which is the hopeful part, and the reason this collection keeps writing chains instead of villains. An unexamined position is not a moral defect. It is a missing line in the methods section. Those can be written. Not:that all perspectives are equal. Haraway calls that a god trick in the same essay, and the geometry agrees: unstated positions give you nothing. Two known baselines beat infinite unrecorded ones. Not:that lived experience is automatically right. Haraway is explicit that subjugated standpoints are "not 'innocent' positions" and stay open to critical examination. Preferred is not the same as unquestionable. Not:that parallax proves any of this. A theorem in trigonometry cannot settle epistemology. It shows the shape of the claim is real in at least one place. We marked that joint contested. Not:an attack on measurement. The zine's hero is a man who measured a coin at thirteen kilometres and published his baseline. The old charts saw a figure holding a sheaf of wheat. The reclaimed chart sees what that figure was doing — finding the signal in the noise, which is what wheat is. It is one of the foundational cognitive capacities of the human species — the one that produced agriculture, mathematics, music theory, taxonomy, and astronomy itself. The pathologizing of pattern-seeking is one of the stranger moves of the diagnostic tradition. The same capacity that lets a person memorize every train schedule in the metropolitan area, map the complete ecosystem of a backyard, or hear the harmonic structure in a piece of music is described, in the diagnostic literature, as a "restricted and repetitive" behavior. The frame is the problem, not the capacity. Spica, this constellation's brightest star, is a binary system — two stars so close together and moving so fast that they've distorted each other into egg shapes. The Flood is one of the oldest constellations in the sky. There are minds that work like this: that provide a fixed reference, a stable orientation point, for everyone around them. They may not be the most dramatic presence in the room. L★S · 008 The Forge formerly · Orion · The Hunter 05h 35m · +5° · mag 0.12 The most recognized constellation in the sky. The old charts saw a hunter with a raised club and a belt of three perfect stars. The reclaimed chart sees what is actually at its center: the Great Nebula, a stellar nursery where new stars are being forged right now, out of gas and gravity and the remains of everything that came before. creationmakingthe processwhat gets made from wreckage ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Forge The Orion Nebula — M42, the middle "star" in Orion's sword — is a stellar nursery 1,344 light-years away and 24 light-years across. Within it, new stars are being born from collapsing clouds of gas and dust. Some of those stars will have planets. Some of those planets may eventually have bones. Those bones will be piezoelectric. The Forge makes star stuff, right now, while you look at it. Betelgeuse is a red supergiant — a star so large that if it replaced our sun, it would extend past Jupiter. It is also dying. At some point in the next hundred thousand years (possibly much sooner; possibly last Tuesday, the light just hasn't arrived yet) it will explode in a supernova visible in daylight and scattered its own star stuff across the surrounding parsecs. The three belt stars — Alnitak, Alnilam, Mintaka — are nearly perfectly aligned, which is why they're so striking. The odds of three unrelated stars lining up like that by chance are low; these are all part of the same young star-forming region, born in the same cloud of gas, traveling together through the galaxy.
