Cosmic Connections Three sites, one web. Nothing here was arrived at in a straight line, and none of it is anybody's alone. This is the page about the links — what travels between Stimpunks, More Realms, and Star Stuff, and why the connections are the content rather than the packaging. Cosmic Connections is Helen Edgar 's phrase for what this collection is doing, and it landed because it was already carrying two histories. The first is Connections , James Burke's BBC series, first broadcast in 1978. Ryan Boren grew up on it, and a good deal of how this collection thinks came from watching it young. Its method is the opposite of the tidy march of great men and eureka moments: Burke's argument is that you cannot understand any piece of the modern world in isolation, because the thing you are holding was assembled out of centuries of unrelated people solving unrelated problems for reasons of their own — profit, boredom, war, faith — none of them aiming at the outcome they produced. An episode starts somewhere medieval and arrives, by way of eight things that have no obvious business with each other, at the object on your desk. Burke went on making the argument across three more series, in 1994, 1997, and 2023. The second is The Cosmic Connection: An Extraterrestrial Perspective , Carl Sagan's 1973 book — the one where he first put the line in print that this whole collection runs on: we are made of star-stuff. Sagan's connection was between our bodies and the interiors of dead stars. Burke's was between a stirrup and a computer. They turn out to be the same move made at different scales: follow the thread, and the thing that looked separate turns out to be continuous with everything around it. Connection isn't a metaphor we apply to the material. It is how the material got made — and how we make it.

Three sites, one web There are three places, and they do different work. Calling them a collaboration is accurate but too flat; what actually happens is traffic. The three sites and what travels between them Stimpunks, More Realms, and Star Stuff drawn as three nodes of one web. Stimpunks sends glossary, patterns, and design method; More Realms sends essays, coinages, and speculative framing; Star Stuff sends both of them back finished, printable, citable artifacts. Every arrow runs in both directions. coinages · citations · corrections glossary patterns design method essays speculative framing felt time · relations STIMPUNKS the garden MORE REALMS the wandering STAR STUFF the flowering no source, no downstream — every edge runs both ways Figure 1 · Not a pipeline with an origin and an output. A web, where each site is upstream of the other two. What actually travels, with receipts From What moves Where it landed More Realms & Autistic Realms Essays, coinages, and the speculative framing — Why Difference Comes First , We Are Made of Relations , My Monotropic Galaxy , the constellation reading of the spiky profile, felt time, shared-air and shared-signal space No. 11 and the Difference-First Frame ; No. 21 ; No. 24 and No. 25 ; No. 29 ; No. 28 and No. 30 in her own voice Stimpunks the knowledge garden Glossary, pattern library, and design method — monotropism, crip time, co-regulation, meerkat mode, ARLES, the ecosystemic model of distress, Cavendish Space, regulation-first No. 17 reads almost entirely out of the glossary; No. 8 turns on Cavendish Space; No. 19 on crip time. Nearly every zine links a term back out. Star Stuff this site Finished artifacts — printable, citable, forkable — plus the fact-checks that go back and correct the sources they came from The ghost pipe entry pairs with Helen's Monotropa uniflora and Monotropism ; Field Guide No. 8 is the companion catalogue to her No. 30 ; every correction lands in the public changelog The Symbioses row is the one that shows the shape best. Helen wrote about Monotropa uniflora — the ghost pipe, which grows no chlorophyll and takes all its carbon second-hand from fungi — as a botanical expression of being monotropic. Monotropa means one turn : the same root as monotropism , the Autistic attention style named by Murray, Lesser and Lawson in 2005. A plant name from Linnaean botany, an attention theory from Autistic researchers, and a mutual-aid ethic about receiving without shame, all sitting on one etymology. Nobody planned that. It was found by following a link.

Why links, and not folders Stimpunks has kept its knowledge as a web of small linked pieces rather than a hierarchy of folders, on the argument that a web of notes with links between them is far more useful than a fixed hierarchical system — the design principle underneath both Tim Berners-Lee's original proposal for the web and Niklas Luhmann's card-index practice. The payoff is not tidiness. It's that connecting notes makes higher-level concepts appear that nobody wrote down , and connecting those makes larger categories appear in turn. The categories are outputs, not inputs. That is emergence , which Stimpunks glosses as the way complex systems and patterns arise out of a multiplicity of relatively simple interactions. It is the same principle physics states as more is different — that a large enough collection of parts obeys laws you cannot read off the parts themselves — and the same one adrienne maree brown builds organizing practice from in Emergent Strategy : small actions and connections create complex systems. Link density and emergence Three panels. In the first, eight notes sit unconnected in a grid — a filing system. In the second, a few links appear between them. In the third, the links are dense enough that a higher-level concept, drawn as a ring around a cluster, has formed without anyone writing it. FILED eight notes, no edges LINKED edges start doing the work EMERGENT a concept nobody wrote Figure 2 · The dashed ring is the point. It is not a folder somebody made; it is a pattern that appeared once the links got dense enough, and it can be named afterward. This is why the collection is built the way it is — every zine cross-linking its siblings, every term linking back out to the glossary, search that indexes down to the individual spread rather than the page. The link density is the argument. A collection where each piece sat in its own folder would make all the same claims and none of the same connections.

Accumulated, not authored The part of Burke that stuck hardest is the timescale. His chains run for centuries, and no single link in them is a breakthrough. Each is a small competent adjustment by someone who could not have known what it would join up with. Progress in Connections is not a person; it's an accumulation. Stimpunks calls this iteration and treats it as the working method rather than a phase: as Cornelius Minor puts it, learning is a series of iterations — not linear, and needing deliberate room made for revision and failure. Which is also why this site publishes its own errors. The changelog and the fact-check ledger are the iteration made visible: what we got wrong, what's right, who caught it. A living document that never shows a correction is just a document making a claim about itself. Everything is a remix The phrase is Kirby Ferguson 's, from his video series Everything Is a Remix (2010–2012, with a fifth part in 2023) — the argument that copying, transforming and combining is not a failure of originality but the mechanism of creativity itself. Stimpunks' license page puts the same thing in the house register: “Nothing comes from nowhere. Punk understood this. So did bricoleurs, rhizome thinkers, and every neurodivergent kid who built something strange and new out of whatever was at hand.” That is why everything here is CC BY-SA 4.0 and made to be printed, forked and passed on. A collection that argued for interdependence and then locked its own doors would be arguing against itself.

The refusals Not: Not a genealogy of geniuses. Burke's whole point is that nobody in the chain saw the end of it, and we are not adding ourselves to a lineage of great minds. Not “everything is connected” as mysticism. Specific links, named and checkable, or it doesn't go on the page. Not interdisciplinary as tourism — borrowing a physics word for its glamour and leaving the physics behind. Not connection as extraction. Crediting the source is the connection; taking the idea and dropping the name is the opposite of one. Not a shared masthead standing in for a shared byline. Where a piece is Helen's, it is hers and says so. Held honestly Emergence is a real property of complex systems, and the physics of more is different is well established. It does not follow that any particular web of notes will produce insight, that our three sites are a complex adaptive system in the technical sense, or that link-density guarantees anything. Burke's chains are also a storyteller's selection: he picks the path that arrives somewhere, and the unchosen paths that went nowhere don't get an episode. We are noticing a rhyme between how knowledge accumulates and how we work, and using it as a method. That's a good reason to link generously. It isn't a proof. So: follow the links. Read a zine, hit a term you don't know, land in the glossary, come back by a different door than you left. That route through the material is not a failure to organize it. The Design System One typeface chosen for legibility, five accents held at near-uniform lightness, and body text that never fades. The visual language of this collection is itself an argument about access — so here it is, with its numbers and its receipts. Every artifact here is a single self-contained HTML file with no dependencies beyond Google web fonts — no build step, no framework, no JavaScript required to read a word. That constraint is the first design decision, and most of the others follow from it. A zine should be one file you can save, print, fork, or hand to someone. Accessibility isn't a layer applied at the end. It is the thing that decides the palette.

Typeface The collection sets its prose in Atkinson Hyperlegible , released free by the Braille Institute in 2019 and named for its founder, J. Robert Atkinson. It was drawn for readers with low vision, and its whole argument is letterform distinction — making characters that are commonly confused resolve differently from each other rather than merely look handsome together. The disambiguation problem I l 1 | 0 O o r n m a e s Look at the tail on the lowercase l , the slashless but narrowed 0 , the distinct apertures on a , e , and s . In a face built for elegance these converge; here they are deliberately pulled apart. For a collection about not being sorted into a norm, a typeface designed by and for people the standard face failed is not a neutral choice. Display · Atkinson Hyperlegible Next Bold The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Body · Atkinson Hyperlegible, 1.02rem / 1.75 Almost every atom heavier than helium was forged in stars and their deaths. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood came from stars that died before the Earth existed. Labels & counters · Space Mono STIMPUNKS FOUNDATION · ZINE NO. 1 · SPREAD 3 / 7 Two other faces earn their place. Space Mono carries every eyebrow, label, page counter, and colophon — a monospace voice for the machinery around the text, deliberately unlike the prose so it never competes with it. Fraunces appears where a piece needs an editorial register rather than a documentary one; Bone Song , Underground , and You Were Never One Thing are set in it with Space Mono, and use no Atkinson at all. The migration, and the bug it uncovered The collection ran on two versions of the face for a while: 18 pages on Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (the 2025 release, which adds five weights, a variable format, and support for over 150 languages), 26 still on the original, and 3 — the Fraunces-set trio above — on neither. All 44 Atkinson pages now load Next. Switching cost nothing in layout: the same measuring string set at 16px came out 286.97px before and 286.78px after, and across 126 measured text blocks not one changed height, width, or line count. The sweep turned up something worse than a split. Every page requesting Next asked Google Fonts for a 200..900 weight range — but Next only publishes 200–800 , so the request returned HTTP 400 and no @font-face rule at all. Those pages had been quietly falling back to system-ui for every visitor who didn't happen to have the font installed locally, which is to say almost all of them. A typeface picked specifically because it was drawn for readers the standard face fails was not reaching those readers. Corrected to 200..800 ; the woff2 now actually downloads.

Palette The canonical tokens live in starstuff.css as :root { --sp-* } — one source of truth for every recurring color. Each page aliases them inline ( --purple: var(--sp-purple) ), so a palette change happens in one place instead of forty-seven. A new shared color means a new --sp- token, never a hex pasted across pages.

Grounds --sp-void-deep #07070f L* 2.1 --sp-void #0a0a14 L* 3.0 --sp-deep #0d0d1a L* 4.0 --sp-page #0f0f1c L* 4.8 --sp-card #0f0f2a L* 5.5 None of them is black. Each carries a violet cast — #0a0a14 sits at hue 290° in CIELAB — so the ground reads as night rather than as absence. --sp-card is the most saturated of the five, which is what makes a card lift off the page without a border or a shadow doing the work.

Accents --sp-purple #a78bfa L* 64.6 · 7.24:1 --sp-pink #f472b6 L* 65.5 · 7.44:1 --sp-gold #fbbf24 L* 80.7 · 11.80:1 --sp-cyan #22d3ee L* 77.9 · 10.90:1 --sp-green #4ade80 L* 79.2 · 11.30:1 Five accents, all of them clustered between L* 64.6 and 80.7 — a spread of 16 points across the whole set. That tight band is the discipline: any accent can replace any other on a given page without changing how heavy the page feels. It's why each zine can be tinted differently (cyan for water, green for aurora, gold for bone) and still be recognizably the same collection. The lowest-contrast accent on the darkest ground still clears 7.2:1 .

Text & neutrals --sp-white #f9fafb L* 98.2 · 18.84:1 --sp-white-soft #f4f2fb L* 95.9 · 17.76:1 --sp-secondary-soft #d4d0e4 L* 84.3 · 13.07:1 --sp-muted #c4b5d4 L* 75.8 · 10.23:1 --sp-secondary #b8aed0 L* 72.9 · 9.38:1 --sp-dim #8a86a0 L* 57.1 · 5.62:1 --sp-dim-soft #807d98 L* 53.5 · 4.97:1 Note what the ladder does not do: it never dips below full opacity to make text quieter. "Muted" here means a different hue at high contrast, not the same hue at 60% alpha. Every value above clears WCAG AA for body text against --sp-void — the dimmest by the smallest margin, and only after being lifted for exactly that reason. The one that failed, and what it cost to fix --sp-dim-soft used to be #63607a — 3.27:1 , under the 4.5:1 AA floor. It styles page counters, series numbers, colophons and refs at 0.5–0.55rem, so it is small text and gets no large-text exemption; publishing a contrast table with that in it was the thing that made it obvious. Raised to #807d98 : same CIELAB hue and chroma, L* 41.9 → 53.5, now 4.97:1 on the void and 4.73:1 on the lightest ground, still visibly softer than --sp-dim . Auditing every text element against its own composited background then turned up four more: an accent pink on a tinted card that came to 4.43:1, three runs of alpha-faded cream on the broadside — the exact "faded gray" this system claims to refuse — and two links left unstyled, falling back to the browser's default blue at 2.11:1 on near-black. All fixed. All 47 pages now pass AA on screen.

Palette lineage The palette began as a Solarized dark variant. That happened before this repository existed, so there's no commit to point at — and it matters less than it sounds, because none of Solarized's sixteen values survive anywhere in the collection. The accents are Tailwind CSS v3's 400-weight ramp, exactly: --sp-purple is violet-400, --sp-pink is pink-400, --sp-gold is amber-400, --sp-cyan is cyan-400, --sp-green is green-400, --sp-white is gray-50. The grounds are ours; no Tailwind gray is that violet. What we kept from Ethan Schoonover is the method , and it's worth naming precisely because the method is the valuable part: A small, fixed, named accent set used as semantic tokens rather than color picked per occasion. --sp-* is that idea. Accents pinned to a narrow lightness band, so substitution doesn't disturb the page. Ours sit at L* 64.6–80.7; Solarized's at L* 49.1–60.1. A ground that refuses pure black and commits to a hue. Solarized's #002b36 leans cyan at hue 230°; our #0a0a14 leans violet at 290°. Warm cream instead of white for paper — --paper: #f5f0e8 in the broadside, --bone: #e8dfc8 in Bone Song , both close cousins of Solarized's base3 #fdf6e3 . And then we threw out its central move. Solarized's stated goal is to reduce brightness contrast while keeping hue separation. We push contrast as high as it goes: Body text against its own ground Scheme Text Ground Contrast Star Stuff #f9fafb #0a0a14 18.84:1 Solarized dark #839496 #002b36 4.75:1 Solarized dark (emphasis) #93a1a1 #073642 4.86:1 "Full-opacity body text, no faded grays" is a direct repudiation of the scheme this palette started from. A low-contrast colorscheme is a lovely thing in a code editor at 2am and the wrong thing entirely for a document meant to be readable by people with low vision, printed on a cheap printer, and handed across a table. Accessibility-first won the argument. Credit Solarized for the discipline, not for the colors.

Principles Full opacity Text is never dimmed with alpha to signal hierarchy. Hierarchy comes from size, weight, and hue at full strength. Generous leading Body copy runs 1.75 line-height. Long measure is capped around 36–38rem so lines stay trackable. 8px radius Cards round at 8px — soft enough to read as an object, tight enough to stay documentary. 3px left border A colored left rule marks anything set apart: claims, callouts, specimens, cards. The system's most reused gesture. Pure-CSS starfield Stars are layered radial-gradient stops on body::before , plus a few absolutely-positioned twinkling dots. No images, no canvas. Spectrum rule A 2px gradient through all five accents, used once per page as a signature — the palette introducing itself.
Motion, and the option to refuse it

Motion, and the option to refuse it The starfield twinkles from one shared @keyframes twinkle-anim in starstuff.css — it used to be copy-pasted into some twenty-five pages. Anyone whose system asks for less motion gets none: a global prefers-reduced-motion block collapses every animation and transition to 0.001ms and disables smooth scrolling, across every page at once. Motion here is decoration, and decoration must be declinable.

The refusals Not: Not low-contrast because low-contrast looks sophisticated. Not gray text on gray backgrounds to signal "secondary." Not a framework, a build step, or a bundle to read one page of prose. Not a design system that can't survive being printed in black and white. Not accessibility as a compliance checkbox added after the visual design was settled.

Print These are meant to be printed and handed to people, so paper is a first-class target rather than an afterthought. starstuff.css strips the site navigation and paging chrome from every printed page — that chrome is never content. On paper the whole collection inverts: white sheet, near-black type, decoration dropped. Because every page aliases the --sp-* tokens, the shared stylesheet inverts them once inside @media print and all forty-seven pages follow. Accents become ink there too — gold #fbbf24 on white is 1.6:1, so an accent that carries meaning as text has to give up its color to stay readable. The one exception is the spectrum rule, a 2px sliver kept in full color with print-color-adjust: exact , which survives the browser's background-graphics setting. Diagrams inherit the same treatment: SVG paints with fill and stroke rather than color , so labels and line art are inverted separately — the diagrams are content here, not ornament. Paged zines also turn inside out for paper. On screen a zine shows one .spread at a time; a single Cmd/Ctrl+P reveals every spread and starts each on its own sheet, so you get the whole zine rather than the visible page. This was broken until it wasn't Worth recording plainly, because the failure is more instructive than the fix. Browsers leave "Background graphics" off by default. For most of this collection's life, no page inverted its colors for print — so a light-on-dark zine sent near-white type to a white sheet and printed blank . Measured with print media emulated, 44 of 46 pages printed illegibly . On one, no pixel anywhere on the sheet was darker than mid-gray. The Bone Song poem — a piece built to be printed and handed to someone — came out as an empty page. Only the changelog was correct. The L★S broadside was half-right: its recto prints as designed, but its verso carried the poem in cream on near-black and vanished too. All forty-seven pages now print legibly, verified two ways — computed text contrast against white for every text element, and pixel sampling of the rendered sheet. A stated principle nobody measures is a wish.

Shared assets What every page pulls in File Carries starstuff.css The --sp-* palette tokens, the .ss-nav site navigation, the shared twinkle keyframe, the reduced-motion block, the print rules, and the injected spread-footer nav styles. starstuff.js Per-spread prev/next controls and #spread-N deep linking for paged zines. A safe no-op on any page that isn't one. favicon.svg The L★S mark. og-card.jpg The 1200×630 link-unfurl card shared by every page. Everything is linked by relative URL, which is what lets any page be saved, moved, or served from a subdirectory without breaking. Each page tints the shared nav by setting one custom property — --nav-accent — on the nav element, which is the whole theming API. Reuse it This system is CC BY-SA 4.0 , like everything else here. Take the tokens, take the contrast floor, take the refusals. If you build something with it, the only ask is that you keep it free and pass it on. Solidarity, not charity. Every correction to this page, and to every piece in the collection, gets published in the changelog — our own errors included. The Difference-First Frame A summary of Helen Edgar's essay Why Difference Comes First (Autistic Realms · More Realms), shared with Stimpunks and used with her blessing. Reference notes behind Love You Down To Your Star Stuff — for a funder, researcher, or skeptical parent who asks why difference gets to be the starting point. A resonant frame, not a proof. What this is, and isn't This is not physics or philosophy proving that our ethic is true. Experts disagree about much of what follows, and relational quantum mechanics in particular is one interpretation among several, not settled consensus. What this is: a resonance — three fields, working independently at wildly different scales, keep arriving at the same shape of idea. That convergence is worth having in our back pocket. It is not evidence, and we will not present it as evidence. Zine No. 9, The Lines We Drew , warns against precisely the move we must avoid here: dressing a human value up as a law of nature, the way the bell curve was recruited to make "normal" look like physics and eugenics followed. So we say it plainly, up front. The atoms do not owe us this conclusion. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof.

The claim, in one line Sameness is the fragile or fabricated thing. Difference isn't a deviation from a baseline — it's the condition anything real, including a self, gets made from. One clarification keeps that line honest, because it braids together two different mechanisms that happen to teach the same lesson. At the cosmic scale, sameness is fragile : near-uniformity was simply the early universe's default, and it was unstable — the smallest unevenness grew into everything. At the social scale, sameness is fabricated : the "typical profile," the flat baseline, is manufactured and then treated as ground truth. Two mechanisms. One moral. We should never blur them into a single tidy slogan, because the precision is where the argument holds.

Three scales, one shape Cosmology · the strongest leg The early universe was almost perfectly uniform: the cosmic microwave background — the oldest light we can see, the Big Bang's afterglow — varies in temperature by only about one part in 100,000 across the whole sky. A truly uniform cosmos would have stayed a dead, featureless fog forever: nothing dense enough for gravity to gather, no stars, no us. Everything that exists, exists because that near-sameness broke. The tiny perturbations are not noise on top of the story; they are the story. This part is well established (Penzias & Wilson 1965; mapped by COBE, WMAP, and Planck). Philosophy · the core Gilles Deleuze argued that Western thought habitually treats difference as secondary — judged by a thing's identity to a concept, its opposition to a contrast, its analogy to a standard, its resemblance to an ideal. All four smuggle in the same assumption: that a fixed baseline exists first, and difference is only the distance from it. Deleuze reverses it — identity is produced out of a prior field of difference, not the ground difference strays from (Deleuze 1994). That is exactly what a diagnostic model does to Autistic people: it measures us against identity, opposition, analogy, and resemblance to a "typical" profile that was never the ground truth to begin with. The flat line is the construct. Difference is what's actually there. Damian Milton's work on the ontological status of autism (Milton 2012) makes a kindred point from inside autism studies — the neurodivergent "spiky profile" gets read as deviation from a flat, typical baseline that was never the ground truth. Quantum physics · the most speculative, most hedged At the opposite end of every scale, Carlo Rovelli's Relational Quantum Mechanics proposes that particles don't carry fixed, standalone properties — what a thing is only becomes determinate in relation to another system (Rovelli 1996). Reading Rovelli from the inside, Helen describes not being a fixed, bounded thing moving through the world but something that emerges in and through its relations and encounters (Edgar 2026). We flag this leg as the shakiest: it is interpretation, offered as rhyme, not as physics settling a question about people. (A related move we add here, not in Helen's essay: Karen Barad's agential realism holds that it is relationships, not pre-given separate objects, that come first — Barad 2007.)
One term we have to handle carefully

One term we have to handle carefully Deleuze's "smooth space" (Deleuze & Guattari 1987) does not mean uniform. It means a field of ungridded, intensive variation — the opposite of striated space, which is fixed, measured, gridded. So the CMB's uniform fog is not "smooth" in Deleuze's sense; it's a pre-individual field, prior to both. The useful move is not "the universe was smooth and that's good." It's that diagnostic categories are the striation — the grid laid over a field that was full of ungridded variation before the grid arrived — and what LYDTYSS protects (the spiky profile, ★stuff, no-wrong-configuration) is the ungridded variation the grid keeps trying, and failing, to fully capture.

The bridge: ethodiversity Between the cosmic argument and the single nervous system sits a middle layer, and it keeps the whole thing from being merely personal or merely abstract. Ombre Tarragnat's ethodiversity — the variety of ways of being and behaving across humans and other animals — makes the same claim at the scale of behaviour, and locates it precisely: not inside one organism, but as a property of a relational field , the way biodiversity belongs to an ecosystem rather than any single species in it (Tarragnat 2025). Its opposite, ethonormativity — the unspoken grid of which ways of being are allowed to count — is functionally striation applied to behaviour: a grid laid over a field that was varied before the grid arrived. Stimpunks keeps this in the ethodiversity glossary ; the term also has earlier roots in conservation biology (Cordero-Rivera 2017), which we note as a Stimpunks aside rather than part of Helen's essay. So the chain runs: CMB perturbations, quantum relation, Deleuzian difference-before-identity (why difference is fundamental) → ethodiversity (the same claim, scaled to behaviour and species) → the spiky profile and LYDTYSS (the same claim again, scaled to one bodymind). Ethodiversity is what lets the cosmic-scale idea land as something ecological and communal, not only intimate. Zine No. 8, The Universe Runs on Difference, already carries this layer.
What it gives LYDTYSS — and how to use it

What it gives LYDTYSS — and how to use it It doesn't make the phrase heavier. LYDTYSS should stay exactly as unadorned as it is; the page works because it stays intimate, not academic, and this material must never be folded into it. What it gives us is an answer , ready when someone asks why difference gets to be the starting point rather than a thing to explain or excuse: because that's the shape reality takes wherever we've actually looked, from the CMB to a nervous system. Not despite the mess — because of it. Hold this as backing material: something to draw on if a funder, researcher, or skeptical parent asks us to justify the framing. Physics and philosophy have been implicit in the zines already; if this becomes a future zine, its distinct claim must stay clear of No. 8. No. 8's point is one of breadth — variety beats monoculture. This page's point is deeper and different: difference is ontologically prior — identity is produced out of a field of difference, not the baseline it deviates from. "Difference comes first," not merely "difference is good." Framed that way, it's a genuine addition, and the ontological floor under both No. 8 and No. 9. If it becomes a zine, it should keep Helen's first-person voice and byline — the essay's intimacy is the point, and flattening it into institutional "we" would lose exactly what makes it land.

On the CMB, for the curious The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light we can observe — the Big Bang's afterglow. For about 380,000 years the universe was too hot and dense for light to travel freely; once it cooled enough for atoms to form, light was released to travel in straight lines, and it has been arriving ever since as faint microwave radiation from every direction. Two things matter here: it is extremely uniform (about one part in 100,000), and the tiny variations that do exist are everything — gravity grew them into galaxies, stars, and us. Stimpunks × More Realms Love Without Cringing Dolly Parton from 1967 to 2023 — forty-four tracks — twenty-five of hers, then nineteen covers — and the argument that runs through all of them. The persona was assigned before she chose it. The copyright stayed in her pocket. And the songs went out to everybody, with no test at the door. A Sound rack · companion to Zine No. 67 One “Dumb Blonde” was not her joke Her first hit, in 1967, was a song called “Dumb Blonde,” in which a woman informs a man that being blonde is not the same as being stupid. She was twenty-one. She did not write it. Curly Putman did. Which means the joke, the persona and the terms of engagement all arrived before she had any say in them, and the first thing the public heard from her was a rebuttal to an accusation nobody had put in writing. She spent the next fifty-nine years working inside that costume, and got so good at it that most people came to believe she had designed it from scratch. That distinction — assigned, then inhabited, then mastered — is worth holding on to, because it is the honest version of a story usually told as pure self-invention. She was extremely deliberate about the wigs and the nails and the laugh. She was also handed a slot marked blonde girl singer by an industry that had exactly one of those, and the alternative on offer was not a different persona. It was no career. And what the blonde was doing Tressie McMillan Cottom’s The Dolly Moment (2021) argues that the costume worked as well as it did because it is aggressively white — that “blonde” operates as an unmarked racial identity, filtering for whiteness without anyone having to name it. That reading sits underneath this whole rack and is not resolved by it. Zine No. 67 gives it a spread rather than a footnote. Two She wrote the dark ones too The received Dolly is relentlessly sunny. The catalogue is not. “Down from Dover” ends with a stillborn baby. “The Bridge” ends, by implication, with a pregnant woman going over one. “In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad)” is a title doing an entire argument’s work — a refusal to let anybody get nostalgic about her childhood on her behalf. Cottom reads this run as gothic motherhood: country music demanded that a woman be a wife or a mother to be taken seriously, and Parton, who never had children, answered the demand by writing an archive of motherhood as painful and complicated as the real thing. That reading is hers and we are borrowing it with the tag on. What it means for this rack is simpler. The sunniest public figure in America had already written the worst outcomes down, in detail, and gone on singing. The optimism was a position taken, not a failure to notice — which is worth carrying into the next two sections, because both are about what she then went and did. Three The Book Lady, and what was on the envelope In 1995 she started mailing books to children in Sevier County, Tennessee. Not the poor ones. Not the promising ones. Every one, birth to five, a book a month, until they started school. Thirty-one years later that is more than 332 million books across five countries, going out at something like three and a half million a month. In all that time, the thing that was never added is a test. No income threshold. No application beyond an address. No reading assessment, no referral, no diagnosis, no waiting list, and no annual review to confirm the child still deserves it. And the parcel does not say to the parent or guardian of. It carries the child’s own name. A two-year-old who cannot yet read gets post. Why that is rarer than it sounds Almost everything else a child needs arrives through a gate — an income threshold, an eligibility determination, a severity cut-off, a screening, a place on a list that can be lost. Each is defended the same way: resources are finite, so they must be targeted. That is true, and it is not the whole sentence. A gate does not only ration; it sorts — and sorting requires somebody to rule on who is worth it. Zine No. 67 spends three spreads on what that costs the people who get through it. She built it for her father. Robert Lee Parton could not read or write, and his daughter called him one of the wisest men she had ever known — both halves of that at once, which is the entire design. She did not conclude that he lacked something. She concluded that something had failed to reach him. The programme is Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, and the children called her the Book Lady. In 2017, at seventy-one, she wrote them an album and handed it the proceeds. It also puts two songs forty-six years apart into a single argument, which is the reason this section sits in a rack rather than only in the zine. “Coat of Many Colors” (1971) is written from inside the laughing — the child in the handmade coat, mocked for it, insisting she was rich and they could not see it. “Makin’ Fun Ain’t Funny” (2017) is the same playground addressed to the other children, the ones doing the laughing. She had been the kid in the coat; when she finally got a room full of six-year-olds listening, she wrote to the ones on the other side of it. Four The copyright in her pocket In 1974 Elvis Presley wanted to record “I Will Always Love You.” The night before the session, Colonel Tom Parker explained the terms. By Parton’s account, the rule was that Elvis did not record anything without half the publishing going to Presley’s side. She had written the song. She had published it herself. She said no — and, by her own account, cried all night about it. I wanted to hear Elvis sing it, and it broke my heart. I cried all night. Dolly Parton, recalling the 1974 decision Eighteen years later Whitney Houston recorded it for The Bodyguard and it became one of the best-selling singles ever made, with the songwriting income going where Parton had kept it. The story gets told as business acumen, and it was. But the shape of it is a refusal, not a strategy: somebody powerful asked her to hand over half of a thing she had made, as the price of being allowed in the room, and she declined to pay a toll she did not owe. That is the same instinct as the mailing label, pointed the other way. She would not put a gate in front of anybody else, and she would not walk through one herself. And then there is what grew on top of that story. In July 2021, on Watch What Happens Live, Andy Cohen asked her what the best thing was that she had bought with the Houston royalties. She said she had bought property in what was then a Black neighbourhood in Nashville — Sevier Park — and that it was “the perfect place for me to be considering it was Whitney… I’m going to be down here with her people, who are my people as well.” It went round the world in days as proof that she had been a friend to Black Nashville decades before it was fashionable. It is still going round: it is in her obituaries this week. And in the part that makes it a story, it does not hold up. What the property records say NPR’s Amanda Marie Martínez checked it three weeks after the broadcast. Nashville Planning Department records show Parton acquired the two parcels at 12th Avenue South and Elmwood in 1990 and 1991 — before The Bodyguard was released in 1992. The royalties could not have bought the property. The Washington Post had reported the purchase as 1997; NPR, which had run the feel-good version itself, published the correction and named its own error in the first paragraph. Two historians told NPR the rest of it. Jessica Wilkerson of West Virginia University put it in a pattern — “[Parton] has a pattern of claiming that when she purchases property, she invests in a place that she’s helping people… It gets trickier to do that with a Black community, where she doesn’t live, she’s not from there, and she’s doing it as a rich white person who can buy up real estate.” Learotha Williams Jr. of Tennessee State University declined the reading altogether: “She invested her money in an area that had a rich Black history, but one that was actively being undermined as a result of gentrification.” Sevier Park is now called 12 South, and is one of the whitest, most expensive and most tourist-driven parts of Nashville. And one detail we are not going to walk past, because the companion zine is built on the absence of exactly this: around the compound, a large gate was constructed. None of which touches the copyright. She wrote the song, she refused the toll, she kept the money, and every word of that is documented. What the sequel shows is how quickly a verifiable refusal gets promoted into an unverifiable virtue once an audience wants one — which is the subject of this essay’s last section, arriving five years early. Cottom, interviewed for that same NPR piece, put it plainly: “This isn’t about Dolly. Loving Dolly is a stand-in for how we can remediate our love for the nation.” Five Known and felt and seen The gate around the compound is a sour note and the last section did not look away from it. This one is the other ledger, and it is longer. On the day she died, Rissi Palmer — who in 2007 became the first Black woman to chart on Billboard’s country chart in almost twenty years, and who has spent the years since running Color Me Country — spent it telling stories about who Dolly had helped. Two of them are checkable. Lenora Ross was from Cincinnati, sang on Lawrence Welk in 1971, and cut two singles for RCA in 1974 and 1975 with Bob Ferguson producing. The press of the day marketed her as “a female Charley Pride”; she is reported to have been the first Black woman signed to a major country label. Neither single charted. This is her account of a Nashville disc-jockey convention, where each label gathered its artists and let the DJs interview whoever they wanted: I wasn’t getting interviewed much, and Dolly of course was, and I guess I looked sort of alone. And she started saying, “Hey, everybody, come over here and talk to Lenora — she’s just a little girl getting started like the rest of us did.” Dolly Parton is a beautiful person. Lenora Ross, c. 1975, on a 1974 convention Note the mechanism, because it is the one that recurs everywhere in this rack: she had the attention, and she spent it on somebody who did not. That is a smaller thing than a foundation and a more difficult one, because it has to be done in the room, in front of the people whose good opinion you also need. Donna Summer is the case usually told slightly wrong, and the true version is better. Summer and her husband Bruce Sudano wrote “Starting Over Again”; Dolly recorded it and took it to No. 1 on the country chart on 24 May 1980, her twelfth chart-topper. Summer never recorded it herself. It is reported to have made her the first Black co-writer of a No. 1 country single. Dolly did not platform her — she cut her song, which in Nashville is not a gesture but the currency that actually pays, in royalties, for decades. The pattern held to the end. In 2024 she is the Dolly P interlude introducing Beyoncé’s “JOLENE” on Cowboy Carter, in the middle of a loud public argument about whether Beyoncé belonged in the genre at all — “Beyoncé is giving that girl some trouble and she deserves it!” In 2021, when Lil Nas X sang a gender-flipped “Jolene” in the BBC Radio 1 Live Lounge — an out gay man keeping the song’s address to a woman intact — she wrote: “Of course, I love him anyway. I was surprised and I’m honored and flattered.” And one story we are going to hold at arm’s length, in the same essay that corrects one You will see it this week: that she spent decades quietly buying band uniforms and instruments for Black high schools across the South and never put her name on it. It traces to a single observation. In October 2022 the journalist Michael Harriot noticed that when he asked people who had been in band or choir at majority-Black high schools how they had paid for uniforms, “a surprising number” answered: Oh, Dolly Parton paid for ours. Others then said the same about their own schools. That is real testimony and we are not waving it away — but it is testimony, not a documented programme, and no organisation of hers confirms it. The bind is genuine: anonymity is the whole of the claim, so a missing paper trail is exactly what the story predicts and cannot settle it either way. We print what it is and let it stand at that height. It matters that almost all of this was done sideways. Cottom is exact about the method, and it is not flattering: Ever the artist of misperception, Dolly leaves unsaid what her core conservative country audience needs to never hear her say. Tressie McMillan Cottom, The Dolly Moment, 2021 Both halves of that are true at once, which is the condition this whole rack keeps arriving at. Except that twice, four years apart, she put it plainly anyway. In 2016, to Larry King: We are all God’s children. If you’re gay, you’re gay. If you’re straight, you’re straight. And you should be allowed to be how you are and who you are. Dolly Parton, Larry King Now, 2016 — in the same answer: “if you’re the fine Christian you think you are, why are you judging people? That’s God’s job.” And in 2020, to Billboard: I understand people having to make themselves known and felt and seen. And of course Black lives matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No! Dolly Parton to Billboard, August 2020 “Known and felt and seen.” She is describing something Cottom herself has a precise word for, in a different essay entirely: Legibility is not the same as visibility. We often confuse the two and our discourse is poorer for the conflation… When I am visible, you can see me in the way you can see a dog or a lamppost. I am socially alive, as it were. I am a category and I exist. Being legible requires other people to have the ability to make sense of me. That means I am a thing that exists but that is also supposed to exist, in a given space or conversation or exchange. Tressie McMillan Cottom, “Why I Hate* California”, essaying, June 2021 That is the whole difference between being let into a genre and belonging in it. Lenora Ross was visible at that convention — a person in a chair nobody was walking towards. What Dolly did in ten seconds was make her legible: somebody who was supposed to be there, like the rest of us. And here is where the two ledgers meet rather than cancel. The legibility Dolly was spending was the one the blonde bought her — the aggressively white, unmarked, instantly-readable persona that is the sharpest thing in Cottom’s critique. That is our reading and not hers, and it does not settle anything: she had that standing because of how the industry sorts people, and she used it to vouch for people the same sorting was keeping out. Both sentences stay. And that 2016 sentence is one we already had. You should be allowed to be how you are and who you are is, near enough word for word, the thing this foundation organises around: authenticity is our purest freedom — a line we take from Neely J., writing in SITI Girl Miami, whose very next sentence asks for “the freedom to BE, fully seen AND heard in all my glory.” Seen and heard. Known and felt and seen. Two people with nothing else in common arriving at almost the same list. And the reason it is a freedom rather than a preference: for neurodivergent and disabled people, inauthenticity is usually a survival strategy rather than a choice. Masking, code-switching, swallowing a stim, flattening an expression, hiding a need — each one costs something, and the bill is paid continuously, all day, for years. Allowed to be how you are is not a request to be indulged. It is the removal of a tax. Which puts her sentence and this rack’s first section into the same argument. She was handed a costume in 1967 that somebody else had written, and she wore it for fifty-nine years — six decades of practice at being legible on other people’s terms. What she asked for on television, in 2016, was that nobody else should have to. She claimed us as family with no conditions attached, and a great many of us claimed her back. She helped write people into being supposed to exist. Six What travelled, and what got left Every song here has been carried somewhere by somebody, and carrying changes things. “Jolene” left home as a plea to another woman and came back as a meme, a metal riff, a slowed-down internet artefact and, in March 2021, four syllables of public-health messaging sung in a hospital chair. “9 to 5” left as a labour song written on acrylic nails on a film set and is now used to sell productivity software. “I Will Always Love You” left as a goodbye to a business partner and came back as the most famous vocal performance of the 1990s, at which point a great many people assumed Whitney Houston had written it. This is the ordinary fate of anything that travels well, and it is the reason this rack keeps naming what a song was for when it was made. Not to police the covers — she was famously delighted by them — but because the smoothed version always travels further than the specific one, and the specific one is usually where the argument lives. The clearest case is the newest In March 2023, administrators at Heyer Elementary in Waukesha, Wisconsin barred a first-grade class from performing “Rainbowland,” her duet with Miley Cyrus, after reviewing it against a district policy on controversial issues in the classroom. The proposed replacement, “Rainbow Connection,” was initially blocked as well. A song about there being no gate, stopped at a gate — and the mechanism was a policy, applied by people following it correctly. And that is what the title of this rack is pointing at. Near the end of her autobiography, having just spent two pages on the fact that people will sometimes take your love and give nothing back and are still all there is, she catches herself being sincere in public and declines to apologise for it: I don’t mean to sound like the inside of a Hallmark card. I do think, though, that it’s time we learned to use the word love without cringing. Dolly Parton, Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business (1994), pp. 297–298 Cottom opens The Dolly Moment by observing that this is exactly the register the culture normally denigrates — that it took a particular political moment to make earnest sentimentality acceptable coming from her. Both things can be true: the moment made room for it, and she had been working in that register for twenty-seven years before the moment arrived, taking the cost of it in reviews the whole time. The songs are where you can hear her not waiting for permission. Twenty-four of them follow. Not a canonisation. This is a rack about a body of work, made three days after she died, by people who are sad. It is not a verdict, and Cottom’s reading is not answered here. Not bootstraps. The rags-to-riches arc is the most extractable thing in the catalogue and gets used to argue that the ladder is fine because one person climbed it. Not claiming her. She was not one of us. The rack is about how her work treated people, not about recruiting her to a community she did not belong to.
One — Underestimated on purpose · 1967–1970 The costume arrives first, written by somebody else. Listen to what she does inside it almost immediately.

The assigned persona Dumb Blonde Dolly Parton · 1967 Her first hit, written by Curly Putman — so the joke was handed to her before she could choose it. A twenty-one-year-old answering a charge nobody had formally made, which turned out to be the job description for the next six decades.

The double standard, named Just Because I'm a Woman Dolly Parton · 1968 Her own song, and a much harder one: a woman telling a man that her mistakes are no different from his, and that the accounting only runs one way. In 1968, on country radio, from a new artist.

What the sunny one also wrote The Bridge Dolly Parton · 1968 Two minutes long, and it stops mid-scene. A pregnant woman, abandoned, standing where the song began. Nothing is stated and there is no possible second reading. Put this next to the received idea of her.

Gothic motherhood Down from Dover Dolly Parton · 1970 A pregnant unmarried woman is sent away to wait for a man who is not coming, and the baby is born dead. Tressie McMillan Cottom reads the whole run of these as Parton answering country music's motherhood demand by making it honest.
Two — Poor is not the same as lacking · 1971–1975 The childhood songs, which are about dignity rather than hardship, and which decline to be inspiring.

The one that says it all Coat of Many Colors Dolly Parton · 1971 Her mother sews a coat from rags and tells her the Joseph story while she sews. The other children laugh. The song's whole weight is on the last turn: she was not poor, she was rich, and they could not see it because they had never been taught how to look.

Lightness on purpose Love Is Like a Butterfly Dolly Parton · 1974 Included precisely because it is slight. She wrote plenty that was not heavy and never treated the light ones as lesser work — which is a position about what art is for, held consistently for sixty years.

Offered as is The Bargain Store Dolly Parton · 1975 A woman describes herself as second-hand goods and invites you to look anyway. Banned by some country stations for the implication. The refusal to pretend to be undamaged is the point, and it is the same refusal the whole catalogue keeps making.
Three — The ones she refused to sell · 1973–1980 Four songs that made her rich, and the reason they made her rich rather than somebody else.

Asking, not fighting Jolene Dolly Parton · 1973 The most-covered song she wrote, and the strangest: the narrator never threatens her rival, never blames the man, and spends four verses telling another woman how beautiful she is. It is a plea to somebody with all the power, and it is unbearably polite.

The copyright she kept I Will Always Love You Dolly Parton · 1974 Written as a goodbye to Porter Wagoner, not a lover — a way of leaving a business partnership without the leaving being a wound. Elvis wanted it; Colonel Parker wanted half the publishing; she said no and cried all night. Whitney Houston, eighteen years later, proved her right.

The crossover Here You Come Again Dolly Parton · 1977 Written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, and the record that took her pop. Country purists called it a betrayal. She pointed out, repeatedly and cheerfully, that a bigger audience is just more people — which is the same arithmetic as the mailing label.

A labour song, actually 9 to 5 Dolly Parton · 1980 Written on set, with the percussion track played on her acrylic nails. It is a song about being used, credited to nobody, and promoted past by men — and it is now most often heard as an upbeat number about the working day. That gap is what the last section of this essay is about.
Four — Walking out, and the light on the other side · 1977–1991 The songs about leaving, and the two that this rack’s companion zine builds a spread of physics on.
Light of a Clear Blue Morning

Deliverance Light of a Clear Blue Morning Dolly Parton · 1977 Written coming out of seven years with Porter Wagoner, on her first self-produced album. It starts nearly a cappella and builds until the arrangement is doing what the lyric describes. If you play one thing here, play this.

Leaving the room Two Doors Down Dolly Parton · 1977 A woman crying alone at a party two doors away decides to go and join it. A very small song about the specific effort of re-entering company when you have been shut in a room with your own bad night.

Pop Dolly, fully committed You're the Only One Dolly Parton · 1979 From the stretch when she was chasing the pop charts and getting told off for it. Worth hearing as evidence that the reinvention was not reluctant — she wanted the bigger room and went and got it.

A hymn for women who carried it Eagle When She Flies Dolly Parton · 1991 Gentle when she's held, and an eagle when she flies. Written at forty-five about the women she grew up watching, and one of the clearest statements of what she actually thought strength was — nothing to do with never needing help.
Five — Claimed as family, and what it cost · 1987–2017 Four decades of declining to make anybody respectable first, including the year it brought death threats.

Three voices, no lead Wildflowers Trio — Dolly Parton, Linda Ronstadt & Emmylou Harris · 1987 She wrote it, and then gave two-thirds of it away. A song about a flower that leaves the garden it was planted in, sung by three women who each had every commercial reason to insist on the top line and did not.
Why'd You Come In Here Lookin' Like That

Camp, on purpose Why'd You Come In Here Lookin' Like That Dolly Parton · 1989 A number-one country single that is also, unmistakably, a drag number — and was received that way by the audience it was aimed at. She never once framed that audience as a demographic. She called them friends, in print, in 1984.

The one that cost her Travelin' Thru Dolly Parton · 2005 Written for Transamerica, drawing on a transgender relative and friend, and nominated for an Academy Award. She received death threats for it and said so plainly. Allyship with a price attached is the only kind that tells you anything.

Stopped at a gate Rainbowland Miley Cyrus ft. Dolly Parton · 2017 In March 2023 a Wisconsin elementary school barred its first-graders from singing this, after reviewing it against a policy on controversial issues. The proposed replacement, “Rainbow Connection,” was initially blocked too. A song about there being no gate, stopped at one.
Six — Books, and the kids they went to · 1999–2023 Where the money went, what she made for children, and the last version of the song she wrote when she walked out.

Going home, commercially unwise The Grass Is Blue Dolly Parton · 1999 After the pop years she made three bluegrass records that nobody asked for, and this one won a Grammy. A song built entirely from things that are not true, sung by someone insisting on them. She was fifty-three and had nothing to prove and made it anyway.

The inner-light song is a labour song Shine Like the Sun Dolly Parton · 2011 Written in 2009 for 9 to 5: The Musical and first sung by three women organising against a boss; she recorded it herself on Better Day two years later. Knowing where it came from changes it from a nice sentiment into a demand.

Written for the Book Lady's kids I Believe in You Dolly Parton · 2017 The title track of her first children's album, all fourteen songs written by her, all proceeds to the Imagination Library. A seventy-one-year-old megastar making a record for two-year-olds and routing the money back to the books.

Anti-bullying, from the child who was laughed at Makin' Fun Ain't Funny Dolly Parton · 2017 The other side of “Coat of Many Colors,” written forty-six years later and addressed directly to the children doing the laughing. She had been the kid in the coat, and she wrote the song for the ones on the other side of it.
Light of a Clear Blue Morning (2023)

Handed on Light of a Clear Blue Morning (2023) Dolly Parton ft. Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, Queen Latifah & Reba McEntire The 1977 deliverance song, forty-six years on, with four other women taking verses. The right last track: the one she wrote walking out of somewhere, given away to people who will keep singing it after she has gone.

Seven — The one time she said it out loud · 2023 A section of one, because it is a category of one. For sixty years her answer was I don’t do politics — and she was explicit about the arithmetic: as many Republican fans as Democrats, and no wish to lose either. Then, at seventy-seven, she opened a rock record by calling somebody a liar.

Sixty years of not saying it World on Fire Dolly Parton · 2023 The lead single from Rockstar, debuted live closing the 58th ACM Awards on 11 May 2023, a show she was co-hosting. The chorus calls someone a liar, says the world is on fire, and asks what they intend to do when it burns down. Asked on Today which lawmakers she meant, she laughed and said “Any of them!” — that they worry more about the party than the people, and that she did not think any of them were trying hard enough. Read it next to section one: the technique never changed. She landed the punch and still declined to name a side, which is the same manoeuvre that kept her legible to everybody for six decades — used, at the end, to finally say something.

Eight — What other people made of her · 1975–2024 The last section of the essay is about what happens to a song once it leaves the person who wrote it. This is that, played: seven Jolenes, four goodbyes, and a Hall of Fame stage singing about a coat.

The one that bent the address Jolene The White Stripes Jack White sings it word for word, which means a man is now pleading with Jolene not to take his man. Nothing is changed and everything is. The first cover to show how far that address could travel without breaking.

On a porch, no production Jolene Miley Cyrus · The Backyard Sessions Guitar, garden chairs, one take and no studio. Stripped this far back the song stops being a hit and goes back to being a woman asking a favour she has no leverage to demand.

Kept exactly as written Jolene Lil Nas X · 2021 BBC Radio 1 Live Lounge, in a low baritone, with the song’s address to a woman left intact. Dolly’s reply was public and immediate: honoured and flattered, and of course, I love him anyway.

Rewritten, on purpose JOLENE Beyoncé · 2024 The one version that refuses the premise. The pleading is gone and a warning is in its place, and Dolly introduces it herself on Cowboy Carter — a blessing issued in the middle of a loud public argument about whether Beyoncé belonged in the genre.

Torch song Jolene Postmodern Jukebox ft. Maris Moved to a smoky 1940s arrangement, where the jealousy reads as glamour rather than fear. Included because it is the least faithful thing here and still unmistakably the song.

A radio session, decades on Jolene Nessa Barrett · triple j Like A Version Fifty years after it was written, a young pop singer picks it for a broadcaster’s cover slot without needing to explain the choice. That is what a standard is.
Children, singing it Jolene School of Rock The final stage of travelling: a song becomes something kids learn. Whatever it was about in 1973, it now belongs to whoever picks up the instrument.

The one that settled the argument I Will Always Love You Whitney Houston · 1992 The reason the copyright mattered. Eighteen years after Dolly declined to hand half the publishing to Colonel Parker, this arrived and became one of the best-selling singles ever made — with the songwriting money going where she had kept it.

Before Whitney, before The Bodyguard I Will Always Love You Linda Ronstadt · 1975 From Prisoner in Disguise, one year after Dolly wrote it and seventeen before the version everyone knows. Proof that the song was already recognised as a standard long before it was famous.

Sung back to her I Will Always Love You Kelly Clarkson · 57th ACM Awards Performed at an awards show with Dolly in the room. The song was written as a goodbye to a business partner; by this point it functions as the thing the industry sings at her.

And everybody else I Will Always Love You Dave Fenley One man, one guitar, no occasion. Here because the previous three are events and this is what the song is the rest of the time — something people sing because they can.

Handed to the people it was written for 9 to 5 Chapel Hart Three Black women from Mississippi taking the labour song. The complaint in the lyric — used, credited to nobody, promoted past — has never needed updating, only re-pointing.
A bar band, at volume 9 to 5 Dwayne Gretzky Played as a party record, which is how most people meet it now. Worth hearing next to the lyric sheet: the gap between the two is section six of the essay.

Slowed until you hear it 9 to 5 Trousdale · Salt Lick Sessions Three-part harmony, taken down to a walking pace. At this tempo the words stop being a shuffle-beat and start being an inventory of grievances, which is what they always were.

The duet, one voice short Islands in the Stream Kylie Minogue · BBC Radio 2 Written by the Bee Gees, made by Dolly and Kenny Rogers, and performed here by a pop star on breakfast radio. A song that needs two people, covered by one, and it still works.
The Last Thing On My Mind

The years she walked out of The Last Thing On My Mind Sierra Ferrell and Timbo The Tom Paxton song Dolly and Porter Wagoner cut as their first duet in 1967 — the beginning of the partnership that “I Will Always Love You” was written to end.

Deep cut, kept alive Here I Am Sierra Ferrell Not a hit and not on a greatest-hits. It survives because working musicians keep choosing it, which is a different kind of afterlife from the one the singles get.

The coat, sung straight Coat of Many Colors Sierra Ferrell No irony, no arrangement getting between you and the story. The song is a child being laughed at and refusing the verdict, and it does not need help.

The coat, at the Rock Hall Coat of Many Colors P!nk, Brandi Carlile & Zac Brown Band · 2022 Sung at her Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction — the induction she initially tried to decline, on the grounds that she had not earned it in rock. They sang the poorest song in the catalogue to put her in.

67 Book lady No One Had to Qualify Dolly Parton, 1946–2026 — on love with no eligibility criterion, and what a gate is really for L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Environment · the thing with no gate Addressed to the child In 1995 she started mailing books to children in Sevier County, Tennessee. Not the poor ones. Not the promising ones. Every one, birth to five, one book a month, until they started school. Thirty-one years later that is more than 332 million books across five countries, going out at something like three and a half million a month. In all that time the thing that was never added is a test. No income threshold. No application beyond an address. No reading assessment, no referral, no diagnosis, no waiting list, no annual review to confirm the child still deserves it. If you live in a participating county and you are under five, the book comes. And it does not come addressed to the parent or guardian of. It comes with the child’s own name on it. A two-year-old who cannot yet read gets post. That is a design decision, and it was made over and over for three decades against every incentive to tighten it up. It is the most checkable thing about her, and it is the whole argument of this zine. The book does not arrive because you qualified. It arrives because you exist, and somebody knows where you live. “I Believe in You,” 2017 · her first children’s album all proceeds to the Imagination Library No One Had to Qualify · Stimpunks

Systems · what a gate is for What a gate is for Almost everything else a child needs comes with a gate. Free school meals have an income threshold. Special education has an eligibility determination. Speech and occupational therapy have severity cut-offs. A gifted programme has a screening. Disability benefits have an assessment, and then a reassessment. Housing has a list, and the list has a position, and the position can be lost. Every one of these is defended the same way: resources are finite, so we must target them. That is true. It is also not the whole sentence. A gate does not only ration. It sorts — and sorting requires somebody to decide who is worth it, using criteria written by people who will never be measured against them. Once that machinery exists, it is available for other purposes, and it gets used for them. We know it from the inside. Many of us got support by being assessed as deficient enough to warrant it, and then lost the support by improving. Some of us learned to present our worst day at a review because the funding turned on it. Parents learn to describe their child in the language of damage, because that is the language the form rewards, and then they have to go home and live with having said it. The cost of a gate is never only the people it turns away. It is what it teaches everyone who gets through. a gate 4 of 12 an address 12 of 12 The same finite budget, two policies one of them also produces a verdict No One Had to Qualify · Stimpunks

Lived experience · one person, not a population Her father could not read Robert Lee Parton could not read or write. His daughter called him one of the wisest men she had ever known. Both halves of that sentence, held at the same time, are the entire design. She did not conclude that her father lacked intelligence, because she had the evidence of him in front of her for fifty years. She concluded that something he needed had never reached him — and that the reaching, not the wanting, was the part that failed. She has said she knew this inability probably kept him from seeing all his dreams come true. Not his ability. The inability to read, treated as a missing supply rather than a missing capacity. It matters enormously that she started from a person instead of a population. A programme designed from a population starts with a deficit profile: a category of children who are failing, a theory about why, and a target to move. A programme designed from one man you loved starts somewhere else entirely — with what would have helped him, and no interest at all in first proving he was broken. The children in Sevier County called her the Book Lady. She has said her father, before he died, told her it was the thing she had done that meant the most. A deficit model asks what is wrong with the person. She asked what had failed to arrive. deficit inside him supply never arrived Same man, same fact, two diagnoses only one of them has a remedy No One Had to Qualify · Stimpunks
A star cannot aim its light

The physics · light does not choose A star cannot aim its light Every photon that leaves a star leaves in a direction the star did not pick. A star is a sphere of plasma held in hydrostatic equilibrium — radiation pressure pushing out, gravity pulling in, balanced for billions of years. Energy made by fusion in the core random-walks outward and finally escapes at the photosphere, and it escapes in every direction at once. There is no mechanism, anywhere in stellar physics, by which a star could send more light one way and less another according to what is standing there. Even the dimming is innocent. The inverse-square law is a fact about the surface area of a sphere — the same energy spread thinner as the sphere grows — and not a judgment about the thing it lands on. Distance is not disfavour. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were assembled inside stars that had no opinion about you whatsoever, and were delivered by an explosion that was not aimed. You did not qualify for your own atoms. She wrote about this light twice. Light of a Clear Blue Morning (1977) came out of the end of her seven years with Porter Wagoner — her song of deliverance, written walking out of something. And Shine Like the Sun is worth knowing properly: she wrote it in 2009 for 9 to 5: The Musical, and recorded it herself on Better Day in 2011. The inner-light song is a labour song. Attention · where she spent it Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine In April 2020 she gave a million dollars to Vanderbilt for coronavirus research. The unproblematic fave is a job

The turn · what we would rather not look at The unproblematic fave is a job In February 2021 — the same month as the vaccine video — Tressie McMillan Cottom published the essay this zine is obliged to answer. The Dolly Moment: Why We Stan A Post-Racism Queen is not a takedown, and reading it as one is the first mistake. Cottom spent months on it, watched hundreds of hours of footage, and says plainly what Dolly gave her: a map of female ambition she could understand, made from stigma and difference rather than inheritance, offering “a repertoire to triangulate the stigmatization of my blackness.” Then she says the other thing. “Dolly is a white Southern multi-millionaire boomer who produces self-consciously white music while wearing a stylized drag of a fallen Southern belle.” Tressie McMillan Cottom, The Dolly Moment, essaying, February 2021 Cottom’s argument, in her terms: the “unproblematic fave” is not a reward for virtue but a job a political moment hands out, and 2020 badly needed someone to hold its contradictions. The drag works, she argues, because it is white — blonde operating as an unmarked racial identity, filtering for whiteness without ever having to name it. She is sharpest on the Billboard line everyone quotes. Asked about Black Lives Matter, Dolly said: “Of course Black lives matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No!” Cottom notes that the radical part is not the first sentence but the last — it is the first time she can recall Dolly describing herself as simply white, with no class modifier softening it. And she notes what is still, carefully, left unsaid. We are not going to resolve this, and putting it here is not a disclaimer. A memorial that leaves it out is not kinder. It is only less true — and the smoothing away of the inconvenient half is the exact operation this whole project exists to refuse. Knowing what we love does not diminish who we love, only how we choose to love them. Down to is not because of

The grammar · down to is not because of Down to is not because of Cottom’s closing line and this site’s own sentence turn out to be the same instrument. Our phrase is Love You Down To Your Star Stuff, and the preposition is the entire mechanism. Down to measures how far the loving reaches. It is never a reason for it. Nobody is loved because they are made of carbon forged in a dying star — that would be the naturalistic fallacy with a nice hat on, and it would leave anyone whose atoms are less flattering out in the cold. Which means loving Dolly Parton down to her star stuff includes the part Cottom named. Not despite it. Not around it. Not with an asterisk at the bottom of the page. Through it — past the wigs and the Horatio Alger story and the thing she declined to say, down to the elements, which the universe has never once sorted into acceptable and unacceptable atoms. And she got there first, in 1994, near the end of her autobiography, with her eyes fully open: “People are not perfect. They will sometimes take your love and give nothing back or, worse yet, use it against you. But they are still all there is. They are the greatest of God’s creations. Loving one another is our only reason for being.” Dolly Parton, Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business (HarperCollins, 1994), pp. 297–298 Read that again, because it is not the sentiment people assume she traded in. She prices the disappointment first and goes ahead anyway. Not people will deserve your love — people will sometimes weaponise it, and they are still all there is. That is what unconditional has to mean if it means anything at all: not a bet that the deserving will show up, but a decision that the deserving was never the mechanism. And then, two paragraphs on, she catches herself being sincere in public and refuses to apologise for it: “I don’t mean to sound like the inside of a Hallmark card. I do think, though, that it’s time we learned to use the word love without cringing.” Same page. Thirty-two years before we needed it. because of the love star stuff a warrant down to the love star stuff a reach One preposition, two different offers only one of them can be revoked No One Had to Qualify · Stimpunks

What we take · a method, not a saint Remove the eligibility criterion A saint is no use to us. A method is. The method is one sentence long: give the thing to everyone in the category, and stop checking. Decide the category honestly and generously, then spend the whole budget on the thing itself rather than on the apparatus that decides who gets it. This is not soft-headedness, and the arithmetic usually supports it. Means-testing costs money to administer. It costs the applicant time, paperwork and dignity, which is a real cost even though it appears in nobody’s budget. It reliably turns away eligible people who cannot face the process — the ones with the least capacity to advocate, which is to say the ones the gate was ostensibly built to protect. Stimpunks does direct aid without means-testing for exactly these reasons. And now the part that a tribute is tempted to leave out. 332 million books is extraordinary, and a country where early literacy runs on one country singer’s goodwill has a problem that no country singer can fix. Philanthropy at this scale is a symptom being read as a cure. She was, on the evidence, unusually good at it — generous, sustained, and unusually free of the ego that normally comes attached. It still should not have been her job, and she is not a reason to stop asking why it was. She died on 25 August 2026, at eighty. She wrote in 1994 that there was plenty of life and love left in her and she planned to enjoy every blessed second. She got thirty-two more years of it and appears to have meant it the whole way through. Not:Not the one-good-thing deal. Appointing somebody our unproblematic fave is a way of feeling decent without changing anything. Cottom named the job; we are not filling the vacancy. Not:Not charity instead of systems. A gift that arrives every month for thirty-one years is still not a policy, and admiring it is not the same as building one. Not:Not bootstraps. The rags-to-riches story is the most extractable thing about her, and it gets used to argue that the gate is fine because somebody once climbed it. Not:Not claiming her for us. She was not Autistic, not disabled, not one of us, and does not need to be. This is about how she treated people, not about recruiting her. Not:Not a spotless record. We put the sharpest reading of her inside the tribute rather than after it, and we did not answer it on her behalf. Not:Not our own metaphor, protected. This zine runs on the absence of a gate — and when she bought two parcels in a Black neighbourhood in Nashville in 1990 and 1991, a large gate was built around the compound. The story that Whitney Houston’s royalties paid for it, which she told in 2021 and which ran again in her obituaries this week, cannot be true: the purchase predates the record. A figure of speech does not get to outrank the property records. “Shine Like the Sun” · written for 9 to 5: The Musical, 2009 the inner-light song is a labour song No One Had to Qualify · Stimpunks

One last thing, and it is small, and it is the reason this zine ends here rather than on the quotation. On page 297 she writes: “The poet Emily Dickinson said, ‘The only thing I know about love is that love is all there is.’” Dickinson did not say that. The poem — J1765 — runs: That Love is all there is, / Is all we know of Love; / It is enough, the freight should be / Proportioned to the groove. Look at what got lost in the carrying. Dickinson’s line is a statement about the limits of knowing — that love is all there is is all we know of it, and that this is enough. Dolly kept the warmth and dropped the epistemics. She did the ordinary human thing with a sentence she loved. So do we. It is the last and smallest proof of the argument: you get loved down to the misquote too.
