The Egg That Is Never Laid

≥115 separate originsno egg is ever laid L★S · 001 The Egg That Is Never Laid Lizards and snakes · Squamata at least 115 separate inventions Live birth is filed as the mammalian way of doing things. In lizards and snakes it has been invented, from scratch, at least a hundred and fifteen times — more often than in the whole rest of the vertebrates put together. ≥115 independent origins~20% of squamate speciesassociated with cold climatesreversibility contested ▸ Field notes Field notes · Lizards and snakes · Squamata The textbook order of operations is that egg-laying is the old way and live birth is the advanced one, arrived at once, by us. Squamates make a mess of that story. Viviparity has evolved at least 115 times in lizards and snakes — set against roughly 140 origins across all vertebrates, which means the great majority of the vertebrate world's independent inventions of live birth happened in this one group. Somewhere near a fifth of all squamate species are live-bearers now. The trigger is generally cold: retaining the young inside the body lets a mother move them into the sun, which an egg buried in cold ground cannot do. What actually varies is the shell, not the egg. Eggshell thickness and the length of retention slide along a continuum, and at the far end some skinks maintain a genuine placenta and pass nutrients across it. So there is no clean line where an egg stops being an egg. What is contested, and stated as contested: Pyron and Burbrink argued in Ecology Letters (2014) for an early origin of viviparity plus multiple reversions back to egg-laying. Blackburn's reply — "Reversibility reconsidered" (2015) — pushes back hard, and whether the transition can run backwards at all is still open. We print the 115 figure, which is not the disputed part, and leave the direction of travel alone. up to ten begintwo are born L★S · 002 The Egg as a Meal Sand tiger shark · Carcharias taurus up to ten begin · two are born In lamniform sharks the mother keeps producing eggs long after mating, and the eggs are not embryos in waiting. They are food, delivered internally, to the young already developing. oophagyadelphophagytwo uteri, one survivor eachthe egg is a supply line ▸ Field notes Field notes · Sand tiger shark · Carcharias taurus This is the entry that most needs its refusals read first, so: it is here for one reason, and the reason is supply. In lamniform sharks — sand tigers, makos, porbeagles, the great white — a pregnant female goes on ovulating well after mating. Those later eggs are oophagy: nutrition, consumed in utero by the young already growing. In the sand tiger it goes further into adelphophagy, where the first embryo in each uterus to develop teeth consumes its remaining siblings along with the unfertilised eggs. A female may carry up to ten embryos and gives birth to two, one from each of her two uteri, each already about a metre long and formidable from the first minute. The reason it earns a place in a guide about eggs is that it is the cleanest case anywhere of an egg functioning as a food source rather than a container — which is the same argument No. 57 makes about the shell of a hen's egg handing its calcium to a skeleton, arriving from the opposite direction. An egg is not one kind of object doing one kind of job. What this is not: a story about the strong deserving to win. Intrauterine cannibalism is one reproductive strategy among the many on this page, it is not a ladder, and pointing it at human beings is exactly the move that How We Got Here exists to name and refuse. The modern reference on the reproductive cycle is Wyffels and colleagues in Frontiers in Marine Science (2022); the cannibalism itself is long-established descriptive natural history and no precise figure beyond the two-pups-per-litter pattern is printed here. the father gestatesplacenta-like pouch L★S · 003 The Pregnant Father Seahorses and pipefishes · Syngnathidae the only vertebrates that do this The female makes the eggs and then hands them over. The male carries them in a sealed pouch, aerates them, regulates their salt, and feeds them across a tissue that works like a placenta. He is not babysitting. He is pregnant. male pregnancyplacenta-like pouchpatrotrophy index 1immune system modulated ▸ Field notes Field notes · Seahorses and pipefishes · Syngnathidae Syngnathid fishes — seahorses, pipefishes, seadragons — are the only vertebrates on Earth with male pregnancy, and the word is not being stretched. At mating the female transfers eggs into a structure on the male's abdomen or tail. Everything after fertilisation is his: he aerates the embryos, osmoregulates for them, and in the most derived pouches the embryos are engulfed by placenta-like tissue and connected to his circulatory system while bathed in pouch fluid. Whether he actually feeds them, rather than merely housing eggs that came pre-loaded with yolk, was a real question, and it has been measured: Whittington and colleagues report a patrotrophy index of 1 in Hippocampus abdominalis, indicating genuine paternal nutrient supplementation during gestation. The cost shows up in his immune system. Carrying another individual's tissue requires not attacking it, and syngnathids have measurable immunogenetic losses and rearrangements associated with the transition to male pregnancy — including, in seahorses, functional asplenia tied to a mutation in tlx1. The reframe here is small and worth making anyway. The popular version of this animal is a novelty item: the fish where the dad has the babies. What is actually going on is that the two halves of reproduction — building the egg, and gestating it — came apart and landed in different parents, and there is no rule of vertebrate life that says they have to travel together. sunk into her backeach one gets a lid L★S · 004 The Lidded Back Common Surinam toad · Pipa pipa eggs ≈6.5 mm · 12 to 20 weeks The eggs are laid and fertilised in open water, then pressed into the skin of the mother's back — where her own tissue grows over each one and builds it a lid. Months later, small toads push the lids off and climb out. eggs implanted in dorsal skina cyst with a horny lidno tadpole stageunusual even among its genus ▸ Field notes Field notes · Common Surinam toad · Pipa pipa This animal gets a gate to itself because nothing else on the list is in the same category. Its eggs are neither retained internally nor carried externally. They are installed. Amplexus happens in open water. As each egg — roughly 6.5 mm — is released and fertilised, the male presses it against the female's back. Over the following hours her skin grows up around each egg and closes over it, forming a cyst with a horny lid. Her dorsum becomes a honeycomb of sealed chambers, each holding one embryo. Then the part that makes it strange twice over: there is no free-living tadpole stage. The embryos pass through tadpole development inside their chambers and stay there. After roughly twelve to twenty weeks the young push the lids off and haul themselves out as miniature toads, dozens of them, within minutes of each other. Five of the other Pipa species release their young as tadpoles — so this is unusual even inside its own genus, which is a useful reminder that "what this kind of animal does" is a much smaller category than it sounds. Held honestly: the account here follows the descriptive literature on Pipa oviposition, including a paper explicitly written to correct circulating misconceptions about the species; figures for clutch size vary widely between accounts and none is printed. glued to the fatherset them down and they die L★S · 005 The Father's Back Giant water bugs · Belostomatinae set them down and they die The female glues her eggs to the male's back and leaves. He carries them, strokes them, pumps water over them, and lifts them to the surface to breathe. It is not sentiment — unattended eggs die every time. eggs on the male's dorsumbrood pumping and strokingbrooding is obligatorycosts him mobility and lifespan ▸ Field notes Field notes · Giant water bugs · Belostomatinae Belostomatidae holds most of the arthropod species known for unilateral post-zygotic paternal care, which is vanishingly rare in animals generally. Within it, the subfamily Belostomatinae — genera such as Belostoma and Abedus — does the thing worth carding: the female cements her eggs directly onto the male's dorsum, and every species in the subfamily has exclusive paternal care from that point. His behavioural repertoire has names: brood pumping, brood stroking, and surface brooding, in which he carries the clutch up to the air, because oxygen is far easier to obtain from the atmosphere than from water. This is where the entry stops being charming and becomes structural. Brooding is obligatory in every belostomatid species studied. Eggs left alone die — in open air and submerged alike. The carrying is not an enhancement to survival; it is the respiratory system. It costs him. Paternal care in these bugs measurably reduces foraging efficiency, mobility and longevity, and he pays it anyway because the alternative is a dead clutch. One precision that matters: the other subfamily, Lethocerinae, does not do this — Lethocerus males guard eggs laid on emergent vegetation above the water rather than on their own backs. "Giant water bugs carry eggs on their backs" is true of one subfamily and not the family, and the distinction is the kind that gets lost first in retelling. The synthesis followed here is R. L. Smith's chapter on the evolution of paternal care in the group. He takes the fertilised clutch into his buccal cavity and holds it, aerating it by rolling it, for up to about thirty days — and through all of it he does not feed. The mouth cannot be a foregut and a nursery at once. The same is true of jawfishes (Opistognathidae) and of many cichlids, and the cost is consistent wherever it has been looked at: brooders lose condition, because the constraint is not effort but anatomy. Two further things are worth having. First, the concealment problem: a mouth full of eggs is conspicuous, and work on male cardinalfish breeding coloration finds it inconspicuous rather than showy, which reads as pressure to hide the brood rather than advertise it. Second, the tidy nuclear reading fails — genetic work on a mouthbrooding Australian species found wildly mixed parentage within single brooded clutches, so the male in question is not necessarily holding one female's eggs, or only his own. Held honestly: the thirty-day figure and the fasting are given as well-established husbandry and field natural history for this species rather than from a paper read for this guide, and no clutch-size figures are printed. From about day eleven of a twenty-one-day incubation, the chorioallantoic membrane presses against the inside of the shell and begins dissolving it. Halgrain and colleagues measured what that does: thickness between day 0 and day 15 shows no significant difference (p = 0.110), while breaking strength between day 11 and day 15 is significantly reduced (p = 0.007). The wall is taken apart from within without measurably thinning. The eggshell supplies more than 80% of all the calcium the embryo gets, and at hatching the skeleton holds about three quarters of the calcium in the animal. Then the opening, which is also not what the word suggests: at internal pipping the beak enters the air cell and the lungs begin working before the shell is broken at all, and the tool that finally scores it — the egg tooth — sits on the inside surface. Afterwards it drops off and the neck muscle that drove it shrinks. The full argument, including what all of this has to do with the trans community's egg crack and with late-identified neurodivergence, is The Shell Was Your Calcium (No. 57). What this card is for is the comparison: hold this against a seahorse, a Surinam toad and a brine shrimp cyst, and the standard egg stops looking standard. the rolling arcis wider than the ledge L★S · 008 The Egg That Does Not Roll in an Arc Common murre · Uria aalge the textbook answer is wrong A murre lays one sharply pointed egg on a bare cliff ledge with no nest at all. Generations of books explain the shape by saying it rolls in a tight circle instead of off the edge. It does not, and the arc is wider than the ledge. pyriform eggno nest, bare rockrolling-arc account unsupportedstability and shell strength instead ▸ Field notes Field notes · Common murre · Uria aalge This is the entry that most belongs on this site, because it is not about an animal being misjudged. It is about us. A common murre lays a single egg directly onto a narrow cliff ledge — no nest, no lining, nothing. The egg is markedly pyriform: fat at one end, sharply tapered at the other. The explanation nearly everyone has met is that this makes it roll in a tight arc, or spin like a top, so that a knock sends it in a circle rather than over the edge. There is no good evidence for it. Ingold's testing in 1980 produced little support. Tim Birkhead and colleagues went at it directly, in a paper whose subtitle asks whether the shape is "not a rolling matter?", and the decisive objection is embarrassingly simple: the arc a murre egg actually rolls is much wider than the ledge it is sitting on. A tighter circle than a sphere's is no help when the circle is still bigger than the available rock. What Birkhead's group put in its place is less quotable and better supported. A pyriform egg is more stable on a sloping surface, so it is less likely to start moving in the first place — and the shape plausibly also confers mechanical strength by spreading impact forces, and keeps the blunt end, where the air cell and the chick's head are, clearer of accumulated filth. So the honest summary is: the shape is doing a job, the job is probably not the famous one, and the famous one survived for decades because it was tidy, visual, and nobody checked. That is this project's own subject arriving in a seabird colony. And in most kiwi species the male does the great bulk of the incubation, which makes the popular framing of the exhausted mother only half the picture. The 15–22% range is given as a range on purpose: it is assembled from record-keeping and reference sources — Guinness World Records, the Smithsonian, Save the Kiwi — rather than from a primary morphometric study we read, and published figures differ. The frequently-repeated explanation for the egg's size, that kiwi descend from much larger ancestors and the egg has not shrunk to match, is a real hypothesis with real argument against it, and is deliberately not asserted here. In a hen the shell is a supply of calcium consumed from inside, as No. 57 argues at length. In a platypus the shell is a permeable interface being supplied from outside. Because she had distinctive scarring, she could be individually recognised on return. Robison, Seibel and Drazen went back eighteen times. She was there every time — over the eggs, keeping them clean, driving off anything that approached, and never observed to feed. When the site was finally found empty, the elapsed brooding period was 53 months: four and a half years, and by a wide margin the longest egg-brooding period reported for any animal. The reason is temperature. At around 3 °C, development is extremely slow, and the pay-off is at the other end — the hatchlings emerge unusually large and well developed, effectively skipping the vulnerable planktonic stage that shallow-water octopus young must survive. Her death at the end of it is not the sad part of the story so much as the design of it: octopuses are generally semelparous, investing everything in one reproductive event. Calling that a sacrifice imports a framework the animal does not have. Published as Robison, B. They use environmental heat — solar, geothermal, or the warmth thrown off by decomposing plant matter — and the Australian brush-turkey builds a large mound of litter whose heat comes from respiring microorganisms. The male's labour goes into managing the mound's temperature, adding and removing material; it does not go into the eggs, and parental care of the emergent chicks has not been observed at all. Which sets the chick a problem no other bird faces. It hatches between 40 and 150 centimetres underground and has to get to the surface with no help. It does: work on brush-turkey chicks following underground hatching puts the ascent at a median of about 40 hours, with a range of 26 to 55. And it arrives ready. Megapodes are superprecocial — hatching in the most mature condition of any bird, with open eyes, full wing feathers, body coordination, and the ability to run and pursue prey immediately. In some species, including this one, a chick can fly on the day it hatches. The reframe is the one this whole section exists for. Judged by the standards of the band above, this looks like the failure state: no incubation, no brooding, no feeding, no parent at all. It is instead the strategy that produces the most independent newborn in the class. Absence of care is not the same as absence of provision — everything the chick needed was loaded into a very large yolk and a well-managed compost heap. Held honestly: mound thermal tolerance in this species is documented by Eiby and Booth in The Auk (2008); the ascent figures come from the Journal of Ornithology work on post-hatching behaviour. Both were read at abstract level. What sex the hatchlings will be has not been decided yet — the sand decides it, and on some beaches it is now deciding almost entirely one way. temperature-dependent sex determinationpivotal temperature ≈29 °Cabove ~31 °C: all female99% female bias on some beaches ▸ Field notes Field notes · Sea turtles · Cheloniidae and Dermochelyidae A sea turtle's clutch is buried in sand and left. Nothing about that is neglect; the temperature of the sand is doing work that in most vertebrates is done by chromosomes. Sea turtles have temperature-dependent sex determination. Below a pivotal temperature the clutch runs male, above it female, and the pivotal value sits around 29 °C — varying by species and population, with some populations measured nearer 30.4 °C. A nest averaging above roughly 31 °C through the middle third of development can produce 100% female hatchlings. That is the part that has stopped being only a curiosity. Rising sand temperatures at some rookeries are already producing extreme skews: green turtle nesting beaches in the northern Great Barrier Reef are reported at around 99% female hatchling production. There is a genuine counterweight — analysis of pivotal temperatures recorded worldwide shows systematically higher pivotal values at warmer sites, which points to local adaptation that could keep producing some males — and it is a mitigating factor rather than a solution, because adaptation of that kind is slow and the warming is not. Deliberately handed off rather than told twice: the other half of the sea-turtle egg story — embryos vocalising inside the shell and hatching in synchrony, and the long assumption that these were silent animals — is drawn in The Hatchery and carried in No. 57. It is not repeated here. The bet being placed is not on any one season. Why it is in this section: nobody comes back for these. The parent is long dead, the lake has evaporated, and the egg is intact in the dust — and when the rain arrives, development resumes from where it stopped, decades of nothing having cost it nothing. A Shell That Has to Pass Inspection

a forgery, one host deepmatched to bird vision L★S · 015 A Shell That Has to Pass Inspection Common cuckoo · Cuculus canorus host-specific female lineages The egg is not just left, it is left in somebody else's nest — which means the shell has a second job no other egg here has. It has to survive being looked at by a bird that would throw it out. gentes: host-specific female racesmimetic egg typesmatched to host vision, not oursarms-race framing contested ▸ Field notes Field notes · Common cuckoo · Cuculus canorus Everything else in this section is left somewhere indifferent — sand, a mound, a dry lakebed. A cuckoo egg is left somewhere attentive, and that changes what the shell has to do. Female common cuckoos form gentes: host-specific lineages, each parasitising one host species and laying a constant egg type that tends to match that host's eggs. In Britain a gens specialising on pied wagtails has evolved mimetic eggs, documented by Brooke and Davies, whose experimental work on cuckoo–host coevolution is the foundation here. The host's countermeasure is inspection — discriminating and ejecting a mismatched egg — and that pressure is what selects for closer matching. The refinement worth carding is about who is doing the looking. Assessing the mimicry by human perception systematically misjudges it; modelling host retinal function instead shows matches that are far better than they appear to us, because birds see into the ultraviolet and process colour differently. The forgery is not aimed at our eyes. And the framing is live rather than settled. "Coevolutionary arms race" is the standard telling, and a 2025 preprint argues that cuckoo egg colour mimicry results from coevolutionary alternation instead — hosts and parasites shifting between targets rather than escalating against each other. A 2025 Science paper works on the genomic architecture of the mimicry and its consequences for speciation. We flag the challenge and lean on none of it: the preprint has not been through review, and we say so rather than reporting it as a result. Handed off: brood parasitism as a nesting strategy — including that not building a nest evolved independently at least seven times in birds — is carded in A Field Guide to Nests (No. 15). This entry is about the shell, not the nest. That apparatus exists because a verdict had been reached about an animal and the verdict was wrong. A murre's egg was said to roll in a safe arc. A father covered in eggs looked infested. A mother who buried a clutch and swam away looked negligent. Nobody has reached a mistaken verdict about the morning your own life rearranged itself behind you. There is nothing to correct, no misreading to overturn, and a column headed actually pointed at somebody's account of recognising themselves would be an insult wearing the costume of rigour. So the table is absent, and the absence is the argument. This is the same rule Field Guide No. 10 set when it declined to run a reframe over the turtles people made out of their own cosmologies: a subject that cannot take the apparatus gets a different card, not a smaller one. The word is not ours, and that is stated rather than glossed. Egg, and getting your egg cracked, are trans community language. No individual coined them so far as anyone has established: Evelyn Bauer's history for Them traces the earliest documented use to an Urban Dictionary entry for egg mode in August 2016, and records Susan Stryker being unable to date her own first encounter with it. A word this good with no owner is not a gap in the record — it is what community language looks like from the inside. We borrowed it, with thanks, and say so. One thing the biology does supply, and it is a limit rather than a licence. Across birds, snakes, lizards, turtles, crocodilians and even the echidna, the tool that opens an egg is on the inside of the shell. Nothing on this page hatches by being opened from outside; an egg opened from outside is not a hatching, it is an egg somebody broke. Which is also the one piece of advice this guide will offer about anybody else's: you cannot do it for them. You can only be audible. The full argument is The Shell Was Your Calcium (No. 57). A man fired for his nervous system

Greenwich · 12 February 1796 A man fired for his nervous system David Kinnebrook was an assistant at the Royal Observatory from 23 May 1794. His job was to catch the exact moment a star crossed the meridian wire. The method was Bradley's — eye and ear. You watch the star approach the wire while counting the clock's beats aloud, and you judge where between two beats the crossing fell. It is a whole-body skill: eyes, ears, working memory, and the timing of your own attention, all at once. Maskelyne set out what it demanded, and the sentence is more revealing than he can have known: "A good ear seems, in this kind of observation, to be almost as useful as a good eye." Nevil Maskelyne, Greenwich Observations 1787–1798, pp. 339–40 In the same published account, the Astronomer Royal recorded that his assistant had "began, from the beginning of August last, to set them down half a second of time later than he should do," and that in January of 1796 "he increased his error to 8/10ths of a second." Kinnebrook was dismissed on 12 February 1796. Maskelyne, who had already tried and failed to correct him, still described him in print as a diligent and useful assistant to me in other respects. He went home to Norfolk, taught school, and computed for the Nautical Almanac from a house in Norwich. He died in 1802, aged about thirty. Nobody at the time thought anything had been discovered. A young man was simply not accurate — which is to say, not the same as his supervisor. On this joint. The dismissal is documented in Maskelyne's own published observations. What is contested is the tidy causal story built on top of it — that this incident is the origin of the personal equation and, through it, of experimental psychology. That telling is under active revision: see Matthew D. Lund, "'A Vitious Way of Observing': Kinnebrook and the Prehistory of the Personal Equation," Isis 116(3), 2025. We have not read it at the primary, and say so. The founding anecdote of this chain is its shakiest link, and putting that first is deliberate. contested Greenwich → the personal equation The eight-tenths gap A clock's second beats drawn as ticks along a line. Maskelyne's mark sits on a beat; Kinnebrook's sits eight tenths of a second later. Königsberg · the 1820s Correct for the observer Two decades later, Friedrich Bessel read Maskelyne's account and did the thing nobody at Greenwich had done. He checked whether it was only Kinnebrook. It was not. Bessel compared his own transit timings against other practised astronomers and found gaps as large as Kinnebrook's, and larger. More importantly, he found they were not random. Each observer ran consistently early or consistently late against each other observer — a stable, personal offset that stayed put across nights and stars. That is a genuine discovery about human beings, made with a telescope: perception and reaction differ between people, systematically, and the difference does not go away when you try harder. And here is what astronomy did with it. It did not screen for fast observers. It did not train the difference out, or grade observers against a standard nervous system. It wrote down, for each person, how they differed — the personal equation — and added that constant to their readings. The variation was accepted as real, published as a number, and built into the instrument's output. The observer was kept. what the personal equation actually is Be careful about why. Bessel was not defending anybody. He wanted accurate stellar positions, and a systematic error is simply a correctable one. Nobody was aiming at dignity. That is the shape of every link in this chain, in both directions — people solving their own problem, producing an outcome they never had in view. documented the personal equation → experimental psychology Two responses to the same finding Left: four observers with different offsets, each given their own published constant, all feeding one corrected result. Leipzig, then New York · 1879–1890 The apparatus leaves the observatory Once you can measure how long a person takes to notice something, you have an instrument that does not care what it is pointed at. Reaction time came out of astronomy as a nuisance to be corrected, and arrived in the new psychological laboratories as a subject in its own right. Wilhelm Wundt opened his laboratory at Leipzig in 1879, and mental chronometry — timing the components of perceiving, deciding, responding — was among the things it was built to do. James McKeen Cattell studied with Wundt, and in 1890 published the phrase that names the rest of this chain: mental tests. He then took it to Columbia. The instrument was invented to answer how long does this person take? It left the observatory answering how much mind does this person have? the step that is not Bessel's Notice exactly where the substitution happens. Bessel measured a difference and used it to correct a reading. The new discipline measured a difference and used it to rank the person. Those are not the same operation, and nothing in the physics licenses the second. This joint is well documented as a matter of who taught whom and what got measured. The inference that a speed is a quantity of mind is not documented at all — it is an assumption the apparatus quietly carried across the threshold, and it is the load-bearing error of the next hundred years. documented Cattell → Thorndike, at Columbia One instrument, two questions A single stopwatch shape with two arrows leaving it. Columbia · 1898 The cat in the box Cattell's doctoral student finished his dissertation in a year. It was called Animal Intelligence, and it put cats in boxes. Edward L. Thorndike built puzzle boxes with a latch inside. A hungry cat goes in; food sits outside; the cat scrabbles until it happens to trip the latch. Put it back in and time it again. And again. What Thorndike published was not the story of any cat. It was the learning curve — escape time on one axis, trials on the other, dropping away as fumbling gives way to the successful move. From it came the law of effect: acts followed by satisfaction get stamped in, acts followed by discomfort get stamped out. Learning had been made into a line on a graph. Anything that is a line has a slope, and anything with a slope can be compared. what the puzzle box actually produced This is the joint where the instrument that started at a telescope reaches something it can shape rather than merely read. A transit time is a fact you record. A learning curve is a fact you can try to bend — by arranging what follows a behaviour. Thorndike went to Teachers College, Columbia, and stayed. "Whatever exists at all exists in some amount"

Teachers College · 1918 "Whatever exists at all exists in some amount" Twenty years after the cats, Thorndike wrote the sentence that made a child measurable. "Whatever exists at all exists in some amount. To know it thoroughly involves knowing its quantity as well as its quality." E. L. Thorndike, "The Nature, Purposes, and General Methods of Measurements of Educational Products," in The Measurement of Educational Products, Seventeenth Yearbook of the National Society for the Study of Education, Part II (1918) Read as epistemology it is almost banal. Read as a warrant for a profession it is enormous, because it converts a question about what schooling is into a question about what schooling can be scored on. And Thorndike said what would be scored: education is known to us, he wrote, only by the products it produces — things made, words spoken, acts performed, and the like. Products. Not children — products, of which children are the raw material. That framing was not hidden or subtextual in this period; it was the textbook. Ellwood Cubberley put it in the standard administration manual of the era, in words nobody has had to dig for: "our schools are, in a sense, factories, in which the raw products (children) are to be shaped and fashioned into products to meet the various demands of life." The second rail · 1869–now The other rail A second track has been running underneath this whole time, and it started in the same place — an astronomer's error curve, turned on people. We have told that story already, and we will not re-tell it here: the curve for observational error becomes Quetelet's average man, becomes Galton's ranking, becomes eugenics. It is The Lines We Drew, zine No. 9, and the corrections we had to make to it are in the public changelog. What matters for this chain is where that rail goes next. Emil Kraepelin extended Galton's sorting logic across the whole range of mental functioning, building the classificatory scheme that descends into the DSM — a system whose business is to say what you are. One rail decides what you are. The other decides what is done to you. Neither is much use to a school without the other. why this zine has two tracks They are separable in principle and they were built by different people for different reasons. But a classification with no intervention attached is inert, and an intervention with no classification has no one to be applied to. A reform, with a long tail

Teachers College · 1914 A reform, with a long tail The multiple-choice test was invented by a man trying to solve an injustice, and he spent his later life trying to undo it. Frederick J. Kelly finished his doctorate at Teachers College, Columbia, in 1914. The dissertation was Teachers' Marks, Their Variability and Standardization, and it had two complaints, both fair. Teachers' grades varied wildly for the same work — a matter of luck for the child. And marking swallowed the hours a teacher should be teaching. His answer was the Kansas Silent Reading Test: the first published multiple-choice test. A whole class at once, no writing, scored by running an eye down a column. It was built to take arbitrary power away from the person holding the pen. It did that. Then it handed the power to whoever held the answer key. the shape of nearly every link in this chain Hold on to how reasonable this is. Kelly is not a villain and the problem he named was real — Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent children have always been on the receiving end of a teacher's private, unaccountable judgment. Standardization is a genuine protection against that, and it is also how a child's morning becomes a set of items with one right answer each. Kelly himself turned against what he had made. As a university president decades later he tried to pull his institution back from standardized testing, and lost his job for it. On this joint. Kelly wrote at Teachers College during Thorndike's long tenure there, and his dissertation is squarely inside Thorndike's measurement programme. We have not established that Thorndike supervised or sat on it. Ohio State · 1924 Built from typewriter parts Sidney Pressey assembled a machine out of typewriter parts that could present a multiple-choice question, take an answer, and score it. The order here is the point, and it is the reverse of how people tell it. The machine did not create the standardized item. The item created the machine. Once a child's understanding had been packed into four options with exactly one correct, a device could handle it — because the hard part, deciding what counts as knowing, had already been done and frozen into the answer key. Automation does not arrive and flatten a rich thing. It arrives after the flattening, and then it is very hard to argue with. the general rule this chain keeps demonstrating Pressey believed he was building a liberation: immediate feedback, self-pacing, a teacher freed from drill. Every claim made for personalized learning in the last decade was made for a box of typewriter parts a century ago, and Audrey Watters' history of these devices is the record of how reliably the claim recurs and how reliably the machines fail commercially while the idea survives. The art of teaching, as a schedule

Harvard · 1954 The art of teaching, as a schedule B. F. Skinner took Thorndike's law of effect, sharpened it into operant conditioning, and pointed it at the classroom in "The Science of Learning and the Art of Teaching." His complaint about schools was, in his own terms, technical. Reinforcement arrives too late, too rarely, and too crudely — a mark on a page days after the work. Behaviour is shaped by what immediately follows it, so schooling is an engineering problem: break the material into small steps and reinforce each one at once. Hence the teaching machines. Two things stayed even though the boxes did not sell. First, the assumption that the observable behaviour is the whole of the learning — that what cannot be counted did not happen. Second, that a person's difference is a schedule problem: with correct contingencies, any behaviour can be brought to the target. Notice this is the exact inverse of the personal equation. Bessel's constant said the difference is stable, so accommodate it. Skinner's schedule says no difference is stable, so remove it. The critique was contemporary, not hindsight. Reviewing Beyond Freedom and Dignity, Noam Chomsky argued that the framework's apparent scientific content evaporates when its terms are applied to human beings — the account, he wrote, is "quite vacuous," and being vacuous it "is as congenial to the libertarian as to the fascist." People said so at the time, in the largest venues available, and it made no difference to the adoption. documented operant conditioning → Lovaas The inversion Two statements set against each other. A room with a child in it

UCLA · 1987 · where the rails meet A room with a child in it This is where the chain stops being history, because from here it is a description of a great many of our childhoods. O. Ivar Lovaas applied operant conditioning to Autistic children at UCLA. His 1987 paper in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology reported that after intensive long-term treatment, 47% of the experimental group (n=19) achieved "normal" intellectual and educational functioning, against 2% of the controls (n=40). Read the outcome measure, because the outcome measure is the argument. What was scored as success was normal-range IQ and passing an ordinary first grade. Not health. Not communication. Not whether a child could ask for what they needed, or was in less distress, or was happier. The endpoint was indistinguishability. Now both rails are visible in one room. The diagnostic rail — Galton, Kraepelin, the DSM — supplies what this child is. Astronomy solved this two hundred years ago

The turn Astronomy solved this two hundred years ago Two disciplines met the same discovery — that human beings differ from one another in perception, timing and attention, stably, and not by choice. They answered it in opposite directions. Astronomy said: the difference is real, so publish the constant and keep the observer. The variation went into the model. The science got better — more accurate, not less — precisely because it stopped pretending its observers were interchangeable. Schooling said: the difference is real, so bring the observer to the standard. Rank, then remediate, then reinforce, then score how close to indistinguishable we got. Accommodation is not a modern concession, or a kindness bolted onto a rigorous system. It is what the more rigorous discipline did with this exact finding, two centuries ago, and the classroom is the outlier. the whole argument, in one And here is why the chain form matters rather than a villain. Nobody authored this road. Maskelyne wanted accurate transits. Bessel wanted good positions. Cattell wanted a science of mind. Kelly wanted children protected from arbitrary marking. Pressey wanted teachers freed from drill. Each solved their own problem competently, and could not have seen what their work would join up with a century downstream. That is not an excuse — the harm is not smaller because it was unintended. It is a route. A thing that was accumulated can be dis-accumulated, one competent adjustment at a time, in the other direction. Nobody has to win an argument with a conspiracy. We have to keep supplying the endpoint the instrument was never able to choose. We are the assistants who got dismissed for eight tenths of a second. And we are also, now, the ones holding the pen — writing our own constants down, and refusing to be corrected away. The stars did not care how fast Kinnebrook was. Neither, in the end, did the astronomy. It just wrote him down and carried on looking. Paris · 1824 A ceiling nobody can lift At twenty-eight, Sadi Carnot published a short book about steam engines that turned out to be about the limits of the universe. The question was practical: how good can an engine get? Engineers assumed it depended on cleverness — better valves, better steam, a better working fluid. Carnot proved it doesn't. "The motive power of heat is independent of the agents employed to realize it; its quantity is fixed solely by the temperatures of the bodies between which is effected, finally, the transfer of the caloric." Sadi Carnot, Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu, 1824 Read what that forecloses. No working substance helps. No mechanism helps. The maximum is set by the two temperatures you have and nothing else, and no engineer who ever lives will beat it. It is one of the strangest results in physics: a ceiling on human ingenuity, derived in advance, that applies to machines nobody had invented yet. And he got it from a theory that was wrong. Carnot worked inside caloric — heat as an indestructible fluid that flows from hot to cold, conserved like water falling through a mill. That picture is false; heat is energy, not substance. Clausius rejected caloric, folded in Joule's work on energy conservation, and Kelvin supplied the absolute temperature scale — and only then did the familiar formula appear. So "Carnot derived the efficiency equation" is a smoothed retelling: the result has layered authorship, and its author reached it by reasoning correctly about something that does not exist. Waste is not a failure. It is the fee.

The second law · what it actually says Waste is not a failure. It is the fee. Here is the part that matters for everything downstream, and it is worth saying slowly because the ordinary use of the word gets it exactly backwards. An engine takes heat from something hot, converts some of it to work, and dumps the rest into something cold. That last step is not sloppiness. It is not a sign that the engineering isn't finished. Without a cold reservoir to dump into, the engine does not run at all. The waste is not the price of doing it badly. It is the price of doing it. A cycle that claims to waste nothing is either measured wrong, lying, or consuming itself. the second law, stated rudely So "eliminate all waste" is not an ambitious engineering goal that we have not yet reached. In thermodynamics it is a category error — a request for a machine that is forbidden, in the way a perpetual motion machine is forbidden. Engineers know this. It is not controversial, contested, or new. It has been settled for two centuries. Hold on to the shape of that sentence: the thing being demanded is not merely hard, it is the one outcome the physics rules out. Under one percent, for ten billion years

The nearest star Under one percent, for ten billion years The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, and in doing so converts about 0.7% of the rest mass involved into energy. The other 99.3% stays mass. By any engineering standard that is a poor conversion. And it is the most consequential energy process in your life: it made the carbon in you, it drives the weather, it is the reason there is a biosphere at all. It has also been running for about five billion years and has roughly that long left. Notice what the Sun is not doing. It is not maximising output. A star sits in hydrostatic equilibrium — the outward push of radiation balanced against the inward pull of its own weight — and that balance is a self-regulating arrangement, not an optimisation. Speed the fusion up and the core expands and cools, which slows the fusion down. The thermostat is the structure. The stars that burn hottest and brightest are the ones that die soonest. The most massive can exhaust themselves in a few million years — a rounding error beside the Sun. output and duration are traded, not stacked So the sky offers a genuinely useful fact, and it is narrower than the one you might want it to offer. Taylor, and a man called Schmidt

1911 · the stopwatch Taylor, and a man called Schmidt Frederick Winslow Taylor published The Principles of Scientific Management in 1911, having serialised the argument in the American Magazine through that spring. The method: take a job, break it into motions, time each motion, discard the ones that don't contribute, and prescribe the remainder as the one correct way to work. The stopwatch is the instrument, and the worker's own account of the job is explicitly not evidence. His most-repeated demonstration involved a pig-iron handler at Bethlehem Steel whom he called Schmidt, loading iron onto railcars. Under Taylor's prescribed regime of work and rest intervals, output rose sharply. The story was told, and retold, and it did more work than any argument. Here it is arriving in a newspaper editorial that Cubberley would later quote approvingly in a textbook for school administrators: "Lately we have had a striking demonstration of what experimental science can do by reducing the motions in laying brick and the fatigue in handling pig iron. It can hardly be pretended that scientific efficiency is of less consequence in the schools." Editorial, Springfield Republican, 1912, as quoted in Cubberley, Public School Administration (1916) Note the move in that sentence, because the whole chain turns on it. Bricklaying and pig iron have been optimised — therefore schools should be. The premise is a factory floor. The conclusion is a classroom. Nothing in between is argued. And hold on to "the fatigue in handling pig iron." We come back to it, and to the question nobody asked, on spread ten. documented Taylor's series → the NEA, one month later What the stopwatch records A job broken into timed motions, with a column of what is measured and a greyed-out column of what is not: the worker's own account, fatigue, and whether the job is bearable. recorded motion 1 · 4.2s motion 2 · 1.8s motion 3 · 6.1s tons / day rest interval not recorded how it felt whether he agreed what it cost him what he wanted the next day the worker's account is not evidence that was the method, not an oversight Figure 5 · two columns, one of them empty the ceiling — provablebounded 5 · Taylor · 1911 Elimination of Waste · Stimpunks

July 1911 · one month later "Or the business world will force them to" The gap between Taylor's factory and the American classroom was about four weeks. Raymond Callahan reconstructed it in Education and the Cult of Efficiency (1962), and the detail is precise enough to date: "In July of 1911, for example, a month after Taylor's series of articles was completed in the American Magazine, a school board member from Allegheny, Pennsylvania told the N.E.A. that the two words which were 'electrifying the industrial world — scientific management' contained a 'message' for every teacher, and near the end of his speech he indicated that if teachers did not voluntarily take steps to increase their efficiency the business world would force them to do so." There is no claim about learning in it at all. It is a warning about who holds the power, delivered to teachers, one month after the method appeared in a magazine. Efficiency procedures were applied, in his summary, "to classroom learning and to teachers, to the program of studies, to the organization of the schools, to administrative functions, and to entire school systems," most of it before 1916 and most of it hung on "the magic words 'scientific management'." 1916 · the phrase, in a school "The elimination of waste" Ellwood Cubberley's Public School Administration (1916) was, in George Counts' judgement, the most widely read and influential book on school administration of its generation. Here is what it told a generation of superintendents that schools are. "Our schools are, in a sense, factories in which the raw products (children) are to be shaped and fashioned into products to meet the various demands of life. The specifications for manufacturing come from the demands of twentieth-century civilization, and it is the business of the school to build its pupils according to the specifications laid down. This demands good tools, specialized machinery, continuous measurement of production to see if it is according to specifications, the elimination of waste in manufacture, and a large variety in the output." The objection · at full strength This argument should not need physics at all Here is the case against the previous spread, made as well as we can make it, because we think it is largely right. The turn Ask what the ceiling is Every serious measure of efficiency ever written down has a maximum. That is what makes it a measure rather than a mood. Carnot's has one, provably. An engine's gauge has a redline. A budget has a bottom. A demand with no ceiling is not a high standard — it is not a standard at all, because nothing can satisfy it and therefore nothing counts as having met it. So the useful question, whenever the word turns up, is short and rude: what is the maximum, and how would we know we had reached it? If there is an answer, you are talking about efficiency. If there isn't, you are talking about obedience with a technical vocabulary. "The elimination of waste in manufacture." There is a well, and it has an instruction attached

Isla Negra, 1973 There is a well, and it has an instruction attached In the last year of his life Pablo Neruda wrote a short untitled poem. It opens by saying that if each day falls inside each night, there is a well “where clarity is imprisoned.” Then it tells you what to do about that: We need to sit on the rim of the well of darkness and fish for fallen light with patience. Pablo Neruda, untitled, El mar y las campanas (1973) · translated by William O’Daly, The Sea and the Bells (Copper Canyon Press, 1988), pp. 94–95 It is a famous image and a kind one. It does not pretend the well isn’t there. It doesn’t tell you to cheer up, or to climb, or to stop noticing that the day fell into the night. It says the light is down there, still, and it can be recovered, and the thing that recovers it is patience. But read the grammar again. We sit. We fish. The poem hands you a rim to sit on and a line to cast — which means the poem has quietly assigned you a role, and there are two roles in it. There is the one who fishes. And there is the light that fell. Even Fallen Light Glows · Stimpunks

The reply, in full Even fallen light glows Helen Edgar read that rewrite and answered it in six syllables. Even fallen light glows. Helen Edgar Look at what the reply refuses to do. It does not argue with a single line of the rewrite. It does not say the rim is closer than it looks. It does not promise that patience comes back. It does not say someone is casting for you right now, or that you will be reached, or that this will pass — all of which would have been kind, and none of which she could know. It makes a much narrower claim, and the narrowness is why it holds: it is a statement about the light, not about the rescue. Whether the fishing works is an open question. Whether the light is still light is not. Those had been welded together by the poem — fallen light is for recovering, its whole role is to be fished out — and six syllables pried them apart. The rest of this zine is one fact that happens to be shaped exactly like that sentence. It is not offered as proof of it. Nothing on a forest floor can prove anything about a person. On the forest floor, fallen wood glows

The fact this zine runs on On the forest floor, fallen wood glows It has a name in English — foxfire — and people have been writing it down for a very long time, because a rotting log giving off a steady green light is not the kind of thing you forget seeing. The current accounting recognises 132 taxa of bioluminescent fungi, across five lineages: the mycenoid lineage (96 species), Omphalotus (18), Armillaria (14), the Lucentipes lineage (3), and Eoscyphella (1). The count has roughly doubled in fifteen years, mostly because people went looking. Here is the part that is not a coincidence. Every one of them is an agaric, and they are saprotrophic white-rot decomposers — or, rarely, plant pathogens. There is no glowing fungus that lives some other way. The thing that glows is the thing that eats fallen wood. This is taxonomy, not metaphor. Every known bioluminescent fungus is a wood or litter decomposer. So the phrase fallen light is not doing poetic work here. On a forest floor at night, the light is in the fallen thing, and it is there because the fallen thing is being taken apart. The glow is built out of the log

Where the light comes from The glow is built out of the log In 2018 a team led by Alexey Kotlobay published the whole pathway — the first, and still the only, completely genetically encodable bioluminescent system in any eukaryote. Four enzymes. It is called the caffeic acid cycle, and it goes like this. Start with caffeic acid. Hispidin synthase turns it into hispidin. A hydroxylase turns that into 3-hydroxyhispidin — the fungal luciferin, the actual fuel. Luciferase oxidises the luciferin in the presence of oxygen, and out comes caffeylpyruvate and a photon, green, at about 530 nm. Then the fourth enzyme, caffeylpyruvate hydrolase, takes the spent molecule and turns it back into caffeic acid. Two things about that are worth sitting with. It is a cycle. The end of the reaction is the beginning of the reaction. Nothing has to be delivered from outside for the next photon. And caffeic acid is a phenylpropanoid — the same chemical family the wood’s own lignin is built from. The fungus is a white-rot decomposer taking lignin apart. The part that glows is the part nobody sees

Which part glows The part that glows is the part nobody sees Say glowing mushroom and you picture a cap. For the whole Armillaria lineage, that picture is backwards. In Armillaria, foxfire comes from the mycelium and the rhizomorphs — the threads and the dark bootlace-like cords running through the wood and under the bark. The mushrooms, the visible fruiting bodies, the part that does the reproducing and gets photographed and has a common name, are consistently reported as non-luminescent. There are known exceptions and honesty requires naming them: A. limonea in New Zealand and an undetermined Brazilian species do form brightly luminous caps. And the pattern is lineage-specific — most mycenoid species glow from both mycelium and fruiting body. But in the lineage that gave English the word foxfire, the rule holds. The showy, productive, reproductive part is the dark one. The glow is in the network underneath, in the wood, where nobody is looking. One proposed reason the caps went dark: the luciferin and its precursor are simply absent from the mature mushroom. Not suppressed for a purpose anyone has demonstrated. Just not there. Continuously, on its own clock, with nobody there

When it glows Continuously, on its own clock, with nobody there In 2015 Anderson Oliveira and colleagues showed that the glow of Neonothopanus gardneri — a large Brazilian species that grows on the leaf litter at the base of babassu palms — runs on a temperature-compensated circadian clock. Temperature-compensated is the technically demanding part. The rhythm keeps its period even as the temperature changes, which is the signature of a real biological clock rather than a chemical reaction speeding up when it warms. The luciferase, the reductase and the luciferin all cycle. And the emission itself is continuous — 24 hours a day, modulated by the clock rather than switched on by anything outside. Which is to say: nothing about the glowing is conditional on a receiver. No creature has to arrive for it to happen. No one has to be walking through that forest. It is not triggered by being approached, it does not brighten for company, and it does not stop when the forest is empty, which is nearly always. It is not a signal being sent to anyone. It is a thing that is the case. Even Fallen Light Glows · Stimpunks
Nobody knows what the glow is for

The honest centre of this zine Nobody knows what the glow is for This is the spread that decides whether the rest of it is worth anything, so here is the state of the question rather than the tidy version. The best-supported story is spore dispersal. Sivinski found that sealed traps baited with glowing fungal material caught more arthropods than unlit traps. Later work in Brazil with lit acrylic mushroom replicas drew significantly more rove beetles, Hemiptera, Diptera and Hymenoptera than unlit ones. Under a closed canopy where there is little wind, insects carrying spades of spores out is a real benefit, and the light plausibly buys it. And that story does not cover the facts. It explains a cap. It does not explain luminescence in the mycelium and the lower stipe — which produce no spores at all, and which in Armillaria are the only parts that glow. A serious rival says it is chemistry, not signalling. Luciferins can act as antioxidants, mopping up reactive oxygen species. On that reading the light is a byproduct of staying alive in an oxidising environment while dismantling lignin. The 2024 review puts it plainly: the hypothesis that fungal bioluminescence is an accidental result of metabolism, rather than any evolutionary benefit, cannot yet be excluded. Perry, Desjardin & Stevani, Journal of Fungi 11(1):19 (2024) So: it has been observed for millennia, the full chemistry was solved in 2018, and we still cannot say what it is for. It may be for nothing. It glows anyway. Even Fallen Light Glows · Stimpunks
It happened once, and has been lost ever since

How common it is to stop It happened once, and has been lost ever since Phylogenomic work points to a single origin of bioluminescence in the Agaricales, roughly 160 million years ago — and then, in the lineages that descend from it, repeated loss or inactivation. 132 taxa glow. The Agaricales contain many thousands of species. The capacity is ancestral; what has happened to it over and over, in branch after branch, is that it stopped. What the phylogeny actually says Claim Status Glowing evolved many times over No — once Glowing is rare because it is hard to acquire No — it is rare because it keeps being lost The non-glowing relatives are lesser fungi Not a claim mycology makes This matters here for one reason, and it is a guardrail rather than a flourish. A zine that says even fallen light glows can slide, in about one sentence, into so you had better be glowing. The phylogeny won’t allow it. Keeping the glow is not an achievement, and losing it is the commonest thing that has ever happened to it. A dark relative of a glowing fungus is not a failed one. It is the overwhelming majority. Two roles, and only one of them is a job

Back to the rim Two roles, and only one of them is a job Neruda’s poem needs both parts to work: somebody at the rim with patience, and light at the bottom of the well. What the burnout rewrite found is that you don’t get to choose which one you are on a given morning. And what the forest floor adds is this. The light at the bottom is not idle. It is not waiting to be useful. It is not in a suspended state pending rescue. It is running a four-enzyme cycle that regenerates its own fuel, on its own clock, continuously, out of the substance of the fallen thing — and it is doing that whether or not anyone is at the rim, because emission was never conditional on detection. If you are the fallen light, glowing is not a task you are behind on. There is nothing to do differently. The casting is somebody else’s work, and it always was — that is not a failure of yours, it is how the poem is built. This is the point at which solidarity stops being a warm feeling and becomes a division of labour. Helen names what sits at the rim: a community, “a constellation made up of all our unique ways of being” — building networks of care, strengthening constellations of love. Somebody is at the rim. It does not have to be you, today. And Love You Down To Your Star Stuff is a claim about reach. Down to measures how far the loving goes, not what earns it. The bottom of the well is not out of range of the claim. It is only out of range of the casting. Not: Notthat the log is glad it fell. Nothing here says the falling was good, or necessary, or secretly a gift. A fallen tree is a dead tree. The glow is not compensation and does not settle the account. Notthat burnout is secretly productive. Decay is not a chrysalis. We are not saying you are composting into something better, or that this is your fallow season. Burnout is damage, it is usually caused by conditions somebody chose, and it is not an ingredient. Notthat you must glow to be worth keeping. Spread ten is in this zine to block exactly that. The glow has been lost far more often than it has been kept, and the dark lineages are not lesser. Notthat the glow is a signal, so try harder to be seen. The opposite. It runs continuously with nobody there, and the one function anyone has evidence for doesn’t even apply to the part that glows in Armillaria. Visibility is not the test. Nota promise that you will be reached. Six words about light are not a rescue plan. “Even fallen light glows” is true whether or not the fishing works, which is precisely why it can be said honestly to someone whose patience has broken. Notnature proving anything about us. A rhyme, not a proof. A fungus in a log says nothing whatsoever about a nervous system, and if you needed mycology to believe you were still here, the problem was never the evidence. Notthe rewrite corrected. Umwelt · the sealed world No view from nowhere A century ago, the biologist Jakob von Uexküll asked a strange question: what is the world like for a tick? The answer is almost nothing — and yet complete. She waits, blind and deaf, for three signals: the warmth of a mammal, the smell of butyric acid, the touch of skin. On those three her whole life turns. That is her Umwelt — not a poorer version of our world, but her entire sky. This is the move that changes everything. Each creature lives within its own perceptual world, and each world is whole — not a partial glimpse of one true reality waiting underneath. There is no underneath. There is no view from nowhere. But whole is not the same as walled: a sky is a soap bubble, not a fortress — permeable, kept aloft by encounter, and never guaranteed. The variety of minds No two alike Nervous systems are roughly 550 million years old, and life has been improvising them ever since — into shapes almost nothing like ours. An octopus keeps most of its neurons in its arms, so each arm half-thinks for itself. A jellyfish has no brain and no centre at all — just a net of nerves ringing its body. A nematode worm runs an entire life on exactly 302 neurons, every connection mapped. No two of these are the same — and no two within a kind are, either. Every nervous system is a one-off, tuned by body and history and the particular world it grew up sensing. So read neurodiversity at face value and it can't mean only us. It means the whole living spread of ways to have a nervous system. There is no standard nervous system, any more than there is a standard mind. Their word for it is ethodiversity — the variety of ways of being and behaving across all animals — and it takes "behaviour" back from the behaviourists. The grid over behaviour The rule that says behave If ethodiversity is the field, ethonormativity is the grid laid over it: the unwritten, humanist rule about which behaviours are allowed and expected in a given animal — human or not — in a given room. And the grid has teeth. The horse who refuses the rider; the frightened or depressed cat who resists being petted and lashes out — for departing from the script, Tarragnat notes, animals like these "are often abandoned or euthanised." Ethonormative violence is real, and often fatal. It is the same move, scaled across species, that pathologises a stimming child or a nonspeaking adult. The reframe is the one this whole collection keeps making. The behaviour read from outside as a malfunction is, from inside, a subjective response that makes sense. Change the environment, not the creature. Neurodivergent people are so often pathologised precisely by being animalised — cast as less-than-human, machine-like, without an inner life. Tarragnat calls the cruel version bestialisation: an apparatus of power working "at the intersection of speciesism and neuronormativity," splitting the world into the "intelligent, sensible human" and the "non-rational, machine-like animal." Judith Butler (2020) names it too — the subjugation of animality by "a specific humanist norm." But there is another move. To (hum)animalise oneself — to claim, without shame, that we are animals — "can be an act of subversion, a way of reclaiming animality." The problem was never being animal. The problem was a norm that made animality abject. So we take it back: not "you're like an animal" as insult, but humanimal as kin. The cat who leaves the lap; the person who goes quiet and still — not abandoning the bond, but protecting it. Withdrawal can be care. Every animal knows this.
