For those cores, the small offering is not a lesser route — it is the route. It even stops itself: past ten to twenty Earth masses the core opens a pressure bump and the pebbles are halted before arrival, so even the sky knows when someone has had enough pebbles. Then the turn, printed on the face of the zine rather than buried in a footnote, because five-for-five is exactly the shape of a claim that circulates for being tidy rather than true. The physics does not justify the love. The universe is not signing anything off, and if it were, its approval would be worthless — a universe that could approve could also decline. This is the same defect the site caught in a sentence of its own: the universe loves you for it makes the star stuff the reason, and a reason can be revoked, where love you down to your star stuff measures how far the loving reaches rather than why it is given. Down to is not because of. Amythest Schaber originated the five; Stimpunks popularized them and put them into currency from 2022, substituting locutions for languages; the term penguin pebbling reached us later, through Lindsey; and Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms has developed the framework furthest, including the Penguin Pebbling game built with Ryan Boren. Eight spreads, five diagrams. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 55 What Looks Like Chaos Stimpunks Zines Seven weavers, twenty-one nests, and a camera say otherwise — and so does a room somebody told you to tidy. Nest building is the textbook example of pure instinct: a bird constructs a thing it has never seen, without instruction, and gets it right the first time. 10 spreads→ Details Nest building is the textbook example of pure instinct — a bird constructs a thing it has never seen, without instruction, and gets it right the first time, so the nest must be something the bird contains rather than something it works out. That claim is falsifiable, because a template predicts one specific thing: sameness, between individuals and within one individual across attempts. Somebody went and measured whether the sameness is there. Southern Botswana, seven colour-ringed male Southern Masked weavers, territories searched daily so a nest was found at the moment it was started; camcorders square to the branch, three nests filmed per bird — twenty-one nests — and the footage coded by a researcher blind to which bird and which date. During the first phase of construction not one measured behaviour was repeatable within a male: not the direction he carried the grass, not how long he wove, not which quadrant he favoured, not how often he lost hold. Then the individuality: two birds consistently pushed the first end of a blade into the right side of the nest, two consistently into the left, three had no side at all — and pooled across all seven, the bias vanished (G = 0.06, p = 0.81). Personal handedness with no species handedness underneath it, which is precisely what a template cannot produce. And they improved: across a season each male dropped grass less often as he built more nests (p < 0.01), while the birds with the most consistent personal style finished the ring phase fastest (R² = 0.25) — a way of one's own was not an eccentricity to be corrected, it was the thing that made him quick. Thirteen years later the harder finding: forty-three white-browed sparrow weaver family groups build architecturally distinct roosts, some with long entrance tubes and some with almost none, stable across years, differing between groups whose territories sit metres apart in the same trees, and not explained by weather, body size, tree height or kinship — then the closer, that the styles are robust to immigration. Not a template and not the environment: a tradition. Set beside all of this is David Gray-Hammond's account of his own room — the diffuser, the books read several at once, the nothing-tidied-away because some days end in a crash rather than a decision — and his sentence about it: to most, it appears that I live in a state of chaos… I know where every item I need resides. The refusals are printed on the zine's face rather than left implied. Not permission from nature, because a universe that could approve could also decline, and down to is not because of. Not instinct versus learning. Not a clever-animal story, since the authors themselves attribute the improvement to increasing dexterity and say any role for cognition still needs demonstrating. And the honest one: not every mess is a nest — burnout collapses the architecture, and the ruins look from the doorway exactly like the curated version. What the science kills is narrower and sturdier for being narrow: the inference that an order you cannot read is not an order. Two centuries of confident observers looked at a nest and saw a machine executing, and were describing the limits of watching while calling it a fact about the bird. Nesting is David Gray-Hammond's; lilipadding is Tanya Adkin and David Gray-Hammond's, with Adkin's name first on both pieces that set it out — a first draft credited it to him alone, and the colophon says so. Ten spreads, two diagrams. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 57 The Shell Was Your Calcium Stimpunks Zines The egg crack moment is borrowed, true, and kinder than its own retelling. More than eighty per cent of a hatchling's calcium came from the wall it broke. The word is borrowed and this zine says so. 10 spreads→ Details In the trans community, getting your egg cracked is the moment somebody knows and accepts that they are trans; the therapist Essy Knopf extended the term to Autistic and ADHD experience in 2025, and credited its origin himself. The word is borrowed and this zine says so — no individual coined it, and Evelyn Bauer's history for Them traces the earliest documented use to an Urban Dictionary entry in August 2016 and finds even Susan Stryker unable to date her own first encounter with it. What the zine argues with is not Knopf but what happens to the metaphor afterwards, when repetition flattens it into a door: one threshold, crossed once, a settled person on the far side. So we checked it against some eggs. The shell does not get thinner. From about day eleven the chorioallantoic membrane dissolves calcium out of the wall, and Halgrain and colleagues measured the result — thickness between day 0 and day 15 not significantly different (p = 0.110), breaking strength between day 11 and day 15 significantly reduced (p = 0.007). Measure it and nothing is happening. Weigh what it can bear and everything is. Nobody could see it; there was nothing to see. Then where the calcium goes: the shell supplies more than eighty per cent of all the calcium a chick embryo gets, roughly 2.2 grams, and at hatch the skeleton holds about three quarters of the calcium in the whole animal. The container becomes the frame, by mass, and there is no moment where one ends and the other begins — and since collagen is piezoelectric, as Iwao Yasuda showed in the 1950s, the wall you broke is now the part of you that turns pressure into charge. Third, the messy middle is a documented stage: at internal pipping the beak enters the air cell and the lungs begin working while the shell is still whole, a staged handover Margaret Vince traced in three parts. From outside, an unmarked egg. Fourth, quail embryos click, and an egg set in a clutch a day late speeds up and hatches with the others — while a slower click rate retards the ones ahead. Synchronisation runs both ways: the ones ahead slow down and wait. And the close, from Mair and colleagues' 2026 study of 225 posts: not a door but an oscillating Grief, Relief, and Belief Cycle, whose fourth theme is post-diagnosis burnout, with the authors asking that identification be treated as a first step rather than a terminal component of a service. The refusals are on the zine's face. Not cracking somebody else's egg — the egg tooth is on the inside of the shell, and you can only click. Not the person before was fake. Not a graduation. Not permission from nature, because chick embryos have no identities and down to is not because of. And not the egg as the enemy, which is the uncomfortable one, because masking cost us enormously and also got some of us here alive. Ten spreads, four diagrams. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 60 Beyond the Optical Image Stimpunks Zines On a measured discrepancy, ninety-three years of refusing to say where it lives, and the same question closed on day one. The most famous rotation-curve paper never uses the word dark. It says mass lies beyond the optical image — exactly what was measured. 13 spreads→ Details Helen Edgar’s first constellation, of twenty, is the Dark Matter Field — “the heavy darkness of neuronormativity… the accumulated weight we carry around of a world that does not meet our needs.” Nos. 45 and 46 both said in their colophons that this naming was being kept back. This is the piece that spends it, and the order of borrowing is stated on spread two: her naming came first, the physics is set beside it afterward, and the reverse move is the one this collection exists to refuse. Then ninety-three years of the most careful attribution on record. Fritz Zwicky (1933) applied the virial theorem to seven galaxies in the Coma cluster and found the average density “would have to be at least 400 times greater than that derived on the basis of observations of luminous matter” — he had the number, he had the phrase dark matter, and he closed the section by calling it “an unsolved problem.” The first thing a careful person does with a discrepancy is decline to place it. Forty-seven years later the famous paper comes apart under reading. Rubin, Ford & Thonnard (ApJ 238, 471, 1980) do not report flat rotation curves: “Most rotation curves are rising slowly even at the farthest measured point,” and the negative claim is narrower still — “Neither high nor low luminosity Sc galaxies have falling rotation curves.” Their conclusion says where and refuses to say what: “must have significant mass located beyond the optical image.” The word “dark” never appears in the abstract, and the subject heading as printed is galaxies : internal motions. In 2000 Rubin was still withholding: “Surprisingly, we cannot yet rule out a modified gravitational potential, rather than dark matter” — and “it is folly to believe that we know what a galaxy is, while the extent, the density distribution, and the composition of ≥90% of its mass are still a dark mystery.” Then the zine corrects itself on the page. It was proposed on the premise that the field is “never directly observed, only detected by its distorting effect,” with lensing offered as proof of that — but lensing is the instrument that made the direct detection. Clowe et al. (2006) measured an “8-sigma significance spatial offset” in the Bullet Cluster that “cannot be explained with an alteration of the gravitational force law.” The premise had to go, and spread seven keeps the correction rather than quietly dropping it. What is still open is the particle, not the mass: LZ and XENONnT have both come up empty, and the searches are widening to axion-like particles and dark photons. Two claims held apart, because collapsing either one is the misuse. The argument itself is structural. A gap between what a model predicts and what a body does can live in exactly three places — the mass, the law, or the measurement — and astronomy has argued all three in public, with rivals named and nulls published. Asked about a child, the same question was closed on day one and the residual placed in the child: not the fluorescent hum, not the unannounced transition, not the six hours of masking, not Milton’s double empathy problem. The claim is precise and the sloppy version is not ours — not that the environmental attribution is obviously right, but that it was never treated as an open question. No rival funded, nothing in the criteria reading “we cannot yet rule out.” Where the analogy breaks is stated at full strength rather than hedged: neuronormativity is unmarked, not unobserved. It is written down — criteria, intervention targets, the compliance goal on an education plan, “culture fit,” the seating chart. Dark matter is hidden by nature; this is hidden by convention, and a convention is a decision that can be read and changed this year. The close is the sharpest thing here. Take the identical fact — unseen mass is most of what holds a galaxy together — and it reads just as naturally as the co-regulation nobody logs and the care work nobody bills. Same evidence, opposite moral, and the physics adjudicates neither: if one fact can carry two opposite morals, the moral was never in the fact. Somebody chooses, and has to own the choosing. Refusals on the face: not dark matter proving anything about a nervous system; not an argument against evidence, since careful public attribution is what we are asking for; not modified-gravity advocacy; not “you are mysterious,” because Rubin’s folly line is about a galaxy; not the inspiration story about Rubin, since borrowing it would do to her what gets done to us; and not Helen’s reading corrected. The neuronormative paradigm is Nick Walker’s (Neuroqueer Heresies, 2021), dated here via Helen Edgar’s own account at Autistic Realms and not read at the book; the double empathy problem is Damian Milton’s (2012); monotropism is Murray, Lesser & Lawson (2005). Zwicky read in translation, not the German. Thirteen spreads, eleven diagrams. A method, not a proof.

Zine No. 61 Thirteen Changes Stimpunks Zines On the number that gave Brontosaurus its name back, a ruler its makers said would not travel, and an appeal they lost in public. A category boundary that publishes its own provenance, fences its own range, names its dissenters, and can be appealed — and lost. Ask that of a cut-off score. 13 spreads→ Details Every kid who loved Brontosaurus got told actually, it’s Apatosaurus, and the lesson attached was that the enthusiasm was the amateur part. Here is the paper trail. Marsh named Apatosaurus ajax in 1877 and Brontosaurus excelsus in 1879; Riggs folded the second into the first in 1903 on differences recorded as “usually considered insufficient to justify generic distinction.” Insufficient is a quantitative word with no quantity behind it — and for eighty years nobody could say insufficient by what measure, because the measure did not exist. Then Tschopp, Mateus & Benson built one, across 298 open-access pages, scoring 81 specimens against 477 morphological characters. Their methods section opens by conceding the soft part: separation “is somewhat arbitrary, in particular in paleontology, where no tests exist for the biological species concept,” and “subjectivity of these interpretations is especially great.” So they published the calibration, which is the spread this zine exists for. They counted the differences between pairs everybody already agreed were one genus — twelve between A. ajax and A. louisae, eleven between D. carnegii and D. hallorum — and set the bar one step past the largest agreed gap: “a minimum of 13 changes is herein considered necessary for generic separation.” Six for a species, deliberately generous, because “a wider margin is preferred herein in order to be more cautious.” You can argue with a number whose derivation is printed. You cannot argue with insufficient. Then the rarest move in the story: they fenced their own instrument. The numbers “cannot be applied to any other analysis, even of the same clade” — a threshold that declares its own range of validity, in advance, in the paper that depends on it. By that ruler Brontosaurus holds its own genus after 112 years, and even the headline is hedged in the abstract: “considered valid by our quantitative approach.” The method was not a rescue machine — the same pass dissolved “Dinheirosaurus” into Supersaurus and raised Galeamopus, cutting against its makers’ own earlier work. And then they filed an appeal and lost. The type specimen anchoring the whole genus Diplodocus is a partial tail the paper calls a nomen dubium, leaving “the otherwise well-known genus Diplodocus typified by a dubious species.” They petitioned the ICZN to move it — Case 3700, with a comment period and supporters — and on the last day of 2018 the Commission said no: Opinion 2425, Diplodocus longus maintained. Refused in print, with a number on it, by a body whose refusals you can look up and cite. Set the five properties beside the label on a child: published provenance, a declared range, named dissent (Prothero, four months later, under his own name), a route of appeal, a citable ruling. A cut-off score arrives already applied, says nothing about who chose it or where it stops meaning anything, and then travels across ages, countries and purposes it was never built for. The ruler that would not travel one clade sideways gets less latitude than the one we hand a five-year-old for life — and there is no Case 3700, nowhere to file, no numbered Opinion. The paperwork is not always kind either, and spread eight says so: Oviraptor means egg seizer, named in 1924 for a clutch it was brooding, corrected by Norell and colleagues in 1994 and 1995, and stuck with the libel forever under nomenclatural priority. Two ways a label outlives its refutation — priority, a rule written down, and repetition, which needs no rule at all. Only one admits it. Then the turn: Velociraptor was feathered, on the evidence of quill knobs on the ulna, and it is smaller and stranger than the movie and closer to a bad-tempered rooster, because birds are dinosaurs. Not one of these corrections made an animal less interesting. Every one made it stranger. The animals were never wrong about themselves; we were wrong about them, and being wrong out loud is what let them get better. And 298 pages is not what growing out of it looks like — it is what it looks like when nobody does. What get serious asks for is never depth, which monotropic attention already has; it is convertibility. Not that we stop being absorbed, but that we stop being absorbed for free. Bettin’s inversion holds: retained neoteny is not developmental lag but a distributed adaptive capacity that keeps a group from setting into whatever the highest-ranking person already believes. The close earns the collection. Apatosaurus louisae is estimated at about 41 tonnes of calcium phosphate, and calcium and phosphorus are made in stars — so a sauropod walked the Late Jurassic on a skeleton of dead stars, every atom second-hand and every atom still in circulation. Bone is piezoelectric, as Yasuda showed, so those animals were writing their own skeletons by walking on them; that this was true of sauropod bone is marked as an inference, not a measurement. And Sander and sixteen co-authors still report “no direct evidence on sauropod food and food processing” — the biggest animals ever to walk, and we do not know how they ate, which never made them less real. Refusals on the face: not an argument against evidence or diagnosis, since published provenance is what we are asking for; not “categories are meaningless,” because thirteen is a real bar doing real work; not a claim that taxonomy is like being labelled; not “the scientists were wrong and the kid was right,” because being corrected was never the injury and not being correctable is; not a demand that every label be revoked, since some of us want ours; and not the naturalistic fallacy, because down to is not because of. Thirteen spreads, eleven diagrams. A method, not a proof.
The Light Arrived Before the Name

Zine No. 62 The Light Arrived Before the Name Stimpunks Zines On light-travel time, the seventy-one years it took one description of us to reach English, and the difference between what a thing is and what it ends up called. Light leaves with nothing written on it, so every name in astronomy is an arrival record and never an origin record. Seven measured delays, and what they say about the observer. 11 spreads→ Details The physics is one sentence and it does all the work: light travels at a finite speed and leaves with nothing written on it. Sunlight is eight minutes and twenty seconds old when it reaches your face; Proxima Centauri’s is 4.2 years old; Andromeda’s is 2.5 million. A photon carries a wavelength and a direction and not a discoverer — everything a star will say about itself is complete at emission, and the name gets attached at the far end, by whoever happened to be standing there with an instrument. Astronomy is honest about this and has a word for the landing: first light is the moment a new telescope opens its eye, and nobody has ever thought the telescope invented the galaxy in the frame. So a name in astronomy is an arrival record, never an origin record — and almost everything in this zine is those two things being confused, with a person in place of a star. Priority is the version written down: credit goes to whoever publishes first, and a comet takes the name of whoever files. Halley earned his fairly — he worked out that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object and in 1705 predicted its 1758 return — and its passages had been recorded for more than two thousand years before him. The rule never claimed otherwise. The trouble starts when the register stops saying what it is a register of. Then 1925, twice. In Cambridge, Massachusetts, Cecilia Payne submitted the thesis showing the stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium; Henry Norris Russell told her it was clearly impossible, and she published with a line saying the abundance was “almost certainly not real.” Russell restated the conclusion in 1929. In Moscow — not Kiev, and the zine keeps its own corrected error on the page rather than fixing it quietly — Grunya Sukhareva finished a clinical description of six boys at the hospital-school she had founded in 1921, recording the aloneness, the flattened expression, the narrow blazing interests and the giftedness underneath. Russian in 1925, German in 1926, English in 1996. Seventy-one years, and half a century after Kanner’s and Asperger’s names were fixed to what she had described. Spread five is the structural spine: a distance is a delay, and the same quantity exists for a finding. Seven crossings, each an interval between two dated events. 168 years from Caroline Herschel’s Royal Astronomical Society Gold Medal in 1828 to the next woman’s, Vera Rubin’s, in 1996. 123 years from Matilda Joslyn Gage mapping the pattern in Woman as Inventor (1870) to Margaret Rossiter naming it the Matilda effect (1993) — the name for late naming was itself a hundred and twenty-three years late, and Rossiter did the one thing the pattern does not do by itself: she looked back down the beam and put the earlier name on it. 71 years to English. 42 years from Annie Jump Cannon joining the Harvard College Observatory in 1896 to Harvard giving her a regular appointment in 1938. 7 years from the first pulsar to a Nobel that went to Hewish and Ryle. 4 years from Payne to Russell. And Mittag-Leffler’s 1925 letter intending to nominate Henrietta Leavitt, who had died in 1921 — there was never a nomination. None of those is a claim about intent; each measures a gap, the way you measure a parallax, and the delay tells you about the observer, not the object. The Bell Burnell spread is deliberately precise where the popular telling is not: she read roughly 96 feet of chart paper a day, found a signal too regular to be noise, and is the second author on Hewish, Bell, Pilkington, Scott & Collins, Nature 217, 709 (1968), period 1.3372795 seconds. She was not written out of the paper. She was written out of the prize. And the pulses had been arriving the whole time — what 1967 changed was the listening. Refusals on the face, because six women is six situations and flattening them would be the second erasure: not that gender explains Sukhareva, since Sher & Gibson give her Jewish identity, her Russian nationality and her Russian- and German-language publication alongside it, and raise the possibility that Asperger omitted her deliberately under Nazi-era antisemitism; not that a missed prize and Stalinist violence are the same harm, since she was attacked at the 1951 Pavlovian Sessions and colleagues around her lost their lives; not that every woman here was silenced alike, since Cannon took the Henry Draper Medal in 1931 and funded the award whose first recipient in 1934 was Payne-Gaposchkin — honoured from outside, unpromoted at home, and she is the exception and forty-two years of the rule; not that recognition and justice are the same, since Herschel took the medal in 1828 and stayed her brother’s assistant on the payroll; not that these men stole, since Russell cited Payne and reported “very gratifying agreement” — the mechanism varies every time and the direction does not; not an argument against priority or citation; and not the naturalistic fallacy. Then the turn that earns the collection. The six children Sukhareva wrote down were Autistic, and so were Autistic children in 1895 and 1795 and every year nobody was taking notes. 1925 is not when we started; it is when somebody was standing there with an instrument. A diagnosis is an arrival record, and the criteria say so out loud — the DSM-5 requires symptoms “present in the early developmental period” while conceding they “may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life.” The manual is describing light-travel time. Somebody diagnosed at forty-seven has not been Autistic since they were forty-seven; the paperwork is forty-seven years old and the light is not. You can’t have been, you’d have been picked up is that confusion said out loud, and it made the receiver the origin for girls, for Black and brown children, for anyone whose flavour of it stayed indoors. There is a version of this history in which the first thing anybody read about us was written by a woman who noticed the giftedness in the same paragraph as the difficulty — because she did, and it did not arrive in time to set the tone. The close: everything heavier than hydrogen and helium was cooked inside stars and scattered when they died, and the carbon, oxygen and calcium in you crossed several billion years to arrive with no name attached and no signature required. The calcium works whether or not Payne was believed in 1925. Publishing Sukhareva’s name does not reach her — she died in 1981 — it fixes our instrument, the one we are using on the next person whose account arrives in the wrong language or the wrong decade. Down to is not because of. Eleven spreads, five diagrams. The light was never wrong. The paperwork was late.

Zine No. 63 Even Fallen Light Glows Stimpunks Zines · after Helen Edgar On Neruda’s well, a rewrite made in burnout, six syllables that answered it — and the fact that fallen wood glows in the dark for no reason anyone has been able to establish. Every known bioluminescent fungus is a white-rot decomposer, so the thing that glows is the thing that eats fallen wood. After 160 million years, nobody can say what the glow is for. 12 spreads→ Details Three texts and one fungus. Neruda’s untitled poem in El mar y las campanas (1973) says that if each day falls inside each night there is a well “where clarity is imprisoned,” and instructs you to sit on the rim of the well of darkness and fish for fallen light with patience (William O’Daly’s translation, The Sea and the Bells, Copper Canyon, 1988, pp. 94–95 — read at the printed page, because every online copy is an aggregator). Read the grammar and the poem has quietly handed out two roles: the one who fishes, and the light that fell. Ryan Boren’s rewrite, made in deep Autistic burnout, moves the speaker into the well — the rim is distant, no casting can reach, patience broke — and the discovery inside it is structural rather than emotional: sitting on a rim with patience is work you can do, being the light at the bottom is not work at all, and once you are the light every instruction in the poem is addressed to somebody else. Helen Edgar answered in six syllables: even fallen light glows. What makes the reply hold is what it refuses — it does not say the rim is closer, that patience returns, or that you will be reached. It is a claim about the light, not about the rescue, and it pries apart two things the poem had welded together. Then the fact. Foxfire. Perry, Desjardin & Stevani (J. Fungi 11(1):19, 2024) recognise 132 taxa across five lineages — Mycenaceae 96, Omphalotaceae 18, Physalacriaceae 14, Lucentipes 3, Cyphellopsidaceae 1 — and every one is an agaric saprotrophic white-rot decomposer, or rarely a plant pathogen. There is no glowing fungus that lives some other way, which makes the thing that glows is the thing that eats fallen wood a statement of taxonomy rather than a figure of speech. The glow is built out of the log: the caffeic acid cycle runs caffeic acid to hispidin to 3-hydroxyhispidin, the luciferin, which luciferase oxidises with oxygen to caffeylpyruvate and a photon near 530 nm — and then caffeylpyruvate hydrolase turns the spent molecule back into caffeic acid. The end of the reaction is the beginning of the reaction. And in the Armillaria lineage the part that glows is the mycelium and rhizomorphs, threads inside the wood, while the mushrooms are consistently non-luminescent: the showy reproductive part is the dark one. Emission runs continuously, on a temperature-compensated circadian clock (Oliveira et al., Curr. Biol. 25:964–968, 2015), so nothing about it is conditional on a receiver — it does not brighten for company and does not stop when the forest is empty, which is nearly always. The honest centre is spread nine: nobody knows what it is for. Lit mushroom models draw more beetles, flies, bugs and wasps than unlit ones, which is real evidence for spore dispersal — and it explains a cap, not the mycelium and lower stipe, which make no spores at all. A live rival says the luciferin is an antioxidant and the light is a byproduct of handling reactive oxygen while dismantling lignin. The review states outright that a non-adaptive, accidental origin cannot yet be excluded. Spread ten is the guardrail: bioluminescence arose once, about 160 mya, and has been lost or inactivated in lineage after lineage since — so keeping the glow is not an achievement and losing it is the commonest thing that ever happened to it. A zine that says even fallen light glows is one sentence away from so you had better be glowing, and the phylogeny is what blocks it. The turn: if you are the fallen light, glowing is not a task you are behind on, and the casting is somebody else’s work — which is where solidarity stops being a warm feeling and becomes a division of labour. Helen’s constellation is what sits at the rim. Refusals on the face: not that the log is glad it fell; not that burnout is secretly productive, because decay is not a chrysalis and burnout is damage somebody’s conditions caused; not that you must glow to be worth keeping; not that the glow is a signal so try harder to be seen; not a promise that you will be reached; not nature proving anything about a nervous system; and not the rewrite corrected — both poems are on the page, unedited, in order. The consolation is deliberately thin, because a thicker one would be a lie to somebody whose patience has broken. Twelve spreads, one diagram. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 69 Your Shadow Is the Centre Stimpunks Zines On the bow that no two people can share, the man who proved it in 1267 with an astrolabe and no theory at all, and why being unable to show someone a real thing was never a reason to doubt it. A rainbow is a circle centred on the shadow of your own head, so there are as many bows as there are observers — and Roger Bacon used that un-shareability as his evidence, not his problem. 11 spreads→ Details The oldest correct thing anybody wrote down about a rainbow is not about colour and not about water. It is about where you are standing. Around 1267, in the experimental-science part of the Opus Majus, Roger Bacon measured the height of the sun against the height of a bow with an astrolabe and reported that a rainbow can never stand more than 42 degrees above the horizon — then wrote something far stranger, as a finding: “From these facts we learn by experiment that there are as many bows as there are observers.” He gave the test. Two people look north at the bow; one walks west and the bow goes west with him, the other walks east and his bow goes east. Hence “it is impossible for two observers to see one and the same bow, although an ignorant person does not grasp this fact” — and the reason, which is this zine’s title: “the shadow of each observer divides the arc of the rainbow into two equal parts.” He put the apex of his cone at the eye and its axis on “the nadir of the sun,” the antisolar point, and did all of it with no theory of refraction at all — forty years before anybody described what happens inside a drop, three hundred and seventy before Descartes could calculate it. Roland Stull’s Practical Meteorology says the same things today: bows are “centered on the antisolar point, which is the point corresponding to the shadow of your head or camera,” and “different observers see different rainbows caused by different light rays interacting with different raindrops” — 42.7° red, ~40° violet, n = 1.3315. The spread that earns the piece is the inversion. Bacon did not treat the privacy of the bow as a puzzle to be explained away; he treated it as data, and ran controls in 1267. A lit cloud takes a colour that “appears the same to different observers, nor does it follow the motion of the observer”; a fish seen through water is displaced but does not follow you; the bow follows you at the speed of “a man running or riding as fast as possible.” One odd answer out of three, and from it he concluded the bow must be made of rays that bounce. He landed on reflection alone and was incomplete — the method was right, and his geometry survived into a downloadable textbook. The feature that makes a rainbow impossible to hand to anybody is the feature that told us what a rainbow is. Then: Les Cowley’s “rainbows possess neither distance nor linear dimension” and “cannot be touched, tickled, walked around or driven through” — a direction, not a place. Your pupils are 63 mm apart, each the apex of its own cone gathering its own drops, so you are not looking at one rainbow with two eyes, which closes the standard exit from our own umwelt argument in No. 15: the perceivers are identical and position alone is sufficient. And the conditions — sun behind, rain ahead, unobstructed, sun under 42° or the ring sinks below the horizon. Bacon worked the arithmetic for Paris (41°12′ at equinox noon) and for a latitude near the Tropic of Cancer, where “no rainbow can be formed at any noon of the entire year.” Rain falling, sun blazing, eyes perfect, no bow: nothing wrong with the observer, and the arrangement is adjustable. The turn: in 759 years nobody has concluded that rainbows are unreal because they cannot be shown to a second person. Nobody asks for corroboration. That courtesy is not extended evenly, and if it were real you could show me has a textbook counterexample in the sky twice a month. Six refusals, the first being the one that matters — not that everybody sees it differently so who’s to say: different bow, same physics, 42.7° for everyone, always. Also not a claim on the Pride rainbow, which already means something specific in our house. Two claims are marked on the page as ours rather than anybody’s measurement. Eleven spreads, six figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 70 Both Arcs, One Drop Stimpunks Zines On the raindrop that makes both bows at once, the lab that tried to erase both of you, and why entwined turns out to be a claim about the source rather than a feeling about the self. A single drop makes both arcs of a double rainbow simultaneously, from one beam — so neither is the second one. And the suppression of queer and Autistic children came out of one lab, with one name on both papers. 12 spreads→ Details A double rainbow is not two rainbows. Roland Stull’s Practical Meteorology: “a single raindrop produces both: entering rays undergo either one internal reflection (primary) or two internal reflections (secondary) before exiting.” One drop, one beam, both arcs, at the same instant — which means the outer bow is never absent, only sometimes outshone. The extra bounce reverses the colours, so red sits outermost on the inner bow and innermost on the outer one and the two reds face each other across Alexander’s dark band (Alexander of Aphrodisias, c. 200 CE) — a band that is not a wall between them but the region neither arc reaches, the shadow left where the light piled up elsewhere. The zine states the awkward number rather than hiding it: the secondary is 43% as bright, because its light must survive two internal reflections instead of one. Dimmer is a fact about path length, not about rank. So spread five refuses the obvious move and will not hand you one arc for being queer and one for being neurodivergent — assign the arcs and one of them is the 43% one, and the shape does the ranking however carefully you write around it. The drop never divided them. Primary and secondary are our words, for our convenience; the drop has never heard them. Then the turn, where entwined stops being a warm word and becomes a citation. In 1974 the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis published Rekers & Lovaas, “Behavioral Treatment of Deviant Sex-Role Behaviors in a Male Child” (7(2), 173–190), whose abstract states its own aim as “the primary prevention of adult transsexualism or similar adult sex-role deviation.” Thirteen years later the same O. Ivar Lovaas, at the same university, published the 1987 autism paper. One name, on both. Our own Eight Tenths of a Second (No. 38) follows the behaviourism chain to a spread called “A room with a child in it” and stops at that door; this zine opens it and reports that there was more than one kind of child at the table. The 1974 paper was read at the paper — PMC holds it as scanned images, so the PDF was obtained and read, which is how the circulating pseudonym “Craig” turns out to be “Kraig”. He was four years and eleven months old. His mother was “trained to be his therapist.” Red and blue poker chips: blue toward a candy bar, red for response cost, timeout, “or (c) physical punishment by spanking from the father.” And the sequencing detail that undoes you — it was judged “clinically safer” to run the chips on ordinary household behaviour first, so the same red chip that had meant tracking dirt on carpet was then extended to playing with girls, playing with dolls, and feminine gestures. His name was Kirk Andrew Murphy; he died by suicide in 2003, reported here as the behaviour-analytic literature reports it, without a causal claim attached, because his family’s grief is not a rhetorical device. JABA issued a Statement of Concern in 2020 and did not retract, reasoning that “the available evidence does not make it clear that the original study was unethical by the standards of that day”; Austin H. Johnson answered in 2022 that it should be retracted. Fifty-two years, and it stands. Neuroqueer credited properly — Nick Walker, independently Athena Lynn Michaels-Dillon, with Remi Yergeau’s neurological queerness — and Gwen Nelson, who created Autistic Pride Day, is a trans woman. Seven refusals, including that queer and Autistic experience are not the same experience, that today’s ABA is not 1974, and that the claim is lineage. Twelve spreads. A rhyme, not a proof — the history is the argument; the rainbow is only how we noticed what shape it was.

Zine No. 71 Nothing Is Pushing Stimpunks Zines On escape velocity as a coasting number, the places inside a well that cost nothing to sit in, and a telescope built so that it cannot brake. Escape velocity is defined for a trajectory with no engine running — and it falls as you rise. Two of the five Lagrange points cost nothing at all to occupy, and which two depends on the system, never on the occupant. 12 spreads→ Details Escape velocity is a coasting number, and almost every use of it drops the condition that makes it true. The 11.186 km/s quoted for Earth is vesc = √(2GM/r), and it is defined for a ballistic trajectory — the speed you need if nothing is pushing you afterwards. Two things follow that the motivational reading gets backwards. First, the figure is local: it falls as the square root of one over distance, so it is 7.91 km/s at two Earth radii and 5.59 at four. The requirement is not a property of what you are leaving; it is a property of where you are asking from. Second, it says nothing whatever about anything under thrust, which is not a loophole but the scope of the definition. Dawn is the demonstration. On 5 September 2012 it left Vesta not by jumping from the floor but by climbing on ion thrust until the bar had come down to meet it — JPL’s own words, “spiral away as gently as it arrived”; Marc Rayman’s, “Thrust is engaged, and we are now climbing away from Vesta atop a blue-green pillar of xenon ions.” The zine is careful to say on the spread, not only in the colophon, that Dawn did eventually cross the local threshold; the claim is that it never had to make the jump from the bottom. Then the half the piece was actually built for. A gravity well contains places that cost nothing to occupy. Of the five Lagrange points, L1, L2 and L3 are saddle points and unstable; L4 and L5 are genuinely stable — not balancing, not holding on — whenever the mass ratio clears a threshold. That threshold is μG = (1 − √(23/27))/2 = 0.0385208965…, the smaller root of 27μ(1−μ) = 1, and here the zine performs a precedence correction: it is usually called Routh’s value after his 1875 paper, and Bruno Sicardy (CMDA 107, 2010) says it “should actually be called Gascheau’s value in view of the precedence of his work” — Gabriel Gascheau, professor at Toulouse, published in Paris in 1843, thirty-plus years earlier. A piece arguing that the environment decides the outcome had no business misattributing the theorem that proves it. And the theorem is the argument: the same rock, unchanged in every respect, stays at Jupiter’s L4 for the age of the solar system and wanders off from the L4 of a pair whose masses are too even. Nothing about the rock did it. About 105 Jupiter Trojans larger than a kilometre are sitting there now (Bottke, Marschall, Nesvorný & Vokrouhlický, 2023) — and, kept deliberately, they were captured during the giant planets’ migration, so the stable place was not where they started and they did not choose it. Then the case that closes the loophole: even the unstable places are cheap. Petersen (AAS 19-806, 2019): “The dynamical region about the SEMB L2 point is inherently unstable” — and JWST holds it, per Rigby et al. (2023), on burns “scheduled every three weeks…with typical durations of tens of seconds,” of which “three…were skipped because the computed correction was negligibly small.” The maintenance schedule for an unstable position includes doing nothing. The final spread is the one the piece exists for: thermal limits forbid sunward-facing thrusters, so “no direct observatory-to-Sun vector maneuver directions are allowed” — Webb cannot brake, drifting past L2 would end the mission, and so every burn is deliberately thrown short. Nobody calls that the telescope’s failing; the whole trajectory was designed around it, at a cost the mission simply paid. Against all of this sits Helen Edgar’s Gravity Well, constellation fourteen of My Monotropic Galaxy, whose naming and frame are hers and whose violet is this zine’s accent — and Buckle, Leadbitter, Poliakoff & Gowen (2021), 32 Autistic adults, whose finding reframes the whole physics: starting, stopping and switching are one tendency, and what helps is another person — “a stuck buddy that I text” — where alarms and lists rarely substitute. The paper’s title is a participant’s phrase, “No Way Out Except From External Intervention,” which is not a confession but a correct statement about where energy enters a system. Seven refusals, including that the burst is not available on request (participants describe “a literal paralysis”), that you’re not stuck, you’re just orbiting is not an accommodation, and that gravity is not the villain — the well is also why there is an atmosphere. One widely-quoted number was hunted, not sourced primarily, and deliberately left out. Twelve spreads, seven figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 73 Measured Against a Tree Stimpunks Zines On six ways a moss fails as a plant, and the finding that the list is backwards — because holding your own water is the newer trick, and the tree is the one that lost the older one. Desiccation tolerance is ancestral. The vascular plants gave it up to get tall and kept it only in their seeds, and some went back for it. The deficit list was accurate line by line, and measuring the wrong thing. 12 spreads→ Details Take a tree as the definition of a plant and a moss fails at six points. No roots — rhizoids anchor and barely absorb. No xylem or phloem. No way to lift water, so no height. No control of its own moisture, because its tissue simply equilibrates with the air. And no photosynthesis at all while dry. Every line is true, and the zine keeps the whole list intact to the last spread. Botany has proper names for the split: a moss is poikilohydric, its hydration tracking the surrounding humidity, where a vascular plant is homoiohydric and holds an interior against the outside — at the price of roots, xylem, a waxy cuticle and thousands of controllable stomata, with a failure mode that is not a pause but death. Drying is a state a tree cannot occupy. Then the finding that inverts the list. Proctor, Oliver, Wood, Alpert, Stark, Cleavitt & Mishler, reviewing desiccation tolerance in bryophytes in The Bryologist 110(4), 2007, record it as a primitive character of land plants, lost in the course of evolution of the homoiohydric vascular-plant shoot system, but retained in spores, pollen and seeds, and re-evolved in the vegetative tissues of vascular resurrection plants. The moss did not fail to acquire the tree’s solution; the tree discarded the moss’s — kept it for the one job where nothing else would do, so every seed in a packet is doing what a moss does, and some lineages later evolved their way back to it. What drying actually is gets stated without comfort. The cytoplasm enters a glassy state in which molecular mobility is severely reduced; a 2013 Journal of Experimental Botany paper on Syntrichia ruralis is titled for the result, “Evidence for the absence of enzymatic reactions in the glassy state.” It is not idling. It has stopped, and stopping is what conserves it — survival bought with the whole of the time. Then water arrives and respiration reactivates almost instantly, photosynthesis within minutes, net rates substantially normal within thirty to sixty. Nothing had to be rebuilt because nothing was dismantled. Syntrichia recovers after decades dry; Roads, Longton & Convey (Current Biology, 2014) grew new shoots from Chorisodontium aciphyllum frozen at least 1,530 years in Antarctic permafrost — and the zine keeps the two apart on the spread rather than blurring them, because that case is cryptobiosis under freezing, not desiccation. The best spread is the boundary layer, and it is Robin Wall Kimmerer’s, read at Gathering Moss (Oregon State University Press, 2003, pp. 14–19). Friction stills the air against every surface, and the layer keeps what it holds — heat, water vapour, and over a rotting log up to ten times ambient carbon dioxide. Being small is the entry requirement, not a shortfall. But the layer is not merely found: friction makes it, so the long narrow upright leaves, the dense hairs and reflective tips and minuscule spines all deepen it. The greater the resistance, the deeper the boundary layer — and the larger the boundary layer, the larger the moss can be. A loop, not a niche: the moss builds the habitat that then permits it to be bigger, and mosses accordingly run from millimetre crusts to ten-centimetre wefts, a range Kimmerer likens to a blueberry bush and a redwood, tracking the layer rather than the moss. And layers nest — a rock’s sits under the forest’s umbrella, so the tree that wins every contest for light is also the reason a moss can be large. That argues against this zine’s own title, which is why it is on the spread and in the closing line. One more inversion: the green cushion is the gametophyte, the generation vascular plants reduced to a few cells in a pollen grain, and the little stalk above it is a periscope whose length correlates with the layer’s depth — the dependent generation is the one built to leave. Closing on Sphagnum: peatlands, ~3% of land, holding roughly twice the carbon of all the world’s forest biomass — the careful wording, kept because the loose one travels further. Six refusals, including that moss is not secretly tougher, that small is beautiful is not on offer, that resilience is never a demand, and that a mechanism recovering in an hour is not a promise made to anyone about burnout. Twelve spreads, three figures. Developed after Helen Edgar’s Mossy Minds & Monotropism. A rhyme, not a proof — the list was true; the ruler was a tree.
The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed

Zine No. 75 The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed Stimpunks Zines on the most expensive smell on earth, and the reason it is not in the mushroom Two people differ functionally at over 30% of their odorant receptor alleles. That is measured, not asserted — and it means “you’re smelling it wrong” is not a sentence that means anything. 12 spreads→ Details Matsutake is among the most expensive foods on earth and the entire price is for a smell — principally 1-octen-3-ol and methyl cinnamate, both of which decline as the fruiting body ages, which is why the grading and the airfreight and the button-stage picking all exist. Then the same molecules, elsewhere: deer choose it over other mushrooms, bears dig ditches for it, and Oregon pickers told Anna Tsing of elk with bloody muzzles from driving their faces into pumice soil to reach it — while in the same ground “slugs, other fungi, and many kinds of soil bacteria are repulsed by the smell, moving out of its range.” One set of compounds; an elk digs until it bleeds and a bacterium leaves. Nothing about the molecules changed between those two sentences. So the fact this zine follows is ordinary sensory biology: a smell is not a property of an object but a binding event between a molecule and a receptor, and if the shape does not fit, nothing happens at all — not a faint smell, nothing. Humans carry about 400 intact odorant receptors, and somebody counted how much they vary. Mainland et al. (Nature Neuroscience, 2014): “63% of the odorant receptors we examined had polymorphisms that altered in vitro function… on average, two individuals have functional differences at over 30% of their odorant receptor alleles” — with OR10G4 genotype explaining over 15% of perceived intensity and over 10% of perceived valence for guaiacol, and explicitly not explaining it for weaker agonists, a limit the zine prints rather than rounds off. The worked case runs from a letter of DNA to a word said out loud: Keller et al. (Nature, 2007) found androstenone “variously perceived by different individuals as offensive (‘sweaty, urinous’), pleasant (‘sweet, floral’) or odourless” — and traced it to two amino acid substitutions in one receptor, OR7D4. Foul, lovely, or absent; three people, one bottle, and nobody misperceiving. Which returns to Tsing’s own account of the autumn aroma: “It’s disturbing. Many people never learn to love it… Some people liken it to rotting things and some to clear beauty.” Not a failure of taste — exactly what a complex volatile predicts against arrays differing at a third of their alleles. And the title’s other half sits underneath it: seventy years have not produced a cultivated matsutake either, because it is a fungus and a pine root exchanging. You cannot farm the first and you cannot standardise the second; it is the same refusal, twice. The turn refuses “everyone has their own truth” hardest — the variation is public, sequenceable and testable, which is the opposite of soft. What it removes is only an excuse: there was no correct experience you were failing to have. Normal is a statistic about a population, not a fact about a person. Held honestly on its own face: no study links matsutake aroma to receptor genotype, and joining them is the zine’s move rather than a demonstrated result.

Zine No. 76 Forty Minutes to See Stimpunks Zines On the second visual system, the forty minutes it takes to arrive, the one bright light that ends it — and the faint thing that only appears when you stop looking straight at it. Dark adaptation is a handover, not a dial. The system everyone calls the worse one runs at the floor physics allows — one quantum per rod — and it is only available off-axis, after forty uninterrupted minutes nobody can feel passing. 12 spreads→ Details Your eyes do not gradually get used to the dark. Two systems hand over, and the handover leaves a kink in the curve. Cone thresholds fall fast and plateau in five to ten minutes; then the trace breaks downward and keeps falling — the rod–cone break — reaching a second, far lower plateau at forty to fifty minutes and an absolute threshold of order 10−5 cd/m². The steep satisfying part is over in ten minutes; the part that delivers the sensitivity takes four times as long and produces no sensation of progress at all, so anyone judging by feel concludes they are finished at about the ten-minute mark. What the second system is for comes from Hecht, Shlaer & Pirenne, “Energy, Quanta, and Vision,” Journal of General Physiology 25, 1942, 819–840 — read at the paper. Thousandth-of-a-second flashes at 510 nm: the minimum visible energy is 2.1–5.7 × 10−10 ergs at the cornea, “between 54 and 148 quanta of blue-green light.” Subtract the eye — ~4% reflected, “almost precisely 50 per cent absorbed by the lens and other ocular media,” “at least 80 per cent passes through the retina without being absorbed” — and 5 to 14 quanta remain, across a field holding “about 500 rods.” And here the zine corrects the most-repeated result in vision science. It circulates as the human eye can detect a single photon. The paper says something narrower and better: “in order for us to see, it is necessary for only 1 quantum of light to be absorbed by each of 5 to 14 retinal rods.” One quantum per rod; five to fourteen rods for a person. The popular version promotes a precise claim about a cell into a boast about an organ. The costs are stated rather than skipped: one pigment means colour is not a defined quantity, not that rods are bad at it; heavy pooling buys the sensitivity and is paid for in acuity; and forty minutes is forty minutes. A tuning is not a ranking. Then the geometry. The fovea — the patch you point at whatever you attend to — is rod-free, and rod density peaks around 20° out, so a faint enough star goes out when you look straight at it. Astronomers train averted vision deliberately. And it is not an amateur’s trick: it is how the 1942 number was obtained. The methods say “we chose a retinal area situated 20° temporally on the horizontal axis” — there was no alternative, because there are no rods at the centre to catch the quanta. The most precise measurement ever made of the limits of human sight was taken by looking away from the thing being measured. The closing move is the asymmetry: forty minutes to build, an instant to destroy, and the person holding the torch spends nothing while the person who waited pays in full — but rods barely respond to long wavelengths, so red light lets you see and keeps the forty minutes. Observatories, bridges, submarines and darkrooms are lit in red. Nobody arrived at that by asking observers to adapt faster. Assemble the description — needs forty uninterrupted minutes, gives no signal while working, resets to zero at no cost to the interrupter, no colour, poor detail, only works off-axis — and it reads exactly like a deficit list, and nobody has ever treated it as one, because everybody has it. Six refusals, the first being that retinal anatomy licenses nothing whatever about how a person should be looked at. Twelve spreads, four figures. Developed after the Nyctous card in Under the Word. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 77 Nothing Melts Stimpunks Zines On how snow grains bond below the melting point without ever becoming liquid, why the joint grows because it is the joint — and why bonding to each other does not fix what you are all standing on. Sintering joins separate things into a structure that carries weight, and none of them stops being separate. The reading is Leanne Betasamosake Simpson’s; only the physics and the avalanche are ours. 12 spreads→ Details Walk on hour-old snow and you go through it; walk on the same snow two days later and it carries you. Nothing was added and nobody packed it. The name for what happened is sintering, and the whole zine turns on what it is not: the obvious way to make a heap of separate things into one thing is to melt them, and that is not what occurs. Grains bond below the melting point, never liquefy, and stay individual crystals with their own boundaries — you can section a snowpack and count them. Held honestly on the spread, because it partly undercuts the title: ice surfaces carry a quasi-liquid premelted layer below the bulk melting point which can assist bonding without bulk melting, and its onset, thickness and relation to liquid water have been argued over for a century. Nothing melts in bulk and no crystal loses its identity; the surface where the joining happens is not a simple solid either. Why the bond forms where it does is the best fact here. Ice sublimes constantly, and the rate depends on the shape of the surface: a convex grain surface gives up more vapour, a concave hollow gives up less. So vapour leaves the rounded outsides and condenses in the crevice between two grains, simply because that is where the vapour pressure is lowest. The neck fills in because it is a neck — and the tighter the curve, the stronger the pull, so the earliest and most awkward stage of a bond is the one the physics favours most. Nothing arrives from outside: the bridge is made of material that left the grains themselves, so the joint is paid for out of the substance of the things being joined. It happens only at contact — proximity is not contact, and the physics has no mechanism for reaching across a gap — and it is strongly temperature-dependent, fast near zero and nearly stalled in deep cold, which makes the capacity to bond a property of grains-in-conditions rather than of grains. What it buys is not hardness but load-sharing: each grain is as fragile as ever, and no grain has to bear the whole thing alone. Then the cost, which is ours and not our sources’. Sintering is also how a cohesive slab is made, and a cohesive slab over a weak layer is the slab-avalanche condition — the same connectedness that carries weight is what lets a fracture cross the whole of it at once. And the failure is not in the necks: it is in the weak layer underneath, which the bonding above cannot reach or repair. Bonding to each other does not fix what you are all standing on. The reading is Leanne Betasamosake Simpson’s, in Theory of Water: Nishnaabe Maps to the Times Ahead, ch. 4, read at the book: “Sintering is a joining. It is a communal transformation that creates a fabric of former snowflakes bonded to each other”; “It weaves itself into its environment, and it does so in a way that doesn’t destroy its neighbours”; “sintering is how Michi Saagiig Nishnaabeg make worlds.” She arrived at it grooming a ski trail — “I wasn’t expecting the snow to teach me how to live in the world” — and she names the cost more honestly than we did: “Sintering is slow deformation,” and “Sintering in the forest is easy for me; sintering with people I’m currently sharing the planet with, much more difficult.” The application to neurodivergent community is Helen Edgar’s. The order on spread ten — her framework, Helen’s application, our physics — is the order the knowledge actually travelled. Six refusals, including that this is not a metaphor extracted from someone’s cosmology, that the physics does not validate the reading, and that community does not fix conditions. Twelve spreads, four figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 78 You Cannot Correct the Sky Stimpunks Zines On why stars twinkle and planets do not, on knowing exactly where a problem lives — and on the fact that correct is not the same as affordable. The flicker belongs to the air, not to the star. Once you know that you cannot honestly blame the star — and you still cannot afford the mirror, which covers a patch, runs on a subscription, and stops when the money does. 12 spreads→ Details A star that appears to be flickering wildly is not flickering. Its light left years ago, crossed the whole distance without incident, and reached the top of the atmosphere as a flat, orderly wavefront. Everything that happened to it happened in the last few microseconds, crossing air made of shifting cells at slightly different temperatures and densities, each refracting the wavefront a little. What lands is corrugated, and the pattern slides across the ground as the cells drift — so somebody standing a few metres away is receiving your missing photons at that instant. The control experiment is free every clear night: through the same air, at the same altitude, planets barely twinkle, because a star is effectively a point and a planet presents a resolved disc whose parts sample different cells at once, so the fluctuations cancel. The standard phrasing is exact — their angular diameters are so large as to quench the scintillations. Quench, not resist: nothing about a planet is tougher, it is simply wide enough that no single cell can speak for the whole of it. If the flicker is caused entirely by the medium, then the flicker is a measurement of the medium, and observatories use it as one — and nobody reads that report as a complaint about the star. Then the hinge the zine exists for. Every remedy is applied to the conditions: wait until the light is higher, spend billions to get above the air, or cancel the distortion with adaptive optics — which needs a natural or laser guide star, is valid over a small patch, and blurs again within milliseconds of the loop opening. It was never a fix. It is a subscription. You can correct a patch of sky. You cannot correct the sky. And somebody already made this argument about people. The social model of disability performs exactly the relocation on spread two: a person is disabled by a world built to a narrow specification rather than by their body. That move was necessary, and it is also the free part — it costs nothing, takes an afternoon, and has never by itself produced a single ramp. Everything after it is the deformable mirror and has the mirror’s properties: expensive, limited in coverage, requiring somebody to keep it running, and failing at once when the funding stops. So the position is uncomfortable in both directions. The people who locate the problem in the person are wrong, and saying so has never built anything. What it does settle is whose problem it is, which is the argument that has to be won before anyone is asked to pay. Six refusals, including that this is not a complaint about the social model but about treating the relocation as though it were the accommodation — a thing done most often by whoever would have to fund it. Twelve spreads, four figures, and a cover that has been running the argument on every page of this site for years: its twinkling points use the shared twinkle-anim keyframe behind the sitewide starfield, and reduced motion leaves them steady. Published hours earlier as The Star Is Not Flickering, framed around glimmers, and repointed the same day when the tie proved thin — the colophon carries that account rather than deleting it. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 82 The Play You Keep Stimpunks Zines On forty-five bumble bees, nine hundred and ten rolls of a wooden ball, and the definition science had to write down before it could see doing nothing at all. The sugar water was already within reach and the bees rolled the balls anyway. Play has five formal criteria, and the first one is that it must accomplish nothing — so the useless thing got studied seriously, on a standard that never once asked it to pay. 12 spreads→ Details Forty-five bumble bees produced 910 ball-rolling actions in a laboratory where a clear, unobstructed lane led to sucrose they could reach without touching anything. Nothing was hidden under the balls; no bee was ever rewarded for moving one. Galpayage Dona and colleagues tested the behaviour against Gordon Burghardt’s five criteria for animal play and it met all five — and foraging, clutter clearing and mating were excluded by the design of the apparatus and by watching what the bees did. The first criterion is the whole argument: to count as play, a behaviour must produce no immediate adaptive outcome. Uselessness is not the absence of a category here; it is the entry condition, written down, and checkable. A second experiment tested whether the activity was rewarding in itself. Bees learned which of two differently coloured chambers held movable balls; when both chambers were emptied they still chose that colour. They came back for the room, not the toy. Younger bees rolled most, particularly three to seven days from eclosion — independent of whether they had met balls before — which is also the window in which bumble bee mushroom bodies are most plastic, though the authors decline to call the overlap causal and this zine prints that hedge. And the paper’s explanation of its own sex difference is the sentence the zine is built on: males rolled individual balls longer because they had more “free time” in laboratory conditions, while females had constant access to pollen and a colony objective. Play expanded into the hours function had not claimed — a fact about environments, not about appetites. Held honestly, at length: the authors cannot exclude that the rolling followed understimulation in captivity, play-like actions have not been shown in the wild, the motivation is unknown, and their conclusion says resembling object play and a form of sentience. All of it stays on the page. Six refusals, including that prescribed play stops meeting the first criterion, that this is not stimming reframed, that joy is not the receipt for hardship, and that an insect settles nothing about a human life. Twelve spreads, two figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 83 The Width of Itself Stimpunks Zines On the root that opens a channel, the lawn that stays compacted, and why we keep asking survivors to do systems change. A dandelion in soil packed to 1.8 grams per cubic centimetre loosened the ground for seventy micrometres, halved that by a hundred and forty, and changed nothing at the scale of the pot. It is a triumph. It is not a repair, and the difference is the whole argument. 13 spreads→ Details Burr-Hersey, Ritz, Bengough and Mooney built the hostile condition on purpose — sandy loam compacted to 1.8 g cm⁻³ with a penetration resistance of 1.55 MPa, roughly fifteen atmospheres — then grew three wild dicots in it for 28 days and imaged the soil by X-ray computed tomography, so the pore structure could be measured without taking it apart. All three species are plants a lawn is designed to exclude; the experiment is a study of weeds without calling itself one. For the dandelion the porosity was 6.9 per cent in the mantle 0–70 µm from the root surface and 3.9 per cent at 70–140 µm, and the paper states plainly that changes were not observed at the whole-column scale. Seventy micrometres is about the width of a human hair. Which makes the sentence everyone repeats — that dandelions break up compacted soil — the smoothed retelling of a result whose conditions were the finding. Not a lie; a claim that kept the verb and dropped every limit attached to it. Then a second complication the metaphor does not survive intact: most dandelions are clones. The genus reproduces largely by apomixis, setting viable seed without fertilisation, and apomicts are triploid or tetraploid while the sexual minority are diploid. Majeský, Vašut, Kitner and Trávníček found apomictic accessions genetically highly homogeneous, with the genus’s real variety most likely of sexual origin — inherited from its lineage’s past rather than being made now. So the tidy reading, grass monoculture against dandelion biodiversity, has a clone-field on both sides. Nick Covington’s line survives all of it and is sharpened by it: in an environment of total control, every dandelion is a triumph. Triumph is the right word. Solution is not — and if even the weed is not the answer to the lawn, the answer was never among the things growing in it. It has to be the ground. The turn is ours: the Autistic kid who found one corridor, the Disabled worker who found the one manager who said yes. A channel opened by force, the width of one person, in ground that stayed exactly as hard — and then read back by the institution as evidence that the column was fine. The closing spread turns on a second dandelion. In Boyce and Ellis’s 2005 borrowing from Swedish the dandelion child is the low-sensitivity one who does tolerably anywhere, and the orchid is exquisitely sensitive to context; Lionetti, Aron, Aron and colleagues added the tulip in the middle across 906 adults — 29 per cent, 40 per cent, 31 per cent. And the orchid half is not fragility: in good conditions orchids do better than dandelions, so every orchid failing in a compacted room is also a result nobody got to see. Set the two dandelions side by side and both say the same thing about the ground — hard ground does not produce variety, it selects for whoever needed least from it, and the survivors get counted as the normal range. Behaviourism is the machinery that presses down, and its offer is that the ground can stay exactly as hard if the child is trained to tolerate it. Unmaking is mostly subtraction; remaking is Cavendish Space, built for caves, campfires and watering holes alike. Six refusals, including resilience as a substitute for accommodation, and the flat statement that surviving is not nothing. Thirteen spreads, two figures. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 86 Older Than Either of Us Stimpunks Zines On the right angles in a pigeon’s forebrain, three papers that disagree about where they came from, and what belonging looks like under either answer. A bird’s forebrain has no layers, and it has the wiring motif layers exist to produce. Whether birds inherited that circuit or built it separately is an open argument between three papers — and the ranking has nothing to stand on either way. 15 spreads→ Details Stacho and colleagues read fibre orientation directly, by three-dimensional polarised light imaging, through the forebrain of a pigeon and a barn owl — and found radially and tangentially organised fibres crossing at right angles along the entire extent of the Wulst and the sensory dorsal ventricular ridge. Lamina-like and column-like, in a brain that builds neither. The motif was iterative, recurring across somatosensory, visual and auditory zones, across two regions and across two species — which is what makes it a finding rather than a slice. The paper also prints its own boundary: the non-sensory dorsal ventricular ridge showed a mosaic-like arrangement instead. Then the obvious explanation fails on its own numbers. A kea carries about 1.28 billion pallial neurons and a raven 1.2 billion against a chimpanzee’s 7.4 billion, and all three perform comparably. What makes the arithmetic work is provisioning — roughly 19 per cent of a primate’s neurons are pallial against 62 in parrots and 78 in songbirds — and cost, since avian neurons run on about a third of the glucose mammalian neurons use. The centre of the zine is a live disagreement. Stacho and colleagues suggest an ancient microcircuit already present in the last common stem amniote, conserved and partly modified. Güntürkün, Pusch and Rose argue the four features required for complex cognition convergently evolved, independently. Zaremba and colleagues, sequencing the chicken pallium across eight stages in the egg, find conserved inhibitory types alongside transcriptomic convergence. Three papers, three answers — and “convergent evolution” is the one that travels, because two independent inventions of a mind is a headline and an open question is a research programme. The belonging claim survives either answer, which is how you can tell it was never resting on the ranking. Fifteen spreads, two figures, six refusals. Companion catalogue: Field Guide No. 23.

Zine No. 11 · Guest Why Difference Comes First Guest zine · Helen Edgar I've been thinking about the connections in-between — physics, philosophy, my own life as an Autistic person. This is me following that thread. A guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), in her own voice — one thread followed down three scales to the same shape: difference comes first. 10 spreads · guest→ Details A guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), in her own voice. One thread followed down three scales — relational quantum mechanics, the cosmic microwave background, and Deleuze — to the same shape: difference comes first, and the baseline is the thing that got built. It ends where the flat line, and even the spiky profile, give way to a constellation of intensities: a self that is dynamic, relational, and never finished. Ten spreads.

Zine No. 22 No One Is the Leader Stimpunks Zines on murmurations, emergence, and the whole that exceeds its parts — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self Each starling tracks only its six or seven nearest neighbours, and the whole emerges from that. After Ballerini & the STARFLAG project. 8 spreads→ Details Emergence and the murmuration — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self. Hundreds of thousands of starlings make vast rolling shapes with no leader and no plan: each bird tracks only its six or seven nearest neighbours (Ballerini & the STARFLAG project), and the whole emerges from that one local rule. Philip Anderson's “More Is Different” (1972) is the spine — the founding statement of anti-reductionism: at each level of scale new laws appear that the parts don't contain, so knowing the parts never rebuilds the whole. The early universe did the same, self-organising faint density ripples into the cosmic web with no architect. Two payoffs land it home: the whole person is realer than any diagnostic checklist of parts (you are not a list of deficits — you are the murmuration), and our best neurodivergent collectives — NeurodiVentures — are leaderless murmurations, not org charts (competency networks and catalysts rather than leaders; decisions where the knowledge lives). A “the whole exceeds the parts” zine. Held with care: leaderless is not structureless. Eight spreads, flock-and-web diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 26 A Mycelium and a Rhizome Stimpunks Zines how neurodivergent knowledge grows: no trunk, no center, many doors A tree has one trunk and a chain of command; you climb it or you're lost. A rhizome has no root to ask permission of, so you can enter anywhere. 8 spreads→ Details How neurodivergent knowledge and community grow, read through star stuff — no trunk, no center, many doors. A tree has one trunk and a chain of command; you climb it or you're lost. A rhizome (Deleuze & Guattari) has no root to ask permission of, so you can enter anywhere — Spiky Profiles → Monotropism → Deep Attention, or in from burnout, or a word that finally fit. No prerequisite, no gatekeeper. And a mycelium is the life in that shape: fungal threads carry nutrients and signals between trees that never touch (the “wood wide web,” Simard), thickening the paths that help and letting the rest fade; a brainless slime mold rebuilds the Tokyo rail network (Tero et al.). Zoom all the way out and the shape returns — the cosmic web of dark-matter filaments, the universe's largest structure, looks like a mycelium, like a neuron: not a pyramid, a web. We're already building it. Gray-Hammond and Munday name it neuro-anarchy; the Autistic Rhizome is “a network with no single point of origin,” members as equals held by a do-no-harm ethic, resilient because nothing depends on a center (with Helen Edgar's watering holes). Where the map meets soil is Cavendish Space. Decentralization isn't disorder — it's the oldest structure there is. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 28 · Guest Wyrd & Weird Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar on the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it Old English wyrd comes from weorþan, “to become,” and is twined with the root of “worth.” A guest zine by Helen Edgar. 9 spreads→ Details On the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it — a guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), rehoused in the Star Stuff style. Long before “weird” meant strange, wyrd meant becoming: Old English wyrd comes from weorþan, “to become,” and is twined with the root of “worth.” Fate was never drawn as a straight line from birth to death but as cloth — the Norns' weaving at the well beneath Yggdrasill, the “web of man” — many threads crossing, none load-bearing alone. The Weird Sisters carried the word down through Holinshed to Shakespeare's Macbeth; over centuries “weird” drifted into an insult, and Autistic and disabled communities have run that drift backward, taking it up again as a name, not a verdict — which is etymologically honest, not just cheek. Held with care: wyrd is not a script, not doom, not a synonym for wrong, not something done to you alone. Under the root, weorþan meant “to become,” never “to be”: nobody is finished, and becoming was never the flaw — it was the design. You were never written; you are still being woven. Nine spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, a “threads already running” map of its kin in the collection, and Helen's own sources & notes.

Zine No. 29 · Guest Only in Relation Stimpunks Zines · after Helen Edgar relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics a particle has no standalone properties. Developed after Helen Edgar's essay “We Are Made of Relations.” 9 spreads→ Details Relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic — a guest zine developed after Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) from her essay “We Are Made of Relations.” In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics a particle has no standalone properties; what it is becomes definite only in relation to another system (Rovelli, 1996). The count gives it away: two distinct coins make four outcomes, but two identical bosons make only three — what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle but the symmetry, the relation (Webster, 2026). Karen Barad calls the relation-before-parts intra-action; the human version, intradependence — made of each other, deeper than interdependence — Helen draws from Barad too. Read through Deleuze, “objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation”: difference first, then relation, and the tidy standalone object is the thing that got built.
