The payoff lands on our own work — the double empathy problem (Milton, 2012) lives in the relation, not one mind, and Helen widens it into DEEP; and in the ARLES ladder Relational sits near the base with Regulation inside it, because regulation is relational, so you change the field, not the person. Held with care: not quantum mysticism, not “everything is connected” as a vibe, not dissolution into sameness — the spiky profile survives the merge. A rhyme, not a proof. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 30 · Guest Always Migrating Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar migration, monotropism, and the galaxy you're already made of A guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), written after Brigit Anna McNeill's The Living Page workshop and rehoused here in the Star Stuff style. 11 spreads · guest→ Details Migration, monotropism, and the galaxy you're already made of — a guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), written after Brigit Anna McNeill's The Living Page migration workshop and rehoused here in the Star Stuff style. Every migrating body is made of matter that already migrated once, so migration was never a metaphor borrowed from animals: it's one of the oldest facts about star stuff. A bird crosses an ocean on a compass sense we still can't fully explain — light striking cryptochrome in the eye makes a pair of electrons whose spins stay linked, and that linked pair is thought to be part of how it reads the Earth's faint field (Hore & Mouritsen; Mouritsen). Entanglement's lesson: once two things have been in relation, they stay in relation — separateness was always the less accurate story, which is Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics in a wingbeat. Zoom out and the pattern holds: the Sagittarius dwarf is still arriving in our halo, and the Milky Way–Andromeda collision everyone called settled is now closer to a coin-flip (Sawala et al., 2025) — a tug, not a destination. Then the turn inward: the bodily restlessness that builds before anything is decided is monotropism's gravity, attention gathered into a few bright points rather than spread as an even glow — and masking teaches us to quieten it until we lose our own north. Neuroqueering is the refusal; Pernille Fraser's “Can we trust the space you offer?” asks it from the other side. Widened by ethodiversity and the double empathy problem, and by Barad's intra-action — the liminal crossing isn't empty transit, it's where the shaping happens. Closes past the spiky profile: not a chart, a constellation of intensities. Eleven spreads, eight diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a threads-already-running map of its kin.

Zine No. 68 · Guest Proportioned to the Groove Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar with Ryan Boren four lines of Dickinson, and why a narrow channel is a fit rather than a shortage Helen Edgar sets Emily Dickinson's J1765 against monotropism and the refrain — and it is the first zine here built to scroll rather than to page. 11 spreads · scrolls→ Details “It is enough, the freight should be / Proportioned to the groove.” A groove in Dickinson's sense is the channel a load runs along, and the four lines say enough is a relation between a load and what carries it — not a quantity you could weigh alone. Set beside monotropism (Murray, Lesser & Lawson, 2005), that stops reading as consolation and starts reading as description. Deleuze and Guattari's refrain then supplies the mechanism in three movements, read at the primary rather than from summaries: a child sings in the dark and makes a centre in chaos; the circle gets drawn and home does not preexist, it has to be built; then the circle is opened a crack to join with cosmic forces — and they insist these are not three stages but three aspects of one thing, so nobody graduates out of the humming. Two passages are Ryan Boren's own, in his voice: the hallway outside his parents' door, and the freight of limerence. Carries its own corrections on the page — a cowbell line drafted as Deleuze and Guattari turns out to be Deleuze alone, speaking in L'Abécédaire, in a translation with only one author behind it; and the Sagan quotation is set in the wording Ryan confirmed against the footage, correcting six instances elsewhere on this site. Refuses retroactively diagnosing Dickinson, “narrow but deep” as a consolation prize, and the naturalistic fallacy. Eleven sections, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 80 One Word for the Opposite Stimpunks Zines On the vocabulary we built for what hurts, the single word we have for what doesn’t — and why a glimmer is probably not a dopamine hit, which is better news than it sounds. Trigger, flashback, hypervigilance, dysregulation, rupture, freeze, shutdown. The opposite got one word, in 2018. The asymmetry is the finding, and you can count it without settling anything. 10 spreads→ Details Write down the words for a nervous system going badly — trigger, flashback, hypervigilance, activation, dysregulation, rupture, freeze, fawn, shutdown, overwhelm — and then write down the words for a small moment in which one registers that things are all right. There is one. It is glimmer, and it was coined in 2018. That asymmetry needs no laboratory to check and no theory to accept: language grows where the pressure is, and the pressure was on harm, because nobody ever had to convince an institution that a moment of quiet was real in order to be believed. What a word does is make a category countable — findable, mentionable, recognisable twice as the same kind of event — which is a smaller and far more defensible claim than the ones usually made for such words. The word is Deb Dana’s (2018), offered as the counterpart to triggers, and it arrived inside polyvagal theory, which is influential and scientifically contested. So the zine answers the obvious question directly: does a good word stop being good if the theory it arrived in is wrong? No — words and theories are different objects with different failure modes, and Helen Edgar says it plainer still: glimmers need not relate to polyvagal at all, being simply the opposite of triggers, moments of joy and comfort, sensory or cognitive. Her monotropic reading is the definition the piece works from: a glimmer as an alignment of focus, sensory needs and emotion — which is why glimmer lists fail as advice, since the alignment is between a particular bodymind and a particular room and nobody else is standing in it. The five nervous-system theories are named and deliberately not used, with the observation the zine exists to make: Porges and Grossman & Taylor are not two parts of a synthesis but the two sides of an unresolved argument, Grossman & Taylor (2007) being the standing critique that RSA is too confounded by respiration to index vagal tone. And the dopamine question gets an honest answer. Berridge and Robinson separated wanting from liking: dopamine carries incentive salience — wanting — and conspicuously fails to raise the pleasure of a sweet taste. Liking runs on opioid and endocannabinoid signalling in hedonic hotspots about a cubic millimetre across, where mu-opioid activity can more than double liking reactions. A glimmer is not the pull toward something; it is the quality of a moment already arriving. So it is probably not a dopamine hit — and that is better news, because the dopamine story quietly makes a glimmer into a reward that has to be chased, and the liking story does not. Six refusals, including that noticing glimmers fixes nothing, that this is not a glimmer list, and that joy is not a duty or evidence of recovery. Filed in Star Gazing, and the colophon says why: three earlier attempts put this in Star Stuff, whose register demands one settled fact, and each either leaned on shaky ground or ended up with rigorous physics tied to the subject by a thread. The topic was never the problem. The collection was.

Zine No. 5 Underground Stimpunks Zines on mycelial networks, decomposition, and the quiet dark where we do our realest work — the below to Bone Song's above The mycelial worldview as an act of love. Six spreads with a prose poem, diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and reflection questions. 6 spreads→ Details Six spreads, and the below to Bone Song's above. The mycelial network and the oldest anarchist in the room; decomposition as bricolage, where nothing is wasted, only waiting; the prose poem; the quiet and the dark; and the line the zine turns on — the work that changes everything is the work no one is watching. It ends on mischief and punk. Diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and reflection questions. On the science, it keeps the kinship and drops the overclaim: mycorrhizal symbiosis is well established, and the popular wood-wide-web picture of forests wired together is named as contested, citing Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023).

Zine No. 14 The Council of All Beings Stimpunks Zines on multispecies justice, more-than-human governance, and the star stuff that convenes Every being at the table is forged from the same stellar matter, so the Council is the universe convening with itself — and you cannot rank what you are made of. 9 spreads→ Details Multispecies justice and more-than-human governance, read as star stuff. Every being at the table — soil, river, beaver, cuckoo, meadow — is forged from the same stellar matter, so the Council of All Beings is the universe convening with itself, and you cannot rank what you are made of. Carries the ethodiversity thread from No. 8 outward: the cosmos varies not only in what it makes but in how its creatures live. Six spreads of argument, then a hydrofeminist coda — the “service provider” critique and the four dimensions of justice, ethodiversity and ethonormativity after Tarragnat, the role-play method (speaking as the soil and the river), the proxy problem and the Umwelt, and Rights of Nature meeting hydrofeminism at Te Awa Tupua, closing on a coda where the council dissolves into flow. Nine spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 15 Every Creature's Own Sky Stimpunks Zines on umwelt, attention-worlds, and why there was never a neutral way to sense Every creature is sealed in its own complete perceptual world — the tick's three signals, the bat's echo, the dog's scent-time — and each world is whole. 8 spreads→ Details Umwelt as star stuff. Every creature is sealed in its own complete perceptual world — the tick's three signals, the bat's echo, the mantis shrimp's light, the dog's scent-time — and each world is whole, not a partial view of one real world underneath. There is no neutral, default way to sense. The animals do the arguing, so that when minds enter, the point lands as recognition: monotropism is an attention-world, Autistic perception a different and complete sky, not a broken copy of a standard one. And when two worlds meet — human and bat, one mind and another — the gap is mutual: the double empathy problem, arrived at without lecturing. Not one correct channel, but mutual translation. Carries the Umwelt thread from No. 14 inward, from von Uexküll through Tarragnat, Manning, Milton, and Despret. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 16 Minor Worlds Stimpunks Zines on niche construction, stimming, and how difference doesn't just see a world — it builds one Organisms don't just adapt to a fixed environment; they remake it — the beaver's dam, the spider's web — and pass the built world on. 8 spreads→ Details Niche construction as star stuff, and the third of a loose trilogy — how we treat other worlds (No. 14), how we sense them (No. 15), and here, how we build them. Organisms don't just adapt to a fixed environment; they remake it — the beaver's dam, the spider's web — and pass the built world on as ecological inheritance. So the neurodiversity turn is plain: don't fix the mind, change the environment (positive niche construction — there is no “normal” brain in a vat). Stimming is worldmaking; minor worlds and niche communities are real, not lesser; and no niche is neutral — the “default” room was built for one kind of mind, so the fix is reconstruction, not accommodation. Grounded in Odling-Smee & Laland, Armstrong, Tarragnat, Manning, Kadodia & Krueger, and Haraway, and rooted in Stimpunks' own glossary. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 27 Every Nervous System Stimpunks Zines on more-than-human neurodiversity, and the animality we reclaim There is no standard nervous system — not across species, and not within one. Read neurodiversity literally and it never stopped at us. 8 spreads→ Details More-than-human neurodiversity, read through star stuff. There is no standard nervous system — not across species, and not within one: the octopus's mind distributed down its arms, the jellyfish's centreless nerve net, the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons. Read neurodiversity literally and it never stopped at the human. Following Ombre Tarragnat's antispeciesist–posthumanist philosophy: there's “no valid reason to be anthropocentric when you talk about neurodiversity,” and ethodiversity — behaviour reclaimed as “a subjective response to a bodymind's situation” — is a fundamentally animal phenomenon. Ethonormativity punishes the ethodivergent (the horse who refuses the rider, the cat who resists petting — abandoned or euthanised). And the core move: neurodivergent people are pathologised by being animalised, so the liberation is to reclaim animality — not bestialisation (the speciesist, neuronormative “less-than-human” split, after Butler 2020) but (hum)animality, kin. Distance is not disconnection: shutting down can be how we keep relation. Every nervous system is the universe wired up to feel itself, no two ever the same. “I would rather be a divergent animal than a typical human.” Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 58 The Stone You Keep Guest zine · after Helen Edgar on otters, monotropism, and the measurable advantage of being specifically yourself One otter population under pressure fans out into individual specialists, each measurably better at its own prey. Some carry a stone and some never do — and the ones with the stone keep their teeth. 10 spreads→ Details Developed after Helen Edgar's essay on the otter cam that runs every Saturday at Solidarity Sesh, where nobody has to watch and that is the part that makes it work. Then past the essay to the papers. Tinker, Bentall & Estes (2008) followed one sea otter population closely enough to tell the individuals apart: where food was scarce it did not converge on one best way to be an otter but fanned out into distinct specialists — snails, clams, urchins, crabs — each with a matched suite of diving behaviours, and each measurably better at its own prey than a generalist. The averaged otter forages nowhere. Hall & Schaller (1964) counted the blows: a mussel took a mean of 35.5, and a range of 6 to 88, so there is no correct number of blows, only yours. Law et al. (2024), across 196 tagged otters, found tool use varies enormously between individuals and that non-users are not behind — they specialise on prey a stone would not help with — while the tool users showed less tooth damage. The accommodation is legible in the skeleton. Also: no blubber, the densest coat measured on any mammal and varying sixfold across one body, a resting metabolism three times what its size predicts from heat leaking out of its own muscle since birth — the calm surface is not the whole cost. They rest in rafts wrapped in kelp, so the holding is done by the forest rather than by anyone's effort; and the kelp is there because the otters are (Estes & Palmisano 1974). Held by what it sustains. Then the fur trade took ninety-nine per cent of them, because they were remarkable, not because they were deficient. Ten spreads, eight diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set of seven that declines cute, inspiring, superpower, rest-to-produce, and the smoothed retellings.

Zine No. 59 The Rest You Keep With Helen Edgar · companion to No. 58 on Autistic rest, monotropism, burnout — and the ledger that was never there Hydra has no brain and it sleeps — and deprive it of sleep and its cells stop dividing properly. Rest is not a reward released after enough work. It is older than the machinery of earning. 11 spreads→ Details Built with Helen Edgar from her essay Reclaiming Rest: Autistic Burnout, Monotropism, and Resistance, whose inversion is the centre of the zine: rest that fights your attention is not rest, and recovery for monotropic people often means going deeper rather than switching off. Then past the essays to the papers. Kanaya et al. (2020) showed that Hydra vulgaris — a nerve net, no brain, nothing gathering it into a decision-maker — meets the behavioural criteria for sleep: it goes quiescent, it is harder to rouse, and after deprivation it rebounds. Deprive it further and the number of dividing cells drops, so rest is when the building happens rather than a pause in it. It also has no circadian clock: under constant conditions the daily rhythm vanishes and a roughly four-hour cycle remains, returning and returning. Great frigatebirds sleep a mean of 42 minutes a day on the wing against twelve hours ashore (Rattenborg et al. 2016), mostly one hemisphere at a time and while soaring rather than flapping — and a separate study found them aloft up to two months without landing (Weimerskirch et al. 2016), so rest is not the opposite of motion. Hibernating grizzlies and black bears go six months without weight-bearing movement and lose no bone at all, because formation and resorption fall together and stay balanced (McGee-Lawrence et al. 2009) — the bear does not out-work the problem, it turns remodelling down at both ends. Meanwhile the den lowers the energy bill: metabolism to about a quarter of basal with core temperature down only five or six degrees (Tøien et al. 2011). Rest as a property of an arrangement, not a feat of will. Closes on Tricia Hersey and the ledger: a debt that was issued can be refused. Eleven spreads, eight diagrams, and a “Not:” refusals set of seven that declines rest-to-produce, “just relax”, rest-as-project, meltdown-as-rest, and natural-therefore-allowed. Interoception gets its own spread, and this zine explicitly does not call meltdown or shutdown a form of rest.

Zine No. 72 The Place Knows You’re There Stimpunks Zines on reciprocity, conditional belonging, and what a place asks of you that a room does not “As long as” is the grammar belonging has usually been offered to us in, so the flinch is well trained. It is just aimed at the wrong sentence — this one describes a relation’s reach, not its terms. 12 spreads→ Details Jessica Hernandez (Maya Ch’orti’ and Binnizá) records a teaching in her father’s voice in Fresh Banana Leaves (2022): as long as we protect nature, nature will protect us. Read as a contract it is frightening, and to anyone handed belonging on terms it reads as a contract immediately. Her own extension settles it — remove ourselves from nature and nature will not be able to protect us. Able, not willing: not a payment withheld but a relation severed, and a party that cannot reach you has no leverage over you. Barry Lopez arrives at the same relation from outside in A Literature of Place (1997), naming three qualities — paying intimate attention, a storied relationship rather than a solely sensory awareness, and living in some sort of ethical unity — and saying what they are for: “a fundamental human defense against loneliness,” because “the place knows you’re there.” The zine keeps his hedge, and keeps the paragraph before it, where he says the framework describes what Indigenous interpreters showed him — so Hernandez is not an illustration of Lopez, she is the tradition speaking for itself without needing the qualifier. Then the turn that makes it ours: Hari Srinivasan’s Presence Without Belonging (2026) names the three conditions belonging requires — recognition, access, sustainability — and shows Autistic loneliness happening in the middle of social participation. A room denies all three routinely. A place denies none, and Lopez’s “intimate attention” is the thing we get pathologized for. Closes on Hernandez again: her Zapotec has no direct word for conservation, only gapanú (to take care of) and rianda (to heal), and on Seattle’s 2018 straw ban, where boxing the world into systems produced an environmental solution that removed disabled people’s access. Twelve spreads, eight figures, and a refusals set of seven. The colophon carries a correction to our own glossary: Lopez never wrote “reciprocal ethical unity.”

Zine No. 81 Already an Entity Stimpunks Zines on a river that is a listed author, and a law that had to be asked In 2020 a river became the first author of an article in a law journal. The tidy rights-of-nature story then breaks on its own primaries — and this is the one zine here that ends with no claim about us. 13 spreads→ Details Martuwarra RiverOfLife is the first-listed author of “Recognizing the Martuwarra’s First Law Right to Life as a Living Ancestral Being,” Transnational Environmental Law 9(3), 541–568 (2020) — reported as the first time a river has authored an article in a law journal, with a research profile at Nulungu. The same year, a paper in Challenges by eight Indigenous authors across four continents carried a dagger on its authorship line: “We formally acknowledge Mother Earth as our senior author, with her own presence and voice.” Both are indexed and citable. Neither is a metaphor. The zine follows that bibliographic fact into the law behind it — and audits settler law rather than explaining anybody else’s, because running our usual method on First Law would make physics the validator and Aboriginal Law an instrument. Aunty Mary Graham (Kombumerri) holds that settler law is incomplete: “it is possible, even commonplace, to commit immoral and unethical acts of destruction that are not illegal.” Quoted from her own Parrhesia paper rather than through an intermediary: “I am located therefore I am,” a reflective self is a communal self, and the Land is the law — a Custodial Ethic against a survivalist ethos. Deborah Bird Rose analysed totemism as “a common property institution for long-term ecological management” and “a jurisprudence of responsibility and right”: sanctuaries where nobody hunts, species-specific prohibitions, named parties with authority to forbid. Which sets up the hinge — terra nullius rested on an ecological claim, given “the mark of scientific authority” by Elkin in 1938, that the land was untransformed and therefore unowned; Rhys Jones reversed it in 1969 with fire-stick farming. Zoe Todd (Métis) shows the same move repeating on the climate and names it aer nullius — a blank commons awaiting Euro-Western theory — and the zine turns that on itself, since No. 26 reaches for Deleuze and this site says “more-than-human” constantly. Then the flattering story breaks: Poelina and Perdrisat record increasing ambivalence about legal personhood, because “the River is already an entity” and should not depend on settler law to become one. To celebrate the conferral is to celebrate the gatekeeping. The last spread is a fence. Every other zine here ends in a claim about neurodivergent belonging; this one does not, and says at length why not — quoting Yunkaporta’s own definition of Indigenous and stating plainly that this project does not meet it. Refuses First Law explained, “Indigenous people believe,” ancient wisdom, validation by physics, and any use of the material as metaphor.
Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not

Zine No. 31 Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not Stimpunks Zines convergence, attractors, and the ones who crawled back out of the valley The crab-like body plan really did evolve at least five times, which is the part everyone quotes. Written after Brett D. Wick's When Everything Becomes a Crab. 12 spreads→ Details Convergent evolution and “attractors,” read against the primary literature — written after Brett D. Wick's essay When Everything Becomes a Crab. The crab-like body plan really did evolve at least five times in decapod crustaceans, which is the part everyone quotes. It was also lost at least seven times — decarcinization, the commoner event — and Wolfe, Luque & Bracken-Grissom (BioEssays, 2021) report that the reasons for the recurrence remain a mystery, with carcinized lineages running from millimetres to metres across nearly every habitat on Earth. So convergence produced no sameness, and the basin is not a destiny. Our eye and the octopus's converged on the same camera and were built backwards from each other, which is why a system that grades the route instead of the outcome will fail an eye. Waddington's canalized landscape gives the picture; “attractor” is named as a metaphor borrowed from dynamical systems. Then the turn: nature's basin permits the millions who never roll in, while engineered systems write the attractor into the rules — engagement chosen as the objective and everything downhill of it becoming vertical video, one route to the answer and a diagnosis for the others. Cavendish monoculture against Cavendish Space, on the ARLES Environment and Systems rungs. Ideas ripen the same way: Ogburn & Thomas's 148 multiples, Merton's singletons-are-the-exception, Tao's “maths at internet speed,” and Brian Eno's scenius quoted from the 1996 primary rather than the altered version in circulation. Closes on our own history — neurodiversity was itself developed collectively. Gould and Conway Morris are left unresolved on purpose. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 32 The Skeleton That Skipped Bone Stimpunks Zines sharks, tesserae, and what happens to a body once somebody decides it's a cure Sharks, rays and chimaeras are vertebrates with no true bone at all. A companion and a counter-song to Bone Song. 12 spreads→ Details A companion and a counter-song to Bone Song, written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. This collection opens on a skeleton that is piezoelectric — press it and it makes voltage. Sharks, rays and chimaeras are vertebrates with no true bone at all: a cartilage skeleton stiffened by thousands of mineral tiles called tesserae, which Dean & Summers (Zoology, 2006) describe as tuned species by species and even to how the animal feeds. Then the finding that changes the story. Sharks were taught for a century as the before picture — cartilage first, bone later, primitive, not there yet. But Brazeau and colleagues (Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2020) describe endochondral bone in Minjinia turgenensis, an Early Devonian fish near the common ancestry of jawed vertebrates. If the shared ancestor had bone, the shark's bonelessness is not a failure to arrive — it is a loss, derived rather than primitive, and the same shape of fact as the crab body plan being lost more often than gained. Which exposes the verdict buried in the word primitive, the same one hiding in low-functioning and delayed. Then the other half: because sharks were said not to get cancer, their cartilage was ground into pills. Ostrander et al. (Cancer Research, 2004) documented 42 chondrichthyan tumours across at least 21 species, at least 15 malignant; Loprinzi et al. (Cancer, 2005) ran the trial and found no benefit to survival or quality of life. A body read as a cure gets harvested — and extraction always starts as appreciation. The skeleton is for the animal. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 33 The Ick Is a Border Stimpunks Zines bone-eating worms, fused fish, a whale that becomes a town — and the reflex that rules bodies out Disgust feels like a fact about the animal. It is a fact about the frame — Rozin & Fallon (1987) treat its objects as largely learned. 13 spreads→ Details Disgust feels like a fact about the animal. It is a fact about the frame. Rozin & Fallon (Psychological Review, 1987) treat disgust as a food emotion at root, whose objects are largely learned — arriving across a child's first eight years and running on the magical law of contagion, where one touch renders a whole plate inedible forever. A reaction that far out of proportion to any physical fact is a rule about categories, and rules about categories are taught. Then three arrangements that read as gross and are, in frame, simply competent. Osedax, the bone-eating worm (Rouse, Goffredi & Vrijenhoek, Science, 2004): no mouth, no gut, a vascularised root system dissolving whale bone, dozens of dwarf males inside the female's tube. The deep-sea anglerfishes, whose fused males cost them their immunity — Swann, Holland, Petersen, Pietsch & Boehm (Science, 2020) found loss of functional aicda, and in permanent attachment loss of rag, abolishing the hallmark of adaptive immunity. To stay joined to another body they gave up the machinery that tells self from not-self. And the whale fall (Smith & Baco, 2003): a pulse of food worth roughly 2,000 years of background supply, a sulphophilic stage lasting decades, a mean of 185 macrofaunal species — richer than any other hard surface down there. Then the turn. The same reflex fires at feeding tubes, drooling, stimming, incontinence and AAC; Nussbaum calls it projective disgust, where a group of people becomes a buffer against the animal nature we would rather deny. Two frames to widen past — the neuronormative and the anthronormative. A house companion to Helen Edgar's Wyrd & Weird: weird was reclaimed, gross gets disarmed. Nobody is guilty of a flinch; everyone is answerable for the two seconds after.
Two Hundred Years Before You're Grown

Zine No. 34 Two Hundred Years Before You're Grown Stimpunks Zines the oldest vertebrate we know of, and the question of who is holding the calendar The Greenland shark does not reach maturity until it is about 156 years old. Nielsen et al. (Science, 2016) radiocarbon-dated the eye lenses of 28 females. 13 spreads→ Details The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate known, and it does not reach maturity until it is about 156 years old. Nielsen et al. (Science, 2016) radiocarbon-dated the eye lenses of 28 females — the lens core is laid down before birth and never replaced, so they read each animal's age against the atmospheric bomb pulse from 1950s nuclear testing — and found a life span of at least 272 years, the largest animal at 392 ± 120. It is also the slowest fish for its size: 0.34 m/s, one tail-beat every seven seconds (Watanabe et al., 2012), and it eats seals anyway, apparently by arriving quietly while they sleep — the strategy needs the trait. Nearly all of them carry a copepod clamped to the cornea, and it costs them almost nothing, because vision is not what the Arctic deep asks for. So late turns out to be a comparison, not a measurement; the ruler was always the variable. But this is not a zine about slow being beautiful: Nielsen's own paper raises the conservation alarm, because an animal needing a century and a half to reproduce cannot recover from pressure arriving in decades, and the species is IUCN Vulnerable. Slow is survivable or it isn't, and the environment decides — which is the social model of disability, stated in fish. Names the standard defence of the clock too: Alfie Kohn's BGUTI, "Better Get Used To It," which almost by definition ignores developmental differences — and cannot survive noticing them. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 35 Everywhere That Turtles Go Stimpunks Zines range, kinship, and the animal every people had to think with A Star Dreaming that “goes everywhere that turtles go — and there are turtles all over the world.” That reads like a figure of speech and is not. 13 spreads→ Details Tyson Yunkaporta writes in Sand Talk that a Star Dreaming Oldman Juma Fejo of the Larrakia People wants to share with all peoples "goes everywhere that turtles go — and there are turtles all over the world, even in desert country, so it connects everybody." That reads like a figure of speech and is actually a range map, so we checked it: roughly 357 species on every continent but Antarctica, in every warm ocean, and in the arid interior, where Chelodina steindachneri buries itself in a dry Pilbara riverbed and waits out a year without water. The primary literature then reverses the obvious reading twice. Lyson et al. (Current Biology, 2016) find the shell began as an adaptation for burrowing, not armour — broadened ribs "provide little protection" and cost you speed and breath; protection is a later exaptation. And Lyson et al. (Nature Communications, 2014) find the price: lock your ribs into a shell and you lose the ordinary way of breathing, so turtles run their lungs off a sling of abdominal muscle instead. Side-necks and hidden-necks answered one problem two ways. Sex is set by the temperature of the sand, not by chromosomes — which makes the Discworld philosophers' failed expedition to determine Great A'Tuin's sex a better joke than they knew. A hatchling learns the magnetic field of one beach and finds it again decades later. And every people had to think with this animal: Turtle Island, ao in the Huainanzi, Kurma — who is a pivot for churning and not a world-bearer — and Great A'Tuin. They are not the same turtle, and that is the connection. Carries the Fibonacci passage and says plainly where it stops being biology. ~48% of turtle species are threatened. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 36 The Layer We Call Essential Stimpunks Zines cetacean brains, the missing layer IV, and a ranking that outlived its evidence The long-finned pilot whale's neocortex holds roughly 37.2 billion neurons — the first animal ever counted above us. Then, in the same paper, the conclusion turns. 13 spreads→ Details Mortensen et al. (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2014) counted the long-finned pilot whale's neocortex and found roughly 37.2 billion neurons — "almost twice as many neocortical neurons as humans," the first animal ever counted above us. Then, in the same paper, they conclude that absolute neuron number is "not correlated with the superior cognitive abilities of humans." The yardstick came back against us and the ranking survived, because it was never resting on the count. Underneath sits the architecture: the cetacean neocortex is agranular, with layer IV — the input layer our textbooks call canonical — absent or underdeveloped, and layer I apparently taking the job instead, giving "a very different connectivity scheme compared to more commonly studied species, like rats and macaque monkeys." Manger (2006) read that missing layer as evidence there is no neural basis for complex cognition in cetaceans; sixteen authors replied in Biological Reviews that these features are "a non-primate route to neuroanatomical (and cognitive) complexity." Difference read as deficit, conducted by neuroscientists, about whales. Held with care: thermogenesis is a serious hypothesis and a brain can do heat work and thought work at once — the claim here is only about which reading you get for free. On neurodiversity, the honest answer: there is no cetacean diagnostic literature and this zine does not invent one. What exists is variation inside single populations — sponging in 15 of 141 known Shark Bay mothers, down one matriline (Krützen et al., 2005), spongers more solitary and foraging longer (Mann et al., 2008) — read through ethodiversity (Ombre Tarragnat), which needs no clinic. Plus 8,719 sperm whale codas resolving into ~143 combinations where 21 had been described, because someone borrowed rubato from music. And eight days off Pico with an S-spined bottlenose dolphin among sperm whales, the rubs returned — a paper titled "Repeated Non-Agonistic Interactions," because "adopted" was the press's word. Douglas Adams got the joke in 1979, ranking us third behind the mice. Then he went to see the baiji. A rhyme, not a proof.
The Village Was Never Just Family

Zine No. 64 The Village Was Never Just Family Stimpunks Zines on alloparenting, reciprocity, and the kin you are not related to Across the cooperatively breeding birds, the species that cannot raise young without helpers are the ones least made of relatives. The prediction ran the other way. 14 spreads→ Details The nuclear family gets offered as nature's own unit, which is an empirical claim, and it has a literature. Riehl (Proc R Soc B, 2013) describes group composition for 213 cooperatively breeding bird species: 55% nest primarily with kin, 15% primarily with non-kin, 30% in groups that regularly hold both — so family is the plurality and never the rule, and 45% of these species routinely raise young alongside birds they are not related to. Then the inversion: 77% of obligately cooperative species regularly include non-kin, against just 38% of facultative ones (χ² = 17.1, p < 0.0001). Where helping is optional, kinship organises it. Where the brood genuinely cannot be raised without a village, kinship mostly stops being what the village is made of. In common vampire bats — who die after about 70 hours without blood — Carter & Wilkinson (2013) fasted 20 individuals across 48 induced sharing days at mixed relatedness and equal familiarity: food received predicted food given 8.5 times more strongly than relatedness, and 64% of sharing dyads were unrelated, against the 67% expected if nepotism were absent altogether. Donors initiated more often than recipients, so not harassment; the network tracked mutual allogrooming, so the bond is maintained rather than inherited. At Taï, Boesch et al. (2010) logged 18 adoptions of orphans across 27 years — half by males, only one of whom was the father, with three genetically confirmed unrelated. And then the spread that costs something: Emlen's (1982) ecological constraints model holds that many helpers stay because the habitat is saturated and there is no opening to breed into. That is a housing shortage with a nest in it, not a chosen family — and it is true of our own households, where people stay because leaving costs more than staying. So the turn is deliberately narrow: the animals license nothing. They remove the warrant for treating biological kinship as nature's default, which is the claim doing the damage on the actual form in the actual corridor. Also inside: "it takes a village" has no traceable village of its own (NPR, 2016; the Dictionary of Modern Proverbs finds no evidence of African origin); Hrdy on human cooperative breeding, marked as argued synthesis rather than measurement; Weston's Families We Choose for the term, and Rosa's "the nuclear family is a scab"; whānau and whanaungatanga from the Māori Dictionary with takiwātanga credited to Keri Opai; Bettin & Mazlum's Autistic translation of the proverb; and Devon Price's strawberry people, a ledger of who fed you kept in a phone. Bound throughout by Companion Stars's correction that most stars are single: this zine promises nobody that they have people.

Zine No. 12 Turn and Face the Strange Stimpunks Zines David Bowie as a way of being star stuff — on unmasking, the freedom of many selves, and difference read not as deficit but as direction From “Changes” and Space Oddity to Blackstar: unmasking as authorship rather than exposure, and authenticity as our purest freedom. 8 spreads→ Details David Bowie as a way of being star stuff — defiantly, joyfully weird. Unmasking as authorship rather than exposure, the freedom of many selves, bringing the hidden to the front, and authenticity as our purest freedom. From “Changes” and Space Oddity to Blackstar, difference read as direction, not deficit. Eight spreads, each with an embedded Bowie performance, plus a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 13 Warriors and Weirdos Stimpunks Zines AURORA as a way of being star stuff — the alien who came home by gathering a tribe of Weirdos, not by being cured into fitting Feeling alien, the mothership's invitation, naming your people, refusing the cure, stimming in the open. Eight spreads, each with an embedded song. 8 spreads→ Details Eight spreads, each built around an embedded AURORA song: a different kind of human; the mothership is coming; warriors and weirdos; there is no cure for me; running with the wolves; and runaway home. The arc is the argument — she came home by gathering a tribe of Weirdos, not by being cured into fitting. Feeling alien, the mothership's invitation, naming your people, refusing the cure, and stimming in the open. A listening companion rack of its own sits in Sound.

Zine No. 66 The Body Understands It First Stimpunks Zines David Byrne as a way of being star stuff — on repetition, prediction, and a stage built so a nervous man could move What he actually wrote about being Autistic, what got lost carrying it, and why Stop Making Sense is built one body at a time. 10 spreads→ Details Ten spreads on one settled finding: groove is measurable and consistent across listeners, so repetition is the mechanism rather than the deficit — and Remain in Light was built by layering one held figure at a time. Byrne reaches the same place himself late in How Music Works, connecting being accused of missing obvious social cues to sensing a musical build; the zine extends that paragraph and declines the mirror-neuron wiring he hangs it on, because the broken-mirror account of autism did not survive review. Two spreads are about transmission instead of music: he wrote “a very mild (I think) form of Asperger's syndrome” and the internet published a coming-out, and in the same paragraph he repeated a 1994 study's 69 percent without the qualification printed in its very next sentence — the same fault, twice, in one paragraph. Then subtraction as access: a performance style he called defined by negatives, down to telling club lighting people to turn the lights on at the start and off at the end. It closes on the budget: Byrne got to be an auteur, and the same nervous system without a record deal gets a behaviour plan. Companion rack: One Body at a Time.

Zine No. 67 No One Had to Qualify Stimpunks Zines Dolly Parton, 1946–2026 — on love with no eligibility criterion, and what a gate is really for 332 million books, no income test and no application — and the critique of her that belongs inside the tribute rather than after it. 11 spreads→ Details Eleven spreads on a design decision anybody can check: the Imagination Library has never had an eligibility test, and the book arrives addressed to the child by name rather than to a parent or guardian. Set that against the gates the rest of us live under — income thresholds, severity cut-offs, the annual review that funds you for being worse — and it becomes an argument, because a gate does not only ration, it sorts, and sorting needs somebody to rule on who is worth it. The physics spread earns its keep: a star has no mechanism for aiming its light, and the inverse-square law is geometry rather than judgement. Two spreads cover what her allyship actually cost, including the death threats over Travelin' Thru. Then the turn — Tressie McMillan Cottom's The Dolly Moment gets a spread, not a footnote, and is not answered on Dolly's behalf; her closing line about knowing what we love turns out to be the LYDTYSS grammar in someone else's words. It ends on a misquote: Dolly attributed a paraphrase to Emily Dickinson in her own autobiography, dropping the hedge exactly as we once did, and gets loved down to that too. Companion rack: Love Without Cringing.

Zine No. 38 Eight Tenths of a Second Stimpunks Zines on a fired astronomer, a cat in a box, and the road to the dashboard In February 1796 the Astronomer Royal dismissed his assistant for marking star transits eight tenths of a second late. Bessel later showed observers differ irreducibly. 14 spreads→ Details In February 1796 the Astronomer Royal dismissed his assistant David Kinnebrook for marking star transits eight tenths of a second late. Bessel later established that observers differ from one another systematically and irreducibly — and astronomy's answer was the personal equation: publish a constant for each observer, build the variation into the model, keep the observer. This zine follows the measuring apparatus out of the observatory: Wundt's laboratory, Cattell's “mental tests,” Thorndike's puzzle boxes and his 1918 credo that whatever exists at all exists in some amount, Kelly's Kansas Silent Reading Test, Pressey's machine built from typewriter parts, Skinner's teaching machines, and Lovaas at UCLA in 1987 — while a second rail runs alongside from Galton through Kraepelin to the DSM. The two meet at a table with a child at it. The first zine built as a Burke-style chain, and every joint is marked documented, contested or leap — six solid, three dashed, one dotted — because two of them are weaker than the story wants. The turn: school found the same human variation astronomy found, and made it the thing to remove. Accommodation is the older answer. Fourteen spreads, twelve diagrams, a running chain spine, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 39 Five Microns Stimpunks Zines on a number that answered a different question, and the room it left you in In March 2020 the WHO posted “FACT: COVID-19 is NOT airborne.” Not a lie — doctrine, faithfully applied, resting on a number that had quietly changed questions. 15 spreads→ Details In March 2020 the WHO posted “FACT: COVID-19 is NOT airborne” and called the alternative misinformation. Not a lie — doctrine, faithfully applied, resting on a number that had quietly changed questions. William Wells put the boundary between droplets that fall and droplets that evaporate into lingering nuclei at 100 micrometres, and never wrote 5; his own table gives a 1 µm particle sixteen hours to fall two metres. The 5 µm figure came from industrial hygiene asking which particles reach the deepest lung — deposition, not suspension — and Alexander Langmuir fused the two in 1951, in a lecture preparing public-health students for biological warfare months after Korea began. Randall, Ewing, Marr, Jimenez and Bourouiba reconstructed it in Interface Focus under the title “How did we get here,” and refuse to solder the load-bearing joint, writing only that the deposition focus “likely” popularised the cut-off — so this zine marks it contested too. Meanwhile Flügge's team in Breslau had grown colonies nine metres from a sneeze in the 1890s, meant “droplets” to cover what we now call aerosols, waited five hours before reading their plates, and recommended ventilation. The 1–2 metre rule has its own separate lineage and turns out to match the width of a 1940s camera's field of view. The second chain zine, every joint marked documented, contested or leap. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a running two-rail spine, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 40 Five Sigma Stimpunks Zines how much evidence is enough before you do something to a child Particle physics will not permit the word “discovery” below five sigma — one chance in three and a half million — and wrote down why. 16 spreads→ Details How much evidence is enough before you do something to a child? Particle physics answered that question carefully and wrote it down. It will not permit the word “discovery” below five sigma — a p-value of 3 × 10⁻⁷, one chance in three and a half million — and the reason is empirical rather than principled: too many 3σ and 4σ results kept evaporating. Louis Lyons, whose paper is the spine of this zine, goes further and argues the bar should not be uniform at all, grading it by degree of surprise, impact, look-elsewhere effect and systematics: single top production 3σ, the Higgs 5σ, supersymmetry 7σ, faster-than-light neutrinos above 8σ. He also prints the statisticians' objection that his own gold standard is unsound. Against all that stands p = 0.05 — about 2σ — chosen by Fisher in 1925 with the word convenient, and unexamined since. The gap is roughly 170,000×, and the asymmetry runs backwards: if physics is wrong it retracts a paper and the particle is unharmed; if we are wrong a childhood already happened and there is no more data to collect. Run Lyons' four dials on an intervention and every one reads high — then the systematics column turns out to be empty, because 150 intervention studies for young Autistic children produced 11 that mentioned adverse events at all. Not an argument against science. An argument against scientism, which keeps the authority and drops the practice. The first chain here with no leap joints. Sixteen spreads, fourteen diagrams, two rails that never meet, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 41 A Conquering Gaze from Nowhere Stimpunks Zines parallax, positionality, and the research done on us For roughly two centuries the strongest objection to a moving Earth was that the stars showed no parallax. The reasoning was valid, and the conclusion wrong. 15 spreads→ Details For roughly two centuries the strongest objection to a moving Earth was that the stars showed no parallax. The reasoning was valid, the observations careful, and the conclusion wrong — partly because the distances required seemed absurd, and partly because telescopic star discs are an artefact of the aperture rather than a property of stars. Then in 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured 61 Cygni at 0.3136 arcseconds from Königsberg — a two-centimetre coin seen from thirteen kilometres. The method carries the whole argument: the baseline is the observer's own displacement across Earth's orbit, so a viewpoint with no location has no baseline, no angle and no depth. A view from nowhere cannot measure distance even in principle; it is the blindest available position. And it is the same Bessel, at the same observatory, who gave us the personal equation in No. 38 — twice showing that knowledge requires a located, particular observer. Every rung of the cosmic distance ladder above parallax is calibrated by the one beneath, and rung two — the period–luminosity relation — was built by Henrietta Swan Leavitt, employed as a Harvard “computer,” paid by the hour, not permitted to observe, and published under her director's name: “has been prepared by Miss Leavitt.” That is the third woman in three chains to do the work and lose the byline, and the zine stops to name all three. Donna Haraway gave the fantasy its name in 1988 — the god trick, the unmarked category claiming the power to see and not be seen — and her positive claim is the one usually dropped: only partial perspective promises objective vision. She refuses relativism just as flatly, calling it “a way of being nowhere while claiming to be everywhere equally.” Then the numbers: 96% of behavioural-science samples from Western industrialised nations, 68% from the US, reported as facts about humans. Then research done on Autistic people rather than with them, and double empathy as a finding that only exists because somebody stood at the other end of the baseline. The correction is neither removing the observer nor declaring all views equal: publish your coordinates. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a single rail with a marked baseline, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 42 Look for the Air Stimpunks Zines two thousand years spent deleting character from the explanation, and the industry that put it back Aristotle explained motion by what a thing is. It is not a foolish theory — go outside and test it and every prediction checks out. 14 spreads→ Details Aristotle's physics explained motion by what a thing is: heavy bodies fall because it is in their nature to seek the centre, faster in proportion to weight, slower in a denser medium. It is not a foolish theory — go outside and test it and every prediction checks out, because everyday observation happens in air. The error is where the explanation was put. Galileo showed the rule contradicts itself (tie a heavy body to a light one and it predicts both faster and slower), rolled balls down inclined planes, and made the strange move of reasoning about a fall with no medium at all — while the famous Leaning Tower demonstration turns out to come from a biography written decades later and is marked contested here. Newton finished it: acceleration is set by the forces acting plus one scalar property, and disposition disappears. Then, on 2 August 1971, David Scott released a geology hammer and a falcon feather together in the lunar vacuum and they landed together, on film. The difference was never in the feather. It was in the air. This chain argues that mindset marketing runs that two-thousand-year move backwards on children. Behaviourism looks like it made the same move but stopped one ring short — it deleted the interior and still left the child as the only adjustable thing. California's task force commissioned its own research, was told the associations between self-esteem and its expected consequences were “mixed, insignificant, or absent,” and shipped in 1990 regardless. Growth mindset fails the same way across 63 studies and 97,672 participants, with higher-quality studies less likely to show benefit — and Dweck and Duckworth both objected to the deployment while it kept growing. The dashboard completes it: a schema with fields for effort, focus and behaviour points, and no field for the room. Along the way the zine corrects its own source — the famous Eric Hoffer line about a movement becoming a business and degenerating into a racket is a misquotation that invents a moral arc he never wrote. It closes on scarcity and slack, on equity literacy, and on the first leap joint since No. 39, marked because it is the sentence a reader most wants to be true. Fourteen spreads, twelve diagrams, two rails running in opposite directions, a “Not:” refusals set.

Zine No. 43 The Elimination of Waste Stimpunks Zines on a word that meant one thing in a steam engine and another in a school In 1824 Sadi Carnot proved a heat engine has a hard, provable ceiling on its efficiency — and that waste heat is not sloppiness, it is the fee. 15 spreads→ Details In 1824 Sadi Carnot proved something strange: that a heat engine has a hard, provable ceiling on its efficiency, set only by the two temperatures available and beatable by no engineer who ever lives. And with it came the result that matters here — waste heat is not sloppiness, it is the fee. An engine with nowhere to dump it does not run at all. So “eliminate all waste” isn't an ambitious goal not yet reached; in thermodynamics it names the one outcome that is ruled out. (He reached this from caloric theory, which was wrong — Clausius and Kelvin supplied the formula later, so “Carnot derived the efficiency equation” is itself a smoothed retelling, and the joint is marked contested.) Then the word left the engine room, and what it shed in transit was the ceiling. Frederick Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management appeared in 1911, and Raymond Callahan's Education and the Cult of Efficiency (1962) dates what followed to the month: in July 1911, one month after Taylor's American Magazine series concluded, a school board member told the NEA that “scientific management” held a message for every teacher — and that if teachers did not voluntarily increase their efficiency, the business world would force them to. By 1916 Cubberley's textbook was listing what schools must take from the factory: good tools, specialized machinery, continuous measurement of production, and “the elimination of waste in manufacture.” Ninety-two years after Carnot, the phrase arrives in a book about children as a specification. By 1912 an educator was already complaining that teachers were “curiously protected in inefficiency.” And the question nobody asked sits in Callahan's own parenthesis: would Schmidt, the pig-iron handler, have agreed that science had reduced his fatigue? It ends at spoon theory — and then spends an entire spread arguing that this argument should not need physics at all, because you are not a heat engine and deriving rest from thermodynamics is precisely the move the collection condemns. Fifteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a spine that crosses its own ceiling, a “Not:” refusals set.
The Sky Was Not Regular Enough

Zine No. 50 The Sky Was Not Regular Enough Stimpunks Zines on cutting a standard loose from the thing it measured, and whether you say so out loud Until 1960 a second was one 86,400th of a day, and the definition pointed at the sky. Then the instrument became steadier than the thing it measured. 16 spreads→ Details Until 1960 a second was a piece of a day — one 86,400th of it — and the definition pointed at something. Not a prototype in a vault, but the sky: you could check it against a star. Then quartz clocks arrived and, for the first time in the history of measurement, the instrument was steadier than the Earth. Scheibe and Adelsberger reported the seasonal wobble in 1936; Stoyko put it at about two milliseconds in 1937. The Earth was never irregular to itself — it became irregular the moment we had something steadier to compare it to. So the tie was cut, twice. In 1956 the second became a fraction of the tropical year 1900, a year that had already ended and could never be re-measured; in 1967 it became 9,192,631,770 caesium transitions, and after that the definition points at no day, no year, no sky at all. Every one of those moves was an improvement, and this zine says so — the collection exists to reclaim science, not to indict it. Since 1972 the gap between the atomic standard and the turning planet has been closed in public by leap seconds: 27 of them, first on 30 June 1972, last on 31 December 2016, and none since, because the Earth started spinning faster and the correction now due is a negative leap second that has never been tested. Duncan Agnew showed in Nature in 2024 that melting Greenland and Antarctic ice slowed the spin enough to postpone it from 2026 to 2029 — climate change bought the world's timekeepers three years, and he refuses to call that good news. Resolution 4 of the 27th CGPM decided in 2022 to widen the tolerance by 2035, and the implementing vote is at the 28th CGPM this October; the proposal is a leap hour. The argument: a leap second is not a bug but an honesty mechanism — a standards body saying in public, on a named date, with a number attached, that its standard and the world disagree by exactly this much. Abolishing it is defensible engineering. What it costs is the announcement. And that is the one thing carried across to us, marked leap because caesium licenses nothing about a person: an accommodation is a leap second, and the objections to it arrive in the same order — it's irregular, it breaks the system, everybody handles it differently — with the same proposed remedy, widen the tolerance and stop announcing. Ends at processing speed and crip time: the Earth is not slow, the second left. Eleven documented joints, one contested, one leap. Sixteen spreads, thirteen diagrams, a running spine that is a plot of its own data, a “Not:” refusals set.
We Learned to Build the Eclipse

Zine No. 52 We Learned to Build the Eclipse Stimpunks Zines on an element nobody would accept because it could not be put on a bench, and on the day we stopped travelling to the Moon's shadow A chain about how a whole branch of physics stopped waiting for the Moon — the corona, for most of astronomy's history available only during totality. 21 spreads→ Details A chain about how a whole branch of physics stopped waiting for the Moon. The Sun’s outer atmosphere is always there and almost never available: the photosphere drowns it, so for most of astronomy’s history the corona and the prominences could only be studied during totality — a few minutes, roughly every eighteen months, along a track a few hundred kilometres wide, usually somewhere difficult, and one cloud ended the expedition. It begins in 1604, where pinhole solar diameters came out systematically too large and nobody could say why until Kepler supplied the theory of how an image forms behind a small hole: the method came first and worked badly; the understanding came second and fixed it. Then Guntur, 18 August 1868, where several observers caught a yellow line near sodium’s — and where what Janssen actually took away was not the line but its brightness. The next morning he observed the prominences again with no eclipse at all, spreading the sky’s glare thin with dispersion while the emission line stayed put. Lockyer, who had wanted this since 1866 and was blocked by glass rather than by ideas, got there on 20 October; both reports reached the Académie within days and it struck a medal for the pair — for the method. Neither report flagged the yellow line, which is the first of four contested joints: the famous sentence “helium was discovered during an eclipse in 1868” is wrong in almost every part, and what the compression deletes is years of argument. Lockyer alone later called it D3 and proposed an element; for a quarter century chemists refused it, not because the spectroscopy was faulty but because nobody could put the gas on a bench — and a thing visible only in light from 150 million kilometres away did not, to them, count as a thing. They were rigorous and they were wrong, and the zine insists on both, because the same method also produced two elements that were never there: coronium and nebulium, dissolved by Bowen in 1927 and Grotrian and Edlén in 1939 and 1942 as forbidden lines of ordinary oxygen and iron — which is also how we learned the corona is millions of degrees hotter than the surface. Ramsay got helium out of cleveite on 26 March 1895, twenty-seven years late, and it had been underfoot the whole time. Then the chain runs downhill, because capability is specific: in 1919 the Moon was needed again to see whether starlight bends, the Sobral astrograph plates were set aside, Earman and Glymour charged Eddington with seeing what he wanted, and Kennefick later established that the call was Dyson’s and that the plates could only agree with Newton if the instrument had also changed magnification — a reason to distrust them other than what they said, which is the whole difference between rejecting bad data and rejecting inconvenient data. Finally Bernard Lyot, chasing stray light up a mountain, photographed the corona with no eclipse on 12 July 1931: an eclipse at a time and place of human choosing, turning minutes per expedition into hours per clear day. We now fly manufactured occulters at other stars. The transfer, marked leap because it is one, refuses the obvious framing first: eclipses were computed years ahead, so the difficulty was never luck but a structural condition — the observation existing only there, only then, with the ocean, the freight, the years and the weather all charged to whoever needed it. An expedition demonstrates what is required and is a catastrophe as a delivery mechanism. So there are three states, not two: reach it, ask for it, or have it — and the middle one is what we named accommodation, which is the word Stimpunks' own page exists to criticise, since the problem is structural and the response is individual. Lyot did not apply for access to the corona; he built an instrument in which it is simply there, and the occulting disc is not a concession but where the precision comes from. Which is a curb cut: Michael Pachovas and friends poured cement into a crude ramp one Berkeley evening and rolled off into the night, and Berkeley cut its first official kerb on Telegraph Avenue in 1972 — while the sledgehammer version of that story is disability lore, not history, which a chain that spends a spread on smoothed retellings could not close on. Angela Glover Blackwell named the curb-cut effect in 2017, and the zine states plainly that it is an observation about what built-in conditions do and never the justification. Twenty-one spreads, twelve documented joints, four contested, one leap, a generated spine, and a “Not:” set that refuses the reading that barriers are valuable for what they reveal. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 56 The Noise Floor Stimpunks Zines every receiver has one, no design removes it, and the biggest discovery in modern cosmology arrived as noise two engineers spent ten months trying to get rid of A chain about a limit nobody beats, and the rooms we build as though it were free. Johnson and Nyquist, printed on facing pages in 1928. 15 spreads→ Details A chain about a limit nobody beats, and the rooms we build as though it were free. In July 1928 one volume of Physical Review printed the measurement and its explanation on facing pages — J. B. Johnson at 97–109, H. Nyquist at 110–113, whose first footnote is three words long: “See preceding paper.” Every conductor above absolute zero hisses, and Nyquist’s conclusion is that the effect is “a universal function of frequency, resistance and temperature and of these variables only” — not the metal, not the workmanship, since “one may be made of silver and the other of lead.” The available power in a band is kTB, and that is in the primary rather than a modern gloss on it. The part that usually goes missing is why it cannot be engineered away. Nyquist did not measure the floor, he deduced it — from the second law. Two resistors at one temperature must pass equal power both ways in every band, or a resonant circuit between them would move heat between equal-temperature bodies for free. The hiss is not permitted, it is required: a silent resistor would be a perpetual-motion machine, which is the same law that says you cannot un-stir the milk from the tea — and nobody files that under insufficient effort. Twenty years on, Shannon’s Theorem 17 turns the floor into a limit on meaning, with the sentence that closes the door: “It is not possible to transmit at a higher rate by any encoding system without a definite positive frequency of errors.” You cannot filter your way to clarity, and that is a theorem rather than a complaint. So engineering stopped hunting for a quieter resistor and changed the question: cool it, shield it, narrow the band — three moves, none of which asks the receiver to beat physics, all of which change the conditions the listening happens in. Which is exactly the instrument at Holmdel, where a maser and a reference load both sat in liquid helium at 4.2 K — a floor lowered deliberately so a remainder would mean something. A remainder was left: 3.5 ± 1.0 K, and the paper is mostly a list of what it was not, down to taping the seams with aluminium and walking a transmitter to ten positions on the ground. The pigeon story is corrected against its primary, and the correction is better than the version that travels: Wilson wrote that evicting them “obtained only a small reduction in antenna temperature” — the floor survived them, and that clause is the one that gets cut. The famous phrase “white dielectric material” is not in his Nobel lecture, and the birds are not in the 1965 paper at all. What could not be removed was “isotropic, unpolarized, and free from seasonal variations (July, 1964-April, 1965)”, and every property that made it impossible to eliminate is a property that made it the universe. Then the 1928 shape repeats mirrored — theory at 414–419, measurement at 419–421, thirty-seven years on. The most consequential discovery in modern cosmology arrived as noise two engineers spent ten months trying to get rid of. Meanwhile the transfer to rooms turns out not to be ours to make: ANSI/ASA S12.60 caps classroom background at 35 dBA because the profession already calls the quantity signal to noise ratio and wants about 15 dB of it — and its instruction is to lower the floor rather than amplify the teacher. Wilkins halved headaches by removing 100 Hz fluorescent flicker, with his own caveat that the harm fell on “a minority that is particularly affected”; Kim and de Dear found sound privacy the largest source of dissatisfaction in any building, and found open plan bought no more ease of interaction than a private office. The last two joints refuse to overclaim, on the page rather than in a footnote: the step to Autistic auditory experience is contested — there is no k for a nervous system — carried by Remington and Fairnie’s finding of increased auditory capacity, one mechanism producing both the distress and the ability, and by Rosas-Pérez’s 2026 acoustics thesis, in which no Autistic respondent among 311 noise-sensitive people found filtering easy — printed with her caveat that the whole sample was already sensitive. Her other finding is where the zine says the analogy breaks, and the break is worth more than the resemblance: no habituation, but an accumulation effect. Thermal noise is stationary; kTB is the same in the tenth hour as the first. The human pattern is cumulative. A resistor never gets tired of being warm — so the floor in a room is crueller than the floor in a circuit, not merely like it. Which also means “you’ll get used to it” is testable, and the exposure hypothesis under it rests on five participants, none noise-sensitive, and two pure tones. The closing analogy is leap, because physics entails nothing about who deserves a quiet room. What it does is remove an excuse. Fifteen spreads, ten documented joints, one contested, one leap, a spine the page calls schematic rather than letting it pass for a plot, and a coda pointing at the practice already written down. A rhyme, not a proof.

Zine No. 65 Everything Else Is Commentary Stimpunks Zines on kin selection, the level you account at, and a clause that fell off on the way to us Twice in the same argument an author wrote the hedge, and the hedge did not survive the trip. The third time, it was our own page. 12 links→ Details The chain the How We Got Here motive was written for, and the one where it turns on us. Darwin stated the two-level problem in Descent of Man (1871) and finished the paragraph "and this would be natural selection." Wynne-Edwards (1962) got the group-level version wrong and Williams (1966) was right to demolish it — a joint kept because any sympathetic account that skips it is selling something. Hamilton (1964) supplied inclusive fitness, which is good science and stays good science. Price (1970) then partitioned selection into within-group and between-group components, so by 1970 both frameworks sat in one formula, before the argument started. Then the other rail: Tom Maschler tried to talk Dawkins out of the title in 1975, and The Selfish Gene’s own introduction says the word to stress is “gene,” that the book “devotes more attention to altruism,” and — in the next sentence — that “altruism might well be favoured at other levels”, which is multilevel selection in everything but name. Chapter one refuses the naturalistic fallacy outright: “I am not advocating a morality based on evolution.” And Dawkins later retracts his own most-quoted sentence, calling “born selfish” misleading and asking readers to delete it. The correction was printed in the same book as the error and it did not travel. Wilson & Wilson (2007) then revived group selection on a careful formulation, stated “the main exception to this rule” immediately after their famous line — and forty pages later compressed it into a one-foot summary, echoing Rabbi Hillel, that drops both the exception and the word single. That compressed version is the one our own Altruism glossary carries, second-hand, and we found it while writing the spread about the mechanism. Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson (2010) and a reply co-signed by more than a hundred biologists show a field still arguing; and for standard models kin selection and multilevel selection turn out to be the same arithmetic added up in a different order. The turn is tagged leap: account at one level only and every other level’s contribution becomes invisible — not disproved, never entered — which decides what repair is thinkable. Nine documented joints, three contested, one leap. Refuses being read as anti-evidence, as anti-Dawkins, and as “group selection won.”

Zine No. 74 Oblivious to Encounter Stimpunks Zines on what the plantation had to remove before it could scale, and the mushroom that has defeated seventy years of trying Sameness is not what the world does when you leave it alone. It is the expensive thing, and somebody paid for it. 10 links→ Details Sugarcane is propagated by pushing a cut piece into the ground, so every plant is the previous plant again — it can be multiplied forever without anything ever meeting anything, which is what Anna Tsing means by “comparatively self-contained, oblivious to encounter.” Portuguese Brazil assembled that cane with land emptied by conquest and with enslaved Africans taken far enough that there were “no established routes for escape.” This chain withholds its own format on that link, visibly and on purpose, because what was done there is not a mechanism for illustrating an argument. Interchangeability was not discovered in people; it was produced in them, by force, because the mill needed it as an input. Sidney Mintz, read at pp. 47–48, documents Barbados holdings cut into equal ten-acre parcels harvested seriatim “assuring a steady flow of cane to the mill,” mills that “operated unceasingly,” a work week broken only from Saturday night to Monday — and part of that pace driven by a belief about boiling syrup he calls “somewhat misleading,” so the demand had already outrun the chemistry it claimed to serve. His verdict is printed here with the hedge he put on it: “I believe it was probably the closest thing to industry that was typical of the seventeenth century.” Industry before the homeland — missed, he says, partly because scholars looking for the factory “began with the artisans and craftsmen of Europe.” Tsing names the resulting idea of progress scalability, the ability to change scale “without any change in project frames,” and states its price: it “banishes meaningful diversity, that is, diversity that might change things.” Then the rails cross. Matsutake has defeated seventy years and millions of yen; the 2020 Mycoscience review still reports cultivation “mostly unsuccessful,” and the only field successes used pine already colonised — so the only way to farm it is to already have the relationship and wait. And in Japan it was lost by abandonment: fossil fuel replaced firewood, the woodlands went shady, the pines died, and by the mid-1970s it was rare — a support removed by improvements aimed at something else. The turn is tagged leap: an accommodation is, by definition, a difference that requires the frame to change, which is exactly what a scalable system is specified to exclude. Nine documented joints, one contested, one leap.

Zine No. 79 Four Decimal Places Stimpunks Zines · chain A chain from atmospheric convection to a paperback subtitle — on the ratio at which a human life was said to begin going well, and the part-time student who read the primary source. 2.9013 was never a measurement of anybody. It was a property of the equations, and would have been the same number if every person studied had answered differently. 14 spreads · 8d 1c 1l→ Details Edward Lorenz published Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow in 1963 — three equations for atmospheric convection whose solutions never repeat, and a real result checked exhaustively for sixty years. What travelled fastest afterwards was not the mathematics but the register: nonlinear dynamics acquired a rigorous-sounding authority outside physics, difficult for a non-specialist to check. In 1999 Marcial Losada fitted Lorenz-type equations to speech coded as positive or negative in business meetings — equations derived for fluid convection, applied to things people say at work, on the justification that both are complicated. Being complicated is not a shared mechanism. In 2005, in American Psychologist, Barbara Fredrickson and Losada joined broaden-and-build to that model and produced a number: people at or above a positive-to-negative ratio of 2.9013 flourish; below it they languish; above 11.6346 flourishing fails again. Four decimal places, on the ratio at which a human life begins to go well. The precision is doing specific work — a number given that precisely claims an instrument was involved. Fredrickson’s 2009 trade book then rounded it away on its own cover: the 3 to 1 ratio that will change your life. The four decimals bought credibility at the journal and were friction at the bookshop. Then a part-time student. Around 2012 Nick Brown, in his fifties, taking an applied positive psychology master’s at the University of East London with no mathematics past school, met the paper on his course and could not find where the data entered the equations. So he went and read Lorenz 1963. With the original in front of him it was visible: the equations had no connection to the emotion data, and would generate the same numbers whatever the participants had said. He wrote to Alan Sokal, of the 1996 Social Text hoax; with Harris Friedman they published in American Psychologist in July 2013. The nonlinear modelling and both ratios were withdrawn as invalid — Losada did not co-sign — while what survives remains contested, Carol Nickerson arguing in 2018 that there is no empirical evidence for critical positivity ratios at all. The chain judges the paper and not the people. Lorenz was right; borrowing across fields is how much good work happens; Fredrickson corrected her own paper, which is the system working, slowly and embarrassingly, which is the only way it works. The failure worth studying is not that somebody was wrong. It is that it took eight years and a stranger. The final joint is marked leap and argues that the precision was the persuasion, and the precision was the empty part — which matters most for people already being scored, since a ratio for flourishing is an instrument for finding those not flourishing correctly. Six refusals, including that this is not an argument against measurement (the method worked), not “do your own research” (Brown read the source the experts cited, which is the opposite move), and not a claim that anyone was a fraud. Spread two draws a boundary with our own shelf: Five Times a Crab borrows attractor from the same 1963 paper, openly and with the source named. Same paper, two borrowings, and the difference is whether you say which one you are doing. Fourteen spreads, ten joints — eight documented, one contested, one leap — and a generated spine. A closing spread that is deliberately not a link asks whether the number reached the classroom, where 4:1 and 5:1 praise-to-correction ratios are repeated throughout positive behaviour support. No citation from that literature to Fredrickson & Losada could be established, and the spread says so rather than inventing one. What is there is a genre with its own ancestry — Gottman’s empirical 5:1, Flora (2000) — and the field’s own verdict, from Sabey, Charlton & Charlton (2019): good face validity, and “a lack of empirical support for any specific ratio.” A chain can be cut at the retraction; a genre reproduces without a source. Positive greetings at the door is the worked example, and the tell is what it measured — academic engaged time and disruptive behaviour, not whether a child felt welcome. With Ehrenreich on positive thinking as an apology for the crueler aspects of the market economy, whose flip side is a harsh insistence on personal responsibility. A rhyme, not a proof.
There Have Been So Many Earths

Zine No. 84 There Have Been So Many Earths Stimpunks Zines · chain Nine links from Theia to Chicxulub, with the state of the land drawn at each one — and the finding that only three of them were moments. Oxygenic photosynthesis was invented once and took something like a billion years to change the sky. Pangea was a hundred and forty-five million years of being a continent. The two events everybody can name are the two whose bars cannot be drawn. 15 spreads · 6d 2c 1l · scroll→ Details The chain is chronological and the sections are as long as the things they describe.
