This is the collection’s second scroll zine, and the second time the form has been the argument: a section’s height is the duration it covers, so Chicxulub is one screen you fall past and the wait between oxygenic photosynthesis and the sky changing colour is three, most of it empty, with a rail down the side so the emptiness reads as elapsed time. Hank Green asked what the most important thing that ever happened was, and defined important usefully — how much depended on it, how easily it could have gone otherwise, and the sharper move underneath: importance is not a property of the universe, so the question is what had to happen for mattering to exist at all. With Cali Moore (PBS Eons) and Joe Hansen (Be Smart), the candidates were the origin of life, the eukaryotic cell, the Earth–Moon system, Chicxulub, the ribosome and oxygenic photosynthesis. Put them in order and something the list format hides comes out. Only three were moments, and all three are impacts — and even those are not three of a kind: Chicxulub is in the ground with a crater and an iridium layer, Theia is an inference from a moon that has never been found, and the rock that may have carried life is imagined, standing in for a transition nobody can describe. One documented, one inferred, one imagined. Everything else was a duration. Photosystem II learned to pull electrons out of water once, and the sky did not change for something like a billion years, because oxygen was consumed on contact by a planet with an enormous appetite; the invention and the consequence are two different events. Eukaryogenesis was, in Green’s own words, a bunch of things in succession, and the date is a neighbourhood rather than a date. Pangea was over a hundred million years of being a continent — roughly a C curled round the Tethys, with a desert down its equator so effective that one landmass still held two worlds — and its assembly dried out the wetlands where lycopsids grew a hundred feet tall, leaving only the ones that could shrink. Two corrections the source did not carry. Its citation for earliest life is Nutman et al. (2016) on 3.7 Ga Isua stromatolites; Allwood et al. (2018) went back to the same rocks and found deformation structures, some of the bumps pointing downward, which stromatolites do not do — the widely accepted floor is the younger 3.48 Ga Dresser Formation. And the famous thirty seconds later and it would have hit ocean is not a result: it traces to a 2017 BBC documentary, not to Kaiho & Oshima’s ~13% of Earth’s surface or Collins et al.’s 45–60° trajectory, and the piece refuses it rather than using it — a stopwatch is a different kind of claim from a probability across a planet. A globe on every link shows the land at that moment, dashed and faint before 1 Ga and reconstructed after it, because that is where Merdith et al. (2021) can hold a full-plate model together and a crisp coastline older than that is an invention wearing a map’s clothes. The art carries its own epistemics, the way the joint tags do. Nine links: six documented, two contested, one leap, plus a leap named inside Link 9 and declined. The turn is the demand for a moment — when did you know, when were you diagnosed, what happened to you — every version of which assumes an impact. Mostly there is no crater; mostly a difference met an environment with no room in it, over years, and the word arrived long after the thing it named. The diagnosis is not the event; it is the sinks finally filling. Ends on four models of the next supercontinent, drawn all four and chosen none, because Earth has never held an arrangement and is not holding this one. Endosymbiosis itself is No. 7’s argument and is pointed at rather than repeated. A rhyme, not a proof.
The Lizard That Was Never There

Zine No. 85 The Lizard That Was Never There Stimpunks Zines · chain On a word that meant “border”, the diagram it turned into, and the eight years by which the refutation beat the bestseller. Karten showed the bird brain carries the same circuit in 1969. The Dragons of Eden won its Pulitzer in 1978. Fifty-one years later it was still in the textbooks. 16 spreads · 10d 2c 1l→ Details Two rails — what was told about the brain and what was observed in it — and the shape is the argument: the observed rail goes live in 1969 and the told rail runs another fifty-one years without touching it. Broca (1878) names a rim of cortex le grand lobe limbique; limbus means border and he claims no function. Papez (1937) proposes a circuit for emotion. MacLean (1952) fuses them into a system — a name for a place becomes a name for a job — then in the 1960s stacks three brains by evolutionary age, each supposedly independently conscious, and chronology pointed at living animals becomes a rank. Karten (1969) shows the bird forebrain has the same neuron types and wiring as mammalian neocortex, in nuclei rather than layers, eight years before Sagan’s The Dragons of Eden carried the model into everyday speech. This site is named out of Sagan’s line about star stuff, and the piece publishes that rather than keeping a clean story. Finlay & Darlington (1995): 131 species, one conserved developmental schedule, nothing bolted on. 2005: the field renames most of the bird forebrain because the old labels were arguments. 2020: 14 of 20 intro psych textbooks discuss brain evolution and 86% of those get something wrong. 2026: 182 mammalian species, and the real division is a trade — olfactory system against neocortex at r = −0.63 — driven not by age but by the shape of the information, since sight, touch and hearing arrive with space in them and smell does not. The armadillo spends its room on smell and is not a failed monkey. The one leap is the last spread.

2 September 2026 Until There Were Ten Glimmers · Ryan Boren A thing that never changes and has no counterexample is very hard to tell apart from a rule. Saturn's hexagon was the only one of its kind for forty-four years. There is now a decagon at the south pole — and it is not the hexagon mirrored. Essay · publication day→ Details The tidy version of this story is two poles, two polygons, how balanced, and the paper refuses to let you have it. Saturn's hexagon sits near 78.5°N, was found by Voyager in 1980–81, and has been in every image since — a lifetime exceeding 44 years with no counterexample anywhere on the planet. The south pole was tipped out of view from mid-2012 until 2023; when it came back there was a ten-sided wave at 58°S to 63°S, wavelength 16,782 ± 1,100 km. But it is not the hexagon mirrored. Where the hexagon's sides and corners are equally contrasted, the decagon is “not uniform in longitude”: three corners very prominent, four less so, three barely defined. Its corners oscillate on a mean 32.5-day period with amplitudes of 4.6° to 8.4°, and the wobble travels — each corner peaking about 2.7 days after its neighbour — which the authors call “a complex dynamical behavior, never observed in the hexagon.” It did not exist in Saturn's previous year, and it “could be a transient evolving phenomenon, whereas the hexagon is a robust wave.” Two candidate causes and no way yet to choose: a jet instability, or a 4,000-km red anticyclone at 55°S resembling one Voyager saw in 1981. Also: a shape drifting at 2.5 m/s inside a 116 m/s jet, so the wind goes through the corners and the corners stay put; a jet whose strength has not changed substantially since 1981; and two of the fourteen authors affiliated to a private observatory in the Australian outback and a French astronomy association rather than a university. The turn is epistemic: one example, held still for forty-four years, had looked exactly like a law.

31 August 2026 Came Back Clean Glimmers · Ryan Boren The pair that comes back clean is the one to worry about. A thousand people buried two thousand pairs of cotton underpants across Switzerland. Land use mattered more than anything else — and the ground that came back cleanest was the lawn. Essay · 4 diagrams→ Details The intuition runs the wrong way, which is why the finding is worth having. Cotton is nearly pure cellulose, so a buried pair of underpants is a standardised meal: how much disappears tells you how much life was down there eating. About a thousand volunteers ran it at a thousand Swiss sites for the University of Zurich and Agroscope, under the excellent project name Beweisstück Unterhose — Proof by Underpants — and land use turned out to matter more than soil chemistry, texture, climate or altitude. Private gardens had the most soil life of any land type studied. Lawns had the least. The most managed surface most of us own is the deadest, which is No. 8's argument about monoculture arriving as a measurement rather than a metaphor. Around 240 of the citizen scientists are listed as co-authors — not acknowledged, not thanked in a footnote, authors — which is a claim about who counts as a knower and is the methods section rather than a slogan. Also: the Tea Bag Index and the published critique that says macrofauna damage gets counted as decomposition, an objection that applies harder to a whole pair of underpants; the 59%-of-global-biodiversity figure printed with its ±15 and its live argument; and the burial protocol, so you can run it in your own garden. Fig. 1 is adapted from the paper's own scale under CC BY 4.0 — the same licence question Flying Free asked and could not clear, asked again and answered yes.

31 August 2026 None of Those Miles Glimmers · Ryan Boren It's happening. It's really happening. It's finally happening. Sunlight is the cheapest electricity we have ever made — with a fourteen-word condition the headline keeps dropping. Four diagrams, a learning curve derived from the data, and a supply line with no gate in it. Essay · 4 diagrams→ Details The good news is real and it is conditional, and the piece keeps both halves. The IEA's 2020 finding was that “for projects with low cost financing that tap high quality resources, solar PV is now the cheapest source of electricity in history” — and the version that travels drops the fourteen-word condition and swaps electricity for energy, which silently extends a claim about 22% of the system to all of it. That is the same fault Rainbow Serpents is about, two days later in a different field, and this page nearly committed it. The mechanism is a learning curve, and it is derived here rather than quoted: module prices fell from $128.27 to $0.258 per watt between 1975 and 2024 — a factor of 497 — while cumulative capacity grew 3.4 million times, 21.7 doublings. Fitted on log–log axes that is 23.5% off the price per doubling at R² = 0.979. It is called Swanson's law and it is not a law: prices rose in six of those fifty years, 2022 by 10.2%. Nobody invented cheap solar; thousands of people iterated it into existence in public, and two governments paid for the early expensive units. Also: silicon as the eighth most abundant element in the universe and a product of massive stars, so a panel is star stuff arranged to catch starlight, both halves literal; the 250-year sequence of US energy crossovers, read twice, because a crossover is not a subtraction; community solar as a watering hole; and Bill McKibben's line about ninety-three million miles, quoted from a dated source after finding that its three circulating versions do not match each other.

30 August 2026 Flying Free Glimmers · Ryan Boren I needed to witness something hopeful and wonder-filled, something to make me feel good about humanity. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope left Kennedy at 7:26 in the morning, bound for Lagrange Two. On the teamwork that put it there, and what a survey telescope is actually for. Essay · launch day→ Details Roman lifted off on a Falcon Heavy and separated 31 minutes later, beginning a hundred-day cruise to a halo orbit 1.5 million kilometres out. Two of the three things it is built to measure have no agreed explanation at all — NASA's own page calls dark energy “just the name that astronomers gave to the mysterious ‘something’” — and the exoplanet census works only because two methods with opposite blind spots run at once. The best fact is the one usually left out: nothing parks at Lagrange Two. It is an unstable equilibrium, and an unattended spacecraft drifts off in about three weeks, so Roman will fire thrusters on a schedule, forever, with fuel budgeted for it from the start. Nobody files that under failure to be independent. A rhyme, not a proof. The first entry in a new collection.

Field Guide No. 6 A Field Guide to Symbioses Star Stuff Field Guides Mutual aid, written into biology. Twelve partnerships across the tree of life — fungi and roots trading underground, a cleaner fish trusted by predators who could swallow it, the fig and its wasp. 12 symbioses→ Details Mutual aid, written into biology — twelve partnerships across the tree of life, read as mutual aid. Fungi and roots trading underground, bacteria making soil, a cleaner fish trusted by predators who could swallow it, algae building reefs that shelter a quarter of ocean life, the fig and its wasp that cannot live without each other. Interdependence is the rule, not the exception: Kropotkin showed mutual aid is a factor of evolution; Margulis, that life “took over the globe not by combat, but by networking.” This isn't “nature is nice” — parasites are real too, and the ghost pipe (Monotropa uniflora) is the honest one-way case, a myco-heterotroph that only takes, modelling receiving without reciprocating — and a bridge to monotropism (with Helen Edgar's tribute to Dinah Murray). It's that nothing living stands alone. What biology has always done, disability-justice communities name and practice: the human specimen is our own care webs and spoon shares (Spade, Mingus, Piepzna-Samarasinha, Kafai, Lewis), and a closing coda swaps the language of management for the language of living systems — symbiosis over competition, competency networks over leadership, coordination over management. Each entry maps who gives what and gets what, with full field notes. Solidarity, not charity; interdependence, not independence.
A Field Guide to Nervous Systems

Field Guide No. 7 A Field Guide to Nervous Systems Star Stuff Field Guides There is no standard nervous system. Eleven ways to have one — the jellyfish's centreless net, the octopus's mind spread through its arms, the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons. Companion to No. 27. 11 systems→ Details Eleven ways to have a nervous system — the companion catalogue to Every Nervous System (Zine No. 27). The jellyfish's centreless net, older than brains; the octopus's mind spread through its arms (two-thirds of its neurons outside the brain); the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons; the honeybee's million-neuron cognition and swarm mind; a jumping spider planning routes with a brain smaller than a pinhead; an electric fish reading a sense we lack; the star-nosed mole's 22-ray touch-world; the corvid's forebrain packed denser than a primate's (Olkowicz 2016); the elephant's 257 billion neurons, almost all cerebellar; a slime mold solving mazes with no neurons at all; and us — about 86 billion neurons, one arrangement among many, not the top of any ladder. Neuroscience hides verdicts in its words — “primitive,” “simple,” “lower” — but the animal kingdom keeps no standard nervous system. Each entry maps its architecture, reframes the deficit reading (“sounds like / actually”), and carries full field notes. There is no standard nervous system.
A Field Guide to the Ways of Migrating

Field Guide No. 8 A Field Guide to the Ways of Migrating Star Stuff Field Guides Say “migration” and most of us picture one shape. Almost nothing does that. Fifteen ways of migrating — the Arctic tern flies ~71,000 km a year and refuses the straight line. The companion catalogue to Always Migrating (No. 30). 15 ways→ Details Fifteen ways of migrating — the companion catalogue to Always Migrating (Zine No. 30). Say “migration” and most of us picture one shape: a long line, north in spring, back in autumn. Almost nothing does that. The Arctic tern flies ~71,000 km a year and refuses the straight line, riding wind in vast S-shaped detours because the long way is the cheap way. A juvenile godwit crossed 13,560 km in 11 days without landing — held with care, since it shrinks its own organs to do it and a migrant who rests is not a lesser migrant. No monarch finishes the round trip: several short-lived generations work north and one “super” generation, living 8–9 months instead of weeks, flies the whole way back. Salmon find one stream by the magnetic field they imprinted on, then die and carry the ocean up into the forest. The largest migration on Earth is a few hundred metres straight up, every night, in the dark — distance was never the measure. Spiderlings rig silk and let atmospheric electricity carry them; trees migrate at metres a year, seed by seed; the Sahara crosses an ocean as dust and fertilises the Amazon; a star gets handed to a wider orbit and the Sun is probably not from here. The centre of the guide is partial migration — populations holding both migrants and residents, described in the literature as the commonest form, the one all others derive from. Variation within a population isn't the anomaly; it's the mechanism. Closes on us: the crossing made in place, when the word arrives and every year behind you rearranges. Held with care throughout — this reads migration as a way of being, never as a frame for forced human displacement. Fifteen entries, route-shape diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set.
A Field Guide to Being a Shark

Field Guide No. 9 A Field Guide to Being a Shark Star Stuff Field Guides One clade, one body plan, four hundred million years — and inside it, almost nothing holds. Twelve ways to be a shark, written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. Companion to Zines 32, 33 and 34. 12 ways→ Details Twelve ways to be a shark — the companion catalogue to the shark set (Zines 32, 33 and 34), written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. These are not distant relatives: one clade, one body plan, four hundred million years. And inside it, almost nothing holds still. The whale shark reaches ~18.8 m and lives on plankton; the dwarf lanternshark tops out near 20 cm and erases its own silhouette by lighting its belly to match the light coming down. The goblin shark cannot give chase in the dark, so it doesn't — the jaws fire forward at up to 3.1 m/s, the fastest protrusion known in any shark. The thresher hunts with the far end of itself, whipping its tail overhead to stun several fish at once. The epaulette shark walks between tide pools on its fins and rides out near-anoxia by suppressing its own metabolism. The cookiecutter, at fifty centimetres, takes a neat plug out of animals hundreds of times its size and everything swims off alive. The bonnethead eats seagrass and — tested in 2018 — digests it, which made "sharks are carnivores" a category nobody had checked rather than a finding. Two entries are here because of a phrase rather than an animal: the great hammerhead's head does not sharpen its electrosense (tested directly, it widens the search area instead), and the frilled shark is not a living fossil, because nothing alive is. One points up, one points down, and both skip what the animal is doing. Twelve entries, schematic diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set. There is no standard shark.
A Field Guide to Being a Turtle

Field Guide No. 10 A Field Guide to Being a Turtle Star Stuff Field Guides Almost every entry is a thing a turtle is supposed to have and doesn't. Twelve ways to be a turtle, and five turtles people made — the leatherback has no bony carapace at all. Companion to Everywhere That Turtles Go (No. 35). 12 + 5→ Details Twelve ways to be a turtle, and five turtles people made — the companion catalogue to Everywhere That Turtles Go (No. 35). Almost every entry is a thing a turtle is supposed to have and doesn't. The leatherback has no bony carapace at all, just hundreds of interlocking ossicles in oily skin — and it dives to 1,280 m and holds its body up to 18 °C above the sea around it, which gives it the largest range of any reptile alive. The mata mata has weak jaw muscles and almost no tongue and is a superb predator, because it never bites: the mouth is a pump, and every "weakness" on the list is a component of it. The Fitzroy River turtle takes about 70% of its oxygen in through two enlarged sacs at the far end of itself. The Chinese softshell excretes urea through the lining of its mouth rather than its kidneys — the head-dipping that looks like drinking is the opposite of drinking. Painted turtle hatchlings spend their first winter in a nest below −10 °C by supercooling, and what decides whether they live is not how tough they are but what touches them. And the Arrau was filed as a silent animal until somebody brought a hydrophone: 2,122 recorded sounds in eleven types, hatchlings calling from inside the egg, and females coming and answering — the first evidence of post-hatching parental care in any turtle. The silence was ours. The last entry is the bill: Rafetus swinhoei, two or three animals left, the last known female dead in April 2023. The five turtles people made — Turtle Island, ao, Kurma (a pivot for churning, not a world-bearer), Great A'Tuin, and a Larrakia Star Dreaming we cite rather than retell — get a separate section and a deliberately different card, because they are not five drafts of one story. There is no standard turtle.
A Field Guide to Being a Tortoise

Field Guide No. 11 A Field Guide to Being a Tortoise Star Stuff Field Guides An arc that runs from the Moon to a graveyard to a beginning. Twelve land tortoises. It opens on 15 September 1968, when Zond 5 carried two Soviet steppe tortoises around the far side of the Moon and brought them back alive. 12 tortoises→ Details Twelve land tortoises — Testudinidae — and an arc that runs from the Moon to a graveyard to a beginning. It opens where this collection has to open: on 15 September 1968, Zond 5 carried two Soviet steppe tortoises around the far side of the Moon and brought them back alive, two months before Apollo 8 carried any human. They lost about a tenth of their body weight and were otherwise fine. Then the ordinary astonishments of a slow land animal: the gopher tortoise digs burrows over fourteen metres long that more than 350 other species live in, which is the argument for building rooms that fit whoever needs them most, stated in reptile. The pancake tortoise has a shell whose bone is full of holes and is the fastest and best-climbing tortoise there is — and the beloved story that it inflates itself inside a rock crevice is now believed to be wrong, so the guide says so instead of repeating it. In July 2020 an Aldabra giant tortoise was filmed hunting and swallowing a tern chick, the first deliberate hunt ever recorded in a wild tortoise, which turned "tortoises are herbivores" from a law back into a summary of what we had happened to watch. Jonathan hatched around 1832 and is still on the lawn. The speckled padloper is six centimetres and complete. And then four entries marked as unfinished, because their endings are decisions rather than facts: the star tortoise, most trafficked tortoise on Earth and trafficked because it is beautiful; the ploughshare, whose shell conservationists engrave to spoil it for the market, and it may not be working; Lonesome George, who died in 2012 and took Pinta with him; and Fernanda, found alive in 2019 after 113 years of "extinct." It ends on Île aux Aigrettes, where an Aldabra tortoise is doing an extinct Mauritian tortoise's job — 529 hatchlings in eleven years. Not restoring what was lost. Finding another way for the function to happen.

Field Guide No. 12 My Monotropic Galaxy Star Stuff Field Guides A guest guide, and the first whose subject is a person. Helen Edgar's deep-field image overlaid with constellation lines and an index of twenty named features of her own Autistic life — rehoused as the field guide it already was. 20 constellations→ Details A guest guide, and the first whose subject is a person. Helen Edgar made a deep-field image of space overlaid with constellation lines and an index of twenty named features of her own Autistic life — and the form she reached for is already a field guide, so this rehouses it as one, in her words, at her numbers. Dark Matter Field is “the weight of neuronormativity before I had words for it.” Stellar Current is the heart of the galaxy, the deep monotropic flow where “my whole bodymind system exhales and time dissolves.” Pebbling Cluster is how she shows love, after the way penguins offer pebbles. Time Drift is lived time “closer to superposition than sequence.” Friction Field is the exhaustion of having needs the world was not designed to meet. Emergence Point is what surfaces when something is finally ready, “trusted rather than forced, arriving in its own time, on its own terms.” It carries no “sounds like / actually” table, and that is the argument rather than an omission. Every other guide here has one, because that table corrects a verdict somebody else handed down — and there is no verdict in these twenty to correct. They are one person's naming of her own life. Field Guide No. 10 found the limit first with its five turtles people made; this is that rule at full scale, and the first guide in the collection to carry it end to end. The astronomy is not gone, it is simply not on the face: open any card and the real object is waiting — galaxies rotating too fast for their visible mass, the quantum tunnelling without which the Sun could not shine, pebble accretion building planets out of small offerings, ram-pressure stripping taking a galaxy's gas because of the medium it is moving through rather than any fault in the galaxy. Five of the twenty have already grown into pieces of their own here, so the index doubles as the hub they hang off. Ends where Helen ends, with the thing she asks for twice: draw your own. Twenty constellations, an index map, a “Not:” refusals set. There is no standard galaxy.
A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Alone

Field Guide No. 14 A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Alone Star Stuff Field Guides A lone wolf is not an outcast. It is a disperser. Twelve ways of keeping your own company among our Terran kin, grown from Betsy Selvam's Stimpunks essay Lone Wolfing: The Joys of Autistic Solitude. 12 ways of being alone→ Details Twelve ways of keeping your own company among our Terran kin, grown from Betsy Selvam's Stimpunks essay Lone Wolfing: The Joys of Autistic Solitude. A lone wolf is not an outcast. It is a disperser — typically nine to thirty-six months old, one of the roughly 15–20% of any wolf population currently between territories, crossing the neutral buffer ground to find a mate and found a pack. The animal we named the loner after was always on its way somewhere. The guide is sorted by four conditions it did not invent: writing in The Atlantic in 2017, Brent Crane quotes the developmental psychologist Kenneth Rubin — solitude is productive only if it is voluntary, if emotion can be regulated within it, if one can rejoin when one wants to, and if relationships outside it are maintained. Crane's own gloss is the hinge: the difference between rejuvenation and suffering is the quality of reflection available, and the ability to come back. So: social bees are fewer than 10% of all bee species (Danforth, Minckley & Neff, 2019) — we built the entire hive metaphor on the outlier. One sweat bee nests solitary in some populations and eusocial in others, and reared side by side each keeps its own way. Giant pandas aim over 80% of their scent marks at animal trails, going out of their way to be found by animals they will never meet — asynchronous is not the fallback channel, it is the majority channel. Territorial neighbours become dear enemies (Fisher, 1954), and sometimes nasty ones (Temeles, 1994), which is kept because both are true. Fission–fusion parties change membership hourly and nobody calls it instability. Cicadas spend seventeen years alone underground to be loud together for a fortnight. Pumas share kills with non-kin and are 7.7 times more likely to share with someone who once shared with them (Elbroch et al., Science Advances, 2017). Orangutan party size tracks fruit availability rather than species — you change the field, not the animal. A wandering albatross takes a sabbatical year at sea and divorces at 0.3%. Then the thirteenth card, which gets no reframe table on purpose: the octopus settlements at Octopolis and Octlantis are not a secret society but dens crowded onto the only hard substrate for miles, with evictions at the edges. Proximity is not company; proximity plus scarcity is a fight. Four gates, a “Not:” refusals set that declines the syntaxin 1a bait outright. There is no standard amount of company.

Field Guide No. 15 A Field Guide to Nests Star Stuff Field Guides Sorted by where the labour actually goes — and the catalogue disagrees with the word. Thirteen homes among our Terran kin. We began meaning to sort by material, and the material sort kept failing: a hermit crab supplies none, and neither does a gall wasp. 13 ways of having a home→ Details Thirteen homes among our Terran kin, sorted by where the labour actually goes — and the catalogue disagrees with the word. We began meaning to sort by material, and the material sort kept failing, because a hermit crab supplies none and a gall wasp supplies none either. What varies is who does the work. The companion to What Looks Like Chaos (Zine No. 55), which asks how a nest gets built; this one asks what gets to count as one, and the answer is much wider. Built: a ten-centimetre pufferfish making a two-metre geometric court on the seabed that divers photographed for years before anyone believed the builder was that small (Kawase, Okata & Ito, Scientific Reports, 2013) — the pattern is not decorative, it sorts fine sand into the centre, which is the part the female inspects. Then the correction that reorganised the whole guide: a termite mound is uninhabited. That is the paper's own word. Fungus-farming termites build massive empty towers above their subterranean nests, and the daily swing of solar heating drives convection through the tunnel network (Ocko, King, Andreen, Bardunias, Turner, Soar & Mahadevan, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2017). The most-photographed animal architecture on Earth is routinely called the wrong kind of thing: it is not shelter, it is infrastructure — closer to a lung than a house. Borrowed: a hermit crab contributes no material to any home it will ever occupy, and when a single shell arrives the crabs gather and queue beside it in descending size order, so that when the largest moves in the whole line moves up at once. Lewis and Rotjan tested the prediction that matters and found it held — vacancy chains distribute benefits across many participants rather than to the first taker. The crab that waits is not being passive; it is standing in the only position from which the chain works. The largest bird nest on record, 2.9 m wide, 6 m deep and over two tonnes, was accumulated across decades until it was more than the tree could hold, which is inheritance and its cost in one object. And a woodpecker's ecological job is not its own nest but the vacancies it leaves behind for everything that cannot excavate. Induced: a gall is oak tissue that the insect made the oak build — the inducer injects effectors including phytohormones that redirect the plant's development, and different wasp species induce distinctively different galls on the same host, which is why the literature calls a gall an extended phenotype of the insect. And not building at all evolved independently at least seven separate times in birds: three times in the cuckoos, once in honeyguides, once in a duck, twice in songbirds (Sorenson & Payne, 2002). A thing discovered seven times over is not a mistake, and that is the sentence the guide would most like a reader to carry. Secreted, or worn: a swiftlet builds from nothing but its own hardened saliva, and the entry states plainly that this is why the species is farmed and harvested at industrial scale rather than leaving it as a footnote. An emperor penguin has no structure at all — an egg on two feet under a fold of belly skin, with the shelter being the huddle, whose walls are other penguins and which moves. If somewhere-to-be requires a structure, the emperor has nowhere and manifestly succeeds, so the definition has to give: some of us have been housed by other people rather than by rooms, and it counted. And a trapdoor spider known as Number 16 held one silk-lined burrow for 43 years, the longest life recorded for any spider — a record that is really about Barbara York Main, who began following that population in 1974 and kept returning for four decades. A long quiet life in one small place is invisible unless somebody decides it is worth watching. Not a nest: the bower, which every list of animal architecture files as the finest nest alive. No egg is ever laid in it and nothing lives there; the female builds the actual nest elsewhere, alone. It is a theatre with deliberate forced perspective — objects graded outward so they subtend a more even visual angle from where she stands (Endler, Endler & Doerr, Current Biology, 2010). We have spent a century calling a stage set a house. And the fourteenth card gets no reframe table, which is a fourth distinct reason for withholding the apparatus. The rooms people build are not graded here. Running a sounds-like/actually over somebody's own room would make us the observer in the doorway with the clipboard — the exact figure No. 55 spends ten spreads indicting — and No. 55 is also explicit that not every mess is a nest, since burnout collapses the architecture and from the doorway the ruins look identical to the curated version. Nobody can sort those two on sight, and the people most certain they can are the reason the guide has a refusals list. The weaver appears in one card that hands off to No. 55 rather than re-running it; the beaver is deliberately absent, already spent in Minor Worlds. Thirteen lineages, thirteen incompatible methods, none ranked, several of them the ones a tidy observer would call failures. The ninth guide to arrive independently at the same sentence: there is no standard nest.

Field Guide No. 16 A Field Guide to Eggs Field Guide · 15 + 1 · companion to No. 57 The egg you are imagining occupies one band out of five. Fifteen beginnings among our Terran kin, sorted by how far the egg gets from the body — because a material sort was tried first and collapsed. 15 ways of beginning→ Details Fifteen beginnings among our Terran kin, sorted by how far the egg gets from the body — and the catalogue disagrees with the picture in your head. The egg you are imagining occupies one band out of five. A material sort was tried first and collapsed, because a hen's egg and a common murre's are the same object by every material measure. So: eggs that never leave, eggs grown over by skin, eggs carried, eggs set down and guarded, eggs left. In the first band, live birth turns out to have evolved at least 115 separate times in lizards and snakes alone — against roughly 140 origins in all vertebrates — and about a fifth of squamate species lay no egg at all; whether the transition ever runs backwards is genuinely contested and is left open here. A sand tiger shark shows an egg working as food: the mother goes on ovulating after mating, up to ten embryos begin, and two are born. Syngnathid fishes are the only vertebrates with male pregnancy, and it is literal — a placenta-like pouch, embryos joined to the father's circulation, a measured patrotrophy index of 1, and immune suppression to tolerate them. A Surinam toad's eggs are pressed into her back and her own skin grows over each one and builds it a lid; there is no tadpole stage, and the toadlets push the lids off after three to five months. Giant water bug eggs are cemented to the male's dorsum, and the carrying is plumbing rather than devotion: unattended eggs die every time, in air or underwater. A Banggai cardinalfish father holds the clutch in his mouth for a month and eats nothing, because a mouth cannot be a foregut and a nursery at once. Then the band everybody pictures, where four of five are strange: a kiwi egg is 15 to 22 per cent of the female (an ostrich's is 2 to 3); a monotreme egg is leathery and porous enough to be fed through its own shell, with ten days of egg followed by four to seven months of milk; and a deep-sea octopus in Monterey Canyon was revisited eighteen times over fifty-three months, guarding one clutch, never seen to feed. The murre is the entry that indicts us rather than an animal: the pointed egg was explained for decades by rolling in a tight arc, Ingold found little support in 1980, and Birkhead's objection is embarrassingly simple — the arc is wider than the ledge. Stability on a slope and shell strength do the work instead. In the last band, walking away turns out not to be the failure state: a megapode chick hatches under 40 to 150 cm of compost, digs out unaided in a median forty hours, and can fly the same day; a brine shrimp cyst waits up to eighteen dry years and resumes where it stopped; and a cuckoo's shell has a second job no other egg here has, since it must survive being looked at — matched to host retinal function rather than to our eyes, by host-specific female lineages, with the arms-race framing now under live challenge. Then the sixteenth card, dashed, with no reframe table: the egg-crack accounts, borrowed from trans communities and credited as unowned, because there is no mistaken verdict about the morning your own life rearranged itself behind you. One thing the biology does supply is a limit rather than a licence — across birds, squamates, turtles, crocodilians and the echidna, the tool that opens an egg is on the inside. You cannot do it for anyone. You can only be audible. The tenth guide to arrive independently at the same sentence: there is no standard egg.

Field Guide No. 17 A Field Guide to Resting Field Guide · 15 + 2 · companion to No. 59 there is no standard way to rest — not an amount, not a posture, not an organ Fifteen ways of resting among our Terran kin, sorted by what is doing the resting. An animal with no brain and no clock. A bird ten months airborne. A squirrel below freezing. And the famous twenty-hour bat, which is one measurement at one temperature. 15 entries→ Details Companion to No. 59, and it asks the question the zine assumes an answer to: what does resting actually look like, across kin who share almost no anatomy? The bands sort by what carries the rest rather than by taxon or by amount. Hydra and Cassiopea have a nerve net and no brain and meet every behavioural criterion for sleep, and Hydra has no circadian clock either — a roughly four-hour cycle instead (Kanaya et al. 2020). C. elegans rests for two to three hours before each of its four moults (Raizen et al. 2008). Great frigatebirds sleep 42 minutes a day aloft, in the soar and never while flapping; common swifts spend over 99 per cent of a ten-month phase airborne, and the record is not uniform — some individuals roosted in midwinter, others never landed (Hedenström et al. 2016). Sperm whales hang vertically and go silent, unresponsive to a boat until it touched them (Miller et al. 2008). Bears keep their skeleton through six months of disuse; arctic ground squirrels hold a core temperature of −2.9 °C by supercooling, with no antifreeze in the plasma (Barnes 1989); lungfish seal themselves in a cocoon of living cells for years. Emperor penguins reach 37.5 °C inside a huddle while it is −19 °C outside, and two thirds of the saving is geometry rather than warmth (Gilbert et al. 2008). Parrotfish build a mucus tent for 2.5 per cent of a day's energy and cut parasite attacks from nearly all to about one in ten (Grutter et al. 2011). Northern fur seals suppress REM for weeks and never pay it back. And the card the guide would keep if it could keep one: the sleepiest-mammal figure of 19.9 hours is a single 1960s measurement at 33 °C on an unknown number of animals, which becomes 11.0 hours at 26 °C — and about one per cent of mammal species have had their sleep measured at all (Harding et al. 2022). Two cards carry no reframe table: sponges, because nobody knows yet and writing actually over an open question is bluff; and plants, because nyctinasty was named by Linnaeus and Darwin himself called the daytime version “improperly” sleep, read here from the 1880 primary. Seventeen cards, fifteen entries.
A Field Guide to Unfinished Animals

Field Guide No. 18 A Field Guide to Unfinished Animals Field Guide · companion to No. 61 there is no final draft — and what varies here is not the animals, it is us Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake and tagged for whether the argument is over. Drawn upside down, then back-to-front. Three animals in three groups. A skull on a tail. Two arms for forty-four years. 16 entries→ Details Companion to No. 61, and it asks the question that zine assumes an answer to: how often does the record actually move? Sixteen animals we reconstructed wrong, sorted by the kind of mistake, and — this guide’s one addition to the house form, borrowed from How We Got Here — every card carries a status: revised (ten cards), contested (four), or name stuck (two). A catalogue of corrections that will not say which corrections are finished would read as a list of settled triumphs, which is the smoothing it is complaining about. Assembled wrong: Hallucigenia was published in 1977 walking on its spines, inverted by Ramsköld and Hou in 1991, and turned end-for-end by Smith and Caron in 2015 when they found the eyes, mouth ring and tooth-lined throat at the other end — wrong on one axis for fourteen years and on the other for twenty-four more. Anomalocaris spent most of a century as three animals in three groups: a shrimp-like appendage, the “jellyfish” Peytoia, and the “sponge” Laggania, united by Whittington and Briggs in 1985 — and then the correction was itself corrected, when Daley and Bergström found a three-plate oral cone in 2012 and Peytoia became valid again. Cope put the skull of Elasmosaurus on the end of its neck in 1868, reading a neck as a tail; and the famous story about who caught him is wrong — it was Joseph Leidy, on 8 March 1870, with Marsh in the room, and Marsh’s claim survives only in a newspaper piece two decades later. Mantell put the Iguanodon thumb spike on its nose; it took thirty-odd whole skeletons at Bernissart for Dollo to move it to the hand. Known from almost nothing: Deinocheirus was two arms found on 9 July 1965 and named in 1970 by Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz, and it stayed honestly unplaced for forty-four years until two near-complete skeletons showed a humpbacked, duck-billed omnivore. The Spinosaurus holotype burned in the Munich bombing of 24–25 April 1944, after Stromer’s requests to move the collection were refused — so every reconstruction since argues from photographs, and the aquatic reading is contested. Helicoprion’s tooth whorl was placed on the snout, the upper jaw, the back and the tail before a 2013 CT scan put it in the lower jaw — of a specimen that had been in a drawer since 1950. The line moved: Brontosaurus (the short form of the zine). Torosaurus, proposed as merely a mature Triceratops in 2010 and rejected in 2012, still unresolved — the mirror image of the Brontosaurus case, a merge rather than a split, with the opposite fate. Nanotyrannus, dismissed for forty years as a juvenile T. rex and reinstated in 2025 by Zanno and Napoli on a near-adult skeleton from the Duelling Dinosaurs block, with a second species nobody had separated out. And Tanystropheus, one species until a CT scan made it two, both size classes fully grown. Three of those four errors were the same error: explaining a difference by age. The name outlived it: Oviraptor means egg seizer and it was brooding its own clutch — and the card is careful that the 1995 brooding specimen is an oviraptorid later named Citipati, not Osborn’s animal, because the tidy version of that story is the one that travels. Basilosaurus means king lizard and Owen showed it was a mammal within five years; he proposed Zeuglodon and priority refused it. Both names are permanent, which is the band the zine cares about: a label outlives its refutation by rule or by repetition, and only one of those admits what it is doing. Tidier than the evidence: the fish-crawls-out story has a date problem — Devonian trackways about eighteen million years older than the earliest tetrapod bodies — and the retelling of that correction is smoothed too, because those trackways are themselves disputed. The film raptor is not the fossil one. And the tail-dragging dinosaur was corrected by a whole field changing its mind, from one 1969 monograph. Two cards are dashed and carry no reframe table. Mary Anning found, prepared and drew the first complete plesiosaur in 1823 and Conybeare presented it without naming her; women could not join the Geological Society until 1904, and on her only London trip no label carried her name. She is not a specimen, and running sounds like / actually down the side of a person would file her with the misreconstructed animals, which is the injury. And the last card has nothing to correct yet: on the guide’s own argument some entries above are currently wrong, and it says where to expect it — the age explanation, the fragment that fits every reading, and the instrument that arrives before the answer. Arrival line: there is no final draft, and the guide says plainly why it departs from the house formula: what varies here is not the animals but us. Eighteen cards, sixteen entries.
A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Family

Field Guide No. 19 A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Family Field Guide · 13 + 1 · companion to No. 64 there is no standard family — and what varies is not how related anybody is, it is what the care runs on Thirteen ways of being family among our Terran kin, sorted by what the care actually flows through. A ledger. A coalition of strangers. A boundary crossed. A pile of pups nobody can claim. 13 entries→ Details The catalogue for No. 64, answering the question that zine leaves open: if care is not keyed to relatedness, what is it keyed to? Sorted by mechanism, because sorting by degree of relatedness collapsed on the first entry that belonged at both ends of the line. In superb fairy-wrens, 76% of offspring (138 of 181) were sired by extra-group males who give no care, and 95% of broods contained such young — and every male in the group feeds the brood regardless (Mulder et al., 1994). Greater anis share one clutch between unrelated pairs with no kin discrimination. Pied kingfishers admit an unrelated helper only when the pair cannot feed the brood alone — hospitality that began in need, kept rather than trimmed. Two bonobos at Wamba adopted infants from a different social group and nursed them, the first such record in a great ape (Tokuyama et al., 2021); a bottlenose dolphin at Rangiroa raised a presumed melon-headed whale calf beside her own (Carzon et al., 2019). Banded mongooses give birth 64% on one night and escorts do not sort pups by parentage — a veil of ignorance, in the literature's own phrase. Because 55% of cooperatively breeding birds really do nest primarily with kin, one section is for them: long-tailed tits identify relatives by call similarity, and post-reproductive killer whale grandmothers help more than breeding ones, because a grandmother carrying her own calf has less to give. A final section corrects us — Komdeur's Seychelles warblers stay as helpers on good territories rather than breed on poor ones, so constraint is arithmetic rather than a wall, and the Damaraland mole-rat, the textbook eusocial mammal, is not an obligate cooperative breeder after all. An overclaim in our own favour is still an overclaim. The families people make get the fourteenth card and no reframe table.

Field Guide No. 20 A Field Guide to Rainbows Field Guide · 16 + 3 · companion to Nos. 69–70 there is no standard rainbow — and rarity, it turns out, is a fact about where the observer was standing Sixteen rainbows sorted by what physically changed — the drop, the path inside it, the light arriving, the surface the cone meets, the instrument at its point. Not a rarity countdown. 16 entries→ Details The catalogue for No. 69 and No. 70, and the guide that takes on a whole genre: every listicle of rainbow kinds sorts by appearance and then ranks by rarity, and both sorts fail. Appearance fails twice, in opposite directions — a fogbow looks nothing like a rainbow and differs only in drop size, its colours all present and diffracted so wide that they overlap into white; a sea spray bow looks identical to a rainbow and is genuinely a different bow, because salt raises the refractive index and shrinks the radius by about 0.8°, so the two stand visibly misaligned in one sky. Rarity fails because it is not a property of any bow: a circumhorizontal arc needs the sun above 58°, which is impossible north of 55°N and happens for roughly 140 hours a year in London against 670 in Los Angeles. Supernumerary arcs cannot be produced by geometric optics at all — Thomas Young explained them by interference in 1804 and they became evidence for the wave theory of light; Airy dismissed him for predicting the wrong angles, and Young had merely missed a 90° phase shift. Third- and fourth-order bows stand around the sun and waited until 2011 for a photograph, found by people who knew exactly where to look. A moonbow carries every colour and a long exposure records them: it is the rods, not the bow, that cannot report them. A dewbow is a hyperbola because a cone met a plane, and a full-circle bow is the only kind there is, seen from somewhere the ground is not in the way. Rainbow light is about 96% polarised, so a lens can switch it off while the sky is unchanged. And the glory is carded as openly unfinished — the surface-wave consensus holds and the precise mechanism is still called obscure. The section on what the light did inside the drop is led by the double rainbow, carded with its mechanism: one bounce leaves at about 42.7°, two at about 50° with the colour order reversed, the outer bow is 43% as bright because a longer path loses more light, and Alexander’s dark band between them is a direction into which neither bow returns any light at all. The mechanism is the catalogue’s; the argument that “secondary” is a rank the physics does not contain stays No. 70’s. Three cards get no reframe table: the ice halos, because they are not rainbows; the antisolar cone — that the bow is centred on your own shadow and no two people see the same one — which is the whole of No. 69; and the flag and the song, which live at the Sound rack. Unique to each observer is not the same as unreal — the guide refuses the word illusion on its own page.
A Field Guide to Third Nature

Field Guide No. 21 A Field Guide to Third Nature Field Guide · 12 + 1 · companion to No. 74 a support nobody named is a support nobody defends Thirteen habitats we made by accident — and, on every card, the improvement now removing it. Insulation. Cleaner seed. Remediation. Regeneration. None of them should be reversed. 12 entries→ Details The catalogue for No. 74, built out of that chain’s tenth link: matsutake became rare across Japan by abandonment rather than destruction, because fossil fuel replaced firewood and the woodlands nobody was cutting grew too shady for pine. That turned out not to be a special case. Anna Tsing’s third nature is what manages to live despite capitalism; this asks what it is actually living on. The sort is by what made the habitat — the work, the structure, the damage — because the sort we tried first, by how damaged the place is, collapsed: a hay meadow and a lead-poisoned spoil heap sit at opposite ends of any damage scale and are the same kind of object here. Corncockle did not tolerate farming, it was farming — harvested, stored and re-sown with the grain until better seed cleaning screened its large seeds out. The corncrake needed a late, slow cut, and when the requirement was finally written into a scheme the population rose from 480 to 589 calling males in five years, reached 1,289 by 2014, and slipped again when the prescriptions changed. The high brown fritillary is the entry that embarrasses an instinct: leave the woodland alone is the mechanism of its loss, because it needed the coppice rotation to keep opening clearings. Black redstarts, a bird of Alpine scree, bred on Blitz rubble and declined city by city with regeneration; 27–74 pairs remain and they now breed on land defined as available for development. Swifts nest in gaps that insulation closes. Chimney swifts we assumed were chimney-dependent — recent work finds many still nesting in big hollow trees, which changes what to do, and a guide about unnamed supports should be the last place to invent a dependence that is not there. East of the Rockies every documented purple martin nests in a box a person put up, an arrangement recorded in Choctaw and Chickasaw gourd housing in the 1700s; nothing needs to be improved to end it, only ignored. Calaminarian grassland is Annex I habitat 6130 — a legally protected community held open by lead and zinc poisoning, whose spring sandwort miners called leadwort because it showed them where the galena was; the North Pennines survey records a lichen abundant at Nenthead smeltmill “until the restoration of Nenthead Mines.” Oil platforms off California are among the most productive fish habitat per unit area measured, and decommissioning law says remove them. The London Underground mosquito is the card where we had it wrong: a 2025 genomic study puts molestus’ origin in ancient Mediterranean agriculture, not the Tube — the accidental habitat was real and three orders of magnitude older, and nobody was careless. The peregrine goes the other way and is here so the guide is not a mood. The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone gets a dashed card and no reframe table, because Deryabina et al. and Møller & Mousseau genuinely disagree and filling in an actually column would be picking a winner in a live dispute. Refuses damage-as-good, ruin as an aesthetic, “nature is resilient,” and any suggestion that the improvements should be undone.

Field Guide No. 22 Under the Word Field Guide · 18 entries · words by Helen Edgar, Marion McLaughlin & Felicity Goodhall eighteen borrowed and invented words for Autistic joy, and what is actually holding each one up Provenance graded rather than flattened — some attested, some real words wearing a word-list gloss, some invented online in the last decade. The sort is by what you find underneath: thirteen have a mechanism, five have a person. 18 entries→ Details Built on Words: Inspired by the experience of being monotropic — a 104-page booklet by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), Marion McLaughlin (Aurora Autistic Consulting) and Felicity Goodhall (Flappy Inky Feathers), January 2025. The words are theirs and the monotropic reading quoted on every card is theirs; what this guide adds is the provenance and the mechanism. The sort was not the one we set out to make: the plan was to file by feeling — joy, longing, solitude, kinship — and it collapsed at once because the feelings overlap almost entirely. What actually divides them is what is under the word. Thirteen have a mechanism, and it is startlingly often variation. A brook’s voice is air bubbles ringing at a frequency set by radius alone (Minnaert, Philosophical Magazine, 1933), so the sound is a chorus that only works because no two bells match. The bright spots under a tree are pinhole images of the Sun, which is why they all turn into the same crescent during a partial eclipse. The glitter path on water is specular reflection from the small fraction of wave facets tilted toward one observer — it points at you, and nobody else’s road shares a single wave. Dark adaptation is a second visual system that takes tens of minutes of rhodopsin to enter and one bright light to destroy. The smell of an old book is the book coming apart, in vanillin and benzaldehyde and furfural. A cloud floats because its water is divided finely enough to fall at a centimetre a second. Blossom order is a chilling requirement — four thermostats, not four runners. Five have a person underneath instead, and that is a firmer foundation rather than a weaker one, because a person can be checked: the famous English definition of toska is Nabokov’s translation note, not a dictionary; duende’s aesthetic sense was argued by Lorca in a 1933 lecture and the everyday Spanish word means a house-sprite; limerence was coined by Dorothy Tennov and published in 1979 and never entered any diagnostic manual, which the card says rather than borrowing the authority of the word psychology; anam cara is two ordinary old Irish words carried into English by one 1997 book; and cynefin is a Welsh word with a second, separate career as a decision framework. Three of these words were invented online within the last decade and one is a Latin word wearing a meaning it never had — marmoris is the genitive of marble — and the cards say so on their faces, because a community that reaches for a word, fails to find one, and makes one is the most Star Stuff thing in the booklet; what would be dishonest is selling recent invention as inheritance. Coddiwomple is not old English slang however often it is sold as such, and the behaviour it names is superbly documented in a desert ant that wanders out and runs home in a straight line. The bouba/kiki figure is printed as 17 of 25 languages rather than “universal,” after Ćwiek et al. (2022), because the three languages where it failed are the interesting part. Five refusals, the first of which is the trap the whole guide is walking past: not that the science proves the feeling is real. The feeling was already real, and physics is not a permit.

Field Guide No. 23 Bird Minds Field Guide · 13 entries · companion to No. 86 thirteen birds, sorted by what we wanted each one to prove Alex, the New Caledonian crow, the kea, the cockatoos of forty-four suburbs, the ravens who wait for tomorrow, the magpie whose famous mirror result failed replication, two cachers with opposite problems — and then four nobody asked, holding the map. 13 entries→ Details The sort is the finding, and it was not the sort we set out to make. By taxonomy you get parrots, corvids and everyone else; by cleverness you are building the ranking this house refuses. What divides these thirteen is the question a researcher brought to them — a fact about us. Three sections hold the birds recruited into an argument: asked to mean it (Alex cross-classifying colour and object; the budgerigar’s open-ended vocal learning, shared with parrots, songbirds, hummingbirds and some cetaceans but not with apes), asked to make a plan (metatool problems solved around tools that are out of sight; ravens refusing food they could eat now for a token worth something only tomorrow; the cockatoo bin culture that reached 44 Sydney suburbs with site-specific styles and provoked a counter-culture of bricks and bungees), and asked to remember when (a nutcracker holding 30,000 caches for six months by landmark geometry — move the landmarks 20 cm and it searches 20 cm off — against a scrub-jay that must hold when because its caches perish at different rates). The fourth section is where the line arrives. The pigeon, the chicken, the barn owl and the ostrich were never candidates for cleverness, and they supplied the fibre architecture, the single-cell developmental atlas, the second species that made one measurement a finding, and the control that breaks brain mass as a predictor. One card corrects our own shipped work — the magpie mirror result rested on two of five birds and failed a 2020 replication, and Field Guide No. 11 had listed self-recognition as established. Two cards carry no reframe table, because the origin of the circuit and the fairness of the corvid-versus-ape comparison have no verdict to correct. There is no standard bird.

Playlist & essay It Take a Joyful Sound Stimpunks × More Realms The loud companion to the L★S Playlist, and the one that argues first. In July 1977 Bob Marley recorded Punky Reggae Party with Lee Perry — a guest list for an alliance that did not exist until it was read out. 36 tracks + essay→ Details The loud companion to the L★S Playlist, and the one that argues first. In July 1977 Bob Marley recorded Punky Reggae Party with Lee Perry after hearing The Clash cover a Jamaican record — a guest list for an alliance that did not exist until it was read out, and the following April roughly 100,000 people marched six miles through National Front territory to hear The Clash, Steel Pulse and X-Ray Spex on one Rock Against Racism bill. Naming a thing helped it happen, which is what neurodiversity did too. Then the physics, because the physics is unreasonably good: sound needs matter — in a vacuum there is none at all — so every note anyone has heard was carried by nitrogen and oxygen forged in stars. A pure sine wave has a pitch and almost no identity; Helmholtz worked out in 1863 that what tells you who is playing lives entirely in the overtones above the note. And distortion, the sound the genre is named by, is a nonlinearity adding harmonics that were never sent in — difference, deliberately added. It reaches you at the skeleton, too: you hear your own voice partly through skull bone, which is why recordings sound wrong. Thirty-six songs from the Stimpunks PSA — Bikini Kill, Dream Nails, Kae Tempest, Le Tigre, The Linda Lindas, Gossip, pink suits — with the door test punk actually contributed, and the honest part: a loud room is itself an access barrier, and acceptance is not any scene's nature but a practice re-won in every room.

Playlist & essay Stimming and Belonging with AURORA Stimpunks × More Realms Weighted toward live performances, because the argument is the body. The companion rack to Warriors and Weirdos (No. 13). It opens on AURORA's own account of seeing herself on video for the first time. 28 performances→ Details The companion rack to Warriors and Weirdos (No. 13), weighted toward live performances because the argument is the body. It opens on AURORA's own account of seeing herself on video for the first time — she was shocked, said she couldn't do anything about it, and kept it: I have to use everything I got. Then the physics of the light she shares a name with, which turns out to be about exactly this. The solar wind delivers energy and nothing else; the colour is the atom's own — that famous green is oxygen's 557.7 nm line. And that line is a forbidden transition: it breaks the electric-dipole selection rules, so instead of the nanoseconds an allowed transition takes, the atom waits about 0.7 seconds before letting go, and the red line waits 110. Which is why altitude decides the colour — lower down the air is crowded and a collision takes the energy first. The most famous light in the sky is a slow release the rules call forbidden, and it only completes where nothing crowds it. Twenty-eight performances across six movements, plus stim-listening (Jim Irion's coinage) and the reason Ryan's own playlist is nearly all live footage. The page is careful about whose word is whose: she calls it emotion; we are the ones calling it stimming, and it says so rather than putting the term in her mouth. The sharpest refusal is saved for last — her movement is celebrated because it is on a stage and lovely, while the same body doing the same thing in a classroom gets a behaviour plan.

Playlist & essay Nobody Got His Eyes Right Stimpunks × More Realms The most-looked-at face in pop, and the one fact everybody repeats about it. Thirty-one songs from Space Oddity to I Can't Give Everything Away — the listening companion to Turn and Face the Strange (No. 12). 31 tracks + essay→ Details The long version of the five Bowie cards that open the L★S Playlist, and the listening companion to Turn and Face the Strange (No. 12) — thirty-one songs from Space Oddity to I Can't Give Everything Away. It starts from the most-looked-at face in pop and the one fact everybody repeats about it, which is wrong. He did not have different-coloured eyes. Both irises were the same colour; in February 1962 a schoolfriend punched him and a fingernail paralysed the muscles that contract the left iris, so that pupil could never close again — anisocoria, not heterochromia. A pupil stuck wide is a hole full of shadow, which is why the eye reads darker in exactly the bright light where a working pupil contracts, which is to say under every stage light and camera flash he ever stood in. That changes what kind of thing the famous feature was: heterochromia is a variation you're born with; this was an injury, reportedly with lasting effects on his depth perception. Glamour is not an accommodation. Then the second thing everyone knows — the constellation named for him in 2016 is not a constellation; there are 88, the list was fixed in the 1920s, and the observatory that made it said plainly it was an invented asterism. Both errors lean the same way: they round a damaged iris and a small tribute up into something more elegant, and the tidier version travels further. Which is Too Good to Check with a soundtrack — and it has a cost, because while the myth is that beautiful nobody asks what a fixed pupil is like under a follow spot.

Playlist & essay One Body at a Time Stimpunks × More Realms Repetition is the mechanism, not the deficit — and the room fills up around you. Twenty-five songs from Psycho Killer to Everybody Laughs — the listening companion to The Body Understands It First (No. 66). 25 tracks + essay→ Details David Byrne from the 1977 CBGB audition to Who Is the Sky? in 2025. The essay runs on one finding — groove is measurable and agreed upon across listeners, and the feature doing the work is repetition, because a figure has to come round again before a body can meet it rather than chase it. Which is how Remain in Light was made: instruments recorded largely one at a time, each part a short figure held without developing, credited openly to Fela Kuti and West African polyrhythm. Then the same method at two more scales — early Talking Heads as a performance style defined by negatives, which is subtraction working as an access strategy; and Stop Making Sense, which adds one body at a time until the stage is full and the man who could not relax is dancing. Nobody fixed him; the room filled up. The synchrony research behind that is real and, per a 2017 meta-analysis, modest, and the page says so. On his own account of being Autistic the rack is careful: self-described, hedged in the original, not upgraded here.

Playlist & essay Love Without Cringing Stimpunks × More Realms The persona was assigned before she chose it, and the copyright stayed in her pocket. Forty-four tracks — twenty-five of hers, then nineteen covers — the listening companion to No One Had to Qualify (No. 67). 44 tracks + essay→ Details Dolly Parton 1967–2023, made three days after she died. The essay opens on something worth checking before repeating: her first hit, “Dumb Blonde,” was written by Curly Putman — the persona arrived before she had any say in it, and the self-invention story is really about what she did once she was inside it. Then the 1974 refusal, told as she tells it: Colonel Tom Parker wanted half the publishing for Elvis, she said no and cried all night, and Whitney Houston settled the argument eighteen years later. A third section pulls the catalogue's dark run forward — “Down from Dover,” “The Bridge,” a stillbirth and a suicide — because the woman who built the Imagination Library was never naive about what happens to people; Cottom's reading of that run as gothic motherhood is borrowed with the tag on, as is her argument about blonde as unmarked whiteness. The last section is about what travels: “9 to 5” sells productivity software now, and in 2023 a Wisconsin school barred first-graders from singing “Rainbowland” under a policy on controversial issues — a song about there being no gate, stopped at one.

Rack · One theme Skepticism and Wonder Playlist & essay The Rainbow Connection — forty songs, and the two uneasily cohabiting modes of thought they carry. A song told a six-year-old that rainbows have nothing to hide, and he took it as permission to love the real thing more than any story about what it was concealing. 40 songs→ Details “Rainbow Connection” — Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher, sung by Jim Henson as Kermit, opening The Muppet Movie in 1979 — grants that rainbows are visions, downgrades them to illusions, and then lands the line that did the work for a science-loving kid: rainbows have nothing to hide. No pot of gold, no other side, nothing withheld. As a closeted queer and atheist child, Ryan found that observational reality better than any story about what a rainbow might be concealing — and the essay is honest that the song gets one word wrong. A rainbow is not an illusion. An illusion is a mistake perception makes; a rainbow is occurring, calculable to a fraction of a degree, and Roger Bacon measured its maximum elevation at 42° around 1267 with an astrolabe and no theory of refraction. What is true is stranger and better: it has no location — a direction rather than a place, centred on the shadow of your own head. Carl Sagan later supplied the vocabulary in The Demon-Haunted World (1995): his parents taught him “the two uneasily cohabiting modes of thought that are central to the scientific method.” Uneasily is the load-bearing word — not reconciled, sharing a house. NeuroTribes’ chapter “Princes of the Air” supplies the lineage, with Asperger forced to walk back his claim that his patients’ interests were remote from real concerns because their imaginations kept anticipating science by decades; and Dorion Sagan — son of Carl Sagan and Lynn Margulis, whose endosymbiosis this collection already runs on — calls detail and breadth “a kind of alembic, an antidote to both.” Then the fact that closes it. In March 2023 the School District of Waukesha, Wisconsin pulled “Rainbowland” from a first-grade concert as potentially controversial — and the song chosen to replace it was “Rainbow Connection,” which was initially banned too, reinstated only after parents pushed back; the teacher who spoke publicly was later terminated. A song whose entire argument is that rainbows have nothing hidden in them was, for a moment, too controversial for six-year-olds. Seven sections: eleven versions of the song; the Garfunkel and Oates joke that reaches the same thesis; eleven of “Over the Rainbow,” which wants the opposite thing; four of “What a Wonderful World,” which wants this one; the colours named as a list and as physics; the rainbow turned inward as identity; and finally Merle Haggard’s sour “Rainbow Stew” against a man on a mountain undone by a double rainbow, the two modes back to back with no attempt to reconcile them. All forty video ids were resolved through oEmbed before anything was written about them — five carried no artist in their link text, and four of those we would have got wrong. No lyric is reproduced anywhere on the page, which is stated rather than worked around.
