Star Stuff Manifesto On the cosmic origins of who we are, the science of how we carry the universe in our bones, and why neurodivergent and disabled people belong — not despite difference, but as difference. L ★ S · Love You, Star Stuff I · Origin
We are all made of exploded stars

We are all made of exploded stars Carl Sagan said it plainly: “The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, the carbon in our apple pies were made in the interiors of collapsing stars” ( Cosmos , 1980, ch. 9). When those stars exhausted their fuel, they exploded across the cosmos. Their debris became clouds. The clouds collapsed into new systems, new planets, new oceans, new life. You. Stellar Nucleosynthesis Almost every atom heavier than helium was manufactured in stars. Carbon, oxygen, calcium, iron — the building blocks of every human body — were forged under conditions of unimaginable pressure and heat, then scattered across the galaxy when those stars died. (Three light elements are the honest exceptions: most lithium came from the Big Bang, and beryllium and boron are made almost entirely by cosmic rays shattering heavier nuclei out in interstellar space. Stars destroy all three rather than build them.) We are, in a literal chemical sense, the remnants of stellar death. This is not metaphor. It is the actual account of where you came from. And it matters — because a cosmology that grounds identity in the violent, generative creativity of the universe is a very different cosmology than one that locates value in conformity, productivity, or neurotypicality. ★ II · The Bones Remember

Your skeleton is piezoelectric In the 1950s, Japanese orthopedic surgeon Dr. Iwao Yasuda and physicist Eiichi Fukada established something remarkable: bone is piezoelectric. Under mechanical stress — compression, tension, bending — bone crystal generates its own electrical charge. This is not incidental. It is how bone knows to grow, where to strengthen, how to heal. The skeleton is a living signal processor, converting force into information. Piezoelectricity Piezo comes from the Greek piezein — to press, to squeeze. Certain materials generate an electric charge when their structure is deformed. In bone the effect comes chiefly from collagen — the protein scaffold, not the mineral — whose fibres are arranged without a centre of symmetry and slip past one another under shear. (Hydroxyapatite, the mineral that makes bone rigid, is symmetric in the way that rules out classical piezoelectricity; recent work gives it a role in bone's electrical environment, but the original effect Fukada and Yasuda measured was collagen's.) Every step you take, every breath, every impact — your bones are generating voltage. Responding. Adapting. Alive. We carry the electrical signature of the cosmos not just as metaphor but as mechanism. The universe built into the architecture of our bodies the same responsive-to-pressure principle it uses everywhere: force begets signal, signal begets change, change begets structure. We are responsive systems, not static ones. Every nervous system that processes the world differently is doing what responsive systems do — responding to the particular pressures of a particular life. "Your bones are piezoelectric. They generate charge under pressure. They respond. They adapt. They remember every load they've carried — and grow stronger at the point of stress. That is not a malfunction. That is the physics of survival written in calcium and light." — Stimpunks Foundation ★ III · The Neurodiversity Paradigm
The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation

The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation The neurodiversity paradigm holds that neurological difference is a natural, valuable form of human variation — not a deviation from a healthy norm to be corrected, but a dimension of the diversity that characterizes our species. Autism, ADHD, dyslexia, Tourette's, and the full range of neurological profiles are not disorders in the sense of broken-ness. They are differences in how nervous systems are organized. The universe is staggeringly, relentlessly various. Stars range from red dwarfs barely massive enough to fuse hydrogen, to hypergiants swollen past a thousand times the sun's radius, to blue monsters near two hundred times its mass. Galaxies spiral, ellipse, collide, merge, scatter. No two snowflakes, no two fingerprints, no two nervous systems. Variation is not the exception. It is the rule. It is the engine. Core Claim The same universe that forged every atom in your body also produced the nervous system you inhabit. There is no astrophysics of typicality. There is only the astonishing variety of what the cosmos can make — and we are part of that variety. The DSM is a human document written at a particular historical moment to describe patterns of distress and difference through a particular cultural lens. The cosmos has no DSM. Turbulence in fluid dynamics is not a pathology — it is a regime of behavior, one with its own laws, its own beauty, its own utility. The same is true of neurological variation. We reframe. Not to deny that neurodivergent and disabled people experience real challenges — many of which are compounded or entirely caused by environments built for a narrow range of bodies and minds — but to insist that the starting point is not deficit. The starting point is this: you came from the same place everything came from. Stars. ★ IV · Love You Down to Your Star Stuff
What it means to say L★S

What it means to say L★S Love You Down to Your Star Stuff — LYDTYSS, L★S — is not a slogan. It is a position. It is a way of saying: I see you at the level of your constituent matter. I love what you are made of. I love the process that made you. I love the particular, improbable, once-in-a-cosmos arrangement of atoms that is you, right now, reading this. This matters in community spaces built for neurodivergent and disabled people because so much of what those community members have been told — by schools, by clinics, by families who meant well — is a story of falling short. Not meeting the threshold. Not reaching the benchmark. Not being the version that fits the space that was already built without them in mind. What L★S says back The threshold is arbitrary. The benchmark is cultural. The space can change. But you — the specific arrangement of matter and electricity and history and nervous system that is you — you are not a problem to be solved. You are a thing the universe made. We love you for it. L★S is also punk. It refuses the frame in which some nervous systems are inherently more valuable than others. It refuses the medicalization of variation without consent. It refuses the premise that the burden of adaptation falls entirely on the person who diverges, rather than on the systems and structures that were built too narrow. It is gentle and it is fierce. It is Sagan's wonder and it is community rage at a world that keeps telling neurodivergent and disabled people they are too much, too little, too loud, too still, too slow, too scattered, too focused, too strange. L★S says: we were made by supernovae. We are not too much. We are exactly as much as we are. ★ V · What We Hold
Declarations of the Star Stuff community

Declarations of the Star Stuff community 01 We hold that every person is made of star stuff. Not metaphorically, but chemically. The iron in your blood was forged in a dying star. This is the baseline of your cosmic belonging, and no diagnosis, no deficit model, no exclusionary system can revoke it. 02 We hold that neurological variation is natural variation. The neurodiversity paradigm is not a denial of challenge. It is a refusal to locate the problem in the person rather than in the mismatch between person and environment. 03 We hold that disabled people belong — fully, without asterisk. Not despite their disabilities, but as people whose full humanity includes their disability experience, and whose knowledge from that experience has value. 04 We hold that your bones remember pressure and grow toward strength. The piezoelectric fact of bone is a reminder that living systems are adaptive. What you have carried has shaped you. That shaping is not damage — it is history, written in calcium. 05 We hold that the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. There is no correct galaxy, no normative star. The cosmos makes what it makes and none of it is a mistake. We extend this to people. 06 We hold that community is a mutual aid structure, not a charity transaction. We are not here to fix each other. We are here to share resources, to amplify each other's signal, to build environments where more kinds of people can be more fully themselves. 07 We hold that love operates at the level of constituent matter. L★S means: I love you down to the atoms. The specific improbable arrangement. Not a performance of you, not a corrected version — this one, as made, as present, as star-forged. 08 We hold that punk and wonder are not opposites. Rage at injustice and awe at the cosmos coexist. Stimpunks carries both. The same voice that says "we are made of exploded stars" also says "build better systems or we will build them ourselves." ★ VI · Carried in the Body
On piezoelectric bones and the neurodiversity paradigm

On piezoelectric bones and the neurodiversity paradigm Your bones are piezoelectric. Under pressure — literal, mechanical pressure — they generate voltage. Collagen fibres in compact bone, sheared against one another, convert load to charge. This is how bone remodels: stress signals the skeleton to grow where it is needed, to reinforce the places that carry load. It is not damage. It is response. It is the body's oldest and most literal act of knowing. Every step is a signal. Every weight you have carried has left its mark — not as fracture, but as architecture. The bone grew denser there. The body remembered. "The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation." — Stimpunks Foundation · Star Stuff Manifesto Neurodivergent nervous systems process signal differently. They amplify some frequencies and damp others. They notice what the typical processing filter removes. They fatigue under loads that weren't in the design spec — because the design spec was never written with them in mind. This is the social model of disability applied to nervous systems: the problem is not the nervous system. The problem is the mismatch. The too-loud room. The eye contact requirement. The assumption of one right rhythm. We carry our cosmology in our bodies: atoms forged in stars, bones that conduct electricity, nervous systems that are — each one — a distinct and unrepeatable way of encountering the world. The universe made all of it. The universe makes all of it still. We are not asking for tolerance. We are not asking to be included in a structure built to exclude us, as a favor, on the condition that we approximate the expected shape. We are saying: the structure was wrong about what shapes are possible. We are made of the same stuff as everything. And everything includes us. Colophon The Star Stuff Manifesto is the founding statement of this collection — the argument every zine, field guide and broadside here is a variation on. It braids two real findings with one paradigm, and the braid is a reading , not a proof. Sources below; corrections are logged publicly in the changelog . I · Origin Stellar nucleosynthesis is established science, traced to Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler & Hoyle, “Synthesis of the Elements in Stars” ( Reviews of Modern Physics 29, 1957) — the B²FH paper — and, for the modern accounting of which sites make which elements, Kobayashi, Karakas & Lugaro, “The Origin of Elements from Carbon to Uranium” ( ApJ 900:179, 2020). Hydrogen is primordial; carbon comes from the triple-alpha process in red giants; nitrogen roughly half from low- and intermediate-mass AGB stars via the CNO cycle; oxygen and calcium from massive stars and core-collapse supernovae; iron roughly half from Type Ia supernovae rather than massive stars alone; iodine and the other r-process elements from neutron-star mergers. Lithium, beryllium and boron are the honest exceptions named in the text — most lithium is Big Bang, beryllium and boron come almost entirely from cosmic-ray spallation in the interstellar medium, and stars destroy all three. The Sagan passage is quoted verbatim from Cosmos (1980), ch. 9, “The Lives of the Stars.” II & VI · The bones Bone piezoelectricity was established by Eiichi Fukada and Iwao Yasuda, “On the Piezoelectric Effect of Bone” ( Journal of the Physical Society of Japan 12:1158–1162, 1957), following Yasuda's earlier work; C. A. L. Bassett and colleagues extended it through the 1960s, and it supplies a mechanism for Wolff's law — that bone remodels along the loads it carries. The effect is collagen's: its fibres are arranged without a centre of symmetry and generate charge when sheared past one another. Hydroxyapatite, the mineral that makes bone rigid, is centrosymmetric, which rules out classical piezoelectricity; recent work gives it a role in bone's electrical environment, but the original measured effect was the protein's, not the mineral's. Greek piezein , “to press.” III · The paradigm The neurodiversity paradigm and the pathology paradigm it refuses are Nick Walker 's formulations, from “Throw Away the Master's Tools: Liberating Ourselves from the Pathology Paradigm” (written 2011; published 2012 in Loud Hands: Autistic People, Speaking ; revised 2013) and Neuroqueer Heresies (2021). Neurodiversity itself is not one person's coinage: per Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley & Walker, “The neurodiversity concept was developed collectively” ( Autism , 2024), “neurological diversity” and “neurodiversity” reached print in 1997 and 1998 through journalist Harvey Blume, who attributed them to the online Autistic community — the InLv list founded by Martijn Dekker in 1996, and the wider movement around Jim Sinclair and Autism Network International. Neurodivergent is Kassiane Asasumasu 's (2000). The mismatch framing is the social model of disability, from the disability rights movement. Stellar variety: red dwarfs outlive the present age of the universe; the largest hypergiants exceed a thousand solar radii ; the most massive star known, R136a1, is about 196 solar masses (169–230; Gemini South, 2022), against a theoretical ceiling near 300. Held honestly The science here is real, and it does not make our ethics true. “The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation” is a statement about us — about what we owe each other — dressed in cosmology because that is where it was easiest to see. The cosmos has no opinion, and deriving an ought from an is is a fallacy we would rather name than commit. Bone's piezoelectricity is a mechanism in a skeleton; it is an analogy for responsive nervous systems, not evidence about them. Nothing in stellar chemistry implies anything about how a school or a clinic should be run. What the science does is more modest and, we think, enough: it removes the excuse that difference is a defect, by showing that variation is the ordinary condition of everything we have ever looked at. As About puts it — we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. 73 Star Stuff Measured Against a Tree on six ways a moss fails as a plant, and the finding that the list is backwards — because holding your own water is the newer trick, and the tree is the one that lost the older one developed after Helen Edgar's Mossy Minds & Monotropism L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely

Assessed against the standard Six ways a moss fails Take a tree as the definition of a plant, and write down every way a moss falls short of it. The list comes out fast, and every line on it is true. Bryophyte, assessed against a vascular plant Faculty Finding Roots Absent. Vascular tissue Absent. Lifting water Cannot. Height Centimetres at most. Water regulation None. Photosynthesis when dry Stops entirely. What a moss has instead of roots are rhizoids, which anchor it and do essentially none of the absorbing. It takes water across its whole surface, directly, from rain and fog and the air. It has no xylem to lift that water and no phloem to distribute it, which is why it cannot be tall: without plumbing there is no way to supply a top. And it cannot keep the water it gets. Its tissue simply equilibrates with the air around it. When the air is dry, the moss is dry, and when the moss is dry it stops. Six faculties, six failures. This is a complete deficit assessment, and there is nothing factually wrong with a single line of it. Hold on to that list. Every item survives to the end of this zine intact. What changes is what the list turns out to be a description of. Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

Two strategies, two names Poikilohydric, homoiohydric Botany has words for these two ways of dealing with water, and the useful thing about them is that neither one is the name of a defect. Poikilohydric — from the Greek for varied — means the organism's water content tracks the water content of its surroundings. It has no interior to speak of. Most bryophytes live this way, and the review literature calls it the poikilohydric habit: tissue hydration closely following environmental humidity. Homoiohydric — from the Greek for same — means the organism holds an internal water status roughly constant against whatever the outside is doing. Vascular plants live this way. So, incidentally, do you. One matches the world. One argues with it. They are two answers to the same problem, and the words for them are descriptive rather than graded. Notice what has already happened. Line five of the deficit list — water regulation: none — has a proper name, and under that name it stops being an absence and becomes a strategy. The same fact, relabelled, changes category. That is not a trick of language. It is what happens when you stop measuring one thing by the standard of another and go looking for what it is actually doing. Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

The bill for a constant interior What holding costs Homoiohydry is not free, and it is not simple. It is an infrastructure project that a plant pays for continuously, for its whole life. To hold an interior against a dry outside, a vascular plant needs roots to reach water that is not at the surface; xylem to lift it, sometimes tens of metres, against gravity; a waxy cuticle to stop it leaving; and stomata — thousands of controllable pores — because a sealed plant cannot take in carbon dioxide, so the seal has to be openable, and every opening is a leak it has chosen. That is four organ systems in the service of one requirement. And the requirement is unforgiving in a specific way: if a homoiohydric plant loses the argument, it does not pause. It dies. Drying is not a state it can occupy. It is the end of the organism. The tree's whole apparatus is the price of not being allowed to dry out. Height is what it bought with the plumbing; vulnerability is what it accepted along with it. So the honest version of the comparison is not tree: capable, moss: incapable. It is two organisms with different fixed costs, different failure modes, and different places they can live. The moss pays almost nothing to run and can be stopped without harm. The tree pays constantly and cannot be stopped at all. Neither of those is a better deal in the abstract. They are only better or worse somewhere in particular. Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

The finding The list is backwards Everything so far has assumed the moss lacks something the tree has. The literature on desiccation tolerance says the opposite, and says it plainly. In their 2007 review in The Bryologist, Proctor, Oliver, Wood, Alpert, Stark, Cleavitt and Mishler set out the evolutionary position: desiccation tolerance is a primitive character of land plants — ancestral, there from the beginning — which was lost in the course of the evolution of the homoiohydric vascular-plant shoot. The moss did not fail to acquire the tree's solution. The tree discarded the moss's. Two details make that more than a reversal of emphasis. First: the vascular plants did not fully let go. The same review records that desiccation tolerance was retained in spores, pollen and seeds. Every seed in a packet is doing the thing the moss does — sitting dry, metabolically stopped, waiting for water. The tree kept the old trick for the one job where nothing else would work, and then spent its adult life unable to perform it. Second: some went back for it. Desiccation tolerance re-evolved in the vegetative tissue of the vascular plants we call resurrection plants — which is to say some lineages, having given it up, evolved their way back to it, because where they ended up living it was the better answer after all. Now read the deficit list again. Not one line of it has changed. But the column heading was wrong. It was never faculties absent. It was the older arrangement, still intact. Where desiccation tolerance was kept, lost and regained A branching diagram of land plants. Desiccation tolerance is marked as present at the base, in the common ancestor. It is retained along the branch leading to mosses. On the branch leading to vascular plants it is marked as lost in the adult shoot, though kept in spores, pollen and seeds. A further branch off the vascular plants is marked as having regained it: the resurrection plants. mosses — kept resurrection plants — regained tolerance: ancestral vascular shoot — lost (kept in spores, pollen, seeds) Figure 1 · kept, lost, and gone back for Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

What drying actually is This is not rest It would be easy, and wrong, to describe a dried moss as resting. Resting is something a running system does. This is not that. As a desiccation-tolerant plant dries, its cytoplasm enters what the literature calls a glassy state — an amorphous solid, not a liquid, in which molecular mobility is severely reduced. Work on the xanthophyll-cycle pigments of Syntrichia ruralis was published under the title “Evidence for the absence of enzymatic reactions in the glassy state”, and that title is the finding: in the dry moss, the chemistry does not merely slow down. It does not run. Nothing is being maintained. There is no idling, no low-power mode, no reduced service. The organism is not doing anything at all, and the reason it survives is precisely that it is not doing anything — a stopped chemistry cannot go wrong. It is not conserving itself. It has stopped, and stopping is what conserves it. Say plainly what the cost is, because there is one and it is real. A dry moss is not photosynthesising, not growing, not competing for anything. Line six of the deficit list stands: photosynthesis when dry, stops entirely. Time spent dry is time not spent living, and a moss in a dry climate may be stopped far more of its life than it is running. This is the trade, stated honestly. Survival bought with the whole of the time. Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

Recovery, measured And then it rains Here is the part that is hard to believe until you see the gas-exchange traces. The moss does not convalesce. It resumes. Infrared gas analysis of rehydrating Syntrichia ruralis shows respiration reactivating almost instantly, photosynthesis beginning within a few minutes, and net photosynthesis returning to substantially normal rates within thirty to sixty minutes. Within the first two hours the protein profile has already changed over: the drying proteins are switched off and a set called rehydrins comes up. There is no ramp, no rehabilitation, no gradual return to duty. Water arrives and the machinery is running again inside an hour. Nothing had to be rebuilt, because nothing had been dismantled. It was intact the entire time it was stopped. How long can it stay stopped? Syntrichia can remain quiescent for decades and recover. And there is a stranger record: Roads, Longton and Convey, in Current Biology in 2014, grew new shoots from a core of Chorisodontium aciphyllum that had been frozen in Antarctic permafrost for at least 1,530 years. New growth appeared after three to four weeks. It was the first demonstration of survival on that timescale in any plant; comparable spans had previously been seen only in bacteria. Keep the two cases apart. The Antarctic moss was frozen, not dried, and cryptobiosis in permafrost is not the same mechanism as desiccation tolerance. The 1,530 years belongs to the freezing case; the decades belong to the drying one. They rhyme, and conflating them would be an overclaim. Net photosynthesis before drying, while dry, and after rewetting A trace of net photosynthetic rate over time. It runs at a normal level, falls to zero as the moss dries, and stays flat at zero for an interrupted stretch marked as lasting anything from days to decades. At the moment water is added the trace rises steeply and reaches substantially normal rates again within thirty to sixty minutes. net photosynthesis normal stopped — days to decades water 30–60 min time → Figure 2 · the gap is not to scale, and that is the point Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

Where the wind stops The still millimetre None of the previous spread works in open air. Drying and rewetting on that schedule needs a place where water lingers — and such a place exists, a few millimetres thick, over every surface in the world. Air is viscous and sticks to things. Away from obstacles it moves in smooth sheets; nearer a surface, friction tugs at it and the stream separates into layers of different speed — fast laminar flow aloft, a turbulent zone of eddies beneath it, and then air that gets slower and slower until, immediately against the surface, it is perfectly still, captured by the friction with the surface itself. Robin Wall Kimmerer calls this that small space where earth and atmosphere first make contact. It is the boundary layer. Because nothing moves there, the layer keeps what it holds: heat radiating back off sun-warmed ground, water vapour evaporating from a damp log, and carbon dioxide. Over a rotting log, where fungi and bacteria are working, the concentration can reach ten times that of the open air. One number, dated on purpose. Kimmerer gives ambient as about 380 ppm, which was roughly right when Gathering Moss was published in 2003 and is not right now. The ratio is the claim; the baseline has moved since, and this zine quotes the multiple rather than the reading. So a moss is a few centimetres tall at most, and that is not a shortfall against the boundary layer; it is the entry requirement. Kimmerer puts the height limit exactly where spread four put it: a plant more than a few centimeters high can't keep itself hydrated. The moss is not a plant that failed to get tall. It is a plant the right size for somewhere a tree can never go. And now the part that is better than any of that. The layer is not simply found and moved into. Friction makes it — so anything that increases friction deepens it. Moss leaves are long, narrow and held upright, which slows the air moving past them; species in dry places carry dense hairs, long reflective leaf tips, minuscule spines. Every one of those textures thickens the still layer overhead. Kimmerer states the rule twice, and the second half is the astonishing one: the greater the resistance, the deeper the boundary layer — and the larger the boundary layer, the larger the moss can be. Read that as a loop, because it is one. The moss builds the habitat that then permits it to be bigger. The ceiling on its size was never a property of the moss. It was a property of the layer — and the layer is something an organism can thicken by being the shape it is. Which is why mosses are not uniformly small. They run from crusts a millimetre high to wefts ten centimetres tall, a disparity Kimmerer likens to the one between a blueberry bush and a redwood — and the difference tracks the depth of the boundary layer in that habitat, not the quality of the moss. One last thing, and it is generous. Boundary layers nest. A rock in a moist forest has its own, sitting under the umbrella of the forest's; the trees slow the wind and their shade holds back the drying, and the mosses on that rock grow lush and tall. So the tree that wins every contest for light is also, intending nothing by it, the reason there is a layer deep enough for a moss to be large in. The ruler was never the tree. But the shelter, quite often, is. Air flow over a moss carpet, and the stalk that escapes it A side view of air moving over a cushion of moss. At the top, straight arrows show fast laminar flow. Below them, wavy arrows show a turbulent zone. Close to the moss, small curls show the still, slow air of the boundary layer. A sporophyte on a long stalk rises out of the cushion and through the boundary layer into the turbulent zone above, where moving air can carry its spores away. laminar flow turbulent zone boundary layer the moss Figure 3 · the moss deepens the layer, and the stalk escapes it Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

Which generation you are looking at The generation the trees spent There is one more inversion in the same shape as the last, and it is hiding in plain sight: the green thing you call “the moss” is not the same kind of body as the green thing you call “the tree.” Land plants alternate between two generations. The gametophyte carries one set of chromosomes and makes the sex cells; the sporophyte carries two and makes spores. Both exist in every land plant. What differs is which one gets to be the plant. In a moss, the green cushion is the gametophyte. The sporophyte is the little stalk with a capsule on the end that grows up out of the cushion — attached to it, nutritionally dependent on it, and short-lived. In a tree, it is the other way round and not by a small margin: the tree is the sporophyte, and its gametophyte generation has been reduced to a handful of cells inside a pollen grain and an ovule. The moss is not a small version of the tree. It is the other half of the life cycle, living in the open, at full size. That little stalk has one job, and the last spread explains it. Spores cannot disperse in still air, and they cannot germinate in their own parents’ carpet — so the seta is a periscope, lifting the capsule up out of the boundary layer and into the moving air above, where eddies can pull the spores out and carry them off. Kimmerer records that its length is strongly correlated with the depth of that layer: tall setae in forests, short ones in exposed places. The dependent generation is the one built to leave. So the two organisms are not even the same part of the same story. One kept both generations visible and let the older one stay in charge. The other put nearly everything into one generation and reduced the other almost to nothing. Twice now the comparison has broken down in the same direction. Not because the moss turns out to be secretly grand, but because tree was never the general case. It was one specialisation, being used as a ruler. Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks
What the small and slow hold

One number, carefully stated What the small and slow hold Mosses in the genus Sphagnum build bogs. They acidify the water they sit in, hold many times their own dry weight in it, and decay so slowly in the resulting cold acid anoxia that their own dead bodies accumulate underneath them for thousands of years. That accumulation is peat. Peatlands cover roughly 3% of the world's land surface and hold on the order of 500–550 gigatonnes of carbon — approximately twice the carbon held in the biomass of all the world's forests. The wording matters and is doing real work. The comparison is against forest biomass — the wood and leaves and roots — not against forests including their soils. The looser claim, “peatlands store twice as much carbon as all the world's forests,” travels much further than the careful one and is not the same statement. We are using the careful one. Still, take the careful one seriously. The organism with no roots, no vessels, no height and no control over its own water is holding twice as much carbon in its slow wet archive as every tree on Earth is holding in its wood. Not because it is stronger. Because it does not decay, and because it has not stopped, and because there has been a great deal of time. Which is the last thing the deficit list got wrong. It was scored on capacities — what can this thing do, right now, compared to that thing. It had no column at all for persistence, and persistence is where the moss keeps its entire answer. Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

What this does not say What this does not say A piece about an organism that survives by shutting down is about four sentences away from becoming something horrible. So, plainly: Not:that moss is secretly tougher than trees. That would just be the deficit list run in the other direction, with the same ruler. Moss is stopped for much of its life, cannot compete for light, and is confined to a few millimetres of still air. The point is not that it wins. The point is that there is no single contest. Not:“small is beautiful.” Smallness here is not an aesthetic or a virtue. It is a specific physical qualification for entry into the boundary layer, with specific costs attached. Consolation is not what the physics offers. Not:resilience as a demand. Desiccation tolerance is not a discipline the moss practises, and nothing here suggests anyone should get better at drying out. An organism that can survive being stopped should still not be stopped for someone else's convenience. Being able to endure a thing has never been an argument for being made to. Not:a claim that stopping is always recoverable. The moss resumes because its chemistry was never dismantled. Autistic burnout is not that, and does not run on that timetable. A mechanism that recovers in an hour is not a promise made to anybody. The rhyme here is about how a state gets classified, not about how long it lasts. Not:that the deficit list was factually wrong. It was accurate, line by line, start to finish. That is the whole difficulty with it, and the reason a list like that is so hard to argue with. It was true, and it was still a description of the wrong thing. Not:a proof. A rhyme, not a proof. Bryophyte physiology establishes precisely nothing about a nervous system. What it supplies is one checkable case of a real and well-documented pattern — an assessment that is accurate in every particular and wrong in its premise, because the standard it measured against was one specialisation mistaken for the general case. Whether that shape is familiar is for you to say. Measured Against a Tree · Stimpunks

L★S Every line of the assessment was true. The column heading was wrong. Holding is the newer trick, and the tree pays for it every day of its life. No. 8 The Universe Runs on Difference — monoculture is efficient and brittle No. 26 A Mycelium and a Rhizome — the other underfoot piece, and its hedges No. 59 The Rest You Keep — rest is not a reward paid out after work No. 71 Nothing Is Pushing — the cost of staying belongs to the place No. 73 Measured Against a Tree — the ruler was one specialisation ← you are here Reflection Which accurate list about you was measuring against something that was never the general case? What have you been told you lack, that is actually the older arrangement still intact? What does it cost the people around you to hold a constant interior — and does anyone bill them for it? Where is your boundary layer, and what is it that slows the air? What have you survived being stopped for, that you should never have been stopped for at all? The boundary layer. Robin Wall Kimmerer, Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses (Oregon State University Press, 2003), ch. “The Advantages of Being Small: Life in the Boundary Layer,” pp. 14–19 — read at the book. Source of the laminar/turbulent/still stratification and of air “perfectly still, captured by the friction with the surface itself”; of the boundary layer as “that small space where earth and atmosphere first make contact”; of the height limit, “a plant more than a few centimeters high can't keep itself hydrated”; of carbon dioxide over a decaying log reaching up to ten times ambient; of the two rules that carry spread eight — “the greater the resistance, the deeper the boundary layer” and “the larger the boundary layer, the larger the moss can be” — of the leaf textures (long narrow upright leaves, dense hairs, reflective tips, minuscule spines) that produce that resistance; of the millimetre-to-ten-centimetre range and its blueberry-bush-and-redwood comparison; of a rock's boundary layer sitting under the umbrella of the forest's own; and of the seta as the stalk that lifts spores out of the still layer, its length correlated with that layer's depth. Rhizoids and the alternation of generations are standard plant biology, not attributed to a single source. Credits The seed is Helen Edgar's. Mossy Minds & Monotropism (Autistic Realms, 2025) is where moss arrives as an invitation to think about monotropism, ethodiversity and neuroqueering our spaces, and where the line about moss's “quiet deep greenness of a million shades” comes from. This zine's accent colour is green because of that sentence. The physiology and the argument are ours, and they go somewhere her essay does not: she reads moss as a model for thriving, where this piece reads the deficit list and finds the ruler broken. Both readings are of the same organism and neither replaces the other. Monotropism is Dinah Murray, Mike Lesser & Wenn Lawson (2005). Ethodiversity is Ombre Tarragnat (2025). Neither is named in the body of this zine, deliberately: the argument here is made entirely out of plant physiology and should stand without the vocabulary. Proposed by Ryan Boren, who asked whether there was something to build around moss, and who then supplied the Kimmerer chapter when the piece stalled on it. Two things the research changed. The zine was outlined as a comparison of two water strategies with the deficit list as a framing device; reading the Proctor review turned it into something sharper — the tolerance is ancestral and was lost, so the deficit list is not merely unfair but inverted, and the tree is the one that gave something up. That is in neither Helen's essay nor Popova's account of Kimmerer. Then the chapter itself changed spread eight twice over. It was drafted as being small is the entry ticket to a layer with better weather — true, and static. Kimmerer has the layer being built: friction makes it, leaf texture increases friction, and the deeper it gets the larger the moss may be, which is a feedback loop rather than a niche. And she has boundary layers nesting, so the forest's own layer shelters the rock's, and the tree turns out to be the reason a moss can be large. That last point argues against this zine's title, which is why it is on the spread and in the closing line rather than quietly left out. Still open Three source items remain, each flagged above where it applies: the Proctor review was read at its abstract and at secondary accounts rather than the paywalled full text, and its three-part claim — kept, lost, regained — is load-bearing enough to want confirmed there; the gas-exchange recovery figures need pinning to a single primary paper rather than to the review literature reporting them; and the peat figures were read at UNEP's summary rather than at the Global Peatlands Assessment itself. None of the three is a quotation, and all three are stated as approximate on the spreads that use them. What this deliberately does not re-argue A Mycelium and a Rhizome (No. 26) owns the underground network, and this piece stays off that ground entirely — no common mycorrhizal networks, no forest-wide claims, none of the material that needs hedging there. The Rest You Keep (No. 59) owns rest and burnout; spread six is adjacent to it and stops short on purpose, and the refusals say why. The Universe Runs on Difference (No. 8) owns monoculture and fragility. A rhyme, not a proof. Nothing in bryophyte physiology establishes anything whatsoever about a nervous system, and nothing here is offered as a cause or a consolation. What the plants supply is one well-documented instance of a particular failure of measurement: an assessment accurate in every line, and wrong altogether, because the standard it used was a specialisation being mistaken for the general case. The list was true. The ruler was a tree — and so, it turns out, was the shelter. the long way round L★S · 001 The Pole to Pole Arctic tern · Sterna paradisaea ~71,000 km a year · pole to pole The longest migration known, flown by a bird lighter than a coffee mug — and it does not fly straight. It follows the wind in enormous S-shaped detours, because the long way round is the cheap way round. longestpole to polenot straightwind-riding ▸ Field notes Field notes · Arctic tern · Sterna paradisaea When Carsten Egevang and colleagues fitted eleven Arctic terns with 1.4-gram geolocators, the tracks came back longer than anyone had guessed: birds from Greenland and Iceland covering roughly 71,000 km in a year, with some individuals exceeding 80,000 — the longest seasonal movement recorded for any animal (Egevang et al., PNAS, 2010). The detail worth keeping is the shape. The tern does not fly the great-circle route. It tracks down the Atlantic in a vast S, pausing mid-ocean, swinging wide to catch prevailing winds. Drawn on a map it looks like inefficiency; measured in energy it is the opposite. The straight line is a human idea about routes, and it is not how the record-holder travels. life builds the world 16 Niche Minor Worlds on niche construction, stimming, and how difference doesn't just see a world — it builds one L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Niche construction Organisms are not passive Since Darwin, we have pictured the environment as the fixed thing: it sets the test, and organisms adapt or die. But that is only half the loop. The beaver builds a dam and turns a stream into a pond. The spider spins a web; the bird weaves a nest; the earthworm rewrites the chemistry of the soil. Organisms are not passive. The environment is a product of organisms. Biologists call this niche construction (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman), and it runs as a second engine of evolution beside natural selection. It even has its own inheritance: descendants receive not only genes but the world their ancestors built — a beaver born into the pond its grandparents dug. So life does not only drift and sense. It builds — and the built world is handed on. Evolution has two engines: the genes you inherit, and the world your ancestors built. the beaver dam · pond the environment is a product of organisms back from the Council, and building the world remade, and inherited Minor Worlds · Stimpunks
Don't fix the head, change the world

fix the person bend the mind to the slot build the world shape the room to the mind two answers to a mind that doesn't fit change the room, not the head Positive niche construction Don't fix the head, change the world Here is what that means for us. The old model says that when a mind doesn't fit, you fix the mind — make it more like the standard one. Niche construction says the standard was never sacred. As Thomas Armstrong argues, there is no "normal" brain kept in a vat at the Smithsonian for all other brains to be measured against. So stop bending the person. Build the environment. This is not soft metaphor; it is how minds actually work. We ease a too-loud world by acting on it — dimming the light, finding the quiet room, laying the routine down like track. Cognitive science frames it as acting on the world to suit our own states; the plainer version is that the place itself helps us think. Cognition is spread across the room we arrange, not sealed in the skull. Change the world, and you change what a mind can do. Don't bend the mind to fit the room. Build a room the mind can think in. Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

A space of one's own Stimming is worldmaking Watch that building up close. The noise-cancelling headphones. The same walk, the same meal, the song on repeat. The desk set just so; the shelf that holds the whole special interest; the stone turned over and over in a hand. From outside, these get filed as symptoms to manage. From inside, they are worldmaking — the patient assembly of a few stable points a self can stand on. Stimming is niche construction at the scale of a body: movement that tunes the sensory field until it is livable. Ombre Tarragnat calls such movements ontological choreographies — dances that bring a small world into being. One Autistic writer describes their nest plainly: this is my space; it lets me hold one small part of a hard world. Own Sky left us inside a soap bubble — whole, but never guaranteed. Here is the reply to that precarity: we build the bubble ourselves, and we keep on rebuilding it. a world assembled from chosen things we build the bubble ourselves Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

the "Major" world small, real, and networked minor worlds, tended and shared small is not lesser Niche communities Minor worlds These worlds are small, and the smallness is the point. A corner, a routine, a fandom, a friendship, a special interest — none of them universal, every one of them real. Erin Manning calls this the minor: not lesser, only not pretending to be the whole. And we build them together. Autistic people all but invented fandom; we assemble niche communities out of necessity and because our ways of being are, frankly, weird (Devon Price). Some grow into NeurodiVentures — non-hierarchical groups run by neurodivergent people for collaborative niche construction, thickening over time into resilient little ecosystems. Small, local, tended by the people who need it — that is not a lesser world. That is a world. A world doesn't have to be universal to be real. It only has to be built, and shared. Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

Reconstruction, not accommodation Whose niche is the default? But not every niche admits that it was built. The hum of fluorescent light, the open-plan clatter, the crowded room — these get called neutral, just the conditions everyone works in. They are nothing of the sort. They are a niche too, built to suit one kind of mind and then renamed the default. Kadodia and Krueger call it the epistemic niche: our shared spaces quietly encode whose senses, whose pace, whose ways of knowing count, and reward the people they were built for. Which is why bolting an accommodation onto a hostile room is not the fix. The architecture itself has to change — reconstruction, not accommodation. There is no neutral sky and no neutral room. And as biodiversity toughens an ecosystem, a wider range of minds toughens a society's knowledge: the default was only ever one niche among the many we could build. Notan accommodation bolted onto a hostile room — reconstruction, not a ramp to nowhere. Nota "neutral" default — a default is just someone's niche, left unmarked. Notbending the person to the room — build a room more minds can think in. Nota world you're only allowed to visit — a world you get to help build. NEUTRAL light · noise · crowd built for one mind a default is someone's niche peel back "neutral" and find a niche, unmarked Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

human dog plant kin tools a niche is always made with we world each other into being The oldest work Worlding together The last thing to notice is that we never build alone. A niche is made with — with the people who share the fandom, the dog who sets the shape of the day, the plants on the sill, the tools on the belt. Donna Haraway calls these companion species: we world one another into being. Step back far enough and it is all one story. The beaver's pond, the spider's web, the quiet room, the niche community, the reconstructed school — every one of them is matter arranging itself into a place where life can hold. The universe builds itself into worlds, and it does it through us. We are star stuff, building — and to make one small, livable world, together, is the oldest work there is. We are star stuff, building. To make a world is the oldest thing matter does. Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

Which "neutral" rooms in your life are really built for one kind of mind? Whose niche gets called the default — and who has to keep visiting instead of building? Minor Worlds is the sixteenth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the third of a loose trilogy: how we treat other worlds (No. 14), how we sense them (No. 15), and — here — how we build them. It is the one where the cosmology comes home to the ground the Foundation stands on. Niche construction — organisms remaking their environments, and passing the remade world on as ecological inheritance — is from Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman (2003), after Lewontin; the beaver, spider, and nest are the textbook cases. Positive niche construction — change the environment, not the child; there is no "normal" brain in a vat — is Thomas Armstrong's (Neurodiversity in the Classroom). That we act on the world to suit our states, and that "the place itself helps us think," draw on active-inference research on Autistic cognition and Annie Murphy Paul's The Extended Mind. Stimming as worldmaking, and the precarious yet buildable bubble, draw on Ombre Tarragnat (Autistic worldings, ontological choreography) and Erin Manning (the minor, Autistic perception); the nest that holds "one small part of a hard world" is from Emergent Divergence. Niche communities and fandom are Devon Price (Unmasking Autism) and Steve Silberman (NeuroTribes); NeurodiVentures and collaborative niche construction are Jorn Bettin / Autistic Collaboration. The epistemic niche — "neutral" defaults built for one kind of mind, reconstruction over accommodation — is Kadodia & Krueger (2026). Companion species is Donna Haraway; "matter worlds" is Karen Barad. Monotropism carries over from No. 15. The reading — that no niche is neutral, no world is lesser, and that building them is the cosmos's oldest work — is ours. You were star stuff, building, all along. The rhizome Not a tree The usual picture of knowledge is a tree. One trunk, a few big branches, everything ranked and traceable back to a single root. To learn it you climb; to belong you find your place on the chart. Miss a branch and you're lost. Deleuze and Guattari offered another shape: the rhizome. Picture ginger root, or crabgrass, or fungal thread — no trunk, no first cause, no top. Any point can connect to any other. It is "a model perpetually in construction or collapsing," they wrote: a map you can enter from any edge, not a tree you must climb from the base. Cut a rhizome and it doesn't die — it regrows from anywhere. There is no root to ask permission of, because there is no root. A map you can enter from any edge — not a tree you must climb from the base. tree one root · a top rhizome any point to any point hierarchy vs network no root, no top A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

enter anywhere spiky mono-tropism deep attn a word that fit burnout a classroom problem no prerequisite · no gatekeeper every door opens onto the whole Entry points Many doors Because there's no beginning, there's no wrong place to start. Neurodivergent knowledge is a rhizome you enter wherever your life opens a door. Come in at Spiky Profiles and you might follow a thread to Monotropism, and on to Deep Attention — or arrive from the far side entirely, through burnout, or a word that finally fit, or a problem in a classroom. No prerequisite. No gatekeeper checking you read the introduction first. No "you're not ready for this yet." The map has as many doors as there are people, and every door opens onto the whole. This matters most for minds that were told they'd learned things in the wrong order, or hadn't earned the next rung. In a rhizome there are no rungs — only the next connection that makes sense to you. No prerequisite. No gatekeeper. As many doors as there are people. A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

The network flows The mycelium moves A rhizome is the shape; a mycelium is the life in it. Underground, fungal threads lace through the soil and trade with the roots they meet — water and scarce minerals for sugar made in the light. Whether those threads also wire whole forests together, elder tree feeding shaded seedling — the "wood wide web" (Simard) — is the contested part, and we hold it loosely (Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, 2023). And the network is not fixed. Where a path is useful, traffic thickens it; where it isn't, it quietly fades. A slime mold — one cell, no brain, no boss — grows across a map of scattered food and settles into almost exactly the rail network human engineers drew for Tokyo (Tero et al., 2010). Decentralised, and still smart. That's how care and knowledge move through our communities too: not issued from a head office, but flowing along the threads to wherever they're needed, strengthening whatever works. Not issued from a head office — flowing along the threads to wherever it's needed. the network learns plenty fed in the shade strong paths thicken · weak paths fade flow · redistribute · adapt smart without a boss A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

same shape, different scale cosmic web mycelium neuron not a pyramid — a web supercluster · mushroom · synapse read the captions to tell them apart the universe's favourite shape Every scale The same shape everywhere Zoom all the way out and the shape returns. The cosmic web — the largest structure there is — is galaxies strung like dew along vast filaments of dark matter, with great voids between and no center anywhere. Matter drifts down the strands to the bright knots where filaments cross. Set a slice of the cosmic web beside a mycelial mat, beside a slime mold, beside a single neuron, and you have to read the captions to tell them apart. The universe keeps reaching for the same answer: not a pyramid, a web. So when we build without a throne at the top, we aren't failing to organise. We're organising the way the universe does at every scale. Decentralisation isn't disorder — it's the oldest structure there is. Not a pyramid. A web. The oldest structure there is. Neuro-anarchy The Autistic Rhizome We are already building this. David Gray-Hammond and Katie Munday name it neuro-anarchy: "the decentralisation of hierarchy as it pertains to neurocultures." The Autistic Rhizome is "a network with no single point of origin. No part of the network depends upon the existence of another." No advocates ranked above followers, no advancing by how much you know — we meet as equals, held together by a do-no-harm ethic instead of a chain of command. Helen Edgar maps the same ground: watering holes and Discords alive at 2am, belonging you don't have to earn. Lose any one node and the network lives on, because nothing depends on a center. That isn't fragility waiting for a leader. It's resilience by design — a community shaped like the minds it's made of. Nota tree — no trunk, and no root to ask permission of. Nota ladder — no one advances by rank or "knowledge level"; we meet as equals. Notwaiting for a leader — decentralisation is the design, not a defect. Notchaos — a rhizome has structure; it just isn't a pyramid. Where have you seen care flow along the threads to whoever needed it, with no one in charge? What path could you thicken, or what new door could you add, this week? A Mycelium and a Rhizome is the twenty-sixth zine in the Stimpunks series. It maps how neurodivergent knowledge and community grow — a rhizome (structure) fed by a mycelium (flow) — and grounds them where they meet reality, in Cavendish Space. It's the map that ties Underground (No. 5) to No One Is the Leader (No. 22). The philosophy: Gilles Deleuze & Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1980) — the rhizome as a map, not a tracing, "perpetually in construction or collapsing." The culture: David Gray-Hammond and Katie Munday on neuro-anarchy and the Autistic Rhizome ("a network with no single point of origin"), and Helen Edgar's Autistic Rhizome and online watering holes. The framing draws on Stimpunks' own A Mycelium and a Rhizome and Cavendish Space, with its pattern language — Spiky Profiles, Monotropism, Deep Attention, Regulation First, Environment Fit. The science: mycorrhizal networks and the "wood wide web" (Suzanne Simard); the decentralised problem-solving of the slime mold Physarum polycephalum, which reproduced the Tokyo rail network (Tero et al., 2010); and the cosmic web of dark-matter filaments — the universe's largest structure, and a rhizome at the grandest scale. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The reading — that decentralisation is not disorder but the oldest structure there is — is ours. no centre L★S · 001 The Net Without a Centre Jellyfish · cnidarian nerve net no brain · a body-wide net · ~600 Myr old One of the oldest nervous systems on Earth: no brain, no head, no centre — a mesh of neurons spread evenly through the body, firing in rings and waves. nerve netno centreoldestdecentralised ▸ Field notes Field notes · Jellyfish · cnidarian nerve net Cnidarians — jellyfish, corals, anemones — are among the earliest animals to evolve a nervous system, roughly 580–600 million years ago. What looks "primitive" from inside a skull-shaped assumption is simply a different, older architecture, whole on its own terms. Ravens will refuse an immediately available small reward in order to take a tool or a token, and use or barter it the next day (Kabadayi & Osvath, Science 357, 2017); New Caledonian crows hold the identity and location of out-of-sight tools in mind while planning a sequence (Gruber et al., Current Biology 29, 2019). This card previously listed self-recognition among the things a corvid does without a neocortex, and did so in the column this table uses to say what is actually the case — which is the worst available place for a result this thin. The corvid evidence is Prior, Schwarz & Güntürkün (PLoS Biology 6(8): e202, 2008): five hand-raised magpies, of which two showed statistically significant mark-directed behaviour, one produced a single spontaneous instance, and two showed none. The authors' own caution, in the paper, is that the number of birds tested is too small for a definitive estimate of the distribution within the population. A close replication with a larger sample — Soler, Colmenero, Pérez-Contreras & Peralta-Sánchez, Journal of Comparative Psychology 134(4), 2020 — then failed to confirm it: the mirror-versus-control difference in social and self-directed behaviour reproduced, but in the mark test self-directed behaviour was more frequent in front of the cardboard control. Hedged narrowly, in both directions. What failed is the mark test, not every mirror response, so "debunked" would be as wrong as the original overclaim. And nothing here touches the tool use or the planning, which stand. The full account is on the magpie card in Field Guide No. 23. Birds reached this without a neocortex at all, building intelligence on a different plan (a densely packed pallium instead of layered cortex). There are many roads to a mind — "bird brain," reclaimed. A correction, 2026-09-03, and it is a different fault from the corvid one on this page. This card previously listed self-recognition in the column above. Two things were wrong with that. First, the species. Every number on this card is the African elephant (Loxodonta africana); the mirror study is Plotnik, de Waal & Reiss, "Self-recognition in an Asian elephant," PNAS 103(45), 17053–17057 (2006) — three adult female Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) at the Bronx Zoo. And the swap is not pedantry: the study's own control depends on it. The paper notes that male African elephants often touch their heads because of temporal gland secretion, whereas in female Asian elephants that gland is bilateral, vestigial and nonsecretory — which is precisely what let the authors rule out a general propensity to touch the marked area. Carry the finding across to an African elephant and you reintroduce the confound the species choice removed. Second, the strength. Happy, Maxine and Patty were all tested; one — Happy — passed the mark test, on the first day of marking, with a significant shift in her head-touching distribution (χ² = 130.83, df = 2, P < 0.001). Maxine and Patty did not. Re-marked two months later, none of the three touched mark or sham. The paper's title is singular for a reason. Held fairly, because this is not the magpie case. There is no failed independent replication here, and the authors answer the one-of-three objection themselves: even in chimpanzees, the most extensively tested species with mirror self-recognition, fewer than half of individuals may pass on some studies — and repeated mark tests on one animal are considered uninterpretable, because they compromise the mark's salience. All three elephants reached the third and fourth stages of the standard progression and showed a total absence of social responses to the mirror image, which is itself evidence. So the honest form is: mirror self-recognition has been demonstrated in one Asian elephant, and it is a real and careful result — it is simply not a general fact about elephants, and it is not a fact about this card's animal at all. So "more neurons" was never a ladder to climb. A brain is shaped by the body and the life it serves, not by a score. The elephant's mind — its memory, mourning, and culture — is exactly its own, built for being an elephant. one shell arriveseveryone moves up at once L★S · 005 The Housing Queue Hermit crabs · Coenobita and Pagurus one shell arrives · a whole line rehouses A hermit crab builds nothing. When a single empty shell turns up, crabs gather beside it and line up by size — and when the largest moves in, every crab behind it moves up at once. owns nothingqueues by sizesynchronous chainsbenefits are distributed ▸ Field notes Field notes · Hermit crabs · Coenobita and Pagurus A hermit crab contributes no material to its home. Every shell it will ever occupy was made by a snail and vacated by circumstance. This looks, at first glance, like the least impressive entry in the guide. It is arguably the most interesting one. Chase, Weissburg and DeWitt described the vacancy chain in 1988: a vacant resource enters the population, an individual takes it and abandons its old one, which a second individual takes, and so on down. One new shell rehouses many crabs. In a synchronous chain, this happens as a piece of visible collective behaviour. Crabs assemble at a newly available shell and queue beside it in descending order of size. When the largest crab moves in, the next takes the shell it left, and the cascade runs down the line. In an asynchronous chain, a lone crab finds a shell and the animals never meet. Lewis and Rotjan tested the prediction that matters and found it held: vacancy chains provide aggregate benefits distributed across many participants, not just the first taker. Read that as a housing system and it is remarkable. Nobody can improve their situation until somebody above them does, so the arrival of one resource lifts a whole queue, and the animals wait for it rather than fight over it. The crab that waits is not being passive. It is standing in the only position from which the chain works. oak tissuewasp’s design L★S · 008 The House You Make the Tree Grow Gall wasps and other gall inducers · Cynipidae and beyond roughly 13,000 described inducers A gall is not built. The insect injects signals that hijack the plant’s own development, and the plant grows a custom chamber — shaped to the insect’s specification, out of the tree’s tissue. plant tissue, insect designan extended phenotypespecies-specific shapesfeeds and shelters ▸ Field notes Field notes · Gall wasps and other gall inducers · Cynipidae and beyond This is the entry that broke the material sort. Ask what a gall is made of and the answer is oak. Ask whose it is and the answer is the wasp's. A gall-inducing insect lays into plant tissue and delivers effectors — including phytohormones — that redirect the host's developmental programme. The plant then grows a structure that shelters and feeds the larva, with tissue layers differentiated for the purpose, developing in step with the insect's own growth. The decisive evidence that this is the insect's design rather than the plant's reaction: different insect species induce distinctively different gall shapes on the very same host plant. The oak is not making a generic wound response. It is being made to build to spec. Which is why the literature reaches for Dawkins's term and calls a gall an extended phenotype of the insect — a body part expressed outside the body, in somebody else's tissue. Roughly 13,000 gall-inducing insect species are described, about 2% of insects, though global estimates run from 21,000 to 211,000, so we give it as a range. Set beside the hermit crab, this section stops looking like cheating. One animal spends its effort finding a home; this one spends it on instructions. Neither assembles anything. Both are housed, and both strategies are tens of millions of years old. the same answerfound 7 separate times L★S · 009 Seven Times, Independently Obligate brood parasites · cuckoos, honeyguides, cowbirds, viduid finches, a duck evolved at least 7 separate times Some birds build no nest, incubate no egg, and raise no young. The phylogeny says otherwise. Interspecific obligate brood parasitism — laying in another species' nest and leaving the rearing to them entirely — evolved independently at least seven times (Sorenson and Payne, 2002): three separate times among the cuckoos, once in the honeyguides, once in waterfowl (the black-headed duck, Heteronetta atricapilla), and twice among songbirds, in the African viduid finches and in the cowbirds. Seven independent origins is the signature of a solution that works. Evolution does not repeatedly stumble into the same catastrophic error in five families across the tree. Recent comparative genomics has gone looking for convergent adaptations across those origins and found them. We are not going to sentimentalise it. Brood parasitism is costly to hosts, and the arms race between parasite and host defence is one of the sharpest in behavioural ecology. The claim here is narrower and it is about our reading, not about the birds: not building is a strategy, not an absence of one. Of everything in this guide, this is the entry we would most like a reader to carry: the option you were told was the failure to do the thing properly may in fact be the thing, arrived at over and over by animals with no contact with each other. a stagethe nest is elsewhere L★S · 013 The Theatre Great bowerbird · Chlamydera nuchalis not a nest · forced perspective The most celebrated "nest" on Earth is not one. Nothing is laid in a bower and nothing lives there. It is a stage — built with a deliberate optical illusion aimed at an audience of one. no eggs, everfemale nests elsewheregraded object sizesforced perspective ▸ Field notes Field notes · Great bowerbird · Chlamydera nuchalis Every list of animal architecture puts the bowerbird near the top, and the entry is misfiled every time. A bower is not a nest. No egg is laid in it. Nothing lives in it. After mating, the female goes away and builds a nest of her own, in a tree, and raises the young alone. The bower is a display court: an avenue of vertical sticks with a decorated area at each end. And what the male does with those decorations is stranger than the mistake. Endler, Endler and Doerr showed in 2010 that great bowerbirds arrange the objects in their courts by size, graded outward, so that from the female's viewing position inside the avenue the objects subtend a more even visual angle than they naturally would. It is forced perspective — the same trick a stage set uses — and males who make it more regular do better. So the structure is a theatre with deliberate scenography, and we have spent a century calling it a house. Why this closes the guide. The other twelve entries correct a reading of an animal. This one corrects the category itself. We are so sure that an impressive structure must be a home that the single most famous builder on the list gets filed under the wrong word — by people who know perfectly well the female nests elsewhere. What counts as a nest was never obvious, and we have been guessing confidently the whole time. 3 Field Guide A field guide to the Neurodiversity Paradigm What the paradigm actually claims. What it means to say variation instead of disorder. Why the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation — and why that matters. The paradigm, plainly stated Neurodiversity · InLv · Nick Walker open edition L★S
Two frameworks. One is a medical model. One is a paradigm.

Two ways of seeing · the same person Two frameworks. One is a medical model. One is a paradigm. The neurodiversity paradigm doesn't replace medicine. It changes the frame — what counts as a problem, who gets to define it, and what solutions are even on the table. Here are the two frameworks, side by side. Pathology Paradigm Neurodiversity Paradigm Neurological difference is a disorder — a deviation from normal functioning that needs to be identified and treated. Neurological difference is a form of natural variation — one point in the full range of human neurological experience. The goal is to identify what is wrong with the person and move them closer to a neurotypical standard. The goal is to understand the person's actual profile and create conditions where they can thrive as they are. Difficulty is located inside the person — as a deficit, a symptom, a dysfunction. Difficulty is located in the mismatch between the person and their environment — the environment is often the problem. Success means the person appears more neurotypical — masks better, behaves more normatively. Success means the person can live well as themselves — with support that fits their actual needs. The diagnostic manual defines the standard from which the person has deviated. The diagnostic manual is a tool for accessing support — useful but not definitive of who a person is. The person's way of being in the world is a problem to be solved. The person's way of being in the world is a valid mode of human existence. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
Not a buzzword. A paradigm with a lineage.

The word · its history Not a buzzword. A paradigm with a lineage. The concept of neurodiversity emerged from the Autistic community in the 1990s — not from academia, not from clinicians, but from Autistic and neurodivergent people describing their own experience and organizing around it. The online community InLv (Independent Living on the Autistic Spectrum), founded by Martijn Dekker in 1996, was one of the primary spaces where this thinking developed. Jim Sinclair's foundational essay "Don't Mourn For Us" (1993) and the work of Autism Network International laid the groundwork. The ideas were built through collective lived experience — no single author, and no one handing them down. This history matters. The paradigm was not handed down from above. It was built from the inside — by the people it describes, from their own understanding of themselves. That is its authority. The definition · plainly stated Neurodiversity (the paradigm) Neurodiversity is the infinite variation in neurocognitive functioning within our species — the diversity of human minds. The paradigm holds that this variation is natural and valuable, that there is no one "normal" brain any more than there is one normal ethnicity, and that neurological differences — autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and others — are not deficits to be cured. Some of that divergence is innate; some is made by experience. Neither kind is an error. — after Nick Walker, Neuroqueer Heresies (2021) Neurodivergent Having a mind that functions in ways which diverge significantly from the dominant societal standards of "normal." Not a synonym for disabled — though many neurodivergent people are disabled. A description of neurological difference, not a diagnosis. — term coined by Kassiane Asasumasu (2000); definition after Nick Walker, Neuroqueer Heresies (2021) Neurotypical Having a neurological profile that aligns with dominant societal standards of "normal." Not a synonym for healthy or good — a description of one position in the neurological distribution. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
The DSM is a tool. Not a truth.

Diagnosis · what it is and isn't The DSM is a tool. Not a truth. The neurodiversity paradigm is not anti-diagnosis. Diagnoses unlock support, accommodations, language, and community. For many people, getting a diagnosis is a profound relief — finally having a word for what their life has been. What the paradigm disputes is the idea that the DSM defines reality — that the categories it creates are natural kinds rather than constructed tools. Diagnostic criteria are written by committees, revised every decade or so, and shaped by cultural assumptions about what counts as "normal" functioning. The DSM describes what deviates from a norm. The paradigm asks: who sets the norm? Who benefits from it? What gets missed when the instrument is calibrated only to detect deviation? Common misreadings · corrected Myth "The neurodiversity paradigm says autism/ADHD isn't real." Fact The paradigm says neurological differences are real — and that framing them as disorders rather than variations changes what we see and what we do. Myth "It only applies to people who are 'mildly' affected." Fact The paradigm applies across the full range of neurological difference — including people with high support needs. Support needs and human value are separate questions. Myth "Neurodiversity means you can't acknowledge that things are hard." Fact The paradigm locates difficulty precisely — in the mismatch between a person and their environment, not in the person's existence. That's a more accurate and more useful place to intervene. Myth "It's just positive spin — trying to make people feel good about deficits." Fact It's a substantive claim about the nature of neurological variation, grounded in disability theory, lived experience, and increasingly, in neuroscience. The goal is accuracy, not reassurance. Myth "If we don't call it a disorder, people won't get help." Fact The paradigm fully supports appropriate support and accommodation — it changes the justification, not the outcome. You don't need to call someone broken to give them what they need. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation.

The core reframe The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. This is not a metaphor borrowed from cosmology for comfort. It is a precise statement about the relationship between variation and value. The universe produces variation at every scale — in stellar types, in orbital mechanics, in the distribution of matter, in the neurological profiles of its most complex structures. No variation in that distribution is intrinsically wrong. The concept of "disorder" requires a norm, and norms are always constructed by someone, for some purpose, from some position. When the calcium in your bones was forged in a dying star, the universe did not ask whether it was being made correctly. It was matter becoming what matter becomes. Your neurology is the same. It is the universe producing variation — which is what the universe does. The paradigm takes this seriously. It says: difference is not deficit. Variation is not disorder. The distribution is not a hierarchy. Five principles · the paradigm in practice Principle 01 Neurological variation is natural Human neurological profiles exist on a distribution. No point on that distribution is intrinsically correct. Autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and related profiles are not errors — they are positions in a natural range. Principle 02 Disability is often environmental Much of what makes neurodivergence disabling is the mismatch between a person's profile and an environment designed for a narrower range. Change the environment and you change the disability. Principle 03 Support needs don't determine worth Having high support needs is not a measure of human value. Every person, regardless of support needs, deserves to have those needs met and to be treated with full dignity. Principle 04 Autistic and neurodivergent people are the experts The people who live a neurological experience have knowledge about it that outside observers don't. The paradigm centers neurodivergent voices — particularly on questions about neurodivergent lives. Principle 05 Nothing about us without us Decisions about neurodivergent people should involve neurodivergent people. This applies to research, policy, education, clinical practice, and every other domain that shapes neurodivergent lives. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks

The paradigm applied · lived experience What this changes The paradigm isn't only theoretical. It has practical consequences for how neurodivergent people understand themselves and how the people around them should respond. When you adopt the neurodiversity paradigm, certain things shift. The question changes from "what is wrong with this person?" to "what does this person need, and what is the environment failing to provide?" That shift has consequences. It changes what interventions look like. It changes what success looks like. It changes whether the goal is making someone appear more normal or helping them live well as who they are. It also changes how neurodivergent people are allowed to understand themselves — not as broken versions of a normal person, but as one valid configuration of the remarkable variation the universe produces. Practical implications 🔬 In assessment: The goal shifts from identifying deficits to mapping a full profile — strengths, challenges, and what environments and supports allow the person to thrive. 🏫 In education: Accommodation isn't charity — it's the environment doing its job. Universal design benefits everyone. The Autistic student asking for written instructions improves outcomes for the whole class. 🩺 In healthcare: Clinicians learn to ask neurodivergent patients how they experience their symptoms rather than assuming a neurotypical baseline. Sensory needs, communication differences, and masking are taken seriously. 👥 In community: Stimming is welcome. Atypical communication is met with curiosity, not correction. People are not asked to perform neurotypicality as the price of belonging. 💛 In self-understanding: You are not a failed version of a normal person. You are a valid configuration of the variation the universe produces. Your neurology belongs here. L★S. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks

The paradigm history draws on the foundational work of Autism Network International, Jim Sinclair's "Don't Mourn For Us" (1993), the Autistic community of InLv — Martijn Dekker's list, founded 1996 — and Nick Walker's Neuroqueer Heresies (2021), whose definitions of neurodiversity, neurodivergent and neurotypical this guide follows.
