Either answer takes the ranking apart

Either way Either answer takes the ranking apart Here is why we can sit inside an unsettled question without losing the thread. The belonging claim does not depend on which way it goes. If it was built twice — then the layered cortex is one implementation among at least two, and the thing our textbooks call the seat of higher thought is, in the field's own word, dispensable. There is more than one way to arrive at a mind, and the one we happen to have is not the entry fee. If it was inherited — then it is stranger and warmer than that. The crossing in the crow's forebrain and the crossing in your cortex are one very old piece of equipment, carried out of the Carboniferous by two lineages that have not shared a body plan in something like 320 million years. Neither of us designed it. Neither of us is the version it was for. The kit is older than either of us. What differs is what each lineage did with it — and what each did with it is not a ranking, it is a natural history. This is the same move the site is built on, in an unfamiliar place. You are made of atoms assembled in dying stars, and so is everything else; the inheritance is not a distinction. A shared inheritance cannot be a hierarchy. It can only be a variety of uses. And the variation is the part that is not in dispute at all. No reading of these papers makes the pigeon a failed owl or the chicken a failed crow. They are different uses of a common toolkit, each sufficient for the life it is in — which is precisely the claim the neurodiversity paradigm makes about us, arriving here from fibre orientation and single-cell sequencing rather than from a manifesto. Older Than Either of Us · Stimpunks
Forty-four suburbs, and a counter-culture of bin locks

The bins Forty-four suburbs, and a counter-culture of bin locks Back to the clip, with the architecture behind it. In Sydney, sulphur-crested cockatoos learned to lift the lids of household waste bins. Klump and colleagues tracked what happened next, and published it in Science in 2021. The behaviour spread by social learning to 44 suburbs. It was not one trick copied exactly: birds opened lids with individual style, and the styles varied by site — local dialects of the same innovation. And the people responded, developing what the paper describes as a counter-culture of technical measures: bricks, bungees, weighted lids. Notice what the whole scene is made of, and that none of it is inside the bird. There is an environment that was built by us and then changed by us again in response. There is a relationship — the behaviour travels bird to bird, which is what makes it a culture rather than a talent. There is attention, sustained across a sequence: a raven will turn down food it can have now to take a tool or a token it can only use tomorrow. And there is a system, which in this story is a municipal waste contract and, in the laboratory version, a century of ranking. None of that is a metaphor for us, and we are not going to make it one. It is the same stack, seen somewhere it is easy to see because nobody's dignity is being adjudicated. When we describe a human being's behaviour without the environment, the relationships, the attention and the system, we are not being rigorous. We are leaving out most of the causes. Older Than Either of Us · Stimpunks

A cheaper neuron is an adaptation, not a gift, and not a moral. NotA ranking with the birds moved up it. If the answer to a bad hierarchy is the same hierarchy, reordered, nothing has been learned. The kea does not need to beat the chimpanzee. Not“Convergent evolution” as the settled answer. It is one of three positions held by working researchers right now. Two of the three have the wrong name on them

The fact-check this page owes Two of the three have the wrong name on them The Science of Discworld books are the ones this site actually learned from. They are also the ones whose authorship almost everybody, including us, gets wrong. They are co-authored: Terry Pratchett with the mathematician Ian Stewart and the reproductive biologist Jack Cohen. And they are not co-authored in the blurred way that phrase usually means. The chapters alternate. The odd-numbered chapters are Pratchett's Discworld narrative — the wizards of Unseen University, who have accidentally made a universe in a jar. The even-numbered chapters are Stewart and Cohen's science, addressed straight to the reader about our universe. Narrativium is his. Lies-to-children is not.

Two lineages, one book Narrativium is his. Lies-to-children is not. Both coinages arrive in the same 1999 book. They come from opposite directions and have completely different parentage, and keeping them straight is the whole job of this spread. Narrativium is Pratchett's, and it is a joke with a knife in it. On the Disc it is an actual element — the substance that makes stories happen, so that the millionth-to-one chance works and the third son succeeds. It is built as a parody of phlogiston, the imaginary fire-stuff that eighteenth-century chemistry invented to explain burning and then had to abandon. The joke: we invent a substance to explain a pattern we have noticed, and sometimes the substance is fictional and the pattern is real. Lies-to-children is not his at all. Jack Cohen and Ian Stewart had been working the idea for years before Discworld carried it anywhere: where lies-to-children actually comes from year book what happens 1994 The Collapse of Chaos Cohen & Stewart discuss the thing: cultural lore passed on in a form that is sufficient but not completely true 1997 Figments of Reality elaborated, and the term used for the difficulty of reducing complex ideas for teaching 1999 The Science of Discworld reaches a mass audience — with a novelist's name on the spine A lie-to-children is the thing your physics teacher does when they tell you electrons orbit the nucleus like planets. It is false. It is also the only way to get you to the next rung, and the honest version of the practice says so out loud: this is a ladder, and you are not at the top of it. Every one of these zines is a lie-to-children. That is not the confession it sounds like — it is the job. The question is only whether we admit the next rung exists. which is the next spread Two lineages converging on 1999 Two tracks. Turned around Every zine here is a ladder If a lie-to-children is a simplification that gets you to the next rung, then this entire site is made of them, and pretending otherwise would be the actual dishonesty. We say bone is piezoelectric — and had to correct ourselves twice, because it is the collagen and not the mineral. We drew a spiky profile and then refused our own chart. The method, credited First Sight and Second Thoughts Here is the debt paid properly. Everything this site does procedurally is a witch's two-part discipline, and Pratchett named both halves better than our documentation does. First Sight is seeing what is actually in front of you — not what you expected, not what the story says should be there. It is harder than it sounds, because the expectation arrives first and feels like observation. Our whole Field Guides collection is First Sight as a form: seven of the twelve arrive independently at there is no standard one of these, which is what you find when you go and look instead of consulting the type specimen in your head. It is the refusal to let a lovely pattern do your looking for you. Second Thoughts are the thoughts that watch the first ones. Not doubt — supervision. The Industrial Revolution books A technology arrives. Who pays? There is a run of Discworld novels that all do the same trick: drop one modern innovation into a medieval city and then refuse to look away from the bill. The pattern is consistent enough to be a method. Moving Pictures gets cinema. The Truth gets the printing press and the newspaper. Going Postal gets the post — stamps, a network, a man made to run it. Making Money gets paper currency and modern banking. Raising Steam gets the railway. In each, the innovation genuinely works, genuinely delights, and genuinely costs somebody something, and the book stays in the room for the third part. That third part is rare. The default technology story has two acts — the invention, and the wonder — and stops before the bill arrives. Pratchett's have three, and the third is always about who was standing where the thing landed: the clacks workers on the towers, the golems who are property, the engravers whose craft the press makes worthless, the people the railway timetable now owns. The question is never “does it work?” It works. That is what makes the question interesting. the shape of an Industrial Revolution book Which lands squarely on techno-solutionism and on the Luddite Sensibilities Stimpunks argues for — and it is worth being precise, because the word gets used as an insult by people who do not know what it means. The Luddites were not against machines. They were skilled workers objecting to a specific arrangement in which the machine's gains went one way and its costs went another. They broke the frames of the employers cutting wages and left the others alone. That is not technophobia. That is a question about distribution, asked with a hammer. It is also the question this site keeps asking about a different set of machines. An assessment instrument works. A behaviour protocol works, for some value of works. Who pays? is the question How We Got Here exists to keep open, and Pratchett was running the experiment in a fantasy city for thirty years. Two acts or three The default technology story runs invention then wonder and stops. The Industrial Revolution novels add a third act asking who pays, with examples: the clacks workers, the golems who are property, the engravers the press displaced, and the people the timetable owns. the default story invention wonder stop what Pratchett does invention wonder who pays? clacks crew golems engravers timetabled it works. that is what makes it interesting the Luddites broke some frames, not all a question about distribution Figure 6 · the act most stories skip One Atom of Justice · Stimpunks

The clacks GNU In Going Postal there is a semaphore network across the continent — towers, shutters, a code, and crews who live up there. Early in the book a young man named John Dearheart dies on one. His father puts his name into the Overhead — the working channel the towers use to talk to each other, which no customer ever sees — with three letters in front of it. G: send it on. N: do not log it. U: at the end of the line, turn it around and send it back. GNU John Dearheart, up and down the towers, indefinitely, for as long as the network stands. A man's not dead while his name is still spoken. Terry Pratchett, Going Postal (2004) — see the colophon on wording Pratchett died on 12 March 2015. Within days, readers on the Discworld subreddit proposed doing the obvious thing to the network we actually have: put him in the Overhead. An HTTP response header, invisible in the page, carried on every request, logged by nobody, meaning nothing to any browser: X-Clacks-Overhead: GNU Terry Pratchett As of today, this site sends it. Every page you load from starstuff.earth carries that header. You can see it in your browser's network panel, under response headers, on this page or any other. It does nothing. That is the point — it is the exact structural joke, an unlogged message that costs one line of config and turns around at the end of the line. stated plainly This is a fan convention, not Pratchett's instruction. He did not ask for it, his estate did not originate it, and nobody should read the header as endorsement by anyone. It is a thing readers started doing in March 2015 because the book gave them a shape for grief and no better one has turned up since. It also belongs in this collection more exactly than anything else here. An easter egg on this site is a real piece behind a small door — and the smallest door we have is a header nobody has to read. GNU, turning around at the end of the line A row of clacks towers. A message travels left to right along the top, marked G for pass it on and N for not logged, then U turns it around at the last tower and it travels back along the bottom, repeating indefinitely. Posterior cortical atrophy The embuggerance In December 2007, at fifty-nine, Pratchett announced that he had posterior cortical atrophy. He gave it a word of his own almost immediately, and the word was not battle or journey. PCA is a rare presentation of Alzheimer's disease that attacks from the back of the brain forward. Because those posterior regions do visual and spatial processing, it takes the seeing before it takes the remembering — reading, judging where things are, recognising what your eyes are pointed at. It typically arrives earlier than typical Alzheimer's, in the mid-fifties or early sixties, which is exactly where it found him. He called it an embuggerance. A nuisance of an unusually total kind. Something in the way. Not a battle he was losing. Not a lesson. A thing that was in the way, named accurately, out loud, by the person it was in the way of. why the word matters here Then he kept writing, by changing the method rather than the ambition: dictating to his assistant Rob Wilkins, and using speech-recognition software. He was knighted in 2009. He went on publishing until he died on 12 March 2015. We are putting this in because Stimpunks is a disability organisation and this is what accommodation actually looks like from inside: the output was never the thing that had to change. The interface did. Dictation is not a lesser way of writing a book; it is a way of writing a book. That is the entire argument of the disability rights movement, demonstrated at length by a man producing novels while his occipital lobe went. What we are not doing with this. Death's challenge One atom of justice Now the objection. In Hogfather, Death is explaining to his granddaughter why humans need to believe in things like the Hogfather. AS PRACTICE. YOU HAVE TO START OUT LEARNING TO BELIEVE THE LITTLE LIES. “So we can believe the big ones?” YES. JUSTICE. MERCY. DUTY. THAT SORT OF THING. 80 Star Gazing One Word for the Opposite on the vocabulary we built for what hurts, the single word we have for what doesn’t — and why a glimmer is probably not a dopamine hit, which is better news than it sounds developed after Helen Edgar’s Glimmers: Autistic Joy and Monotropism L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely

An asymmetry you can count Count the words Here is something checkable that needs no laboratory. Write down the words we have for a nervous system going badly. Trigger. Flashback. Hypervigilance. Activation. Dysregulation. Rupture. Freeze. Fawn. Shutdown. Overwhelm. Startle. Collapse. Every one of them is in common use. Several have entered ordinary speech. They are precise, they are distinguishable from each other, and a person can say which one is happening. Now write down the words for the opposite — not for happiness in general, but specifically for a small moment in which a nervous system registers that things are all right. There is one. It is glimmer, and it was coined in 2018. That asymmetry is the finding of this zine, and it does not require anybody to agree about physiology. You can verify it by trying the exercise. One vocabulary was built out over decades by clinicians, researchers and survivors who needed to name what was happening to them. The other was not built. The reason is not mysterious. Language grows where the pressure is, and the pressure was on harm — on explaining it, treating it, getting it recognised. Nobody had to convince an institution that a moment of quiet was real in order to be believed. One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks
A thing with a name is a thing you can count

What a word does A thing with a name is a thing you can count Before the word, these moments were not rare. They were uncountable — not in the sense of being too many, but in the sense of not being the kind of thing anybody was counting. A category with a name behaves differently. It can be looked for. It can be mentioned to somebody else without a paragraph of explanation. It can be noticed twice and recognised as the same kind of event. None of that is a change in the moments. All of it is a change in what attention can get hold of. The word did not create the experience. It created the possibility of keeping track of it. Which is a much smaller claim than the ones usually made for such words, and a more defensible one. Nobody has to believe anything about vagal tone to accept that naming a category makes its members findable. That is what nouns do. And it is the reason this zine is in this collection rather than the one next door. A piece in Star Stuff is supposed to take one settled fact and follow it until the belonging claim is already inside it. This piece has no settled mechanism to offer and is not going to pretend otherwise. Star Gazing exists for exactly this — possibility rather than proof — and Helen Edgar named it. One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks

Whose word Deb Dana, 2018 The word is Deb Dana’s, from The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy: Engaging the Rhythm of Regulation (Norton, 2018). She proposed it as the counterpart to triggers: the small cues that register as safety rather than as threat. It travelled fast, which tells you the gap was real. A word that fills nothing does not get taken up by people who were not looking for it. And it arrived inside a framework this house treats carefully. Polyvagal theory is influential and scientifically contested — the same note we carry on The Nearest Body (No. 72). Which raises the obvious question, and it is worth answering directly rather than stepping around. Does a good word stop being good if the theory it arrived in turns out to be wrong? No. Words and theories are different objects with different failure modes. A theory makes claims that can be false. A word makes a category available, and the category either earns its keep in use or it doesn’t. Glimmer has earned its keep by being immediately usable by people who have never heard of the vagus nerve. Helen Edgar puts it plainly, and her version is the one this zine works from: glimmers do not need to relate to polyvagal at all. They are just the opposite of triggers — moments of joy, comfort, sensory or cognitive. One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks
When the tunnel and the room agree

The monotropic reading When the tunnel and the room agree Helen Edgar reads glimmers through monotropism — attention gathered on fewer things at a time — and the reading is specific enough to be useful. A glimmer, in her account, is a small but powerful moment when everything aligns: focus, sensory needs and emotions coming together in a way that feels right. Not a mood, and not an achievement. An alignment. That is a more exacting definition than it first appears, and it explains why glimmers are so specific to the person having them. If a glimmer requires the attention tunnel, the sensory environment and the emotional state to agree at the same instant, then it is not transferable. Somebody else’s conditions are different, so their alignments happen elsewhere, over different things, and cannot be recommended. This is why glimmer lists do not work as advice. The alignment is between a particular bodymind and a particular room, and nobody else is standing in it. It also explains something the word-book this collection came from noticed independently: that the moments people reach for words to describe are so often sensory and small — light through leaves, the shine on water, the sound of a brook, the smell of a book. Those are catalogued in Under the Word (Field Guide No. 22). One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks
The five theories, and why we are not using them

Held at arm’s length, on purpose The five theories, and why we are not using them There is a list, circulated in trauma-informed circles and useful to know, of five existing theories about the nervous system, offered as things a practitioner might synthesise. Polyvagal theory (Porges) · neurovisceral integration (Thayer, Hansen, Saus-Rose & Johnsen) · the biological behavioural model (Grossman & Taylor) · the resonance frequency model (Lehrer) · the psychophysiological coherence model (McCraty & Childre, HeartMath). The list reaches us via Janae Elisabeth’s Trauma Geek, crediting Sarah Schlote. Here is the thing worth knowing before treating that as five bricks to stack. They are five competing interpretations of largely one measurement — heart-rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia — and two of them are the opposing sides of an unresolved argument. Grossman & Taylor (2007) is the standing critique of Porges: it argues that RSA is too confounded by respiration to serve as an index of vagal tone, and that polyvagal misdescribes the evolution of vagal cardiac control. The disagreement is live. One and three are not two parts of a synthesis. They are the two sides of a fight, and a piece that blended them would be flattening a live dispute into a smooth story. That is a familiar shape here. Our chain Four Decimal Places (No. 79) follows what happens when a smooth story is built on borrowed authority and left unchecked for eight years. So this zine names the five and uses none of them. Not because the science is worthless — neurovisceral integration in particular is well regarded — but because none of it decides whether the tea was good. The moment does not become more real if a model backs it, and it does not stop being real if the models are still arguing. One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks

The question everybody asks Probably not dopamine Ask what a glimmer is made of and almost everyone reaches for the same answer. A little hit of dopamine. It is the folk chemistry of our moment, and it is very likely the wrong molecule. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson spent decades separating two things that ordinary language runs together: wanting and liking. Wanting is the pull toward a thing — anticipation, seeking, the tug of a cue. Liking is the hedonic impact of the thing when it actually arrives. Dopamine turns out to do the first and not the second. It carries incentive salience — wanting — and it is conspicuous for its failure to increase the pleasure of a sweet taste in the experiments designed to measure exactly that. In people, dopamine tracks ratings of wanting a reward better than ratings of enjoying it. Liking runs somewhere else, and somewhere strikingly small. It depends on hedonic hotspots — regions roughly a cubic millimetre across in rats, in the shell of the nucleus accumbens and the ventral pallidum — where opioid and endocannabinoid signalling, not dopamine, does the work. Mu-opioid activity in one of those spots can more than double the liking reaction to sweetness. A glimmer, as Helen describes it, is not the pull toward something. It is the quality of the moment already arriving. That is liking, and liking is not the dopamine system. And this is better news than it sounds. The dopamine story quietly makes a glimmer into a reward — something obtained, chased, hit. The liking story does not. It says the moment is not a payoff for anything, was not earned, and is not on a schedule. Nobody has to go and get it. Held honestly, since this zine spent a spread refusing to lean on neuroscience. The wanting/liking dissociation is far better supported than the polyvagal claims, and it is still an active research programme, mapped mostly in rats, and the human picture is more tangled. It is here as a correction to a popular claim, not as a foundation. What it establishes is narrow: if you were going to name a molecule, dopamine is the wrong one. One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks

What it is for A practice, not a discovery Put the pieces together and a modest, defensible account is left standing, with nothing in it that requires anybody to settle a scientific argument. The moments are real and always were. The vocabulary for their opposite is enormous and theirs is one word old. A word makes a category findable. And what the word is for is not explanation — it is noticing. A glimmer is not a discovery about the nervous system. It is a practice of attention, and the practice is the whole of it. Which is why it sits so naturally beside monotropism. If attention is the medium a person lives in — gathered, narrow, hard to move and enormously rich where it lands — then a word that directs attention toward small alignments is not a small intervention. It is an intervention in the only place the person actually is. And it needs no permission from a model. The tea was good. The light through the leaves was worth stopping for. Somebody said the right thing in the right tone and something in you unclenched. None of that is waiting on a replication. This is why the piece is filed here rather than next door. Not everything worth printing is a settled fact, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of dishonesty. One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks

What this does not say What this does not say A zine about noticing good moments is about four words from becoming something insufferable. So, plainly: Not:that noticing glimmers fixes anything. It is a practice of attention, not a treatment, not a substitute for support, and not something to be recommended to a person who is drowning. “Have you tried noticing the good moments” is a sentence that has done real harm. Not:a case against polyvagal theory, or for it. The framework is contested; this zine says so once and then does not rest on it. Deb Dana’s word is good independently of it, which is the argument on spread four, and Helen Edgar makes the same point in her own words. Not:that the dopamine correction is the new explanation. Spread seven exists to remove a wrong molecule, not to install a right one. If you were going to name a chemical, it is not dopamine — and the better move is not to name one. Not:a glimmer list. If the moment is an alignment between a particular bodymind and a particular room, then somebody else’s list is a list of their rooms. Prescribing them is the fastest way to turn a noticing practice into another thing to fail at. Not:joy as a duty, or as evidence of recovery. Nobody owes anybody a glimmer count. A hard week with none in it is a hard week, not a failure of practice, and the word was never meant to be a target. Not:a proof, and this time not even a rhyme. The other pieces in this series follow a settled fact until the belonging claim is inside it. This one cannot, and does not try. What it offers is an asymmetry you can count, a correction to a popular claim about a molecule, and an argument that a word which makes something findable is worth having on its own terms. Star Gazing is where we put the things we mean but cannot demonstrate. One Word for the Opposite · Stimpunks

Polyvagal theory is Stephen Porges’ and is an influential but scientifically contested framework — the wording this site carries on The Nearest Body (No. 72), reused deliberately rather than reinvented. The five theories named on spread six — Porges; Thayer, Hansen, Saus-Rose & Johnsen; Grossman & Taylor; Lehrer; McCraty & Childre — reach us through Janae Elisabeth’s A Neurodiversity Paradigm Lens on Polyvagal Theory (Trauma Geek), which credits Sarah Schlote for the list. Nothing here is a criticism of Janae Elisabeth’s article, which is a practitioner setting out the models she works between; the point is only that they cannot be stacked. Wanting and liking. Kent C. Berridge & Terry E. Robinson, across the incentive-salience literature — dopamine mediating wanting rather than hedonic liking; hedonic hotspots of roughly a cubic millimetre in the nucleus accumbens medial shell and ventral pallidum; mu-opioid neurotransmission in a hotspot more than doubling liking reactions to sucrose; and dopamine’s conspicuous failure to raise hedonic impact in taste-reactivity work. Open: cited at the level of the literature’s standard summary rather than to a single paper read in full, and stated on the spread as a correction to a popular claim rather than as this zine’s foundation. Much of the hotspot mapping is in rats; the human picture is more tangled, and the spread says so. Credits. The seed is Helen Edgar’s Glimmers: Autistic Joy and Monotropism (Autistic Realms), and the definition this zine works from is hers in her own words: that glimmers need not relate to polyvagal at all, being simply the opposite of triggers — moments of joy, comfort, sensory or cognitive. Why this is in Star Gazing Three earlier attempts to build this piece failed in the same way, and the failure is worth recording. Each tried to put glimmers in Star Stuff, whose register is one settled, checkable fact followed honestly until the belonging claim is inside it. Glimmers has no such fact under it — the framework it arrived in is contested, and the joy literature has its own retraction attached — so each attempt either leaned on shaky ground or, having refused to, ended up with rigorous physics tied to the subject by a thread. The topic was never the problem. The collection was. Star Gazing exists for possibility rather than proof; Helen named it; five of its members are her guest zines. Filed correctly, the piece needs no mechanism and stops straining for one. A rhyme, not a proof — and on spread nine, not even that. The tea was good. That did not need checking, and it was never going to be settled by a model that is still arguing with itself. ↑ ↓ the relation comes first 29 Relation Only in Relation relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic after Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · a relation, still becoming L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The physics Only in relation A particle, on its own, doesn't quietly hoard its properties in private. In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics, a system's properties become definite only relative to another system it interacts with (Rovelli, 1996). There's no view from nowhere in which an electron already "has" its values, waiting to be read. What is real is what happens between systems. An honest caution before we go further: RQM is one interpretation of quantum theory among several, and physicists still argue it. We're not smuggling physics in to prove anything about people. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. "There is no absolute, observer-independent description of a person that tells the whole truth about themselves." — Helen Edgar, We Are Made of Relations (2026) the same particle, two situations in isolation ? no fact of the matter in relation ↑ definite — for that system a value is something two systems have between them not something one holds alone Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

count the outcomes two coins — distinct H H H T T H T T 4 two bosons — identical H H H T T T (H T = T H) 3 the missing 4th is the tell nature can't tell the two apart so it doesn't count them apart What is actually real Count the bosons Flip two coins and you get four outcomes — HH, HT, TH, TT — because the coins are distinct objects, so "heads-then-tails" and "tails-then-heads" are two different things. Do the same with two identical quantum particles — two bosons — and nature counts only three. The two mixed cases collapse into one, because there is no fact about which particle is which (Webster, 2026). That vanished fourth outcome is measurable, and it is the tell: what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle. It's the symmetry — the relation — that says these two can't be told apart. "What is fundamentally real are not particles as such, but rather the laws and symmetries … that govern their behaviour." — George Webster, IAI (2026) Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Relation before relata Made of each other Entangled particles can't be described one at a time. The pair carries correlations the parts simply don't have on their own — measure one and you've said something about the other, however far apart they've drifted. The physicist-philosopher Karen Barad calls this intra-action: not the meeting of two things that already exist separately, but a relation out of which the parts come to be distinct at all (Barad, 2007). The relation is first. The "things" are what it leaves behind. There's a word for the human version, one Helen draws from Barad: intradependence — not two finished people who later depend on each other, but selves made of each other from the start. Deeper than interdependence. We don't arrive as sealed units who only later reach out. We are, from the start, relations wearing the shape of a person. inter- vs intra- inter-action two wholes, then a link intra-action one relation, then parts the bond is the origin, not the bridge the parts are what the relation leaves behind made of each other Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

what comes first difference · relation objects (late arrivals) first the differentiating, then the things the object is what got built The order of things Difference, then relation Reading the physics through Deleuze, George Webster puts the metaphysics plainly: "Objects do not come first and then differ; rather, objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation." — George Webster, reading Deleuze (2026) First there is difference and relation; the tidy, standalone object is the late arrival — the thing that gets built. It's the same move Star Stuff has made from the start in Why Difference Comes First: the measured, average "normal person" was never the ground floor. Difference is. Turn it one notch further and relation is. Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

What it means for us The gap is two-way When an Autistic person and a non-Autistic person misunderstand each other, the old story put the deficit in one of them — the Autistic one. Damian Milton named the truer picture: the double empathy problem. The misunderstanding runs both ways — a mismatch between two differently-built minds, not a fault inside one (Milton, 2012). Relational physics says: of course it does. The trouble was never sitting inside a single object. It lives in the relation. Helen widens double empathy into DEEP — Dynamic, Embodied, Ecological, Political — because the mismatch isn't a static glitch between two heads. It's alive, bodily, environmental, and shaped by power. Change the lighting, the pace, the assumptions, the room — and the "deficit" you were measuring moves. It was in the relation all along. where the gap lives one mind another mind not one side — the space between double empathy, made DEEP a mismatch is a property of the pair it has no single owner Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Regulation isn't a skill you own privately and keep failing to deploy. We co-regulate: nervous systems settle, or don't, in relation to other bodies, other pacing, a room that holds us or doesn't. So the support that actually works doesn't try to repair an isolated person. It changes the relational field — the sensory environment, the pacing, the temporal texture, a community's capacity to hold different ways of being. If it's not working, it's not the person. Held with care What we are not saying Relational physics rhymes with how we already know support works. It is not a licence for the traps that show up whenever "quantum" meets "people." Notquantum mysticism. No "quantum consciousness," no mind magically collapsing reality. In physics the "observer" is any system at all — a speck of dust will do. Not"everything is connected" as a vibe. This is a specific claim about how properties come to be, not a warm fog. Notdissolution into sameness. Being a relation doesn't melt you. Where two rivers meet they run braided for miles — one current, still distinct. The spiky profile survives the merge. Notphysics proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. The receipt There was never a No. 37 Count the zines on this site and you will find a hole. Nos. 36 and 38 sit next to each other with nothing in between. This is the page about the hole, and it has to start by correcting itself. We were going to tell you we skipped it by accident. That is not what happened, and it took about four minutes of reading our own notes to find out — which is roughly how long the check always takes, and roughly how often it gets skipped. What actually happened: on 11 August 2026 a zine about the last stage of a supernova remnant was drafted and given the next number in the sequence, No. 37. Then it stopped, because it leaned on Helen Edgar's writing closely enough that the honest thing was to ask her before building it. So it waited. And while it waited, seven other pieces were finished and took the next seven numbers. When it was finally built on 13 August it was No. 45 — The Cloud Phase. Our own decision log is blunt about what that means: The number moved 37 → 45 because seven pieces shipped while it sat — the number says when, and that gap is the rule working, not a renumbering. DECISIONS.md · 13 August 2026 So 37 is not a mistake. It is a receipt for a question asked rather than assumed. Which is a much better thing to find in your numbering than a tidy unbroken run, and it is why this page fills the slot without pretending to repair it. Why the false version mattered enough to catch. “We lost track and skipped one” is a smoother story than “we deferred a piece to ask someone, and the sequence recorded the wait.” Smoother stories travel further, which is exactly the failure Too Good to Check catalogues and the broadside hands out on a card. Shipping it here would have been this house committing its own named fault, in a piece about honesty, for a joke. The famous one Your temperature is not 37 The most famous 37 in the world is a body temperature, and it is out of date by about a century and a half. It comes from one man with a very long thermometer. Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich published Das Verhalten der Eigenwärme in Krankheiten in Leipzig in 1868, reporting over a million readings from roughly 25,000 patients. His instrument was about a foot long and had to sit in the armpit for twenty minutes. The mean of that vast, patient, hand-tallied dataset was 37 °C — 98.6 °F — and he called it the physiological point. It was a fine number. It is no longer our number. In 2020 Myroslava Protsiv and colleagues put three American datasets spanning 157 years side by side and found body temperature has been falling the whole time, monotonically, by about 0.03 °C per birth decade: decline in mean body temperature by birth cohort cohort span change men born 1800 → 1997 −0.59 °C women born 1890 → 1997 −0.32 °C both per birth decade −0.03 °C Modern adult oral means land nearer 36.6 °C. So 37 is not wrong the way a typo is wrong — it is an accurate 1868 average that got promoted to a constant and then quietly stopped describing anybody. Nobody lied. A number was measured carefully, published honestly, and then outlived the population it was measured on — and kept being taught. the failure mode, without a villain Our own field card calls this one the number that went stale, and it is the third of six ways a fact goes wrong. Worth sitting with, because it is the failure mode with no bad actor in it at all: the only way to catch it is to go back and measure again. How long to look Spend 37% not choosing There is a second 37, and this one is a theorem. It answers a question everybody actually has: how long should I keep looking before I commit? Set it up strictly. Options arrive one at a time, you can rank the ones you have seen, and every decision is final — no going back to number three. The optimal strategy has a shape that is not obvious: look at the first 1/e of them and reject every one, however good, then take the first option after that which beats everything you have seen. 1/e is 0.368. Roughly 37%. And the payoff is the strange part: It finds the single best option about 37% of the time — whether there are a hundred options or a hundred million. the 1/e law of best choice The number does not decay with scale. A third of a very long search is a lot of looking, and it is still the right amount. Which is where this zine's own subject walks back in. The Cloud Phase spent its looking time. It could have been built on 11 August with an assumption in it; instead it sat while a question went out, and the sequence recorded the waiting as an absence. The number of the wait, and the fraction of any search you are supposed to spend not choosing, are the same 37. And that is a coincidence. A delightful one, sitting right at the centre of this piece, with nothing behind it. The next spread is about not pretending otherwise — because this is exactly the moment a zine reaches for a mechanism it does not have. We will not solder these together

Three unrelated 37s We will not solder these together Here is the trap this whole zine is walking toward, and it is the most fun thing about the number, which is precisely why it is dangerous. Three 37s in a row. A body temperature. An optimal stopping fraction. And the number people apparently reach for when told to be random. Lay them beside each other and something in the head starts reaching for a because — as if the brain picks 37 because of something to do with 1/e, or as if 37 recurs because 37 is somehow special. They are not connected. Not loosely, not deeply, not at all: what each 37 actually is the 37 what kind of thing 37 °C a 19th-century arithmetic mean of armpits, in one unit 37% 1/e, rounded — a limit, in no unit at all “pick 37” a fact about people, in a base-ten range of 1–100 The 37 in the temperature is a decimal accident of the Celsius scale — in Fahrenheit the same fact is 98.6, and the coincidence evaporates. The 37 in the stopping rule is 36.79 rounded, and it is a percentage, not a count. The 37 people pick only exists because somebody offered them 1 to 100. A coincidence dressed as a mechanism is not a small mistake. It is the specific move that lets a real finding get pointed at people, and it is why this collection exists. the fault this piece was built to name This is the same shape as Five Sigma's complaint: keeping the authority of a number while dropping the practice that earned it. And it is why the joke here stops short of a punchline. Three 37s is a nice thing to notice and nothing to conclude from. We are allowed to enjoy it. We are not allowed to explain it. The genuinely lovely part Thirty-seven, honestly Strip out the coincidences and the number is still worth the apology. All of the following is checkable on paper in a couple of minutes, which is the nicest property a fact can have. It is the 12th prime. Reverse the digits and you get 73, which is also prime — and which is the 21st. The digits of the number reverse, and so do the digits of its position. That is not deep. It is just very pleasing, and it is exact. It is the third star number: 6n(n−1)+1 gives 1, 13, 37, 73 — so 37 and 73 are consecutive star numbers as well as digit reversals of one another. Which means a site built entirely out of starfields skipped the star number. It is also the fourth centered hexagonal number, 3n(n−1)+1: 1, 7, 19, 37. Triple it and you get 111, because 111 = 3 × 37. So 37 × 6 = 222, 37 × 9 = 333, and so on up — a repdigit machine hiding in a prime. And the biggest one: every positive whole number, without exception, is a sum of at most 37 fifth powers. Thirty-seven is exactly enough and no smaller number will do. That is the value of g(5) in Waring's problem, and Chen Jingrun nailed it down in 1964. Every number there has ever been, or will be, is thirty-seven fifth powers or fewer. It is a strange thing to be the exact size of. g(5) = 37 None of this makes 37 special in a way that means anything about anybody. It just makes it good company — which is all we promised it. Held loosely on purpose The number people reach for The third 37 is the one everybody wants to be true, and it is the one this zine holds at arm's length — which is the honest thing to do and also, awkwardly, the whole point of the site. Ask a lot of people to pick a random number from 1 to 100 and the answers are not flat. They avoid round numbers, avoid the ends, avoid the exact middle, avoid repeated digits — and they pile up on a few odd, prime-looking numbers. In a survey of roughly 200,000 responses run by Veritasium, 37 and 73 came out near the top, close to tied. We like this a great deal. We are still going to say what it is: Contested A large, self-published survey, not a refereed finding. The data is real and the effect is plausible, but we have not read a peer-reviewed paper reporting it, and every account of it we could reach is secondary. It is on this spread as somebody's experiment, never as a law about human beings. What the result would mean, if it holds, is nicer than the number anyway. Primes feel random to us because nothing divides them — no pattern to catch the eye, so the mind reads “no structure” and offers it up as randomness. But primes are the most rigidly determined objects in arithmetic. There is nothing arbitrary about 37 whatsoever. So the thing we reach for when we want to be unpredictable is one of the least arbitrary things there is. That is a fact about us, not about the number. if the finding holds Which is a familiar shape here. Something gets called disordered, or random, or arbitrary, because the person looking cannot see the rule it is running on. The Lines We Drew has the long version. Owed, Not Earned Inclusion safety is the first stage of psychological safety. It is not a reward for the worthy, and not a prize you win. It is the baseline we owe one another simply for being here. Be human. Be harmless. Meet both and you are in · that is the whole qualification 01 No litmus test Not your diagnosis, your speech, your output, your history, or how easily others can make sense of you. There is no audition at this threshold. 02 Worth, not worthiness Worth is a thing you have, entire, already. Worthiness is no one's to weigh at the door — and if it is ever anyone's business, it is not here. 03 The one disqualifier Acceptance is owed to everyone. So is safety from harm — and harm is the single thing that can cost you your place. Not your way of being. Only harm. “Inclusion safety is not earned but owed. Every human has title to it as a nonnegotiable right.” Timothy R. You do not have to earn your way in. You were ★stuff all along. The four stages, the definitions, and the quoted lines are Timothy R. Clark 's, from The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety: Defining the Path to Inclusion and Innovation (Berrett-Koehler, 2020) — the inclusion-safety material is Stage 1, including “if you have flesh and blood, we accept you,” the worth-before-worthiness distinction, and be human and harmless as the qualification. Frederick Douglass's line is his own, from Our Composite Nationality , delivered in Boston on 7 December 1869 (the Library of Congress manuscript is catalogued 1867). The move past common humanity to common origin — that belonging is constitutive because we are made of the same star stuff — is ours. the full creed and every source: starstuff.earth/inclusion-safety-creed · stimpunks.org · morerealms.com print freely · share freely · CC BY-SA 4.0 L S

Designing for Paper Notes & Rationale · how the broadsides are built Every number here was arrived at by printing something and finding out it was wrong. This page is the working — the spec, the inks, the gates, and the faults that no gate can see. Backing material for the Print collection , which argues what earns a sheet. This one covers how a sheet is made, and is deliberately outside the reading chain — it is reference, not a stop on the tour. For the site-wide visual language, see The Design System ; this page is only about the artifacts made for paper.

The format One fixed specification for every sheet. The point of a fixed format is that eight different arguments come off the printer as the same object — a rack, not a pile — and that a reader in any country gets the same artifact from the same file. 190 × 259 mm The intersection of A4 and US Letter. At 9 mm page margins, A4 gives a box of 192 × 279 mm and Letter gives 198 × 261 — so a sheet inside both is one file that prints uncropped in either country, with no “US version” to maintain and get out of sync. 9 mm margins, not 10 At 10 mm the Letter box is 259.4 mm against a 259 mm sheet. That 0.4 mm of slack was thin enough for sub-pixel rounding to tip the whole thing onto a third page . Found by printing to PDF and counting, not by reading the arithmetic — the arithmetic said it fit. Two sides, A and B Side A is the face; side B does the work. Enforced structurally: each side is a .sheet element with page-break-after on the first, so the file is two printed sides or it is broken. Breakpoint below 700 px The one that looks like a screen concern and isn't. Print media queries resolve against the page box, not the screen — and the narrowest real page box here is A4 less its margins, 192 mm, or about 726 px. A mobile breakpoint set at 820 px was therefore matching on paper , collapsing a two-column card into one 190 mm column at roughly 95 characters a line, long enough that side B overran and was silently clipped.
Ink on white, in both media

Ink on white, in both media The rest of the site is light on dark, and starstuff.css inverts it inside @media print so a zine survives being printed. The broadsides never enter that machinery: they are drawn as ink on white on screen and on paper, so what you see in a browser is a preview of the sheet rather than a different design that will be converted later. The reason is blunt. Browsers leave Background graphics off by default , so a light-on-dark page reaches paper blank — which is exactly what happened to 44 of the 46 pages on this site until somebody measured it. A broadside cannot depend on a reader finding a checkbox in a print dialog, because the whole premise is that it gets handed to people and photocopied by people who never saw the web page at all.

Borders, not backgrounds Same constraint, one level down. The registration bar across the top of each sheet is a border-top , not a background — because borders survive that checkbox and background colours do not. An earlier design put the cream stock in a background-color and a halftone in a background-image , and neither ever reached paper. What did print was the gold misregistration shadow, because it happened to be text: at 1.84:1 on white, a faint smudge. The reader got the flaw of the effect and none of its charm.

Type Atkinson Hyperlegible Next throughout , with Space Mono for labels and chrome. Atkinson was drawn by the Braille Institute for letterform distinction at exactly the small sizes a hand-out uses — the 6–9 pt range where a broadside does most of its work. No display serif. Fraunces was inherited from the earlier risograph costume and went with it. It is Bone Song 's editorial voice, not a broadside's, and more to the point it is a high-contrast serif whose hairlines are the first thing to drop out of a photocopy or a tired laser printer — which is most of a broadside's life. Worth recording that before this was fixed, the sheets loaded Atkinson and rendered 0% of their characters in it. The star is drawn, not typed. Atkinson has no U+2605 , so a typed ★ silently comes from whatever font the reader's system happens to supply — measurably so: the character rendered at exactly the generic-serif advance width. For a logotype on a sheet meant to print identically everywhere, that is not good enough, so the L★S mark is an SVG path with an inner radius 0.382 of the outer, filled currentColor so it inherits the surrounding ink.

Two spot inks An explicit exception to a house rule. starstuff.css flattens all five accents to near-black inside @media print on purpose — print is monochrome by default here. The broadsides keep two colours each, declared as literal hex rather than aliased to the --sp-* tokens, and forced through with print-color-adjust: exact . They have to be declared literally because the screen accents measure 1.6–2.7:1 on white and are unusable as paper ink. So each is the house hue darkened until it clears WCAG AA on white, and each sheet takes a different pair — which means the bar across the top tells you which sheet you are holding when five of them are face-down in a stack. That is the registration bar's real job. Gold · #92400e 7.1:1 · L★S & Elements faces Violet · #5b21b6 9.0:1 · Six Ways & BGUTI faces Pink · #9d174d 7.9:1 · Refuse face, Elements verso Green · #166534 7.1:1 · Owed face, Shared Air verso Cyan · #164e63 9.1:1 · Water & Air faces, BGUTI verso

What we check, and how For about a year, both of the original broadsides said “two-sided single sheet” in their own copy, and both were lying. Measured by printing to PDF and counting pages: the L★S sheet came out as three sides on US Letter and two on A4 — a different physical object depending on the reader's country — and Six Ways came out as four sides on both. Nothing in the repository could see it, because the checks that existed measured whether ink was legible, not whether it landed on the page. Three committed tools now run before a sheet ships. Each exists because something shipped broken in a way the others could not detect. tools/check-sheets.mjs Prints each sheet at both paper sizes and counts pages, and separately measures content height against the box. The separate measurement is the subtle part: a fixed-height sheet whose content overruns does not paginate — it is silently clipped — so a clean page count can still hide a cut-off final line. It measures at the real page-box width rather than a desktop viewport, for the breakpoint reason above. tools/check-contrast.mjs Composites every text element against its real ancestor background stack, on screen and under print emulation, at WCAG AA. It runs a separate pass for SVG text fills, because color never reaches fill and a CSS-only pass is structurally blind to diagrams. The print pass composites against the bare white sheet rather than trusting emulated print media, which still paints backgrounds a real reader will not get. tools/check-markup.mjs Reads source rather than the DOM, and that is the design: it catches markup the browser silently rewrites — nested or

Take it and reuse it The whole specification is four numbers and two rules: 190 × 259 mm at 9 mm margins , ink on white in both media, borders rather than backgrounds for anything that must survive to paper, and two inks darkened until they clear AA on white. Everything else is editorial. The sheets are CC BY-SA 4.0 , the tools are in tools/ , and the whole repository is public. If you make broadsides for your own community with this, that is the intended outcome, not a tolerated one — and you will not need our colours, only the method. 68 Proportioned to the Groove four lines of Dickinson, and why a narrow channel is a fit rather than a shortage Words: Helen Edgar With Ryan Boren Scroll ↓ the groove opens as you go

01 · The Poem Four lines, nothing left over That Love is all there is, Is all we know of Love; It is enough, the freight should be Proportioned to the groove. — Emily Dickinson, The Single Hound (1915), poem CX A groove, in the sense Dickinson is using, is the channel a load runs along — a rut, a track, a rail. The freight is what the channel carries. She is not saying love is small. She is saying it is matched: enough is a relation between a load and the thing that carries it, not a quantity you could weigh on its own. On the number This poem is usually cited as 1765, which is Thomas H. Johnson's number from his 1955 edition — the numbering this collection already uses, as J1765, in No. 67. Dickinson titled and dated almost nothing, so a number is an editor's decision rather than hers. We could not confirm the corresponding Franklin number and so do not give one. The text above is quoted from the poem's first printing, where it appears untitled as poem CX on p. 118.

02 · The Groove A channel, not a limit Dickinson isn't describing a shortage. She's describing a fit. Love doesn't need to be vast to be complete — it needs to match the channel it moves through. A groove that carries everything it was built to carry is not a smaller love. It's a finished one. Monotropism describes attention working the same way: interest pulled into a small number of deep channels rather than spread thinly across many at once (Murray, Lesser & Lawson, 2005). Read against that, proportioned to the groove stops sounding like a consolation and starts sounding like a description — of how focused, monotropic love already works. The freight was never supposed to spread thin. It was supposed to fit.

03 · The Refrain A child in the dark Deleuze and Guattari open their plateau on the refrain — 1837: Of the Refrain — with exactly this kind of groove. A child in the dark, gripped by fear, comforts himself by singing under his breath. Lost, he takes shelter, or orients himself with the little song as best he can. “a rough sketch of a calming and stabilizing, calm and stable, center in the heart of chaos” Deleuze & Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus, trans. Massumi (1987), on the child's song That's the groove doing its first job. Not confinement — shelter. A pattern repeated until it becomes somewhere safe to be. They are careful to add that the song is itself a skip: it jumps from chaos to the beginnings of order, and it can come apart at any moment. The shelter is real and it is not guaranteed. A reader's own refrain I was that child humming in the dark. Fear was the prevailing feeling of my childhood. I was scared of everything and felt tossed about by forces I didn't understand and had no hope of controlling. I spent my nights sitting in the hallway outside my parents' bedroom door, staring at the light in the ceiling and humming to myself as I feared the world at either end of the corridor. The hum in my chest and the hum in the light offered a comforting groove, carved from unknowable chaos. — Ryan Boren

04 · The Circle Home does not preexist The second movement of the refrain is the one that gets skipped in the retelling, and it is the one that matters most here. The song stops being a point in the dark and starts being a space. Deleuze and Guattari put it flatly: “Now we are at home. But home does not preexist” Deleuze & Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus, trans. Massumi (1987) It has to be drawn. A circle around an uncertain centre, marked out and held, so that the forces of chaos stay outside and something fragile inside gets room to work. Their own second example is a hallway light away from the one above: a child hums to summon the strength for the schoolwork she has to hand in. This is the part worth saying plainly to anyone who has been told their coping is a symptom. The repetition is not the residue of the fear. It is the construction of the room.
One opens the circle a crack

05 · The Opening One opens the circle a crack Then the third movement. The circle that was built to keep chaos out is opened — not on the side where the old forces press against it, but somewhere the circle itself made possible. One opens it, they write, “in order to join with the forces of the future, cosmic forces.” “One ventures from home on the thread of a tune.” Deleuze & Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus, trans. Massumi (1987) And then the line that keeps this from being a ladder: these are not three successive moments in an evolution. They are three aspects of one thing. The shelter, the room and the opening are not stages you graduate through, leaving the humming behind. They are happening at once, in the same small repeated tune. Nothing about the groove has to widen for that to happen. It only has to open. The channel that made the shelter possible is the channel that makes the cosmic connection possible — not despite its narrowness, but through it. A correction we made in the building This spread was drafted around a line about a cowbell being “promoted to the status of celestial noise” through sheer repetition, cited to A Thousand Plateaus. It is not in that book. Searching the Massumi translation, cow bells appear once, in a list making a different argument, and celestial appears elsewhere again. The image is genuinely Deleuze's — but he says it aloud, alone, in the filmed interviews L'Abécédaire, in the letter R comme Ritournelle. The only English we could reach is one scholar's own translation of spoken French, so we give the image as a paraphrase and let the verbatim quotations above, which we read at the primary, carry the argument instead.

06 · Star Stuff The freight is literal “Because the cosmos is also within us. We're made of star-stuff. We are a way for the cosmos to know itself.” Carl Sagan, Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, ep. 1, “The Shores of the Cosmic Ocean” (1980) Not a metaphor, and not a flourish. The calcium in the bones doing the humming, the iron in the blood, the carbon in every cell — forged in the interiors of stars that finished burning before the Earth existed, and scattered when those stars came apart. So the freight in Dickinson's four lines is not only a figure of speech either. Something actual is being carried, and it has to take the shape of whatever carries it: a body, a relationship, a hallway at night, a line of a poem.
Down to is not because of

07 · LYDTYSS Down to is not because of This is where the groove, the refrain and the star stuff meet. Love You Down To Your Star Stuff is this house's central phrase, and its grammar is doing careful work. Down to measures how far the loving reaches. It does not say the star stuff is the reason for it. The elements are the extent of the claim, not its warrant — which is exactly the distinction Dickinson's line is already making. The freight is proportioned to the groove; the groove is not what earns the freight. So: to love someone down to their star stuff is not to love them despite the narrowness of their channel. It is to love the specific, elemental material that channel is carrying, without asking it to widen first.
What the channel was carrying all along

08 · The Freight What the channel was carrying all along A monotropic love often looks like one interest returned to again and again; one person's whole attention offered rather than divided; an info-dump handed over like a gift, because it is one. None of that is love running low. It's the freight, exactly proportioned, moving through the only channel it was ever going to fit. It does not need translating into a broader, more diffuse shape to count. It was already enough. A reader's own refrain I've felt the freight of limerence, and of requited love. The attention tunneling, furrowing, following its groove. — Ryan Boren A companion reading runs through No. 66, which arrives at the same place from the other direction: a groove is a loop with a body attached. Dickinson's groove is a channel; Byrne's is a repetition you can dance to. Both are patterns that hold a person up.

09 · An Invitation What's your groove carrying? Think of the channel your own love travels through — the single interest, the one person, the particular way you show up for someone. Has it been met at the size it actually is? Or has it been asked to widen before it was allowed to count? Sit with that for a moment before you scroll on.

10 · Colophon L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff Refusals monotropic attention as a deficit to be broadened into something more respectable. “narrow but deep” offered as a consolation prize for not being the other thing. a poem as evidence. Dickinson's four lines are a rhyme with monotropism, not a proof of it, and she is not a witness we get to call. retroactively diagnosing Emily Dickinson. Reclusiveness is not a diagnosis, we have no standing to hand her an identity she never claimed, and the argument does not need her to be one of us to work. the naturalistic fallacy. That the universe is built out of difference does not by itself make difference good; we love people down to their star stuff because we choose to, not because physics instructs us. Sources Dickinson, E. “That Love is all there is” [poem CX], in The Single Hound: Poems of a Lifetime, ed. Martha Dickinson Bianchi (Boston: Little, Brown, 1915), p. 118. Commonly cited as J1765 after Johnson's 1955 edition. Text checked against the transcription of the scanned first edition at Wikisource; all four lines match. Deleuze, G., & Guattari, F. A Thousand Plateaus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia, trans. Brian Massumi (University of Minnesota Press, 1987; original French 1980), plateau 11, “1837: Of the Refrain.” All quotations on spreads 03–05 were read in the Massumi translation, not taken from summaries. Deleuze, G. L'Abécédaire de Gilles Deleuze, interviews with Claire Parnet, prod. and dir. Pierre-André Boutang, letter R comme Ritournelle — the cowbell-as-celestial-noise image, given here as a paraphrase. The English in circulation is Léopold Lambert's own translation, published on The Funambulist and collected in The Funambulist Pamphlets 3: Deleuze (punctum books, 2013); the two are the same author, not two sources. The French transcript was not reached. Murray, D., Lesser, M., & Lawson, W. (2005). Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism. Autism, 9(2), 139–156. doi:10.1177/1362361305051398 Sagan, C. Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, episode 1, “The Shores of the Cosmic Ocean,” first broadcast 28 September 1980. Wording confirmed against the footage at 6:14 by Ryan Boren. This corrects a quotation this house had been circulating with Universe in place of cosmos — see the changelog. Credits Written by Helen Edgar (More Realms), who brought the poem, the refrain and the argument. The two first-person passages are Ryan Boren's, in his own words, and are his alone. The Dickinson poem reached us sideways, through Dolly Parton's autobiography, while building No. 67 — which is how most things here arrive. On the form. This is the first zine in the collection built to scroll rather than to page: one section per screen, in a single continuous channel. That is not decoration. Every other zine here is a sequence of discrete spreads you step between; this one is a furrow you follow, which is the shape the piece is about. It still prints — on paper the screens collapse back into continuous prose and the scroll furniture disappears.
