The Quillery Eight Esmx · drawn for the sky Our mascot is a bundle of spikes whose tips come loose and drift, as if they are made of energy . This page takes that literally eight times over, and puts a source line under every one. Esmx the Porkypine — part pig, part porcupine — is the Stimpunks Foundation's community mascot, drawn by Kaya Oldaker and released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with an explicit invitation: feel free to customise, make variants of Esmx to represent your community. This is us taking that up. Star Stuff's community is a collection about what the sky is made of, so ours are eight Esmx pointed at the sky. What this is, and what it is not These are variants, not reproductions. Kaya's original artwork is not reproduced here and is not ours to redraw stroke for stroke; it lives at its own page , with a download of every official variant. What is on this page is Esmx built again from scratch in this site's line, the way the A'Tuin drawing and the twelve cosmic eggs were. The licence is share-alike , this whole site is already CC BY-SA 4.0, and the credit is at the foot of every drawing below. One figure, eight manes — and that is the design, not a shortcut. The official variant set works exactly this way: the same Esmx, recoloured, so a community can make one that looks like itself. The mane is where Esmx is meant to be remixed, so the mane is where all eight of these differ. It also keeps the promise the drawings make: if the figure were redrawn each time, a difference between two cards could be an accident of the pen rather than the thing the card is about. Every drawing carries alt text, because the source asked. Kaya's page ships alt text for each official variant with the instruction if you share these, include alt text . Honouring a licence is the easy half of honouring a maker. Each drawing below has a real description, not a filename.

The eight Esmx in Emission A drawing of Esmx — a porkypine, part pig, part porcupine, with a teal and pink colour scheme, an earring in one ear and a missing chunk in the other. Esmx's mane sweeps to the right and breaks apart into a row of separate vertical bright lines, like the emission spectrum of a star. One line, taller than the rest, is labelled helium, 587.6 nanometres. He · 587.6 nm found in the Sun first

Esmx in Emission No. 1 · the mane as a spectrum Split a star's light and it does not come out as a smear. It comes out as separate bright lines , at fixed places, and each set of lines belongs to one element and no other. It is the closest thing astronomy has to a signature: you can name what a thing is made of from a distance you will never cross, without touching it, without asking. On 18 August 1868 , watching a total eclipse from Guntur in India, Pierre Jules Janssen found a yellow line in the light of the Sun's prominences that sat where no known element sat. Norman Lockyer, working in London, reached the same line that October and named the thing behind it helium , for the Sun. Nobody found it on Earth for another twenty-seven years. An element was catalogued in a star before anyone had held it. Esmx's mane already does the thing the prism does: it starts as one mass and comes apart into discrete, separated, differently-coloured lines. That is not a metaphor we added. It is in the original design , and in the alt text — the spikes trail off and separate. Sources: Janssen's eclipse observation, 18 Aug 1868, and Lockyer's of 20 Oct 1868 — American Physical Society, This Month in Physics History . Terrestrial isolation: William Ramsay, 1895, from cleveite, with Per Teodor Cleve and Abraham Langlet independently. Related here: A Field Guide to the Elements , Not a Line (No. 21), which uses the same fingerprint fact. The Quill Is a Hair A drawing of Esmx the porkypine, with an earring in one ear and a missing chunk in the other. One spike of the mane runs off to the right and is drawn again, hugely magnified, as a single quill whose tip carries rows of tiny backward-pointing barbs. Arrows show that the barbs make the quill easy to push in and hard to pull out. in: easier out: harder keratin · the same protein as a fingernail

The Quill Is a Hair No. 2 · what a spike is made of A quill is not a thorn, not a bone, not a claw. It is a hair — a hair that grew stiff and hollow and enormous. It is made of keratin, the same protein as your fingernails and the hair on your head, and it grows from a follicle in skin the way any hair does. In 2012 a group at Harvard and MIT put the North American porcupine's quill under proper measurement and found the tip is not smooth. It carries rows of microscopic backward-facing barbs , and those barbs do two things at once. They make the quill harder to pull out , which everyone expected. They also make it easier to push in — the barbs concentrate stress along the tip and let it cut rather than shove, cutting the penetration force substantially. Both properties come from the same feature. We like this one because it refuses a tidy story. The thing that makes a spike good at going in is the same thing that makes it hard to take back. That is not a moral, and we are not going to make it one. Source: W. K. Cho, J. A. Ankrum, D. Guo, S. A. Chester, S. Y. Yang, A. Kashyap, G. A. Campbell, R. J. Wood, R. K. Rijal, R. Karnik, R. Langer & J. M. Karp, “Microstructured barbs on the North American porcupine quill enable easy tissue penetration and difficult removal,” PNAS 109 (52), 21289–21294 (2012), doi:10.1073/pnas.1216441109 . Quills as modified hairs: standard mammalogy. Esmx Does Not Shoot A drawing of Esmx the porkypine with a full mane. To the right, three dashed arcs show quills supposedly flying through the air; each arc is crossed out. Below them a solid line shows what actually happens: a quill leaves only where something touches it. never happens contact only the quill releases; the porcupine does not throw it

Esmx Does Not Shoot No. 3 · the popular verdict, corrected Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. They cannot throw them, fire them, or launch them. The quill is held in the skin by an attachment that gives way under a particular kind of push — so when something makes contact, the quill stays in the thing it touched rather than in the porcupine. An attacker has to come to it. The myth is easy to see the shape of: you find a predator studded with quills and no porcupine within reach, and the story writes itself backwards. It is also the exact fault this collection keeps finding — a mechanism invented to explain a coincidence , then repeated until it sounds like something everyone has always known. We are keeping this one at the front because our mascot is a porcupine and a spiky mascot invites precisely this reading: that the spikes are for attacking, that they go out looking. They do not. A quill is what happens at the boundary, and only there. The animal is never the punchline , and neither is the animal's armour. Source: Uldis Roze, Porcupines: The Animal Answer Guide (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2012) — Roze's own field work on the quill's release mechanism is the standard account. Related here: True Facts About True Facts (No. 47), A Field Guide to Watching Animals , whose reframe tables correct the popular verdict on the animal and nothing else. Spikes, Independently A drawing of Esmx the porkypine beside a simple branching tree. Four separate branch tips each end in a spiky silhouette — porcupine, hedgehog, tenrec and echidna — and the branches meet only far down at a common ancestor drawn with no spikes at all, showing that spines were arrived at four separate times. porcupine hedgehog tenrec echidna a common ancestor with no spines at all

Spikes, Independently No. 4 · there is no standard way to make a spike Porcupines have spines. So do hedgehogs, tenrecs, and echidnas. Take those four back down their branches and they do not meet at a spiky ancestor — they meet at an animal with ordinary fur, and in the echidna's case you have to go back past the split between egg-laying mammals and everything else. Spines were arrived at separately, four times, in four lineages that were not talking to each other. A hedgehog is not a small porcupine; it is not even a close relation. An echidna is not a porcupine that lays eggs. They are four independent answers, built from different starting material, to a problem that has more than one solution — which is what convergence keeps demonstrating and what a single standard keeps denying. Seven of our twelve field guides have arrived at some version of this sentence without being pointed at each other: there is no standard star, nervous system, migration, shark, turtle, tortoise, galaxy. Add spikes to the list. The universe keeps solving the same problem more than one way, and keeps declining to rank the answers. Related here: Five Times a Crab (No. 36), on carcinisation — where the real finding is that the crab shape was lost more often than it was gained; the Field Guides , where the no-standard sentence keeps recurring. The four lineages sit in four different mammal groups (Rodentia, Eulipotyphla, Afrosoricida, Monotremata), which is what makes the independence uncontroversial rather than a close call. Sulfur, and the Last Days A drawing of Esmx the porkypine whose mane spikes are drawn as chemical bonds: pairs of sulfur atoms joined by a short link, the disulfide bridges that make keratin stiff. Behind them, two oxygen nuclei collide and fuse into sulfur-32, labelled as oxygen burning in a massive star. S–S · what makes a quill stiff O O S oxygen burning a massive star, near the end

Sulfur, and the Last Days No. 5 · the whole argument, in one spike Keratin is a protein, and what makes the hard kind hard — quill, claw, horn, nail — is that its strands are stitched to each other by disulfide bridges : two sulfur atoms, from two cysteines, holding hands across the gap. Pull the sulfur out and a quill is a limp thread. The stiffness is not in the shape. It is in the bond. And sulfur is made in a specific place, at a specific point in a star's life. When a massive star has run through hydrogen, helium, carbon and neon, its core turns to burning oxygen — two oxygen nuclei fusing, throwing off products of which sulfur-32 is one of the most abundant . This is late. It is the accounting a big star does in its last stretch before the core gives way. So: the reason a porcupine's spike stands up is a bond made of an element assembled in the final days of a star that died before the Sun existed. Not a resemblance. Not a rhyme. The same atoms. This is the whole site in one drawing, and it is why Esmx belongs here at all — love you down to your star stuff reaches all the way down to the thing that makes a quill a quill. Sources: disulfide cross-linking in hard α-keratins — standard protein biochemistry. Sulfur's origin: all sulfur isotopes are synthesised in hydrostatic or explosive oxygen burning, which happens only in massive stars and Type Ia supernovae — Chin, Henkel et al. , “Interstellar sulfur isotopes and stellar oxygen burning,” A&A (1996), arXiv:astro-ph/9505067 . Related here: A Field Guide to the Elements , Bone Song (No. 1). Not a Chart A drawing of Esmx the porkypine. Behind the mane, a faint measuring grid with a dashed baseline and an axis fades out toward the right, while the mane's spikes carry on past the edge of the grid entirely. A note reads: no baseline, no axis, not one moment. baseline no baseline · no axis and not measured at one moment

Not a Chart No. 6 · the mascot outruns its own diagram Esmx's spikes are there for a reason: they evoke the spiky profile , the observation that a neurodivergent person's abilities are not one level but a range with real peaks and real troughs. The idea is Damian Milton's , building on Francesca Happé . It also turns up in the workplace literature, where a 2020 paper describes it as large, statistically-significant disparities between peaks and troughs of the profile and suggests it “may well emerge as the definitive expression of neurominority” — a study using the term, which is not the same thing as being where it came from. And we have already published the argument against it . No. 21 grants that the spiky profile beat the single severity dial, then names what it kept: it still plots you as distances from a flat expected baseline, still needs axes, and still freezes you at the one moment somebody assessed you. A better chart is still a chart. Which is exactly what makes the mascot better than the diagram it came from. Esmx's mane has no baseline. There is no zero line under it, no axis beside it, nothing it is a deviation from , and the tips keep going after the drawing stops. The same move the cosmic egg on our door makes: keep the jag, throw away the grid. Sources: the spiky profile is Damian Milton 's, building on Francesca Happé — the attribution this collection carries throughout. The two quoted phrases are from Nancy Doyle, “Neurodiversity at work: a biopsychosocial model and the impact on working adults,” British Medical Bulletin 135 (1), 108–125 (2020), doi:10.1093/bmb/ldaa021 , which is the wording Esmx's own page quotes; it is cited here as a use of the term in the workplace literature, not as its provenance . Related here: Not a Line (No. 21) and its broadside . The Trailing Spikes A drawing of Esmx the porkypine whose mane tips come loose and become the stars of a constellation, joined by faint lines into a figure. Underneath, a depth scale shows the same stars at wildly different distances from the viewer, so the figure exists only from here. nearer much farther the figure exists from here, and nowhere else

The Trailing Spikes No. 7 · a pattern is a place you are standing The best thing in Esmx's design is the part that comes apart. The mane does not end — the tips separate and drift , and Kaya's page says they can trail off and make patterns. Draw them far enough out and you have made a constellation, which means you have made the mistake this whole collection was built to notice. A constellation is a line of sight . The stars in one are, in the general case, nowhere near each other; they sit at wildly different distances and are held together by nothing but the angle you happen to be looking from. Move a long way sideways and the figure dissolves. It was never out there. It was a fact about your position, wearing the costume of a fact about the sky. Which is the friendliest possible warning about a mascot. Esmx's spikes make a pattern because we are standing here. That is a good enough reason to enjoy a pattern, and not a good enough reason to believe it is a structure. Related here: A Field Guide to Constellations ; The Lines We Drew (No. 9), which had to correct its own version of this — its depth argument originally ran on Orion's Belt, whose three stars turn out to be at essentially one distance and genuinely related. The general claim survives; the example did not. Esme A drawing of Esmx the porkypine. The tallest spike of the mane rises into the pointed silhouette of a witch's hat against a field of stars, and the letter x at the end of the name is drawn large beneath, marking the name Esmx as a variant of Esme. Esme → Esm x they / them

Esme No. 8 · where the name came from Esmx is named for Esme — for Esmeralda Weatherwax and the Witches of Discworld. The x is deliberate: it marks gender neutrality and fluidity, and Esmx's pronouns are they/them. Kaya's page adds that if you build your own variant from the blank template, you pick pronouns to fit what you made. That the name is a Discworld name is not a small coincidence for this particular collection. The Easter Eggs already hold No. 49 , a credit to Terry Pratchett that turned up three attribution corrections and ended by conceding that our own masthead is a promise rather than a finding. And the method it credits him for — First Sight and Second Thoughts , seeing what is actually in front of you and then watching yourself think about it — is Granny Weatherwax's inheritance more than anyone's. So the mascot was carrying a citation the whole time. Our porkypine is named after a witch who is famous for refusing to be fooled, including by herself. That is a better fit for a fact-checking collection than anything we would have arrived at on purpose. Source: the naming, the x , and the they/them are stated on Esmx's own page — primary, being the mascot's own account of itself. Related here: One Atom of Justice (No. 49); the Turtle at the foot of the collection.
What we left out, and one we nearly got wrong

What we left out, and one we nearly got wrong Notes The goblin stays in. Kaya's design notes name a bit of goblin in the mix, after goblin mode — refusing a social norm in order to be comfortable, and being frank about being weird. We have not drawn that as a feature because it is not a feature; it is the posture the whole character is standing in. It is also the closest thing Esmx has to a thesis, and it is the same one as Wyrd and Weird . We did not draw the pig. A porkypine is pig plus porcupine, and the temptation was to make something of the fact that porcupines are rodents and are not pigs at all — that the Latin behind the name calls it a spiny pig and the animal politely declines. We left it out because it is a joke about a word rather than a fact about an animal, and this page had eight better things to carry. It is written down here so the next person does not think we missed it. One distinction this page nearly got wrong, in the direction it warns about. A draft of card No. 6 cited the 2020 British Medical Bulletin paper as the source of the spiky profile , on the reasoning that it is the wording most often quoted and that its author's name appeared nowhere in this project. That is the error, not the fix. Using a term in a study is not being part of its provenance — a paper that defines a phrase in order to work with it is a use , and the citation belongs to whoever the idea came from, which here is Damian Milton building on Francesca Happé. Caught by Ryan Boren before it shipped. It is recorded because it is precisely the substitution Too Good to Check catalogues: the most quotable source standing in for the actual one, which is how a citation ends up pointing at the wrong person while looking more rigorous than the alternative. “Esmx” by Kaya Oldaker is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 · these eight variants likewise Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms stimpunks.org · morerealms.com · starstuff.earth open edition · print freely

Stimpunks × More Realms Skepticism and Wonder The Rainbow Connection — forty songs, and the two uneasily cohabiting modes of thought they carry. A song told a six-year-old that rainbows have nothing to hide, and he took it as permission to love the real thing more than any story about what it might be concealing. A Sound rack · companion to Zines No. 69 and No. 70 One 1979, and a six-year-old I grew up with The Muppet Show. The Muppet Movie came out in 1979, when I was six, and I was captivated by its opening song. “Rainbow Connection” was written by Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher and sung by Jim Henson as Kermit, sitting on a log in a swamp with a banjo. It was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song, the American Film Institute later placed it 74th among movie songs, and in 2021 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry. None of which is why it mattered to me. It mattered because of what its first verse does in the space of six lines. The verse opens by asking why there are so many songs about rainbows and what is on the other side. Then it grants that rainbows are visions — and immediately downgrades them, calling them only illusions. And then it lands the line that did the work: rainbows have nothing to hide. On the lyrics, which are not printed here This page discusses “Rainbow Connection” closely and quotes almost none of it, because reproducing a copyrighted lyric is not ours to do. The verses are characterised rather than transcribed, individual words appear where the argument turns on that exact word, and the full lyric is one link away at Genius. If a sentence here seems to be circling a line rather than quoting it, that is why. Two Nothing to hide To a science-loving kid, nothing to hide was the whole song. It recognises that a rainbow is an artifact of observation. There is no pot of gold in its reaches. There is no other side, because there is no side. Rainbows are not withholding anything from you, and they are not keeping a secret at the end that you might reach if you walked far enough. Rainbows just are. As a closeted queer kid and a closeted atheist, I found the observational reality of rainbows better than any story of what they might hold if they were fixed and finite. The science of them filled my head with more wonder and awe than the stories told about them ever did. That is an unusual thing for a song aimed at children to allow, and it is why this one stuck. A thing with nothing to hide is not a thing with nothing in it. Three The one word the song gets wrong And here the rack has to be honest about its own opening track, because the verse contains a word that our own Zine No. 69 spends twelve spreads refusing. “Illusions.” A rainbow is not one. An illusion is a mistake your perception makes — something you seem to see that is not occurring. A rainbow is occurring. It is light, refracted and reflected in falling water, arriving at your eye along a path that is calculable to a fraction of a degree from a refractive index of 1.3315. Roger Bacon measured its maximum elevation at 42 degrees around 1267, with an astrolabe and no theory of refraction at all, and the number has not moved. What is true is stranger and better than illusion: a rainbow has no location. It possesses, in Les Cowley's words, “neither distance nor linear dimension.” It is a direction rather than a place, centred on the shadow of your own head, and no two people have ever seen the same one. That is not a thing failing to be real. That is a real thing that is not an object. So I read the chorus — so we've been told, and some choose to believe it — not as negating the verse but as refusing the reduction in it. The true nature of rainbows is more wonderful than any of the flattenings, and it opens far more metaphorical room, not less. They are perfect circles, centred on the observer, made of solar light and falling water and a working eye, all three in real-time collaboration. How connected and wonderful is that? Four Two uneasily cohabiting modes The next verse asks who decided that a wish on a star would be heard, notes that somebody thought of it and somebody believed it, and then says, flatly: look what it's done so far. I was a skeptical kid and a closet atheist. Fascinated by stars; unconvinced by wishing on them. What I liked was the ambiguity — that line can be read as praise or as indictment and the song does not tell you which. It holds the good and the bad of belief in the same hand. I chose to hold both the skepticism of science and the wonder of dreaming, and the song let me. Sixteen years later, Carl Sagan gave me the words for what I had been doing. In The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (1995), writing about his parents: But in introducing me simultaneously to skepticism and to wonder, they taught me the two uneasily cohabiting modes of thought that are central to the scientific method.Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World, 1995 Uneasily cohabiting. Not balanced, not reconciled — sharing a house and not always comfortably. That is the correct description, and it is what “Rainbow Connection” had already modelled for me before I had a name for it. The song is skeptical in the verse and hopeful in the chorus and does not resolve the tension, because the tension is the point. Five Princes of the air Autistic, skeptical minds have been looking at the stars and inventing the future out of their dreams for a long time. NeuroTribes has a chapter about it — “Princes of the Air” — documenting the stargazing visionaries who turned science fiction into working technology and connected the world through the air. Steve Silberman notes that Hans Asperger may have been the first clinician to see that his patients' imaginations sometimes anticipated developments in science by decades, which forced him to walk back his own claim that their interests were remote from real-world concerns: But his joking suggestion that the designers of spaceships themselves must be autistic also turned out to be prescient.Steve Silberman, NeuroTribes — ch. “Princes of the Air” The joke was that we were unworldly. The record is that we were early. Six The alembic There is a third voice worth adding, and the lineage is not a coincidence. Dorion Sagan — son of Carl Sagan and of Lynn Margulis, whose endosymbiosis this whole collection already runs on — puts the same two modes together as a piece of laboratory glassware: Science's eye for detail, buttressed by philosophy's broad view, makes for a kind of alembic, an antidote to both.Dorion Sagan, Cosmic Apprentice: Dispatches from the Edges of Science An alembic is a still: two vessels joined, one heating and one condensing, and neither of them useful alone. An antidote to both is the sharp part — detail without breadth curdles into scientism, breadth without detail into vapour, and each is the cure for the other's excess. Which is the same claim Sagan the elder made about skepticism and wonder, and the same one a frog made on a log in 1979. Seven What the song was later found to cost In March 2023, first-graders at Heyer Elementary in Waukesha, Wisconsin, were preparing a spring concert on a theme of world unity and peace. Their teachers picked “Rainbowland,” the Miley Cyrus and Dolly Parton duet on this rack. The district vetoed it, reviewing the song against a board policy on controversial issues in the classroom. The music teacher was asked to find something else, and what she landed on was “Rainbow Connection.” That was initially banned too. It was reinstated only after parents pushed back. The teacher who spoke publicly about the first ban, Melissa Tempel, was later terminated. Sit with the shape of it. A song whose entire argument is that rainbows are ordinary optical phenomena with nothing hidden in them — written for a puppet, nominated for an Oscar, entered in the National Recording Registry — was, for a moment, too controversial for six-year-olds. Not because of anything in the song. Because of what the word in its title had come to be suspected of. Which is the skepticism half of this rack arriving from a direction I did not expect when I was six. The wonder half is easier and it is still true: the light is real, the water is real, your eye is real, and the three of them are collaborating right now. Nothing is being hidden from you. That was always the good news. What this rack is not saying Not that “Rainbow Connection” is a queer anthem or an Autistic one. It is a song about wanting to believe things, written by two songwriters for a film, and it did not have me in mind. What it did was leave room, and room is what a closeted kid can use. Not that skepticism and wonder resolve into one comfortable thing. Sagan's word was uneasily, and the discomfort is doing work — drop the skepticism and you get credulity, drop the wonder and you get the flattening this collection spends most of its time arguing against. Not that every song here agrees with the others. “Over the Rainbow” wants somewhere else; “What a Wonderful World” wants this one; “Rainbow Stew” thinks you are being sold something. They are on the same rack because the argument is between them, not inside any one of them. Not a claim on the Pride flag. It is a chosen set of colours, not the physical spectrum, and the Philly stripes were added precisely because a “natural” spectrum was being used to leave Black and brown queer people out. No. 70 holds that line and this rack does not cross it.

One — The song itself · eleven ways through it Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher, 1979. The verse is skeptical, the chorus is not, and nobody has ever resolved that — they just pick which half to lean on.

The original, handed over Rainbow Connection (Sing Along) The Muppets · Jim Henson as Kermit The Muppets’ own sing-along cut, which is the right way to meet it: the song was written to be joined, and Henson performs it as a small voice thinking out loud rather than a big voice declaring.

The song as a room A Special Performance of “Rainbow Connection” The Muppets Kermit alone with the banjo. Strip the film away and what is left is a character admitting he keeps being drawn to something he has just finished calling an illusion.

Sung by a crowd “Rainbow Connection” with Choir! Choir! Choir! Kermit the Frog & New Yorkers · Lincoln Center A room of strangers taught the song on the spot. The lyric is about lovers and dreamers finding each other; this is the only version where you can watch that happen in real time.

The outlaw reading Rainbow Connection Willie Nelson Nelson sings it as a plain statement of fact from someone who has had a long time to consider the question, which turns the wistfulness into something closer to patience.

The unreleased one The Rainbow Connection (Outtake) Carpenters An outtake, surfaced on the Carpenters’ catalogue channel rather than issued at the time. Karen Carpenter’s voice does something specific to the sceptical verse: she declines to be arch about it.

The full-throated one Rainbow Connection Barbra Streisand The maximalist reading, and on the rack precisely because it is the opposite of Henson’s — proof that the song survives being sung as though it were certain.

The soft-rock reading Rainbow Connection Kenny Loggins Loggins takes it at face value and lets it be pretty. A legitimate choice and a useful control: this is what the song sounds like with the scepticism sanded off.

The one you would not guess from the link Rainbow Connection Weezer feat. Hayley Williams From Muppets: The Green Album (2011). The link text carries no artist at all; oEmbed returned Weezer. Two voices trading a song about not being sure, which suits it.

The punk one Rainbow Connection Me First and the Gimme Gimmes A covers band who play everything fast and mean it anyway. Speeding it up removes the room to be wistful and leaves only the questions, which is a reading rather than a joke.

The lullaby Rainbow Connection JJ Heller Sung to a child, which returns the song to its actual audience and raises the stakes of the verse: this is the version where somebody is being told rainbows have nothing to hide for the first time.

The duet nobody expected Rainbow Connection Debbie Harry & Kermit the Frog Blondie’s singer and a frog, on television. The Muppets’ standing method — put the icon next to the puppet and let neither condescend — is the move this collection keeps making with facts.
Two — The joke that agrees with the song One track, because it earns its own section: a comedy duo arriving at the essay’s thesis by the shortest possible route.

The pun that is also the point Rainbow Connections Garfunkel and Oates A song about the connections you make with people, hung on the rainbow of the title. The joke depends on the listener already knowing a rainbow is about relation rather than location — which is the argument of No. 69, reached by comedians first.

Three — Somewhere over · the wish, eleven times Harold Arlen and E. Y. Harburg, 1939. The other great rainbow song, and it wants the opposite thing: not that rainbows have nothing to hide, but that there is somewhere on the far side worth reaching.

The original wish Over the Rainbow Judy Garland The Wizard of Oz, 1939; it won Best Original Song. The rainbow here is explicitly a threshold to somewhere else — the exact reading “Rainbow Connection” would push back on forty years later.

The one carrying two songs at once Somewhere over the Rainbow Israel “IZ” Kamakawiwoʻole His medley folds “What a Wonderful World” into it, which is why this rack has a section for each: IZ had already noticed the two songs answer the same question. Also carded on the L★S rack — one of the few songs held in two racks here.

Recorded in a small room Over The Rainbow (Blues Alley) Eva Cassidy Live at Blues Alley in 1996, the year she died at thirty-three, and almost unknown at the time. The recording found its audience long afterwards, which is its own comment on arrival and delay.
The quiet one somewhere over the rainbow Christina Perri Taken slowly and small — the wish read as something you say to yourself rather than announce, which is closer to how wishes actually get made.

The two songs spliced on purpose “Somewhere Over the Rainbow / I’m Yours” GENTRI An arrangement that follows IZ’s instinct and pairs the wish with a song about being present. The seam is the interesting part.
The young voice Over The Rainbow (RAWsession) Nikki Yanofsky A jazz reading that refuses the sentimental default and treats the melody as a set of intervals to be worked, which is a form of respect.

No words at all Over the Rainbow (Tokyo 1984) Keith Jarrett Solo piano. Strip the lyric and the wish is still legible in the shape of the tune — that famous octave leap is the reaching, and it is there without anybody saying so.
Over the Rainbow (Live at Jazz at Lincoln Center)

Live, 1958 Somewhere Over The Rainbow Sarah Vaughan From Holland, 1958. Vaughan’s control is the argument: she could place the note anywhere and chooses restraint, so the longing reads as decided rather than helpless.

Four — The world as it is · the counterweight The answer song, whether or not it was written as one. Not somewhere over anything — here, and already sufficient.

Here, not elsewhere What A Wonderful World Louis Armstrong 1967. Armstrong lists ordinary things and declines to wish for others. Beside “Over the Rainbow” it is a rebuttal; beside “Rainbow Connection” it is agreement.

Played across borders What a Wonderful World Playing For Change · Song Around The World Musicians in many places recorded separately and assembled into one take. The method is the message: the wonderful world is demonstrated rather than described.

“What A Wonderful World” w/ National Symphony Orchestra

With an orchestra behind it “What A Wonderful World” w/ National Symphony Orchestra Jon Batiste · The Kennedy Center The same reading at scale — useful next to the previous track for what does and does not change when you add ninety people.
Five — Naming the colours Two songs that treat a rainbow as a thing with parts, which is what the skepticism half of this rack is for.

Six — I am a rainbow · the metaphor turned inward At some point the rainbow stopped being in the sky and became a description of a person. These are the songs that made that move — and the reason a word in a song title can now get a first-grade concert cancelled.

The skepticism Rainbow Stew Merle Haggard 1981, and the sourest rainbow song here. Haggard lists the utopia he is being promised — free energy, free everything — and does not believe a word of it. On a rack about wonder this is the necessary corrective: somebody is usually selling something.

Rainbow Serpents Entropy increases in an isolated system. Not a closed one, and not an open one — and the qualifier keeps falling off. On a law applied where it does not belong, three of our own pieces that walked up to that line and stopped, and three infinities that are not the same infinity. You’re never too far from a snake. — Tyson Yunkaporta, Snake Talk This essay is about a qualifier. Four words long , taught in every thermodynamics course, and almost always gone by the time the idea reaches daylight. Here is the law with it: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. And here is how the idea usually arrives: Entropy always increases. Everything runs down. The four words that went missing are of an isolated system . They are not decoration. They name the only kind of system the sentence is true of — and almost nothing you will think about today is one. What the loss produces is a picture of the universe as a thing winding down like a clock, and that picture has been doing work far outside physics for a very long time. The person who put it to us most sharply is Tyson Yunkaporta , of the Apalech clan , western Cape York, a Wik Mungkan speaker who writes about knowledge systems. His charge is not that our physics is wrong. It is that we took a true law and sang it somewhere it does not belong, and that the consequences have been enormous. Two things this essay will not do. It will not explain the Rainbow Serpent, which is not one being, not one nation’s, and not ours to describe. And it will not claim that Aboriginal Law is validated by thermodynamics — that would make our instruments the judge of somebody else’s jurisprudence, which is the argument in Already an Entity (No. 81) and we are not going to undo it a week later. What it will do is take a criticism of our physics, from outside our discipline, and check it.
Three times we walked up to this and stopped

Three times we walked up to this and stopped Before anything else, the confession, because it is what gives this essay its subject. The Elimination of Waste (No. 43) follows the word waste from Carnot’s heat engine into scientific management and then into the school. On its last spread it stops dead and argues against itself: “you are not a heat engine. The second law governs closed systems and cyclic processes; a person is neither. Fatigue is not waste heat, spoons are not joules.” It marks that step as its leap and declines to take it. The Noise Floor (No. 56) uses the same law in the other direction — Nyquist deduced the thermal noise floor from the second law, because a silent resistor would be a perpetual-motion machine. The hiss is not a shortfall. It is required . Your Shadow Is the Centre (No. 69) establishes that a rainbow is a cone of directions with its apex in your own eye: there are as many bows as there are observers, and Roger Bacon reasoned his way to it around 1267 with an astrolabe and a measured 42°. Three pieces, three edges of one argument, and each of them stops just short of it. Yunkaporta does not stop. He puts the three together and says the arrangement is a curse.

The qualifier, stated properly Thermodynamics distinguishes three kinds of system, and the distinction is not pedantry — it decides which sentence is true. System Exchanges with its surroundings What the second law says about its entropy Isolated neither matter nor energy tends to a maximum, and does not decrease Closed energy but not matter can decrease , given work or energy input Open both matter and energy can decrease, while entropy production inside stays non-negative The familiar sentence — entropy always increases — is true of the first row only. Conflating closed with isolated is a well-documented error, and it is the one that matters here, because almost nothing anybody cares about is isolated. Both statements are written down, side by side, in a review of exactly this subject in Reviews of Modern Physics . Martin Singh and Morgan O’Neill give the restricted form first: entropy S of an isolated system must not decrease with time… d S /d t ≥ 0. (isolated system) Singh & O’Neill, Rev. Mod. Phys. 94 , 015001 (2022), eq. (1), after de Groot & Mazur Look at where the qualifier is. It is not in a footnote or a preamble. It is printed as a parenthetical label on the equation itself — (isolated system) — because the equation is not true without it. And their definition is the strict one: “an isolated system… does not exchange mass or energy with its environment.” Then, four paragraphs later, they say the climate system exchanges energy with space as radiation “and it is therefore not isolated,” and give the general form: d S /d t = Š e + Š i eq. (3) — Š e is the net import of entropy from the surroundings, Š i the production of entropy inside the system by irreversible processes; the second law requires Š i ≥ 0 That is the whole thing in two lines. The law is not weaker out here. It has one more term. Entropy produced inside is still never negative — the second law is intact and unnegotiable. But a system that exports entropy faster than it makes it can have its own total entropy fall , and no law is broken. And we made the same slip Read the No. 43 sentence again: “the second law governs closed systems and cyclic processes.” The precise word is isolated , and ours was loose. Yunkaporta uses both words, and where he puts each one is worth noticing. Naming the thermodynamic term he writes closed system , which is the ordinary shorthand and what most physics writing says. But describing what the worldview actually demands, he writes: “systems must be isolated and exist in a vacuum of individual creation.” That is exact. Isolation is the stronger condition, it is the one the doctrine requires, and he uses the stronger word in the place where it belongs. So this is a correction to us, not to him. It is how anything alive works. A seed does it. A forest does it. You did it this morning. The Earth is not isolated. It receives a stream of low-entropy sunlight and radiates high-entropy infrared to space, and it is that gradient — not any exemption from physics — that pays for every ordered thing on the planet. The tell Somebody says “everything runs down — second law” about a thing that is plainly exchanging matter and energy with its surroundings. Ask which system they mean, and where its boundary is.

Running through, not down If the running-down picture is the wrong one, the obvious question is what the right one is. There are two answers, at two scales, and they are not the same answer. Keeping them apart matters. The first is ours, and it is not in dispute. Singh and O’Neill open their review by stating it plainly: “The Earth is a highly irreversible thermodynamic system. It receives energy and entropy from the sun and radiates energy and entropy to outer space.” What arrives is a focused beam of shortwave radiation with an effective emission temperature of about 6,000 K . What leaves is diffuse longwave emission at about 250 K . The energy in and out are, in their words, “roughly in balance” — the planet is not hoarding it. What changes is the entropy those photons carry: while the incoming and outgoing fluxes of energy are roughly in balance, the Earth exports vastly more entropy than it receives … the second law of thermodynamics requires that this net export of entropy be balanced by irreversible production of entropy within the climate system. Singh & O’Neill, Rev. Mod. Phys. 94 , 015001 (2022) That difference is the entire budget out of which every ordered thing here is paid: a forest, a reef, a body, a sentence, this page. The planet is not running down. It is running through . Held honestly No ratio is printed here, and note that the review does not print one either — it says vastly more . Figures are quoted elsewhere and depend on exactly which fluxes are compared. The mechanism is solid; the multiplier is not ours to round off. The second answer is Yunkaporta’s, and it is about time rather than energy. This is where the disagreement he is describing actually sits, and it is worth having in full rather than in summary: First Peoples and Second Peoples seem to have a fundamental disagreement on the nature of reality and the basic laws of existence. It all comes back to notions of time, and the existential acrobatics required for Second Peoples to make time run in a straight line, to create a beginning, middle and end of things. First Peoples’ law says that nothing is created or destroyed because of the infinite and regenerative connections between systems. Therefore time is non-linear and regenerates creation in endless cycles. Second People’s law says that systems must be isolated and exist in a vacuum of individual creation, beginning in complexity but simplifying and breaking down until they meet their end. Therefore time is linear, because all things must have a beginning, middle and end. Tyson Yunkaporta, “A rainbow serpent theory of time,” Garland Magazine Read that against the four missing words and the shape of the thing is plain. The linear model is not a finding about time. It is what you are left with once you have assumed isolation — because an isolated system really does have a beginning, a middle, and an end, and really does run down. Assume the box, and the arrow follows. What Yunkaporta is pointing at is that the box was assumed. He pairs his own First Law with the first law of thermodynamics himself, and directly: “First Law always means nothing is created or destroyed, but just keeps going around if you look after your place, whether you’re an Elder or a physicist.” That pairing is his and we report it as his. We are not offering thermodynamics as confirmation of anybody’s Law — that is the move refused below, and in No. 81 before it. What we can say is narrower and still worth saying. Of the two models, one of them describes the planet we are on. Earth exchanges matter and energy continuously, in every direction, at every scale. The straight line requires a container that is not there.
A true law, sung where it does not belong

A true law, sung where it does not belong Here is the argument as Yunkaporta makes it. It is his, it is in print, and we are reporting rather than extending it. He describes how a curse works in an Aboriginal worldview: you take part of a system, observe the pattern of the whole in that fragment, “then you sing a false pattern… into the whole from the part, powering it with another system in constant motion.” And then: The curse is a deception made real—either an outright lie or a true law or pattern applied where it doesn’t belong. It is like a computer virus, a sneaky line of code that ends up crashing the whole system. The application of the second law of thermodynamics to open, interconnected systems does the same thing. It is a curse. Tyson Yunkaporta, Sand Talk (2019), pp. 48–49 Note the precision of the definition. A curse is not superstition here and it is not a lie, necessarily. It is a true pattern, correctly observed, deliberately applied outside its domain, and powered by something that keeps moving. That is a description of a category error with a delivery mechanism — and as a description of what happened to the second law between the textbook and the culture, it is uncomfortably exact. He goes further, and this is the part that is his interpretation rather than a physics claim: that the appetite for closed systems is why the built world is so full of “fences and walls, borders, great divides, and great barriers.” If your model of time requires an isolated system, you will find yourself manufacturing them. We are not in a position to adjudicate that. We can say that the physics half is right, that our own No. 43 half-said it and stopped, and that the question he ends on is a fair one to leave standing: In reality we do not inhabit closed systems, so why choose the second law of thermodynamics to create your model of time? Yunkaporta, Sand Talk , p. 47
A club that says two things depending on how you hold it

A club that says two things depending on how you hold it The argument has an object attached to it, and the object is the best short explanation of it. Yunkaporta carved a club. Around its head he etched an ouroboros — the snake swallowing its own tail — to stand for the second law and a world that must end. But the club is three-dimensional, and when you roll it across clay the etching releases something the flat image could not hold: “an endless procession of snakes, head to tail.” One carving. Rolled, it prints a line with no last snake in it. The ouroboros closes because something is being consumed. The procession does not close, and nothing is eaten. That is the first law and the second law rendered as a tool you can hold, and it is worth saying plainly that this is a better teaching object than most of the diagrams in a physics textbook . It also carries his sharpest line about the figure itself, from earlier in the same book: the ouroboros was supposed to be a metaphor for infinity, “However, it contained the same curse, the same contradiction: How can this serpent be a symbol of infinity if it will eventually eat itself?”
The bow was always a circle

The bow was always a circle One piece of pure physics, which belongs to nobody, and which this site has already worked over twice. A rainbow is not an arc. It is a cone of directions, roughly 42° from the antisolar point, with its apex at your eye. You see an arc because the ground cuts the cone. From an aircraft, with nothing in the way, the same bow is a complete circle — and it always was. Which means the bow moves when you move, and two people standing on two hills are not looking at one rainbow from two angles. They are looking at two rainbows. Yunkaporta makes exactly this point, and reaches the same conclusion an optics textbook does: When we see that arc in the sky… we are only seeing one part of it, and it is subjective, just for us. If we move the rainbow also moves, only appearing in relation to our standpoint. A man on the next hill will see it in a different position from where we are seeing it. Yunkaporta, “A rainbow serpent theory of time,” Garland Magazine We are not claiming a convergence here, and we are certainly not claiming that physics confirms anything. It is one fact about light, available to anyone who looks, and two traditions noticed it. That is what a fact about light is like. The full argument, with Bacon’s astrolabe and the reason there are as many rainbows as there are observers, is Your Shadow Is the Centre . The catalogue of every other kind of bow is A Field Guide to Rainbows .

Not one serpent This is the section where the essay stops. The Rainbow Serpent is not a single figure with regional variants, and treating it as one is the specific error this site has undertaken not to make. There are many beings, many nations, many names, and some of the knowledge is restricted. Yunkaporta says so himself, of the serpent he is describing: “There are infinite variations of him in all shapes and sizes throughout the world—wyrm, dragon, uraeus, and many different names in different regions, taking the shape of the spirit of those places.” So: quoted, credited, and not explained. We are not going to summarise a Law we do not hold, or produce the tidy paragraph that would let a reader think they now know what the Rainbow Serpent is. Why the restraint, specifically Not squeamishness. The Rainbow Serpent has one of the heaviest histories of commodification in Australian art — reproduced on tea towels and airport canvases for decades, usually without a nation attached and usually without payment. A settler-run project adding one more explanation to that pile is not a contribution. What we can do instead is the boring thing: cite the person, name the clan, quote rather than paraphrase, and link out.
The head does not take the tail

The head does not take the tail The Autism Infinity Dragon — Kaya Oldaker “The Autism Infinity Dragon” by Kaya Oldaker , released by the artist into the public domain : “This is the autism symbol as a dragon. I did this to represent the influence my autism has on my art. This is a public domain drawing and anyone can use it for any reason.” — Kaya’s Kosmos · kayaskosmos.com . Credited here because attribution is courtesy even where it is not required. This is the autistic community’s own infinity symbol , drawn as a dragon by an autistic artist for whom dragons are a long-standing special interest — and drawn, in her words, “to represent the influence my autism has on my art.” Kaya Oldaker also drew Esmx, the Stimpunks mascot. It belongs in this essay for a reason that is about geometry, and that you can check by looking at the picture. Look at the crossing point. The mouth is open, and the violet plume of the tail passes beneath and past it. Nothing is gripped and nothing is being consumed. This is a lemniscate — a single continuous curve that crosses itself and carries on — and a lemniscate is not an ouroboros. An ouroboros closes by eating. The ouroboros is an isolated system. The infinity loop is an open one. The difference is whether anything has to be eaten for the figure to continue. We are not going to claim Kaya drew a thermodynamics diagram. She drew a dragon, for a reason she has stated, and it is a better dragon than the argument needs. But the autistic community chose an unclosed figure for itself, and the distinction between the figure that closes and the figure that does not is exactly the distinction on the club. And a note about our own sequencing This essay has just spent a section on Rainbow Serpents and then shown you a rainbow-coloured serpentine figure a few hundred words later. That juxtaposition does work whether we intend it or not, so: the resemblance is an artefact of our running order. Kaya’s dragon is not a Rainbow Serpent, is not descended from one, and is not answering to one. It is an autistic artist’s symbol for autistic people, and the only reason the question comes up at all is that we put the two things near each other. That is ours to manage, not hers to disclaim. They rhyme, and rhyming is not descent.
A deficit assessment is an isolated-system model of a person

A deficit assessment is an isolated-system model of a person Here is the one claim in this essay that is ours, about us, made with our own symbol, and routed nowhere near anybody’s Law. An assessment measures a person alone. It scores them against a standard, in a room, on a day, with the environment held constant and unrecorded. Whatever comes out is treated as a property of the person — something they have, or lack, or are losing. That is an isolated-system model, and people are not isolated systems. The support in the room, the noise, the lighting, whether anyone believed you last time, whether you are allowed to move — all of these cross the boundary constantly, and none of them appear in the score. When the number comes back low, the model has nowhere to write down that half the apparatus was outside the box. Nothing in thermodynamics licenses that observation. The physics does not say how anybody should be treated, here or anywhere — that argument is A Promise, Not a Finding , and it holds. Down to is not because of. What the physics does is take away an excuse. If you are going to model a person as a system, you have to say which kind, and if you say isolated you are wrong before you have measured anything.

What this essay is not Not an explanation of the Rainbow Serpent. Quoted from a named author of a named clan, and left there. It is not one being and we do not hold it. Not Aboriginal Law validated by physics. The traffic here runs the other way: a criticism of our physics, arriving from outside our discipline, which we checked and found correct. See No. 81 for why the reverse would be a colonial move with better manners. Not a claim that the second law is wrong or optional. It is exactly right, in its domain, and No. 56 is built on it holding. Entropy production in an open system is still never negative. Not “the second law proves rest is mandatory.” No. 43 refused that on its own last spread and we are not un-refusing it. You are not a heat engine, and spoons are not joules. Not a lineage. The ouroboros, the Rainbow Serpent and the autism infinity loop are three different things that happen to be snakes bent into curves. They rhyme. Rhyming is not descent, and noticing a rhyme is not discovering a connection. Not ancient wisdom. Yunkaporta is a working academic who published a book in 2019 and an essay in a magazine. Filing living argument under timeless folklore is another way of filing it under not-current.

Coda: processes rather than objects The last word should be his, unglossed. Speaking about serpent law, in conversation rather than in print: …it’s mostly about balance, and it’s mostly about maintaining fluidity between arbitrary designations that want to make the world into things, objects. Edges bleed, and they’re supposed to. Things migrate, things flow, systems interact. And that’s what the serpent law does. It helps us to be like that, to recognize ourselves as processes rather than objects . And if you’re making your relationships based on that understanding — that the snake, that wisdom that the serpent brings — that’s where that phase shift happens. That’s why the snake’s so important. We all need to share our next stories with each other. Tyson Yunkaporta, in conversation — transcribed from speech, false start elided, punctuation ours We are not going to interpret that. But it is worth saying where it lands against everything above, because it lands squarely. An isolated system is a thing. An open system is a process. That is the entire content of the two equations: one describes a box with contents, and the other describes a flux — a rate, terms crossing a boundary, a quantity defined by what passes through it rather than by what it holds. d S /d t = Š e + Š i is not a description of an object. It is a description of a process, and it has a boundary in it that you had to choose. Which is also the whole of the deficit assessment. A score is an object. A person is a process, with edges that bleed by design — and the assessment’s error is not that it measures the wrong thing but that it measures a thing at all .

None of these is Yunkaporta’s and none should be attributed to him. The universe doesn’t pathologize its own variation. And the running-down story is not a fact about you, a community, or a forest — it is a fact about a box that exchanges nothing with anything, and nothing you care about is that box. The Bow With Its Colours Spread Too Wide

small dropbands overlap = white L★S · 001 The Bow With Its Colours Spread Too Wide Fogbow · droplets under about 0.05 mm radius 30–45° · white, broad, banded within A fogbow is filed as the colourless rainbow, the ghost, the one that did not develop properly. Nothing failed. The colours are all present and all in order — the bands have simply been widened, by diffraction, until each one overlaps its neighbours and the sum reads white. droplets ≲ 0.05 mmdiffraction widens the bandsstrong supernumerarieswhite by addition, not absence ▸ Field notes Field notes · Fogbow · droplets under about 0.05 mm The single most useful entry in this guide, because it is the one where sorting by appearance fails hardest. A fogbow and a rainbow look nothing alike. They differ in one parameter: the size of the drop. Rain falls in drops around a millimetre across. Fog and cloud droplets rarely exceed 100 micrometres and a fogbow needs them at roughly 0.05 mm and below. At that scale the light no longer behaves as a tidy ray: it diffracts around the droplet, and diffraction widens each colour band. Widen every band far enough and they stop sitting side by side and start sitting on top of each other. Overlapping colours across the visible range add to white. The white is the sum of the colours, arrived at by addition. This has a clean, testable consequence, and it is the reason to trust the account rather than merely accept it: the effect runs on a slope, not a switch. As droplet diameter increases the fogbow narrows and colour returns at the edges, and at the intermediate sizes found in waterfall spray — roughly 100 to 500 micrometres — you get intermediate bows, neither white nor fully coloured. There is no boundary at which a fogbow becomes a rainbow. The two names describe two regions of one continuum, and the naming is ours. The same physics that smears the main band sharpens something else: fogbows carry unusually strong supernumerary arcs inside them, for the reason given three cards along. A phenomenon losing colour in one place and gaining structure in another is not a degraded version of anything. Held honestly: the radius is given as a range (about 30–45°) because it genuinely varies with droplet size — quoting a single figure would contradict the card's own argument. What changes is where the observer is standing, and that is worth a card of its own precisely because the genre treats it as a fact about the bow. The cloudbow sits opposite the sun around the shadow of the aircraft, with its scattering angles running roughly 135° to 165°, and very often with a glory inside it. It is the ordinary companion to the third card in the next section. The reason it is here is the rarity argument. A cloudbow was not rarer in 1850 than it is now — cloud decks with the sun behind the observer were exactly as common. What was rare was anybody being above one. Every rarity ranking in this genre is quietly a ranking of human vantage: who could get high enough, who lives far enough south, who was awake, who was looking the right way. Move the observer and the "rarity" moves with them, which means it was never a property of the phenomenon being ranked. Modern satellite work uses cloudbow polarisation to retrieve droplet sizes from orbit — the same signal, read as an instrument rather than a sight. rain: 42.0°salt: 0.8° smaller L★S · 003 Two Bows, One Beam, Different Water Sea spray bow · saltwater against rainwater radius ≈ 0.8° smaller than a freshwater bow Salt raises the refractive index of water. Very slightly — but a rainbow is an angle, and an angle answers to the refractive index exactly. Where sea spray and rain fall in the same sky, two bows stand side by side, misaligned by less than a degree, and the misalignment is visible to the naked eye. salt raises the refractive indexradius ≈ 0.8° smallerboth bows visible at onceidentical in appearance ▸ Field notes Field notes · Sea spray bow · saltwater against rainwater The exact inverse of the fogbow, and the pair is why this section leads the guide. A fogbow looks like a different phenomenon and is the same one at a different drop size. A sea spray bow looks identical to a rainbow and is a genuinely different bow. Appearance gets both cases wrong, in opposite directions, and no amount of looking harder fixes either. Dissolved salt raises seawater's refractive index above fresh rainwater's. The rainbow angle is set by that index and nothing else, so the seawater bow's radius comes out roughly 0.8° smaller. Where surf spray and falling rain occupy the same air with the sun behind an observer, both bows form from the same beam at the same instant, and the pair is reported and photographed as two arcs visibly out of step — the spray bow sitting just inside its freshwater twin. The important part is that you cannot get to this by looking. The two arcs are the same colours in the same order at the same brightness. What separates them is a number, and the number came from chemistry that the eye has no access to. A guide that sorted by appearance would have to file these as one entry and would be wrong. Held honestly: the 0.8° figure is the one quoted in the atmospheric-optics literature for typical seawater salinity, and it is a function of salinity, so it is not a constant of nature. Salinity varies; so does the offset. small: sphericallarge: flattened 2.5% L★S · 004 One Bow Whose Drops Disagree Twinned rainbow · two drop populations at once oblateness of 1–2.5% is enough A rare bow in which the primary itself splits into two arcs sharing a base. It is not a double rainbow and it is not two rainbows. It is one rainbow being made by two crowds of drops that are not the same shape as each other — because falling flattens a large drop and leaves a small one alone. not a double rainbowlarge drops flatten in fall1–2.5% oblateness sufficestwo showers, one cone ▸ Field notes Field notes · Twinned rainbow · two drop populations at once Everybody has seen the diagram of a spherical raindrop, and it is right — for small drops. Surface tension holds a drop under about a millimetre very close to a sphere. Larger drops meet air resistance on the way down and are flattened by it, into oblate shapes that can oscillate as they fall. (The teardrop shape of the picture books is not among the options.) A rainbow's angle depends on the drop being a sphere. Ray-tracing shows that departures of a mere 1–2% from sphericity noticeably distort the primary bow. So when two showers fall through one observer's cone at once — one of small spherical drops, one of large drops flattened by around 2.5% — the two populations produce two slightly different primaries with a common base, and the bow appears to split. The modelling is the interesting part and the honest limit at the same time. Simulations combining spherical drops with oblate spheroids reproduce the twinned bow; the shape data comes from ray-tracing through realistic drop models built as two conjoined half-spheroids of different oblateness, and Debye-series work on polydisperse distributions shows that anomalous drop-size distributions can twin the primary, secondary, tertiary and quinary bows at certain solar elevations. Why it is in this guide. Every other card here is one parameter moved. This one is the same parameter holding two values at once in the same sky — and the result is not an average. The bow does not compromise into a single fatter arc. It shows you both. Held honestly: this explanation is simulation-led and reconstruction-led rather than settled by direct measurement of the drops in a photographed twinned bow, and it is presented that way in the literature. The Bow In A Liquid That Is Not Water

Not water — methane, falling through a thick orange haze onto a world where water is bedrock. Methane has its own refractive index, so it has its own rainbow angle: a bow of about 49° radius instead of 42°, the same colours in the same order, with an orange cast from the sky it hangs in. liquid methane, n ≈ 1.29radius ≈ 49°same colour orderinfrared bows more likely than visible ▸ Field notes Field notes · Methane bow · Titan The furthest this section's parameter can be pushed: not a different size of drop, or a different shape, or a different salinity, but a different liquid entirely. Liquid methane has a refractive index of about 1.29 against water's roughly 1.33. Run the same geometry and the primary bow comes out at a radius of about 49° rather than 42°. Colour order is unchanged — blue inside, red outside — with an overall orange tint contributed by Titan's sky rather than by the drops. The practical difficulty is honest and worth keeping: rainbows need reasonably direct light, and Titan's air is thick with haze, so a visible methane bow may well be rare. But Titan's atmosphere is substantially clearer in the infrared, and infrared bows there are considered likely — which means the bow may be routine and simply outside the band our eyes happen to read. Geometric optics — light as rays, in one face of the drop, off the back, out again — cannot produce supernumerary arcs. Not "does not predict them well." Cannot, in principle. They were a standing refutation of the complete ray account sitting in plain sight above every rain shower on Earth. Thomas Young explained them in 1804, by interference: two geometrical rays can leave a drop at the same scattering angle having travelled different distances inside it, and when they recombine they reinforce or cancel by wavelength. That produces exactly the fringing observed. Because the account requires light to have a phase, supernumerary arcs became evidence for the wave theory of light at precisely the moment that argument was live. The history has a second half that we keep, because it is the more useful half. In 1838 George Airy produced the integral treatment that still bears his name — and dismissed Young's account as "the imperfect theory of interference," on the reasonable ground that it put the arcs at the wrong angles. Airy was right that Young's numbers were off. He was wrong about why: Young had not known that a ray crossing a focal line picks up a 90° phase shift. Put the phase shift in and Young's interference theory becomes surprisingly accurate. Airy's success then overshadowed Young's contribution for well over a century. So the record is: a correct mechanism, published first, rejected by a better mathematician for a real defect that turned out to be a missing term rather than a wrong idea. We are not going to draw a moral from that about people. We are going to leave it on the page. The privacy was the clue. Roland Stull's Practical Meteorology says the same thing 759 years later. And the turn is that zine's, not ours to repeat: nobody has ever doubted a rainbow on the grounds that it cannot be handed over. What this guide does with it instead. Two entries lean on the geometry without re-arguing it. The glory puts your own silhouette in the middle of the rings so the anchoring is impossible to miss. The full-circle bow depends on the antisolar point being below the horizon whenever the sun is above it. Both cite the cone and neither retells it, which is the whole rule: told twice is told worse. no hub · no clock L★S · 001 The One With No Ledger Hydra · Hydra vulgaris a nerve net, no brain · a ~4-hour cycle, no clock A freshwater animal a centimetre or two long, related to jellyfish and coral, with no brain and no central nervous system — just a mesh of nerve cells with nothing anywhere gathering it into a decision-maker. Hydra is the standing objection. It has neurons — a few thousand — but they form a nerve net with no centre, no ganglion, nothing that could be called an organ of control. And it sleeps. Kanaya and colleagues established it against the behavioural definition, which is the one that works across species that share no anatomy: the animal becomes quiescent, it is harder to rouse, and if you deprive it of the state it takes more of it afterwards and falls into it faster. That third criterion is the whole test. Being still is not sleep; being still and then owing stillness is. Two findings from the same paper make this the card the guide opens on. The first is that melatonin, GABA and the PRKG1 kinase all push Hydra towards sleep, exactly as they do in animals with brains — the machinery predates the organ. The second is what deprivation costs: cell proliferation falls off. Rest here is not a pause in the animal's real work. It is when a good deal of the building happens. And it keeps no time. Put Hydra in constant light or constant dark and its daily rhythm simply vanishes — there is no free-running circadian clock underneath. What remains is a cycle of roughly four hours, returning and returning. So the oldest resting animal available to us is not answering to a day at all. The authors call it a sleep-like state before they call it sleep, and that hedge is kept here. What is established is that it meets the criteria, not that a polyp experiences anything. The argument this card serves is No. 59: an account of rest as something earned needs a ledger to keep score in, and there is no ledger in a nerve net. On its own that proves nothing; plenty of things slow down at night. What made it sleep was the other two tests. Roused at night, the animal took longer to respond and longer to right itself. Bone answers to load. Take the load away — bed rest, spaceflight — and resorption outruns formation and the skeleton thins. McGee-Lawrence and colleagues compared hibernating and active grizzlies and black bears and found no difference in bone volume fraction or tissue mineral density. It has downshifted the whole process evenly and come out even. The physiology around it is just as counterintuitive. Tøien and colleagues measured metabolic rate and body temperature continuously through natural winters and found metabolism suppressed to about 25 per cent of basal while core temperature was regulated between roughly 30 and 36 °C in multi-day cycles — a drop of only five or six degrees. Plasma sampled from animals below 0 °C had normal solute concentrations and no evidence of antifreeze molecules — none of the cryoprotectant chemistry that lets some insects and fish tolerate freezing. This is the other one: aestivation, a response to drought, and it is at least as extreme. As its pool dries, an African lungfish burrows into the mud and produces mucus in quantity until the mucus stiffens into a case around its body, leaving an opening at the mouth. The Twenty Hours That Was One Warm Room

33 °C26 °C19.9 h · 11.0 h L★S · 011 The Twenty Hours That Was One Warm Room Little brown bat · Myotis lucifugus 19.9 h at 33 °C · 11.0 h at 26 °C The sleepiest mammal, in every table and every listicle, at just under twenty hours a day. In a cooler room the same measurements give eleven hours. the number is one measurementtemperature-dependent~1% of mammals measuredthe tables are old ▸ Field notes Field notes · Little brown bat · Myotis lucifugus This is the card the guide would keep if it could keep only one, and it is not about a bat. It is about how a number becomes a fact. Everyone has met the sleepiest mammal. It appears in infographics, in trivia, in science journalism, and in the comparative databases those draw on, at 19.9 hours a day. Harding and colleagues went back to where the figure came from. Almost all of the extreme-bat-sleep record traces to two studies by Brebbia and co-workers in the 1960s and 70s, on Myotis lucifugus and Eptesicus fuscus. The 19.9-hour measurement specifically was taken at an ambient temperature of 33 °C, and it "rests on a single study using an unknown number of specimens." Then the finding that should be printed somewhere permanent: the same body of measurement gives 11.0 hours at 26 °C. The most-repeated sleep statistic about any mammal nearly halves depending on how warm the room was — which for a bat is not a detail, because a bat in a cool room enters torpor, and torpor is not sleep. Two fruit bat species measured properly come in at about 14.8 and 14.7 hours, comparable to a Syrian hamster, an animal that features in nobody's list of champion sleepers. The paper's wider argument is the one this band is built on. Roughly one per cent of mammal species have had their sleep measured at all; a great deal of the comparative record is decades old and was gathered under artificial conditions, notably social isolation and controlled temperature, which for many species is a description of stress rather than of life. The familiar giraffe and cat figures come out of the same thin literature, and the giraffe circulates at both 1.9 and 4.6 hours depending on which secondary source you land on — a factor of nearly two and a half, which is the tell. So this card carries no headline number of its own, and the missing bar in its diagram is deliberate: there is no honest single figure to draw. Which is why the guide's claim is what it is. There is no standard way to rest — and for most of the animals alive, there is not even a standard measurement of it. Its sleep has two modes. Hauled out on land it sleeps as a land mammal does: both hemispheres in slow-wave sleep together, with REM. In the water it converts to a largely unihemispheric pattern — one hemisphere in slow waves, the other awake — and REM sleep is profoundly reduced or eliminated. Kendall-Bar, Lyamin, Siegel and colleagues measured what the eyes do while this happens: the eye contralateral to the sleeping hemisphere stays closed about 99.4 per cent of the time, while the eye on the waking side opens in brief bouts averaging 1.9 seconds, around eight times a minute. Half the animal is watching, in glances. Then the result that gives the card its title. Lyamin and colleagues found fur seals suppress REM sleep for very long periods — weeks — without subsequent rebound. No catch-up. In most mammals REM deprivation produces a measurable debt that is paid back with interest, and it is one of the better arguments that REM does something necessary. A fur seal at sea appears to simply not owe it. This is not a licence to skip sleep, and the guide will not pretend otherwise: the seal is a specialist, and its physiology is not ours. But it belongs in a catalogue about rest because it breaks the tidiest available story. Sleep debt is not a universal law of animals with brains. It is how the accounting works in the species where it has been measured, and here is a species where it does not. Gilbert, Ancel and colleagues instrumented huddles and measured what that is worth: a maximum ambient temperature inside the huddle of 37.5 °C — close to the birds' own deep body temperature — recorded while the air outside was −19 °C. About two thirds of the metabolic saving comes not from the warmth but from the reduction in cold-exposed body surface — from there being less of you facing the weather at all — and about one third from the mild microclimate the group creates. So most of the benefit is structural rather than thermal. It is a fact about shape. And the huddle is not static. It moves in travelling waves: roughly every 30 to 60 seconds a bird takes a small step, and its neighbours follow, so the whole mass slowly reorganises and birds on the edge cycle inward. No individual is managing this. There is no penguin in charge of fairness. Which is why the card is here rather than in band three. Nobody in this huddle is resting harder than anybody else. They built a condition, and the condition does the work. openfoldednot sleep, and never claimed L★S · 017 The Word Was Borrowed, And They Said So Nyctinasty · Linnaeus’s Somnus Plantarum (1755) no reframe offered — the misnaming was ours Bean and pea and prayer-plant leaves fold at dusk and open at dawn, on a circadian clock, and the movement has been called the sleep of plants since Linnaeus.
