Here there is a common belief — that plants sleep — but it was never a verdict passed on plants. It was a convenience of ours, and it has been flagged as one by its own authors for two and a half centuries. The provenance is worth reading from the primary rather than from summaries of it, and the primary is out of copyright. In The Power of Movement in Plants (1880), Charles Darwin, assisted by his son Francis, writes that "the so-called sleep of leaves is so conspicuous a phenomenon that it was observed as early as the time of Pliny; and since Linnæus published his famous Essay, 'Somnus Plantarum,' it has been the subject" of continuing study. So: the phenomenon is ancient, the word is Linnaeus's, from a 1755 essay, and Darwin inherited it with visible reservations. He is blunter about the daytime version — "The leaves of some plants move during the day in a manner, which has improperly been called diurnal sleep" — and elsewhere says of it that "we believe it to be of an essentially different nature from the nocturnal movement." The modern name is nyctinasty: nastic leaf movement at the onset of darkness, driven by the circadian clock, documented from legumes to the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha. It is real, it is rhythmic, and it is not sleep by the three criteria this guide has used throughout — there is no arousal threshold to raise and no homeostatic rebound to measure. A plant deprived of its night-time leaf position does not fold harder the next evening. None of which is a deficit, and that is why there is no actually column. A reframe table corrects a misreading of an organism. Nothing here has misread the plant; a folk usage borrowed a good word for a movement that deserved one, and the borrowing was labelled from the start. Recording that is bookkeeping, not rescue. It sits at the end of the guide because it names the guide's own risk. Rest is a word we carry across enormous distances — to a polyp, to a nematode, to a bird asleep on one side — and every one of those carries is a judgement about whether the word still means anything. Linnaeus made one and Darwin queried it in print. The least we can do is say which ones we are making. No reframe offered no reframe offered · L★S —

Notless true for being thinner — a thinner signal still carries a real rhythm. Notranked beneath presence — signal is a form of presence. Notalways spoken — written and AAC words carry understanding too, sometimes better. Nota lesser community for having no address — a watering hole doesn't need a building. Shared Signal · Stimpunks

Every star you see is a signal that outran its source — light that left so long ago that some of those stars are already gone. We wrote a whole zine about it: the dead stars still reach us. The reaching is real even when the one who sent it is out of reach. That is the deepest thing a signal does: it lets connection cross a gap that touch cannot. The same physics that carries a dead star's light to your eye carries your voice to someone alive but far away. Presence, sent ahead of the body. So no channel is the master channel — not voice, not video, not text, not breath. Connection is built between two people, in whatever medium lets both of them be understood (Milton, 2012). 01 of 05 · The origin LYDTYSS The full phrase, initialed. Love You Down To Your Star Stuff. Every word present. Nothing lost. LLove YYou DDown TTo YYour SStar SStuff Etymology · LYDTYSS The phrase before it became portable LYDTYSS is the full acronym — every word present, nothing compressed, the whole sentence rendered in seven letters. It's the version you type when you want someone to know exactly what you mean before you've established the shorthand. At seven characters it's already private — this is a phrase that belongs to a community, spoken in spaces where the full meaning is known. The acronym doesn't explain itself. It assumes shared ground. The weight of the phrase is preserved here: the downward direction (D), the possessive (Y — Your), the movement through scales. Every syllable that earns "star stuff" its landing is still visible. How it's used In writing, in channels, in early use — when the phrase was still new and the shorthand hadn't settled yet. The form that remembers all seven words. Shorthand Evolution · Stimpunks2
Drop the scaffolding. Keep the weight.

02 of 05 · The first softening LYSS The first compression. Down To Your dissolves — the structural words, not the emotional ones. What remains: Love, You, Star, Stuff. LLove YYou SStar SStuff —D, T, Y dropped Etymology · LYSS Drop the scaffolding. Keep the weight. The compression from LYDTYSS to LYSS removes the three structural words — Down, To, Your — the ones that indicate direction and possession but don't carry the emotional payload. What's preserved: the verb (Love), the subject (You), and the cosmological anchor (Star Stuff). The compression is surgically precise — it removes exactly what can be inferred from context and nothing else. LYSS has a quality LYDTYSS doesn't: it's almost speakable. Four letters, one syllable — rhymes with "kiss." It starts to feel like a word rather than an abbreviation. How it's used In community, between people who know the phrase. Faster to type than LYDTYSS, still readable without explanation. The form that trusts the reader. Shorthand Evolution · Stimpunks3
One letter changes. The sound opens up.

03 of 05 · The warm variant LUSS An alternate four-letter compression. The U where the Y was — a different mouth feel, a rounder sound, a different kind of warmth. LLove UYou (phonetic) SStar SStuff →Y becomes U Etymology · LUSS One letter changes. The sound opens up. LUSS and LYSS carry the same four words — Love, You, Star, Stuff — but LUSS makes a phonetic substitution: U for Y. The letter U is the phoneme of "you." It sounds like what it represents. That single swap changes the feel of the shorthand. LYSS is clean and consonant-led. LUSS is rounder, warmer, more vowel-forward. It reads more like an embrace than an acronym. LUSS also sounds better spoken aloud — "luss" sits in the mouth differently than "liss," closer to "lush" or "love" in its phonaesthetics. Some uses of the shorthand preferred this version for exactly that reason. How it's used A parallel form to LYSS — used by those who preferred the phonetic U, who wanted the shorthand to feel more like the word it stands in for. Both remain valid. Six Principles and a Room A counsellor's code of ethics is addressed to two people. The distress is usually coming from a third thing, and the third thing cannot be struck off. On what a relational ethic owes after the door — and on a professional body that has just moved, and where its step stopped. This page starts with a question somebody else asked. Helen Edgar sat an evening session on ethics as part of her BACP training, came out of it, and wondered whether there was a Star Stuff version — whether everything this site keeps saying about difference, relation and belonging adds up to an ethics, or only to a mood. It is a fair challenge and it deserves a specific answer rather than a warm one. So this is not an essay about ethics in general. It is an essay about one document, which is real, public, free to download, and about to be replaced.

Six principles The Ethical Framework for the Counselling Professions is what BACP members in the UK are bound by. The edition in force as this is written was first published in 2018 and took effect on 1 July that year. It has three parts — a commitment to clients, a section on ethics, and a long section on good practice — and at the centre of the ethics section sit six core principles, given here in full because the whole of this essay is a reading of them. Being trustworthy: honouring the trust placed in the practitioner. Autonomy: respect for the client's right to be self-governing. Beneficence: a commitment to promoting the client's wellbeing. Non-maleficence: a commitment to avoiding harm to the client. Justice: the fair and impartial treatment of all clients and the provision of adequate services. Self-respect: fostering the practitioner's self-knowledge, integrity and care for self. BACP · Ethical Framework for the Counselling Professions, 2018 · Ethics, paragraph 5 Before anything else: this is a good document. Nothing that follows is a complaint about counsellors, who are for the most part the people trying, inside services that have been cut to the bone. The framework is careful in ways that documents of its kind usually are not. It knows its own principles collide, and instead of pretending otherwise it says so and tells you what to do about it. “A decision or course of action does not necessarily become unethical merely because it is controversial or because other practitioners would have reached different conclusions in similar circumstances. A practitioner's obligation is to consider all the relevant circumstances with as much care as possible and to be appropriately accountable for decisions made.” BACP · Ethical Framework 2018 · Ethics, paragraph 7 That is a grown-up sentence. It refuses the fantasy of a code that resolves cases for you, and it puts the weight on reasoning you can be held to. We have no improvement to offer on it. Read the six principles again anyway, and count the nouns that are doing ethical work. Practitioner. Client. Services. That is the cast. Every principle is a duty running between two people, with one half-clause — the provision of adequate services, inside Justice — reaching past them.

The word that appears once That reading is an impression, and impressions are cheap. The document is public and machine-readable, so it can be counted instead. How these counts were made Both frameworks were downloaded as published PDFs from bacp.co.uk and converted with pdftotext -layout ; words were counted with grep -oiw on the extracted text. The 2018 extraction runs to 6,825 words , the 2026 to 4,124 . Anyone can reproduce this in about two minutes, and should — a count you have not run yourself is a claim somebody made, and this site has been wrong that way before. In the 2018 framework, the word environment appears once . Not in the principles, not in the values, not in the commitments to clients, not anywhere in the long good-practice section. It appears in paragraph 8, in a sentence about the practitioner's inner life. “Personal moral qualities are internalised values that shape how we relate to others and our environment. They represent a moral energy or drive that may operate unconsciously and unexamined.” BACP · Ethical Framework 2018 · Ethics, paragraph 8 The environment is present as something the practitioner has an attitude toward. It is a direction their moral energy points. It is not a party to anything. What the 2018 framework has words for — 6,825 words of it Word Times Where client / clients 173 throughout practitioner / practitioners 35 throughout relationship / relationships 34 throughout context 3 the client's cultural context; contracting; supervision setting 2 both about tailoring your conduct to where you work environment 1 paragraph 8, quoted above organisation 1 BACP's own charity registration, on the copyright page system / systemic / structural / institutional 0 — The single organisation is the best detail in the table, and it is not a gotcha — it is the shape of the thing. The only organisation named in a professional ethics framework is the professional body's own company number. The two uses of setting are worth stating precisely, because they are the closest the document comes and they do not get there. Both instruct you to apply the framework in ways that are appropriate to your role and your service's setting. The setting is a variable that modifies your duty. It is never a thing that can be at fault. None of this is an oversight, and reading it as one would be the lazy version of this essay. A professional code regulates professionals. Its sanction is registration, and you cannot strike off a building. The framework says who it is for in its own opening: it exists so that BACP conduct panels have a reference point when a complaint is made against a member. A document built to answer did this member act well? is going to be composed almost entirely of members and the people they saw. The trouble is not that the code is wrong about its job. It is what happens to everything the code has no slot for.
Where the fault goes to live

Where the fault goes to live Picture the referral. An Autistic teenager is not coping at school. By the time they reach a counselling room, a good deal has already happened to them, and almost none of it happened inside them. The lighting is fluorescent and flickers at a rate most people cannot consciously see. The timetable moves them through six rooms and six social configurations in a day, with the transitions unbuffered. The corridor at changeover is louder than a nightclub. The uniform policy specifies fabric they cannot wear. The reasonable adjustment was agreed in March and has not been implemented, because the person who agreed it left. The waiting list ran eleven months, and in month seven they stopped sleeping. The diagnostic category they were given routes them toward a service commissioned to reduce behaviours rather than to change any of the above. The school is judged on attendance, so every accommodation costs somebody a number they are measured on. Now open the code. Six principles. Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, self-respect, being trustworthy. Every one of them is a question about how the practitioner conducts themselves toward this young person. There is no line to write the lighting on. There is no line for the eleven months. There is no line for the commissioning incentive, and none for the adjustment that evaporated when a member of staff resigned. When the only parties to an ethic are two people, everything that is not one of those two people has to be recorded somewhere else — and the only somewhere else on offer is inside the person who came in. This is the deficit model arriving by paperwork rather than by prejudice. Nobody has to believe anything cruel. The form simply has one box, the box has a name in it, and the lighting is not eligible. There is a serviceable word for the thing that actually produced the distress, and it is assemblage — a temporary gathering of unlike things (bodies, buildings, timetables, categories, funding cycles, lights) that between them make some outcomes easy and others impossible. It comes from Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, and it is genuinely useful here, so we will use it and then be careful with it. A note we owe, from four pieces ago This site recently audited its own habit of reaching for French philosophers to say things that people with a much older claim have been saying, in print, with names and nations attached. Zoe Todd calls the pattern aer nullius , and her charge is not that Deleuze is wrong — it is who else could have told you, and whether they got a line in the bibliography . Relational selfhood is not a 1980 invention, and an ethics that locates the self in its relations has addresses far older than this one. The honest response is narrow: use the word, credit the two men it came from, and do not present it as the discovery. It would be worse to reach past that for somebody else's jurisprudence to lend weight to an argument of ours — so we are not going to. No. 81 makes that case at length , including the paragraph it decided not to write.

The floor is already poured There is an obvious way for this argument to go wrong, and it is worth naming before going further, because it is the reason a lot of people are wary of relational ethics in the first place. If harm is produced by assemblages, if selves are made in relation, if nothing is fixed and everything is becoming — then what stops any of it from dissolving into well, that's just another assemblage ? An ethics with no floor is not an ethics. It is a way of being unavailable for blame, and the people it fails first are the ones with the least power in the room. This site put its floor in some time ago, and it is one sentence. “There is exactly one disqualifier at this door, and it is not difference — it is harm.” Star Stuff · Inclusion Safety: Owed, Not Earned The Creed is a doorway ethic: it settles who belongs, and the answer is everybody, because belonging is constitutive rather than conferred. This essay is the other half — what is owed once people are through the door — and it inherits the floor unchanged. So: a relational ethic does not weaken do no harm . It widens the list of things capable of doing it. The practitioner's duty is untouched. What is added is that a timetable can be an agent, a waiting list can be an agent, a commissioning incentive can be an agent, and none of them stop being answerable just because they cannot attend a hearing. Somebody set that timetable. Somebody signed that contract. Difference is not the problem. Harm is, and harm has more authors than a two-party code can list.

Then the profession moved Here is where an essay of this shape normally ends, with the writer having proved something about a profession that was not consulted. That is not available, because while this was being written the profession moved — further and more deliberately than most. BACP spent four years revising the framework. The replacement was published in 2026. Its own copyright page says it takes effect from 1 November 2026; BACP's guidance page says it becomes mandatory at midday on Tuesday 3 November 2026, and members are committed to the 2018 edition until then. Both dates are given here because both are published and they are not the same date. The new edition puts a sentence on its cover, under the title, where a subtitle goes. “Working ethically is working within relationships” BACP · Ethical Framework for the Counselling Professions 2026 · cover The relational turn that this site has been arguing for from the physics end is, as of this November, the front cover of Helen's professional body's code of conduct. It is worth sitting with that for a second before saying anything clever about it. And the change is not cosmetic. The whole document is rebuilt. There are now three sections — Working ethically within relationships , Ethical principles , Core responsibilities — and the first of them is a method for reasoning rather than a list of duties. The Latin is gone: autonomy , beneficence , non-maleficence and self-respect appear zero times in the new edition, replaced by plain English — Do no harm , Best interest , Respect . Six principles have become twelve. And one of the twelve is this: “ Anti-oppression: Be aware of relational power dynamics, ensuring relational power imbalances do not create or lead to marginalisation or minoritisation” BACP · Ethical Framework 2026 · Ethical principles A mainstream professional body in the United Kingdom now lists anti-oppression as a core ethical principle, alongside honesty and confidentiality, binding on tens of thousands of practitioners. Elsewhere the new edition requires collaboration with the person a decision will affect, requires a written rationale when collaboration is not possible, and defines collaboration as “taking deliberate steps towards mitigating potentially harmful power dynamics and inequalities between people.” It even opens a slot for the outside: practitioners must now account for external factors , meaning “those factors that sit outside the relationship but may impact the relationship,” explicitly including “organisational expectations and requirements.” That is a real step, taken deliberately, over four years. Say so plainly before saying anything else.

Where the step stopped Now run the same count on the new document, because the interesting thing about a step is where it stops. The same words, both editions Word 2018 · 6,825 words 2026 · 4,124 words relationship / relationships 34 27 relational 2 2 organisational 0 3 environment 1 0 setting / settings 2 0 systemic 0 0 structural 0 0 institutional 0 0 Relationship language is up sharply once you account for the shorter document. Organisational language appears for the first time. And environment , which appeared once, now appears not at all. The two occurrences of relational in the 2026 edition are the ones that matter, and they are both inside the anti-oppression principle: relational power dynamics , relational power imbalances . Read the principle again with that in view. The framework has learned to see power — and it has located power between the people in the relationship , twice, by name. Oppression, in the new code, is something that happens in the space between a practitioner and the person in front of them. A great deal of it does. That is a true and hard-won thing to have written down. But it is not where most of it comes from, and there is a body of work saying so precisely. “But these injustices are not merely interpersonal – they are structural. They arise from socio-material environments that facilitate ease for neurotypical ways of being while simultaneously marginalizing neurodivergent ways of being.” Zamir Kadodia & Joel Krueger · Epistemic injustice, niche construction, and neurodiversity · Philosophical Psychology, 2026 Kadodia and Krueger are writing about epistemic injustice — Miranda Fricker's term for the harms done to us specifically as knowers, when our testimony is discounted because of who is giving it, or when the concepts we would need to describe our own experience have been crowded out. Their move is to say that the niches we think in are built, maintained and reproduced, and that neuronormative assumptions get built into them, so that some ways of being are afforded ease and others are made to work for it. The injustice is in the room's construction, not only in anybody's manner. That is exactly the gap between relational power and structural power, stated by people whose subject is us. And there is one more thing in the 2026 edition worth reading slowly, because it is where the room finally does appear. “Contracts and context of work – our commitment through the application of this Ethical Framework is to collaborative working, however, there may be occasions when our contracts for work, or the context where we are working, specifically exclude collaborative working. Where this is the case, the reasons need to be documented clearly.” BACP · Ethical Framework 2026 · When collaboration might not be possible This is honest drafting and we would not want it removed — a code that pretended practitioners are free agents inside services that constrain them would be worse, and lying. But notice the grammatical position the room has been given. The environment enters the new code chiefly as a reason you could not do the ethical thing, and the requirement is to write down why. It arrives as an exemption rather than as a defendant. Which is not a failure of nerve; it is the limit of what a professional code can be. Registration is the only sanction it holds, and no room has ever been registered. So the step stops where the instrument stops, and pointing at that is not an accusation. It is a description of the next problem, and the next problem does not belong to counsellors alone.

The third ecology There is a small book that names the missing piece exactly, and it was written by somebody who spent his working life in a clinic. Félix Guattari — the second name in Deleuze and Guattari, and a practising psychotherapist at the La Borde clinic for four decades — argued in 1989 that any adequate ethics has to run across three registers at once, which he called the three ecologies: mental , social , and environmental . His claim was that treating them separately guarantees failure in all three, because a mind is not repairable in isolation from the relations it sits in, and neither of those is repairable in isolation from the material world they sit in. Set the two frameworks against that and the shape is unmistakable, and unmistakably progressive. Three ecologies, and how far each edition of the code reaches Three stacked bands, labelled from the top: mental, social, environmental. Two vertical brackets run alongside them. The 2018 bracket covers the mental band only, marked "the practitioner's own moral qualities, and their conduct toward one client". The 2026 bracket covers the mental and social bands, marked "relationships, collaboration, and power between people — the word relational, twice". Beside the third and lowest band, environmental, there is no bracket, and the note reads "no bracket: environment 0, systemic 0, structural 0, institutional 0 — and this is where the lighting, the timetable and the waiting list live". Guattari, 1989 · the three ecologies Mental how we relate to ourselves Social how we relate to each other Environmental the material world we do both inside 2018 six principles 2026 twelve principles, anti-oppression no bracket reaches the third band environment 0 · systemic 0 · structural 0 · institutional 0 The 2018 edition reaches the practitioner's interior and their conduct toward a client. The 2026 edition reaches the relationship and names power inside it. The third band is where the lighting, the timetable and the eleven-month wait live — and it is the one whose word went from one to zero. Guattari is not being invoked here as a proof of anything. He is being used the way a name for something is used: the profession has taken the second rung, and there is a third, and it already has a name and a literature. That is a lead, not a verdict, and the mapping above is our reading of two documents rather than a finding either of them would recognise.
What it looks like on a Tuesday

What it looks like on a Tuesday An ethics that stops at the diagnosis of a gap is not much of an ethics. The practical question is what changes on an ordinary day, and the answer to that one is not ours — it is already written, by the person who asked the question at the top of this page. Helen Edgar's Ethodivergent Hearth Building came out of a planning conversation with Stimpunks for the Neuroqueer Learning Spaces project, and it asks what it takes to build spaces that sustain neurodivergent people rather than merely include us. The hearth is the image: a warm centre people return to, which may not be a room at all. “In ethodivergent hearth building, these sensory and relational centres become vital anchors, places to return to without performance, where our difference is held with warmth rather than shame or stigma.” Helen Edgar · Ethodivergent Hearth Building: A Relational Neuroqueering Community Practice · Autistic Realms, 10 July 2025 The word underneath it is ethodiversity , Ombre Tarragnat's term, which extends the neurodiversity paradigm past the human brain to the whole range of ways of sensing, moving, attending and relating — across species, across the living and the non-living. It is the vocabulary this site has been using for a year in its more-than-human pieces, and it turns out to be an ethical vocabulary rather than a descriptive one, because once ways of relating are the unit, the material conditions of relating stop being scenery. Read as an answer to the gap above, the hearth is unglamorously concrete. It is time that bends to bodyminds instead of bodyminds bent to timetables. It is fallow rest, stim time, quiet time. It is co-regulation, sensory consideration, bodily autonomy, relational consent. It is access intimacy — Mia Mingus's term for the feeling of not having to explain your access needs — treated as an ordinary design requirement rather than a lucky accident. None of that is a therapeutic technique. All of it is a change to the third band. Which is the practical form of the whole argument. If the distress is being produced in the room, then the ethical act is often a change to the room , and the person best placed to make it is frequently not the practitioner — it is whoever set the timetable, wrote the commission, chose the lighting, or built the waiting list. A relational ethic does not let those people out. It is the only kind that has ever had a place to write their names.

What this is not Not: Not an attack on therapists, or on BACP. The 2018 framework is a careful document that knows its own principles collide. The 2026 revision moved further than most professional bodies have. Both are quoted here at length precisely because they are worth reading. Not an argument that rules are oppression. Codes with teeth are how people with less power get recourse. The complaint is about the size of the frame, never about having one. Not a dissolution of responsibility. An ethic in which everything is an assemblage and nobody is answerable is worse than the one it replaced. The floor is the Creed's, unchanged: harm is the disqualifier, and rooms have authors. Not physics proving philosophy. Nothing about relational quantum mechanics establishes anything about ethics, and this site has a whole page about why we do not make that move. A rhyme, not a proof. Not somebody else's law recruited to settle ours. There is an older and more complete answer to “what is missing from a code that cannot name the land,” and it belongs to people who are not us. See No. 81 , which declines the same shortcut at greater length. Not a finished ethics. This is one document read closely, and a gap named. The gap is real; the filling of it is a much larger job than an essay.

The line Helen's question was whether this site's commitments add up to an ethics. They add up to at least this much, and it can be put in one sentence that a practitioner could actually use on a Tuesday: An ethic you can only point at a person is an ethic that will keep finding the fault in the person. Everything else follows from taking that seriously. Belonging is owed rather than earned, which the Creed already settled. Harm is the one disqualifier, which it also settled. What this page adds is the third thing: the list of possible authors of harm is longer than the list of people in the room , and an ethics that cannot write the longer list will keep producing the same verdict about the same people, in good faith, forever. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Codes do, occasionally, by having nowhere else to put the blame. Read the doorway half → Primary documents. Six Ways a Fact Goes Wrong

Six Ways a Fact Goes Wrong A story that fits gets less scrutiny, which is exactly when it needs more. Six shapes the failure takes — and the tell for each. 01 The quote nobody said What circulates is a compression — true in spirit, absent from the text. Tell More quotable than anything anyone says out loud. Do Search the actual book. 02 The number that went stale Measurements get superseded. The old value circulates for decades with nothing marking it expired. Tell Repeated everywhere, dated nowhere. Do Check the source you cited gives your number. 03 The story told backwards The facts survive the retelling and the emphasis doesn't, so the meaning inverts while every sentence stays defensible. Tell The paper's own hedge is missing. Do Read what the authors said they don't know. 04 The credit that drifted Attribution decays toward tidiness. A collective becomes a founder; a documenter becomes a coiner. Tell One name where a community was. Do Find the first printed instance, not the famous one. 05 The press release, not the paper A layer whose job is to make the finding interesting. Its output isn't a lie — it's a livelier verb. Tell The vivid verb is doing the work. Do Open the abstract. See which word the authors chose. 06 The finding that flatters you The other five are accidents. This one is an appetite, and it comes looking for you. Tell You wanted it true before you read it. Do Slow down here. Where we started The skeleton you were promised This whole collection opens with a bone. Bone Song starts where you'd expect: your calcium was forged in stars, and the skeleton it built is piezoelectric. Press on it and it makes voltage. Iwao Yasuda found that in the 1950s. Your bones are listening to how you move. That's the founding image here. Star-forged mineral, laid down in a living lattice, humming quietly under load. And then the ocean says: sure. Or don't. There is a whole class of vertebrates — sharks, rays, skates, the strange deep chimaeras — that never turns up to the bone. Same phylum. Same backbone-having club. No true bone anywhere in the body. Not a lesser version of yours. A different answer to the same question, and it has been working for a very long time. two vertebrates, two skeletons us mineralised bone press → voltage piezoelectric shark soft core cartilage + tiles bends, then springs no true bone both are vertebrates · neither is the draft same club, different build yasuda 1954–1957 · dean & summers 2006 Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
A mosaic where the bone would be

What's in there instead A mosaic where the bone would be "Cartilaginous" makes it sound floppy. It isn't. A shark's skeleton is cartilage with a mineral crust laid over it — thousands of small blocks, packed edge to edge like paving, sitting on top of an uncalcified core. The blocks are called tesserae, from the word for mosaic tiles, and that is exactly what they look like. Mason Dean and Adam Summers, reviewing the tissue in 2006, describe a skeleton whose mineralisation comes in distinct types — areolar, globular, prismatic — arranged differently depending on the animal's age, its species, where in the body you're looking, and how it feeds. The skeleton is tuned to the life. And the design does something bone can't. A tiled surface over a soft core bends further before it breaks, then springs back. It's lighter than bone. It doesn't need marrow cavities or a blood supply threaded all the way through. None of that is a workaround. It's a different set of trade-offs, chosen — over deep time — by an enormous number of successful animals. You were taught one skeleton and told it was the skeleton. There are others, and they are not rough drafts. tessellated cartilage, in section uncalcified cartilage core tesserae — mineral tiles, laid edge to edge the seams between tiles are where it flexes stiff enough to bite · springy enough to swim areolar · globular · prismatic — three ways to mineralise dean & summers 2006 · zoology a mosaic, tuned to the life it carries Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
They didn't miss it. They let it go

The part that changes the story They didn't miss it. They let it go For most of a century the shark was taught as the before picture. Cartilage first, bone later — sharks as a living snapshot of the stage vertebrates passed through on the way to becoming us. Primitive. Ancestral. Not there yet. The fossils stopped cooperating. In 2020 Martin Brazeau and colleagues described Minjinia turgenensis, an Early Devonian fish from Mongolia on the placoderm grade — close to the common ancestry of all jawed vertebrates — and it is full of endochondral bone. The kind sharks don't have. Which flips the sequence. If the shared ancestor already had bone, then the shark's bonelessness isn't something it never got round to. It is something its lineage gave up. A derived condition. A loss. We have run into this exact shape before, one zine ago. The crab body plan was gained five times and lost seven — leaving turned out to be the commoner event. Here it is again in the skeleton: subtraction is not the same as never having arrived. And whatever they traded away, they have been fine. The chondrichthyan record runs back to the early Silurian — call it 440 million years, on scales and teeth at first. Four mass extinctions. Still here. The animal you were told hadn't got there yet had been there, and chose otherwise. who had bone, and when shared ancestor HAS BONE Minjinia turgenensis early Devonian bony fishes → us kept the bone sharks & rays let the bone go loss derived, not primitive · brazeau et al. 2020 nature ecology & evolution, 2020 the before picture was never before Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

The word doing the damage "Primitive" is a verdict Watch how it works. Primitive has a technical meaning — a trait resembling an ancestral state — and it carries a second meaning it never declares: unfinished. lesser. earlier on the way to better. Both meanings ride in the same word. So a real observation ("this trait resembles the ancestral condition") arrives already sentenced. And here the technical meaning was also wrong. The shark skeleton isn't ancestral. It's a later change. The word was carrying a verdict it hadn't earned, about a fact that wasn't a fact. Our field guide to nervous systems flagged the same habit in neuroscience — jellyfish nets called primitive, worm brains called simple. Same move, different tissue. It's the move that gets made about us, too. Low-functioning. Developmentally delayed. Behind. Every one of them a measurement with a destination smuggled inside it, and the destination is always somebody else. one word, two cargoes "primitive" what it declares resembles the ancestral state what it smuggles unfinished · lesser · behind and for the shark skeleton: the declared meaning was false too a sentence, passed before the evidence the verdict inside the description low-functioning · delayed · behind Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
Then someone decided it was a cure

The turn Then someone decided it was a cure Here is what happened next to the skeleton we've just spent five pages admiring. Somewhere along the way a claim got loose: sharks don't get cancer. Cartilage has no blood vessels of its own; tumours need a blood supply to grow; therefore — the reasoning went — a shark must be carrying something that stops them. Grind it up. Take it as a powder. It became an industry. Capsules, powders, whole shelves of them, sold to people who had just been given the worst news of their lives and were looking anywhere at all. Notice the shape of the claim, because it is the important part. The animal is no longer an animal. Once you've decided a body contains the answer to your problem, the body stops being a life with its own reasons and becomes a supply. And then there's the small matter of whether it was true. the chain of reasoning cartilage has no vessels true so sharks don't get cancer false so grind them into pills didn't work one true premise does not carry a conclusion a body that contains an answer stops being read as a life the premise, the leap, the shelf an animal becomes a supply Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

The record Sharks get cancer They always did. Somebody just had to go and count. In 2004 Gary Ostrander and colleagues went through the literature and the Registry of Tumors in Lower Animals and found 42 documented tumours in cartilaginous fishes — across at least 21 species, in nine families and seven orders. Twenty-four in sharks, sixteen in skates and rays, two in chimaeras. Tumours of the nervous system, the gut, the skin, the blood-forming tissue, the reproductive organs, the endocrine system — and of the skeleton itself. At least fifteen were malignant, invading normal tissue. Their paper's title says the quiet part: Shark Cartilage, Cancer and the Growing Threat of Pseudoscience. Then it was tested properly. Charles Loprinzi and colleagues ran a randomised trial in patients with advanced cancer and reported in 2005: no difference in survival, no difference in quality of life, and side effects bad enough that people struggled to keep taking it. So: the premise was false, the product did nothing, and the animals were killed anyway. 42 documented tumours ≥ 21 species · 7 orders 0 benefit to survival or quality of life The claim was never checked because it was useful. That is usually the reason. 42 tumours, by group sharks 24 skates & rays 16 chimaeras 2 at least 15 malignant · invading normal tissue ostrander et al. 2004 · cancer research the count that was there all along nobody had asked Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
A body read as a cure gets harvested

The pattern underneath A body read as a cure gets harvested This is the sentence the zine exists for, so here it is plainly. The shark was not harmed because anyone hated it. It was harmed because somebody decided its body contained something useful, and once that decision is made, everything else follows without anyone needing to be cruel on purpose. You stop asking what the animal is doing with its own skeleton. You start asking what the skeleton can do for you. And then you go and get it. It is the same operation when it's aimed at people. We know this frame very well: the search for the cause, so there can be a cure. The interest in Autistic people that arrives only as what are they good at, could we use that. The inspiration story where a disabled life is raw material for somebody else's lesson. The research funding that goes to prevention rather than to the things we've actually asked for. All of it starts the same way — not with hatred, with usefulness. A body is read for what can be extracted, and the reading feels like appreciation right up until the moment it costs you something. What the skeleton is actually for

Back to the animal What the skeleton is actually for It's for the shark. That's the whole answer, and it's worth sitting with, because it is the answer that got skipped. The tiled cartilage is doing a job every second of that animal's life. It holds a jaw that has to bite without shattering. It carries a body through water with the springy recoil that makes the swimming cheap. It grows with the animal, tuned — species by species, region by region, feeding style by feeding style — to the exact loads that particular life puts on it. It is not a message to us. It is not a resource with an animal wrapped round it. It is a body, solving the problem of being that body, in a way that has held up across four mass extinctions. Your skeleton is doing the same thing. Yasuda's finding wasn't that your bones are useful to somebody — it's that they're listening, minute by minute, to the life you are actually living. You don't owe anyone a reason

Closer to home You don't owe anyone a reason Everything in this zine turns on one question, and it's a question that gets asked about people constantly. What is it for? Asked of a shark's skeleton, it produced a shelf of pills that didn't work and a lot of dead animals. Asked of a person, it produces the same shape: what are you good for, what does your difference get us, where's the upside. You've probably been handed the flattering version. Autistic people are so detail-oriented — brilliant for quality assurance. It sounds like praise. It's a receipt. It says the welcome is conditional on the yield, and quietly hands you the bill if the yield stops. So here is the plain form of the refusal, which is the same one we'd make on the shark's behalf if it could be bothered to care what we think: The skeleton is for the animal. Your mind is for you. Not a resource. Not a lesson. Not a supply. A body doing the work of being itself, which is the only justification anything in this universe has ever had, and it has always been enough. Four hundred million years of no bone at all, and nobody down there is apologising. The tiles aren't a rough draft of a spine. The Star Stuff You're Made Of Eight elements essential to your body, traced to where the universe forged them. Almost every atom heavier than helium was made in stars and their deaths — and none of it was made for you, which is somehow the better story. H Z 1 Hydrogen The First Light ~10% of you The Big Bang, ~13.8 billion years ago. No star ever made it — every other atom in you is younger. O Z 8 Oxygen The Weight of You ~65% of you Massive stars, scattered by core-collapse supernovae. Mostly the water you're built from, not the air. C Z 6 Carbon The Scaffold ~18% of you Aging stars, by the triple-alpha process — three helium nuclei fusing almost at once. N Z 7 Nitrogen The Borrowed Letters ~3% of you Dying stars, via the CNO cycle. You breathe it constantly and can't use a molecule of it raw. Ca Z 20 Calcium The Bone Note ~1.5% of you Massive stars and their supernovae. Your skeleton, and the spark behind every heartbeat. Fe Z 26 Iron The Death Rattle ~4 g · trace Two kinds of stellar death: roughly half from core-collapse supernovae, half from Type Ia. K Z 19 Potassium The Spark ~0.25% of you Explosive burning in supernovae. Every nerve signal you have ever had. A little of it is radioactive. I Z 53 Iodine The Rare Catastrophe ~15–20 mg · trace Colliding neutron stars, by the r-process. Star light Making in the open, in the shine of the cosmic latte This repository is public — every page, every tool, every error. The reason is one sentence of Brandeis's, and one colour that had to be corrected in public before anybody could use it. Average the light of two hundred thousand galaxies and you get a colour. It is a warm off-white, and somebody reading the newspaper over a coffee named it cosmic latte . That is the fact this page is named after, and it is not the interesting half. The interesting half is that the first answer was wrong, and the astronomers said so out loud.
The colour of the universe is a correction

The colour of the universe is a correction The colour was never the point. Ivan Baldry, Karl Glazebrook and the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey team were measuring the cosmic spectrum — the volume-averaged light of present-day galaxies — to constrain how fast the universe used to make stars. What colour that spectrum would look like to a human eye was a footnote . Footnote 3, to be exact, and you can still read the original on arXiv: “Integrating these through the cosmic spectrum we have computed RGB values of 0.269, 0.388, 0.342. This corresponds to a blue-green color, the closest match in standard RGB color lists… is ‘pale turquoise’.” Baldry, Glazebrook et al. · astro-ph/0110676 · footnote 3, as posted It travelled. The universe is turquoise is a lovely sentence and it went everywhere, which is how it reached Rochester, New York, and the desks of people who do colour for a living. They spotted the problem in the arithmetic that turns a spectrum into a colour: the software had been handed the wrong white point . A white point is the colour your eye has decided counts as white, and it is not a property of the light being measured — it is a property of where you are standing . Tungsten bulbs push it yellow. A monitor pushes it blue. The program had been set to a reddish white, and anything measured against a reddish white looks green by comparison. The galaxies had not moved. The observer had. Within weeks the team put out the correction themselves. Two sentences from Glazebrook in that announcement are the reason this page exists: “It's our fault for not taking the color science seriously enough. I'm very embarrassed.” “I don't like being wrong, but once I found out I was, I knew I had to get the word out.” Karl Glazebrook · Johns Hopkins University announcement, 13 March 2002 Corrected, the colour is a beige-white. NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day describes it with a care worth stealing: “a conditionally perceived shade of beige.” Not is beige. Conditionally perceived as beige — by an eye, adapted to a particular dark, standing somewhere. Then they ran a naming contest. Skyvory and univeige were among the entries. Cosmic latte won. The same spectrum, before and after the white point was corrected Two colour swatches side by side. On the left, the colour as first announced in January 2002: a pale turquoise, labelled with the paper's computed RGB values of 0.269, 0.388 and 0.342, and its footnote's name, pale turquoise. An arrow runs from left to right labelled "white point corrected", noting that the software had assumed a reddish white and that the galaxies did not move, the observer did. On the right, the colour as published in March 2002: a warm off-white, hex FFF8E7, named cosmic latte. Beneath both: same spectrum, same two hundred thousand galaxies, different observer. one spectrum, two white points announced · jan 2002 pale turquoise rgb 0.269 0.388 0.342 footnote 3, still on the preprint white point corrected the software assumed a reddish white published · mar 2002 cosmic latte #fff8e7 the correction, in public same spectrum. same 200,000 galaxies. the galaxies did not move. the observer did. a colour is a relation between light and somebody looking at it Figure 1 · the retracted colour and the published one, and the knob between them Marking the rung #FFF8E7 is not a constant of nature. It is one sRGB rendering of a colour that only exists relative to an observer — which is the same thing the astronomers said, in the words “conditionally perceived.” The sample is around two hundred thousand galaxies in one survey's volume, not every star there is. And the colour moves : APOD notes the cosmic spectrum has grown much less blue over the past ten billion years as redder stars became more common. We are painting this page in it anyway, and saying all of that out loud, because a simplification is honest exactly where it marks where it stops . So the most-shared fact about the colour of the universe is an erratum . The reason anyone can trust the number is that the people who got it wrong put the correction where the mistake had been, under their own names, before the journal version went out. It cost Glazebrook an afternoon of being embarrassed in public and it bought everyone since a usable answer. That is the entire argument for working in the open, and it happens to be lit in the exact colour we are borrowing.
“Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants”

“Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants” The line everybody quotes is Louis D. Brandeis's, from a Harper's Weekly essay of 20 December 1913 that became chapter five of Other People's Money and How the Bankers Use It . Two things go missing every time it is repeated, and both are worth having back. “Publicity is justly commended as a remedy for social and industrial diseases. Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants; electric light the most efficient policeman.” Louis D. Brandeis · “What Publicity Can Do” · Harper's Weekly, 20 December 1913 The first missing piece is the second clause. Sunlight and electric light are doing two different jobs — one kills what is already there, the other deters what would otherwise arrive. A public changelog is sunlight: it cleans up what we already got wrong. A public repository is the electric light: it changes what we are willing to write in the first place, because somebody can read the diff. The second missing piece is smaller and, for a project with a fact-checking ethic , more interesting. Brandeis did not write sunlight is the best of disinfectants . He wrote “is said to be.” He was passing on a proverb and marking it as one. The most quoted sentence in the literature of transparency is itself hedged by its author, and the hedge is the first thing a century of quoting filed off.

What “open” means here, in nouns Open is a word that survives being meant loosely, so here it is as a list of things that exist and can be checked. Every one of these is in the same public git repository as the pages themselves, at the same commit. the artifact, and where its working is kept what you can read where the working is 115 pages — zines, field guides, broadsides, essays the repository, and every revision of every one of them the claims FACTCHECK.md — 114 pieces logged, 122 items VERIFIED , 24 CORRECTED , 19 PLAUSIBLE , 1 REMOVED the errors the changelog — 21 dated releases, 169 entries, 50 of them fact-checks , each naming what was wrong, what is right, and who caught it the reasoning DECISIONS.md , plus the design system and the print rationale as public pages the checking tools/ — six gates, about 2,850 lines, runnable by anyone with a browser and Node the search search-index.json , a committed build artifact — 1,270 records across 114 pages the licence CC BY-SA 4.0. Print it, copy it, hand it to somebody One thing is deliberately closed, and it belongs in the same list. Search runs entirely in your browser against that committed index. There is no server to send a query to, no analytics on it, and no log of it anywhere. We are open about our work; we are not curious about yours. Openness that only ever flows one way — institutions private, readers observed — is the ordinary arrangement, and inverting it is the point.

The machines Six automated gates check this site. None of them was planned. Every one exists because something shipped broken and a person found it — which turns out to be the most important sentence in this section, and we will come back to it. six gates · what each asks, and what made it necessary the gate the question the fault that created it contrast check-contrast.mjs What colour is it — on screen, and on paper? Browsers leave background graphics off by default, so a light-on-dark page prints blank. 44 of 46 pages did. Nobody noticed until somebody pressed print. markup check-markup.mjs What shape is the tag tree? Four links nested inside a link on a collection page. Anchors cannot nest, so the parser closed the outer one early and the cards came apart on the live site. collision check-overlap.mjs Where is it? One zine shipped with three pieces of text sitting on top of other text. All five other gates passed it , and none of them was wrong to. sheets check-sheets.mjs Does it fit the paper? A broadside describing itself on its own face as “a two-sided single sheet” printed as three sides on US Letter. sitemap check-sitemap.mjs Does the sitemap agree with the filesystem? A live zine, linked from the front page, that had never been listed — uncrawlable for weeks — and a broadside listed twice. search index build-search-index.mjs Is every word findable? A page whose text was indexed at 12% and which passed the coverage check, because the check counted records instead of measuring words. The gates are only half the story. What each failure taught is the other half, and those lessons are now the operating rules of this repository.

Measure, don't count The search indexer used to check its own work by counting records: did this page produce at least as many chunks as it has sections? One page has exactly three of the blocks it was chunking on, produced three records, and shipped 12% of its own text into the index looking perfectly healthy. Now every page's records are measured against that page's actual words, and anything under 90% gets re-segmented and a remainder record appended. The run prints a percentage per page, because a page that indexes an eighth of itself looks exactly like a clean one if all you print is a count.
Wait on a condition, never a clock

Wait on a condition, never a clock Two of these tools drive a headless browser, and both used to wait a flat 1.3 seconds for a page to render before reading it. That makes every run a race. On 11 August the indexer lost it: one build produced 629 records where the builds either side produced 637 — eight records and fifteen kilobytes of text gone, with exit code 0 and no warning. Now both tools wait for the page to stop changing, then read it twice and require the two reads to agree, and a page that never settles is a hard error rather than a quiet truncation. Removing the sleep also made the whole run faster, which is the usual reward for replacing a guess with a question.
A tool's worst failure is the page it didn't look at

A tool's worst failure is the page it didn't look at Zero failures out of zero elements measured looks exactly like a clean page. Worse: when a page silently drops out of a sweep, its failures leave the total, so the number goes down and reads as progress. So the contrast checker reports any page it could not measure as UNREAD , never as ok , counts those separately from the failures, and fails on them on their own terms before contrast is even considered. The same instinct runs through the rest. Where a check genuinely cannot answer — a heading painted with a clipped gradient has no single pair of colours to compare — it says unmeasured, check by eye rather than guessing. A tool reporting “I can't check this” is reporting a gap, not clearing it. That list once ran to 196 entries and was being read as a footnote — while 90 elements across 45 pages printed invisibly, including the site's own wordmark, so the front page came off the printer with no title on it. The tool had been saying look here the whole time.

Keep every baseline at zero All six gates sit at a baseline of zero, and that is a maintenance decision rather than a compliment to the code. The contrast gate stood at 110 failures on the morning of 13 August and was cleared that day. A gate that reports “110, same as yesterday” requires a human to remember yesterday's number; a gate at zero requires nothing. A green number you have to read past stops being read. Two more rules earned the same way. A check that has to be rebuilt is a check nobody runs — the contrast tool was written three separate times as a throwaway scratch script before anyone committed it. And a comment is a note, not a control : one zine's source carries a warning that anything drawn past a certain coordinate lands on the words. The warning was accurate, it was correct, it was right there, and it did not stop the next page from doing it. That is the whole difference between documentation and a gate.
The first honest run is the argument for the gate

The first honest run is the argument for the gate The collision checker's first real run over the finished site found seven pre-existing defects nobody had seen — four covers with a caption printed over the title, an unbreakable label overflowing its column onto the body text, and a shipped page where a reader was being shown “ight-years.” None of these was subtle. All of them had been live for weeks, on a site with five other automated checks and a fact-check ledger, being read by people.
What machines are good at, and what they are not

What machines are good at, and what they are not There is a name for the method these gates implement, and it is not ours. The previous essay takes it from Terry Pratchett: First Sight is seeing what is actually in front of you rather than what you expected; Second Thoughts are the thoughts that watch the first ones. Not doubt — supervision. Second Thoughts can be built. First Sight cannot. Which is the honest shape of every tool in tools/ . Look again at the table above and notice what it is a list of: six faults that a person found first. Not one gate anticipated the fault that created it. The sequence is always the same, and it does not reverse. How every gate in this repository came to exist Four steps in a row. First, a fault ships and nothing sees it. Second, a person notices — marked as the only step that cannot be automated. Third, a gate is written. Fourth, the gate holds that ground on every run afterwards. A return arrow runs from the fourth step back to the second, labelled: attention freed for the next thing nobody has noticed yet. Beneath: machines hold ground, people take it. a fault ships nothing sees it a person notices first sight a gate is written second thoughts it holds that ground every run, forever attention freed for the next thing nobody has noticed yet machines hold ground. people take it. It is a precise one, and it is what makes the machines worth having: a gate never has to notice the same thing twice, which means the noticing can move on. Two thousand eight hundred and fifty lines of checking code is two thousand eight hundred and fifty lines of attention that nobody has to spend again. the division of labour, stated honestly what a machine is good at what it structurally cannot do Exhaustive. 115 pages, 94,718 tags, 1,648 ids, 1,270 index records — every one, every run Notice that a beautiful pattern is doing your looking for you. It does not care how much you love a finding, or how long the draft took Decide a subject cannot take the apparatus. A repo-wide sweep can touch 66 pages in one pass and check all of them Be embarrassed. Which is what Glazebrook was, and it is the mechanism — the correction was published by the feeling, not by the arithmetic Repeatable. The same question, asked identically, on every commit Decide what is worth making at all , or who it is for, or what this project owes the people in it

Generative AI, said plainly This is the first page on this site to state it, which is itself a small failure of the openness it is arguing for. Generative AI facilitates a great deal of the work here — drafting, the gates and their output, index and sitemap maintenance, the ledger, source legwork, and the sweeps that touch every page at once. Star Stuff is, among other things, an experiment in whether that can be done in service to accessibility, accuracy and transparency rather than at their expense. So, in nouns, on both sides. what it does here, and what it is never allowed to do does does not Draft, revise, and build pages against a written house style Decide what is worth making, or what this project believes Run and extend the six gates; rebuild the search index; keep the sitemap and the chain honest Stand as a citation for anything, ever Do the legwork of finding primaries — fetch the paper, grep the out-of-copyright book, pull the preprint Be the last check on a quotation. A person reads the primary before it ships Maintain FACTCHECK.md and write the public changelog entries, including the ones about its own errors Be trusted about anything it merely recalls The rules constraining it are the ordinary house rules, applied without an exemption: aggregators are leads, not citations ; a quotation is traced to the book, essay, paper or talk; a paraphrase is never dressed as a quote; the check is logged before the piece ships. With one addition that exists specifically because of the machine — your own summary is an aggregator. A model's account of a source is a secondary source about that source, and it is not exempt from the rule just because it is the thing writing the sentence. Why the rule is shaped that way One collection here exists to separate science from three things that wear its clothes: pseudo-science, scientism, and the smoothed popular retelling — the version with every hedge filed off, because the tidy version travels further. A language model is, structurally, a machine for producing the third one : the fluent, confident, average account, at scale. That is an odd thing to build a fact-checked site with, and the answer is not to trust it more carefully. It is to make everything it produces answerable to something that is not it — a primary source, a gate that measures, and a person who reads the paper. The smoothing is exactly why the machinery had to be built. And the mechanism has already failed here, in a way worth publishing. This repository keeps a working-notes file that tells the AI how the site works. A sign-off sentence in those notes got absorbed as house voice, promoted to “our masthead,” and shipped in a zine — where it was quoted with the three words that repaired it removed, and then argued against. It had never been the masthead. It was a colophon on one zine, and it had corrected itself in the next breath. Ryan Boren caught it , and both the essay and the notes now say the same thing: context is not evidence. Working notes are a lead about the site, exactly like any other aggregator. That is one of three attribution errors published in the last week alone. Another credited five neurodivergent love locutions to a single person on the strength of a citation chain that led, at every step, back to our own pages — a closed loop with no primary at the bottom of it, in which the aggregator being over-trusted was us. The third credited an organisation where it owed a person: Betsy Selvam's byline was on the essay the whole time. Each is in the changelog with what was wrong, what is right, and who caught it. None was caught by a gate.

A public entity There is a reason a foundation whose subject is learning builds in the open rather than merely publishing when finished. Seymour Papert and Idit Harel gave it a name: constructionism , which takes constructivism's idea of learning as building knowledge structures and adds one condition. “…this happens especially felicitously in a context where the learner is consciously engaged in constructing a public entity, whether it's a sand castle on the beach or a theory of the universe.” Seymour Papert & Idit Harel · “Situating Constructionism,” in Constructionism, 1991 A public entity. Not a finished one — a public one, while it is being made. That condition is the whole of this page: the repository, the ledger, the tools, the errata and the changelog are not documentation of the learning, they are it. It is what the Stimpunks Learning Space practices, and this site is the foundation eating its own cooking rather than recommending a recipe. And it is why the errors are the most valuable thing in the repository. A private error log teaches one person, once. Fifty published fact-checks are a curriculum — in what a closed citation loop looks like, in how a hedge goes missing, in why the tidiest version of a story is the one to distrust. We would not have any of that if we had waited to be right. A knowledge garden is how star stuff comes to know itself. It cannot do that behind a login. Which lands where the self-portrait already had it, and where the essay before last put the observer: there is no view from nowhere, only an unstated view from somewhere. The astronomers' white point makes that literal. Every measurement carries an observer, and the honest thing to do with an observer is name them and show your working — which is the same reason the changelog says who caught each error, and the same reason this page says how it was made. Not: Not a claim that open equals accountable. Publishing a correction does not un-publish the error. People read the misattributed quote, printed the blank page, followed the citation loop. Sunlight disinfects; it does not undo. Not a claim that the gates make the site correct. Six gates at zero, 122 verified items, and we shipped three attribution errors last week. The gates measure colour, structure, position, paper, coverage and completeness. None of them can read. Not an argument that transparency substitutes for structure. Brandeis was arguing for publicity alongside regulation, not instead of it, and the sentence is regularly quoted by people who want the first without the second. Not an advertisement for AI. The honest summary is that a language model is a smoothing machine pointed at a project built to resist smoothing, and it earns its place here only under constraints that a human maintains and enforces. Take the constraints away and you get a fluent, confident, well-formatted version of exactly what this site exists to argue against. Not a claim that the machines caught the interesting things. Every gate here is downstream of a person noticing. The gate's value is that the noticing never has to happen twice — not that it happened at all. Not open-washing. Open is a licence, a repository, a runnable toolchain and a published error log, or it is a word in a footer. If any of the four goes away, so does the claim. Not everything. Your search query is yours and never leaves your browser, and there is no personal data in this repository. Open about the work is not the same as open about the people, and the second one is somebody else's business model.

The shorter version The average colour of the light in this universe is a warm off-white, and the first published value for it was wrong. It got fixed because two astronomers put their own erratum where their mistake had been, and because colour scientists who had nothing to do with the paper could see enough of the working to spot the flaw in it. That is the arrangement we are copying. The pages, the tools, the reasoning, the ledger and the errors are all in one public place, at the same commit, under a licence that lets you take them. The machines here are second thoughts made durable — they hold ground that a person already took, so the person can go and look at something new. And the looking is still ours, because it has to be. Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants. We work by the light of a colour that had to be corrected — in public, by the people who got it wrong, with everything shown. It makes no chlorophyll and does no photosynthesis; it glows waxy-white in deep shade, living entirely on carbon it siphons from mycorrhizal fungi that are themselves fed by trees. Botanists call it a myco-heterotroph, or epiparasite: a one-directional relationship, not a mutualism. Named plainly, it belongs here precisely because not every symbiosis is gentle, or even. That a living thing takes what it needs and returns nothing in kind is not a moral failing — it is how a forest floor works, and how mutual aid works too: to each according to need. Some seasons, some bodies, can only receive, and the network holds them anyway. No one earns belonging through output; no one is disposable for being, this season, a taker. There's a deeper rhyme, too. "Monotropa" means one turn — the same root as monotropism, the Autistic attention-style (Murray, Lesser & Lawson, 2005). Helen Edgar calls the ghost pipe "one of the most perfect botanical expressions of being monotropic": thriving in the dark others can't use, nourished through a hidden mycelial network of care. Her essay Monotropa uniflora and Monotropism is written in tribute to Dinah Murray, who named monotropism and spent her last years studying the very fungi that feed this ghost. Energy is only transformed, never gone. it falls back in 45 Star Stuff The Cloud Phase on the last stage of a supernova remnant, and how long the in-between actually lasts after Helen Edgar · a cloud, not a waiting room L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely

The cloud phase Astronomy already named it A big star does not simply stop. It explodes, and what is left is called a remnant — the star's own material, thrown outward at thousands of kilometres a second. The version most of us were handed ends about one step past that. The shell expands, thins, cools, and disperses into the interstellar medium. Fade out. The star is finished, and the sentence is finished with it. But the physics runs further than the sentence does, and there is another word waiting at the end of it. In 2024 Leonard Romano, Manuel Behrendt and Andreas Burkert followed remnants through their long cold decline in three-dimensional simulation. They found the late evolution divides into four stages — and the one at the end they call the cloud phase. Not the end phase. Not the dispersal phase. The cloud phase — a named, described, modelled stage of a remnant's life. Romano, Behrendt & Burkert · ApJ 965, 168 · 2024 That is the whole reason this zine exists. We did not go looking for a metaphor and bend the astronomy to fit it. The astronomers got there first and wrote the word down. What is left of a dead star is understood as a cloud, studied as a cloud, and given a stage of its own in the literature. Held as proposed, not as settled. Romano et al. is a 2024 hydrodynamic simulation study, not textbook consensus, and the four-stage subdivision is their result. It may be revised. We are flagging that here, in place, the way this collection flags the wood wide web — and nothing later in this zine leans on it. The argumentative weight sits on spread five, which is an observation. Where the usual story stops A remnant's life shown as four boxes — free expansion, Sedov-Taylor, radiative, cloud phase. A marker shows the popular account ending after the third box, while the literature carries on to the fourth. freeexpansion Sedov–Taylor radiative cloudphase where the retelling stops and it keeps going the last stage has a name Romano et al., 2024 · proposed Figure 1 · the word at the end of the sentence The Cloud Phase · Stimpunks

It falls back in The shell comes back The intuitive picture of a remnant is a bubble that just keeps growing until it is too thin to see. Outward, all the way down. That is not what the simulations do at the end. Romano and colleagues find four stages inside the radiative phase: the radiative phase, subdivided stage what happens pressure-driven snowplow the hot, overpressured bubble inside is evacuated and pushed into the cold shell momentum-conserving snowplow nothing is driving it any more; the shell coasts and broadens implosion cold material from the back of the shell floods into the central vacuum cloud phase the infalling gas settles as a central, compact overdensity The third stage is the turn. Once the shell is no longer being pushed from behind, and the pressure inside has fallen to match the pressure of the medium outside, nothing is holding the cavity open. So the remnant falls back into itself. The collapse inward is not the failure of the expansion. It is the next thing the remnant does. stage three of four And what settles in the middle is not thin leftover. In these simulations it is highly chemically enriched, can reach a thousand to ten thousand solar masses, and can become self-gravitating within a few million years — which the authors call an attractive, novel pathway for supernova-induced star and planet formation. The timescales are long. The implosion takes a few hundred thousand to a few million years to launch. The cloud takes a few million to about ten million more to form. Nothing here is quick, and nothing here is idle. Grains that did not exist before

The debris makes new material Grains that did not exist before On 23 February 1987 a star exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, close enough to see with the naked eye. It was the nearest supernova since 1604, and we have been watching it continuously ever since. In 2014 ALMA resolved the millimetre emission from the middle of that remnant and measured what was sitting there: at least 0.2 solar masses of dust — the largest mass then measured in any supernova remnant — concentrated at the centre, in the cold inner ejecta, not yet reached by the reverse shock. Later work with Herschel and further ALMA data puts the cold dust nearer half a solar mass. Here is the part worth sitting with. That dust is new. Silicate and carbon grains condensed out of the cooling wreckage, assembled from atoms forged in the star's last seconds and in the explosion itself. Before the star died, that material did not exist in that form anywhere. The debris field is not where things end up. It is where the next material gets made — not after the wreckage, but in it. SN 1987A, thirty-odd years in Dust is not incidental, either. It is what lets a cloud cool, what shields molecules from starlight, what eventually accretes into rock. The grains in your bones were made in places like this. Some fraction of them, in something's ejecta, in some galaxy's slow afterwards. What is contested here. The ≥0.2 M☉ measurement is the firm floor; the total, the composition, and the timing are still argued. Sarangi & Cherchneff and Dwek & Arendt find silicate-dominated dust forming early; Wesson et al. find carbon-dominated dust forming mostly after day 1500. And how much of it survives the reverse shock over the coming millennia is genuinely open. We are using the floor, not the ceiling. Most of a cloud never becomes a star

Ninety-two percent stays cloud Most of a cloud never becomes a star This is the middle of the argument, and it is not a simulation. It is a measurement. In 2011 Norman Murray took the thirteen most luminous free-free radio sources in the Galaxy — responsible for a third of the Milky Way's free-free emission — matched them to their host giant molecular clouds, and asked how much of each cloud had actually been turned into stars. The star formation efficiency ran from 0.002 to 0.2, with an ionizing-luminosity-weighted average of 0.08. Eight percent. In the most vigorously star-forming clouds in the Galaxy — the bright ones, the ones you would pick deliberately if you wanted star formation to look efficient — ninety-two percent of the cloud does not become a star. And that is the flattering figure. Murray gives the Galactic average efficiency as 0.005. Ninety-two percent is the number from the clouds chosen for being the most productive. Galaxy-wide, more than ninety-nine percent of a molecular cloud stays cloud. Murray · ApJ 729, 133 · 2011 Read that as a shortfall and you have read it wrong. There is no rate the cloud is failing to hit. Nobody set a target. There is no efficient cloud somewhere, meeting expectations, against which these are underperforming. Ninety-two percent is not what the cloud failed to do. It is what a cloud is. What a cloud turns into Two bars. The first, for the Milky Way's most productive clouds, shows eight percent becoming stars and ninety-two percent staying cloud. The second, the Galactic average, shows half a percent becoming stars. the most productive clouds 8% 92% stays cloud the Galactic average 0.5% 99.5% stays cloud gold is the part that lights Murray, ApJ 729, 133, 2011 Figure 4 · the argumentative centre The Cloud Phase · Stimpunks

So the in-between is not the short part The long condition The same paper measures the other half of it: how long a giant molecular cloud lasts. 27 ± 12 million years, at the mean mass of that sample — a bit less than three free-fall times. Tens of millions of years of being a cloud. And the bright episode inside that span is short, late, and terminal: Murray finds the luminous clusters in his sample are actively tearing their host clouds apart. The star formation does not crown the cloud's life. It ends it. So the arithmetic runs the opposite way from the story we get told. Put the two measurements side by side and the shape is unmistakable: The bright part is brief and it destroys the cloud. The cloud part is long, and it is nearly all of what there is. two numbers from one paper Which means the in-between is not the gap between the real states. It is the majority state — by mass, and by duration — and the luminous thing is the exception that terminates it. We are not offering that as consolation, and it would be a weaker piece if we were. It is simply what the measurements say. The refusal to rush this to a bright resolution is not editorial restraint. It is the data. A discrepancy worth naming. The arXiv preprint of Murray (2011) gives cloud lifetimes as 17 ± 4 Myr and “about two free-fall times”; the published ApJ version says 27 ± 12 Myr and “a bit less than three.” We cite the published paper, which is the version of record — and we are telling you the preprint disagrees, because you may go and find it. Remnants entangled in new ways Re-assembly, not return Helen Edgar names this stage from the inside, and she named it before we went looking for the physics.
