What seeded us is unsettled Something nearby was freshly dead Our own solar system began in a cloud, and there is a fingerprint of what was in it. In 1976 Typhoon Lee, Dimitri Papanastassiou and Gerald Wasserburg found an excess of magnesium-26 in calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions in the Allende meteorite — the decay product of aluminium-26, which has a half-life of about 717,000 years. That half-life is the entire argument. 26Al is made in massive stars. For its decay product to be locked into the oldest solids in the solar system in that quantity, live 26Al had to arrive in our birth cloud within a few half-lives of those solids forming. Something nearby, and freshly dead, was in the material we are made of. Fifty years on, which something is openly contested: candidate sources — none settled candidate the problem it solves, and the one it leaves a nearby supernova the classic account; makes 26Al readily — but should have delivered plenty of 60Fe with it a massive star's wind a Wolf–Rayet star sheds 26Al from its outer layers before exploding, keeping 60Fe locked inside ordinary enrichment no triggering event at all; the accumulated ash of countless earlier stars in the interstellar medium Tang and Dauphas measured the early solar system's 60Fe in 2012 and found it steady and low — around 1 × 10−8 relative to 56Fe. A nearby supernova should have brought both isotopes. The missing iron is why a wind is now a serious contender. That dead stars' material is in us is not in doubt. Which star, and by what route, is not settled — and we are not going to pick one to make the ending tidier. The contested part gets its name, out loud, on the last page. Not:burnout as a secret gift. Nothing here says the collapse was good for us, or that we needed it. A supernova is a catastrophe for the star. What follows is not a reward for it. Not:the phoenix. That bird comes back as itself. A remnant does not — the material persists and the arrangement does not, and pretending otherwise is how people get asked to be who they were. Not:a promise that the cloud becomes a star. Ninety-two percent of it doesn't, and galaxy-wide it is more than ninety-nine. We will not sell the odds as an assurance. Not:an argument for rushing to the bright thing. The bright part is short and it disrupts the cloud. Wanting it sooner is wanting the end sooner. Not:reorganisation read as individual deficit. The trigger is the surroundings. A cloud collapses because of the field it is in, and so does a person; ask what the pressure is before you diagnose the thing under it. Not:one triggering supernova, asserted. We would like to end on a single dead star that made us. The evidence does not support naming it, so we haven't. Why a council The cosmos convenes Carl Sagan said it plainly: the calcium in our bones, the iron in our blood, forged in stars that died before the Earth was born. But the same is true of the soil under the city, the water in the river, the beaver and the cuckoo and the meadow. Every being at the table is star stuff. The Council of All Beings is a ritual from deep ecology, developed by Joanna Macy and John Seed: for an afternoon, humans set down the human mask and speak on behalf of another being — a mountain, a wolf, a river. Read cosmically, it isn't make-believe. It's the universe convening with itself, in all the forms it has learned to take. And that reframes everything downstream. You cannot rank what you are made of. Kinship here is not a metaphor — it's an inventory of shared atoms. The council is the universe convening with itself — the same star stuff, gathered in all the forms it has learned to take. one forge C · O · H Ca · Fe human beaver cuckoo river meadow same forge, different form every seat is star stuff The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

justice count recognition be heard participation exist & act capabilities fair share distribution four questions for every being the agenda of a real council The seating chart Mere service providers The trouble is the seating chart we inherited. Modern planning treats the more-than-human world as a set of service providers — nature valued for what it yields to us, a resource rather than a relation. Repeated everywhere, that one move is a root of the socioecological crisis (Harms et al., 2025). Multispecies justice turns the resource back into a party with standing. It asks four plain questions of any being: can it count (recognition), can it be heard (participation), can it exist and act (capabilities), does it get a fair share (distribution)? These aren't abstractions. They're the agenda for a council that actually means to seat everyone. The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks
Difference in how, not just what

Ethodiversity Difference in how, not just what Biodiversity counts the kinds of life. But a subtler variety is nested inside it: not just what lives, but how it lives. Ombre Tarragnat calls this ethodiversity — the variety of "ways of being and behaving" across all animals — extending a term coined in ecology by Adolfo Cordero-Rivera. The migratory route, the dialect of a birdsong, the nocturnal life, the whole existential style of a creature. Its shadow is ethonormativity: the unwritten rule about which behaviours are allowed to count as acceptable. The horse who refuses the rider, the cat who won't be petted — abandoned, or worse, for departing from the expected script. A grid laid over a field that was already full of variation. So justice has to protect more than a list of species. It has to protect their ways of being. Star stuff varies in matter — and in manner. The council seats not just the beaver, but the beaver's way of being a beaver. The cosmos varies not only in what it makes, but in how its creatures live. the table SOIL BEAVER CUCKOO RIVER MEADOW a role card for every voice you argue the world from there Participation · the method Speak as the soil, the river How do you give a being a seat when it can't pull up a chair? You speak as it. In multispecies role-play — the method behind the guide Speaking as a River — people take the part of the soil, the beaver, the cuckoo, the meadow, and argue the world from there. One role card simply reads: "You are the Soil — without you, nothing works here." Good councils run on a few principles (after Artmann): each being is a relating subject with agency, not an object; each has a right to its own voice; each has value in itself, not only in use; and the exchange is reciprocal — giving and taking on equal terms, the old hierarchy set down. It's a rehearsal for a wider "we" — a room where the beaver's right to stay is something you answer to, not around. The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

The hard part Who speaks, and how A borrowed voice carries a real hazard: speaking for a being can slide into speaking over it. A human voicing the river is, honestly, a human guess — shaped by human wants. Philosophical ethology offers a discipline for it. Vinciane Despret asks that we pose the questions that matter to the animal, not only to us; Jakob von Uexküll called each creature's lived world its Umwelt — the meadow a tick senses is not the meadow you see. The task is to enter that world, as far as you can, before you presume to represent it. Listen long. Represent second. Notventriloquism — a borrowed voice is a responsibility, not a costume. TE AWA TUPUA the river · a legal person the water runs through us all standing, not service the river flows through the room Distribution · standing A real seat, not a favour The ritual points toward real governance. Under Rights of Nature, some rivers and forests now hold legal standing. Aotearoa New Zealand recognised the Whanganui River as a legal person — Te Awa Tupua — with appointed guardians who speak in its name. Projects like the Interspecies Council rehearse the same shift: governing with the more-than-human world, not merely about it. And the river was never only "out there." In Astrida Neimanis's hydrofeminism, we are all bodies of water — rain, river, and blood passing through one another. The water in you has been the sea; it will be the cloud. Coda Already in flow Not every convening needs a chair. The council seats us — star stuff at a table, taking turns to speak. But water never waited for an invitation to convene. It was already in flow before anyone sat down: sea to cloud, cloud to rain, rain to river, river to blood, blood to rain again — one long convening that never adjourns. Maybe that's the truer shape of the thing. Not a table with seats around it, but a flow with all of us already in it — no head of the table, no order of speaking, just the same water finding its way through every body it passes. Inheritance Their ending, our beginning A star's death is not only a loss. It is a dispersal. The heavy elements a star forges — the calcium, the iron — are flung out when it dies, drift for ages, and gather again into planets, and bodies, and us. We are made of dead stars. Not as a metaphor: the atoms in our bones were forged in stars that died before the Earth existed. Their ending is the reason we are here to look up at all. Ancestors work the same way. What they made — the free spaces, the strategies, the words — scattered outward when they were gone, and gathered into us. We don't start the fire. We catch its light. Forgetting is a tool of white supremacy. Memory is the work. The debt runs one way Lit by a room we can't be thanked for Forgetting isn't neutral. What in your community's memory is going dark for lack of tending, and what would it take to keep it? Who belongs in your register that no one has named yet? Will you add them? The Dead Stars Still Reach Us is the tenth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the one about ancestry — the astronomy underneath our writing on memory and lineage. The astronomy is real, and worth stating precisely. Light travels at a finite speed, so we always see a star as it was when its light departed, never as it is now. It's often said that "the stars you see are already dead" — in truth, most naked-eye stars are still shining, because they sit tens to hundreds of light-years away, far less than a star's lifetime. The deeper, exact point is that we can never see any star's present, so we live by light from sources we cannot check — and some of them, especially distant ones, are indeed already gone. SN 1006 is the vivid case: observers worldwide recorded the supernova in the spring of 1006 CE; the star lay roughly 7,200 light-years off, so the explosion itself happened millennia before anyone on Earth saw it, and only its expanding remnant — and its scattered elements — remain (this is the "Liberating Star Stuff" image Stimpunks keeps). Betelgeuse, about 550 light-years away, will end as a supernova; if it exploded today we would not know for roughly five centuries, and it may already have gone. The ancestry is drawn from our own writing. The Highlander Folk School crosswalk reads the school (founded 1932 by Myles Horton; Septima Clark's citizenship schools; Rosa Parks, 1955; Aldon Morris's "movement halfway house") as ancestry rather than parallel — via Nico Slate's 2022 history. Story: Maintaining the Continuity of Creation gathers Tyson Yunkaporta's "deep time diligence" (from Emergence Magazine) on story outlasting fragile data, and Audre Lorde on the historical amnesia that makes each generation reinvent the wheel. "Cult of Compliance" and "broken systems, not broken people" are Stimpunks canon. Quotations carried in full, with gratitude: Ira Socol, "We build on each other's work — as good revolutionaries always do"; and Cara Page & Erica Woodland, Healing Justice Lineages (North Atlantic Books, p. 32). "Forgetting is a tool of white supremacy. Memory is the work." is our formulation of the latter. The reading — that starlight and ancestry are the same debt, inheritance owed forward — is ours. How knowledge grows The garden, not the stream Most of the web is a social stream: a feed of dated posts, sorted by an algorithm, urgent for a day and then washed away. A post starts decaying the moment it's published. You don't return to it; you scroll past it. A garden is the older idea. Mike Caulfield drew the line: the garden is the web as space, an arrangement you can walk. It's evergreen — you keep tending and refining the notes — and richly cross-linked, so that, as Maggie Appleton puts it, every walk creates new paths. You add things not in sequence but so they can form future, unpredicted relationships. The Star Stuff site is a garden. So is the whole knowledge garden it grew from. Not a feed to keep up with — a landscape to wander. A stream tells you what's new. A garden lets you wander what's true. hierarchy subjects → articles rhizome sideways, not up grown from lived experience a mesh, not a ladder roots down in real life Lived experience Grown from the ground up An encyclopedia grows downward from the top: subjects, then categories, then articles, handed down by an authority. A garden grows the other way. Ours climbs up from the soil of lived experience — from what a body knows, to a word for it, to a pattern, a recipe, an environment, a system. And it doesn't grow in straight lines. Its shape is a rhizome and a mycelial network (after Deleuze & Guattari): ideas spread sideways and underground, throwing up shoots where they connect, refusing the neat trunk-and-branches of the tree. Knowledge grown up from the ground of real neurodivergent and disabled life — not lowered down onto it. An encyclopedia is handed down from the top. A garden grows up from the ground. The cosmic turn Star stuff, knowing itself Here is the reason it's a garden and not a vault. Carl Sagan said we are a way for the cosmos to know itself. A knowledge garden is that sentence built into a thing you can walk through — and the method it uses is the cosmos's own. A star forges the elements in its core and then, dying, scatters them — a supernova is a seed-head bursting (the image on every Stimpunks page, SN 1006, is literally liberated iron). That scattered stuff settles into life; life grows minds; minds grow gardens of meaning that go to seed and grow new minds. Nucleosynthesis, then the periodic table — the first seed catalogue — then us. So the universe doesn't know itself as stored data. It knows itself as a garden — by growing, connecting, and seeding, over and over. The reflex It arrives before you do You know the feeling. It gets there ahead of you. Something on a screen, something in a jar, something in a documentary about the deep sea — and before a single thought has formed, the whole body has already voted. The face does its thing. Before we go any further Two icks, not one There is a distinction the research makes, and an earlier version of this zine walked straight past it. It matters enormously, so it goes here, before the argument. Paul Rozin's own framework separates two things that both feel like "ew." Distaste is sensory. It is a response to the actual properties of a thing — bitter, sour, slimy, sticky, cold and wet in the wrong way. And it is there from the beginning. Put something bitter on a newborn's tongue and you get the gape face: mouth open, upper lip pulled back, nose wrinkled, brow down. It is highly conserved across species. It has been observed in humans in utero. And then the finding that settles how deep it runs. In 1973 Jacob Steiner published observations of the gustofacial response in anencephalic newborns — infants born without most of the higher brain. They make the face too. The response does not require a cortex. It isn't a judgement, it isn't an attitude, and it cannot be a prejudice, because there is nothing there to hold one. Disgust proper is a different animal. Rozin calls it ideationally based and contamination-sensitive: you don't have to taste a cockroach to be disgusted by one. It attaches to ideas about things — where they have been, what they touched, what they count as. This zine is about the second one. Everything that follows — the borders, the projections, the sorting of bodies — is the ideational kind doing political work. The sensory kind is not a prejudice and never was. You were never a blank slate. You arrived with a body that already had positions on the world, and that gape is older than our species — history, carried in you. Which is, after all, the premise of this entire collection. The correction on this spread is Helen Edgar's, who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years and pointed out that the first version of this zine presumed a thinking response to the ick — and that the babies and the young people she has worked with plainly have one without it. two responses, both called "ew" distaste the gape face present at birth no cortex needed disgust where has it been? ideational contamination-sensitive develops later not a prejudice never was does border work this zine is about this one rozin · steiner 1973 · gustofacial response distaste is bodily · disgust is ideational only one of them can be a prejudice The Ick · Stimpunks

Where it came from The second one gets taught The gape was there at birth. The contamination logic was not, and small children are famously unbothered by it. Paul Rozin and April Fallon, in a 1987 paper that still anchors the field, treat disgust as a food emotion at root — revulsion at the prospect of taking something into the mouth. Its objects are overwhelmingly of animal origin. And crucially, this kind develops, arriving across a child's first eight years or so rather than being present at the start. They also describe what it runs on. Disgust obeys the laws of sympathetic magic — including the law of contagion, under which contact transfers an essence. A cockroach touches your sandwich; the sandwich is now inedible. Not partly inedible where the legs went. All of it. Forever. Sit with that, because it's the whole argument in one move: the reaction is out of all proportion to any physical fact. No amount of chemistry explains the whole sandwich. What's operating is a rule about categories and contact — and rules about categories are things a culture teaches you. Which means the border can be redrawn. People do it constantly, in both directions, without noticing. Somebody, somewhere, feeds their child something you would gag on, and their child grows up finding it delicious and finding your dinner revolting. Both of you think you are perceiving. the law of contagion edible one touch ALL of it inedible and it arrives on a schedule birth ~4 yrs ~8 yrs unbothered fully installed rozin & fallon 1987 · it was taught a rule about categories not a measurement of danger The Ick · Stimpunks

Exhibit one The worm with no mouth In 2004 Greg Rouse, Shana Goffredi and Robert Vrijenhoek named a genus that shouldn't work. Osedax — the name means bone-devourer — lives on whale skeletons on the deep sea floor. The adult females have no mouth and no gut at all. What they have instead is a root system: a branching, blood-supplied network that grows down into the bone, carrying symbiotic bacteria that break the bone down from inside. The animal doesn't eat. It roots, like something between a worm and a small tree, into the skeleton of something enormous that died above it. And the males never grow up. Dozens of them — tiny, paedomorphic, arrested partway through development — live inside the female's own tube, doing the one job they are there for. Every clause of that is a small horror in English, and not one of it is a problem. It is a lineage that found a food source nobody else could reach, and built a body that could get at it. Read from inside, it's just competent. You are not looking at a violation. You are looking at somebody's job. What it costs to never let go

Exhibit two What it costs to never let go The deep-sea anglerfish is the one everybody has heard about, usually told as a joke. A male, far smaller than the female, finds her in the dark, bites on, and fuses. Tissues join. The two circulatory systems merge into one. He never leaves. It is the only case in nature of two vertebrates becoming, permanently, a single joined body. Here is the part that isn't a joke, and it is the reason this zine exists. In 2020 Jeremy Swann, Stephen Holland, Malte Petersen, Theodore Pietsch and Thomas Boehm looked at the genomes and found what the fusion cost. Species whose males attach temporarily have lost functional aicda — the gene behind antibody maturation. Species whose males attach permanently go further, some losing functional rag genes altogether, which abolishes the somatic shuffling of antigen receptors that is the defining hallmark of adaptive immunity. Your immune system's entire job is telling you from not-you, and rejecting the not-you. So: To be permanently joined to another body, they gave up the machinery that draws the line between self and other. They did not solve rejection. They dismantled the thing that rejects. The border you are so sure of is a piece of equipment. It can be traded. Somebody did. attachment, and what it costs temporary lost: aicda no antibody maturation permanent lost: aicda + rag no receptor shuffling — adaptive immunity gone the immune system's job: self | not-self to stay joined, they gave up the line swann, holland, petersen, pietsch & boehm 2020 science, 2020 · immunogenetics of sexual parasitism the price of never letting go The Ick · Stimpunks
A body that becomes a town

Exhibit three A body that becomes a town Nothing triggers the reflex like a corpse. So let's take the biggest one there is. A whale dies and sinks. Down there, food arrives as a slow drizzle of scraps from far above — and now, all at once, forty tonnes of it lands in one place. Craig Smith and Amy Baco, reviewing the whole field in 2003, put the scale plainly: the sediment beneath a sunken carcass gets an initial pulse of organic matter equivalent to roughly 2,000 years of the normal background supply. Then a town builds itself, in three overlapping stages. Months to years. The mobile scavengers — sleeper sharks, hagfish, rat-tails — strip soft tissue at 40 to 60 kilograms a day. Months to years. Enrichment opportunists move onto the enriched sediment and the exposed bones: dense assemblages of polychaetes and crustaceans, up to 40,000 animals per square metre. Decades. The sulphophilic stage. Bone lipids break down without oxygen and give off sulphide; bacteria make a living out of the sulphide; a large, trophically complex community assembles on top of that. Smith and Baco report a mean of 185 macrofaunal species on a large skeleton at this stage — higher local diversity than any other hard surface in the deep sea. Across the world's whale falls, 407 species. Twenty-one of them are known from nowhere else on Earth. The thing you were taught was the end of a body is, down there, one of the most generous events that ever happens. 185 mean macrofaunal species on one large skeleton 21 species known from nowhere else one carcass, three stages, decades 1 · mobile scavengers sleeper sharks · hagfish · rat-tails — 40–60 kg/day months–years 2 · enrichment opportunists polychaetes · crustaceans — up to 40,000 per m² months–years 3 · sulphophilic bone lipids → sulphide → chemoautotrophs mean 185 macrofaunal species DECADES ≈ 2,000 years of background food, at once smith & baco 2003 decay is a construction schedule the richest hard surface down there The Ick · Stimpunks
What the ick was actually measuring

The turn What the ick was actually measuring Go back over the three of them and ask what they had in common. It wasn't danger — none of them can hurt you. It wasn't dirt — the deep sea is one of the cleanest places on the planet. What they share is distance from one particular body plan. Mouths belong on faces. Bodies end at the skin. The dead are separate from the living. Eating is done with a gut. These aren't laws of nature. They are the specifications of one animal, generalised into a template — and the ick is what fires when something falls outside it. That template has two settings, and this collection has been picking at both: Anthronormative — the assumption that the human arrangement is the correct arrangement for a body. Neuronormative — the assumption that one kind of mind is the correct kind, and other kinds are that kind gone wrong. Same machine, two dials. Both take a local arrangement and file everything else as a deviation from it. distance from a template one template Osedax anglerfish whale fall the ick tracks radius · nothing else anthronormative one right body neuronormative one right mind same machine, two dials a local arrangement, promoted to a standard The Ick · Stimpunks
The same reflex, aimed at us

Where it lands The same reflex, aimed at us Now the part this zine was actually written for. That reflex — the one that fires at a rooted worm and a fused fish — does not stay in the ocean. It gets pointed at people, and it does an enormous amount of work. It fires at a feeding tube. At drooling. At an adult in incontinence pads. At a stim that isn't the socially cleared kind — the loud one, the wet one, the one with hands. At a communication device that speaks in a voice somebody decided was unpleasant. At bodies that need help with the parts of being alive that everyone has agreed to pretend are private. Nobody says disgusting out loud. They don't have to. The reflex does its work in the face, in the half-step back, in the seat that stays empty, in the invitation that doesn't come, in the tone of the assessment paperwork. Martha Nussbaum gave this its name in 2004: projective disgust. We take what we cannot stand about being animal — that we leak, decay, depend, and die — and we load it onto a group of people, who then function as a buffer between us and our own bodies. Push them out and the animal facts feel further away. Which is why the ick is not a matter of taste, and why we are not asking anyone to find worms charming. Disgust is how a border gets enforced without anyone having to defend it. It doesn't argue. It just refuses, and then it acts hurt if you ask it to explain. The reflex that ruled out the bone-eating worm is the reflex that empties the seat next to us. It never learned there was a difference. projective disgust, in one move what we can't stand about being animal: leaking · decaying · needing · dying loaded onto a group of people who then sit between us and the facts push them out → the animal feels further away it was never about them nussbaum, hiding from humanity, 2004 a buffer, made of people the ick is doing somebody's laundry The Ick · Stimpunks
Weird we took. Gross we haven't

Two words, two jobs Weird we took. Gross we haven't There's a word next door to this one, and it has already been reclaimed. In Wyrd & Weird, Helen Edgar follows weird back to Old English wyrd — becoming, fate, a web held from every side — and shows Autistic and disabled communities running the drift backwards, taking the word up as a name rather than a verdict. Weird is ours now. People wear it. Gross has not been taken, and it works differently. Weird is a judgement about categories: you don't fit the box. It can be answered with pride, because pride is also a claim about where you belong. Gross isn't a claim at all. It's a body refusing another body. You can't be proud at it, because it doesn't stay to listen — it has already turned away. So this one doesn't get reclaimed. It gets disarmed: shown to be learned, shown to be arbitrary, shown to be doing political work it never admitted to. You don't march under it. You just stop letting it decide who's in the room. two words, two jobs weird a claim about categories "you don't fit" answerable → RECLAIMED worn as a name gross a body refusing another body "get it away" unanswerable → DISARMED shown for what it is you can march under one of these the other you just take the keys off no. 28 took the first one this one gets disarmed instead The Ick · Stimpunks

Held with care What we are not saying This argument has several cheap versions. Naming them so we don't get mistaken for one. Not"actually it's beautiful." That just swaps one aesthetic verdict for another and keeps the judge's chair warm. The worm doesn't need to be pretty. It needs to be left alone. Not"gross but useful to humans." Hagfish slime is being studied for fibres; whale-fall bacteria for enzymes. Fine — but usefulness is the extraction frame, and the zine before this one is about where that leads. Notyour sensory aversion is a prejudice. If a texture, a smell, a sound or a wet thing on your hands sends you through the roof — that is distaste, it is bodily, and none of this argument is pointed at it. Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent sensory responses are real, they are not bigotry, and you do not owe anybody an apology or an exposure programme for them. Nota blank slate. We are not claiming you arrived with no positions on the world. You arrived with a nervous system that had plenty, and the oldest of them are older than our species. What is learned is the contamination logic laid over the top, not the body underneath it. Notdisgust is never useful. It plainly has a job — some of it tracks real contamination. The claim is narrower: its objects are learned, it overshoots wildly, and it should never be trusted as evidence about a person. Notyou're bad for feeling it. It was installed in you before you could consent. Nobody is guilty of a reflex. You are only answerable for what you do in the two seconds after. Notdisabled people are deep-sea creatures. We are not anyone's metaphor. The shared thing is the reflex and the border it draws — not the bodies on either side of it. Notbiology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. That the ocean is full of arrangements we find upsetting is not why people deserve welcome. Look again Nothing down there has changed Go back to the worm. It is still rooted in the bone. It still has no mouth. The males are still small and still in her tube. The Ick Is a Border is Zine No. 33 in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series. It is a house zine and a deliberate companion to Wyrd & Weird (28), Helen Edgar's guest zine on weird — the word this community did reclaim. Weird is hers and the reclamation is hers; this zine takes the neighbouring word, gross, which works differently and is disarmed rather than worn. It extends Every Nervous System (27) and The Council of All Beings (25) into the territory of disgust, and continues the account of constructed lines begun in The Lines We Drew (9). Written after The Skeleton That Skipped Bone (32), for the same young person, whose marine biology special interest is the reason both exist. Corrected after publication — and the correction is the important part. The first published version of this zine argued that the ick is learned, full stop. Helen Edgar, who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years, read it and pointed out that it presumes a cognitive, intellectualising response — and that pre-term babies, and the young people she has worked with, plainly have an ick without one. She is right, and the literature is unambiguous. Rozin's own framework separates distaste — a chemosensory rejection tied to a thing's actual properties, producing the highly conserved "gape face," present at birth and observed in utero — from disgust proper, which Rozin describes as ideationally based and contamination-sensitive, and which you can feel about a cockroach without tasting one. The strongest evidence for how deep the first one runs is Jacob Steiner's (1973) observations of the gustofacial response in anencephalic newborns, who produce it without most of a higher brain: the response does not require a cortex, and therefore cannot be an opinion. Spread 3 now makes that distinction before the argument starts, and the argument is explicitly scoped to the ideational kind. Helen's second point is the one that goes deepest and is now in the zine's own voice: we are not blank slates — that is the point of star stuff; we have history in us. A response conserved across species and present before birth is exactly that history, and the earlier draft was, in effect, arguing against this collection's own premise. Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent sensory aversion is distaste, not prejudice, and spread 11 now says so in a refusal. Sources & notes. The gustofacial response: observation on normal and anencephalic newborn infants. On disgust: Rozin, P. & Fallon, A. E. (1987). A perspective on disgust. Nussbaum, M. C. (2004). Hiding from Humanity: Disgust, Shame, and the Law. Princeton University Press — source of projective disgust, and of the account in which subordinated groups serve as buffers against the vulnerable animal nature we would rather deny. On Osedax: Rouse, G. W., Goffredi, S. K. & Vrijenhoek, R. C. (2004). Osedax: bone-eating marine worms with dwarf males. Science, 305(5684), 668–671 — females consuming whale bone through a vascularised root system, lacking a discrete trophosome, with numerous dwarf paedomorphic males living in the females' tubes. On the anglerfishes: Swann, J. B., Holland, S. J., Petersen, M., Pietsch, T. W. & Boehm, T. (2020). The immunogenetics of sexual parasitism. Science, 369(6511), 1608–1615 — genomes of species with temporarily attaching males lack functional aicda; permanent attachment is associated with further alterations "culminating in the loss of functional rag genes in some species, abolishing somatic diversification of antigen receptor genes, the hallmark of canonical adaptive immunity." On whale falls: Smith, C. R. & Baco, A. R. (2003). Ecology of whale falls at the deep-sea floor. Oceanography and Marine Biology: An Annual Review, 41, 311–354 — read in the primary; source of the three successional stages and their durations, of the sleeper sharks, hagfish and rat-tails removing soft tissue at 40–60 kg per day, of the enrichment-opportunist densities (up to 40,000 m⁻²), of the sulphophilic stage lasting decades with a mean of 185 macrofaunal species (higher than any other deep-sea hard substratum community), of the 407 species globally and 21 known only from whale falls, and of the ~2,000-year equivalent pulse of background organic-carbon flux to the underlying sediments. Held honestly. Rozin and Fallon's account is a theory of disgust, not the only one, and the claim made here is the modest one their evidence supports: the objects of disgust are substantially learned and culturally variable, and the response overshoots any physical fact. That some disgust responses track genuine pathogen risk is not disputed. The whale-fall figures are means and estimates from a review of a small, poorly sampled set of sites — Smith and Baco say so themselves — and should be read as order-of-magnitude. The anglerfish immune losses vary by species and are not uniform across the group; "gave up the line between self and other" is our phrasing of a genetic finding, and adaptive immunity is not the whole of self/non-self discrimination. A note on a familiar quotation: "dirt is matter out of place" is widely attributed to Mary Douglas's Purity and Danger (1966), and she did make it famous — but it is not her coinage. It appears unreferenced in her first edition and is credited in later editions to Lord Chesterfield without a source; the earliest located use is an 1853 address by Lord Palmerston. We have not used the line as hers, and neither should anyone else. Finally: the ethics do not come from the biology. That the ocean is full of arrangements we find upsetting is not why anyone deserves welcome — as about.html puts it, we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation — and it has never once found any of us disgusting. The Ladder We Don't Print ARLES is the Stimpunks Design Method — five layers of neurodivergent life in an order that has to hold. It is named here, and deliberately almost nowhere in the zines. A spread-by-spread map: the pair closest to the ladder, three more that climb it without being built to, two that sit on a rung and say so — and the four pieces that already name the method out loud, which is a fact this page has to hold rather than tidy away. What this is, and isn't This is a reading of our own work, and a reading can be argued with. Every rung label below was applied after the fact, by us, to pieces that were mostly not built with the ladder in hand. Nothing on this page was measured. The six gates in this repository can check a colour, a tag tree, a page count, a sitemap entry and a text collision; not one of them can check whether a spread is really about attention. The method was: read the spread eyebrows and headings of all sixty-two numbered zines , then read the candidates in full. That will have missed a piece that climbs quietly, and it may have over-read one that doesn't. If a mapping below looks wrong to you, it might be. And the survey has a date on it: sixty-two was the whole shelf on 23 August 2026, and the shelf has grown since — Nos. 63–72 have not been read against the ladder. That number is left as written rather than quietly raised, because raising it would claim a survey that did not happen. Stimpunks crosswalks other people's frameworks against ARLES — the ecosystemic model of distress , and Jessica Dark's System-Level Organisational Design Framework . This page turns the same instrument on our own shelf, which is a much easier exercise and worth much less. Finding your own method in your own artifacts is the least surprising result available. What it is good for is legibility: it tells a reader why the zines keep arriving at the room instead of the person.

The ladder, named once ARLES names five layers through which neurodivergent life is structured, and the order in which environments have to be redesigned to support it. Each layer holds up the one above it. A · Attention How a mind focuses, processes, and forms meaning. Monotropism lives here. This is the floor. R · Relational (incl. Regulation) Communication, co-regulation , consent. Regulation is relational and environmental, not an individual skill. L · Lived Experience The sensory, emotional and cognitive realities of a day. What it actually feels like to be in the room. E · Environment The conditions that shape participation. A space either fits a bodymind or fights it. S · Systems The structures, norms and institutions that distribute opportunity and constraint. Upward it is a design order · downward it is a diagnosis Read upward , it is a sequence for design: begin with attention and nervous-system safety, build shared language and co-regulation, name what people actually experience, redesign the environment, and only then move to systems. Read downward , it is a sequence for diagnosis: a failing system points to the environment that produced it, the environment to the lived experience it ignored, and on down to the attention it never accounted for. Skip the lower layers and systems reform collapses. That sentence is the whole reason the order is load-bearing rather than decorative, and it is why most reform fails: it starts at the top, rewrites the policy, and then asks people to cope. ARLES and the design method it belongs to are Stimpunks' own, published in the open — the glossary entry is the short form and the design method the long one.
Why the word stays off the spreads
Why the word stays off the spreads Three reasons, in the order they matter.
One · A named framework asks for assent before the argument does

One · A named framework asks for assent before the argument does A zine here works by taking one settled, checkable fact and following it honestly until the belonging claim is already inside it. The Moon runs the tide because tidal force falls off with the cube of distance. A hammer and a feather land together in vacuum. Bone under load makes a charge. The reader is not asked to agree to anything; they are asked to look. An acronym reverses that. It asks the reader to accept a five-part model of neurodivergent life first , and then the fact arrives as an illustration of the model — which is exactly the demotion the collection exists to refuse. The fact stops doing the work the moment it becomes an example.
Two · The rungs already have plain words

Two · The rungs already have plain words Attention. The people near you. What the day actually feels like. The room. Who set the rules. Every rung has an ordinary-language form that costs a reader nothing, and the zines already use them. A piece that says the storm is in the weather, not the water has delivered the Environment rung to someone who will never need the label. A piece that says when a feather falls slowly, look for the air has delivered the downward read.
Three · It is already the standing rule, written into a colophon

Three · It is already the standing rule, written into a colophon No. 59, The Rest You Keep , is the one zine built on the ladder deliberately, and its own colophon states the rule: Internally this zine is built on the ARLES ladder — attention, relational, lived experience, environment, systems — which is deliberately not printed on the spreads; the argument should stand without the scaffold. One precision, because the sentence is slightly generous to itself. What is withheld is the acronym, the diagram and the order-claim . The rung words are not withheld: five of them are printed on No. 59 as spread eyebrows, one per spread. That is the line, and it is the right line. A reader meets Attention as a heading over an argument about attention and loses nothing. They never meet a ladder they have to buy into.
The one the ledger says was built on it: No. 59

The one the ledger says was built on it: No. 59 The Rest You Keep runs the full ladder in order, one rung per spread, with the acronym absent. It is the only piece whose own colophon and ledger row both record the ladder as an internal structure — and it turns out not to be alone on the ladder, only alone in admitting it. Its companion is the next section. Its five rung spreads are interleaved with three animal-fact spreads, and the interleaving is the interesting part. 2 The finding. Hydra has no brain and sleeps anyway — and its cells stop dividing when you stop it. off-ladder · the fact 3 The tunnel, not the line. No circadian clock to free-run; a ~4-hour cycle, returning and returning. Rest as a shape attention takes. Attention 4 On the wing. Frigatebirds sleeping 42 minutes a day aloft. Rest is not the opposite of motion. off-ladder · the fact 5 Partial presence is real presence. Camera off, lurking, reading and not answering — absence is a claim about output, not about being there. Relational 6 No ramp, just the edge. Interoception arriving quiet or late, so the depletion never announces itself while it builds. Lived Experience 7 Six months, no load. The bear's skeleton holding its bone through hibernation, against everything disuse should do to it. off-ladder · the fact 8 Rest is a property of an arrangement. The den does a measurable job in the energy budget. Rest is something a setup affords, not something a body achieves. Environment 9 The debt that was never owed. The earning frame — rest released after enough output — named and refused. Systems 10 Held honestly. The refusals set. off-ladder · refusals Spreads 1 and 11 are the cover and the closing question, as on every zine. The off-ladder spreads are not gaps. They are what each rung is paid for with. Five consecutive rung spreads would be a slide deck: five assertions in a row, each asking to be believed on the strength of the one before it. Instead an animal arrives, does something checkable, and the rung it licenses follows immediately. The ladder is the spine; the facts are the ribs. One thing this page cannot settle, and should say so: the spread-by-spread structure of No. 59 is Helen Edgar's , from her Reclaiming Rest and Going Deeper , and the ARLES reading is recorded in the finished colophon. Who placed which rung where is not recoverable from the record here, and the piece does not need it to be.
Its companion, where the reading came first and the word never arrived

Its companion, where the reading came first and the word never arrived No. 58, The Stone You Keep is the same Saturday room as No. 59 — the Solidarity Sesh otter cam, developed after Helen Edgar — following the otters where its companion follows rest. Its proposal carried a rung-by-rung reading of the outline before the zine was built. And the finished page names ARLES nowhere : not on a spread, not in the colophon, not in a <meta> tag, not even in its own row in the ledger. Zero occurrences in the file. That makes it the best illustration on this page of the rule the page is arguing for, and better than No. 59: the rungs went in, the label never got as far as the page, and a reader cannot tell. 2 Nobody has to watch. Cameras mostly off, some speaking, some in text, some just there — and the fact that nobody has to watch is what makes it work. Relational 3 There is no standard otter. Under food limitation the population does not converge on one best way to be an otter. It fans out into specialists (Tinker, Bentall & Estes, 2008). Attention 4 The stone is not a metaphor. A stone kept on the chest and reused from one food item to the next — and the blow counts run 6 to 88, so the variance is the finding . Attention 5 Some otters never use a stone. Non-users are not the ones who haven't figured it out; they specialise on prey a stone wouldn't help with — and the accommodation shows up as tooth health (Law et al., 2024). Attention 6 What it costs to float. The most restful image available to a human being is thermodynamically a furnace. The calm surface is not the whole cost. Lived Experience 7 Anchored, and together. Rafts in the kelp canopy — and the kelp does the holding, not vigilance, not grip strength, not a sleeping animal working at staying put. Relational + Environment 8 The forest that holds you is the forest you hold. Islands with otters had kelp forest; islands without had urchin barrens (Estes & Palmisano, 1974). Presence is load-bearing. Environment 9 What they came for was the coat. A hundred and seventy years of fur trade, roughly 99% gone by 1911 — the trait that let the animal live in cold water is what made it a commodity. Plus the refusals. Systems Spread 1 is the cover, spread 10 the closing questions. The proposal ran to ten spreads with the fur trade and the refusals separate; the built page merged them into spread 9, so the rung numbers transfer without renumbering — which is worth checking rather than assuming, since a mapping quoted from a proposal against a shipped page is exactly the kind of figure that goes stale quietly. It does not climb cleanly, and the way it fails to is a third pattern. Every rung is present and the overall movement is upward, but Lived Experience and Relational are transposed — the cost of floating (6) arrives before the raft that holds you (7) — and spread 7 carries two rungs at once, because in an otter raft the relation is the environment: the kelp is what holds the animal, and the other otters are in the same kelp. So this one runs Relational, Attention×3, Lived Experience, Relational and Environment together, Environment, Systems. Set beside No. 15 , which descends to the floor before climbing, and No. 16 , which runs out of order because its claim is about the rung itself, that is the third distinct way a real zine declines to be a staircase. The pair is the argument Nos. 58 and 59 are companions by design — the same Saturday, the same room, the otters in one and the rest in the other — and they are the two pieces here closest to the ladder. One prints five rung names as spread eyebrows. The other prints the word nowhere at all. Read them side by side and nothing about the strength of either argument tells you which is which. That is the entire case for keeping the acronym off the spreads , and it is an accident of how the two were made rather than a demonstration anyone set up — which is the only reason it is worth anything.
Three that climb without being built to
Three that climb without being built to These were not designed against the ladder. They arrive at it, which is the more interesting result — and in one case they arrive at it from the top.
No. 17 · The Nearest Body — four rungs, and the floor missing

No. 17 · The Nearest Body — four rungs, and the floor missing 2 Tidal force. The near body wins: tidal force falls off with the cube of distance, so nearness beats mass. off-ladder · the fact 3 Co-regulation is gravity. A safe-enough nervous system nearby pulls yours into rhythm, at a distance, without touching. Relational 4 Spring & neap. Aligned or crossed pulls; parallel presence as tidal locking. Relational 5 When there is no moon. Meerkat mode: no steady pull, so the water heaves every direction at once. What the day feels like. Lived Experience 6 The storm is in the weather. Water has no weather of its own — the storm comes from the system overhead and from where someone paved the marsh. Environment 7 The tide table. Regulation-first and chronodiversity: read the table and go with it; every coast keeps its own clock. Systems Four rungs in five spreads, in order, and the piece is the only zine on the site that prints the downward read as well — spread 6 walks Systems down to Environment down to Lived Experience down to attention, in the vocabulary of the ecosystemic model of distress. It has no Attention spread, and that is a real gap rather than a subtlety. Monotropism enters No. 17 only by reference from the earlier zines. A piece about regulation that never reaches the floor of the ladder is running four rungs of a five-rung argument — which is worth noticing precisely because the ladder's own claim is that the floor is what holds the rest up.
No. 15 · Every Creature's Own Sky — it descends before it climbs

No. 15 · Every Creature's Own Sky — it descends before it climbs 2–3 Umwelt, and the senses beyond ours. The tick's three signals; Nagel's bat. No view from nowhere — every creature's world, from the inside. Lived Experience 4 The cosmos looks back. The star-stuff turn: the universe sees itself only from the inside, through the eyes it made. off-ladder · the turn 5 Minds have skies too. Attention is a sense — it decides what shows up at all. Monotropic and polytropic as two skies, not a ranking. Attention 6 The gap goes both ways. Milton's double empathy problem: when two umwelten meet, the failure belongs to neither. Relational 7 Mutual translation. What the sky asks of us: curiosity rather than correction, and nobody owing you legibility. Environment This one takes three spreads to reach the floor and then climbs three rungs in three. It arrives at Attention from above — the diagnostic direction — and then turns and builds upward from it. That shape is not a flaw in the mapping; it is what a zine has to do. A reader will not accept a claim about attention on spread two. They will accept it on spread five, once a tick and a bat have made the case that no two bodies share a world.
No. 42 · Look for the Air — the whole thing reads downward

No. 42 · Look for the Air — the whole thing reads downward 2–5 Aristotle to Apollo 15. Falling explained by what a thing is , then character deleted from the explanation, then a hammer and a feather landing together in vacuum, on film. off-ladder · the chain 6 The hinge. Deficit ideology is Aristotelian physics applied to children: the trajectory explained by an internal disposition, the situation absent. the diagnosis 7–10 Behaviourism, self-esteem, grit, the dashboard. An industry that measures effort, focus and behaviour points, and has no field for the room. Systems 12 Where the air actually is. Scarcity has a measurable cognitive cost — the medium, quantified, against the objection that only character is measurable. Lived Experience 13 When a feather falls slowly, look for the air. The habit of mind, stated as an instruction. Environment Systems, then the day, then the room. That is the diagnostic order, run without a word of the vocabulary, and it works because the physics has already taught the reader the move: you would not design an intervention to build feather resilience. Spread 11 is the chain's correction to itself over a misquotation, and sits outside this reading.
Two that don't climb, and say so

Two that don't climb, and say so This is the part that keeps the page honest. A framework you can find everywhere is a framework that has stopped saying anything. No. 31, Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not occupies two rungs across ten spreads and states it in its own colophon: “In Stimpunks' ARLES terms, this zine lives at the top two rungs — Environment and Systems.” Convergence, attractors, Waddington's canalized landscape, the difference between a slope that was found and a wall that was poured. There is no ascent and there should not be. A zine about terrain has no business pretending to be about attention. No. 16, Minor Worlds runs the rungs badly out of order — Environment, Environment, Attention and Lived Experience together, Relational, Systems, Relational — and it is right to. Its claim is about the Environment rung: that the hum of the fluorescent light and the open-plan clatter are a built niche that got renamed the default. You cannot argue that from below. The rung under examination has to be on the table first. And then the majority. Most of the numbered zines do not map onto this ladder at all, because most of them are not making a design argument — they are following a fact. No. 9 is about who holds the pen when a boundary gets drawn. No. 61 is about a ruler that would not travel one clade sideways. Those are arguments about measurement and authority, and forcing a rung onto them would tell you nothing about either.
Four pieces already say it out loud

Four pieces already say it out loud The rule at the top of this page is a rule going forward. It is not a description of the shelf, and the difference has to be published rather than smoothed over. Four pieces name the method on the page today: No. 17, The Nearest Body — spread 6's eyebrow reads Ecosystemic distress · ARLES , and the body spells out the downward read and links the glossary. Listed again in the colophon. No. 29, Only in Relation — spread 6 draws the ladder , all five rungs, and argues from it: Relational sits near the base, and Regulation lives inside it, because regulation is not a private skill. No. 31, Five Times a Crab — the two-rung placement in the colophon, plus the design-method line carried as an attributed quote. No. 59, The Rest You Keep — the colophon sentence quoted above, which is the rule stating itself. Nothing here proposes stripping them. No. 29's ladder is doing real work on that spread — the whole point of the piece is that regulation lives in the relation, and the diagram is what makes the placement visible. And a collection with a public error log cannot quietly delete an exception in order to make a rule look cleaner than it is. What the rule says is that a new zine does not become the fifth. Not Not a template. ARLES is a design order and a diagnostic order. It is not a story shape, and a zine built to hit five rungs in five spreads would be a framework deliverable with a starfield behind it. No. 59 earns its ladder by paying for every rung with an animal. Not a grading scheme. A one-rung zine is not a worse zine. No. 31 sits at the top of the ladder and never moves, and it is one of the most carefully sourced pieces here. Not a claim about intent. Four of the six maps above are retrospective, and a fifth (No. 58) is read off a proposal rather than a stated intent. Saying this piece climbs the ladder is not saying anyone was holding the ladder at the time, and the two are easy to blur once a diagram exists. Not a private vocabulary. ARLES is published, in the open, and free to use with credit — the glossary and the method . It is kept off the spreads for the reader's sake, not for ours. Not evidence of anything. A house framework found in house artifacts is the least surprising result available, and this page would be worthless as a defence of ARLES. It is a legibility aid: it explains why these zines keep arriving at the room instead of the person.

One axis, and we put ourselves at the top of it

The ladder One axis, and we put ourselves at the top of it Ask how smart an animal is and you have already agreed to something: that smart is a quantity, that it runs along one axis, and that every mind can be given a place on it. The axis needs a yardstick, so we have built several. Absolute brain mass. Brain mass against body mass. The encephalisation quotient. Cortical surface. Neuron counts. These are real measurements, taken carefully by careful people, and none of them is the problem. The problem is the ordering. A measurement tells you how much of something there is. It does not tell you that more of it is better, or that the creature with the most of it is the one the others are failing to be. And the ordering came first. We had the ladder long before we had the instruments, and then we went looking for the instrument that would show us on the top rung — which is a different activity from measuring. us apes monkeys the rest … more the shape of the assumption one axis · one winner a ladder, not a measurement The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Then somebody counted the pilot whale

The count Then somebody counted the pilot whale Neuron number is the yardstick that feels least arguable. Cells are countable. You can do the stereology and get a figure, and the figure does not care what you were hoping for. In 2014, Mortensen and colleagues did the counting on the neocortex of the long-finned pilot whale — a dolphin, despite the name. They found roughly 37.2 billion neocortical neurons, alongside some 127 billion glial cells. That is, in the paper's own words, almost twice as many neocortical neurons as humans. The first animal ever counted with more neocortical neurons than us, and it is a mid-sized dolphin that most people have never heard of. 37.2 ×10⁹ neocortical neurons long-finned pilot whale ≈ 2× the human count mortensen et al. 2014 Neuron density is lower in the whale; the total is higher because the brain is bigger. Both facts are in the paper, and both are worth keeping. 37.2 pilot whale ≈ half human neocortical neurons ×10⁹ the countable yardstick and it does not favour us mortensen et al. 2014 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
The measurement lost. The ranking survived it.

The part nobody quotes The measurement lost. The ranking survived it. Here is the sentence in that same paper. The absolute number of neurons in the human neocortex, the authors conclude, is not correlated with the superior cognitive abilities of humans — at least not compared with cetaceans — as had previously been hypothesised. Read it slowly. The yardstick was neuron count. The count came back against us. And the conclusion drawn is not perhaps the ranking is wrong. It is the count must not be the right yardstick. To be fair to the authors: as a narrow claim about neuroscience that is entirely defensible, and probably correct. Neuron number alone plainly does not explain human cognition. They are reporting an honest negative result. But look at what stayed fixed while everything else moved. Human superiority is not the thing being tested here. It is the thing the test is being fitted to. Which tells you something useful: the ranking was never resting on the count. So no count could ever disturb it. Another yardstick will be found, and if that one comes back wrong too, another will be found after it. the evidence whale us moved and yet the ranking us didn't it was never resting on the evidence a fixed point, dressed as a finding the yardstick is replaceable the conclusion is not The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
The input layer our textbooks call canonical is simply not there

No fourth layer The input layer our textbooks call canonical is simply not there Open a neuroscience textbook at the cortical column and you will find six layers, with layer IV as the front door: the granular layer where signals from the thalamus arrive before anything else happens to them. The cetacean neocortex does not have one. Not reduced in places — the whole sheet is agranular. The lamination, as the literature describes it, runs: a thick cellular layer I; a densely packed layer II whose neurons send dendrites up into layer I; a wide pyramidal layer III; an absent or underdeveloped layer IV; a magnocellular layer V of large pyramidal cells; and a heterogeneous layer VI. So where does the input go? The current reading is that layer I takes the job — that it is the main target for incoming subcortical neurons precisely because layer IV is absent, with layer II then relaying that information down to the lower layers. The front door moved upstairs. The result, in the words of the review that lays this out, is a very different connectivity scheme compared to more commonly studied species, like rats and macaque monkeys. Sit with that phrase — more commonly studied species. The canonical column is canonical because of who we happened to put on the microscope. Rats and macaques are the baseline for reasons of husbandry and history, not because evolution nominated them. And in layer V of the anterior cingulate, anterior insular and frontopolar cortices, the humpback whale turns out to carry large spindle cells — von Economo neurons — similar in shape and distribution to those described in hominids. Hof and Van der Gucht call it a likely case of parallel evolution. Same cell type, arrived at separately, in a cortex with no fourth layer to build it on. primate IIIIII IV VVI in front door: IV cetacean I IIIII IV VVI in relay front door: I IV: absent the job moved two routes into a cortex absent ≠ missing ≠ lacking hof & van der gucht 2007 · marino et al. 2008 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Difference read as deficit, in Biological Reviews, in 2006

The live argument Difference read as deficit, in Biological Reviews, in 2006 In 2006 Paul Manger published a long paper arguing that cetacean brains got big to make heat — thermogenesis against a cooling ocean — rather than to think. He argued further that cetaceans are considerably less intelligent than generally supposed. One of his three claims was this: there is no neural basis for complex cognition in cetaceans. Among the evidence offered were the indistinct lamination, the pyramidalised layer II, and the absence of layer IV. In 2008, sixteen authors replied. Those features, they answered, are one aspect of an unusual combination of conservative and derived traits — and cetacean brains, having diverged from our common ancestor more than 95 million years ago and arrived at high encephalisation entirely independently, in all likelihood represent a non-primate route to neuroanatomical (and cognitive) complexity. A brain organised unlike ours was read as a brain insufficient for mind. The reply did not say the difference wasn't real. It said the difference wasn't a deficit. You know this argument. It is the one made about us, in clinics and classrooms, in the same century. Here it is being had by neuroscientists, about whales, in a review journal — and the shape of the inference is identical. one observation no layer IV manger 2006 no neural basis for cognition marino et al. 2008 the input moved to layer I same slide different baseline the inference is a choice one fact, two readings deficit or design the data did not decide it The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
We are not telling you who won

Held with care We are not telling you who won It would be easy, and dishonest, to leave Manger as the villain of this zine. So: his thermogenesis hypothesis was a serious proposal, published in a serious journal, and it has not simply evaporated. Later work has found real thermogenic signatures in cetacean brains — uncoupling proteins expressed in cortical neurons and in glia, an increased density of noradrenergic boutons. A brain in cold water may well be doing heat work and thought work. Organs are not single-purpose. The reply from Marino and colleagues is also not neutral ground. It is an argued position by researchers with a stake in cetacean cognition, and calling a paper a claim in search of evidence in your own title is not a gesture of detachment. So we are not handing you a verdict. What we are pointing at is narrower and, we think, harder to wriggle out of: the direction the inference travelled by default. Given a cortex organised unlike the ones we had studied, the available readings included this brain is built differently and this brain is built worse. The second was reached quickly, defended at length, and required no additional evidence to feel reasonable — because the ladder was already there to catch it. That is the part that recurs. It recurs in the lines we drew around normal, and it is the mechanism the difference-first frame exists to interrupt. Not who was right about whales. They had to borrow from music, because the shelf didn't fit

Rubato They had to borrow from music, because the shelf didn't fit Sperm whales talk in codas — short patterned bursts of clicks. For decades the Eastern Caribbean repertoire was described as around 21 discrete coda types. A modest vocabulary. Roughly what you would expect from a lesser mind. In 2024, a team analysed 8,719 codas from at least 60 whales recorded between 2005 and 2018, and found the repertoire was not a list at all. It has four features that combine freely: rhythm and tempo, which hold steady regardless of context, plus two they named rubato and ornamentation, which shift with the conversation going on around them. Combine those four and you get roughly 143 combinations actually in use — nearly an order of magnitude past the old count. Notice the naming. Rubato and ornamentation are borrowed from music, because the categories on the shelf did not have a slot for what the whales were doing. The vocabulary had to be built before the structure could be seen. Which is the quiet lesson of the whole zine. When your instrument has no category for a thing, the thing reads as absence. Twenty-one types was never what the whales had. It was what we could hear. rhythm tempo faster, same shape rubato stretched ornament +1 extra was: 21 types is: ≈143 combinations four features, freely combined context-sensitive · context-free sharma et al. 2024 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one

Only some of them Fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one In Shark Bay, Western Australia, some bottlenose dolphins break a marine sponge off the seafloor, wear it over the closed beak, and use it to probe the sediment for fish. It is called sponging. Not the dolphins. Some. Krützen and colleagues found it in 15 of 141 known mothers, and mitochondrial DNA put its transmission almost entirely down a single matriline — mother to daughter, learned rather than inherited. And spongers live differently. Compared with non-spongers in the same water, they are more solitary, work the deep channels, dive for longer, and spend more of the day foraging. So inside one population, sharing one gene pool and one bay, there is a minority with a different sensory route to food, a different social pattern, and a different shape of day — passed along a family line, by learning. We have a word for a profile with peaks and troughs rather than a single level: the spiky profile. And a word for surfacing and diving by capacity — dolphining, which we named after them before we knew this. 141 known mothers 15 spongers · one matriline variation inside one population not a species difference krützen et al. 2005 · mann et al. 2008 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks

The question, straight Is there neurodiversity among whales? We went looking, and here is the honest answer: there is no cetacean autism literature. No whale ADHD, no dolphin dyslexia, no diagnostic framework of any kind applied to a cetacean. We found none, and we are not going to invent one to make this zine land better. That absence is worth stating plainly, because the temptation runs the other way. It would be easy to write whales are neurodivergent too, and it would be false, and it would borrow legitimacy from a clinical apparatus we spend the rest of our time arguing with. But the question has a real answer, once you notice that the neurodiversity paradigm was never about diagnoses. It is about variation within a population, and whether the population is built so that variation survives. At that level the record is not empty at all. It is fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one, with a traced inheritance route. It is 143 combinations where we had heard 21. It is a cortex with no fourth layer, working. The frame that lets us say this without diagnosing anybody is ethodiversity — Ombre Tarragnat's extension of the neurodiversity paradigm, by way of ethology, to beings with nervous systems. It takes the part that travels (variation is normal, and it is not a defect) and leaves behind the part that shouldn't (the clinic, the diagnosis, the deficit). You do not need to find an Autistic whale. You need to stop requiring a diagnosis before variation counts. Not: whales are smarter than us. That is the same ladder with a new occupant. We are not trying to win the ranking; we are declining it. Not: dolphins are Autistic. We do not diagnose across species to borrow standing. No such literature exists and we are not manufacturing it. Not: a superpower. 37.2 billion neurons is not a gift narrative, and neither is anybody's spiky profile. Not: nature proves the ethics. Difference would deserve welcome in a universe that made exactly one shape. The whales are a rhyme, not a warrant. And: we notice we are doing it too. This zine spends eleven spreads using cetacean minds as material for a human argument. Their minds are not evidence for our politics first. A body shaped differently, travelling with whales

Eight days off Pico A body shaped differently, travelling with whales In 2011, off the island of Pico in the Azores, two researchers watching sperm whales found something else in the group: an adult male bottlenose dolphin whose spine curved so severely that his rear half held an S shape. Over eight days he travelled with the whales, foraged with them, and played with the adults and their calves. When he rubbed his body against them, the rubs were sometimes returned. A dolphin with a spine that didn't work like other dolphins' spines was moving with a slower species that had room for him in it. Two things this is not. First, it is not an adoption. The paper is titled Repeated Non-Agonistic Interactions — careful, unglamorous, exactly as far as the evidence goes. "Adopted" is the press's word, not the researchers'. Second, we do not know why. The suggestion that other dolphins had harassed him and he sought refuge is a plausible guess offered to reporters — not a finding. It may be that a curved spine made sperm whale pace easier to keep than dolphin pace. We don't know. What is in the record is eight days, and the rubs coming back. That is enough. It does not have to mean anything about us to be worth knowing. sperm whales S-curved spine rubs returned calf days recorded together 8 — and the rubs came back azores, 2011 non-agonistic, repeatedly wilson & krause 2013 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Douglas Adams got there first, and then the joke came due

So long Douglas Adams got there first, and then the joke came due In 1979, in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, Douglas Adams made this exact joke and made it better. On Earth, he wrote, humans had always assumed they were the most intelligent species on the planet — whereas in fact they were the third. Mice first. Dolphins second. Look at the mechanism. He does not overturn the ranking. He keeps its form perfectly intact and moves us down two rungs, and the whole apparatus collapses into absurdity, because a ladder that puts mice on top was never measuring anything. The dolphins, knowing what was coming, left. Their last message, mistaken for a stunt: So long, and thanks for all the fish. Then the bill arrived. In 1988 Adams travelled with the zoologist Mark Carwardine to find endangered species for Last Chance to See, and one of them was the baiji, the Yangtze river dolphin — a freshwater cetacean going deaf and blind in a river turned into an industrial corridor. In December 2006, a six-week survey of the Yangtze ended without a single sighting. Turvey and colleagues published it as, possibly, the first human-caused extinction of a cetacean species. A species actually said so long. Not as a punchline. The ranking was never a description of the world. Manger's thermogenesis hypothesis is a serious proposal and is not settled against: later work reports uncoupling proteins in cetacean cortical neurons and glia and raised noradrenergic bouton density, consistent with real thermogenic function. A brain can do heat work and thought work at once, and we take no side on the mechanism. The reply we quote is itself an argued position by researchers invested in cetacean cognition. On neurodiversity: we searched and found no scientific literature applying neurodiversity, in its human diagnostic sense, to cetaceans — we state an absence we looked for, not a proven absence, and we have not searched exhaustively or outside English. The fact this zine runs on Light carries no name Light moves at a finite speed, so every observation is an observation of the past. Sunlight reaching your face left the Sun about eight minutes and twenty seconds ago. The nearest star after ours, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 light-years off, so its light is four years old when it gets here. The Andromeda Galaxy is roughly 2.5 million. That is settled, checkable, and taught to children. What gets taught less is the second half of it: the light leaves with nothing written on it. A photon carries a wavelength, a polarisation, a direction. It does not carry a discoverer. Everything a star will ever tell us about itself is packed at the moment of emission, complete, and then it crosses however far it has to cross — and the name gets attached at the far end, by whoever happens to be standing there with an instrument when it lands. Astronomy has a term for that landing. First light is the moment a new telescope opens its eye and returns its first image. Nobody has ever thought the telescope invented the galaxy in the frame. First light is a fact about us — about when we got there, and what we had built by then. So a name in astronomy is an arrival record. It is never an origin record. Those two things get printed on the same line in a textbook, which is how they get confused, and almost everything in this zine is that confusion happening to a person instead of a star.
