Priority is a rule about who was standing there

The rule as written Priority is a rule about who was standing there Priority is the convention that scientific credit belongs to whoever publishes a finding first. In astronomy it is not a sentiment, it is administration: a comet or a minor planet takes the name of whoever reports it to the right body first, and the paperwork settles it. Halley's Comet is a clean case. Edmond Halley used Newton's gravitation to work out that the bright comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object making return trips, and in 1705 he predicted it back for 1758. It came. The name is his, and by the rule it is his fairly — he did the thing the rule rewards. He also did not see it first, and nobody claims he did. Its returns had been recorded for more than two thousand years before him, the earliest firmly identified passage being the one Chinese astronomers logged in 240 BCE. Naming a thing and observing a thing were never the same act, even where we teach the history as though they were. Notice what the rule is honest about. Priority does not pretend to record when the comet started existing, or when a human first looked at it. It records who filed. Everyone involved knows that, and the convention runs cleanly because nobody mistakes the register for the sky. The trouble is not the rule. The trouble is what happens when the filing system loses its own honesty and starts being read as a record of origin — because then whoever was late, or far away, or writing in the wrong language, stops looking late and starts looking absent. And a register does not lose its honesty on its own. It is kept by people. Committees, editors, prize panels, the handful of journals that got read and the two or three languages they got read in — and in the 1920s the people holding all of that were overwhelmingly white, Western and men. That is what does the accounting. So be exact about what the physics is for here. Light-travel time gives you the shape of the error — a thing complete at one end, named at the other, with a measurable gap between. It does not give you the cause. The cause is bias, and bias is not a property of light. It has names, addresses and letterheads, and it decides where the receiver points. The Light Arrived Before the Name · Stimpunks

One year, two continents 1925, twice So here is that accounting, twice over, in one year. Two women finished work in 1925 that their fields would be built on. Both were talked into sounding less certain than they were. Neither name arrived with the finding. In Cambridge, Massachusetts, Cecilia Payne submitted Stellar Atmospheres — the thesis showing that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, which is the single most consequential fact about what the universe is made of. Henry Norris Russell, a senior man in American astrophysics, told her the result was clearly impossible. She published anyway, with a line in it saying the enormous abundance of hydrogen and helium was “almost certainly not real.” Russell restated the same conclusion in 1929. Otto Struve later called her thesis “undoubtedly the most brilliant Ph.D. thesis ever written in astronomy.” In Moscow, Grunya Efimovna Sukhareva finished a clinical description of six boys who had spent about two years at the hospital-school she had founded in 1921. She was a Jewish woman, working in Soviet institutions, publishing in Russian. Every one of those facts is in the account of why you have not heard of her, and none of them is a shortfall in her. She recorded the aloneness, the flattened expression, the narrow blazing interests — and the giftedness running underneath. It is now widely read as the first clinical account of autism, eighteen years before Kanner and nineteen before Asperger. She published in Russian, then in German the following year so more of the world could read it. The English translation arrived in 1996 — seventy-one years later, and half a century after the two men's names were fixed to the thing she had described. A note on Moscow, kept on the page. An earlier draft of this zine placed her in Kiev, following a shorthand that circulates in the secondary literature — Manouilenko and Bejerot's 2015 paper calls her “Kiev-based.” She was born in Kiev in 1891 and moved to Moscow in 1921, where the hospital-school and the 1925 observations were. A zine about miscrediting that quietly repaired its own propagated error would be doing the smoothing it is complaining about, so the error is logged here and in the changelog rather than swept. Neither woman was wrong. Both were made to sound less certain than they were, by men whose certainty was not asked to justify itself in the same way. The finding, in each case, was already complete and already in flight. The Light Arrived Before the Name · Stimpunks

The name for late naming arrived late

A hundred and twenty-three years The name for late naming arrived late In 1993 the historian of science Margaret W. Rossiter published a paper called The Matthew Matilda Effect in Science, and gave the pattern in this zine a name it could be cited by. She was answering Robert Merton's Matthew effect — that credit accumulates on scientists who already have it, so the famous get more and the obscure get less. Rossiter's addition was the mirror: women's work is minimised, misattributed, or folded into a nearby man's name, and the two effects are the same accounting error seen from opposite ends. Here is the part that belongs in this zine rather than a general one about sexism in science. Rossiter did not name it for herself, and she did not name it for a scientist. She named it for Matilda Joslyn Gage, a suffragist and abolitionist who had already mapped the whole mechanism in a pamphlet in 1870 — Woman as Inventor, expanded thirteen years later for the North American Review. The pattern was described in 1870. It got a citable name in 1993. The concept of the late name was itself a hundred and twenty-three years late. That delay is the argument's best evidence. If the effect were rare, the description of it would have travelled at the ordinary speed of a good idea. Instead the description sat, in a nineteenth-century pamphlet by a woman outside the academy, doing exactly what it described — waiting for somebody with enough standing to be standing there when it landed. And when somebody was, she did the one thing the pattern does not do by itself: she looked back down the beam and put the earlier name on it. The Light Arrived Before the Name · Stimpunks
The signal had been arriving the whole time

Ninety-six feet a day The signal had been arriving the whole time In 1967 Jocelyn Bell was a graduate student working through the output of a radio telescope she had helped build, reading roughly 96 feet of chart paper a day by hand. She found something occupying about a quarter of an inch of it: a signal too regular to be noise. Her supervisor thought it was interference. She kept pulling the thread, and it was a pulsar — a rotating neutron star, sweeping a beam past us with a period the discovery paper gives as 1.3372795 seconds, stable to within two ten-millionths. Take the fact from spread two seriously for a moment. Those pulses had been arriving before anyone was there to receive them. The star had been doing this the entire time; the regularity was not created by the observation. What changed in 1967 was that somebody built a receiver and then read every foot of what came out of it. She is the second author on the paper that reports it — Hewish, Bell, Pilkington, Scott and Collins, Nature 217, 709 (1968). This is worth stating precisely, because the shorthand version of the story gets it wrong in both directions. She was not written out of the paper. She was written out of the prize: the 1974 Nobel in Physics went to Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, and not to the author standing second on the discovery. She has said since that she is not bitter, and that in 1974 students simply were not who prize committees looked at. That is a description of the instrument, not an absolution of it. A committee that cannot see a graduate student is a receiver with a known blind spot, and the signal it misses was never faint. Sukhareva spent her career on the other side of a comparable blind spot, and it is worth naming the blind spot rather than what she supposedly lacked. She was a woman. She was Jewish. She published in Russian and German, from the Soviet Union. Not one of those is a deficiency in her. Each is something the committees of the period were built not to see. A pulse train, older than its receiver Evenly spaced pulses run the full width. The left half is faint because nothing was receiving them; the right half is bright. The refusals What this does not say Six women, one pattern, and six quite different situations. Flattening them into a single shape would be the second erasure, so here is what is deliberately not being claimed. Not:that gender explains Sukhareva. Sher and Gibson give four reasons together, and rank none of them: her gender, her Jewish identity, her Russian nationality, and publication in Russian and German — which they call, plainly, not an efficacious recipe for worldwide attention in the 1920s. They also raise the possibility that Asperger omitted her deliberately under Nazi-era antisemitism. Her erasure was Jewish and Soviet as much as it was gendered, and a zine that files her under “women in science” and stops has taken three quarters of the mechanism out. Not:that a missed prize and state violence are the same harm. They are not, and the difference is not one of degree. Sukhareva was attacked at the 1951 Pavlovian Sessions for “anti-Marxist views” and self-censored the bibliography of her 1955 work; colleagues around her lost careers and lives. Nobody's life was at stake in a committee room in Stockholm. Both belong on the page; they do not belong on the same axis. Not:that every woman here was silenced the same way. Annie Jump Cannon built the stellar classification scheme still in use and was honoured in her lifetime: first woman to take the National Academy of Sciences' Henry Draper Medal, 1931. And she joined the Harvard College Observatory in 1896 and got no regular Harvard appointment until 1938. Honoured from outside, unpromoted at home, for forty-two years. She is the exception and she is forty-two years of the rule, which is why she is on this page rather than left off it. Not:that recognition and justice are the same thing. We are not new. Our records are

Which brings it to us We are not new. Our records are The six children Sukhareva wrote down in 1925 were Autistic. So were Autistic children in 1895, and in 1795, and every year in between that nobody was taking notes. 1925 is not when we started. It is when somebody was standing there with an instrument. This is the whole of spread two, arriving at a person. A diagnosis is an arrival record. It is a dated statement about when a clinician, working in a particular decade, in a particular language, using a particular set of criteria, first wrote something down. It is not, and has never claimed to be, a record of when the thing began. The criteria say so out loud. The DSM-5's third criterion for autism requires that symptoms “must be present in the early developmental period” — and then adds, in the same breath, that they “may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life.” The manual is describing light-travel time. It is telling you the emission was early and the detection can be decades late, and that the delay lives in the demands and the masking, not in the person. Somebody diagnosed at forty-seven has not been Autistic since they were forty-seven. The paperwork is forty-seven years old and the light is not. Many of us know this in the body, because we have had a version of it said to us: you can't have been, you'd have been picked up. That sentence quietly makes the record the origin. It says that whether we existed depends on whether the receiver was switched on, in our town, in our decade, for a child who looked like us. Girls, and Black and brown children, and anyone whose flavour of it stayed indoors, got the receiver switched on late or never. And it runs the other way too, which is the part that stings. The names on our diagnoses are Kanner's and Asperger's because of when translations happened. Sukhareva's account was eighteen years earlier and seventy-one years from English. We are not asking to be discovered. We were never undiscovered. We are asking the record to be read for what it is: a log of when the looking happened, kept by the people who were doing the looking. Two lines that are not the same line One line runs the whole width: what was always the case. A second, shorter line begins only part way along: what the paperwork records. Made of the same star stuff, unsigned

The last crossing Made of the same star stuff, unsigned One more thing that crossed a great distance without a name on it, and it is the reason this piece is in this collection rather than a history-of-science shelf. Payne's thesis said the stars are hydrogen and helium. Everything heavier than those two was cooked afterwards, inside stars, and scattered when they died — the carbon in your cells, the oxygen in your blood, the calcium in the bone your hand is resting on. Those atoms crossed interstellar space and several billion years to get into you, and not one of them arrived with a discoverer's name attached. They did not need one. The calcium works whether or not Cecilia Payne was believed in 1925. The hydrogen did not become more abundant when Russell restated it in 1929, and it was not less abundant during the four years in between, while the most consequential fact about the universe sat in a Harvard thesis with a hedge in it that its author had been talked into. That is the whole premise of this collection put as plainly as it goes. Belonging runs underneath the record. The record is a human artefact — late, partial, in whichever languages the committees happened to read, and revisable. The thing it is a record of is not. She is not a footnote version of herself, waiting for us to notice. She was the whole star the entire time. We are only now getting the light. Which is the honest scale of what a correction can do. Publishing Sukhareva's name does not give her back the credit; she died in 1981 and nothing here reaches her. It fixes our instrument — the one we are using right now, on each other, on the next person whose account arrives in the wrong language or the wrong decade or the wrong body. And there is one thing available to us that is not repair. Her atoms are still in circulation; that is chemistry, not consolation. What we can carry forward is not her credit, which was never ours to hand back — it is her method. Notice closely. Write the giftedness down in the same paragraph as the difficulty. Then turn the instrument toward whoever is arriving right now in the wrong language, the wrong decade or the wrong body, and be the one who is standing there. The bell curve is a vantage point

The same trick, on us The bell curve is a vantage point The curve that sorts us into normal and abnormal began in astronomy. It was the "error curve" — the math for how repeated measurements of a star's position scatter around its true one. In the 1800s, Adolphe Quetelet — an astronomer — turned that instrument on people, and invented l'homme moyen, the average man. What had described the error in a measurement now described the ideal human, with everyone else scattered around it as deviation. Francis Galton took the next step, reading the curve as a ranking, and built eugenics on it. So the tool that mapped the indifferent stars got turned on our minds — and the average, a made-up midpoint, was handed to us as the shape we were supposed to be. The Lines We Drew is the ninth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the companion argument to Field Guide No. 1 — where that guide redraws the constellations, this one is about why redrawing is legitimate at all. The astronomy moved, and this page moved with it. An earlier version of this zine said the belt was a line-of-sight accident — Alnitak ~740 light-years, Mintaka ~690, Alnilam ~2,000, "nearly three times farther." That was wrong, and we have corrected it. Those were Hipparcos-era parallaxes, and Hipparcos measured these bright, distant, multiple O and B stars badly: its parallax for Mintaka (212 ± 30 pc) is about half the figure that spectroscopy, cluster membership and Gaia DR3 now agree on, and both Hipparcos reductions of Alnilam proved incorrect. Current distances put all three at essentially the same depth — Alnitak 1,260 ± 180 ly (387 ± 54 pc), Alnilam 1,250 ± 26 ly (384 ± 8 pc, from VLTI interferometry: Oplištilová, Brož, Hummel, Harmanec & Barlow, "VLTI observations of the Orion Belt stars: I. ε Orionis," Astronomy & Astrophysics 704, A204, 2025), and Mintaka ~1,240 ly (381 ± 8 pc, Gaia DR3). All three belong to the Orion OB1b association, and the ε Ori paper places its star at that association's median distance: they are siblings from one cloud, not strangers in a row. APOD, cited in our earlier draft, likewise gives the three as a group "about 1,500 light-years away" — it never supported the numbers we hung on it. The depth is real; it is just in the figure rather than the belt. Bellatrix lies 250 ± 10 ly away, Betelgeuse about 548 (uncertain by as much as 100), Saiph 650 ± 30, Rigel about 863, and the belt near 1,250 — so the hunter is assembled from stars strung across roughly a thousand light-years. We think the correction improves the zine. A page arguing that confident lines get mistaken for facts of the sky had drawn one of its own, in depth, from superseded data — and better instruments moved it. That is the argument arriving uninvited, and it now runs on the spread. The lineage from stars to people is real and well documented. The bell curve entered science as the astronomer's "law of error": in his Theoria Motus (1809), Gauss used it to model how imperfect measurements scatter around a celestial body's true position — the same method that recovered the lost asteroid Ceres — with Legendre and Laplace close behind. Adolphe Quetelet, who directed the Brussels observatory, carried that error law from the sky to the census in his Essai de physique sociale (1835), inventing l'homme moyen, "the average man" — and, crucially, treating the average not as merely typical but as an ideal from which real people "deviate." Francis Galton kept Quetelet's curve but flipped its meaning: in Hereditary Genius (1869) he ranked human ability along what he called the "law of deviation from the average" and graded groups above and below the line. He coined the word eugenics later, in Inquiries into Human Faculty and Its Development (1883), where a footnote to the introduction proposes it for "the science of improving stock." His protégé Karl Pearson gave the field its machinery — the standard deviation (1894) and the correlation coefficient — in the Mathematical Contributions to the Theory of Evolution series, and was later appointed the first Galton Professor of Eugenics at University College London (1911–1933); the mathematics came first, the chair after. The statistical sense of the word "normal" arrives in the 1870s alongside all of this — used apparently independently by C. S. Peirce (1873), Galton, and Wilhelm Lexis (1877), with "normal distribution" settling into place in Pearson's writing by 1897. The sleight of hand was never the curve — some traits really are close to normally distributed — but the leap from deviation-as-measurement-error to deviation-as-human-defect, and the mistaking of a made-up midpoint for a law about how a person ought to be. Robert Chapman's Empire of Normality (2023) follows this same thread forward, into psychiatry and capitalism. On Chapman's account, Galton reframed the statistical centre as mere mediocrity rather than an ideal — so that deviation above it read as superiority and deviation below as defect — founding the frame that, carried through Kraepelin into the DSM, the neurodiversity movement later arose to name and refuse. That frame's name — the pathology paradigm, and its counterpart the neurodiversity paradigm — is Nick Walker's, articulated in "Throw Away the Master's Tools: Liberating Ourselves from the Pathology Paradigm" (written 2011; published 2012 in Loud Hands: Autistic People, Speaking; revised 2013), not Chapman's; Chapman works with the terms rather than coining them. The "normal" mind, in other words, has a history — and a contestable one. The border really does move: the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from the DSM beginning in 1973; Asperger's disorder was added in DSM-IV (1994) and merged into Autism Spectrum Disorder in DSM-5 (2013). "Epistemic injustice," with its testimonial and hermeneutical forms, is Miranda Fricker's (2007). "Neurodiversity" is not one person's coinage, though it is often credited to Judy Singer (1998). Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley & Walker, "The neurodiversity concept was developed collectively: An overdue correction on the origins of neurodiversity theory" (Autism, 2024), show that "neurological diversity" and "neurodiversity" reached print in 1997 and 1998 in the work of journalist Harvey Blume, who attributed them to the online Autistic community — and that the concept and its theory were developed collectively by neurodivergent people. We follow that correction here. The neurodivergent / neurodivergence coinage is Kassiane Asasumasu's (2000), as logged for Zine No. 3; the paradigm's articulation is Nick Walker's and the wider community's. The reading is ours: that the constructed line was never the sky, and so is ours to redraw. Everybody has a lizard brain, and nobody has one

The question Everybody has a lizard brain, and nobody has one You have heard it, and you may have said it. That was my lizard brain. My amygdala hijacked me. The reptile took over. It is a way of apologising for a reaction by attributing it to an older, dumber animal living downstairs. There is no such animal. There is no such downstairs. The model behind the phrase is called the triune brain, and a paper published in April 2026 disposes of it in a single sentence that is worth reading slowly, because of how little hedging is in it: the “triune brain” theory persists to this day in the evocation of “my lizard brain” to explain uncontrolled emotional excess using the utterly false evolutionary tale that reptiles have brain only “up to” the emotional limbic system, grown over later by the logical neocortex, reaching its full flower in humans. Imam, Kielo, Trude & Finlay, Science Advances, 22 April 2026 “Utterly false” is not a phrase working scientists spend lightly. And the model has been contradicted in the specialist literature since 1969. So this chain is not really about whether the lizard brain is real. It is about how a claim that was refuted before most of us were born ended up in everyone's mouth — and what is actually dividing the brain, which turns out to be better than the story it replaces. Thirteen links. We are implicated in one of them. The Lizard That Was Never There · Stimpunks
A word that only meant “the edge”

Link 1 · Paris, 1878 A word that only meant “the edge” documented Paul Broca, describing mammalian brains, notices a rim of cortex curving around the brainstem like a collar. He calls it le grand lobe limbique — the great limbic lobe. The word is limbus. It means border, edge, hem. Broca is naming a shape, and a position: the stuff at the margin, where the cortex folds round. His grouping takes in the cingulate and parahippocampal gyri, the hippocampus, the primary olfactory cortex, the diagonal band, retrosplenial and medial prefrontal areas. It says: what happened in you just now was the old animal, the part that predates reason, breaking through the floor. It is said about anger and about panic, about a meltdown, about a startle response, about someone who could not mask any longer. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed

75 Star Stuff The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed on the most expensive smell on earth, and the reason it is not in the mushroom one settled fact · followed all the way down L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·
You are not buying a mushroom

The thing itself You are not buying a mushroom In a good year matsutake is among the most expensive foods on earth. It is not especially nutritious. It is not rare in the way a truffle is rare. It is firm and a little woody and, by the standards of the mushrooms people eat for pleasure, unremarkable to chew. The entire price is for a smell. That is not a flourish. It is what the trade is organised around. Matsutake are graded on aroma before anything else; they are picked at the button stage, before the cap opens, because the smell is strongest then; they are flown rather than shipped; and the same mushroom that commands a fortune fresh is worth a fraction of it a few days later — not because it has spoiled, but because it has stopped smelling like that. Anna Tsing spent years following this mushroom around the northern hemisphere and opens her account with the smell rather than the money. Her word for the aroma is the autumn aroma, which is the phrase Japanese poetry has used for it for centuries: not a flavour note, a season. So the object at the centre of this economy is not an object. It is a volatile compound leaving a surface, and something on the other side detecting it. Which raises a question the price makes urgent. If the entire value is the smell, and the smell is what people disagree about — then where, exactly, is the thing being paid for? The smell has a chemistry, and it is running out

Named, measured, and leaving The smell has a chemistry, and it is running out The autumn aroma is not mysterious at the chemical level. It has been pulled apart by gas chromatography and it has names. Two compounds dominate the volatiles that matsutake mycelia and fruiting bodies put into the air: 1-octen-3-ol — the compound most people would call “mushroom” if asked to name the smell of mushrooms — and methyl cinnamate, which is sweet and spicy and is the part that is not like other mushrooms at all. Around them sit 1-octen-3-one, 3-octanone, 3-octanol, benzaldehyde, phenylacetaldehyde, linalool, methional and others, each contributing at its own threshold. The grading practice turns out to be chemistry rather than superstition. As the fruiting body ages, methyl cinnamate and 1-octen-3-ol both decline. The mushroom is not degrading into something unpleasant; it is emitting less of the two things it was being bought for. A price that falls with the hour is tracking a measurable quantity. So far this is a tidy story about an object with a property. A mushroom emits molecules; the molecules are the smell; the smell is the value. Every step of that sentence is wrong after the next spread, and it is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with mushrooms. A note on the noun. “Matsutake” is doing some work here. Across Eurasia most matsutake are Tricholoma matsutake; in western North America the local one is usually treated as T. magnivelare. Tsing notes that some scientists prefer to keep the general term because the dynamics of speciation are still unclear. What held the category together, before any of the genetics, was the smell — the mushrooms that had it were matsutake. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed · Stimpunks
What the elk did, and what the bacteria did

The same molecules, elsewhere What the elk did, and what the bacteria did The forest is full of things that meet these molecules, and they do not agree about them even slightly. Deer choose matsutake over other mushrooms. Bears turn over logs and dig ditches for it. Oregon pickers told Tsing about elk with bloody muzzles from driving their faces into sharp pumice soil to get at it, the smell taking them from one patch straight to the next. Flying insects circle underground caches the way they do over truffles. And in the same soil, meeting the same compounds: slugs, other fungi, and many kinds of soil bacteria are repulsed by the smell, moving out of its range. Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing, The Mushroom at the End of the World, 2015 One set of molecules. An elk digs until it bleeds. A bacterium leaves. Nothing about the molecules changed between those two sentences. It is tempting to file this as a difference in taste — the elk likes it, the slug does not, animals are different. That reading is comfortable and it is the wrong shape. The elk and the slug are not weighing the same experience and reaching different verdicts on it. They are not having the same experience. There is a laboratory version of this, and it is blunt: 1-octen-3-ol and methyl cinnamate have been shown to repel a mycophagous springtail — an animal that eats fungi — away from the fungus producing them. A smell is not a property. It is an event.

The mechanism A smell is not a property. It is an event. Here is the settled fact this whole zine rests on, and it is ordinary sensory biology rather than anything contentious. A volatile molecule leaves a surface and drifts. If it reaches a nose, it has to fit — physically fit — into a protein sitting in the membrane of a sensory neuron. That protein is an odorant receptor. If the shape works, the receptor changes conformation, the neuron fires, and a signal goes to the brain. If the shape does not work, nothing happens at all. Not a faint smell. Nothing. Humans carry about 400 intact odorant receptors. Any given molecule activates some combination of them, weakly or strongly, and what we experience as one smell is the pattern across that combination. The smell is not in the mushroom. It is in the meeting — and the meeting needs both halves. Which means the question “what does matsutake smell like?” is incomplete in the same way “how heavy is this?” would be incomplete without saying in what gravity. It smells like whatever it produces in the receptor array it lands in. Change the array and you change the smell, without touching the mushroom. The elk and the soil bacterium have wildly different arrays, so it is no surprise they end up somewhere different. The interesting question — the one with a number attached — is how different the arrays are between two people. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed · Stimpunks
Two people differ at over 30% of their receptor alleles

Measured, not asserted Two people differ at over 30% of their receptor alleles This is the spread the zine exists for, and the reason it is filed under a settled fact rather than a nice idea. Somebody went and counted. Mainland and colleagues screened human odorant receptors in a laboratory assay, found which molecules switched them on, and then asked how often the ordinary genetic variation between people actually changes whether a receptor works. The abstract states the results plainly: 63% of the odorant receptors we examined had polymorphisms that altered in vitro function. On average, two individuals have functional differences at over 30% of their odorant receptor alleles. Mainland et al., Nature Neuroscience 17, 114–120 (2014) Over thirty per cent. Not in exotic cases. Not between distant populations. Between any two people, on average, roughly a third of the equipment differs in ways that change what the equipment does. And they checked it against actual perception rather than stopping at the bench. Variation in one receptor, OR10G4, explained over 15% of the variation in how intense people found the smell of guaiacol, and over 10% of how pleasant or unpleasant they found it. The hedge is in the finding, and it stays. The same paper reports that OR10G4 genotype did not explain the variation for vanillin and ethyl vanillin, which bind that receptor more weakly. The effect is specific to a strong pairing rather than general. That limit is theirs and we print it, because a zine arguing that people are not interchangeable should not quietly make its own evidence broader than it is. Two people standing over the same mushroom are not running the same instrument. That is not a metaphor for anything. It is a measurement of protein function. Two amino acids decide what you are smelling

One molecule, three experiences Two amino acids decide what you are smelling The general figure is striking. The worked example is the one that is hard to argue with, because it goes all the way from a letter of DNA to a word a person says out loud. Androstenone is a steroid derived from testosterone. It turns up in sweat, in pork from uncastrated boars, in truffles. Keller and colleagues open with what people report when they smell it: variously perceived by different individuals as offensive (“sweaty, urinous”), pleasant (“sweet, floral”) or odourless. Keller et al., Nature 449, 468–472 (2007) Foul, lovely, or not there. Three people, one bottle. Then they found the mechanism. A single human receptor, OR7D4, responds to androstenone and its relative androstadienone — and to essentially nothing else, having been tested against a panel of 64 other odours and two solvents. A common variant of that receptor carries two amino acid substitutions, R88W and T133M, which severely impair how it works in the dish. People carrying the impaired version were, as a group, less sensitive to both steroids and found them less unpleasant. The genotype accounts for a significant share of both how strong the smell seems and whether it is horrible. So the argument about whether androstenone stinks was never an argument about androstenone. It was two proteins, differing at two positions, doing different things — and each person accurately reporting what their own equipment returned. Nobody in that room was wrong. There was no fact of the matter about the smell to be wrong about. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed · Stimpunks

Back to the autumn aroma Rotting things, or clear beauty Now the mushroom again, with the mechanism in hand. Tsing is unusually direct about the smell for someone who wrote a book in its praise, and her honesty is the thing to keep. It’s not an easy smell. It’s not like a flower or a mouth-watering food. It’s disturbing. Many people never learn to love it. It’s hard to describe. Some people liken it to rotting things and some to clear beauty — the autumn aroma. Tsing, on first being handed a matsutake in an Oregon forest Read that against the last two spreads and it stops being a remark about taste. Some people liken it to rotting things and some to clear beauty is exactly what you would predict of a complex volatile mixture landing in receptor arrays that differ at a third of their alleles. The usual framings for that disagreement are all available and all wrong in the same way. An acquired taste. A cultural preference. You have to learn to appreciate it. Each of them assumes one smell is arriving and people are responding to it well or badly — that there is a correct experience, and a distance from it that can be closed with effort or breeding. There may be no distance to close. If the arrays differ, the smells differ, and the person who says rotting things may be reporting their own arrival accurately and completely. Held honestly. Tsing’s sentence is ethnography, not a survey — she is reporting what people said to her over years of fieldwork, and nobody has run a controlled cross-population study of matsutake aroma perception that we could find. The receptor findings are general and do not name this mushroom. The link between them is ours, and it is a plausible mechanism rather than a demonstrated one. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed · Stimpunks

And the title, at last Two things nobody can standardise There is a second thing about matsutake that will not sit still, and it sits directly underneath the first. Nobody can farm it. Not for want of trying: Japanese research institutions have put decades and enormous sums into it, and the most recent review of the field still opens with the verdict that cultivation “has been mostly unsuccessful.” Commercial supply is still people walking into forests. The reason is that matsutake is not a self-contained organism. It lives in a transformative mutualism with the roots of particular trees, taking carbohydrates from the pine and foraging for it in return — and the field successes that exist were achieved using trees the fungus had already colonised, then waiting years. The only known way to farm it is to already have the relationship. Set the two facts side by side, because they are the same fact at two scales: What refuses to be standardised, and where Scale What it actually is Why it will not standardise In the ground a fungus and a pine root, exchanging take the tree away and there is nothing left to farm In the nose a molecule and a receptor, binding change the receptor and there is nothing left to agree about Both halves of this economy are relationships that somebody has mistaken for objects. The mushroom is not a product with a yield; it is the visible few days of an exchange decades old. The smell is not a property with a value; it is what happens when that exchange’s by-product meets a particular array of proteins. You cannot farm the first. You cannot standardise the second. It is the same refusal, twice. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed · Stimpunks
“You’re smelling it wrong” is not a sentence that means anything

There is no standard nose “You’re smelling it wrong” is not a sentence that means anything Everything above is chemistry and protein function. Here is what it does not license, and then what it does. It does not license everyone has their own truth. The variation here is the opposite of that: it is public, physical and measurable. You can sequence the receptor. You can express it in a dish and see what binds. Two people disagreeing about androstenone is not a breakdown of objectivity — it is an objective fact about two different proteins, and the disagreement was predictable before either of them opened the bottle. What it does license is narrower and harder. When someone reports a sensory experience you do not share, “you are exaggerating” and “you will get used to it” are not the modest, sceptical positions. They are the extravagant ones. They require that one receptor array be the real one and the others be errors relative to it — and no such array exists. There is no reference nose kept in a vault in Paris. “Normal” here is a statistic about a population, not a fact about a person. It tells you where most of the alleles fell. It does not tell you what arrived in anybody. Those of us who are Autistic hear the correction constantly, and rarely about mushrooms. The lights are fine. The shirt is fine. Nobody else can hear that. The last of those is often literally true and is being offered as though it settled something. It does not settle anything, because the question was never whether the room is loud. It is what arrived. The universe does not run a reference implementation of a nose. It just makes receptors, and they vary, and every one of them reports honestly. We love you down to your star stuff — not because the chemistry says so. The chemistry says nothing about who deserves what; it never has and it never could. Down to is not because of. What the chemistry removes is only an excuse: it takes away the pretence that there was a correct experience you were failing to have. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed · Stimpunks

What this is not Not: Not: “everyone has their own truth.” This is the reading to refuse hardest, because it sounds like the same thing and is its opposite. Receptor variation is public: sequenceable, expressible in a dish, testable against a panel of 64 odours. Two people smelling androstenone differently is not evidence that facts are soft. It is a hard fact about two proteins. Different instruments are not the same as no measurement. Not: a claim that all sensory reports are equally reliable about the world. A smoke alarm is right and your nose can be wrong about whether the house is burning. What varies here is what a molecule produces in a person — not whether the molecule is present. Both are checkable, and they are different questions. Not: a superpower story. Nobody here has a better nose. The person who cannot smell androstenone at all is not deficient and the person who finds it unbearable is not gifted. The array is not a score. Reaching for “heightened senses” regrades the same ruler instead of putting it down. Not: nature says be kind. That receptors vary is not why anyone deserves to be believed. Difference would deserve welcome in a universe where every nose was identical, and the argument for it was never resting on biology. See A Promise, Not a Finding. Down to is not because of. Not: an argument that accommodations are unnecessary because “everyone is different.” That sentence gets used to flatten specific needs into a general shrug. The finding is the reverse: the variation is specific, large and mapped, which is exactly what makes a particular request answerable rather than a matter of temperament. And: a limit we are keeping. No study links matsutake aroma to receptor genotype. The receptor work is general; the mushroom is the case that made the question vivid. The join between them is ours, and it is a mechanism we find plausible rather than one anybody has demonstrated. The Mushroom That Cannot Be Farmed · Stimpunks

Tidal force The near body wins The tide is the ocean answering to the sky. The Moon pulls hardest on the water directly beneath it, a little less on the rock of the Earth, less still on the far ocean — and that difference in pull, stretched across the planet, lifts a bulge on each side. Two bulges, turning under us: two high tides a day. Here is the strange part. The Sun is 27 million times more massive than the Moon, and it hauls on the Earth with over 170 times the raw force. Yet the Moon runs the tide. Tidal force falls off not with distance but with distance cubed — so the small, close body overwhelms the vast, far one. Distance matters more than mass. You are pulled most by what is nearest — not by what is largest. The Sun is 27 million times heavier. The Moon still owns the tide. Nearness beats mass. SUN 27,000,000× heavier far · loses the tide the ocean MOON near · wins force ∝ 1 / distance³ the small near body wins tidal pull falls off as the cube The Nearest Body · Stimpunks

a safe-enough body your nervous system pull across the gap gravity acts at a distance the moon never touches the sea Co-regulation · polyvagal Co-regulation is gravity Now read yourself as the water. Co-regulation is what it feels like when a safe-enough nervous system comes near: soft gaze, an unhurried voice, a steady heartbeat — and yours begins to fall into time with it. You don't settle by force of will. You are pulled into rhythm by a nearby body. Polyvagal theory offers a name for it: resonance with another regulated nervous system as the deepest safety signal there is, letting your body drop into a calm, social, at-ease state. (Polyvagal's finer physiology is contested; the settling you feel in safe company is not.) And gravity crosses a gap. Being with someone can be a felt presence, not a hand on the shoulder: a shared game, music in a chat, someone in the next room. Near enough to pull; not so near it overwhelms. You do not have to be touched to be moved. The moon never touches the sea. It only has to be near enough to pull. The Nearest Body · Stimpunks

Spring & neap · parallel presence Two high tides No body of water answers to a single pull. The Sun tugs too — and when Sun and Moon line up, their pulls add into a spring tide: high highs, low lows, a deep and easy rhythm. When they sit at right angles, the pulls half-cancel into a neap tide — flat, muddled, hard to read. So it is with us. When your people, your places, and your routines are all in safe mode at once, regulation comes easy; everything is pulling the same way. When they pull against each other, you go slack and confused, no tide to speak of. And two bodies can settle into one rhythm without ever merging. The Moon turns once for every orbit, forever showing the Earth a single face — tidally locked. That is parallel presence and body doubling: two people in one orbit, each a steady face for the other, together and separate at once. Aligned, the pulls add. Crossed, they cancel. We regulate best when our moons agree. SPRING · aligned pulls add → big tide NEAP · crossed half-cancel flat tide aligned moons deepen the tide crossed pulls flatten it The Nearest Body · Stimpunks

VENTRAL · safe moon SYMPATHETIC · meerkat no moon · no rhythm DORSAL · ebbed flat gone still swell · chop · flat a sea needs a moon to keep time Meerkat mode When there is no moon Take the moon away and the water doesn't rest — it churns. No steady pull to organize it, so it heaves every direction at once, hunting for anything to lock onto. Autistic and AuDHD folks know this state: meerkat mode — up on the hind legs, scanning for threat, unable to settle or focus, an overwhelmed monotropic mind desperate for a hook into flow. It gets misread as clinginess, as over-attachment, as too much need. It is none of those. It is a nervous system starved of a moon. The constant reaching for a safe person isn't a flaw in the water — it's a tide with nothing to answer to. You do not settle a churning sea by ordering the waves to stop. You restore its moon. A churning sea isn't broken. It's a tide that lost its moon. The Nearest Body · Stimpunks
The storm is in the weather

Ecosystemic distress · ARLES The storm is in the weather When the sea won't settle, we go looking for the fault in the water. But water has no weather of its own. The storm comes from the system overhead; the flooding comes from where someone built the seawall too low, dredged the channel, paved the marsh that used to drink the surge. Stimpunks calls this the ecosystemic model of distress: dysregulation lives in the relationship between a bodymind and its environment, not inside the person. Read ARLES downward and a failing system points to the environment that made it, the environment to the lived experience it ignored, and down to the attention and the nervous system it never once accounted for. Broken systems, not broken people. Nota broken nervous system — a body of water doing exactly what water does near a storm. Notover-attachment or "too needy" — a tide reaching for the moon it was starved of. Notlimerence: co-regulation is mutual and safe; limerence is one-sided and uncertain. Not every strong pull regulates you; some only pull you under. Notcalm-down-by-willpower — you settle a sea by restoring its moon, not by scolding the waves. Nota fault in the person — the storm is in the weather and the seawalls. the system seawall the water is not the problem look up, not down broken systems, not broken people The Nearest Body · Stimpunks

high low predictable · and yours read the table, go with it every coast keeps its own clock Regulation-first · chronodiversity The tide table The oldest gift the tide gives is that it can be known. Sailors don't fight the sea; they read the table and go with it. Regulation-first is the same discipline — settle the nervous system before you ask anything of it. Learn your own rhythms; build rooms that publish theirs. And no two tables match. Every coast keeps its own clock; chronodiversity means your high tide is not mine — and a world worth living in stops treating one timetable as the only real one. Come in with the tide. You were never meant to hold the ocean still. Find your moons — the near ones, the safe-enough ones — and let them pull you into time. Be a moon for someone. Let someone be a moon for you. The Nearest Body is the seventeenth zine in the Stimpunks series. After the more-than-human trilogy (Nos. 14–16), it picks the water back up and turns it inward: from a council of beings dissolving into flow, to the single body of water pulled by the bodies nearest it. The science is settled and citable. Tides are the ocean answering to the difference in gravity across the Earth, raising a bulge on each side — two high tides a lunar day. The Sun out-masses the Moon roughly 27 million times and out-pulls it more than 170-fold, yet the Moon raises the larger tide, because tide-generating force falls off as the cube of distance rather than the square: distance matters more than mass (NOAA Ocean Service; Stanford Solar Center). The teaching A father told his daughter The sentence this zine is about did not arrive as a slogan. It arrived as something a man said to his child, more than once, the way you say a thing you want someone to still have after you are gone. Jessica Hernandez is Maya Ch'orti' and Binnizá — Zapotec — an environmental scientist who writes about Indigenous science and the landscapes it heals. In Fresh Banana Leaves she sets the teaching down in her father's voice, not her own: “He always told me that as long as we protect nature, nature will protect us.” Jessica Hernandez, Fresh Banana Leaves, 2022 — reporting her father It sits inside a larger thing he taught her: that our animal and plant relatives are watching over us too, and that the more we take care of them, the more they take care of us. Later she restates it in her own voice — “nature protects us as long as we protect nature” — and adds that this is something Western science has failed to understand or explain. Keep the chain. A teaching has a direction and a household, and both are part of what it means. Strip them and you get a bumper sticker; the words survive and the relation they came out of does not. Why this matters before anything else. A great deal of what follows depends on this being a specific teaching from a specific tradition, transmitted person to person — not a general truth about Nature that anyone may pick up. We are quoting a daughter quoting her father, and that is how it will be cited on every page here. what a teaching carries her father Zapotec · Ch'orti' Hernandez writes it down this page names the chain what a slogan does to it keeps the words drops who said it to whom and out of what the relation is the part that gets lost Figure 1 · A teaching has a household. Keep it. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks
Three words we have heard before

The conditional Three words we have heard before Read the sentence again and notice what it opens with. As long as. For a lot of us that is not a neutral phrase. It is the exact grammar in which belonging has been offered to us our whole lives, and always with the same shape: you may stay, on terms. As long as you can make eye contact. As long as you keep up. As long as the accommodation doesn't cost anything. As long as you're the good kind. As long as you don't stim in the meeting, don't go non-speaking at the wrong moment, don't need the thing you need twice in one week. As long as you're not too much. Every one of those is a conditional, and every one of them means the same thing underneath: your place here is a payment plan, and you are always one missed instalment from losing it. So when a sentence arrives saying as long as we protect nature, nature will protect us, a lot of us hear a contract — and hearing it is not a failure of reading. It is a well-trained ear doing exactly what it learned to do. The flinch is correct. It is just aimed at the wrong sentence. If you have been offered belonging on terms, you learn to hear the terms first. That reflex has kept people safe. It is worth keeping — and worth checking. the conditional, as we usually meet it belonging (behind the gate) as long as you mask as long as you keep up as long as it's free as long as you're the good kind as long as you're not too much a place you can be evicted from Figure 2 · Conditional belonging. The reflex it trains is a good one. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks
One word settles the whole thing

Able, not willing One word settles the whole thing A few pages after the teaching, Hernandez extends it — and the extension is where the contract reading dies. She writes that as long as we continue to remove ourselves from nature, nature will not be able to protect us from environmental impacts. Able. Not willing. Not prepared to. Not obliged to, having received nothing. That is a claim about capacity, and a contract has nothing to do with capacity. A party to a contract who is not paid withholds. It still could; it declines to. That is what makes it leverage, and leverage is what makes the conditional frightening. What Hernandez describes is the other thing entirely. Remove yourself far enough from a system and it does not start refusing you — it simply can no longer reach you. The protection was never a service being rendered. It was a property of being inside the relation, and you have stepped outside it. Nobody is withholding. Nobody is keeping the account. There is no gate, and there is no gatekeeper, and the thing you were braced for was never there. Not a payment withheld. A relation severed. Nature is not refusing to pay us. We walked out of the room. A sibling to this argument. The Rest You Keep (No. 59) makes the same move against a ledger — rest is not a reward released after enough work, because nothing was ever keeping score. This one makes it against a contract. Different machinery, and both of them missing. two ways a thing can fail to reach you contract us nature payment withheld it COULD. it declines to. = leverage = something to fear relation nature us out of reach it CANNOT. we left. = no leverage = nothing to earn Hernandez wrote ABLE. that is the right-hand box. Figure 3 · Withheld, or unreachable. Only one of them is a threat. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks
Three qualities, one of them hedged

Attention Three qualities, one of them hedged If the relation is not a contract, what is it made of? Barry Lopez answered that in 1997, in an essay called A Literature of Place, and he was careful in a way that matters. He names three qualities that make a lasting connection to a place: paying intimate attention; a storied relationship to a place rather than a solely sensory awareness of it; and living in some sort of ethical unity with a place. Read that third one slowly. Some sort of. Lopez is describing something he is sure is there and not sure how to name, and he leaves the uncertainty in the sentence where a reader can see it. That hedge is not weakness. It is a writer refusing to sound more certain than he is about somebody else's relationship to the ground. Start with the first. Paying intimate attention is the whole entry point, and it is also — read from where we are standing — a description of monotropic attention: a deep single channel that goes far into one thing rather than thinly across many. Lopez calls it the beginning of connection. We get told it is a symptom. The same attention. Two completely different names, depending on who is doing it and whether anyone thought to ask what it was for. The child who can tell you every stone in one creek is not failing to be interested in the world. They are doing the first of Lopez's three things, and doing it well. Lopez, 1997 — as he actually wrote it paying intimate attention no hedge a storied relationship — not a solely sensory awareness of it no hedge living in SOME SORT OF ethical unity with a place hedged — and he meant to “a fundamental human defense against loneliness” Figure 4 · Three qualities, and what Lopez says they are for. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks

Relational Where Lopez got it Here is the part that usually gets left out, and it changes the shape of everything. In the paragraph immediately before the three qualities, Lopez explains where he found them. He travels to remote places and depends on interpreters, and, he writes, “eminent among such helpers are indigenous people” — for whom he then gives three reasons: they attend more closely to nuance in the physical world and see more; their history in a place runs deep, which gives a spatial landscape a dimension in time; and they tend to occupy the same moral universe as the land they sense. Then, and only then, the three qualities. The framework is a description of a relationship Lopez was shown. He says so himself, in order, on the page. Which means Hernandez is not a supporting citation propping up a Lopez idea. It is the other way round. She is the tradition, speaking for itself, in the first person, without needing an interpreter. And notice what happens to the hedge. Lopez, honestly and from outside, writes some sort of ethical unity. Hernandez's father, from inside, needs no qualifier at all. He just tells his daughter how it is. “Indigenous people tend to occupy the same moral universe as the land they sense. Their bonds with the earth are as much moral and biological.” Barry Lopez, A Literature of Place, 1997 — the paragraph before the three qualities “As long as we protect nature, nature will protect us.” Hernandez's father — the same claim, from inside, unhedged “Many of us, I think, long to become the companion of a place, not its authority, not its owner.” Barry Lopez, A Literature of Place, 1997 The order of citation is the argument. It is easy — and common — to quote Lopez's three qualities as a tidy framework and then reach for an Indigenous writer as illustration. That inverts the direction the knowledge actually travelled, and Lopez's own paragraph is the evidence against doing it. We put him second here on purpose. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks

What it is for The place knows you're there Lopez does not leave the three qualities hanging as an aesthetic. He says what they are for, and the answer is not stewardship, or virtue, or a healthier planet, though he cares about all three. He says they are “a fundamental human defense against loneliness.” And then he says how it works — which is the sentence this zine is named after: “If you're intimate with a place, a place with whose history you're familiar, and you establish an ethical conversation with it, the implication that follows is this: the place knows you're there. It feels you. You will not be forgotten, cut off, abandoned.” Barry Lopez, A Literature of Place, 1997 Sit with what is being claimed. Not you will feel better. Not you will have communed with something. Something much more specific: you will be known. Somewhere will hold the fact of you. That is a claim about recognition — and recognition is the thing a great many of us have been going without in rooms full of people. Held honestly. Lopez writes the implication that follows, and the sentences after it are the shape of a felt conviction, not a measurement. We are not claiming a creek has a mind, or that it registers you the way a friend does. The claim on this page is about what the relation does to the person in it — and that part is not mystical at all. what the three qualities are for intimate attention storied relationship ethical unity a fundamental human defense against loneliness the mechanism he gives: the place knows you're there Figure 5 · Not virtue. Not stewardship. Recognition. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks
Lonely in a room full of people

Lived experience Lonely in a room full of people Lopez said loneliness. So let us be precise about which loneliness, because there is a version of it that the usual advice cannot touch. Hari Srinivasan's Presence Without Belonging (2026) is about exactly this. Autistic loneliness, he argues, is routinely misread as social isolation or low social motivation — when in fact it very often happens in the middle of ongoing social participation. We are at the job, in the class, at the table. And still not there. His framework separates presence from belonging, and names three conditions belonging actually requires: Recognition — being understood and taken seriously as a social subject. Access — being able to participate without extraordinary communicative, sensory or temporal effort. Sustainability — participation you can keep up over time without disproportionate cumulative cost. Take away any one and you get presence without belonging: contact without connection, which is lonelier than being alone and much harder to explain to anyone. Now hold that beside Lopez. He is describing a relationship that delivers recognition — the place knows you're there — and it asks no mask for it, charges no extraordinary entry cost, and runs on the kind of attention we already have rather than the kind we have to perform. That is not nature being therapeutic. That is a relation whose access requirements we happen to meet. three conditions belonging needs a room a place recognition access sustainability understood, taken seriously no extraordinary effort no cumulative cost presence without belonging belonging not every room fails these, and not every place is reachable. this is the common case, not a law. Environment No word for conservation Hernandez makes an observation about her own language that does more work than a whole shelf of argument. In the Zapotec variant her family speaks, there is no word that translates directly to conservation. The nearest they could arrive at are gapanú — to take care of something — and rianda — to heal. Neither one carries what conservation means. And she draws the conclusion herself: conservation was not needed before colonization, so Indigenous languages can serve as indicators of what has been introduced into our lands. She therefore chooses to say healing rather than conservation, because healing is what her culture actually holds. Think about what a missing word is evidence of. Not a gap in the language. A gap in the problem. You do not build a word for setting a bone in a world where nobody falls. And this is the same move the whole zine has been making, arriving from a different direction. A vocabulary of protection-as-transaction — conserve, offset, manage, steward the resource — is not the older layer that got covered over. It is the newer one. The relation came first, and it did not need contract language, because it was never a contract. Not a claim about all Indigenous languages. This is one variant of Zapotec, described by one speaker about her own family's speech, and she says plainly that languages adapt and vocabularies grow. It is evidence about a specific language, offered by someone entitled to offer it — not a general law about Indigenous thought. reaching for a word that isn't there gapanú to take care of something rianda to heal “conservation” no direct translation a missing word is evidence about the world, not about the language Figure 7 · What was never needed did not get a name. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks
The straw ban, and who paid for it

Systems The straw ban, and who paid for it Hernandez has one more thing to say, and it is the reason this zine belongs on a site about disability rather than a site about nature. She argues that Indigenous holistic thinking is not systems thinking, because many Indigenous communities do not divide the world into systems in the first place. Western knowledge separates everything into systems and boxes — which is why the environmental sciences fan out into an array of disciplines that do not speak to each other. And then she gives the example, and it is ours: Seattle's 2018 ban on plastic straws. An environmental solution, designed inside the environment box. Outside that box, disabled people lost access to an essential tool. She quotes Alice Wong on why plastic straws are essential — the harm was documented by the people it landed on, as it always is. Her point is not that the ban was well-meant but clumsy. It is structural: when everything is separated into systems, more harm can be done with the solutions that are thought of. The box is what produces the harm. Draw the boundary and everything outside it becomes somebody else's department. Which is the same severance the whole zine has been circling. Remove ourselves from the relation and nature cannot reach us. Remove disabled people from the environmental box and the solution cannot see us. Same cut, two casualties. An environmental policy that harms disabled people is not a trade-off between two goods. It is one failure — the failure to have been in relation with everyone the decision touches. what a box does to a solution boxed environment disability: outside = not consulted not boxed both in the room straw ban, 2018 access removed a solution that costs no one the box is not a simplification. it is the harm. Figure 8 · After Hernandez on holistic thinking, and Alice Wong on straws. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks

Held honestly What this zine refuses This is an argument about belonging that runs through land, and that is a road with a great many potholes in it. Here are the ones we are steering around, named so you can hold us to them. The largest is the easiest to fall into and the hardest to see from inside: the slide from a place can offer recognition to nature is good for you. The second sentence sounds like the first being friendly. It is not. It turns a relation back into a service, which is precisely the thing spread 4 spent its whole length taking apart. And one that is ours specifically. An argument that we find recognition outdoors must never become another room with a door on it. Plenty of us cannot get to a creek — because of pain, money, transport, safety, a body that does not do stairs or heat or distance, a neighbourhood with no green in it. A windowbox counts. A pigeon on a ledge counts. One tree you know the state of, all year, counts. Lopez's requirement is intimacy, not acreage. Nota contract. Protection is not a payment we render and nature returns. As long as here describes a relation's reach, not its terms. Nobody is keeping the account. Notnature as therapy. We are not prescribing the outdoors, and a place is not a treatment that works on us. Extracting wellbeing from land is the same logic as extracting anything else from it. Not“neurodivergent people are closer to nature.” That is the noble-savage move pointed at us, and it has been used to explain why we belong outside rather than in the building. We are not more natural. The access requirements simply differ. Notspeaking for other beings. The collection's standing refusal, and it applies double here: saying a place knows you are there is not a claim to know what it would say. Notthe naturalistic fallacy. Nothing here argues that because the relation is old or natural, it is therefore right, or that your belonging is licensed by an ecosystem. The universe does not owe us a precedent. Nota general Indigenous wisdom. Every claim on these pages belongs to a named person from a named tradition — a Zapotec and Maya Ch'orti' scientist, quoting her father. Not a mood. Not a category. Notone more thing to be failing at. If this reads as a standard of connection you are not meeting, put it down. It is a description of something available, not an assignment. The Place Knows You're There · Stimpunks

Pick a room you are in every week. Which of the three is missing? Sources & notes. Hernandez, J. (2022). Fresh Banana Leaves: Healing Indigenous Landscapes Through Indigenous Science. The teaching quoted throughout is her father's, reported by her — “He always told me that as long as we protect nature, nature will protect us” — alongside his fuller teaching that our animal and plant relatives watch over us and that the more we care for them the more they care for us. Her own restatement, “nature protects us as long as we protect nature… this is something Western science has failed to understand or explain,” and the extension the argument on spread 4 turns on, “as long as we continue to remove ourselves from nature, nature will not be able to protect us from environmental impacts,” are both hers. Srinivasan, H. (2026). “Presence Without Belonging: A Conceptual Analysis of Loneliness in Autism.” Autism in Adulthood, DOI 10.1177/25739581261448524 — the Presence Without Belonging framework and its three conditions, recognition, access and sustainability. On the ecological reading of Autistic experience this piece sits beside, see Helen Edgar's Neuroqueering Relational Ecologies: Autistic Weathering and the Body Without Organs (More Realms), which takes the same relation through Ombre Tarragnat's weather-body and Astrida Neimanis's bodies of water. Stimpunks' place-based education and nature glossary entries are where this zine started. A correction, and it is ours. Lopez's three qualities circulate widely — including in our own Stimpunks glossary, and in a Stimpunks post — under the name “reciprocal ethical unity,” presented as his framework. He never wrote that phrase. What he wrote is “paying intimate attention; a storied relationship to a place rather than a solely sensory awareness of it; and living in some sort of ethical unity with a place.” The word reciprocal appears in the next paragraph, in a question he asks on the reader's behalf — “How can you find such a reciprocity?” — and again later, in “an ethical and reciprocal relationship with everything around us.” So the familiar phrase is a portmanteau of two separate moves, and in fusing them it does something worse than compress: it hardens Lopez's deliberate hedge, some sort of, into a term of art, and converts a question into a listed quality. We carried the compressed version ourselves before checking the essay, which is the only reason we can describe how it happens. The glossary entries are flagged for the same fix. Related, and found in the same pass: a Stimpunks post attributes to Lopez the line about living “as if your children's future mattered” — that is Robin Wall Kimmerer, in Braiding Sweetgrass, and it is not quoted here because we have not yet confirmed it against the book rather than against quotation sites. Honesty notes. Three things held loosely. First: Lopez writes “the place knows you're there. It feels you” as an implication that follows — the shape of a conviction, not a measurement, and no claim is made here that a landscape registers a person the way a person does. What is claimed is what the relation does to the human in it. Second: the pairing of Lopez's loneliness claim with Srinivasan's framework is ours, not theirs. Lopez died in 2020 and never read Srinivasan; Srinivasan's paper is about human social participation and says nothing about land. Two authors, twenty-nine years apart, are being put in a room together by us — the resemblance is a rhyme, not a result, and the columns in Figure 6 are our reading. Third: reading Lopez's “intimate attention” as monotropic attention is likewise our move and not his; monotropism is a theory of Autistic attention, not a theory of place, and the overlap is a description we find useful rather than a finding either literature reports. You do not have to earn the ground. Go and be known by something. Love you down to your star stuff.
