82 Star Stuff The Play You Keep on forty-five bumble bees, nine hundred and ten rolls of a wooden ball, and the definition science had to write down before it could see doing nothing at all for everyone asked what the point of that was L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely
Nine hundred and ten times, for nothing

What they actually did Nine hundred and ten times, for nothing In a laboratory at Queen Mary University of London, forty-five bumble bees were given a clear, unobstructed path to a dish of sugar water. Along the sides of that path, out of the way, somebody had left some small wooden balls. The bees did not need the balls. They could reach the sucrose without going near one. Nothing was hidden underneath them, nothing was gained by touching them, and no bee was ever rewarded for doing so. Over the course of the study, forty-five bees rolled those balls 910 times. Some bees went back again and again. They pushed the balls in different directions, over different distances, in patterns that were not the same twice. Then they went and got their sugar, which had been there the whole time. The paper is called Do bumble bees play? — and the reason it takes thirteen pages to answer is that the answer had to be defended against every cheaper explanation first. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks
Somebody had to write down what doing nothing means

The definition Somebody had to write down what doing nothing means This is the part worth stopping on, and it is easy to read past. Before anyone could say whether a bee was playing, the field had to agree on what play is — formally, in criteria you can fail. That work is Gordon Burghardt’s, in The Genesis of Animal Play (2005), and the criteria are deliberately strict, because play is exactly the thing a hopeful observer sees everywhere. Ball rolling was tested against all five. Burghardt’s five criteria, and what the bees did The criterion What it rules out Met? Not fully functional food, mates, shelter — any immediate adaptive outcome yes Intrinsically rewarding anything the animal had to be paid to do yes Different in form ordinary working behaviour, done in the usual way yes Repeated, not stereotyped a one-off accident; a fixed, identical loop yes Begun unstressed anything driven by hunger, threat or distress yes The authors also excluded, by the design of the apparatus and by watching what the bees did, that the rolling was foraging, clearing clutter out of the way, or mating behaviour. Read the first row again. The opening requirement for something to count as play is that it must not accomplish anything. Uselessness is not the absence of a category here. It is the entry condition, it is written down, and it can be checked. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks
Repeated, and never the same twice

Criterion four Repeated, and never the same twice The fourth criterion is the subtle one, and it is the one that carries this zine’s argument furthest. Play has to be repeated — otherwise it is a one-off accident, an animal bumping into something. But it must not be stereotyped: not a fixed loop run identically each time. The amount of ball rolling varied within individual bees and between them. A bee came back to it, and did it differently. Repetition was not the problem. Sameness would have been. That distinction is worth holding, because we are so often handed the opposite one. A returning, absorbing, repeated interest gets read as a rut — something to be interrupted, redirected, or counted in a column. The formal literature on play makes precisely the reverse move: it asks whether the repetition varies, and treats variation as the evidence of something alive rather than something stuck. A thing can be done over and over and still be free. The bees were not running a program. They were doing it again, which is a different word. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks
They came back for the room

The second experiment They came back for the room Criterion two says the behaviour has to be rewarding in and of itself. That is a strong claim about an insect, so the authors went and tested it separately. Bees were given two chambers of different colours. In one, the balls could be moved. In the other, they could not. The bees learned the difference. Then both chambers were emptied — no balls in either — and the bees were offered the choice again. They chose the colour of the room where the rolling had happened. There was nothing to roll. There was nothing to eat. What was left was the place, and a colour associated with having done something worthless there, and that was enough to bring them back. This is what makes the finding hard to argue away. A bee that rolls a ball might be confused about something. A bee that returns to an empty room because of what it once did there is reporting on how the doing felt. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks

Sufficient on its own terms Joy is not a compensation Ask what the literature on Autistic lives is about, and the honest answer for a long time was: what is hard. Deficit, burden, cost, risk, outcome. The vocabulary for the other half arrived late and arrived thin. Elliot Wassell’s study of Autistic joy (Disability & Society, 2025) asked 86 of us a question the field had mostly skipped: what makes you happy? A majority reported experiencing joy often. Three themes came back — that the Autistic sensorium is itself a source of joy, that our interests matter enormously, and that joy needs circumstances being just right. Notice what the third one costs, and hold it for two spreads. Joy is not the receipt for having endured something. It does not settle a debt, and it is not evidence that the hard parts were worth it. The bees are useful here for one narrow reason: nobody asked what the ball rolling was for before agreeing it counted. The paper did not have to show that play made the bees better foragers to publish the finding that they play. The activity was permitted to be its own justification, which is a courtesy the science extends to a bumble bee more readily than the world extends to us. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks
The young ones rolled the most

Three to seven days The young ones rolled the most Bees rolled more when they were younger — most of all between three and seven days from eclosion, which is when a bee emerges as an adult. The pattern rises and then falls, which is the shape play takes in young mammals too. It was not about experience. Bees that had met balls before and bees that had not showed the same age effect. Being young was the thing. And there is a second fact sitting next to it. A bumble bee’s mushroom bodies — the parts of the insect brain that handle sensory information and memory — are at their most plastic in the first seven days after eclosion. The play and the plasticity occupy the same window. The authors decline to close that gap, and so do we. Whether the overlap between play and neural plasticity in any animal is causally linked, they write, will require further research. It is a striking coincidence that has not been shown to be more than one. What the age curve does not support is the reading we get handed constantly: that play is a stage, and growing up means coming out the other side of it. The older bees did not stop. They rolled less. Nobody in this study called the older bee cured. days 3–7 age — days from eclosion → ball rolling less — not none Schematic, not plotted from the published data. The shape is the reported one; the axis values are not. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks

The sentence in the limitations The time nobody had claimed Male bees rolled individual balls for longer than female bees did. The authors offer an explanation, and it is the most useful sentence in the paper. The females had constant access to pollen and nectar — which is to say, they had a job. The colony’s work was in front of them and available at all times. The males had no such call on their hours. In the authors’ own phrasing, the males had more “free time” in laboratory conditions: less motivation to stop. The motivation for carrying out functional activities may limit how long individuals can engage with a play activity at any one time. Galpayage Dona et al. (2022), paraphrasing Burghardt (2005) Read plainly, that is a claim about environments rather than about bees. Play did not expand into the animals with more capacity for it. It expanded into the hours that function had not already claimed. The variable was not who wanted to play. It was who was free to. We know this one from the inside. The question “why don’t you do things you enjoy any more” is almost always answered by an audit of the week rather than an audit of the person — and the audit is rarely the thing anybody offers to change. Wassell’s third theme was circumstances being just right. Circumstances are somebody’s decision. claimed by function a job that is always available unclaimed — the play goes here same animal, different week Schematic. The paper reports a duration difference by sex; the account of why is the authors’ own, and is offered as one. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks

What the paper says against itself Held honestly A finding this charming is exactly the kind this collection is supposed to be careful with. So here is what the authors say against their own result, in their own paper, without being asked. They cannot exclude captivity. Object play in bumble bees may, they write, follow a lack of stimulation that the natural environment would otherwise provide. Captive animals are given play opportunities as enrichment for exactly that reason. The bees were in a box. It has not been shown in the wild. Their own recommendation is that future work should examine whether play-like actions occur outside the laboratory. Nobody has watched a bumble bee do this in a meadow. The motivation is unknown. Further research is needed, they say, to identify what actually drives the rolling. And the conclusion hedges its own verb. What they report is a behavioural phenomenon resembling object play — not a proof of an inner life. They say it adds to a growing body of evidence for a form of sentience in insects, which is a careful sentence and should stay careful. None of that is a retreat. It is what a finding looks like when the people who found it would rather be right than quoted. We are keeping the whole of it, hedges included, because a fact that has to be trimmed to carry an argument was never carrying it. The criteria were met. The place preference held. The age curve is real. What is unsettled is unsettled on the page. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks

Who set the test Productivity was never the test There is a habit of mind that hears “a bee played” and immediately asks what advantage it conferred. That reflex has a history, and it is not a neutral one. Robert Chapman’s Empire of Normality (2023) gives the structural account: normality is manufactured and enforced rather than found — a standard produced under industrial capitalism, against which people are sorted by what they yield. Nick Walker names the same machinery as the neuronormative paradigm, in Neuroqueer Heresies (2021). Neither is a claim that difference is imaginary. Both are claims about who wrote the ruler. This zine adds one narrow thing to that, and it comes from the method rather than from us: A formal scientific standard exists for doing something worthless, it has five criteria, and not one of them asks what the behaviour was for. Burghardt’s framework does not require play to pay. It requires the opposite — it disqualifies anything that pays. A whole research literature runs on a definition in which usefulness is disqualifying, and it has been running for decades without collapsing into incoherence. So the demand that our interests justify themselves by output is not the rigorous position in the room. It is the parochial one. The rigorous people gave a bumble bee the benefit of the doubt and wrote down criteria that would let them be wrong. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks

What this does not say What this does not say A zine about play is unusually easy to turn into homework. So, plainly: Not:play as therapy. The moment play is prescribed for an outcome — regulation, skills, engagement, progress toward a goal somebody else set — it stops meeting the first criterion. A thing that has to justify itself is not the thing described in this zine, whatever it is called on the form. Not:“even insects play, so you have no excuse.” That converts a finding into an obligation, and an obligation is the one thing play cannot survive. Spread eight is the answer: if it is not happening, look at the week before you look at the person. Not:stimming reframed as play. Stimming is regulation, it is ours, and it does not need a second job. The play literature separates play from what it calls habitual ticks — that is a behavioural category inside an ethology paper, carrying no verdict about anybody, and we are not importing it as one. Not:joy as the payment for hardship. Nothing here says the difficult parts were worth it because of the good ones. Joy is not a receipt, a silver lining, or evidence that a system was survivable. It is sufficient on its own, which is a smaller and much better claim. Not:a claim about what it is like to be a bee. The authors say resembling object play, and a form of sentience, and we are keeping both hedges. We do not know what the rolling felt like. We know it was worth returning to an empty room for. Not:a proof. A rhyme, not a proof. Bombus terrestris settles nothing about a human life, and nothing that is true of us is made true by an insect. What the study supplies is one carefully measured case in which a behaviour that accomplishes nothing was studied seriously, on criteria that never once asked it to pay for itself. The Play You Keep · Stimpunks

no brain. it sleeps anyway. 59 Rest The Rest You Keep on Autistic rest, monotropism, burnout — and the ledger that was never there L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff with Helen Edgar · open edition · print freely

The finding Nobody files a report Hydra is a real animal, not a thought experiment. A freshwater creature a centimetre or two long, related to jellyfish and coral, usually found clinging by its foot to a pond plant with a ring of tentacles at the other end. It has no brain. No central nervous system at all — just a loose mesh of nerve cells spread through the body, with nothing anywhere gathering that mesh into a decision-maker. And Hydra sleeps. It goes still. It is harder to rouse. Keep it awake and it sleeps longer afterwards to make up the debt, and falls asleep quicker when you let it — which is the homeostatic signature, the thing that separates sleep from merely sitting there. Keep it awake long enough and the number of dividing cells drops off. So rest is not a bonus feature bolted onto a body's real work. In an animal with no brain to argue the point, rest is part of how the body gets built and stays working at all. Which puts the usual story in a strange position. The assumption that rest must be earned — tracked, justified, released once enough has been put in — requires something keeping score. A ledger. An account with a balance. Hydra has no ledger. It rests anyway. Held honestly, and early. This is not the argument that Hydra rests, therefore your rest is natural, therefore it is allowed. Using natural to mean permitted is its own trap, and this collection refuses it everywhere else — the universe does not owe us a precedent, and a resemblance is a rhyme, not a proof. Hydra is not evidence that you are allowed to rest. Hydra is evidence that the thing you were asking permission from was never there. one animal · no brain · three criteria Hydra vulgaris nerve net · no centre 1 · goes quiescent 2 · harder to rouse 3 · rebounds after loss all three · met dividing cells slept deprived rest is when the building happens Kanaya et al. 2020 · Science Advances a sleep-like state, in an animal with no brain The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Attention The tunnel, not the line One more thing about Hydra, because it is the hinge. Put it in constant light or constant dark and its daily rhythm vanishes — it has no circadian clock to free-run. What is left is a cycle of roughly four hours, returning and returning. So the oldest resting animal we can point to is not keeping time against a day. It rests on a rhythm of its own that comes back around. Which is the shape a lot of us already know. Autistic attention often does not spread thinly across many things at once; it pools, and goes deep into a few. That is monotropism — Dinah Murray, Mike Lesser and Wenn Lawson, 2005 — and time inside that kind of focus has its own shape. Not slower or faster. Helen Edgar calls it spiral time: not a line you are falling behind on, but a spiral you are moving through, returning to the same place on purpose. Now the consequence, which is the whole reason this spread exists. If rest is offered by pulling that attention away — the meditation app, the walk, the gentle activity, when what the mind actually wants is stillness with the interest still in view — then it is not rest. It is another demand, wearing a rest costume. Rest that fights your attention is not rest. Helen Edgar · Reclaiming Rest (2025) For attention that works this way, rest often means staying in the tunnel. Going further into the one thing. Not being pulled out of it and told to relax. What this is not. Hydra's four-hour cycle is not monotropic time, and no shared mechanism is being claimed — one is a cnidarian ultradian rhythm and the other is how human attention is organised. The rhyme is worth noticing and it is not evidence. The monotropic account stands on its own literature, and on us. two shapes of time the line you fall behind on one direction · no returning the spiral you move through returning is the method attention, not exhaustion Murray, Lesser & Lawson 2005 · Edgar on monotropic time deeper in is a direction, not a retreat The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks
Rest is not the opposite of motion

On the wing Rest is not the opposite of motion A great frigatebird can stay in the air for up to two months without landing. Weimerskirch and colleagues tracked them across the Indian Ocean, riding thermals up and gliding down in a roller-coaster that costs them almost nothing. That is one study, and it is about where the birds go. A different team asked a different question of the same species: what is the brain doing up there? They fitted EEG recorders and followed non-stop foraging flights of up to ten days and three thousand kilometres — different birds on different trips, not the two-month records. Over those flights the birds slept an average of 42 minutes a day. Back on land: over twelve hours. The detail that matters is how. Slow-wave sleep arrived in bouts that could run several minutes; the REM episodes lasted only seconds. It was more often one hemisphere at a time in the air than it ever is on land, with the open eye generally facing the direction of the turn — though both hemispheres did sometimes go under together, so half a brain awake is not a requirement for staying up. And it happened while the birds soared on rising air, never while they flapped. So rest here did not require stillness. It required a system that could rest part of itself while another part kept working — and a glide, rather than a wingbeat, to do it in. It slept in the glide. Nothing stopped. Two studies, two claims, and not a target. The two-month figure and the 42-minute figure come from different work and are not one finding; the sleep study's own flights ran up to ten days. And 42 minutes is sleep restriction, not an achievement — the birds catch up on land, and nothing here suggests a body thrives on less. The point is narrower: rest was possible mid-flight, in pieces, without the motion stopping. one bird · two hemispheres asleep awake · watching more often aloft than ashore sleep per day 42 min in flight 12+ hrs on land it slept in the glide Rattenborg et al. 2016 · Weimerskirch et al. 2016 part of a system rests while the rest keeps flying The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Relational Partial presence is real presence Lurking in a group chat without posting. Camera off. Texting instead of calling. Reading every message and answering none of them today. Being in the room with the sound down. None of that is absence. What gets counted in each of those cases is output — messages sent, words spoken, a face on screen. But absence is a claim about somebody not being there, and not one of those is that. They are all being there, with the output turned down. Every Saturday the Stimpunks Solidarity Session leaves an otter cam running while the conversation drifts in and out. Some cameras on, most off. Some people speaking, some in text, some just there. Nobody has to watch it. That is the part that makes it work — and the reason it works is that the room does not price presence by output. Because a relationship that only holds when everyone shows up at full intensity was never built to hold a nervous system that varies. And they all vary. Ours vary visibly, which is a difference in legibility, not in kind. Presence does not need full output to count as presence. No animal on this spread, on purpose. Every other spread here has one, and the obvious move was to set the frigatebird's half-lit brain beside a camera-off Saturday and let the resemblance carry the claim. That is the metaphor this zine refuses five spreads later — and it would misdescribe the bird, which sleeps about 42 minutes a day in short bouts inside its glides, never while flapping, and is awake for the rest of the flight rather than cruising along permanently half-lit. The distinction is Helen Edgar's, from No. 58: the otters are evidence; we are testimony. This spread is testimony. It does not need a bird standing behind it. one room · four ways of being in it camera on in text only lurking stepped out still connected no mode outranks another presence without performance Solidarity Sesh · the low-demand shared watch a reason to stay in the room The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Lived experience No ramp, just the edge Interoception is the sense that reports the inside of your own body. Hunger. Heartbeat. Thirst. Tiredness arriving. For a lot of us that signal comes through quiet, or late, or in a shape that is hard to read. Which means the depletion does not announce itself while it builds. You feel fine. Then you do not. There is often no slope in between. Meltdown and shutdown live at that edge. They are not chosen and they are not a rest strategy — they are what a nervous system does when the cost has already been accumulating and no warning arrived in time to spend it differently. An emergency stop, where a signal should have come first. It would be easy to read that as proof that rest is optional if you are only careful enough — that with better monitoring you could time it precisely. It is proof of the opposite. Missing the signal costs too much. Rest cannot wait for a warning that may never come. Said plainly, because the framing gets this wrong. This zine does not call meltdown or shutdown a form of rest. Describing them as enforced rest makes an injury sound like a strategy, and then makes the person responsible for having needed it. They are the cost of rest having been unavailable. Everything else in here is about the rest that gets chosen, before the edge. what the signal does not do the ramp you were promised warning the edge you get “fine” emergency stop not a strategy · a cost interoception · and what it does not report the flat line is not the same as capacity The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Six months, no load The bear's bone Bone answers to load. That is why this whole collection opens with Iwao Yasuda's finding that a bone under pressure generates a charge — a skeleton is not scaffolding, it is a tissue that reads what is being asked of it and rebuilds accordingly. Which sets up a problem. Take the load away and bone is supposed to go. Put a person on months of bed rest, or in orbit, and it does: resorption outruns formation and the skeleton thins measurably. A hibernating bear goes roughly six months with no walking, no weight-bearing, none of the loading that is supposed to keep a skeleton honest. It loses no bone. Researchers compared hibernating and active grizzlies and black bears and found no difference in bone volume fraction or mineral density. Cellular activity dropped — but resorption and formation dropped together, staying balanced. The bear does not out-work the problem. It turns the remodelling down at both ends and comes out in spring with its skeleton intact. Long rest cost this animal nothing structural. So the loss is not a law. A bear is not a person, and this is not advice. Humans do lose bone in prolonged disuse; nothing here suggests skipping movement, and the researchers study bears precisely because we cannot do what they do. The claim is narrow and it is about the rule, not the routine: there exists a physiology in which half a year of stillness is not paid for in skeleton. What looked like an inevitable trade is a fact about particular bodies in particular arrangements. six months of disuse · two outcomes a person on bed rest loss a bear in the den held bone volume & mineral density · unchanged remodelling, turned down at both ends formation resorption balanced McGee-Lawrence et al. 2009 · Bone not pushing through — turning it down evenly The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks
Rest is a property of an arrangement

Environment Rest is a property of an arrangement The bear's skeleton is doing its own work from the inside. The den is doing a different job, and that one is measurable in the energy budget. A hibernating black bear drops its metabolic rate to about a quarter of basal while its core temperature falls only five or six degrees, and its heart runs as low as nine beats a minute. That is the striking part of Tøien's work: the metabolic suppression is largely uncoupled from the cooling. Deep rest here is not the body going cold and switching off. Holding that state still costs something, and the den is what lowers the bill. Bears select dens for insulation — buried, snow-covered, sheltered from wind and disturbance — and a well-insulated den measurably reduces what has to be spent on staying warm. The animal's contribution is to be somewhere that will hold the conditions steady, and then to stop. So rest is not only a capacity a body either has or lacks. It is what happens when a body and its surroundings are arranged so that resting is possible without effort being spent on making it possible. Temperature. Darkness. Safety. Nobody needing anything right now. Change the surroundings and the same body can no longer do what it just did. Two findings, deliberately not merged. The den lowers the energy cost of hibernating; the preserved bone is an internal remodelling result. Nobody has shown that a worse den costs a bear its skeleton, and this spread does not imply it — the bone would likely hold in a poor den and the animal would simply pay more to be there. Keeping them apart is the honest version, and it is the stronger one: the body and the room are each carrying a documented share. the room, doing the holding safety no demand insulation metabolism falls · temperature barely does ~25% basal −5–6°C only deep rest is not going cold Tøien et al. 2011 · Science · den microclimate literature the arrangement carries part of the cost The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks
The debt that was never owed

Systems The debt that was never owed Underneath most of how rest gets talked about sits an earning frame: rest as something released after enough output. A balance paid down. Never quite yet. Tricia Hersey, who founded The Nap Ministry, names what that frame is doing: Rest is a form of resistance because it disrupts and pushes back against capitalism and white supremacy. Tricia Hersey · Rest Is Resistance: A Manifesto (2022) Her ground is specific and it is not ours to blur: rest stolen from Black people under slavery and its long afterlives, and a grind culture that reads bodies as machinery. She names what the machinery story is: Rest pushes back and disrupts a system that views human bodies as a tool for production and labor. It is a counter narrative. We know that we are not machines. Tricia Hersey · The Nap Ministry, 21 February 2022 A counter narrative. That is the precise word for it, because the earning story is a narrative and not a measurement — and the argument is a Black liberationist one before it is anything else. What it hands us is the shape of the accounting. If rest must be earned, someone is holding the ledger, and whoever holds it decides who is behind. That is a mechanism for withholding, and it works best on people whose output is already read as suspect — which is to say, on us, routinely, from the first time a report card described us as not applying ourselves. And this is where Hydra comes back. There is no ledger in a nerve net. The debt was not discovered in the body; it was issued — and a debt that was issued can be refused. Not flattened into wellness. Hersey's rest is a demand made from inside Black liberation struggle, not a self-care tip and not a general theory we get to lift clean. We cite her because the accounting she describes is the same accounting we are handed, not because our situation is hers. two accounts of the same body earned · owed · behind issued, not found baseline no balance to clear a ledger is a tool for withholding and it is used hardest on whoever is already read as not trying a debt issued can be refused Hersey 2022 · The Nap Ministry rest as refusal, not as recovery time The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

Held honestly What this zine refuses Every piece in this series ends by naming what it will not claim. The refusals are load-bearing: a zine about rest is unusually easy to turn into its opposite, and most of the ways that happens are kind-sounding. Rest gets recommended to us constantly. Almost none of it survives contact with how our attention actually works, and a surprising amount of it arrives as one more thing to do properly. If it needs to be justified afterwards, it was not rest. It was unpaid work with the lights off. Not:Rest so you can produce. Hydra is not recharging in order to divide more efficiently on Monday. Rest is not a maintenance interval on a working machine, and framing it that way just moves the ledger. Not:An animal metaphor for people. The bear is not a model of who to become and the frigatebird is not an instruction. They are kin, doing their own thing, in bodies that are not ours. Not:“Just relax.” Offered as advice it is usually a demand — for stillness that fits somebody else's nervous system, delivered to someone with no spare capacity to perform it. Not:Rest as a project. Optimised, tracked, done correctly, reviewed. That is the grind with a softer noun on it. Not:Meltdown as rest. Calling a shutdown enforced rest turns an injury into a strategy, and then hands the person the bill for having needed it. Not:Natural, therefore allowed. The animals are not a permission slip. Nature grants nobody anything, and a belonging claim resting on biology can be revoked by the next paper. Not:The smoothed version. The hedges in here are not padding — no circadian rhythm in Hydra, two months and 42 minutes from two different studies, a bear that is not a person. The true versions are stranger and they are enough. The Rest You Keep · Stimpunks

L★S Rest is older than the brain, older than the ledger, and older than anyone's opinion of how much you have done today. An animal with no nervous centre sleeps, and its cells divide because it did. Nothing was ever owed. Love you down to your star stuff — and down to the rest you keep. Phase transitions Water doesn't get gradually stiffer Cool a glass of water and it does not slowly thicken toward solid. It stays liquid, liquid, liquid — and then, at a single temperature, it flips all at once into ice. Not a gradual stiffening; a sudden change of state. It is the same H₂O on both sides — the very same molecules, only rearranged. Physicists call this a phase transition: a substance holding steady until a threshold in its conditions is crossed, then reorganising completely — solid, liquid, gas — with nothing added and nothing taken away. Nothing about the water got better or worse. It crossed a line. Nothing about the water changed. It crossed a line. state colder → liquid ice 0°C not a ramp — a cliff the flip happens all at once The Same Water · Stimpunks

pressure temperature → solid liquid gas one substance, many states the conditions decide The phase diagram The conditions, not the substance Whether that water shows up as ice, liquid, or steam depends entirely on the conditions around it — temperature and pressure. Scientists chart it on a phase diagram: a map with a region for each state and lines where one becomes another. Read it and the point lands quietly. Ice is not defective water; steam is not water trying harder. There is no best state and no failed state — only one substance, and the conditions it happens to be in. So if you want a different state, you change the conditions, not the substance. We said this once about rooms and minds. Here it is again, about states. Ice isn't broken water. It's water somewhere colder. The Same Water · Stimpunks
Why could you do it yesterday?

Fluctuating capacity Why could you do it yesterday? Here is the question so many of us brace for: why could you do it yesterday and not today? The same person crosses from managing to not managing, the way the same water crosses from liquid to ice on one degree of difference. Not unreliable. Not lazy. Not putting it on. The same you, in changed conditions. You are not inconsistent. cooling · the universe changing state → one hot symmetry gas star ice · you same stuff, meeting its conditions the oldest change there is The oldest change The same water This is the oldest move there is. The early universe didn't cool smoothly; it changed state — dropping past threshold after threshold, its forces freezing out of a single hot symmetry the way ice forms out of water. A cloud of gas drifts unchanged for ages, then crosses a threshold of density and collapses, all at once, into a star. The same star stuff is plasma, gas, dust, rock, ocean, ice — and us. None of those is the broken version of the others. And the water in you is partly older than the Sun, carried in from the cold of space: it has been vapour and ice and rain and ocean, the same substance every time. So when your state shifts with your conditions, you aren't failing. You're doing the most ancient thing matter knows how to do. You were never broken. The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing

the horizon the shadow 2.6× wider 48 Star Stuff The Shadow Is Bigger Than the Thing on the black hole nobody photographed, and what can only be known by its effect on everything else Eight telescopes · six sites · 3.5 petabytes · one dark circle · a rhyme, not a proof L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff open edition · print freely
Nobody has photographed a black hole

The honest problem Nobody has photographed a black hole Start with the thing everyone gets wrong, including most of the headlines in April 2019. A camera works by catching light that left the subject. That is the whole mechanism — the apple sends photons at your eye, and you see an apple. A black hole sends nothing. Not a little. Not faintly. The event horizon is the surface where the geometry has tipped so far that every path leading outward has stopped existing; there is no direction that is away. Light does not struggle out slowly. It does not get out. So the ordinary way of knowing about a thing is simply unavailable, and no better camera will fix it. This is not a limit of our instruments. It is a fact about what the object is. There is no picture of a black hole and there never will be. What exists is a picture of everything else, arranged by one. the situation, stated plainly Which sounds like the end of the enquiry, and is instead the beginning of it. Because a thing that emits nothing still does a great deal — to gas, to stars, to the paths of passing light — and all of that is visible. The rest of this zine is about what you can learn from the second-best option, and about the one number that makes it dangerous. Why the ordinary method fails On the left, an apple sending light rays out to an eye, labelled this is how seeing works. The second-best option Only what bends around it Gas falling toward a black hole does not go quietly. It compresses, shears against itself, and gets hot enough to shine — so the object that emits nothing is generally surrounded by something that emits a great deal. Now put that glow behind a lens made of gravity. Light travelling near a massive body does not go straight; its path bends, and the closer it passes the harder it bends. At a particular radius the bending becomes exactly enough to curve a beam right around into a circle — the photon sphere, at three GM/c² from the centre. Light there is orbiting. So what arrives at a telescope on Earth sorts itself into two kinds. Light that passed far enough out escaped and reached you. Light that came in closer than the critical approach spiralled in and never left. The result is a bright ring around a dark middle — and the dark middle is not an object. It is the set of directions in which any light you might have received went into the hole instead. You are not looking at a black hole. You are looking at the shape of a hole in everything else. what the image actually is The astronomers' word for that dark middle is the shadow, and the word is well chosen — a shadow is defined entirely by what it happens to, never by itself. The shadow is bigger than the thing

3√3 against 2 The shadow is bigger than the thing Here is the fact this zine is built on, and it is a piece of exact geometry rather than an impression. For a non-spinning black hole, all the relevant radii can be written in one unit — GM/c², which is just the object's mass expressed as a length: radii, for a non-spinning black hole, in units of GM/c² radius what sits there 2 the event horizon — the actual boundary of the actual object 3 the photon sphere, where light can orbit 3√3 ≈ 5.196 the edge of the shadow — what a distant observer sees Divide the last by the first. 3√3 / 2 ≈ 2.598. The dark circle in the picture is about two and a half times wider than the object casting it. Gravity does not merely hide the black hole; it magnifies the hiding, throwing the darkness outward well past the horizon's true edge. The shadow overstates its cause by a factor of about 2.6 — and it does so consistently, which is the only reason anyone can work backwards from it. the number the whole piece turns on One more thing makes this usable, and it is close to a fluke. Real black holes spin, and spin drags spacetime around with it — so you would expect the shadow's size to depend on how fast it turns and how it is tilted toward you. It barely does. Across the whole range of spins and viewing angles, the shadow's angular radius stays at 5 ± 0.2 GM/Dc² — a spread of about four percent, with the non-spinning case (3√3 ≈ 5.196) sitting near the top of it. That near-constancy is a quirk of the equations rather than a principle, and it is what turns a dark smudge into a measurement: if the shadow's size is fixed by mass over distance and almost nothing else, then measuring it tests the geometry itself. 10 April 2019 · M87* Forty-two microarcseconds The first one they got was not the nearest. It was the one whose shadow happened to be biggest in our sky. M87* sits at the heart of a giant elliptical galaxy about 55 million light years away, and it is enormous — the ring measurement implies a mass of 6.5 ± 0.7 billion suns. Distance shrinks it; size restores it. The two nearly cancel, and what is left is a ring 42 ± 3 microarcseconds across. A microarcsecond is a millionth of a second of arc, and a second of arc is already a 3,600th of a degree. Put it in terms of a thing: Forty-two microarcseconds is roughly the angle subtended by an orange, sitting on the Moon. our own arithmetic — see the sources note Nothing on Earth resolves that. A telescope's sharpness is set by the wavelength it works at divided by the width of the dish, and to see 42 µas at the 1.3 mm the hot gas shines at, the dish would have to be about as wide as the planet. So they used the planet. That is spread seven. The image released on 10 April 2019 came from data taken two years earlier, over six nights in April 2017 — the gap is not delay, it is the checking. And what the checking looked like is the next spread, because it is the most quietly admirable thing in the whole story. Four teams who weren't allowed to talk

The discipline Four teams who weren't allowed to talk Here is the awkward part of the method, and the reason the result is trustworthy. An array of separate telescopes does not record a picture. It records how much the incoming waves agree between each pair of dishes — a scatter of measurements across a plane, with enormous gaps where no pair happens to sit. Getting from that to an image means filling in what was never measured, and there are infinitely many images consistent with the data. So the choice of method is doing real work. And every person involved knew exactly what general relativity predicted they should find. That is the classic way to fool yourself, and they took it seriously. The collaboration split into four imaging teams, each kept blind to the other three, working with two quite different families of algorithm — the long-established CLEAN and the newer regularized maximum likelihood. Four groups, forbidden to compare notes, using different mathematics, all produced a ring of about the same size in about the same place. First M87 EHT Results IV, 2019 The blinding is not bureaucracy. It is the only available answer to a question nobody can answer about themselves: did I find this, or did I draw it? This is the same instinct as the five-sigma rule in No. 39 and the whole of Too Good to Check. Wanting a result is not a disqualification. Failing to build a guard against wanting it is. A telescope the size of a planet

April 2017 · six sites A telescope the size of a planet You cannot build a dish the width of the Earth. You can, it turns out, use the Earth. Eight radio telescopes at six sites — Arizona, Mexico, Hawai'i, Chile's Atacama, the Sierra Nevada in Spain, and the South Pole — pointed at the same patch of sky on the same nights and recorded what arrived, each stamped against an atomic clock. Nothing was combined at the time. There is no network that could carry it: the array wrote roughly 350 terabytes per telescope per day, about 3.5 petabytes in all, onto racks of helium-filled hard drives. The drives were then flown to two correlator supercomputers and played back against each other, and only there did the separate recordings become one instrument. The South Pole's drives could not leave. No aircraft flies out of Amundsen–Scott through the Antarctic winter. That station's share of the observation sat on a shelf at the bottom of the world until the season turned — the picture was waiting on the weather, which is a very old condition for astronomy to be in. Consider what this instrument is. Its aperture is a planet. Its resolution comes not from any one dish being good but from the dishes being far apart, and knowing precisely how far. No site saw the ring. No site could have. The image exists only in the relationship between them. Nobody saw it alone, and no part of the instrument was capable of seeing it alone. The seeing happened between them. what an interferometer is The Earth as one aperture A globe with six marked observing sites, and lines joining every pair of sites, labelled the aperture is the distance between them. The subject that won't hold still

12 May 2022 · Sagittarius A* The subject that won't hold still Three years after M87*, the same array released the one at home: Sagittarius A*, about four million solar masses, roughly 27,000 light years away, at the centre of our own galaxy. Its ring came out at 51.8 ± 2.3 microarcseconds — slightly larger in our sky than M87*'s, because although it is around 1,600 times less massive it is also vastly closer. It should have been the easy one. It was much the harder one, for a reason that is worth sitting with. Everything near a black hole orbits on a clock set by its mass, and a small black hole runs fast. The innermost stable orbit around M87* takes something like thirty days to go round. The same orbit around Sagittarius A* takes about thirty minutes. M87* holds a pose for a month. Sagittarius A* rearranges itself several times over a single night's observing. why the near one was the hard one An interferometer builds its image out of the Earth's own rotation, sweeping the pairs of telescopes across the sky over hours. That method assumes the subject is the same subject from the first hour to the last. For Sagittarius A* it plainly wasn't, and the methods had to be rebuilt to cope with a source that changes while you are still looking. Being nearer did not make it easier to see. It made it faster, and fast is its own kind of invisible. Known by the orbit it puts things into

The turn Known by the orbit it puts things into Everything anyone knows about a black hole is a fact about something else. The heat of the gas. The bending of the light. The orbits of stars whipping around the galactic centre. The width of the dark patch. Not one of those is a measurement of the object; every one is a measurement of what the object does to its neighbourhood — and together they pin it down to within a few percent. This is not an exotic epistemic situation. It is an extremely ordinary one, and most of us live inside it. Monotropism is not visible. What is visible is where the attention went, and what it cost to pull it away. Pain is not visible. A sensory environment is not visible — only what someone does to survive it. You cannot point a camera at an access need. the same shape, at human scale And the response this usually gets is the one the EHT refused: if it can't be seen, treat it as absent. Every unphotographable thing in a person's life gets met with that sentence in some form — you don't look Autistic, you seem fine, you managed last week. The astronomers had a far stronger version of the problem — a thing that emits literally nothing, not merely something inconvenient to observe — and they did not conclude it was absent. They built an instrument out of a planet and measured what bends around it. The absence of a photograph was never evidence of an absent thing. It was a fact about cameras. the turn, in one line Inferring the unseen centre An empty dashed circle at the centre with several orbits and bent paths curving around it, each labelled as something measurable, showing that the centre is known only from what surrounds it. never seen orbits stellar motion bent light bent light every arrow is a measurement of something else and together they locate the centre Figure 8 · knowing by the surroundings The Shadow Is Bigger · Stimpunks

The uncomfortable half And the shadow overstates it Most versions of this argument stop at the previous spread, on the warm note. This one doesn't, because the physics has a second half and the second half is the useful one. Go back to the number. The dark circle is not the same size as the object. It is about 2.6 times wider. Measure the black hole by its shadow and forget the factor, and you will conclude it is two and a half times the thing it is. Now carry that across, carefully. What an observer sees of an unmet need is almost never the need. It is the disruption — the shutdown, the meltdown, the missed deadline, the sudden absence, the job that ended badly, the reply that came out wrong. Those are real, and they are genuinely caused by the thing. They are also systematically bigger than it. They are bigger because they include everything that had to bend. Years of compensating, the effort of masking, the accumulated cost of a hundred small accommodations made privately and never counted. All of that is bent light. None of it is the horizon. What people see of an unmet need is the disruption, not the need — and the disruption is the larger object. the second half of the geometry Two things follow, and they cut in opposite directions, which is how you know it isn't a slogan. For anyone doing the observing: do not size the need by the disruption. You are looking at magnified darkness. The person is not as large a problem as the wreckage suggests, and treating the wreckage as the measurement is how support plans get built for a person who does not exist. And for anyone being observed: the disruption is not the measure of you either. It was inflated on the way out — by the bending, by the years, by an environment that made a small thing throw a long shadow. In physics the magnification is exactly 3√3/2 and you can divide it out. In a life there is no such factor, which is precisely why you ask the person rather than measuring their shadow. Unseeable is not a blank cheque

The guardrail Unseeable is not a blank cheque There is a comfortable misreading of everything above, and it needs closing off on the page rather than in a footnote. The misreading is: since it can't be photographed, no claim about it can be checked, so any claim will do. That is not what happened here, and the EHT is its refutation. They could not see the thing. They measured it anyway — Sagittarius A*'s ring at 51.8 ± 2.3 microarcseconds, matching what general relativity predicts for an object of about four million solar masses at that distance, to within a few percent. Not being able to see something is not the same as not being able to know anything about it. It only means the evidence arrives sideways. So the claim this zine actually makes is narrow, and it is worth saying in one sentence: an unphotographable thing can still be measured, argued about, constrained, and got wrong. Which is also the honest version of the human half. Self-report is not magic and it is not beyond question; it is the instrument available, and like every instrument it is checked against consequences, against other people's accounts, against what happens next. Asking is not a lowering of standards. It is the measurement. Not:that anyone is a black hole. That reading is right there — devouring, dark, pulling everything in — and we refuse it flatly. Nothing in this zine is a description of a person. The black hole is the observation problem, not the human being. Not:that being invisible is romantic. It is a measurement failure, and it costs people diagnoses, benefits, jobs and belief. There is nothing beautiful about going unseen; the beautiful thing is the eight telescopes. Not:that "you can't see it" settles anything. Three and a half petabytes on hard drives, flown off a continent, exist because a collaboration declined that sentence. Not:a proof about people. Spreads nine and ten are a rhyme. The geometry is exact and checkable; the analogy is neither, and it licenses nothing on its own. A rhyme, not a proof. 57 Star Stuff The Shell Was Your Calcium The egg crack moment is borrowed, true, and kinder than its own retelling. More than eighty per cent of a hatchling's calcium came from the wall it broke. L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · ten spreads ·
Once the egg cracks, there's no going back

Two · the claim as received Once the egg cracks, there's no going back There is a moment a great many of us recognise on description alone. Nothing new happens to you. Somebody says a sentence, or you read a list, and every year you have already lived rearranges itself behind you. The struggles were not personal failings. They were a nervous system doing what it does, in a world built to a different specification. The therapist and author Essy Knopf — Autistic, ADHD, queer, disabled — set this out in March 2025, and named where the language comes from: the trans community, where getting your egg cracked is the moment somebody knows and accepts that they are trans. Knopf's argument is that Autistic and ADHD people have their own version of it. Because once the egg cracks, once you see yourself for who you truly are, there's no going back — but that's a good thing. Essy Knopf · The “Egg Crack” Moment: Realizing You're Neurodivergent · 2025 He is right about the feeling, and this zine is not an argument with him. The relief is real. So is the grief that arrives behind it, and the anger about the years, and he names all three. The argument is with what happens to the metaphor after it leaves his mouth. Repeated enough, the egg cracks flattens into a door: one side undiagnosed and struggling, the other side self-aware and free, a threshold between them that you pass through once. It is a tidy story, and tidy stories travel. So we did what this collection does. We went and looked at some eggs. The incubator does not agree with the door. It agrees with something better. The Shell Was Your Calcium · Stimpunks

Three · whose egg it was first The word is not ours Before anything else, the debt. Egg, in this sense — a person who is trans and does not know it yet, an embryo of the person they will hatch into — is trans community language. We are borrowing it, and borrowed words get carried carefully or not at all. Who said it first is not known, and that turns out to be the interesting part. Evelyn Bauer, writing for Them in December 2024, went looking. The earliest documented use is an Urban Dictionary entry for egg mode — “someone who is trans but doesn't know it yet” — posted by a user called bitplane7 on 23 August 2016. The subreddit r/egg_irl followed on 26 July 2017. Before that, nothing written down. Bauer asked the historian Susan Stryker, who could not say when she first heard it, only that by 2019 it felt intuitively obvious. When the person who wrote the field's standard history cannot date a word, the word did not come from a book. A word this good with no owner is not a gap in the record. It is what community language looks like from the inside. Our own vocabulary works the same way. Neurodiversity has a first author and a contested one; much of the rest of it — the phrasings that actually get used, the ones that arrive already fitting — came out of mailing lists and comment threads and group chats, from people who were not building a canon and did not sign anything. The InLv list is where a great deal of it happened, and most of the individual sentences are unattributable now. That is not sloppiness. It is the shape of a thing made by a community rather than issued to one. We say so here because the alternative — quietly letting a borrowed word sound like ours — is the small theft that the most-quotable-source failure is made of. The borrowing also comes with a warning attached, and Bauer states it plainly. We keep it, and it returns on spread eight. The Shell Was Your Calcium · Stimpunks
The shell does not get thinner

Four · what the shell actually does The shell does not get thinner Here is the first thing the door story gets wrong, and it is worth the whole zine. A hen's egg incubates for twenty-one days. From about day eleven, an extraembryonic membrane called the chorioallantoic membrane presses against the inside of the shell and begins dissolving it — pulling calcium out of the wall and passing it to the embryo. This is not damage. It is supply. In 2022 a team at INRAE measured what that does to the shell. Halgrain and colleagues compared shells across incubation, and found something that sounds like a contradiction. Thickness between day 0 and day 15: no significant difference (p = 0.110). Breaking strength between day 11 and day 15: significantly reduced (p = 0.007). DAY 0 DAY 15 SAME WALL Thickness, day 0 to day 15: no significant difference (p = 0.110) Breaking strength, day 11 to day 15: significantly reduced (p = 0.007) Halgrain et al., Frontiers in Physiology, 2022 The wall is being taken apart from the inside and it is not getting visibly thinner while it happens. Measure it and you would say nothing is going on. Weigh what it can bear and you would know everything is. Nobody could see it. There was nothing to see. Every one of us who got a late answer has had some version of the same conversation. But you seemed fine. You did well at school. Nobody noticed anything. And the honest reply has always been that there was nothing to notice, because holding it together is the thing that was happening. The masking was load-bearing right up to the week it wasn't. The shell agrees. Intact, correct, full thickness, and by day fifteen it will fail under a load it carried easily on day one. The Shell Was Your Calcium · Stimpunks

Five · where the shell went Into the skeleton So the calcium comes out of the wall. The obvious next question is the one the metaphor never asks, because the metaphor is busy with the door: where does it go? The eggshell supplies more than eighty per cent of all the calcium a chick embryo gets — roughly 2.2 grams per egg — and in altricial birds, the ones that hatch helpless, more than ninety. Between days eleven and fifteen the embryo's skeleton holds more than eighty per cent of all the calcium in the animal, and at hatching it holds about three quarters. Put those two sentences next to each other and read them again. SHELL BONE >80% of the embryo's calcium comes from the shell · at hatch the skeleton holds ~75% of it Halgrain et al., 2022 The container becomes the frame. Not metaphorically — by mass. The thing that held the animal in is, by the time the animal leaves, most of what holds the animal up. There is no moment where the shell is discarded and the skeleton begins. They are the same calcium at two addresses. And that calcium has a longer history than the egg. Every one of those atoms was assembled inside a star that is no longer there — fused in the shells of a massive one, scattered when it failed. It has been a shell before. It has been seawater and limestone and somebody's tooth. Then it becomes bone, and bone does the thing this whole site is named for. Press on it and it answers in current: collagen is piezoelectric, as Iwao Yasuda showed in the 1950s and Bassett and colleagues confirmed after him. Load a bone and it generates a charge, and the charge is part of how it decides where to grow. The wall you broke is now the part of you that turns pressure into signal. You did not escape the shell. You stood up in it. The Shell Was Your Calcium · Stimpunks

Six · the messy middle Breathing, and still inside This spread is for whoever is reading it and does not know yet. At the blunt end of an egg there is a pocket of air, the air cell, which grows through incubation as water evaporates out through the shell's pores. Near the end, the embryo pushes its beak through the inner membrane into that pocket. This is called internal pipping, and it is the moment the lungs go to work — respiration transfers from the chorioallantoic membrane, which has been doing the gas exchange all along, to the animal's own airways. Margaret Vince traced how that changeover happens in the domestic fowl, and found it is not one event but three: the major airways aerate, then respiratory movements begin, then the finest branches aerate slowly (Vince, Journal of Physiology, 1976). A staged, unhurried handover. All of it happens before the shell is broken. AIR CELL LUNGS WORKING SHELL UNBROKEN Internal pipping · the lungs start before the shell does Vince, Journal of Physiology, 1976 Set that egg in front of an observer and it is an egg. Whole, unmarked, apparently nothing happening. Inside it is an animal that has already started breathing air and has not broken anything yet. The messy middle is a respiratory stage. There is a period — hours, in a hen — where you are doing the new thing and still entirely inside the old container, and from outside there is no evidence whatsoever. Not hesitation. Not failing to commit. Not being a bit Autistic, or trying on a label, or whatever else gets said to people who are mid-changeover and cannot yet produce a certificate. It is a stage with a name, and everything that hatches goes through it. The Shell Was Your Calcium · Stimpunks
You crack when you hear others cracking

Seven · the clicking You crack when you hear others cracking A clutch of quail eggs is laid over days but hatches together, near enough. For a long time this was filed as one of those things. Margaret Vince, working in Cambridge in the 1960s, put instruments on the eggs and found out why. In the last days before hatching the embryos click — an audible, intermittent sound in time with their breathing — and the clicking is not incidental. It is a signal, and the neighbours act on it. An egg placed in a clutch a full day behind the others will speed itself up and hatch with them (Vince, 1964). Development accelerates, on the strength of hearing other embryos further along than itself. And then the part that matters most here. Vince went looking for the other direction, and found it: a slower click rate — around 0.9 clicks per second — retards embryos that are ahead (Vince, 1968; 1984). Synchronisation is not the stragglers being dragged up to standard. It runs both ways. BEHIND SPEEDS UP AHEAD WAITS Bidirectional synchronisation · the behind accelerate, the ahead are retarded Vince, Animal Behaviour 1964, 1968 · J. Exp. Zoology 1984 We keep saying that community is what makes this survivable, and we usually mean it as encouragement. In an incubator it is not encouragement. It is the mechanism. The clicking is how the clutch hatches together — remove it and they don't. Which is a fair description of how most people's egg actually cracks. Almost nobody works it out alone in a room. It is a video, a thread, a friend saying have you ever looked into this, somebody one step further along making a noise where you could hear it. You were not given information. You were given a rate. The ones ahead slow down and wait. That is the finding we would least have predicted and like the most. Not everyone hurrying to catch the fastest embryo. A clutch arriving at the same time because it is worth more to arrive together, and the cost of that is paid by whoever was ahead. The Arrau turtle does its own version of this, calling from inside the shell and going on calling in the river; it is drawn in The Hatchery and its story there is about who was listening. Eight · the refusals What this zine is not An egg is a good enough image that it will carry almost anything, including several things it should not. So, plainly: Not: cracking somebody else's egg Bauer's warning, kept as given: naming somebody an egg — especially in a gossipy, pejorative or confrontational way, and most of all to their face — can push a person further into the closet, not out of it. The biology says the same thing with no ambiguity at all. The egg tooth is on the inside of the shell. Nobody pips from outside; an egg opened from without is not a hatching, it is an egg somebody broke. You cannot do this for a person. You can only click. Not: the person before was fake The tidiest and most damaging reading — that there was an impostor and now there is the real one. The shell was your calcium. It is in your legs. Every year spent holding it together was spent by you, in a body that was already this body, and none of it was somebody else's life. Not: a graduation Mair and colleagues read 225 posts about late identification and one of the four themes they came back with is post-diagnosis burnout. Hatching is not the end of the hard part; in a good deal of the testimony it is where a particular hard part starts, generally with no support attached. Anyone selling the crack as an arrival has not read the follow-up. Not: permission from nature Chick embryos do not have identities, or closets, or a diagnosis waiting at twenty-nine. Nothing in an incubator authorises anything about us, and a universe that could approve could also decline — we would not take the verdict either way. This is a rhyme, and rhymes are for holding a thing in mind, not for proving it. Down to is not because of. Not: the egg as the enemy The container gets cast as the villain because the story needs one, and it will not hold. That shell kept an animal at the right temperature and humidity for three weeks, exchanged its gases through its own pores, and then handed over most of its substance. Masking is like this too, which is the uncomfortable part: it cost us enormously and it also got some of us here alive. You are allowed to be angry about a thing that worked. What the science does kill is narrow and holds well. It kills the door — the idea that this is one threshold, crossed once, with a settled person on the far side. Nothing about hatching is a threshold. It is a supply chain, a staged handover of breathing, a negotiated arrival time, and a tool you grow and then lose. The Shell Was Your Calcium · Stimpunks

Nine · not a door Not a door. A cycle In 2026 Ally Pax Arcari Mair and colleagues at Edinburgh went looking for what actually happens to people after a late identification. They gathered 731 public posts about grief and neurodivergence across seven platforms, kept the 225 that spoke to grief and relief in relation to identifying late, and read them. They did not find a door. They found a process, which they named the Grief, Relief, and Belief Cycle — and they were explicit that it is oscillating, non-linear, and different for everyone. Four themes sit inside it: Theme one The Life I Could Have Had — the loss and the regret. The jobs, the friendships, the school years that would have gone another way. Theme two Grieving for My Younger Self — looking back at the child who was called lazy and difficult, now knowing what was actually happening to them. Theme three Feeling Gratitude — the relief, and the self-understanding it buys. This is the part the popular version keeps. Theme four Post-Diagnosis Burnout — the emotional and physical toll, and the absence of anything waiting to help. This is the part the popular version drops. A cycle means it comes round again. The gratitude does not retire the grief; you can be four years into knowing and get flattened by the life you could have had, on a Tuesday, for no reason. That is not you failing at having hatched. That is the documented shape of the thing. And the authors are blunt about who should be doing something with that. Their recommendation is a paradigm shift in which identification is treated as a first step, rather than a terminal component of a service — wraparound support before, during and beyond. The cycle is not a personal weather system to be endured privately. It is a care gap with a citation. Diagnosis is a first step, not a terminal component. Mair, Gonzalez-Figueroa, McConachie, Goodall & Gillespie-Smith · Autism · 2026 One last thing about hatching, for whoever needs it. The tool that does the breaking is temporary. Birds grow an egg tooth, a small hard point of keratin on the beak, purely to score the shell from inside; turtles and crocodilians grow a caruncle on the snout, lizards and snakes a true tooth, and even the echidna — a mammal, hatching from an egg — has both. It evolved over and over, because getting out is that important. Behind it works the musculus complexus, a neck muscle that swells specifically for this job. And afterwards: the egg tooth drops off, or is resorbed, within days. The hatching muscle shrinks. The stereotyped thrusting movements stop and never return. None of that apparatus is part of the animal's ordinary life. The one who did the cracking was built for the cracking. Whoever you had to be to get out of that shell — the one who read everything at 3 a.m., who rehearsed the sentence for a fortnight, who was furious for a year — was the right animal for that fortnight. They were also grown for one job, and they are allowed to be put down. Mair's second theme is grief for a younger self, and this is the near end of it: you can mourn the version of you who did the hard part, and still not need them any more. You are not the shell and you are not out of it either. You are what the shell became, standing in a wider room, still made of the same star. Love you down to your star stuff. Credit where it is owed Egg and getting your egg cracked, in the sense used throughout, are trans community language, and we are borrowing them. No individual coined them so far as anyone has been able to establish: Evelyn Bauer's piece for Them traces the earliest documented use to an Urban Dictionary entry for egg mode by the user bitplane7 on 23 August 2016, and r/egg_irl to 26 July 2017, and records Susan Stryker being unable to date her own first encounter with it. We state the origin as unknown rather than picking the most citable name, which is the failure Too Good to Check catalogues. A second used to be a piece of the day

the definition · until 1960 A second used to be a piece of the day One 86,400th of it. Twenty-four hours, sixty minutes, sixty seconds — multiply and that is the whole of it. The definition pointed at something. Not at a prototype in a vault in Paris, the way the kilogram did, but at the sky. If you wanted to check a second you watched a star cross a wire, waited for it to come round again, and divided. Everyone was inside the standard. The Earth turned under all of us at once, and the unit was a share of that turning. Nobody owned it and nobody had to be trusted about it. A second was not a quantity somebody had decided. It was a fraction of something everyone was standing on. what got given up, stated at the start The rest of this zine is the story of that tie being cut — carefully, deliberately, by people with good reasons, in three documented moves. None of them was a mistake. Then the instrument got steadier than the standard

Berlin and Paris · 1936–37 Then the instrument got steadier than the standard Quartz clocks arrived, and for the first time in the history of measurement the clock was more regular than the Earth. In 1936, A. Scheibe and U. Adelsberger, working with quartz-crystal clocks at the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt in Berlin, reported that the Earth's rotation varies with the season. In 1937, N. Stoyko at the Bureau International de l'Heure in Paris put a number on it: the day in January ran about two milliseconds longer than the day in July. The causes are all real and all still with us. Tidal friction from the Moon, bleeding rotation away over geological time. Seasonal exchange of angular momentum with the atmosphere — winds and weather, pushing back. Coupling between the mantle and the liquid core. The slow rebound of continents still rising after the last ice sheets came off them. The Earth was never irregular to itself. It became irregular the moment we had something steadier to compare it to. the joint the whole chain turns on This is the reversal that makes everything after it possible. As long as the sky was the most regular thing available, the sky was the standard by definition and could not be wrong. The demand came before the physics

the day of two noons · 18 november 1883 The demand came before the physics It is tempting to read the chain in the other direction — physics gets precise, and society is dragged along. The dates say the opposite. Before 1883 every town in North America kept its own noon, set by the Sun where it stood. That is not disorder; it is the most literal accuracy there is. Noon means the Sun is overhead here, and it was. Then railways. A schedule spanning two towns with different noons is not an inconvenience, it is a collision. Towns reset their clocks as the new noon arrived, and many of them had two noons that day. Nobody discovered that local solar time was wrong. Five years later, the clock started keeping records

Auburn, New York · 20 november 1888 Five years later, the clock started keeping records Standard time is a shared reference. It becomes something else the moment somebody writes it down next to your name. On 20 November 1888, Willard Le Grand Bundy, a jeweller in Auburn, New York, patented a workman's time recorder. The collection this zine belongs to exists to reclaim science from the things that wear its clothes. Processing speed is a fit, not a rate

Saturdays, 10am Central Nobody has to watch Every Saturday the Stimpunks Solidarity Session leaves an otter cam running while the conversation drifts in and out. Some cameras on, most off. Some people speaking, some in text, some just there. Nobody has to watch it. That is the part that makes it work. Our co-creative director Helen Edgar wrote down what the cam was doing for her: on a day when listening and speaking were both off the table, it gave her somewhere to put her attention and a reason to stay in the room — a way to exist in parallel with people she wanted to be near. Then she noticed the resemblance. The otters float, juggle a stone, somersault off alone for a while, drift back for a minute of shared play, and peel away again into their own absorption. The finding There is no standard otter Here is what happens when you actually follow one sea otter population closely enough to tell the individuals apart. Where food was plentiful, everybody ate more or less the same things. Where food was scarce, the population did not converge on one best way to be an otter. It fanned out. Distinct individuals settled into distinct diets — one on snails, one on clams, one on urchins, one on crabs — and each carried a whole matched suite of behaviours to go with it: where to dive, how deep, how long, what to do on the surface. And the crucial part: each specialist was measurably better at its own prey than a generalist would have been. That is not variation as noise around an average. It is variation as the answer. The averaged otter — snail-and-clam-and-urchin-and-crab, all at once, moderately — is a number, not an animal. It forages nowhere. A population of specialists is not a population that failed to standardise. Held honestly. The fanning-out showed up under food limitation — the crowded, hungry site, not the comfortable one. Scarcity is not a gift and we are not going to call it one. What the finding says is narrower and better: when the pressure came, difference was what let the population keep eating. one population · four specialists snails clams urchins crabs foraging efficiency, own prey no bar is the “real” otter the average otter forages nowhere · eats nothing Tinker, Bentall & Estes 2008 specialisation, not a spread around a mean The Stone You Keep · Stimpunks
The stone is not a metaphor

Point Lobos, 1964 The stone is not a metaphor Two observers sat on the California coast for six days and wrote down thirty separate instances of a sea otter using a tool. The otters floated on their backs, laid a stone on the chest, and pounded shellfish against it. The same stone was frequently kept and reused across one food item after another. They also counted the blows. A mussel took an average of 35.5 strikes to open — and the range ran from 6 to 88. Sit with that range. It is the same animal, the same tool, the same job. One otter is done in six. Another is still going at eighty-eight. Nobody is doing it wrong. There simply is no correct number of blows, and an average of 35.5 describes no single mussel that was ever opened. Helen read the kept stone as a stim tool: something reliable and joyful to return to, the way a special interest or a sensory object works — regulation through flow. The reading holds. And the stone is not standing in for anything. It is a rock, and it is load-bearing. There is no correct number of blows. There is your number of blows. blows to open one mussel 0 22 45 67 90 6 88 mean 35.5 describes no mussel one stone, many meals retained, item after item Hall & Schaller 1964 · 30 instances, 6 days the range is the finding The Stone You Keep · Stimpunks
Some otters never use a stone

The part that matters most Some otters never use a stone Follow 196 tagged sea otters over years and tool use turns out to vary enormously between individuals. Some reach for a rock constantly. Some essentially never do. The non-users are not the otters who haven't figured it out yet. They specialise on prey a stone wouldn't help with — urchins, crabs, smaller bivalves that open under a bite. The frequent tool users are on the snails and clams that don't. Two routes to a fed animal, and the route is chosen by what you're built and practised for. Then the finding that should be printed on a wall somewhere: the tool users showed less tooth damage. Cracking hard shells with your teeth costs you your teeth. Using the rock spares them. So the accommodation is not a shortcut, and it is not a crutch, and it is not less than doing it unaided. It is the difference between arriving at old age with your teeth and arriving without them. The support is legible in the skeleton. An accommodation is not a discount on the task.
