The One That Got Its Name Back

thirteen changes apart L★S · 008 The One That Got Its Name Back Brontosaurus excelsus merged 1903 · separated again 2015 Contested Named in 1879, folded into Apatosaurus in 1903 on differences called insufficient, and separated out again in 2015 by a 298-page analysis that published the exact threshold it used. A hundred and twelve years of children being told they had the name wrong. The argument is still live. named 1879merged 1903separated 2015argument still open ▸ Field notes Field notes · Brontosaurus excelsus The short version of No. 61, which this guide accompanies. Othniel Charles Marsh named Apatosaurus ajax in 1877 and Brontosaurus excelsus in 1879. In 1903 Elmer Riggs folded the second into the first, on differences that were usually considered insufficient to justify generic distinction. Insufficient by what measure? None existed. In 2015 somebody built one. Tschopp, Mateus and Benson published a 298-page, open-access revision of Diplodocidae, scoring 81 specimens against 477 characters — and rather than assert a judgement, they published the calibration. They counted the differences between pairs everybody already agreed were a single genus, got twelve and eleven, and set the bar one step past: a minimum of thirteen character changes for a genus, six for a species. Then the move that makes it exemplary rather than merely convenient: they wrote that the numbers cannot be applied to any other analysis, even of the same clade. A threshold that declares its own range of validity. And it is still contested, which is why the chip says so. Their own abstract hedges: Brontosaurus is considered valid by our quantitative approach. Donald Prothero published a dissent four months later under his own name. There is no consensus, and this guide is not going to invent one. The other half of the story is in the zine and belongs here in one line: the same authors petitioned the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature over a separate problem with Diplodocus, and lost, in a numbered published Opinion in 2018. A field where the revisers can be refused in print is a field worth trusting. The One That May Be A Grown-Up

one genus or two · open L★S · 009 The One That May Be A Grown-Up Torosaurus latus merge proposed 2010 · rejected 2012 · unresolved Contested A large horned dinosaur with holes in its frill. In 2010 two researchers argued it is not a separate genus at all but simply a fully mature Triceratops. In 2012 others answered that the growth evidence does not support it. More than a decade on, there is no consensus — and this is the mirror image of the Brontosaurus case. merge proposed, not a splitgrowth stage or genusanswered in 2012no consensus ▸ Field notes Field notes · Torosaurus latus In 2010 John Scannella and Jack Horner argued in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology that Torosaurus Marsh, 1891 is Triceratops Marsh, 1889 — synonymy through ontogeny. Their case: cranial change in Triceratops continues late and fast, the parietal fenestrae open and the squamosals lengthen at the very end of growth, and the result is exactly what has been catalogued as Torosaurus. No juvenile Torosaurus has ever been found, which is what you would expect if they are the oldest individuals of something else. In 2012 Nicholas Longrich and Daniel Field answered, in PLOS ONE, that the growth evidence does not carry it — looking at epoccipital development and fusion, the closing of skull sutures, and bone surface texture, and clustering specimens by developmental sequence rather than by size. Their conclusion: Torosaurus is a valid, distinct genus. More than a decade later there is no settled answer. Several rounds of publication have sharpened what is actually being disagreed about without resolving it. Put this card beside Brontosaurus and something useful appears. That one is a proposed split; this is a proposed merge. They are the same operation run in opposite directions, and they have had opposite fates — the split is broadly (not universally) taken up; the merge is broadly (not universally) rejected. The direction of a proposal has no bearing on whether it is right, and a field that can take one and refuse the other on the evidence is doing the thing correctly. There is also a plain lesson about growth. Two very different-looking skulls can be one animal at two ages. How different does something have to look before it is a different kind of thing? is not a question anatomy answers on its own, which is the whole subject of the companion zine. The One They Called A Juvenile

two species L★S · 010 The One They Called A Juvenile Nanotyrannus lancensis dismissed 40 years · reinstated 2025 Revised A small tyrannosaur named in 1988 and, for most of the four decades since, dismissed as simply a young Tyrannosaurus. In 2025 a near-adult skeleton from the Duelling Dinosaurs block established it as a genus in its own right — and turned up a second species nobody had separated out. named 1988dismissed as a teenagerreinstated 2025and a second species ▸ Field notes Field notes · Nanotyrannus lancensis This is the card that most resembles what the companion zine is actually complaining about, and it resolved while that zine was being written. Nanotyrannus lancensis was named in 1988 from a skull from the Hell Creek Formation. For most of the following four decades the mainstream position was that it is not a genus at all — just a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex. Small, lightly built, more teeth: exactly what a young animal of a big species might look like. In 2025 Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli published in Nature on specimen NCSM 40000, from the block known as the Duelling Dinosaurs — a tyrannosaur preserved together with a Triceratops. The specimen is near somatically mature, and it shares distinguishing features with the original N. lancensis skull. Combining comparative anatomy, growth modelling, tests of which characters actually change with age, and a new phylogenetic dataset, they find that the taxon is distinguishable from Tyrannosaurus, sits outside Tyrannosauridae, and contains two species. The second is named N. lethaeus, after the river of forgetting, for having sat unnoticed. Independent work the same year reached a compatible conclusion from a different direction, finding a growth-arrest line in the hyoid — a small throat bone nobody had thought to section — indicating that the original specimen was an adult after all. Hold the shape of the forty years. The dismissal was not unreasonable; juveniles really do look like that, and the sceptics were doing their job. What is instructive is the difference between a hypothesis held sceptically and a category treated as settled. For a long stretch, “it is just a juvenile” functioned as the second — an answer applied rather than a question kept open — and the reopening took an exceptional specimen and somebody willing to cut a bone nobody had cut. The authors note the obvious implication: if this one was hiding in plain sight, others are. This is the card the companion zine is built around. Because a label can outlive its own refutation in two different ways. Until There Were Ten By Ryan Boren · Stimpunks Foundation Occasion: Sánchez-Lavega et al., Science Advances , 2 September 2026 · Published 2 September 2026 For forty-four years Saturn's hexagon was the only one of its kind, and its refusal to change is exactly what made it look like a law. There is now a ten-sided wave around the south pole — and it is not the hexagon's twin. Three of its sides are drawn strongly, four less so, three are barely there. Its corners wobble on a cycle the hexagon has never shown. It may not last. Saturn's north pole has a hexagon on it. Not a metaphor and not an artefact — a jet stream running eastward around the pole that has bent itself into six straight sides and six corners, wide enough to swallow the Earth, sitting near 78.5°N . Voyager found it in 1980 and 1981 . Ground telescopes, Hubble and Cassini have all looked since, and it has been there every time, which puts its lifetime at more than 44 years . That is the part worth holding onto before anything else. It is not just that Saturn has a hexagon. It is that in decades of looking, nobody had ever found a second one — not in the southern hemisphere, not at any other latitude, not on any other planet in quite this form. One example, unchanging, for longer than most people reading this have been alive. A thing that never changes and has no counterexample is very hard to tell apart from a rule.
The south pole came back into view

The south pole came back into view Saturn is tilted, and it takes about 29 Earth years to go round the Sun, so its poles take turns facing us. From mid-2012 the southern hemisphere was closed to us — tipped away, not observable from Earth. It did not come back into view until 2023 . When it did, there was something there. In October 2023 , Hubble's red-filtered images showed a ten-sided shape around the south pole, near 63°S . In August 2024 , with a better viewing angle, the sides and corners were clearer. By August and September 2025 all ten corners were fully developed, and ground-based telescopes were picking it up too. A decagon. Wave number ten, where the hexagon is wave number six. Its mean wavelength around the latitude circle is 16,782 ± 1,100 km — each side longer than the diameter of the Earth. Saturn's two polar waves compared Two polar views side by side. The north pole carries a six-sided hexagon near 78.5 degrees north, drawn with six sides of equal weight. The south pole carries a ten-sided decagon near 63 degrees south, drawn with sides of deliberately unequal weight: three heavy, four medium, three very light, because the paper reports three vertices very prominent, four less prominent and three less well defined. NORTH · hexagon 78.5°N · seen since 1980 · sides equally drawn Red Spot 55°S SOUTH · decagon 63°S · seen since 2023 · three sides strong, three barely there Fig 1. Schematic, not to scale — the two waves sit at different latitudes and are drawn here at the same size for comparison. The uneven line weights on the decagon are the finding, not a drawing style: the paper reports three vertices very prominent, four less prominent, three less well defined.
It is not the hexagon's twin

It is not the hexagon's twin The tidy version of this story is two poles, two polygons, how balanced . The paper will not let you have it, and the refusal is the best thing in it. Start with the sides. The hexagon's six sides and corners are equally contrasted — it looks drawn with a ruler. The decagon does not. Of its ten corners, three are very prominent, four are less so, and three are barely defined at all. The strongest corners sit near a large red anticyclone at 55°S; the mushiest section of the wave is on the opposite side of the planet. In the authors' words, “the decagon is not uniform in longitude, unlike the hexagon whose sides and vertices are equally contrasted.” Then the wobble. Track each of the ten corners in longitude and they do not sit still: they oscillate, with a mean period of 32.5 days and amplitudes from 4.6° to 8.4° . And the wobble itself travels — the moment of peak swing arrives at each corner about 2.7 days after its neighbour, so the oscillation walks around the pole. The paper is blunt about what that means: this is “a complex dynamical behavior, never observed in the hexagon.” The corners wobble, and the wobble travels around the pole Four stacked sine curves representing four of the decagon's ten vertices oscillating in longitude over about sixty-five days, roughly two cycles. Each curve is shifted about 2.7 days later than the one above it, so the peaks form a diagonal march down the figure. A vertical scale bar shows the mean amplitude of 4.6 degrees. Schematic of the vertex oscillation reported in the paper — four of the ten corners shown, curves idealised as sinusoids. For comparison, Jupiter's Great Red Spot oscillates with a period near 90 days and an amplitude near 1°.
A shape standing almost still in a 116-metre wind

A shape standing almost still in a 116-metre wind Underneath the decagon runs an eastward jet, peaking at 116 m/s near 60.5°S. The shape itself drifts eastward at 2.5 ± 0.2 m/s . It is very nearly parked. Which means that relative to the wind blowing through it , the pattern is moving backwards at 113 m/s . The air rushes through the corners and the corners stay put. This is the same arrangement the hexagon has in the north, and it is the signature of a wave rather than a thing: nothing is being carried around the pole: a shape is being held in a moving fluid. What is actually blowing Worth saying plainly, because “jet”, “wind” and “fluid” all get used for this and they are the same thing. It is gas — overwhelmingly molecular hydrogen , roughly nine parts to one of helium by volume, with traces of methane, ammonia, water and phosphine. A gas is a fluid, which is why atmospheric scientists model it with the same equations they would use for an ocean. There is no ground underneath it. NASA puts it flatly: as a gas giant, Saturn “doesn't have a true surface—the planet is mostly swirling gases and liquids deeper down.” Go down far enough and the hydrogen does not meet a floor; it just gets denser, stops being distinguishable as gas or liquid, and eventually starts conducting electricity like a metal. So the jet is not blowing over anything. It is a fast band inside a fluid that continues all the way down. And what the telescopes actually see is not the gas at all. Hydrogen and helium are transparent. The images track clouds — ammonia ice near the top, ammonium hydrosulfide and water deeper — which is why the paper gets slightly different latitudes at different wavelengths: 763 nm reaches deeper cloud, the 889 nm methane band sees haze higher up, and the wave shows up at both. The decagon is not a structure. It is a pattern in where the clouds are , held in place by where the wind is. One more number, quietly remarkable. That southern jet's shape and strength have not changed substantially since 1981 — the same is true of Saturn's other non-equatorial jets. The wind was already there, doing this, the whole time the south pole was turned away from us. Only the pattern is new. Nobody knows what made it, and the paper says which two guesses it has

Nobody knows what made it, and the paper says which two guesses it has Here is where a lesser write-up says scientists are baffled . The authors are not baffled; they have two candidate mechanisms and no way yet to choose between them, which is a different and more interesting condition. The first candidate is that the jet simply went unstable — that a fast, sharply curved current will spontaneously buckle into a regular number of lobes. The curvature here is roughly eight times the planet's own vorticity gradient, so there is plenty to work with. The second is the red spot. There is a large anticyclone at 55°S , about 4,000 km across, drifting at 23 ± 1 m/s, tracked from 2023 to 2025 — and it resembles a spot Voyager saw at the same latitude in 1981, informally nicknamed Anne's spot . The decagon's sharpest corners are the ones nearest it. In shallow-water simulations, dropping an anticyclone like that beside the jet can set a periodic pattern going. What the simulations could and could not settle The team ran a shallow-water model three ways. Seed the jet with ten evenly spaced disturbances and you get a stable ten-lobed pattern — but it travels far too fast. Introduce the red spot and, for some depths, it perturbs the jet into a periodic pattern. Impose a ten-wave directly and it fragments into a ring of alternating cyclones and anticyclones that moves at 46 m/s — faster than the real decagon, but well below the jet. None of the three reproduces the observed drift. The authors' own conclusion is that they “cannot therefore rule out the possibility that the formation of RS is ultimately the cause of the decagon” — which is a careful sentence, and not the same as saying the red spot did it.
It may not last, and the hexagon probably will

It may not last, and the hexagon probably will This is the line that changes the shape of the story. The decagon did not exist in Saturn's previous year — when Voyager passed through this same season, four decades ago, there was nothing like it. And it has been visibly developing across 2023, 2024 and 2025 rather than sitting there unchanged. So the authors offer this: the decagon “could be a transient evolving phenomenon, whereas the hexagon is a robust wave, as shown by its long lifetime and stability.” Two polygons on one planet, and they are not the same kind of object. One has held its shape through forty-four years and a great deal of nearby storm activity. The other arrived recently, is drawn unevenly, wobbles on a 32-day cycle, and might be gone before anyone works out where it came from. One example had looked like a law

One example had looked like a law For forty-four years there was exactly one of these, and it never changed. That is a hard combination to argue with. It is also, on reflection, a terrible basis for a general claim — a sample of one, held still. What the south pole has produced is not a confirmation and not a contradiction. It is a second case , and the second case is different in almost every way that could be measured: different number of sides, different evenness, different behaviour over time, possibly different durability. Same planet. Same physics. Same kind of jet, running at a speed it has held since 1981. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation — and it does not tidy it up, either. The second example is not the first one mirrored. It is its own thing, drawn unevenly, wobbling, and possibly temporary. We spend a lot of this site's pages on the difference between a distribution and a defect — on what happens when a single well-documented case gets promoted into the standard, and everything else becomes a deviation from it. Saturn is not an argument for that. It is a rhyme : a very clean illustration of how confidently a rule can be inferred from one long look at one example, and how quickly the rule turns back into an example when a second one shows up. The hexagon did not become less real on 2 September 2026. It stopped being the only way for a jet on Saturn to arrange itself. Two of the fourteen authors are not at a university or an agency The longitude tracking that produced the 32.5-day wobble needed images across months, from many places. Alongside Hubble, the paper draws on ground-based observations archived in the ALPO Japan and Planetary Virtual Observatory Laboratory databases, covering 26 June to 11 October 2025, and on PlanetCam at the 2.2-metre telescope at Calar Alto. Two of the co-authors are affiliated not to a university or a space agency but to Broken Hill Observatory in Australia and an astronomy association in France. Planetary weather is slow and needs watching, and the people who watch it that patiently are not all professionals. The last entry in this collection was about a thousand volunteers burying underpants; this one has a private observatory in the outback in the author list. Not Not a twin. The decagon is not a southern hexagon, and the paper spends its discussion section saying so. The symmetry is the thing to resist here, not the thing to enjoy. Not a message. A ten-sided cloud pattern is a jet meandering. It is not geometry with intent, and Saturn is not drawing. Not settled. Two candidate causes, three simulation runs, and none of them reproduces the observed drift. Nobody knows yet is the honest state, and it is not the same as baffled . Not a new rule. One example looked like a law for forty-four years. Two examples are not a law either — they are two examples. Not because of . Saturn declining to standardise its own two poles is a rhyme, not a warrant. Down to is not because of : nobody's belonging rests on what a gas giant does with a jet stream.

And that rhythm turned out to be one of the most useful things in all of astronomy: Cepheid variables pulse with a period that reveals their true brightness, which let Henrietta Leavitt — and everyone since — measure distances clear across the cosmos. Energy that comes and goes on its own cycle isn't lesser. Here, it's how we learned the size of the universe. Trait Sounds like Actually Brightness rises and falls can't hold steady pulses on a reliable cycle Never constant unstable the change is how it works Its fluctuation a defect how we measure the whole universe Its way rhythmic, not constant · L★S 003

main sequence hot cool brightnesspulsar L★S · 004 The Precise Signal Pulsar · rotating neutron star spins up to ~700×/second · ms-precise The collapsed core of a dead massive star — a Sun's mass in a city-sized sphere — spinning fast and sweeping a beam past us like a lighthouse, with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks. neutron starmillisecond precisiontiny, densea galactic clock ▸ Field notes Field notes · Pulsar · rotating neutron star A pulsar is a neutron star — the collapsed core of a dead massive star, a whole Sun's worth of mass packed into a sphere the size of a city — spinning fast and sweeping a beam of radiation past us like a lighthouse. Some spin over 700 times a second, and their pulses arrive with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks. Small, dense, easy to overlook, and quietly one of the most precise things in the universe. Astronomers use pulsars to navigate, to test gravity, to hunt for gravitational waves. A tremendous, exact signal in a tiny package the eye would never notice. Trait Sounds like Actually Tiny and dense collapsed, spent a city-sized cosmic clock Spins wildly out of control keeps time to the millisecond Faint to the eye insignificant its beam sweeps the galaxy Its way precise, not spent · L★S 004

main sequence hot cool brightnessbinary L★S · 005 Never Alone Binary system · two or more stars 44% of Sun-like stars have a partner Multiplicity climbs steeply with mass: about a quarter of M dwarfs, 44% of Sun-like stars, and nearly all of the most massive live bound to a companion, orbiting a shared centre. Shaped by relationship, not in spite of it — where it happens. pairedrelationalshared orbitdepends on mass ▸ Field notes Field notes · Binary system · two or more stars We picture stars as solitary points of light, and for most of them that picture is right. Multiplicity is a steep function of mass: roughly 26% of M dwarfs have a stellar companion, 44 ± 2% of Sun-like stars do, and the most massive stars almost all do. Because the galaxy is overwhelmingly made of M dwarfs, two-thirds of stellar systems in the disk are single (Lada 2006; Raghavan et al. 2010; Duchêne & Kraus 2013). Where a pair does exist, both stars orbit a shared centre of gravity that lies in neither of them, sometimes trading streams of matter across the space between. A star's whole life can be shaped by the one it circles. Being paired isn't a lesser or dependent way to exist — and neither is being single. Identity here is relational: what a star becomes depends on who it's with, when there is anyone. Corrected 2026-08-14. This entry previously said "most stars live bound to another" and "most of the sky was never single." That is the popular retelling, and it is wrong — see Companion Stars (No. 46), which opens on the correction. Trait Sounds like Actually Bound to another dependent a system, and a common one at the massive end Shares mass and orbit entangled shaped by relationship, not despite it Two, not one incomplete alone whole together — and a single star is whole too Its way relational, not solitary · L★S 005

main sequence hot cool brightnessred giant L★S · 006 A Later Way of Being Red giant · late-life phase what the Sun becomes in ~5 billion yrs When a Sun-like star spends the hydrogen in its core, it doesn't fail — it transforms: swelling huge, cooling to deep red, and forging heavier elements it sheds into space to seed new worlds. Change, not decline. transformedoff the main sequenceforges elementsnot decline ▸ Field notes Field notes · Red giant · late-life phase When a Sun-like star exhausts the hydrogen in its core, it doesn't fail — it transforms. It swells enormously, its surface cools to a deep red, and it begins fusing heavier elements, forging carbon and oxygen and shedding them into space where they'll seed new worlds. In about five billion years, this is what our own Sun will become. It's tempting to call that decline. But the red giant is the same star living a different phase — larger, cooler, and doing some of the most generative work of its whole existence. Aging, here, is not diminishment. It's another way of being — and a fertile one. Trait Sounds like Actually Left the main sequence past its prime entered a new phase, not a decline Swollen and cooler falling apart forging the elements of new life Utterly changed no longer itself the same star, living differently Its way transformed, not declined · L★S 006

main sequence hot cool brightnesswhite dwarf L★S · 007 The Long Afterward White dwarf · stellar remnant Earth-sized · a teaspoon weighs tonnes What remains after a red giant sheds its outer layers: the exposed core, a Sun's mass packed into the size of Earth. It fuses nothing anymore — and shines on, on stored heat alone, for billions upon billions of years. remnantstopped fusingstill shiningan enduring end ▸ Field notes Field notes · White dwarf · stellar remnant After a red giant sheds its outer layers, what remains is a white dwarf: the exposed core, roughly the mass of the Sun packed into the size of the Earth, so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh tonnes. It no longer fuses anything. And yet it shines — on stored heat alone — for billions upon billions of years as it slowly cools. We tend to file "stopped working" under "finished." The white dwarf declines the framing. Its fusing life is over, and it goes on glowing longer than most stars ever live: a quiet, luminous afterward that is still, unmistakably, a way of being a star. Trait Sounds like Actually Stopped fusing dead shines on for billions of years Small and faint finished the enduring core, cooling slowly An end-state nothing left a quiet, luminous afterward Its way enduring, not ended · L★S 007

main sequence hot cool brightnessblue giant L★S · 008 Bright and Brief Blue giant · O/B-type supergiant tens of solar masses · gone in millions of yrs The showpieces — tens of times the Sun's mass, blazing hot and staggeringly bright. If brightness were the measure, these would win. But they burn out in a cosmic instant, and they're the rarest stars of all. brilliantfast-burningrarestnot the standard ▸ Field notes Field notes · Blue giant · O/B-type supergiant Blue giants and supergiants are the showpieces — tens of times the Sun's mass, blazing hot and staggeringly luminous. If brightness were the measure of a star, these would win outright. But they pay for it: they tear through their fuel and live only a few million years, a cosmic instant, before dying as supernovae. It's worth noticing which way of being a star we're tempted to call the "best" — the brilliant, fast-burning one — and then noticing that it's the rarest and shortest-lived of them all. Brightness was never the measure. It's one way among many, and far from the way most stars go. Trait Sounds like Actually Blazing and huge the ideal star one way among many — a costly one Burns fast the best spent in a few million years Brilliant the standard to meet brilliance was never the measure Its way one way, not the standard · L★S 008

We Are All Star Stuff Zine No. 4 · In progress Open call for contributors The first three zines in this series made arguments. This one holds space for something different: the actual voices of the people the series is for. Zines No. 1, 2, and 3 built the framework — the piezoelectric bones, the cosmology of care, the neurodiversity paradigm. They explained why you are made of star stuff and why that matters. We Are All Star Stuff is the zine that asks: what does that mean to you? We're collecting short pieces — a few sentences to a few paragraphs — from Autistic, ADHD, dyslexic, disabled, and otherwise neurodivergent people, and from the family members, educators, and community members who love them. No expertise required. No particular format. Just your honest answer to the question of what it means to be loved down to your star stuff, or to love someone that way. This zine will be offered freely, the same as the rest of the series — print-at-home, shareable, open edition. Every contributor will be credited exactly as they choose: full name, first name only, initials, role, or anonymous. Prompts You don't need to answer any of these directly — they're starting points, not requirements. Write toward whatever feels true. "When I first encountered the phrase 'Love You Down To Your Star Stuff' — or the idea behind it — something shifted. Here's what shifted, and why." "The neurodiversity paradigm says my neurological difference is variation, not deficit. Here's what that reframe has meant in practice — in my life, my work, my relationships, my sense of myself." "Here's a moment when I felt — or gave — the kind of love that goes all the way in. Past the hard parts. Down to the star stuff." "The idea that the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation: here's what that means to me, or what I wish it had meant to someone in my life earlier." "Something I want other neurodivergent people — or the people who love them — to know. Anything. L★S." Format Length A few sentences to a few paragraphs. No minimum, no hard maximum — but shorter pieces are easier to fit and we'll work with you on longer ones. Form Prose, fragment, list, letter, poem — any form that fits what you want to say. Write in your own voice. Formal or casual, both welcome. Credit You choose: full name, first name, initials, role ("an Autistic parent"), or anonymous. You can also add a brief bio line if you'd like. Edits We'll share any edits with you before publication and won't change your words without your approval. Rights You keep all rights to your words. We ask for permission to include your piece in this zine and future print editions of it, nothing more. Deadline No hard deadline yet. We'll publish when we have enough voices to fill a zine. Earlier submissions mean earlier inclusion. A note on anonymity: You're welcome to share as much or as little about yourself as you want. You don't need to disclose a diagnosis, a label, or a relationship. If you want to write "someone who has been loved this way" and nothing more, that's a complete and welcome contribution. 55 Star Stuff What Looks Like Chaos Nest building is the textbook example of pure instinct. Seven weavers, twenty-one nests, and a camera say otherwise — and so does a room somebody told you to tidy. L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · ten spreads ·
To most, it appears that I live in a state of chaos

Two · a completely curated space To most, it appears that I live in a state of chaos David Gray-Hammond describes his room. There is a bed with enough pillows and a duvet that doesn't overheat him. A galaxy projector on the ceiling. LED lights wired to respond to the television, because synchronised sound and light is a sensory need and not a flourish. An oil diffuser — sweet peas, lavender, sometimes cedarwood — so that even his sense of smell is something he chooses rather than something that happens to him. On the bed: snacks, medication, notebooks, and several books at once, because his attention moves between them rather than down through one. A tripod and a light ring within reach, so a thought can be recorded the moment it arrives. Nothing gets tidied away before sleep, because some days end in a crash rather than a decision, and the room has to be survivable on those days too. To most, it appears that I live in a state of chaos, but in actual fact I have my needs fulfilled in this space, and what appears to be chaos is actually a completely curated space. I know where every item I need resides. David Gray-Hammond · AuDHD and me: My nesting habits · 2023 He calls it nesting. Two people can stand in that room and see two different things, and only one of them is looking at a plan. What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks
The bird that was said to already know

Three · the bird that already knew The bird that was said to already know There is a claim about birds so old and so comfortable that most of us absorbed it without ever being taught it directly. A bird builds a nest it has never seen, without instruction, and gets it right the first time. The nest is therefore not a thing the bird works out. It is a thing the bird contains — a fixed action pattern, a genetic template, running to completion. It is a good story, and it was for a long time the default position in the literature rather than a fringe one. Walsh and colleagues state it plainly as the thing they set out to test: if nest building runs on fixed action patterns or is predominantly under genetic control, as is often assumed, then the behaviours should vary little between birds and should repeat reliably within one (Walsh et al., 2011). That is a real prediction, and it is falsifiable, which is the only reason any of this is interesting. A template predicts sameness — between individuals, and within the same individual across attempts. So somebody went and measured whether the sameness is there. A template predicts sameness. Not beauty, not competence — sameness. That is the whole of what it predicts, and it is the only thing that can be checked. What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks

Four · seven weavers, twenty-one nests Seven weavers, twenty-one nests Southern Botswana, a farm outside Gaborone. Seven male Southern Masked weavers, each one colour-ringed so it could be told from the others. Territories searched daily through the building season, between half past five in the morning and quarter to seven at night, so that a nest was found at the moment it was started rather than halfway through. Camcorders on adjustable tripods, set square to the nest. Three nests filmed per bird — twenty-one nests. Then the footage was coded by a researcher who did not know which bird they were watching or on what date, which is the part that makes the rest of it worth reading. What got counted: which side of the beak the grass protruded from, which side of the nest it went into, which quadrant of the structure the bird wove in and for how long, and every time a blade of grass was lost or dropped (Walsh et al., 2011). Not the finished nest. Almost everything known about how birds know what to build had come from examining structures that were already complete — which is a little like judging a life by the tidiness of the room. What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks
Four birds had a side. The species had none

Five · a hand of one's own Four birds had a side. The species had none During the first phase of construction — attaching the first blades to a bare branch — not one of the measured behaviours was repeatable within a male. Not the direction he carried the grass, not how long he spent weaving, not which part of the structure he favoured, not how often he dropped a blade. The template predicted sameness and got none. Then the individuality. Two of the seven consistently pushed the first end of a blade into the right side of the nest. Two consistently pushed it into the left. The remaining three had no side at all. And pooled across all seven birds and hundreds of insertions, the bias vanished — no lean either way (G = 0.06, p = 0.81). Personal handedness, with no species handedness underneath it. If there were a template, that is precisely what could not happen. ↑ INSERTED INTO THE RIGHT SIDE BLGMLP ORPBPYWP all seven pooled: no bias · p = 0.81 ↓ INSERTED INTO THE LEFT SIDE seven males · solid = a real, tested side-preference; dashed = none four birds lean, the species does not — after Walsh et al. 2011, fig. 2 What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks
They dropped less grass every time

Six · they got better They dropped less grass every time Here is the finding that finishes the template off. Across a season, as each male built more nests, he lost hold of the grass less often (p < 0.01). Not the species improving over evolutionary time. One bird, over three nests, in a few weeks, getting better at the thing. And the birds with the most consistent personal style paid for it in the right currency: the more strongly a male leaned to his own side, the faster he finished the ring phase (R² = 0.25, p = 0.01). A way of one's own was not an eccentricity to be corrected. It was the thing that made him quick. None of this was new in kind. Elsie and Nicholas Collias had watched Village Weavers move from juvenile to adult in 1964 and found that experienced birds build neater, more tightly woven nests than inexperienced ones — the first nest is crude, and the bird is not born knowing better (reported in Walsh et al., 2011). The authors are careful about what this does and does not show, and so are we: they attribute the change most readily to increasing dexterity, and say outright that whether cognition is involved needs further work. We are not going to sell you a clever bird. Practice is enough for the argument. A template does not improve. Improvement is what something does when it was never finished to begin with. What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks

Seven · forty-three families Forty-three families, forty-three styles Thirteen years later, a different weaver and a much harder question. White-browed sparrow weavers live in family groups and build two kinds of structure: nests for breeding, and single-occupant roosts for sleeping. Forty-three groups were measured (Tello-Ramos et al., 2024). The groups build differently from each other. Some make long roosts with extended entrance tubes; others make short ones with barely any tube. The differences hold across years, and they hold between groups whose territories sit metres apart in the same trees. Then the eliminations, one at a time: not the weather, not the size of the birds, not the height of the tree, not how closely related the groups were. And the finding that closes it — the styles are robust to immigration. A bird arrives from a group that builds one way, and the structures keep coming out the other way. That is not a template, and it is not the environment either. It is a tradition — a way of building held by a group, taught by living in it, outlasting the particular birds who happen to be there. GROUP A · long tube same trees · metres apart GROUP B · short tube not weather · not body size · not tree height · not kinship and it survives a bird moving in from somewhere else What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks

Eight · the refusals What this zine is not Two findings, thirteen years apart, in two species of weaver. It would be easy — and it would be wrong — to walk them straight across into a claim about us. So, plainly: Not: permission from nature The birds do not authorise anything. A universe that could approve of us could also decline, and we would not accept the verdict either way. Nobody's room is justified by a weaver in Botswana. Down to is not because of. Not: instinct versus learning These birds are not learning instead of being birds. Development is not a contest between what came with you and what you did with it, and the finding is not that the template was replaced — it is that there was never a template doing the work anyone assumed. Not: a clever-animal story The authors themselves say the likeliest explanation is increasing dexterity, and that any role for cognition still needs demonstrating. We are not going to inflate that, because the inflated version is the one that gets repeated and then quietly corrected years later. Not: every mess is a nest This is the honest one. Gray-Hammond is explicit that burnout collapses the architecture — spaces stop being maintained, and what is left can look, from outside, exactly like the curated version. A nest and its ruins are not the same thing. The difference is never visible from the doorway, which is the entire point. What the science does kill is narrower, and sturdier for being narrow. It kills the inference that an order you cannot read is not an order. Two centuries of confident observers looked at a nest and saw a machine executing. They were describing the limits of watching, and calling it a fact about the bird. What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks
Every needed thing where the attention already is

Nine · an architecture of continuity Every needed thing where the attention already is Gray-Hammond puts nesting beside lilipadding — the practice, set out by Tanya Adkin and David Gray-Hammond, of moving between small safe places by deliberate steps rather than leaps, honouring the tunnel of attention you are in while gently inviting the next one (Adkin & Gray-Hammond, 2025a). Nesting, in that frame, is the physical design of the lilypad. A hostile room makes us leap too far, too soon, just to get out of it. A well-nested one opens channels: a desk that runs into the bookshelves that run into somewhere soft to decompress, each area inviting the next, so that a transition costs a step instead of a rupture. He calls the result an architecture of continuity. When his therapist suggested keeping a feelings journal across the room, he declined — because crossing the room in that moment is not two steps, it is fifteen. The journal within reach is a gentle pad. The same journal, six feet away, is a wall. Which is why rest alone does not fix burnout. If burnout is the collapse of an architecture — the physical space, the relationships, the sense of continuity with yourself — then recovery means rebuilding the structure, not just lying still inside the rubble. Nesting is rehabilitative, not only preventative. And it is why Prakash Nair's finding about schools stings. The cave — the space for going quiet and going deep — is one of the primordial learning spaces David Thornburg named, alongside the campfire, the watering hole, and a fourth that usually gets dropped, life (Thornburg, 2004). Nair's observation is that the cave is never the priority in a new school building, and that millions get spent on buildings that will not change outcomes because nobody costed a place to withdraw to. A room to be alone in is the one that gets value-engineered out, in a school and in a life. Compassion is not simply an action performed by others. It is the environment we are invited to inhabit — and the space we provide to ourselves. David Gray-Hammond · Autistic Nesting as the Physical Architecture of Lilipadding Nobody is born knowing how to build their own room. Every weaver's first nest is crude. Every weaver gets better at it. No two of them do it the same way, and the species has no opinion about which side the grass goes in. Our rooms are ours the same way — worked out, revised, improved by living in them, unreadable to anyone standing in the doorway with a clipboard. Stimpunks keeps two sentences side by side on the subject, and the pair is worth more than either alone: It took me decades to learn how to change my environment to make myself comfortable. @willaful It took decades to learn I was allowed. @steve_asbell The weavers only need the first sentence. A bird gets better at building because it builds — that is the whole of it, and it is in the data. There is nothing in twenty-one nests in Botswana that corresponds to the second sentence, because nobody had ever told those birds they were not allowed to weave. That is exactly where the rhyme stops. The first sentence is a fact about learning, and the birds have it too. The second is a fact about permission — and permission is not a feature of nature, it is something people hand out or withhold. Which means it is the half that can be changed by deciding to. So when an institution takes a room away from us, it is not confiscating clutter. It is demolishing the thing that was holding us together, and calling the demolition tidiness. And when it takes decades to learn you were allowed, somebody spent those decades not telling you. What Looks Like Chaos · Stimpunks

What We Refuse Nearly every piece we publish ends by naming the traps it won't fall into. Lay them side by side and the same refusals keep coming back — and how often each returns is the finding, not the decoration. ✕ A rhyme, not a proof 9 pieces That a pattern recurs in nature is not why difference deserves welcome. It would deserve welcome in a universe that made exactly one shape. Deriving an ought from an is is a fallacy we would rather name than commit. Crabs · sharks · turtles · whales · the deep sea · the fungal network · relational physics ✕ Not anyone's metaphor 9 pieces We are not making anyone an animal, and we are not borrowing a creature to stand in for a person. Where a piece uses one, the shared thing is the frame — a body read for what can be taken out of it — never the bodies. Strongest where the animal is most useful to us ✕ Not a superpower 5 pieces The troughs are real and support is not a consolation prize. A gift narrative is still a ledger — it just pays out before it charges. Nobody has to be extraordinary to be owed a place. And not inspiration: you are not a lesson for anyone's comfort ✕ Not extraction recurring Usefulness in disguise — difference mined for productivity, the “cognitive diversity” business case, “ecosystem services” putting the service provider back at the centre. Being valuable is not the same as being welcome. The frame our more-than-human pieces watch hardest for ✕ Not flattened into sameness recurring “Everyone's a little bit neurodivergent” is the monoculture again, wearing a kinder face. And there is no normal to deviate from in the first place, so there is nothing here to be a deviation of. Belonging never asks you to lose your shape ✕ Not the person bent to the room recurring Not an accommodation bolted onto a hostile room — a ramp to nowhere. Build a room more minds can think in. Broken thresholds, not broken people; change the conditions, not the substance. And never a reason to withhold support while we wait every piece, and every refusal in full: starstuff.earth print freely · share freely · CC BY-SA 4.0 See reverse Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms what the refusals are protecting Broadside · Open edition Side B of B What's left Belonging is constitutive. Not conferred. True of you before you arrived, and true whether or not anyone ever tells you so. Difference is variation, not deficit. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Neither do we. The troughs are real. Support isn't a consolation prize for failing to be exceptional. It's the point. Change the conditions, not the substance. Ice isn't broken water. It's water somewhere colder. Kinship is material. The same hydrogen from the same beginning; the same calcium from the same dying giants. Not a courtesy we extend. Credit stays where it was earned. A collective is not a founder. A documenter is not a coiner. How a refusal works A refusal is not a mood. Each one names a specific move the piece could make and won't — and it is placed exactly where that piece is most tempted to make it. A refusal parked somewhere safe is decoration. They are load-bearing. Take “a rhyme, not a proof” out of the natural-history pieces and what's left is an argument that biology licenses a politics. That is a fallacy, and it has been aimed at us far more often than for us. The most-repeated one points inward. Nine pieces carry the same sentence because nine pieces reach for the same shortcut. The count isn't a boast about our standards — it's a measurement of our appetite. Refusing is not the same as debunking. A refusal closes a move we might make. It doesn't score a point off anyone who made it, and the pleasure of the debunk is its own trap. And: we notice we are doing it too The Layer We Call Essential spends eleven spreads using cetacean minds as material for a human argument, and says so in its own refusals set: their minds are not evidence for our politics first — they are theirs first. That is the shape of the honest version. Not a claim to have escaped the trap, but a note, in the piece itself, saying where we are still standing in it. The refusals are the part we would most like to skip. That is how we know where they go. the collection, and how we check ourselves: starstuff.earth/too-good-to-check · stimpunks.org · morerealms.com print freely · share freely · CC BY-SA 4.0 L S

Who Is Holding the Candle Carl Sagan learned skepticism and wonder at the same time and called them uneasy neighbours. His son Dorion says the objective voice is a lie about where knowledge comes from. Two Sagans, one method — and the reason this site says we . The Demon-Haunted World is remembered as the skeptic's book. It is the one with the baloney detection kit in it, the one people reach for when someone is selling a crystal or a cure, and its subtitle — Science as a Candle in the Dark — has been quoted so often it has worn smooth. The sentence in it that matters most to us is not about baloney at all. It is about two people who knew no science whatsoever. “My parents were not scientists. They knew almost nothing about science. But in introducing me simultaneously to skepticism and to wonder, they taught me the two uneasily cohabiting modes of thought that are central to the scientific method.” Carl Sagan · The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, 1995 Read it slowly, because three things in it are load-bearing and all three are easy to walk past. It is two modes, not one. Not skepticism with a bit of enthusiasm attached — two whole ways of thinking, both required. They cohabit uneasily . Sagan does not say they harmonize or balance; he says they live together badly, which is a strange thing to say about the thing you are recommending. And his parents taught him — people one step out of poverty who knew almost nothing about the subject. The transmission did not come from an institution, from credentials, or from a curriculum. It did not come from school either, and he is blunt about that on the very next page. “I wish I could tell you about inspirational teachers in science from my elementary or junior high or high school days. But as I think back on it, there were none. There was rote memorization about the Periodic Table of the Elements, levers and inclined planes, green plant photosynthesis, and the difference between anthracite and bituminous coal. But there was no soaring sense of wonder, no hint of an evolutionary perspective, and nothing about mistaken ideas that everybody had once believed.” Carl Sagan · The Demon-Haunted World, 1995 The institution had all the content and none of the thing. It could hand him anthracite and bituminous coal and it could not hand him either mode — no wonder, and no mistaken ideas that everybody had once believed , which is the skeptical half stated as a curriculum item and left out of every curriculum. This is a familiar shape around here. The place with the resources delivered the surface and missed the substance, and the people with no standing at all delivered the real thing at the kitchen table.

The two uneasily cohabiting modes Take either one away and you get something that still looks like thinking and reliably fails. Wonder without skepticism is the subject of the other essay in this collection. It is how a forest-wide fungal network became settled fact in three of our own pieces: the finding rhymed with everything we believe, so nobody asked it a hard question. A story that fits gets less scrutiny, which is exactly when it needs more. Skepticism without wonder fails differently and more quietly, because it never has to admit to being wrong about a fact — it is wrong about what the exercise is for. It arrives at the pleasure of the debunk, at correcting people as a hobby, at treating Myth! as a destination. And that failure mode is not hypothetical for a site like this one: the deficit literature about neurodivergent and disabled people is written almost entirely in the skeptical register, skeptical of us specifically, and remarkably little of it has ever been curious about us. Two modes, and what each becomes alone Two boxes side by side. On the left, skepticism: the question "what would show me this is wrong?", and alone it becomes the pleasure of the debunk. On the right, wonder: the question "what else could possibly be true?", and alone it becomes too good to check. Arrows run down from both into a third box beneath them: the two uneasily cohabiting modes, held at full strength and arguing. Between the arrows, the words "braided, not balanced". neither mode survives the other's absence SKEPTICISM what would show me this is wrong? alone: the pleasure of the debunk WONDER what else could possibly be true? alone: too good to check THE TWO UNEASILY COHABITING MODES held at full strength, arguing this is what a method is BRAIDED, NOT BALANCED Figure 1 · Not a midpoint between the two. Both at full strength, permanently disagreeing.

Why “uneasily” is the load-bearing word The obvious reading of Sagan's sentence is that the two modes need moderating — be a bit skeptical, be a bit amazed, meet in the middle. That reading is wrong, and his son wrote the line that explains why. In the introduction to Cosmic Apprentice , Dorion Sagan reaches for Niels Bohr: “…while the opposite of a trivial truth is false, the opposite of a great truth is another great truth.” Niels Bohr, as quoted by Dorion Sagan · Cosmic Apprentice, 2013 That is the mechanism. Check everything and the universe is stranger than you can currently imagine are both great truths, which means each one's opposite is also true and neither can be diluted into the other without ruining both. A half-skeptic is not moderate, they are careless. A half-wonderer is not sensible, they are incurious. You do not average them. You hold both at full strength and let them argue, permanently, and the friction is not a defect in the method — the friction is the method. Uneasy is the correct state. A method that felt comfortable would have stopped checking.

The alembic Dorion Sagan's own version of this braid is not skepticism and wonder but science and philosophy, and he gives it a chemist's metaphor. An alembic is the still — the vessel that separates a mixture into what it actually contains. Electrum is the natural alloy of gold and silver, valuable as itself rather than as either metal waiting to be refined out. “Science's eye for detail, buttressed by philosophy's broad view, makes for a kind of alembic, an antidote to both. This intellectual electrum cuts the cloying taste of idealist and propositional philosophy with the sharp nectar of fact yet softens the edges of a technoscience that has arguably lost both its moral and its epistemological compass, the result in part of its being funded by governments and corporations whose relationship to the search for truth and its open dissemination can be considered problematic at best.” Dorion Sagan · Cosmic Apprentice: Dispatches from the Edges of Science, 2013 An antidote to both. Not a defence of science against philosophy or the reverse — a claim that each is the cure for the other's characteristic poisoning. Philosophy left alone goes cloying: elegant, self-consistent, and about nothing. Science left alone goes compass-less, and Dorion is precise about the mechanism rather than gesturing at it. Not that scientists are corrupt. That the funding decides which questions get asked , and an institution whose relationship to open dissemination is “problematic at best” will keep producing true findings while losing the ability to say why any of them matter, or to publish the ones nobody paid for. This is the argument our How We Got Here chains exist to make, and No. 40 makes it outright: particle physics demands five sigma, pre-registration and a published record of everything that did not work, while the interventions run on disabled children have historically demanded far less and been compulsory for somebody. The compass, missing. The guard on this argument Everything above can be misread as a complaint about science, and it is the opposite one. We are not asking for less evidence. We are asking for the parts that got left behind — the pre-registration, the blinding, the reported harms, the published nulls, the hedge the paper carried and the press release dropped. Three things get mistaken for science and are its opposite: pseudoscience , which keeps none of the method; scientism , which keeps the authority and drops the practice; and the smoothed popular retelling , which files off every hedge because the tidy version travels further. Pointed at human beings, all three flatten exactly the variation the science elsewhere insists is real — and they do it with a citation attached, which is far harder to answer than a plain insult. If this page ever starts reading as anti-science, it has gone wrong. Which Dorion also says, a few paragraphs later, better than we just did: “Science's spirit is philosophical. It is the spirit of questioning, of curiosity, of critical inquiry combined with fact-checking. It is the spirit of being able to admit you're wrong, of appealing to data, not authority, which does not like to admit it is wrong.” Dorion Sagan · Cosmic Apprentice, 2013 Critical inquiry combined with fact-checking. That is Carl's two modes again in different clothes — the curiosity that goes looking, and the checking that keeps it honest — and the last clause is the one with teeth. Authority does not like to admit it is wrong. That is why a changelog that publishes our own errors with dates and names is not housekeeping and not humility theatre. It is the only available evidence that we are appealing to data rather than to our own standing.

Who is holding the candle Now the passage that this page is named for, and the one that changed how we write. Dorion arrives at it from a deliberately provocative direction — that in the calculus of writing genres, fiction is nonfiction and nonfiction is fiction — and the reason is not a paradox for its own sake: “…the passive voice, ‘objective’ stance, anonymity, and depersonalization of the scientist and journalist betray the fundamental phenomenological reality that each of us has a specific perspective. All observations are made from distinct places and times, and in science no less than art or philosophy by particular individuals.” Dorion Sagan · Cosmic Apprentice, 2013 Betray is doing a lot of work, and both of its senses are live. The objective voice gives away the truth it means to hide, and it is unfaithful to the thing that actually happened. Somebody was somewhere, at a time, with a history and a funder and a hope about the result, and they looked. The grammar deletes them. What is left reads as though the finding arrived unaccompanied. Sagan's candle is a good image precisely because a candle has to be carried. It does not illuminate a room evenly from nowhere. It is held, at some height, by somebody, and everything behind them stays dark. The passive voice is not neutral — it is a set of deletions The sentence What the grammar deletes What we write instead “Deficits were identified in the social communication domain.” A person, from outside, made a judgement against a norm they did not have to state or defend — and the norm is the whole argument Who assessed whom, against what, and how it reads from inside. See No. 9 on where the lines came from “Studies show…” Which studies. Who funded them. Which ones found nothing and were never published Named authors, year, journal, and the hedge the paper actually carried “It is widely accepted that…” Accepted by whom — and whether anyone re-checked, or whether repetition has been standing in for evidence What we checked, when, and what we found. The ledger is dated per piece “The error has been corrected.” Who made it, who caught it, and how long it was live — which is the only part anyone can learn from “We shipped this. Helen Edgar caught it. Fixed on this date.” Our changelog is written this way throughout So this is the argument underneath a house rule that otherwise looks like a style preference. We write about neurodivergent and disabled people in the first person plural — we, us, our — because it is true and the alternative is not. Third person here would not be neutrality. It would be a claim to be standing outside a room we are in fact sitting in, and Dorion's point is that the claim is unavailable to anyone, including the people best trained to make it. There is no view from nowhere. There is only an unstated view from somewhere. The same commitment runs through the small print. Helen Edgar's zines are hers and say so on their faces, in her voice, under a shared masthead — the masthead is collaborative, authorship is not. Every correction carries the name of whoever caught it, including the ones that were embarrassing to publish. The fact-check ledger records who checked what and on what date, because checked without a checker is exactly the deletion described above. And it is why the sharpest sentence in Too Good to Check belongs to this page as much as that one: the primary source for an Autistic life is an Autistic person. That is not a slogan bolted onto a fact-checking rule. It is the fact-checking rule, applied where it costs something. Donna Haraway named the general case situated knowledges in 1988 and argued the harder half of it — that the honest alternative to a false objectivity is not anything goes but a stronger accountability, because a perspective you have declared is one somebody else can finally hold you to.
What this licenses, and what it refuses

What this licenses, and what it refuses Every argument on this page has a cheap version that sounds identical, and the cheap versions are common enough that leaving them unnamed would be negligent. Not: Not relativism. “All observations are made by particular individuals” is a claim about where knowledge comes from, not about whether it can be wrong. Orion's Belt is at one depth or it isn't, and we were wrong about it in public. Not a licence to skip the check. It is the reverse: because we are in the room, our own findings need more scrutiny, not less. Every gate on this site exists because we write from a position. Not anti-science. The complaint is that the compass got lost and the hedges got filed off, and the remedy is more of the method rather than less of it. Not a rule that only insiders may speak. The claim is that everyone speaks from somewhere and should say where. Declaring a position is available to anybody; pretending not to have one is available to nobody. Not contempt for the passive voice. It has real uses, including where the actor genuinely doesn't matter. The failure is using it to make a positioned judgement look like a reading off a dial. Not resolved. The two modes still cohabit uneasily on this page and will keep doing so. That is the state Sagan described, and we have no plan for improving on it.

Two Sagans, one method It is a nice accident that these two passages come from a father and a son, and it would be sentimental to make more of the inheritance than the pages support. They are not saying the same thing. Carl is describing how a method feels from inside — two habits pulling against each other, taught to a boy at a kitchen table by people with no science between them. Dorion is describing what the method's official prose does to that boy once he grows up and writes it down: files off the pulling, deletes the table, deletes the parents, and reports the finding as though it had arrived by itself. Put the two together and you get something usable. Keep both modes at full strength, and keep the person holding them visible. The candle and the hand. Everything on this site — the citations, the ledger, the published errors, the credits, the first person plural — is one or the other of those, and mostly both. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Neither does an observer who has admitted they are standing somewhere. Read the checking half → Sources. Sagan, C. (1995). The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark. Random House. Both quotations are from the opening chapter, verified against the text (Kindle locations 89–94 of 7157). The second is given with one elision, marked; nothing between the omitted words changes its sense. Sagan, D. (2013). Cosmic Apprentice: Dispatches from the Edges of Science. University of Minnesota Press. All three quotations are from the introduction, “Condensed — The Questing Spirit,” verified against the text (Kindle locations 70–94 of 4589). The passage on the passive voice opens mid-sentence; the elided words are “In the counterintuitive calculus of writing genres, ‘fiction’ is nonfiction and nonfiction is fiction. By that I mean that” — summarized above rather than quoted, because the setup is doing rhetorical work the excerpt would otherwise inherit without explaining. On the Bohr line. “The opposite of a great truth is another great truth” reaches us through Dorion Sagan, who introduces it with “as Niels Bohr impressed.” We have primary-confirmed that Dorion wrote it; we have not primary-confirmed Bohr saying it, and the usual source given elsewhere is a son's recollection rather than Bohr's own writing. So it is attributed here as quoted-by, which is what we can actually stand behind. This is failure mode one caught in advance rather than after publication, and it is an open item. Haraway, D. (1988). Situated Knowledges: The Science Question in Feminism and the Privilege of Partial Perspective. Feminist Studies , 14(3). Cited for the concept, which is characterized rather than quoted. Both quotations also appear together on Stimpunks' Facts, Fire, and Feels: Research-Storytelling from the Edges , which is where this page started. 11 Guest Zine Why Difference Comes First Inspired by our collaborative Stimpunks work, and my own neuroqueering Deleuze project, I've been thinking about the connections in-between — physics, philosophy, my own life as an Autistic person. This is me following that thread. Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · More Realms L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · guest edition ·

Two · I'm not a fixed thing I'm not a fixed thing A little while back I wrote about something called relational quantum mechanics — a way of thinking about physics where tiny particles don't have fixed qualities all on their own. They only become something in relation to whatever's around them (Rovelli, 1996). I'm not a physicist — it's one idea among several, and physicists argue about it. As a multiply neurodivergent person, that's always been closer to how I experience myself — not as a fixed, separate thing moving through the world, but as something that shows up through my relationships and encounters with everything around me (Edgar, 2026a). I'm still working through what that means. Physics, philosophy, and my own life keep circling the same ideas about being interconnected, unfixed, always transforming. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Three · my monotropic galaxy My monotropic galaxy The oldest light we can see is called the cosmic microwave background — it's the afterglow of the Big Bang, and it's almost perfectly smooth. It only varies by about one part in 100,000 across the whole sky — almost uniform, but only almost. Those tiny variations — slightly denser here, slightly thinner there — were the beginning of everything. Gravity pulled the denser bits together, and over billions of years they became stars, galaxies, planets, you, me, all of it. If the universe really had been perfectly uniform, it would have stayed a flat, empty fog forever. Nothing to see, no one to see it. Structure only exists because that near-sameness broke. That's the same shape I recognise in my own monotropic attention — energy pulled gravitationally into a few bright points, rather than spread out in an even, undifferentiated glow. And yet it's exactly that unevenness, that refusal to flatten, that so many of us — anyone who's ever been called too much, not enough, or too different — have been measured against. the "almost" is where everything comes from almost uniform · not quite the tiny unevenness seeds the stars Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Four · neuronormative time Measured against neuronormative time I've spent a lot of my life being measured against a flat line. Nobody always said it in those words, but that's what was happening — a standard chart, a "typical" way of communicating or paying attention or experiencing the world, treated as the baseline everyone should be smoothed toward. And me, positioned as the deviation that needed explaining, or fixing, or at least accounting for. That flat line was never just about behaviour — it was also about time: a single approved tempo, a single approved rhythm, everyone expected to arrive and finish and transition together, in step with a clock that was never actually neutral. So there's something that genuinely steadies me in learning that the universe itself never once managed that. what was already there, moving the "typical" baseline you = "deviation" a straight line, laid over what was already moving the grid comes after the field, not before Uniformity was never the achievement. It's the thing that would have stopped everything before it even started. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar
There is no normal or baseline

Five · no normal or baseline There is no normal or baseline Gilles Deleuze, working with Félix Guattari, made a version of this same argument. Deleuze noticed that a lot of Western thinking treats difference as secondary — judged by how much it resembles some ideal, some average, some "normal" category. All of that quietly assumes the baseline came first, and difference is just a deviation from it. The baseline is the thing that got built. The idea of normality is what has shaped our capitalist society (Chapman, 2023) and is what we are judged against (Deleuze, 1994). Difference is what's actually there, first — and identity is what eventually forms out of it, temporarily and locally, the way a crystal settles out of a solution along the gaps and spaces in between — the places where those of us most marginalised live, and where we build our own networks, our own solidarity. This is where Deleuze and Guattari's idea of smooth space becomes useful (Deleuze & Guattari, 1987). Smooth space is full of local, variable difference — it hasn't had a fixed grid laid over it yet. Striated space is what happens when that grid arrives: when a field gets measured, divided, standardised. Difference doesn't get smoothed into existence by that process. Smoothing is what a system does afterward, only if it insists on it — striation laid over what was already smooth. Nothing gets smoothed into existence. Smoothing is what happens to something afterward — only if a system insists on it. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Six · smooth ≠ flat Smooth doesn't mean flat Smooth space isn't empty of movement — it's just ungridded. It cuts against how regulation usually gets talked about, as though it means being still, quiet, zen: a flat line of its own. But smooth space is defined by what it lacks — a grid — not by what it's doing. It can be full of movement and still be smooth — which is closer to how neurodivergent regulation actually works: through stimming, through bodily autonomy, through movement rather than stillness. That's closer to what I recognise when I try to describe my own attention — my porousness to my environment, the way my sensory system stays open to everything around it, the way time folds back on itself instead of running in a straight line. Not flat. Not gridded. Full of shape that never quite resolves into one measurable thing. SMOOTH · ungridded STRIATED · gridded smooth is not empty · it's ungridded the fog was neither — a field before either one Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Seven · ethodiversity What ethodiversity means This is where Ombre Tarragnat's work on ethodiversity has become important to me. Ethodiversity is the variety of ways of being and behaving, across humans and other animals — and Tarragnat is precise about where it actually lives: not inside any one person, but as a property of the relationships between us, the way biodiversity belongs to a whole ecosystem, not to any single creature in it (Tarragnat, 2025). Ethonormativity, in their framing, is the unwritten rule about which ways of being are allowed to count as normal in a given room. Put next to Deleuze, I don't think it's a stretch to say ethonormativity simply is that grid — applied to how we're allowed to behave. A fixed grid laid over a field that was already full of variation before the grid ever showed up. Ethonormativity reaches further than neuronormativity, though. Neuronormativity is about which neurotypes get treated as the default — Autistic brains judged against non-Autistic ones, for instance. Ethonormativity is the wider grid underneath that: it governs which ways of being and behaving, across every species, get to count as acceptable at all. It holds neuronormativity inside it, but it isn't limited to brains, or even to humans (Tarragnat, 2025). Ethonormativity simply is that grid — a fixed grid laid over a field that was already full of variation before the grid ever showed up. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Eight · a constellation of intensities A constellation of intensities I recognise that grid in every space I've ever masked in — education, the workplace, wherever something that was moving gets asked to hold still long enough to be measured. And I recognise its absence, with real gratitude, in the spaces I'm part of — NeuroHub Community and David Gray-Hammond, Stimpunks: an Autistic rhizome, a mycelial network of care, non-hierarchical, no fixed centre, connecting wherever it meets (Deleuze & Guattari, 1987). I used to think the shape of my own mind was something like a spiky profile — a way of picturing uneven ability across different areas, real peaks and real troughs, instead of one flat line running across the whole of who you are. At least it's truer than a flat line. But a profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges — and that's exactly where I want to push further, past even the spiky profile. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all. It's a constellation of intensities: a galaxy, always in relationship with itself, always in motion, never finished (Edgar, 2026b). Some stars I've lived in for decades. Others I've only just learned to name. None of them sit on an axis. They just belong to the same galaxy — we are all made of stardust. flat line a grid spiky profile still axes, still edges a constellation no axis · in motion flat line → spiky profile → no chart at all even the spiky profile is still a grid A profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar
The universe doesn't do flat lines

Nine · permission The universe doesn't do flat lines I still don't have this fully settled or finished. But every time I follow this thread — from the sky, down through physics and philosophy, into the actual shape of my own attention — I end up in the same place. Not a tidy conclusion. More like a kind of permission. The universe doesn't do flat lines. It never really tried to. It went straight from near-uniform fog to unrepeatable structure, without ever pausing at sameness for its own sake. I think that's worth remembering, gently — the next time any of us is asked to explain why we don't match the line. We are all star dust. We are neuroqueering the spiky profile: no edges, limitless ways of being. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

L★S · 001 The Inner Ocean Europa · moon of Jupiter a global ocean under ~15–25 km of ice A quiet, cracked marble of ice on the outside — and underneath, a global ocean of liquid salt water, possibly holding more water than all of Earth's seas combined. Kept warm by tides, not sunlight. inner oceantidal heatunder icemaybe life ▸ Field notes Field notes · Europa · moon of Jupiter Europa looks, from outside, like a still, cracked marble of ice. Underneath is one of the most exciting places in the solar system: a global ocean of liquid salt water, kept warm not by sunlight but by the constant tidal flexing of Jupiter's gravity kneading the moon's interior. There may be more water there than in all of Earth's oceans combined. No sky, no sun — no problem. The warmth comes from within, and the seafloor may host the same kind of chemistry that feeds life around Earth's deep-sea vents. A still surface is not an empty one. Some of the richest worlds keep the whole ocean on the inside. L★S · 002 The Other Chemistry Titan · moon of Saturn methane rain · −179°C · thick orange haze Titan runs Earth's whole weather system with the labels swapped: clouds, rain, rivers, and seas — of liquid methane, under an orange haze, where water ice is as hard as rock. A world that senses on a different chemistry. methane seasorange hazeother chemistrya full water cycle ▸ Field notes Field notes · Titan · moon of Saturn Titan runs Earth's weather system with the labels swapped. It has clouds, rain, rivers, lakes, and seas — but made of liquid methane and ethane, beneath a thick orange haze, at −179°C where water ice is as hard as granite. It is the only place besides Earth we know of with stable liquid on its surface. It senses and moves through the world on a different chemistry entirely. To call it inhospitable is really just to say it isn't Earth. On its own terms it is complete: a full hydrologic cycle, a landscape carved by flowing liquid, a sky with its own weather. A different medium, a different light, a whole world getting on with it. L★S · 003 What Has to Come Out Enceladus · moon of Saturn geysers venting to space · ~500 km wide A small, bright moon that cannot keep its ocean to itself. From cracks at its south pole it fires plumes of water vapour hundreds of kilometres into space — and that spray is how we learned what its hidden sea contains. plumeshidden oceanexpressiontasted from space ▸ Field notes Field notes · Enceladus · moon of Saturn Enceladus is a small, brilliant-white moon that cannot keep its ocean to itself. From four warm cracks at its south pole — the "tiger stripes" — it fires enormous plumes of water vapour and ice grains hundreds of kilometres up, straight into space, feeding one of Saturn's rings. The Cassini spacecraft flew through the spray and sampled the sea without ever landing. There's something to love in a world whose inner life simply has to come out — and whose expression turned out to be exactly how we learned what it holds. What it couldn't contain is what let us know it was there.
